11213116.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11213116.value: Statistical Process Control (SPC) was traditionally established for the manufacturing industry. In recent years, SPC has gained considerable attention as it has been found effective in applications in important areas such as healthcare, education, hospitality industry, energy management, and public service. However, for SPC to be effective in non-manufacturing systems, it has to have the ability to handle situations associated with multivariate and/or non-normal distribution. In the past, we have investigated time-between-events (TBE) control charts that have proven to be very effective with reference to the monitoring and control of high quality manufacturing processes. In this proposed research, we will develop and investigate some advanced control charts for TBE and related process characteristics targeted for more generalized applications, with a focus on multivariate situations. We will also investigate the modelling and monitoring of extreme-value characteristics, such as those related to peak usage, extreme damage or performance levels in important areas beyond manufacturing, such as found in service and administrative systems. An important application of our research is to develop cost-effective maintenance procedure based on TBE data monitoring. Almost all existing studies have focused on the univariate data monitoring system, while most systems/equipment deteriorates with usage and age which will be studied in this project. Usually an event has two dimensions, one is the event magnitude and the other one is the event frequency and they are traditionally monitored separately. In this proposal, we will develop and study some monitoring procedures, especially those based on bivariate distributions that could incorporate the dependence of these two characteristics as well. The PIs are internationally known researchers having extensive experience in statistical process control research. The proposed research is expected to considerably advance the current field of knowledge, providing cutting edge innovation for applications in SPC. The research issues (multivariate monitoring, effects of estimated parameters, monitoring with reliability data, joint monitoring of the frequency and magnitude of events, etc.) covered in this proposal are in line with the need for efficient applications in the real word as suggested in a very recent review paper by Woodall and Montgomery (2014) in the Journal of Quality Technology. 统计过程控制（Statistical Process Control，SPC）最初应用在制造行业中。近年来，人们发现SPC可以有效地应用在一些其他的重要领域，如医疗、教育、酒店行业、能源管理和公共服务业，因此SPC受到了更多关注。然而，为了能够使SPC在非制造系统中得到有效运用，其必须具有处理多变量和（或）非正态分布情形的能力。过去我们大量研究了事件间隔时间（time-between-events，TBE）控制图，发现其对于高质量制造过程的监测和控制非常有效。在本研究中，我们将开发和研究一些面向TBE和相关过程特性的高级控制图，以期更一般化的应用，其中重点关注多变量情形。我们还将研究服从极值分布的变量的建模和监测，比如制造业之外其他一些重要领域如服务和管理系统中所发现的那些关于峰值负荷、极端损坏或性能水平的情况。本研究的另一项重要应用是开发一个基于TBE数据监测的经济维修过程。几乎所有的现有研究都是针对单变量的数据监测系统，而大部分的系统或者设备会随着使用量和使用年限退化，这将在本项目中进行研究。通常一个事件有两个维度，一个是事件峰值，另一个是事件频率，而传统上这二者被分别进行监测。在本研究中，我们将开发和研究一些基于双变量分布的监测过程，这些过程考虑到这两个维度间的相关性。本计划中涉及到的研究问题（多变量监测、参数估计的影响、可靠性数据的监测、事件频率和峰值联合监测等）符合发展SPC在现实世界中的有效应用的需求。

11213116.label: Realisation of objectives
11213116.value: The research objectives are fully achieved as planned. In fact, we have accomplished much more beyond our original plan. Several excellent students were recruited and they are well-trained with the help of project funding. A few have taken on faculty or research positions and are continuing with the research in their careers. The group published a number of good papers (see the list – I am not co-author in all papers, but all lead authors are my student or postdoc, and I asked them to take the lead and learn to be more independent researcher). Below are some main points on how and to what extent the project objectives have been achieved. Some publications are related to more than one objective. (1). Further studies on advanced control charts for the monitoring of time-between-events. In the research proposal, “One focus of this project is on developing new and advanced procedures for monitoring Time-Between-Events (TBE).” Several advanced procedures suitable for different application contexts are developed. Some of the research results and publications are described in the following. In Huang et al. (2018), we developed two new CUSUM schemes for simultaneous monitoring of parameters of a shifted exponential time to events. One is based on the max statistic combining MLE estimators of origin and scale parameters, namely CUSUM-MLE-MAX chart; the other is based on the likelihood ratio statistic, namely CUSUM-LR chart. We presented the implementation strategies and the implementation steps are shown using two real datasets. Non-normal distributions are common in time to event processes, but the functional form of the process distribution may not be explicitly known a priori. Li et al. (2019) investigated two distribution‐free cost‐efficient Shewhart‐type schemes. The proposed schemes are applicable to any unknown continuous univariate processes, including time to event processes. Sanusi et al. (2017) developed an EWMA monitoring scheme for estimated parameters. An auxiliary variable is introduced at the estimation stage to monitor the location parameter of a process distribution. The proposed chart, denoted as MrEWMA, is an EWMA-type control chart based on the ratio mean estimator. This motivation further enhances the sensitivity of the control chart, especially in detecting shifts of small magnitudes. As for counting process in discrete manufacturing, the number of defective items found over time is very low. Such processes are known by high-quality or high-yield processes. Mahmood and Xie (2019) presented a review of models and monitoring of zero‐inflated processes. It provides a summary of past and current trends of monitoring methods under the zero‐inflated models and presented some further research issues. One is the follow-up work by Mahmood (2020) that developed a generalized linear model based monitoring methods for high‐yield processes. (2). Control charts for bivariate/multivariate time-between-events distribution. In this task, we planned to “focus on process monitoring with multiple characteristics.” Cheng et al. (2017) presented a multivariate exponentially weighted moving average (MEWMA) procedure for TBEs data. The frequency and magnitude of some event should be investigated together as a bivariate process monitoring problem due to the correlations between both the frequency and severity measurements in general. In our study, we proposed a control chart based on a bivariate gamma distribution with an association parameter to characterize the dependence between event frequency and event magnitude. Comparison is conducted between three kinds of charts under eight shift domains and showed good results. In another piece of work, Wang et al. (2018) proposed a multivariate sign chart for monitoring dependence among mixed-type data. This work integrates ordinal categorical factors and continuous factors into a unified framework of standardized ranks, which can preserve the dependence among original mixed-type factors and the change of it. Then this work combines standardized ranks and spatial signs to achieve affine invariant charting statistic and significantly improve the efficiency of the consequent control charts in detection of dependence shifts among mixed-type data. An additive manufacturing process is monitored by the proposed control chart to show its implementation in real life. Huang et al. (2018) investigated some multivariate distribution-free EWMA Schemes for simultaneous monitoring of time between events and event magnitude. Specifically, we studied two distribution-free monitoring EWMA schemes, namely EWMA-Mathur and EWMA-JKBWS respectively, for simultaneous monitoring of TBEs and event magnitude. In addition, a comprehensive performance comparison is shown and the procedure is applied to two manufacturing processes. (3) Some useful charts for frequency and magnitude monitoring. For this task, we stated that “When monitoring the occurrence of incidence, we should consider both the frequency and magnitude. Control charts have been developed considering this problem, although more should be done.” The corresponding research activities are as in the following. A PhD student and a research fellow studied an adaptive distance based procedure for the simultaneous monitoring of time between events and event magnitude in Sanusi and Mukherjee (2018). An MT scheme to simultaneously monitor the magnitude (M) and time (T) between events. It is based on the amalgamation of the max-type and the distance-type schemes to capitalize the advantages of both schemes. Unlike previous works, our proposed scheme is capable of monitoring almost all types of shifts in all the process parameters. In addition, we use a real-life data to show the implementation of the proposed scheme. Sanusi et al. (2020) developed a Max-EWMA control chart for simultaneous monitoring of the magnitude and time-between-events. Unlike earlier works, a single maximum EWMA (Max-EWMA) scheme for simultaneously monitoring the magnitude of each occurrence and time interval between two consecutive occurrences of the event which contains historical information in a weighted form. It is more effective than the T&X and the rate chart for detecting small shift domain. It also competes strongly in detecting large shifts. The result shows that the Max-EWMA scheme performs best for detecting small to moderate shifts. (4) Study the TBE data monitoring for maintenance reliability applications In the research proposal, we proposed “One important application of our research in reliability is to develop cost-effective maintenance procedure based on TBE data.” The corresponding research activities are as in the following. We have investigated an integrated model of SPC and maintenance policy in this research. We incorporated type II error in our optimization model assuming the shifts can occur simultaneously in mean and variance of manufacturing process. Then recommend synthetic T2 chart to monitor the underlying process. A paper has recently been published. In Li et al (2020) presented a dynamic control charting scheme for early detection of reliability problems for maintenance related decision making. Instead of specifying a constant control limit, we determine the control limits progressively by considering stochastic product sales and non-homogeneous failure processes, simultaneously. Simulation and comparison studies, as well as a real-data application, showed that the proposed scheme is able to detect an underlying reliability problem promptly and meanwhile estimate the change point with an acceptable accuracy. (5) Application to real-world problems and actual processes In almost all the publications, we have included application examples. Some are real case study and some are based on published data or simulated data from realistic scenario. Implementation procedures are shown for general applications. Specific recommendations and insights are also presented. These research projects were also developed through the implementation issues from manufacturing industry and are suitable in the new and advanced/intelligent manufacturing environment.

11213116.label: Major findings and research outcome
11213116.value: In this project, together with my students, we have presented a number of studies on advanced control charts for the monitoring of time-between-events. Especially, bivariate and multivariate time-between-events distributions are used and studies on the monitoring of frequency and magnitude are carried out. Some are briefly described below. Sanusi et al (2019) presented some useful studies on simultaneous monitoring of magnitude and time-between-events data. A new scheme combining a Max‐type and a Distance‐type schemes to monitor the time of occurrence of an event (T) and the magnitude of an event (X) simultaneously and efficiently. It is very competent in detecting a shift in the process distribution of T or X or both and has a distinct advantage over its traditional counterparts in detecting moderate to large shifts. In another piece of work, Sanusi et al (2020) presented a performance study to show that the Max-EWMA chart outperforms its existing counterparts with the same objective of detecting small shifts in process parameters. The Max-EWMA control chart also competes strongly in detecting large shifts. The work of PhD student and research fellow led to Li and Mukherjee (2019) that investigated nonparametric procedures considering cost-minimisation. Another distribution-free hybrid scheme is studied in Sanusi et al. (2019) in a different application and a large-scale Monte Carlo simulation has shown that the scheme has a robust competitive performance with their existing counterparts. Further research on zero-inflated Poisson distribution has been carried out. We developed and studied PR-ZIP and PR-ZINB charts (Mahmood, 2020) that enables us to detect a change in the process as well as also able to accumulate the effect of covariates. When the covariate is accumulated with the variable of interest than the model-based control charts, the new procedure provides better performance as compared to data-based control charts. Li et al. (2019) is an interesting study on a dynamic control charting scheme that is able to detect an underlying reliability problem promptly and meanwhile estimate the change point with an acceptable accuracy. This has already led to more follow-up work. In summary, the study has resulted over 10 publications in reputable journal and 5 PhD students partially supported by the grant have graduated. A journal special issue was edited, a recent paper was selected by IISE Transactions as highlight article. We also presented several invited talks at different conferences.

11213116.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11213116.value: There are a number of research directions and some are already followed up by students recently graduated. One is to consider process monitoring of mixed-type of data, both categorical and variable data. A popular area of research is to consider monitoring changes with image information, which could be linked to other important fields of artificial intelligence and applications. Another problem we started to investigate is the monitoring of networks as there are many dynamic issues and changes that should be incorporated into the modelling, although there is no simple way to deal with the problem. Various application problems such as monitoring procedure for additive and intelligent manufacturing could be other important issue to be further studied. Generally, many real-world problems involve high-dimensional mixed-type data and we should also consider the magnitude of economic loss caused by the products’ nonconforming events, as further extension of this project.

11213116.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11213116.value: Manufacturing processes are highly capable of producing a large number of items with near-zero defect quality today. Such processes are known as high-quality or high-yield processes. For this type of processes, an effective approach is to monitor the time between the occurrences of defects so that potential issues could be detected earlier and actions before many defective items start to be produced. In this project, several advanced research studies are carried out on this problem. We have considered bivariate and multivariate processes and incorporation of advanced statistical monitoring techniques. In addition, the information could include the severity of defect, and zero-inflated distributions might be more appropriate. Monitoring frequency and magnitude has also shown to have wide applicability beyond manufacturing processes. The results and procedure in this research provides simple and effective way for decision making, such as in predicting warranty claims and in maintenance policies.

11214116.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11214116.value: Program testing is a method to execute a multithreaded program over a test case and determine whether the program execution reveals any error or the output of the program is incorrect. It is the most widely practiced method in the industry to ensure program correctness. With the advent of multicore processors, more and more programs are multithreaded. Bug reports of useful multithreaded programs such as MySQL or Eclipse are still filed by users every now and then, reporting symptoms like halts and crashes, which are critical. On the other hands, program developments of this class of programs are increasingly mature, indicating that some basic kinds of concurrency bugs like data races should now be able to detect and fix. The continual reporting of severe symptoms on the use of such useful multithreaded programs indicate that research efforts should be placed to address the next level of fundamental concurrency bugs. Atomicity violation is a fundamental kind of concurrency bugs. Even an execution without any data race or deadlocks may incur atomicity violations. A code block execution in a trace usually contains a sequence of accesses to one or more memory locations as well as synchronization operations. Atomicity violation occurs when an execution fails to protect some of its code blocks. Such a code block is marked to be atomic. However, in actual execution, it is not the case. Such a failure of protection indicates that the intermediate results being processed by a particular code block may mistakenly be read or corrupted by some concurrently executing code blocks. Static analysis and model checking techniques in analyzing large-scale multithreaded programs are either imprecise or impractical. Dynamic approach to testing is essential to demonstrate the presence of atomicity violations instead of merely reporting the potentials of the code to produce them. Nonetheless, the state of the art techniques can only reveal such concurrency bugs by using excessive memory overheads and can be ineffective. They may exhaust all the memory even on analyzing medium-scale programs, not to mention the industry-scale ones. This project aims at developing a novel FAVOR framework to support the detection of atomicity violations in large-scale multithreaded programs. FAVOR addresses the key challenge in tracking cross-thread dependency and interleaving-sensitive issue in generating thread schedules with and without atomicity violations. This project will also educate students so that they can effectively contribute to the growth of the software industry after graduation. 程序测试是一种在测试用例下执行多线程程序的方法，用以判断是否程序在执行中发生错误或程序的输出不正确。它是行业中用来确保程序正确性最被广泛实践的方法。随着多核处理器的出现，越来越多的程序被设计成多线程。广泛应用的多线程程序例如MySQL或Eclipse，仍然不断被用户提交像程序停止或崩溃这类严重症状的Bug报告。另一方面，此类程序的开发越来越成熟，标志着如数据冲突（Data Race）这样一些基本种类的并发性Bug（Concurrency Bug）如今应该能够被检测并修复。这些广泛应用的多线程程序在使用过程中不断被提交具有严重症状的Bug报告，表明研究精力应该放在解决下一阶段的基本并发性Bug上。违反原子性（Atomicity Violation）是一种基本的并发性Bug，甚至在没有任何数据冲突或死锁（Deadlock）的程序执行中都有可能违反原子性。在一次执行跟踪中一个代码块的执行经常包含对一个或多个内存地址的访问序列及一些同步操作（Synchronization Operation）。违反原子性发生在程序在（并发）执行时未能保护它的一些代码块（不被其他代码块干扰），这些代码块被标记为原子性的（Atomic）。然而，在实际程序执行中情况并非如此。这种保护失败预示着被特定代码块处理的中间结果可能被错误地读取或被某些并发执行的代码片段损坏。对大规模多线程程序而言，以动态方式进行测试以证明违反原子性的存在而非仅仅评估代码对违反原子性的潜在保护是非常必要的。然而，当今的技术水平只能通过极度的内存开销暴露此类并发性Bug，并且很可能效率低下。它们甚至可能在分析中等规模程序时就出现内存耗尽，更不必说工业级程序。此项目的目标是开发一个新颖的FAVOR框架用以支持大规模多线程程序的违反原子性检测。FAVOR解决了在生成具有和不具有违反原子性的线程调度过程中跟踪跨线程依赖（Cross-thread Dependency）和交错敏感（Interleaving-Sensitive）问题的关键挑战。此项目也将培养学生以便他们毕业后可以有效地为软件行业的发展做出贡献。

11214116.label: Realisation of objectives
11214116.value: The first objective was to investigate the challenges in exposure of atomicity violation bugs from multithreaded programs. To realize this objective, we collected the source code of representative multithreaded programs, including the DaCapo, Java Grande, Splash2x, benchmarks as well as real-world applications such as mysql and a testchain implementation of blockchain. We used two methodologies to study these program code and traces. The first methodology was a typical method used in dynamic analysis and testing of such programs for concurrency bug detection. For each program, we ran it over each applicable test case several times. To analyze the situations of atomicity violations, we implemented different types of atomicity violation detectors, including detectors that only produce true positives from the observed traces, detectors that may produce false positives, but they can produce all true positives. We applied each detector on each collected trace and collected the sets of events and dependencies captured by these detectors. We analyzed their extent of trace monitoring and the event dependencies in the collected datasets with respect to each atomicity violation they detected to identify new opportunities and challenges in detecting atomicity violations. We attempted to analyze the scenarios that a slight change in traces and what information not captured caused these detectors unable to detect atomicity violations precisely and efficiently. We also examined the source code of these atomicity violations to identify why some atomicity violations were more difficult to detect than others. We found that the monitoring and logging processes are very heavy weighted which prevent the adoption of atomicity violation detectors to be applied on production runs. The second methodology is our original proposal to address the above problem. We observed that atomicity violation detection required the same test cases to be executed several times. After a detector parsed a trace, the dependencies among events and the outcome of atomicity violation detection were known. The follow-up traces can reuse these pieces of information to make the recording process more lightweight. We thus examined each trace to check how the execution points before or after an atomicity violation (or a concurrency bug such as data race) can be paired up so that details can be abstracted out to identify challenges therein in reproducing the trace. We have then designed a new approach, called TPlay, to reproduce concurrent traces. The second objective and the third objective were to formulate a cross-thread dependency strategy and search-based strategy for atomicity violation detection. To realize them, we studied how different function calls are related across program threads and when the across-thread information should be kept. In simple cases, all information could be kept, yet by doing so created an impractically large runtime overhead to fail the execution of the detector. We thus systematically analyze why some dependencies could be removed with respect to each possible execution point of atomicity violation occurrence. We then designed a new type of cross-thread dependency maintenance strategy, which propagated essential information for subsequent atomicity violations before deleting each dependency. To identify which information was essential, we seeked from modeling the dependencies in a mathematical model and took the view of online analysis. Our methodology is to systematically analyze the model to answer a series of research questions. They include whether a newly generated dependency should be kept for a subsequent atomicity violation detection, the location to keep such dependencies that ought to be kept so that the subsequent inference on atomicity violation can be efficient and effective, and the execution point to delete each such dependency. We further studied whether some events were non-essential in analyzing a trace. Based on the analysis result, we mainly designed a new strategy called RegionTrack, which is a detector without producing false positives or false negatives, while able to detect each true positive case. We wondered whether certain kinds of events might be completely skipped from analysis, thereby making detectors more lightweight. Our methodology was to re-examine each kind of event or dependency used in RegionTrack and review the theory behind the above-mentioned analysis on maintaining dependencies. If a kind of event or dependency in the theory can be abstracted out, then at least in theory, i.e., without considering the efficiency aspect, that kind of event or dependency can be eliminated. This process was tedious. Therefore, we resolve to use mathematical proofs for assistance. Once we identified such a kind of event or dependency, we reformulated our model on RegionTrack to eliminate that kind of event or dependency. From this point, we identified that there were two lines of research. The first line was to realize the reformulated model as a new detector, which resulted in EpochPairCheck, and the second line was to realize the model by transforming a trace while keeping RegionTrack intact, which resulted in ConPlay. Our method to formulate EpochPairCheck was to decompose each dependency as a pair of timestamp-thread pairs, and thus only a part of each dependency was required to maintain. Our aim was to use the epochs kept in each thread to recover the dependency sequence that corresponds to each atomicity violation occurrence through a search-based strategy, thereby generating the chain event to assist developers to debug their programs. Our method to formulate ConPlay was to transform event sequence into a parallelized version. The idea was that in replaying a trace, the information on the recorded trace was read-only. Therefore, if the trace information about the partial orders of dependencies were kept precisely, threads in the replay traces could reproduce the partial orders without synchronization among these threads in the reproducing execution. The fourth objective was to develop and evaluate the proposed FAVOR framework. We compared TPlay, RegionTrack, EpochPairTrack, and ConPlay with their respective existing techniques. To achieve it, we implemented our suite of techniques as tools to support the analysis of C/C++ or Java multithreaded programs with and without atomicity violations and/or data races. Our tools were developed in C++ and Java with the use of both industry-strength dynamic instrumentation framework and a direct modification of a high-performance Java Virtual Machine (JikesRVM). We used the benchmark suites to comprehensively evaluate our techniques via these tools in terms of detection effectiveness and runtime overheads such as precision, memory overheads, logging overheads, and replay probability. By comparing the results of the prior arts, we identified the merits and limitations of our techniques and iteratively refined them.

11214116.label: Major findings and research outcome
11214116.value: We have found that the set of traces generated by the same program on the same input may produce different traces, and yet at a higher level of abstraction, many detailed variations of event ordering could be unified and consolidated into the same high-level dependency [C8, C14]. This finding enabled the replay of such traces at a higher level of abstraction while the information to be logged after the abstraction in these traces can be significantly reduced. This resulted in a novel technique TPlay [C12], where the record log size can be reduced by more than 80% in the experiment. The use of a precise atomicity detector in TPlay also enabled the replay probability to be higher than 90% in the experiment. We also found that a key reason on why existing detectors could not precisely detect atomicity violations was due to the need to keep a dependency for later use and yet have to balance the runtime overhead for online analysis. As such, these existing detectors may have to prematurely remove the dependency [J6]. We developed the RegionTrack detector based on implicit dependency propagation [J6]. It used vector clocks to model dependency and propagated the timestamps in the clocks to some other clocks to overcome the problem of keeping information for a dependency that could be deleted. This resulted in state-of-the-art detection precision and efficiency. EpochPairCheck [J8] further the state of the art represented by RegionTrack. We proved that the partial orders among subregions in RegionTrack can be eliminated after the timestamp propagation process. By keeping epochs instead of dependencies through the propagation process, we showed that it was possible to recover at least one cyclic chain of dependencies among threads to pinpoint each detected atomicity violation, which was not possible for the state-of-the-art atomicity violation detectors including RegionTrack. ConPlay [J9] was to record both the event index of each write event of each thread and how two cross-thread indexes form a write-write pair. To resolve the omission of write-read or read-write event pairs in recording traces, we discovered that it was possible to use the read events in the replay traces to recover whether a write event has reached a particular index. ConPlay showed that this strategy was feasible. From the experiment, we found that ConPlay reproduced large traces with 80% in replay probability, where previous state-of-the-art techniques using write-write dependencies cannot replay these traces.

11214116.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11214116.value: RegionTrack and EpochPairCheck show the potential of vector clocks for precise and efficient atomicity violation detection observable in the trace. However, traces after some subtle thread interleaving may still hide concurrency bugs. A research direction is to detect these hidden atomicity violations from the traces. These two detectors still incurred large overheads. TPlay used RegionTrack to record traces to produce high-level traces and encode the high-level traces as a novel kind of trace record log. The major overhead is to profile the memory accesses. The recent advances in data race detection should also provide insights on how to lower the runtime overheads of atomicity violation detection further. Moreover, from the development of ConPlay, we observed that write-write event pairs may accomplish a search-based strategy to partially recover read-write and write-read dependency information. By using static analysis with dynamic write-write information, some function calls can be skipped from profiling the detailed memory accesses. There is a strong connection among single-variable atomicity violation, multi-variable atomicity violation, and transactional atomicity violation. Our project focuses on the transactional atomicity violation and non-serializable traces. It is interesting to have a unified method to detect all these kinds of atomicity violations and data races.

11214116.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11214116.value: Atomicity violations occurring between code regions executed in parallel by different units of the same multithreaded programs are high-level bugs. Leaving them in programs may cause these programs to produce critical failures with severe consequences. These bugs should be detected and removed before these failures produce severe damages to our society. In this project, we analyzed the mathematical models behind a major kind of atomicity violations, and formulated a series of new detection tools to help developers to detect and debug them. Two developed tools can find atomicity violations in program executions. They produced state-of-the-art precision and efficiency. One tool can further provide the information on the execution history that produces the detected atomicity violation. The fourth tool used the atomicity property, verified by the above tools, to simplify the relationship between the function calls performed by different parallel units of the program in execution. It reduced the record log size for subsequent trace reproduction. This tool chain helps developers to detect these programs against atomicity violations productively.

11214316.label: Project Objectives
11214316.value: Develop a clustering algorithm to divide the switches of a data center into clusters and place a WR in each cluster, such that the number of WRs used to cover all switches is minimized and the control traffic demand of each switch is met. Design a wireless backbone network for each domain and design resource allocation algorithms for the wireless links, such that the WRs within the domain are all connected to the domain controller and the aggregated control traffic demand over wireless links is met. Design an efficient distributed scheme for multiple domain controllers in the data center, such that global congestion control and load balancing can be achieved through the collaborations among the controllers.

11214316.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11214316.value: Software Defined Networking (SDN) is an emerging technology that decouples the software that controls a network from the devices that implement network functions, which is the separation of the network control plane from the data plane. The control plane usually uses an independent network for communication between the controller and the switches, which is physically separated from the data plane network. However, building an additional wired network for control plane in a data center involves complex construction work of cabling installation, which hinders the wide deployment of SDN in data centers. The principal goal this project is to investigate the current wireless and SDN technologies and develop a wireless solution for adopting SDN for data center networks. This project consists of three major tasks: 1) Develop a clustering algorithm to divide the switches of a data center into clusters and place a WR in each cluster, such that the number of WRs used to cover all switches is minimized and the control traffic demand of each switch is met. 2) Design a wireless backbone network for each domain and design resource allocation algorithms for the wireless links, such that the WRs within the domain are all connected to the domain controller and the aggregated control traffic demand over wireless links is met. 3) Design an efficient distributed scheme for multiple domain controllers in the data center, such that global congestion control and load balancing can be achieved through the collaborations among the controllers. 軟件定義網絡（Software Defined Network, SDN）是一項可以將控制網絡的軟件與實現網絡功能的設備分離（即網絡控制平面與數據平面的分離）的新興技術。控制平面通常用一個獨立網絡進行控制器與交換機之間的通信，從而實現與數據平面網絡的物理隔絕。然而，在數據中心裡面建立額外的有線網絡將涉及到佈線等複雜的工作，這勢必成為SDN應用于數據中心的最大障礙。本項目旨在對現有無線和SDN技術進行深入調研，并提出一項無線解決方案以實現將SDN應用在數據中心網絡。本項目主要包含三個主要研究任務：1）設計一個聚類算法用以將數據中心里的交換機分為不同的簇，并在每個簇中佈置一個無線路由器，從而實現使用最少的無線路由器去覆蓋所有的交換機並且滿足每個交換機的控制流量需求。2）為每一個域設計一個無線骨幹網絡以及為每條無線鏈路設計資源分配算法，從而實現域中所有的無線路由器都連接到域控制器並且滿足無線鏈路上的聚合控制流量需求。3）為數據中心里的域控制器設計一個高效的分佈式方案，從而通過控制器之間的協作以實現整體擁塞控制與流量均衡。

We also investigated multicast applications in SDN data center networks, and developed a delay-sensitive multicast scheme for inter-datacenter networks. 11214316.value: Software Defined Networking (SDN) is an emerging technology that decouples the software that controls a network from the devices that implement network functions, which is the separation of the network control plane from the data plane. The control plane usually uses an independent network for communication between the controller and the switches, which is physically separated from the data plane network. However, building an additional wired network for control plane in a data center involves complex construction work of cabling installation, which hinders the wide deployment of SDN in data centers. The principal goal this project is to investigate the current wireless and SDN technologies and develop a wireless solution for adopting SDN for data center networks. 11216416.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11216416.value: Mobile cellular systems are now evolving towards the fifth generation (5G). For 4G cellular networks, multiple access techniques are mainly orthogonal, especially for users associated with the same base station. The advantage of using orthogonal multiple access is that interference becomes easier to manage, as the whole radio spectrum can be partitioned into orthogonal pieces in time or frequency domains, which are also commonly called resource blocks. The function of radio resource management then reduces to the task of allocating resource blocks to users, which includes channel assignment for allocating frequency subcarriers and packet scheduling for allocating time slots. While such an approach can effectively eliminate intra-cell interference, the densification of cells and full resource reuse in 4G cellular systems cause severe inter-cell interference, especially for cell-edge users. To further improve system performance, more advanced interference management techniques are needed. To provide high spectral and energy efficiencies, non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) based on user superposition is a promising candidate for 5G cellular systems. This technique represents a major change from previous generations of cellular networks, as NOMA allows multiple users to share the same resource block via power-domain multiplexing. Signals of different users are linearly added and distinguished at the receiver by multi-user detection, which can be realized, for example, by successive interference cancelation. Instead of naively treating interference as noise, the structure of interference is exploited by advanced receivers for detection and decoding. This represents a new paradigm of interference management. To ensure effective operations of successive interference cancelation, power control is indispensable, as the received signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) of a connection must match with its selected code rate. To maintain target SINRs for all users, the classic power control theory has been well developed since the launch of 2G cellular systems, with the basic assumption that interfering signals are treated as additive Gaussian noise. For NOMA systems, interference structure needs to be exploited and classic power control results are not directly applicable. A revisit of the theory is therefore needed. In this project, a new power control framework for NOMA systems will be established by rigorous mathematical techniques. The results will be integrated into a resource optimization framework, which includes user grouping and channel allocation. Efficient decentralized resource allocation methods based on game theory and advanced optimization techniques will be proposed and their performance will be evaluated by computer simulations.

11216416.label: Realisation of objectives
11216416.value: The objectives of the project have been achieved. First, we have extended the classical power control theory to more complicated interference structure, which includes the scenarios of multicast transmissions and interference cancellation. The results are obtained by rigorous mathematical analysis, which laid a foundation for the design of practical schemes. Second, iterative distributed power control algorithms for multi-cell NOMA systems have been designed. This is based on the power control theory we have developed and also on mathematical analysis. The most difficult part of this problem is that the decoding order in each cell can be changed during the iterative process. By carefully analyzing the algorithms, convergence properties are proved. Third, our work is further extended from power control to more general resource management tasks, which include subcarrier allocation, user grouping, and beamforming. Using advanced optimization techniques, we have designed practical algorithms, which can be used to improve system performance of future wireless networks. In summary, we have obtained fundamental mathematical results, which increase the understanding of power-controlled wireless networks. Furthermore, we have designed distributed algorithms, which can be used for the optimization of practical wireless systems.

11216416.label: Major findings and research outcome
11216416.value: We have obtained necessary and sufficient conditions for the feasibility of a target signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) in a wireless multicast system with and without power constraint. The feasible SINR region and its geometric properties are studied. Besides, an iterative algorithm is proposed, which can efficiently check the feasibility condition and compute the boundary points of the feasible SINR region. The results were published in Journal Paper 3 stated in Part C. We have also investigated the power control problem for the downlink of a multi-cell NOMA system. The problem aims to minimize the total transmit power of all the base stations subject to the data rate requirements of the users. Its feasibility and optimality properties are characterized. Furthermore, a distributed algorithm is designed and its convergence is proved. Numerical results quantify the improvement of our proposed method over some existing schemes in terms of power consumption and outage probability. The results were published in Journal Paper 1 stated in Part C. Our work is extended to consider the joint subcarrier and power allocation problem for the downlink of a multi-carrier NOMA system. A novel three-step resource allocation framework is designed to deal with the sum rate maximization problem. Numerical results show that our proposed three-step resource allocation algorithm could achieve comparable sum rate performance to the existing near-optimal solution with much lower computational complexity and outperforms the power-controlled orthogonal multiple access scheme. Besides, a tradeoff between user fairness and sum rate performance can be achieved by applying different user power constraint strategies in the proposed algorithm. The results were published in Journal Paper 2 stated in Part C. Our work is also extended to consider the power minimization problem for multi-cell multiple-input single-output NOMA systems. The associated joint user grouping, beamforming and power control problem is a mixed integer non-convex programming problem. Based on an iterative distributed methodology, we designed our resource management methods. Simulation results show that they outperform various existing schemes in several aspects, including power consumption, outage probability, energy efficiency, and connectivity efficiency. These results were published in Journal Paper 4 stated in Part C.

11216416.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11216416.value: Non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) allows multiple users in the same cell sharing the same frequency spectrum at the same time by superposing signals of multiple users together. The mutual interference between these users is called intra-cell interference. In a cellular environment, there is interference from neighboring cells, which is called inter-cell interference. To decode the signals, inter-cell interference is typically treated as additive noise while intra-cell interference is handed by successive interference cancellation, which decode the signals of users in the same cell one by one sequentially. Such a delicate interference structure poses a difficult optimization problem for efficient power control. This project investigates the problem and obtains fundamental results on system optimality. For practical applications, iterative distributed algorithms that always converge to the optimal point are designed. These results are further extended to more complicated resource allocation problems in NOMA-based wireless networks. Several resource management algorithms are designed and their performance are shown to outperform existing methods, which lead to more efficient operations of wireless systems.

11225216.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11225216.value: The Internet and telecommunication are becoming indispensable to our daily lives. Without the Internet or telecommunication, there would be NO email, World Wide Web, e-commerce, online stock trading, Facebook, or even smartphones, etc. Indeed, a smartphone is not “smart” without Internet access. About 97% of international and intercontinental Internet communications are transported via fiber optic submarine telecommunication cables, which are the physical backbones of the entire cyber world. Submarine telecommunication cables are often either laid directly on the seabed or buried at shallow depths within the seabed. Over the last decade, damage to submarine telecommunication cables has been observed when significant seabed movement occurred due to geo-hazards (e.g., earthquakes and submarine landslides). For example, in 2006, a magnitude-7.1 earthquake struck Hengchun, south of Taiwan, severely damaged seven submarine telecommunication cables and disrupted international telecommunications to Hong Kong, Taiwan, China, Korea, Japan and Singapore. After the earthquake, Hong Kong suffered from very slow Internet connection and disruption of other telecommunication services (e.g., international direct dial) for more than a month. Similar scenarios of multiple submarine telecommunication cable damage occurred twice in the Mediterranean Sea during 2008, compromising Internet connection in Europe, Asia and Africa. Although the economic cost of the damage was very difficult to measure accurately, a report from the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology (ETH) Zurich in 2005 suggested that a one-week Internet blackout costs 1.2% of the GDP (i.e., many billions of dollars). This proposed research aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the interaction between submarine telecommunication cables and seabed movement and develop risk assessment methodologies for submarine telecommunication cables. The major research components include finite element numerical simulations and full-scale physical modeling using a soil testing chamber. The numerical and full-scale physical models will reveal the failure mechanisms of submarine telecommunication cable damage due to seabed movement. The modeling results will be used to develop design charts and methods for evaluating the seabed movement-induced risk of submarine telecommunication cable damage. The proposed research will quantify the risk of seabed movement-induced damage to submarine telecommunication cables. The research outcome will be applicable to submarine telecommunication cables worldwide and contribute to the development of a fast and reliable global Internet, which is becoming increasingly vital not only to Hong Kong, but also to many other countries around the world. 互聯網和電信在現代生活中變得越來越重要。沒有互聯網和電信，就沒有電子郵件、各種電子社交媒體、電子商貿、甚至智能電話。沒有互聯網數據服務的智能電話的確並不〝智能〞。海底光纜是互聯網和電信系統的骨干組成部件，97%的國際互聯網流量是通過淺埋在海床上的海底光纜來傳送。過去10多年，由於地震或海底滑坡等地質災害引發的海床運動導致的海底光纜破壞時有發生，造成巨大的經濟損失。如2006年台灣恆春地震破壞了7條海底光纜，癱瘓了香港、台灣、中國大陸、韓國、日本和新加坡等地的國際互聯網和電信服務。2008年地中海的海底光纜被地震破壞，嚴重影響了歐洲、亞洲和非洲的國際互聯網和電信服務。本項目將系統地研究海床運動與海底光纜的相互作用，並建立一套科學的海底光纜地質災害風險評估方法。

11225216.label: Realisation of objectives
11225216.value: All project objectives have been successfully achieved. Both finite element (FE) numerical models and full-scale physical models have been developed to investigate the interaction between submarine telecommunication cables and seabed movements. The FE numerical model results have been validated using results obtained from full-scale physical modeling. Probabilistic methods have also been developed to characterize the spatial varying seabed conditions along the cable routes from sparsely measured data obtained during site investigation. In addition, random finite element methods (RFEM) has been used to investigate the effects of uncertainty in seabed conditions on cable responses. The project has resulted in publications of 11 papers in top journals, three conference papers (e.g., ASCE Lifelines Conference 2021), and training and graduation of one PhD student (see sections 8, 9, and 10). This project also contributes to a US patent granted in 2019 (see section 11). Some details on the numerical models, physical models and probabilistic analyses are given in the following paragraphs, respectively. FE numerical models and full-scale physical models have been developed to investigate the responses of submarine telecommunication cables to lateral seabed movements (Wang et al. 2021, see paper 11 in section 8). A FE model was firstly developed using ABAQUS and validated by full-scale physical test results. The full-scale model experiment was performed in a large-scale split-box test apparatus. The internal dimensions of the split-box are 5m*1m*1m (length*width*height). One half of the box is secured to the ground, and the other part can move along a certain angle with respect to the longitudinal axis of the split-box. A submarine telecommunication cable was buried in soils inside the split-box, and one half of the split-box was pushed to move laterally for modeling of seabed movements. The full-scale model experiments investigated the response of telecommunication cables subjected to abrupt lateral ground movement and to provide a basis for the validation of FE simulations. Reasonable agreements were obtained through the comparison of the results from FE analysis and the full-scale tests. After validation of the FE model, a series of FE parametric studies was performed to systematically study the effects of various parameters involved in cable-soil interaction when subjected to lateral seabed movements. In total, 7610 FE runs were performed, covering various combinations of typical soil properties, cable characteristics and seabed movement characteristics. The parametric study results were summarized in a dimensionless plot, followed by a regression analysis. The parametric study results indicated that the maximum cable strain induced by lateral seabed movements is influenced by the normalized load and the relative cable-soil stiffness. The normalized load dominates the maximum cable strain. Regression equations for the best-fit curve and upper and lower bounds of the 90% prediction interval were provided. Using the proposed formula, the maximum cable strain can be quickly estimated when the normalized load and relative cable-soil stiffness are known. Safety criteria and evaluation chart for submarine telecommunication cables were also developed for evaluating safety of the cable directly using soil properties, cable characteristics and seabed movement characteristics. To probabilistically model the spatially varying seabed conditions along the cable routes from sparsely measured data obtained during site investigation, a novel random field generator has been developed (Wang et al. 2018 see paper 4 in section 8). The random field generator is based on Bayesian compressive sampling (BCS) and Karhunen–Loève (KL) expansion, denoted as BCS–KL generator. The BCS-KL generator is able to directly generate random samples that account for spatial distribution (i.e., spatial auto-correlation) of soil properties along the cable routes, as well as cross-correlation among different soil properties at the same locations from sparse measurements (Zhao and Wang 2018, see paper 6 in section 8). The random samples generated were used as input to the FE numerical models for performing random finite element analysis and investigating the effects of various uncertainties (e.g., spatial variability of soil parameters) on cable responses under a Monte Carlo Simulation (MCS) framework. Statistical analysis of the MCS results was performed to prioritize the effects of various uncertainties on cable damage probability. The results show that uncertainty of the anchored cable length has the most significant effect on cable damage probability, while the effects of uncertainties in soil friction angle and effective unit weight are minor. In addition, spatial variability of soil parameters has significant effect, and ignoring spatial variability of soil parameters may lead to misjudgment of cable damage risk.

11225216.label: Major findings and research outcome
11225216.value: Submarine telecommunication cables, which carry more than 97% of international telecommunications, are usually buried shallowly beneath seabed and vulnerable to seabed movements. In recent years, many submarine cable damages have been observed when significant lateral seabed movements occur due to geohazards, e.g., earthquakes and submarine landslides. This calls for a need of methods to evaluate the cable safety when subjected to lateral seabed movements. This project developed finite element (FE) numerical models and full-scale physical models to investigate the responses of submarine telecommunication cables to lateral seabed movements. A FE model was developed first and validated by full-scale physical test results. After validation of the FE model, a series of parametric studies is performed covering typical ranges of soil properties, cable burial depths, cable characteristics and seabed movement characteristics. The parametric study results are summarized in a dimensionless plot, followed by a regression analysis. A simple but effective equation is developed to predict the maximum cable strains induced by lateral seabed movements. The dominant parameters that control submarine cable responses are identified and incorporated into the formula. Safety criteria for submarine telecommunication cables are also proposed for evaluating the cable safety when subjected to lateral seabed movements. As summarized in Part C, this project has led to 11 papers published in top international journals, three international conference papers, and one USA patent. One PhD student has been trained under this project and successfully graduated.

11225216.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11225216.value: In this project, the seabed movement was imposed to the submarine telecommunication cables as displacement boundary conditions, without explicit modeling of the development of seabed movement induced by earthquakes or submarine landslides. To model the development of seabed movement, e.g., during submarine landslides, a large deformation numerical simulation tool is needed, such as material point method. However, the model complexity and computational cost will increase dramatically. High-performance computing technology is needed for such modeling.

11225216.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11225216.value: The Internet and telecommunication are becoming indispensable to our daily lives. More than 97% of intercontinental Internet communications are transported via fiber optic submarine telecommunication cables, which are the physical backbones of the entire cyber world. Submarine telecommunication cables are often either laid directly on the seabed or buried at shallow depths within the seabed. Over the last decade, damage to submarine telecommunication cables has been observed when significant seabed movement occurred due to geo-hazards (e.g., earthquakes and submarine landslides), leading to severe disruption of international telecommunications. This project developed finite element numerical models and full-scale physical models to investigate the responses of submarine telecommunication cables to lateral seabed movements, leading to a comprehensive understanding of the interaction between submarine telecommunication cables and seabed movement and risk assessment methodologies for submarine telecommunication cables. The research outcome is beneficial to submarine telecommunication cables worldwide and contributes to the development of a fast and reliable global Internet, which is becoming increasingly vital not only to Hong Kong, but also to many other countries around the world.

11226716.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11226716.value: The research objective of this project is to develop robust design and tolerance design methods for time consuming computer models with random field inputs. Robust design and tolerance design are important methods for building quality into a product. Due to the rapid increase in computing power, computer models of physical systems are increasingly being employed for product design. In such models, the outputs are physical quantities that are functions of space and time. Each physical quantity is a solution of a partial differential equation (PDE) with boundary and initial conditions, and the equations are solved numerically with the finite element or finite difference method. Inputs to the computer model include the geometry of the physical system, parameters of the PDE (e.g., material properties and source term), and boundary and initial conditions. Most of these inputs are uncertain functions of space that can be modeled as random fields. For example, the thermal conductivity of a solid body can be modeled as a lognormal random field. The input uncertainty of main interest in this research represents uncertainty about the actual properties of a unit of manufactured product or environmental noise. In the former case, the mean function of the random field input is a control factor, and the variance function of the input represents inherent variability in the manufacturing process, which can be reduced by improving the manufacturing process. The random field variation about its mean, whether it represents product property or environmental variation, is always noise. The problem considered in this research is that of robust design (choice of random field mean) and tolerance design (choice of variance) in the presence of random field noise. We will develop methodologies for choosing the control factor settings (means and variances) to minimize the expected total cost (sum of quality and manufacturing cost) due to variation in the response caused by noise. Our research will focus on time consuming computer models that require the use of metamodels/ surrogates constructed with a computer experiment. The proposed project is an extension of current work on uncertainty quantification (UQ), which focuses on estimating the probability distribution of scalar summaries of the solution of a PDE induced by input uncertainty. UQ has recently received widespread interest from applied mathematicians, engineers, and statisticians. Our project will provide novel and computationally tractable statistical modeling and optimization methods for robust and tolerance design with random field inputs.

11226716.label: Realisation of objectives
11226716.value: Objective #1 is addressed by Article #1 and Article #4. Article #4 develops a radial basis function metamodel/emulator to efficiently predict and optimize the expected cost/desirability value of the output of a time-consuming stochastic simulator, where the cost/desirability objective function (OF) contains uncertain parameters. The expected OF at each experiment design point is estimated with the sample mean of the replicates at the point, and these sample means are used as the response data for metamodel fitting. While the metamodel is applied to predict the expected OF, it can be used to predict quantiles of the OF by replacing the sample mean response data with sample quantile response data. Article #1 considers integrated parameter and tolerance design for mixture proportion inputs and it derives a globally optimal tolerance region that is applicable to any tolerance design problem. To compute the optimal tolerance region, the total cost (sum of quality and tolerance costs) is calculated by stochastic simulations and optimized via a Gaussian process (GP) emulator fitted to the stochastic data. Article #7 is related to Objective #1. It explores an application related to robust design, i.e., prediction of degradation rates of emerging contaminants based on stochastic data. Objective #2 is addressed in Article #2, Article #5, and Article #8. Article #2 proposes a GP emulator for predicting the solution of a partial differential equation (PDE) that respects Dirichlet boundary and initial conditions imposed on the PDE. The emulator provides improved prediction performance over standard GP emulators when the boundary and initial conditions are variable inputs, and it works well for high-dimensional input domains. It is useful for robust design with random field noise factors, as these noise factors often manifests as boundary or initial conditions. The emulator is applied to approximate a simulator of the temperature in a tissue containing a tumor subjected to thermal ablation. Note that the design of the thermal ablation process can be formulated as a robust design problem with a random field noise factor, i.e., skin surface temperature, imposed as a Dirichlet boundary condition. Article #5 applies a GP emulator to solve a real problem on high-dimensional simulator-based integrated parameter and tolerance design of a centrifugal compressor faced by collaborators at Beihang University, where random field noise in the form of the deviation from nominal geometry is present. The geometry of the centrifugal compressor is parameterized by 10 design variables, and the objective is to determine the optimal nominal value and tolerance for each of the 10 variables. The total cost to be optimized is the sum of the quality and tolerance costs, where the quality cost is a linear combination of the failure probability for each of three output quality characteristics. A computationally efficient formula for computing a conservative estimate of the quality cost based on the GP emulator is derived, which allows a thorough search for the optimal nominal values and tolerances in the high-dimensional decision space. Article #8 develops a shifted log loss GP model for expected quality loss prediction in robust design. The model is applicable to robust design with any continuous loss function. It is superior to existing models in predicting the expected loss. Article #3 is related to Objective #2. Article #3 develops the ANOVA-MOP method for optimization of multiple outputs of a time-consuming simulator with a high-dimensional vector of inputs. In the method, an emulator is used to estimate the total sensitivity indices for the functional relationship between each output and the inputs, and these indices are used to determine which inputs are unimportant for optimizing an output. This input screening approach is relevant to Objective #2, as it reduces the input dimension, which facilitates construction of accurate emulators. While Article #3 does not apply the ANOVA-MOP method to robust design with random field inputs, the method can be extended to such problems. Objective #3 is addressed in Article #4, Article #5, and Article #6. In Article #4, a Cartesian product design is used for enabling efficient fitting of the proposed radial basis function metamodel with stochastic simulation data. In Article #5, a two-stage experiment design approach is used in an attempt to reduce the input dimension of the centrifugal compressor design problem for facilitating GP emulator construction. In the first stage, a fractional factorial design is used as initial design to screen the inputs. In the second stage, a follow-up Latin hypercube design is added. In general, this experimental design approach is useful for reducing the input dimension of robust design problems with many inputs (e.g., problems with random field noise represented by many random variables) for the purpose of model fitting. Article #6 develops an experiment design approach for efficiently estimating the optimal point with generalized linear models (GLMs) and applies it to a robust design problem based on a Poisson regression model fitted with physical experiment data. The approach is also applicable to stochastic computer experiments, as GLMs are useful for such experiments. All noise inputs for simulator-based robust and tolerance design (RTD) examples/problems considered in this project are modeled as finite-dimensional random fields (which are represented/parameterized by finite noise vectors, i.e., finite-dimensional random vectors) as it is difficult to develop simulators for realistic problems with noise inputs modeled as infinite-dimensional random fields. An infinite-dimensional random field noise input is a stochastic process that cannot be exactly represented by a finite noise vector (but is approximated by a finite noise vector in computations nevertheless). This difficulty is due to the need for sophisticated simulation/modeling software (e.g., ANSYS), which is not included in the budget of the project, and scarcity of published data for estimating infinite-dimensional random field noise models. To attempt to overcome these problems, an effort to collaborate with other researchers was made. This led to collaboration with researchers from Beihang University, who provided the computational fluid dynamics software and computer model for the centrifugal compressor RTD problem reported in Article #5. Nonetheless, the noise inputs for this problem are modeled as finite-dimensional random fields. Articles 1. 11226716.label: Major findings and research outcome
11226716.value: In this project, statistical modeling, optimization, and experimental design methods for robust and tolerance design (RTD) with time-consuming simulations that improves on the capabilities of existing RTD methods are developed. Simulations of real systems for RTD with inputs modeled as infinite-dimensional random fields often require sophisticated software. Moreover, such simulations involve first parameterizing the infinite-dimensional random field inputs with a finite number of random variables using approximations such as a truncated Karhunen-Loève expansion, as discussed in Article #8. Thus, after this initial dimension reduction step, a RTD problem with infinite-dimensional random field noise reduces to a RTD problem with finite-dimensional random field noise, i.e., a finite noise vector. Due to these reasons, the methods/models for RTD developed in this project are directly developed for the finite noise vector case and applied to problems with finite-dimensional random field noise models that are tractable to simulate. There are several important research outcomes. A globally optimal tolerance region for product tolerance design is derived in Article #1 and a computationally efficient stochastic simulation and GP-emulator based method is proposed for finding the region. It gives large improvements in quality cost over the existing hyperrectangle tolerance region. Article #4 develops a radial basis function emulator for predicting the expectation of a parameterized objective function for robust design based on a time-consuming stochastic simulator. The emulator predicts the expected objective function over an interval of values of its parameter, which allows a solution robust to objective function uncertainty to be found efficiently. Article #2 develops an improved GP emulator for predicting numerical partial differential equation solutions that respects given Dirichlet boundary and initial conditions. This model is useful for robust design with random field noise as such noise factors often manifest as random boundary and initial conditions. Article #8 develops a GP modeling approach for predicting the expected loss corresponding to any continuous loss function that improves over existing approaches. Article #5 reports a real RTD problem based on a time-consuming simulator of a centrifugal compressor with a high-dimensional input space, where the quality cost depends on the failure probabilities of some output quality characteristics. This challenge is solved by developing a computationally efficient method to estimate the failure probability based on a GP emulator, and a two-stage sequential design strategy to reduce input dimension. Article #6 develops an approach to generate optimal Bayesian designs for estimating the optimal robust design solution with generalized linear models.

11226716.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11226716.value: There are two areas with potential for further development. First, it is prevalent to use common random numbers in stochastic simulations. The use of common random numbers can give a more precise estimate of the difference in expectation values or quantile values of the objective function for pairs of alternative control factor settings. Thus, it is of interest to extend the modeling approach in Article #4 to accommodate stochastic simulations with common random numbers and apply it to solve robust design problems with these types of simulations. Second, when a simulator is extremely time consuming (e.g., the simulator for a centrifugal compressor described in Article #5), it is of interest to employ a lower fidelity and faster simulator to provide additional data for improving accuracy and precision of the robust and tolerance design results. This leads to the problem of robust and tolerance design based on multifidelity simulations, which is an area in need of more research.

11226716.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11226716.value: This project developed statistical modeling, optimization, and experiment design methods for robust and tolerance design (RTD) that improves on the capabilities of existing methods. RTD with time-consuming simulators are widely used in optimizing product quality. This project produces novel contributions to the areas of optimization in RTD, statistical modeling for RTD with stochastic simulations, statistical modeling for RTD with high-dimensional inputs, and experimental design for RTD. The developed methods and models give significant improvements over existing methods and models in terms of computational efficiency, prediction accuracy, and quality of the RTD solution found. We made a notable advancement in product tolerance design, where a globally optimal tolerance region that minimizes the total cost is proposed. We developed a modeling approach for robust design with stochastic simulations to efficiently find a solution that is robust to objective function uncertainty. We proposed a Gaussian process (GP) emulator with improved accuracy that respects boundary and initial conditions imposed on partial differential equations. Finally, we considered a RTD problem involving a centrifugal compressor modeled with a time-consuming simulator, where we developed a practical two-stage design approach for input dimension reduction, and efficient formulas for estimating and optimizing the total cost based on a GP emulator.

11228316.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11228316.value: Qualitative and quantitative detection of biological species are central to many areas of healthcare and life sciences. Recently, 1-D nanostructured semiconductors have become a class of popular building block for transducer elements with promising properties for biosensing applications. Despite the fact that real-time, label-free, and highly sensitive detection of proteins, nucleic acids, and virus have been demonstrated by single-nanowire field-effect transistor based biosensors, clinical applications of these biosensors are rare. The device-to-device performance variation among the single-nanowired biosensors is the principal obstacle to their utilization and mass production. One possible strategy to minimize such variation is to construct multi-nanowire field-effect transistor biosensors. In this project, we will concentrate on the development of practical multi-nanowire field-effect transistor biosensors for the detection of protein tyrosine kinase-7 (PTK7). PTK7 is an important biomarker for various leukemias and solid tumors, including T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, acute myeloid leukemia, B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, lung cancer, gastric cancer, and colon cancer, and so far no nanowire-based PTK7 biosensors have been developed. We plan to (1) establish a cost-effective technique to prepare multi-nanowire field-effect transistors with good transconductances from non-cytotoxic semiconductor nanowires, (2) develop surface modification technique to conjugate PTK7-selective recognition units on nanowires, and (3) build and optimize multi-nanowire biosensors which allow real-time PTK7 sensing. It is anticipated that these PTK7 biosensors not only would allow early detection of various cancers, but they would also provide a platform to study the relationship between the dynamics of PTK7 and the formation of different diseases. 定性和定量的生物檢測是許多保健醫療和生命科學領域的重要課題。一維半導體納米結構近日已成為有前景的生物傳感器元件構建塊。儘管單納米線場效應晶體管已經被演示用於實時和無標記的蛋白、核酸和病毒的高靈敏度檢測，其臨床應用仍然罕見。單納米線生物傳感器之間的性能差異是使用和大規模生產這類生物傳感器的主要障礙。構造多納米線場效應晶體管生物傳感器則是一個可能減少傳感器之間性能差異的策略。在這個項目中，我們將集中發展檢測蛋白酪氨酸激酶-7（PTK7）的實用多納米線場效應晶體管生物傳感器。PTK7是多種白血病和腫瘤的重要生物標記，包括T細胞急性淋巴細胞性白血病，急性骨髓性白血病，B細胞急性淋巴細胞性白血病，肺癌，胃癌和結腸癌。目前，基於納米線的PTK7生物傳感器還沒被開發出來。我們計劃（1）建立具有成本效益的技術來製備多納米線場效應晶體管，（2）開發表面化學技術使多納米線場效應晶體管能夠選擇性識別PTK7，以及（3）優化多納米線生物傳感器，使它允許實時PTK7檢測。我們預期，這些PTK7生物傳感器不僅可以允許早期癌症的檢測，還可以提供一個平台來研究PTK7與不同疾病之間的關係。

11228316.label: Realisation of objectives
11228316.value: In order to develop our proposed InAs nanowire biosensor, we have optimized the growth conditions of InAs nanowires (NWs) by fine tuning different CVD parameters, including the concentration of catalyst (nickel), amount of InAs precursor, flow rate of carrier gas (hydrogen), growth temperature and duration. The best growth condition for long and straight InAs NWs have length > 4 micron with diameter of less than 50 nm. Multi-NW FETs were fabricated and their transport properties were investigated in both air and PBS buffer. Upon the fabrication of the multi-NW FETs, the bio-stability and cytotoxicity of the devices were investigated. We discovered that the InAs nanowires exhibit moderate cytotoxicity to several cell lines, including HeLa, MCF7, Hep G2, and A549. These results suggest that the as-grown InAs NWs can release cytotoxic ions, hampering the application of our proposed FETs for real-time bio-sensing. Attempts were made to modify the surface of the InAs NWs by various thiol-containing organic molecules. Although the cytotoxicity of the surface-modified InAs NWs can be significantly reduced, the gating properties of the FETs were compromised. Our investigations revealed that the stronger the thiol-containing molecule binds to the InAs NWs, the lesser will be the gating ability of the resultant FET. While the InAs NWs may not be the best candidate for the proposed biosensing application, we explored its application as phototransistors. Our results indicate that the sulfur binding on the surface of the InAs NWs plays a critical role in the enhancement of the negative photoconductivity. In line with our proposal to explore different bio-sensing platform based on nano-materials, we developed a nano-theranostic system, denoted as Ce6-CuS/MSN@PDA@MnO2-FA nanoparticles (NPs), which combines photodynamic therapy (PDT), photothermal therapy (PTT), magnetic resonance (MR) imaging with hypoxia-relieving and tumor-targeting functionalities. In vitro and in vivo measurements clearly demonstrated that all these functionalities worked synergistically as expected. The system, having a low dark cytotoxicity, can be effectively internalized by 4T1 cells and decrease the cell viability to 2% upon 660 nm/808 nm laser irradiation. Tumors in 4T1 tumor-bearing mice can almost be completely destroyed in 2 weeks via combined PDT/PTT. Moreover, several new anti-cancer systems were developed/explored in this project. For example, we developed the synthesis of two series of phosphonium ring-fused bicyclic ruthenafuran and osmafuran complexes via a one-step synthesis procedure. The complexes were found to exhibit stronger cytotoxicity against several common human cancer cell lines compared with their corresponding metal precursors and the classic anticancer agent cisplatin, and are able to induce mitochondrial dysfunction in cells, which suggests that the metallafurans may potentially serve as alternative anticancer agents. A new series of ruthenium-indolizinone complexes with anticancer properties was also prepared by an unexpected alkyne activation pathways.
