11273116.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11273116.value: Conventional Ultraviolet germicidal irradiation (UVGI) disinfection technology uses low-pressure mercury lamps and has some drawbacks. The UV light-emitting diode (UV-LED) is an emerging and attractive alternative to traditional mercury vapor lamps for bioaerosol disinfection. In this project, we tested different UV-LED wavebands under individual and coupled operations. UV irradiations with three typical wavebands (UVA, UVB, and UVC) were studied. A synergistic disinfecting effect was observed by utilizing UV-LEDs with the coupled UVB/UVC (288/271 nm) wavelengths for selected bacteria. Besides, the performance of the pulsed UV-LEDs was tested and compared with the continuous UV-LEDs. The results showed a comparable disinfection efficacy for UV-LEDs operating under pulsed and continuous modes. We developed a rotating upper room UVGI-LED (UR-UVGI-LED) air disinfection system and tested its bioaerosol disinfection performance in a full-scale chamber. The rotating UR-UVGI-LED system under a poorly-mixed condition, compared to the stationary system, enhanced its performance considerably. Thus, our proposed rotating irradiation offers great potential for future applications in environments where bioaerosols are unevenly distributed in a built environment. The findings of this work provide valuable information to the general public. It delivers useful engineering strategies for the enhancement of the bioaerosol disinfection performance of UVC-LED devices in indoor applications.

11273416.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11273416.value: The behaviour of cemented sands and weak sandstones has been the subject of a large amount of research over several decades, yet there remain significant gaps in our understanding, notably the precise relationship between the micro-mechanics and the macroscopic behaviour. More specifically, our understanding of the relative roles of breakage of the inter-particle bonds and crushing of the particles has been hampered by the difficulty of separating their effects with traditional laboratory techniques that might be used in uncemented sands and by our lack of direct measurement of the mechanics of cemented particle contacts. Comparisons have been made between triaxial test data over the years for a wide range of cemented sands and sandstones. These have led to considerable speculation about the relative roles of particles and cements in determining the overall mechanics, but verification of this is also inhibited by the lack of micro-mechanical understanding. This project proposes an original approach to investigate the mechanics of weak sandstones from micro-scale observations to modelling the macroscopic stress-strain behaviour. The research will integrate the results of triaxial tests over a wide range of stress levels with micro-CT observations of the developing particle and cement damage, so building on the expertise of each of the applicants. While these are both commonly used methods, the cornerstone of the work will, however, be a the first ever thorough investigation of the micro-mechanics of single cemented sand contacts using new apparatus that directly measure the input parameters needed for micro-mechanical modelling. This will make the research unique in its ability to close the micro to macro circle. N/A

11274016.label: Realisation of objectives
11274016.value: 1. Determine critical components, design, and manufacture flight module prototypes. The first objective concerns (i) identification of minimally required components to construct the proposed modular vehicles, and (ii) the physical implementation. This objective is comprehensively realized as described in the publication in a highly prestigious journal, IEEE Transactions on Robotics [1]. The research has proposed to construct a robot from multiple "flight modules" and a single "control modules". Each flight module houses a motor, propeller, speed controller, an IMU, and a battery while the control module incorporates a primary flight control unit as found in conventional flying robots. The decision to separately include a battery on each module gives rises to a scalable design. In the meantime, the use if multiple IMU facilitates the automated calibration process. The developed algorithm-driven pre-flight calibration process that uses multiple IMUs is the novelty of the work. 2. Develop flight control algorithms capable of learning the unknown geometry and vehicular dynamics. This objective is tightly related to the first objective, but focusing on the theoretical aspect. This has been thoroughly fulfilled in [1]. Here, we proposed to devise a method to stabilize a vehicle that is made up of a payload of which its physical properties (mass, size, shape, moment of inertia) are not known in advance. The payload significantly affects the dynamics and stability of the robot. For flying robots, flight performance and stability is highly sensitive and critical. To overcome the difficulty introduced by an unknown payload, we divided the task into two steps. The first step is to obtain rough estimates of the payload's properties. This provides sufficient information for the flight controller to stabilize the robot (without crashing). The second step is to perform an online update to refine the initial estimates to radically improve the flight performance. For the first task, to compute initial system parameters, which include the mass, moment of inertia, and locations of the propellers with respect to the center of mass (CM) of the robot, we incorporated an inertial measurement unit (IMU) into each flight module. Under the assumption that all propelling modules are approximately upright, the measurements from the IMUs are used to deduce the relative distances between all the flight modules. Critical parameters required for flight are then estimated based on this knowledge. The estimates are inevitably inaccurate. To further improve the flight performance, we developed an adaptive geometric flight controller that is capable of refining a large number of uncertain robot parameters. The stability and convergence of the proposed flight controller is provided via a Lyapunov analysis. 3. Demonstrate stable flight of the fabricated prototype and devised algorithms with and without the motion capture system. As shown in [1], we have demonstrated stable hovering and trajectory tracking flights with six manufactured prototypes using the proposed flight modules, estimation schemes, and the devised adaptive flight controller. Six prototypes vary in configuration and the numbers of propelling modules (4-8). The experiments were carried out using the motion capture system for position feedback and showed that all robots stabilized to the desired trajectory over time. A simple human-assisted trimming process was introduced to facilitate the liftoff for some prototypes with highly asymmetrical configurations. We, however, have not carried out flight tests without the motion capture system in an outdoor environment. This is primarily because the technical research contribution gained from accomplishing such tasks is very limited. The process only requires the incorporation of a few hardware components and previously developed algorithms. The outdoor flight would, undoubtedly, contribute to the practical sides and translation of the research results, but not the technical impact. Instead, we opted to explore other research avenues. We consider relaxing the previous main assumption on the alignment of propellers. Without this, the flight dynamics of the robot follows an unconventional form. The problem of trajectory generation and flight control of such vehicles has not been previously addressed by the research community. We have published our early finding on the trajectory generation in a conference in 2019 and succeeded in developing a flight control for robots with such novel configurations. Flight experiments were performed to validate the proposed methods. The manuscript is in the final stage before submission. We aim to submit the results to a major robotics journal (IEEE Transactions on Robotics or IEEE/ASME Transactions on Mechatronics) in a few weeks [2]. [1] B. Mu and P. Chirarattananon, "Universal Flying Objects: Modular Multirotor System for Flight of Rigid Objects," in IEEE Transactions on Robotics, vol. 36, no. 2, pp. 458-471, April 2020, doi: 10.1109/TRO.2019.2954679. [2] B. Mu, X. Cai, and P. Chirarattananon, "Trajectory Generation and Control of Underactuated Multirotor Robots with Tilted Propellers," under preparation for submission to IEEE Transactions on Robotics or IEEE/ASME Transactions on Mechatronics.

11274016.label: Major findings and research outcome
11274016.value: Major project objectives, namely the development of flight modules that can be incorporated to a rigid body payload to create a flying vehicle, have been completed. To this end, the prototypes, in the form of control and propelling modules, were designed and manufactured. The automated algorithm-based calibration method was devised. And a novel flight controller capable of dealing with a large range of uncertain system parameters was developed. Together, we have demonstrated a complete engineering solution that can be further scaled for commercialization. The main results outlined above were consolidated into one comprehensive paper published in IEEE Transactions on Robotics. Publication in the prestigious journal requires an entirely novel work that is considered impactful in the robotics community. Due to its competitiveness, the journal only publishes about 100 papers per year and is considered a gold standard for the field. During the project, we also trained one PhD student, who is now about to graduate after working on the project for almost four years. In addition to the published manuscript, the second part of the research focusing on a multirotor vehicle with tilted propellers has also produced promising results. This paper is also expected to be submitted and published in a high impact journal. This part of the research is no less significant than the results presented in the first publication, attributing to approximately half of the content in the thesis of the graduating student.

11274016.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11274016.value: A promising direction for further development has been identified and outlined above (the end of 5.3). That is the topic of dynamics and control of underactuated multirotor vehicles with unaligned propellers. This is motivated from one major simplifying assumption of the work that requires all propellers to be parallel as seen in conventional robots. The the propellers are not all aligned, the coupling between translational and rotational dynamics of the robot is increasingly sophisticated. To date, the problem has not been addressed, possibly owing to the complexity and the lack of motivation. We have started working on this topic and achieved satisfying results, with the findings being written up for submission in a very near future.

11274016.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11274016.value: In this research, we have developed Universal Flying Objects (UFOs)—a modular aerial robotic platform for transforming a rigid object into a multirotor robot. To achieve this, we designed and constructed flight modules, in the form of a control module and propelling modules that can be affixed to an object. The object, or payload, serves as the airframe of the vehicle. The modular design produces a highly versatile platform as it is reconfigurable by the addition or removal of flight modules, adjustment of the modules’ arrangement, or change of payloads. To facilitate the operation, we devised an automated calibration and flight control methods. When combined, stable flights are accomplished with minimal manual intervention or tuning required by a user.

11274516.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11274516.value: Vertical greenery systems (VGSs) are increasingly popular features of building façades all over the world. However, the fire hazards of VGSs have not yet been thoroughly studied. Many countries have neither fire safety codes nor standard fire tests specifically designed for VGSs. In particular, a fire scenario in which a window flame plume moves out of a room fire should be scientifically investigated in the context of VGSs. Plants and the associated combustible components of a VGS located near a window can be ignited easily. The heat, flames, toxic gases and particulate matter emitted would spread upward along the green façade. Burning leaves and branches in the VGS may fall and firebrands may blow to other locations, causing greater hazards. In addition, as an outdoor attachment, VGSs might easily catch fire from burning materials from a fire at another location or as a result of arson. The major aim of this project is to conduct a thorough investigation of the behaviour of VGSs in the above fire scenario. The fire behaviour of three VGSs – the panel system, the felt system and the container system – will be studied and compared. Three popular species of green plants – ivy (Hedera helix), Chinese evergreen (Aglaonema or ‘Lady Valentine’) and baby rubberplant (Peperomia obtusifolia) – will be investigated. Ignition of plants by a flame and their consequent burning will be affected by the moisture content, which varies with the plant species and irrigation conditions. The plants will be studied with three moisture contents: normal watering, no watering for 10 days and no watering for 20 days. The likelihood of igniting the plants and the accessories in the VGSs will be evaluated with a cone calorimeter. The heat and smoke emitted will be measured. The vertical upward fire spread over the green façade will then be examined using physical reduced-scale experiments. The results of the mathematical models of fire spread will be combined with the cone and the physical reduced-scale modelling experimental results to achieve an integrated understanding of the fire hazards of VGSs. Experiments will be carried out on a portion of a real-scale VGS to verify the phenomena observed in the scale modelling experiments and the predictions from the mathematical models. The results will be used to develop standard fire tests for the assessment of VGSs. Appropriate fire protection, fire-fighting and rescue strategies for buildings with VGSs can then be recommended.

11274516.label: Realisation of objectives
11274516.value: Vertical greenery systems (VGSs) are increasingly popular features of building façades all over the world. However, the fire hazards of VGSs have not yet been thoroughly studied. There are no detailed specifications of the fire safety objectives of green constructions in the updated building fire safety codes in many places such as Hong Kong. Fire hazard of exposing VGSs to a window plume was explored thoroughly and scientifically in this project. All four objectives listed in the proposal were achieved as following: Objective 1. To examine the heat and smoke emitted by burning three commonly used plant species at different moisture levels in vertical greenery systems using a cone calorimeter. Three plant species Hedera helix, Peperomia obtusifolia and Aglaonema are commonly used for vertical greenery systems (VGSs). These three species were studied in this project with different moisture contents (MC), and tested by a cone calorimeter. When the plants were fresh and green with high MC, no ignition was observed for all three species. Hedera helix was not able to ignite once MC was higher than 243 % under a heat flux of 50 kWm-2. Peperomia obtusifolia was not ignited for MC above 200 % under a heat flux of 20 kWm-2. Aglaonema commutatum ignition occurred once MC was below 316 % under a heat flux of 50 kWm-2. The transient heat release rate per unit area, the concentrations of carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide were measured. Cone calorimeter data on the time to ignition, peak heat release rate, total heat released, and peak carbon monoxide concentration were used to calculate three parameters of flashover propensity, total heat released and fractional effective dose. Analysis shows that plants with high MC were not even ignited under high heat flux. They were ignited only under low MC and so have a high risk of flashover. Thermal risk and smoke toxicity hazard also increase for dry plants. These findings demonstrate the importance of maintaining healthy live plants by regular watering to give adequate fire safety. Results measured from the cone calorimeter were used to develop a mathematical flame spread model in Objective 3. Objective 2. To study the fire hazards of green façades adjacent to a room with a flashover fire. The behaviour of part of a VGS at different moisture levels exposed to the window flame plume scenario was studied by scale modelling experiments first, and then by full-scale burning tests. Flashover was set by burning a small propanol pool fire with adequate fuel in a scale room model. The objective of scale modeling experiment is to identify the hazardous scenarios to be further explored by larger-scale tests. Window plume spread out except under high heat flux post-flashover room fire would act on the façade. The spread of heat and smoke in the façade were examined. Flame impingement would ignite the plants, with time to ignite depending on their MC. Two points on flame spread over VGS were identified and to be further justified by full-scale burning tests. Wet plants are not easy to be ignited. Dry plants can be ignited readily with flame spread. Results were also used to study flame spread modeling in Objective 3. Objective 3. To study fire spread along the green facade with plants with different moisture levels. Full-scale burning experiments on VGSs were carried out in Lanxi, Harbin, Heilongjiang, China. A portion of each of the three VGSs was designed by the Research Assistant recruited and constructed in summer 2018. The real-scale VGS was 7 m tall and used to study fire hazards of VGS with those three plants at different MC. Flame spread over plants in VGS were observed. The temperatures outside the VGS put above the fire room were measured. Ignition of plants by window plumes depends on the shape of the leaves and how fast water moisture evaporated from the plants. Plants have lower initial MC can be dried rapidly within a few hours even under natural environment. Therefore, fire hazard can be very serious for plants without appropriate watering to give adequate moisture. For small leaves plants with lower initial MC, continuous flame was observed upon ignition because of more leaves. Flame spread rapidly along both the horizontal and vertical directions. A thermal model was developed to study heat transfer through green façade. Results were applied to study annual cooling load reduction for different buildings and scenarios in Hong Kong. The approach was extended to give a simple mathematical model of flame spread over the green façade. A model was then developed based on the associated experimental studies on cone calorimeter, scale modeling and full-scale burning tests in the above tasks. Potential fire risk in underground green corridors was also studied. Numerical simulations with computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and physical scale modeling experiments were performed. Heat release rate data obtained from the cone calorimeter experiments for three plant species were conducted for a green wall. Results showed that a fire does not occur in underground corridors with fresh and live plants. However, fire risk increases gradually with drying out of plants. One approach was used to study convective heat transfer and smoke movement to adjacent buildings. Objective 4. To propose an appropriate testing method to evaluate the fire behaviour of vertical greenery systems. Vegetation grown along building façades provides fuel for the spread of fires. The direct action of a window flame plume from a post-flashover room fire is confirmed to ignite dry plants, planter boxes, foams and laminar layers of felt sheets. Heat, flame, smoke and hazardous chemicals generated from burning plants can spread to different parts of the building and to nearby areas. The heat and toxicity of the smoke can affect firefighters if they lack appropriate personal protection equipment. Based on the above study, the fire scenario due to window flame plume should be considered to work out appropriate regulations to assess the risks of green façade fires. Testing standard should be established by the Authority to complement the current specified requirements on green facades. Plant selection principles of VGS were discussed on plant characteristics. Plants were proposed to be ranked by their potential ignitability first. Modifications on current fire tests based on this study were suggested for testing VGS. As identified in this project, very wet plants with high MC are difficult to ignite. However, dry plants of VGS will be very hazardous. A more important point is to enhance fire safety management to ensure proper irrigation of VGS plants. Further, effects of integrating VGS to concrete wall was considered. Advanced approaches with an emphasis on sustainability are explored in conjunction with the development of new materials such as carbon nanotube that can be used in concrete.

11274516.label: Major findings and research outcome
11274516.value: The behaviour of VGSs in the fire scenario under window plume from a flashover fire was investigated. Three popular species of green plants for VGS – ivy (Hedera helix), Chinese evergreen (Aglaonema or ‘Lady Valentine’) and baby rubberplant (Peperomia obtusifolia) were evaluated. Ignition of plants by a flame and their consequent burning are affected by the moisture content, which varies with the plant species and irrigation conditions. The likelihood of igniting the plants were evaluated with a cone calorimeter. The vertical upward fire spread over the green façade was then examined using physical reduced-scale experiments. Experiments were carried out on a portion of a real-scale VGS to verify the phenomena observed in the scale modelling experiments and the predictions from the mathematical models. Window flame plume ejecting out from the opening would ignite dry plants easily, but not the wet plant. Flame would spread up rapidly along the VGS after igniting the dry plants. Vertical temperature profiles along the façade confirmed the observed flame spread. Vertical upward fire spread over the green façade was modeled first using the physical reduced-scale data. A mathematical model of fire spread was developed by the cone and the physical reduced-scale modelling experimental results to achieve an integrated understanding of the fire hazards of VGSs. Results on the mathematical models of fire hazard of façade fire were combined with CFD simulations on studying convective heat transfer and smoke movement to adjacent parts of the buildings. Flame spread over VGS due to window flame plume observed in this project experiments should be considered in developing standard fire tests for assessing VGSs. Appropriate fire protection, fire-fighting and rescue strategies for buildings with VGSs can then be worked out. Results had been published as 5 journal papers and 2 conference papers up to this moment. Major findings in this project are summarized: • Window flame plume from a post-flashover room fire would act on the VGS. Flame impingement would ignite the dry plants faster. This scenario is confirmed to be hazardous. • Wet plants with high MC are not easy to be ignited. Dry plants with low MC can be ignited readily with flame spread. • Irrigation is important to provide wet plants. However, watering plants might not be allowed in dry seasons. Fire safety management is needed to work out further research on irrigation.

11274516.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11274516.value: Vertical greenery systems (VGSs) are increasingly popular features of building façades all over the world. However, the fire hazards of VGSs have not yet been thoroughly studied. Basically, only the fire scenario in which a window flame plume moves out of a room fire was scientifically investigated in the context of VGSs in this project. Fundamental research on wind effects is strongly recommended. More full-scale burning tests on VGS with more plants are needed. As identified in this project, appropriate fire safety management has not yet been specified for buildings with VGSs. The window flame plume hazard scenario should be included. Integration with green concrete is proposed as fundamental study. Further development works on VGSs are proposed to apply research findings of this report:  Providing guidelines for authorities to evaluate the fire safety of new projects with VGSs.  Drafting fire regulations for VGSs by putting in the above typical fire scenarios.  Studying more on fire service installations, firefighting and rescue strategies for buildings with VGSs.  The heat and toxicity of the smoke would be hazardous to firefighters. Appropriate development work on training firefighters based on this study is required.

11274516.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11274516.value: The fire hazards of vertical greenery systems (VGSs) were thoroughly studied. A fire scenario in which a window flame plume moves out of a room fire was scientifically investigated. Three popular species of green plants – ivy (Hedera helix), Chinese evergreen (Aglaonema or ‘Lady Valentine’) and baby rubberplant (Peperomia obtusifolia) – were investigated. Ignition of plants by a flame and their consequent burning will be affected by the moisture content, which varies with the plant species and irrigation conditions. The likelihood of igniting the plants in the VGSs were evaluated first with a cone calorimeter. The vertical upward fire spread over the VGS was then examined using physical reduced-scale experiments. A mathematical model of fire spread was developed by combining with the cone and the physical reduced-scale modelling experimental results. Experiments were carried out on a portion of a real-scale VGS to verify the phenomena observed in the scale modelling experiments and the predictions from the mathematical models. The results were used to develop standard fire tests for the assessment of VGSs. Appropriate fire protection, fire safety management on keeping plants wet with appropriate irrigation, firefighting and rescue strategies for buildings with VGSs were then recommended.

11274616.label: Realisation of objectives
11274616.value: The project has successfully completed with all the objectives been addressed. The major achievements of the project were summarized in this final report. Following listed activities and achievements in detail. 1. Development of Upy-based supramolecular polymers and nanocomposite. We have successfully synthesized a couple of low-molecular-weight polymers/oligomers composed of UPy motifs. Either bi-functional or multi-functional UPy motifs could be incorporated into the final synthesized polymers. Polymers with polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) backbone with bi-functional, tri-functional or multiple UPy motifs have been developed, which are further used for the development of composites for antifouling applications. Figure 1a illustrated a typical synthetic route for a three-arm oligomer (denoted as (UP)3T) with both UPy motifs and PDMS fragments. The UPy motifs could form dimers and facilitate the assembly of the oligomer into large-scale network. Further AFM and TEM imaging showed that the UPy dimers will form nanoscale stackings during the assembly of the oligomers, leading a novel supramolecular composite. The PDMS fragments are expected to provide hydrophobicity and antifouling properties, and the UPy motifs are expected to provide self-healing properties due to the hydrogen-bonded dimerization. The synthesis of the (UP)3T and its application in self-healable nanocomposites for coating related applications have been published in Angew. Chem. Int. Ed., 2018, 11242-11246 (Featured as VIP Paper), and Science Advances, 2019, 5, eaaw5643, for which the PI served as the corresponding author. Besides the polymer synthesis, we also successfully grafted the UPy-tethered polymers onto silica nanoparticles for functionalization. The modified silica nanoparticles could assemble with the UPy-tethered polymers to form polymer nanocomposite. 2. Study on the surface slipperiness, mechanical durability and healing process of the Upy-based supramolecular nanocomposites. The nanoscale domains of the UPy dimers and dimer stackings would reinforce the mechanics of the composite. The measured Young’s modulus of the composite films is 47.39 MPa by tensile testing, storage modulus approximately 151.4 MPa by dynamic thermomechanical analysis, respectively. The nanocomposites are damage-healable and the cut damage could be fully healed when the sample is heated at 70°C for 12 hours in air, due to the reversible association and dissociation of UPy motifs. Surprisingly, the healing procedure could be accelerated when the sample is put in high humidity environment or under water. Regarding the performance on healing time and the mechanical strength, our sample is outstanding within reported damage-healable supramolecular silicones. Further study showed that water molecules play a key role in the accelerated procedure of damage-healing. Water molecules could penetrate the gas-permeable PDMS moieties and facilitate the dissociation of the UPy dimers and dimer stackings, leading to the reduced glass transition temperature and thus the damage-healing procedure. The developed nanocomposite films are hydrophobic due to the existence of the PDMS backbone. Water contact angle on the nanocomposite was around 100 degree. Moreover, the nanocomposites show low contact angle hysteresis to a range of oils such as hexadecane, ethanol and grape seed oils. This is because the high poor solubility PDMS chains is those non-polar liquid would lead to immiscibility of the probing liquid to polymer network. the high crosslinking density contributed from the UPy dimers would further prevent the penetration of oil liquids and thus wetting of them. Furthermore, the composites could be casted onto diverse surfaces and present both damage-healing ability and very high shear strength, making them extremely useful for coating related applications. For example, when casted onto glass slides, copper foil and aluminum, the measured shear strength could be ~31 MPa, 31 MPa and ~20 MPa, respectively. This is because the dissociated UPy motifs at the coating/substrate interface would provide abundant hydrogen bond to facilitate the bonding, and the high mechanical strength of the coating would also contribute to the high shear stability of the coating. 3. Investigation for antibiofouling properties of the developed supramolecular nanocomposites. The antibiofouling performances were evaluated by using typical biomolecules and bacterial strains. Specifically, the BSA proteins, E. coli and P. aeruginosa have been used in this project. The prime nanocomposite samples actually show certain adhesion to the tested proteins and bacteria strains, probably due to the existence of the dissociated UPy motifs at the interface. As addressed previously, water could facilitate the dissociation of the UPy dimers, and the dissociated UPy motifs could provide additional binding sites to those biomolecules and cells. To improve the antibiofouling performance of the coating, a small amount of silicone oils were added to the precursor of the coating. The silicone oils show high affinity to the PDMS backbone and could slightly swell the developed coating. It is demonstrated that a large amount of silicone oils would lead to phase separation from the nanocomposite because the UPy-riched domains show poor solubility to silicone oils. And the longer chain (high molecular weight) of PDMS backbone would improve the incorporation ability to silicone oils. After systematic study, silicone oils with less than 10% weighting percentage, and PDMS backbone with molecular weight of 3000 are selected for best antifouling performances. The Young’s modulus of the prepared sample is 2.15 MPa by tensile testing, and 7.53 MPa by probe nanoindentation. Comparing to the prime sample (3.67 MPa and 11.8 MPa respectively), the addition of silicone oils would reduce the mechanical strength according. While the addition of silicone oils would facilitate the damage healing procedure, the sample could be healed within 30 hour when heating at 70°C and 5 min when heating at 90°C, respectively. The prepared sample has smooth surface topography. Droplets contained proteins or bacteria cell would slide easily without any pinning, minimum fouling was observed on the sample surface after sliding. When the sample was immersed in bacteria medium for 24-72 h incubation, bacteria cells show minimum adhesion for the whole period. When there is damage cut applied to the sample, slight staining was found at the cut area caused by bacteria cells. Indeed, the bacteria staining is subject to the recovery of the damaged area. Based on our results, it is found that for film with 200 micron thickness, the scratch or cut gap smaller than 100 micron, the incorporated silicone oils could refill the gap and prevent the bacteria fouling even though the full recovery take longer time. In summary, we have successfully completed the objectives proposed in the project, and a couple of research articles have been published which the PI is the corresponding author, including Angew. Chem. Int. Ed., Science Advances and ACS Nano. Furthermore, an invited review entitled of “Emerging Applications of Bioinspired Slippery Surfaces in Biomedical Fields” was contributed by the PI’s group and published at Chemistry - A European Journal, and featured as Frontispiece.

11274616.label: Major findings and research outcome
11274616.value: 1. We have developed a couple of UPy-based supramolecular polymers that could assembly into large-scale network. The UPy motifs could form dimers and dimers stackings which would undergo multiphase separation within the supramolecular network to form semi-crystalline domains. The UPy-based supramolecular polymers could also be grafted onto silica nanoparticles to help develop multifunctional nanocomposites. 2. The as prepared supramolecular nanocomposites show high mechanical strength, high binding ability to various substrate and intrinsic damage-healing ability. Particularly, the damage-healing ability could be enhanced by putting the sample in humid air or underwater for which water could facilitate the reversible dissociation and association of the UPy dimers. The nanocomposite is also hydrophobic, and shows low contact angle hysteresis to a range of oils including hexadecane, ethanol and grape seed oils. 3. The antibiofouling performance the nanocomposite would be largely improved by adding a small amount of silicones. Using PDMS fragment of larger molecular weight could further enhance the surface slipperiness, reduce damage-recovery time and help reduce the adhesion to biofoulants such as proteins and bacteria. 11274616.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11274616.value: With the knowledge and skills gained in this project, we have successfully developed a couple of supramolecular polymers that could assembly into bulk films and membranes. Their performances including liquid-repellency, damage-healing, shear stability are outstanding, making them excellent candidates for coating related applications. Further research focused on supramolecular coating/adhesive is ongoing. Furthermore, through the project, we have successfully developed protocols on the polymer synthesis and nanoparticle fabrication, gained skills and knowledge on advanced characterization methods particularly the AFM mapping on adhesion forces and modulus, all of which would form a solid and fundamental basis for the PI’s lab on the material innovation as well as on the exploration of other cutting-edge projects.

11274616.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11274616.value: We have developed a couple of supramolecular polymers which could assemble into large-scale network through hydrogen bonding. The hydrogen bonding motifs would form large aggregates which would further undergo multiphase separation within the polymer matrix, leading to semicrystalline nanodomains. Such unique assembly status of the hydrogen bonding motifs would improve the mechanical performances of the nanocomposites. When applied as a coating, the nanocomposites show high mechanical strength, high shear strength, readily oil sliding and intrinsic damage-healing ability. The supramolecular polymers could be grafted onto nanoparticles to develop multifunctional nanocomposites. Furthermore, by incorporating silicone oils into the nanocomposites, the surface slipperiness and antibiofouling properties could be significantly improved.

11274916.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11274916.value: The output regulation problem, also called the servomechanism problem, is to design a feedback control law for the system such that asymptotic tracking for a class of reference inputs and disturbance rejection for a class of external disturbances can be achieved while the stability of the closed-loop system can be maintained. One of the most important features of output regulation is that both reference inputs and external disturbances do not need to be known exactly. Arising from practical control problems in engineering, such as trajectory tracking of mobile robots, disturbance rejection in airplane taking-off and landing, and vibration suppression of high speed trains, the output regulation problem has attracted extensive attention for scientific research for several decades. Due to information collection, transmission, and processing, time-delay is ubiquitous in practical systems. It is well understood that a very small time-delay may devastate the stability of a well-designed control system. However, due to the complexity of involving time-delay in analysis and synthesis, most of existing results on output regulation focus on systems without time-delay. More recently, some efforts are devoted to addressing the output regulation problem for linear time-delay systems. However, they only consider linear systems with known and constant time-delays, which are not the case for many engineering systems in practice. The objective of this project is to investigate several fundamental problems in output regulation of linear and nonlinear time-delay systems in more practical settings. We aim to explore both feedforward design and internal model design control methodologies and develop novel approaches for output regulation of time-delay systems. In particular, we will investigate controller design for linear systems with time-varying delays, linear systems with time-varying delays and model uncertainties, linear systems with unknown time-delays and model uncertainties, and a class of nonlinear systems with time-delays. The theoretical results will also be applied to a practical engineering problem in trajectory tracking and disturbance rejection of mobile robots. Based on deep exploration of the internal model principle for time-delay systems, a general framework for handling the robust output regulation problem for time-delay systems will be established. The success of this research project will enable us to address a number of critical and fundamental problems in trajectory tracking control and disturbance rejection control of practical systems. The anticipated theoretic results will expand the applications of output regulation in more practical situations. This project is thus of both significant academic interest and practical importance. 輸出調節問題，也被稱為伺服控制問題，其目的是設計反饋控制律使得系統的漸近跟蹤問題和擾動抑制問題得以解決同時能夠保持閉環系統的穩定性。輸出調節問題的典型特點是不需要參考輸入和外部擾動的信息是精確已知。輸出調節問題源於實際工程領域，例如移動機器人的軌跡跟蹤，飛機起降時的擾動抑制，高鐵行駛過程中的振動控制等等。正因為其如此廣泛的應用前景，輸出調節問題在過去的幾十年裡得到了大量的關注與研究。 時滯現象在實際系統中無處不在，例如信息的採集、傳遞和處理。眾所周知，很小的時滯都可能破壞系統的穩定性。然而，在實際系統的分析及設計中考慮時滯會使問題變得十分複雜。正因如此，現有的大部分關於輸出調節的研究結果是針對非時滯系統。直到最近，研究者們才開始關注時滯系統的輸出調節問題並得到了一些初步的結果。這些結果的研究對象主要是時滯已知的線性系統。然而在實際工程領域的被控系統中時滯往往是未知的。 此項目的主要目標是研究線性及非線性時滯系統輸出調節中的基本問題。我們將設計前饋控制策略和內模控制策略，並且研發新穎的控制策略以解決時滯系統的輸出調節問題。具體來講，本項目將分別研究含時變時滯的線性系統，含時變時滯並帶有模型不確定的線性系統，含未知時滯並帶有模型不確定性的線性系統，和一類含時滯的非線性系統。並且，這些理論研究的結果將用於解決移動機器人的軌跡跟蹤問題。 基於對解決時滯系統內模原理的深入探索，本項目將建立一個廣義的理論框架用於處理時滯系統的魯棒輸出調節問題。此項目的成功實施將有助於解決實際系統軌跡跟蹤任務中的一些難題。並且，此項目預期得到的結果將進一步豐富現有的輸出調節理論並擴展其在實際工程控制中的應用。綜上所述，本項目具有重要的理論價值及應用價值。

11274916.label: Major findings and research outcome
11274916.value: Several fundamental problems in output regulation of linear and nonlinear systems with time-delays in more practical settings have been investigated. In particular, we designed controllers for linear systems with time-varying delays, linear systems with unknown time-delays and model uncertainties, and a class of nonlinear systems subject to external disturbances. The output consensus problem, which can be viewed as a special case of the output regulation problem, for nonlinear uncertain multi-agent systems with time-varying communication delays has been considered. Output consensus of all systems is achieved with some robustness not only to heterogeneous dynamics with uncertainties but also to unreliable network communication in terms of network connectivity and communication delays. In particular, we allow the presence of time-varying communication delays in network. A distributed dynamic output feedback control law is designed by the internal model control strategy. The proposed control approach offers great flexibility to incorporate the internal model approach. The result has been published by the top-tier journal in the area. We have also solved some engineering problems such as target enclosing and trajectory tracking for a mobile robot subject to a class of disturbances, adaptive nonlinear ship tracking control problem and adaptive tracking control of uncertain Euler-Lagrange systems subject to external disturbances. These studies enable us to answer a number of critical and fundamental questions in trajectory tracking and disturbance rejection of practical control systems. These results have also been published in the top-tier journals in the area. Then we further extended our research to unbounded delays. A low gain approach is proposed for consensus of linear multi-agent systems with distributed infinite transmission delays. Some semi-global stabilisation results are established for linear systems with distributed infinite input delays and actuator saturations. The results from this project expand the applications of single and multi-agent systems in more practical situations and thus considerably narrow the gaps between theories and applications.

11274916.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11274916.value: A number of results have been obtained and published on different but related control problems for linear and nonlinear systems with time delays and model uncertainties, or external disturbances. Several engineering problems have also been studied. During this process, many intriguing problems in delayed systems are identified. For example, when we investigated systems with unbounded delays, we found that there is no systematic ways to solve several fundamental control problems. However, applications of systems with unbounded delays arise in many fields including biology, mechanics, and social science. Thus, it deserves more attention. It has been one of our recent interests and could be one of the future research focuses.

11274916.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11274916.value: Several fundamental problems on control of linear and nonlinear systems with time-delays and model uncertainties, or external disturbances have been studied. Time-delay exists in many practical control systems and a very small time-delay may devastate the stability of a well-designed control system. In this project, several fundamental control problems including stabilisation and output regulation problems have been addressed. A number of critical issues, including time-varying delays, unknown delays and unbounded delays, have been tackled in this project. The developed techniques and approaches will considerably narrow the existing technical gaps in control of single and multiple linear and nonlinear systems with time-delays and enhance their control performance in real life applications. The expected outcomes of this project will provide a wider scope of applications for dynamic control systems under more practical situations.

11275216.label: Project Objectives
11275216.value: Design and fabricate structured surfaces with 1D or 2D gradient in structural morphology. Optimum morphology that promotes the vectoring and confinement of droplets to the boiling region, suppresses vigorous shape fluctuation and thermal Marangoni flow, and facilitates the alleviation of local hotspots will be designed. Control surfaces with homogeneous post arrays will be fabricated for comparison. Investigate droplet dynamics on as-proposed surfaces at high temperature. We will study the droplet vectoring and boiling dynamics under different temperatures. Emphasis will be placed on the characterization of how the presence of Janus thermal state enhances the droplet motion and subsequent stabilization for fast boiling off. The effect of substrate inclination on the droplet motion will also be investigated. Develop analytical models to elucidate the effect of surface topography on the thermal states. The efficacy of our model will be validated using our experimental results. Characterize the heat transfer performances. We will compare the heat transfer coefficient of a Janus thermal state droplet on the gradient surface with that of the control surface under the condition of identical substrate temperature. We will measure the heat flux of the proposed surface based on droplet chains produced by the spray.

11275216.label: Realisation of objectives
11275216.value: The objectives have been fully addressed and several important results have been achieved with publications in leading journals such as Nature Physics, Nature Communications and Science Advances. The insights learned from this project will lay down important foundation for the rational design of effective energy system. 1: We designed and fabricated structured surfaces with 1D or 2D gradient in structural morphology that promotes the vectoring and confinement of droplets to the boiling region, suppresses vigorous shape fluctuation and thermal Marangoni flow, and facilitates the alleviation of local hotspots. Control surfaces with homogeneous post arrays were also fabricated for comparison. We investigated droplet dynamics on and characterized the droplet vectoring and boiling dynamics under different temperatures. 2: We studied the droplet vectoring and boiling dynamics under different temperatures. To gain more detailed insights into the droplet transport dynamics, we also compared the flow fields inside Leidenfrost droplets using Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV). Regardless of different velocities and directions on various planar ratchets, Leidenfrost droplets always present the asymmetric and preferential rotating circulation cell, following the directions of their propagation. Moreover, the occurrence of the maximum velocity field at the liquid/vapor interface in both cases strongly suggests that the different droplet dynamics arise from the varying viscous shear induced by the asymmetric vapor flow. 3. We also developed analytical models to elucidate the effect of surface topography on the thermal states. Our model was also substantiated by experimental measurements on planar ratchets with diverse first-order and second-order geometries. 4. We also compared the heat transfer coefficient of a Janus thermal state droplet on the gradient surface with that of the control surface under the condition of identical substrate temperature. We also measured the heat flux of the proposed surface based on droplet chains produced by the spray.

11275216.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11275216.value: This project is focused on the fundamental understanding and controlling of Janus droplet at high temperatures for efficient heat transfer. Since our ability to remove or harness thermal energy is often contingent on water droplet as a mediator, the fundamental understanding of droplet dynamics at high temperatures is of critical importance. The project has resulted in new insights for the development of new materials, devices, and systems for efficient thermal energy conversion, transport and utilization, as well as cultivating several young scholars.

11275916.label: Project Objectives
11275916.value: To establish the cost-effective chemical vapor deposition to obtain high-quality ternary In2xGa2−2xO3 nanowires with the controlled composition, crystallinity, dimension, surface morphology and electrical properties. To fabricate highly efficient memristive or resistive random-access memory devices on glass substrates based on the single In2xGa2−2xO3 nanowire as the active channels and transparent conductive metal-oxide thin films as the electrodes. To evaluate the corresponding key memristive device performance metrics in the switching speed, power density, uniformity, endurance and retention. All these valuable information is essential to further optimize the nanowire stoichiometry, electrode composition, device dimension and structure for the enhanced memory performance and reliability. To construct the large-scale In2xGa2−2xO3-nanowire-based memory device arrays on transparent and flexible substrates. The ultimate target is to achieve the corresponding device performance limits to establish relevant design guidelines of nanowires-based memory devices, to go beyond the conventional thin film technologies, for the future memory circuit implementation.

11275916.value: 近年來，由於消費者對增強的設備性能和更好的移動體驗的要求，移動設備技術已取得了突飛猛進的發展，推動了更高性能和更小尺寸的存儲芯片的發展。然而，通過簡單地縮小存儲單元以獲得更快的編程速度和更低的功耗，是不足以提供滿足消費者需求的增強型移動體驗。此外，由於在消費電子產品中觸屏設備的日益滲透，小型化的個人電子設備的出現將引起對緊湊型透明柔性系統的探索。就這一點而言，迄今為止大量的工作都集中在透明柔性憶阻器（電阻隨機存取存儲器，RRAM）的開發，即通過使用金屬氧化物的薄膜作為有源溝道材料，透明導電氧化物（TCO）作為電極的下一代存儲器技術。雖然所獲得的開關特性遠遠好於其它競爭技術，但由於所有這些薄膜元件仍然需要光刻做圖案定義，獲得超出光刻尺寸的单体电芯對於可持續的縮小尺寸將是非常難以實現的。同時，由於納米技術的出現，高度結晶的金屬氧化物納米材料，諸如納米線（NWs）已經被用作有前途的透明柔性記憶器件的功能塊，這得益于其非常小的尺寸、優良的機械可塑性、完善划算的合成方案和易於調製的材料性能，更重要的是可以充分地開發設備的縮小潛能。例如，這些單晶的納米線可以容易地生長在晶格失配甚至無定形的基板上，然後可以將納米線轉移到透明柔性的基板上用作後續的器件製造。另外，與傳統的無定形或多晶系薄膜器件相比，由於納米線較少的晶界對切換性能產生較小的負面影響，納米線的這種晶體性質可以顯著改善由其製造的憶阻器件的性能。即便如此，在控制納米線的合成，了解它們的基本性質，將這些高品質的納米線整合到透明柔性的RRAM設備中，并評估其相應的性能和可靠性，這些過程中仍然充滿許多顯著的挑戰。在本提案中，我們集中于將三元的In2xGa2−2xO3納米線作為有源器件的通道，這歸功於其優良的結晶度和化學、電和熱穩定性，以及優良的電阻開關性能，這些優點已在與其配置相對應的薄膜器件中得到了證明。這項工作的目標是通過進一步對納米線通道的化學計量和尺寸、電極構成、器件結構以及存儲器操作方案的進一步優化，來評估其性能極限。最後，我們為以後的記憶電路的實現計劃建立一個基於金屬氧化物納米線相關的設計指導，以超越傳統的薄膜技術。

11275916.label: Realisation of objectives
11275916.value: In this project, we have successfully accomplished all the objectives with 100% of completion. To be specific, we have achieved a new synthesis technique, known as solid-source chemical vapor deposition, to synthesize single-crystalline ternary In2xGa2−2xO3 nanowires and quaternary InGaZnO (NWs) controlled composition, crystallinity, dimension, surface morphology and electrical properties (Objective 1). For example, InGaZnO NWs with different chemical stoichiometry were grown on the surface of Si/SiO2 substrates by the ambient-pressure CVD method. The substrates were first deposited with a thin layer of Au catalyst film by thermal evaporation. For the growth of InGaZnO NWs, a varied mass of Ga granules, In granules, zinc and graphite powder were used as the precursor source. During the growth, the source was placed at the sealed end of a quartz tube (10 cm in length and 1 cm in diameter) while the substrate, predeposited with the catalyst, was positioned 2 cm away from the source. This quartz tube was then put in the center of a large quartz tube (1 inch in diameter) within the single-zone horizontal tube furnace. Next, the set-up was heated up to 990 °C in 20 min and held for 7 min with the flow rate of gas mixture (10 vol.% O2 + 90 vol.% Ar) and Ar maintained at 20 and 80 sccm, respectively. When the growth was done, the system was naturally cooled to the room temperature. This growth process was then repeated twice (i.e., 2nd and 3rd growth runs) with fresh substrates but using the same precursor source. It is noted that the 3rd growth was held at 990 °C for 10 min. Interestingly, pure ZnO and In doped ZnO NWs were collected for the first two growth runs, respectively, while InGaZnO NWs with different chemical stoichiometry could be reliably obtained after the 3rd growth run. In this case, we employed this growth sequence to controllably fabricate the InGaZnO NWs. Simply by varying the mass of Ga source, different NW composition could be obtained. Importantly, the periodic dark-bright layered structures perpendicular to the NW radial direction are obviously witnessed in the high-resolution transmission electron microscopy images in which the dark contrast corresponds to the InO2- layers and the bright contrast correlates with the GaO(ZnO)3+ blocks. The corresponding diffraction spots appeared in a distinctive layered superlattice structure are as well found in the selected area electron diffraction pattern. All these results explicitly elucidate the formation of layered superlattice structures, inducing quasi-2D electron gases (quasi-2DEG), of InGaZnO NWs. Once the optimal NW growth was obtained, the NWs were then fabricated into highly-dense parallel NW arrays by well-developed contact printing method for the construction of memory devices on different substrates (e.g. mechanically flexible, transparent or stretchable substrates) in order to study their device performance (Objective 2). Technically, the device operation mechanism could be understood in terms of the oxygen adsorption–induced charge trapping and subsequent electrically or optically induced charge release are highlighted. The quasi-2DEG devices presented here changed its conductance by regulating the number of adsorbed oxygen according to the applied electric and light pulse. This shows the potential of building artificial neuromorphic devices using such strongly electron-correlated quasi-2DEG superlattice NWs. When the devices were fabricated on flexible polyimide substrates, they still exhibited impressive device characteristics. To be specific, the flexible quasi-2DEG devices could implement a human memory model. While an intensive stimulation (e.g. 1 mW/cm2, 10 s light pulse) was applied onto the NWs, the giant light-to-dark current ratio of ~5E3 was observed. With the aim to minimize the influence of read voltage on the charge retention, a small read voltage of 10 mV was used in the charge retention measurement. The retention loss in the quasi-2DEG photonic synapses bears many similarities to the memory loss in biological systems. The fitting result indicated that the current decay process accords well with the Kohlrausch stretched exponential function. The value of lifetime was fitted to be ∼1.3E4 s, suggesting a good nonvolatile charge retention characteristic, being better than those of the recently reported ITO/Nb:SrTiO3 Schottky junction synaptic memristors and the native oxide–inspired InSe synaptic memory devices (retention time ~1E4 s). On the other hand, the multibit data storage capability of NWs is also evaluated (Objective 3). It is found that when the quasi-2DEG synapse was exposed to successive stimuli (e.g. light pulses in 0.05 mW/cm2, 10 ms at intervals of 0.5 s), they would lead to a progressive output current increase controlled by the number of pulses. This progressive increase signified the direct writing of surface states onto the quasi-2DEG NW surface and the continuous injection of electrons into the superlattice NW core. This way, the memory function with 400 distinct programmable states could be successfully demonstrated, which was equivalent to a data storage ability over 8 bits (i.e., 256 programmable states). This observation was akin to a well-studied posttetanic potentiation, in which if many stimuli follow closely one after another, the synaptic transmission would gradually grow with the increasing number of stimuli. In this manner, the existing biological synaptic facilitation model that describes the transmitter release dynamics during repetitive stimulation could be used to predict or distinguish these conductance states (or synaptic weights) of the quasi-2DEG synapses. Since the quasi-2DEG photonic synapses are capable of high-performance light detection (i.e. excellent ultra-violet (UV) photodetector as demonstrated in our previous works (ACS Nano, 13, 12042-12051, 2019), brain-like information processing and multibit-level data storage, all these functionalities can be combined together and implemented into device arrays as human visual systems (Objective 4). In this case, to further shed light on the functionality and scalability of these devices, an artificial visual system, consisting of a 6 × 5 pixel array (i.e., total 30 devices), was fabricated to record the information of the applied stimuli (e.g. patterned light). As an individual pixel has a feature size of 100 um in our artificial visual system, a pixel density of 254 pixels per inch is achieved. Such high pixel density makes our quasi-2DEG artificial visual system able to recognize very tiny objects. This pixel size is substantially smaller than those of previously reported artificial visual systems, such as the pixel size of 250 um in two-terminal MoOx optoelectronic resistive random access memory arrays and the pixel size of about millimeter level in artificial flexible visual memory system using UV-motivated memristors. For instance, a human hair with diameter around 80 um was used to pattern light. This way, only devices exposed under the patterned light could be triggered. After removing the light, a clear hair-shaped pattern could be observed from the output current mapping that read directly from the quasi-2DEG visual system. This system not only can detect optical patterns but also can store them for later read out. After powering off the devices for 1 hour, the memory arrays could still retain the hair-shaped pattern with little attenuation, demonstrating the capability of imaging, data processing, and memorizing here. A higher pixel density can be used to distinguish more sophisticated patterns in the future. In summary, we have achieved to assess the corresponding device performance limits to establish relevant design guidelines of nanowires-based memory devices, to go beyond the conventional thin film technologies, for the future memory circuit implementation.

11275916.label: Major findings and research outcome
11275916.value: In this project, there are several key findings, which lead to 16 high-impact journal publications (1 Science Advances, 1 Advanced Materials, 4 Nano Research, etc) as well as 9 invited presentations at different international conferences. In specific, as reported in Nano Research 2018, utilizing in-situ Ga alloying, highly crystalline, uniform, and thin In2xGa2−2xO3 nanowires (NWs) with diameters down to 30 nm were successfully prepared via ambient-pressure CVD. Introducing an optimal amount of Ga (10 at.%) into the In2O3 lattice was found to effectively enhance the crystal quality and reduce the number of oxygen vacancies in the NWs. When configured into global back-gated NW field-effect transistors, the optimized In1.8Ga0.2O3 NWs exhibit significantly enhanced electron mobility reaching up to 750 cm2·V–1·s–1 as compared with that of the pure In2O3 NW, which can be attributed to the reduction in the number of oxygen vacancies and ionized impurity scattering centers. Highly ordered NW parallel arrayed devices were also fabricated to demonstrate the versatility and potency of these NWs for next-generation electronic devices. At the same time, as reported in Science Advances 2020, we propose and demonstrate the quasi-two-dimensional electron gas (quasi-2DEG) memory devices based on InGaZnO superlattice NW arrays using an unreported device operation concept by combining the oxygen adsorption-desorption kinetics on the NW surface and the strong carrier quantum-confinement effects in the superlattice core. These quasi-2DEG devices could process information in an in-memory computing approach with an ultralow energy consumption down to subfemtojoule per synaptic event. During the programming process, the electrons can efficiently transfer into superlattice NW cores, leading to the storage of localized electrons in multiple quantum wells, which results in the persistent charge retention and the multibit-level memory capability. By regulating the number of adsorbed oxygen or trapped electrons through the applied light pulse, resembling the Ca2+ ions flux and neurotransmitter release dynamics in biological synapses, we can achieve a truly brain-like cognitive system (i.e. mechanically flexible device arrays) to perform data-intensive tasks such as orientation selectivity and image memorizing. All these results can evidently provide a promising device scheme to build artificial neuromorphic systems using quasi-2DEG in future memory applications of bionic devices, electronic eyes, etc. In summary, all these major findings are significant, which would bring forward the deployment of complex metal oxide NW memory devices, to go beyond the conventional thin film technologies, for the future memory circuit implementation.

11275916.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11275916.value: Although there are many significant findings produced from this work, there are still several major areas required for the further study of these mechanically flexible metal oxide NW memory devices. For example, as the device operation mechanism is based on the oxygen adsorption–induced charge trapping and subsequent electrically or optically induced charge release, the effective surface area of nanowire channels would play a major role in the device performance. In this case, it is essential to understand the device characteristics as a function of different NW diameters. Another one is to further explore the integration of these flexible nanowire devices into the artificial visual systems. Since these flexible devices can be attached onto any curved surface, they can then be attached onto a semi-hemispherical object to mimic human eyes. Particularly, the device size, such as the channel length and electrode dimension, will be reduced to yield a higher pixel density for the device arrays such that these flexible devices can be used to distinguish more sophisticated patterns. All these further works would push forward the substantial technological development of metal oxide NW memory device arrays for practical utilizations.

11275916.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11275916.value: In the past decade, as demanded by consumers aiming for enhanced device performance and better mobile experience, the mobile device technology has been progressed at unbelievably fast pace, driving the memory chips with higher performance and smaller form factor. Nevertheless, by simply down-scaling the memory cells with the faster programming speed and lower power consumption are not enough to provide the improved mobile experience that consumers need. Fortunately, the advent of nanotechnology has facilitated unique properties of semiconducting nanowires contributing ideal active materials for the memory devices, even for mechanically flexible platforms. In this project, we have successfully developed a hybrid and low-cost approach utilizing the bottom-up high-performance multifunctional In and Ga based metal oxide nanowire arrays with the conventional top-down device fabrication processes to achieve large-scale, heterogeneously integrated nanowire memory circuitry. For example, the nanowire devices exhibit the excellent crystallinity in the device channel and chemical, electrical and thermal stability, as well as the superior resistive switching performance as demonstrated in artificial neuromorphic devices configured with their thin-film counterparts. Ultimately, we established a versatile and powerful technology platform to realize the mechanically flexible memory device arrays for practical utilization.

11276116.label: Project Objectives
11276116.value: To characterize the seasonal composition and diversity of the fungal populations of air, surfaces and occupants’ skins in residences of Hong Kong To determine the potential correlations within and between the bacterial and fungal total and active populations in residences over time

11276116.label: Realisation of objectives
11276116.value: One of the main objectives of this project is to investigate the fungal populations that are present in the indoor built environment over seasons and to understand their relationships with the bacterial populations. Another key objective is to investigate the microbial populations that are metabolically active. Both objectives in this proposal have been successfully achieved. Specifically, in Objective 1, we elucidated the seasonal dynamics, diversity, transferability between air, surface and occupant skin, and city-scale transport of fungi in mechanically and naturally ventilated built environments. Furthermore, the cross-domain relationships, and the similarities and differences between bacteria and fungi in air, surface and occupant skin were determined. We further applied the Sloan neutral model and determined that stochastic forces such as passive dispersal and ecological drift were key to the assembly of the occupant skin fungal populations, which have important implications to the built environment microbiome. In addition to detecting the presence of microbial populations, it is also important to determine their metabolic status. Due to the low density of microbial populations in the built environment, capturing sufficient quantity and quality of total RNA to evaluate metabolic activity is inherently challenging. As part of Objective 2, we first conducted an extensive benchmarking and comparison of different methods to analyze total RNA in built environment samples. After establishing the methods, we applied it to study the active microbial populations in naturally and mechanically ventilated built environments. We found that microbial members that were low in abundance tended to exhibit disproportionately high metabolic activity. This observation was consistently observed in different indoor environments and over seasons, suggesting that only a restricted group of taxa can survive and thrive in the oligotrophic and regulated indoor conditions. Overall, through this study, we have gained insights into the total and active built environment microbiomes, and such knowledge enhances our understanding on occupants’ microbial exposure. The findings have important implications for safeguarding occupants’ health. As part of the education plan of this study, we have trained a number of undergraduate students on microbiology and molecular techniques, and the importance of studying the built environment microbiome.

11276116.label: Major findings and research outcome
11276116.value: The results from this project have been published in a number of high-impact journals (Part C). The goal of Objective 1 is to characterize the seasonal fungal communities that are in air and on surfaces and occupants’ skins in naturally or mechanically ventilated residences in Hong Kong. As reported in Tong et al. (2017), we found using amplicon sequencing of the ITS1 region of samples collected from 19 residences over four seasons that the fungal members in the indoor environment were mostly sourced from skin and environment, and surfaces were strongly influenced by touch frequency. We provided evidence that fungal members can be transferred bi-directionally between surfaces and skins but transfer between surface or skin and air are weaker. In Tong et al. (2017), we also reported the correlations between bacterial and fungal populations, which is part of the goal of Objective 2. Interestingly, the cross-domain analysis between bacteria and fungi revealed strong positive correlations in diversity and composition, suggesting that the two communities are modulated in a coordinated manner. In order to further understand the dynamics of the skin fungal communities over seasons, we reported in Tong et al. (2019) that intrapersonal variation increased over time. In particular, stochastic assembly processes such as passive dispersal and ecological drift were the main drivers. Despite the presence of stochastically distributed members, well-adapted members were also important as shown by co-association networks. Taken together, the dynamic nature of occupant skin fungal communities can contribute to the variations observed in the built environment. The goal of Objective 2 is to investigate the microbial members in the indoor environment that are metabolically active, which requires examining total RNA and is inherently challenging due to low density of biomass in the samples. To facilitate the investigation, we first conducted an extensive benchmarking of different methods as reported in Gomez-Silvan et al. (2018). After establishing a robust method, we applied it to investigate the microbial members that were active in residential environment. We found that only a fraction of the taxa present were considered metabolically active. Further investigation in mechanically ventilated environments over four seasons revealed that taxa low in abundance consistently had a disproportionately higher metabolic activity (Zhou et al., in submission). Overall, the findings from this project enhanced our fundamental understanding of the microbial members that are not only present but also active in the built environment, which have important public health implications.

11276116.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11276116.value: In light of the on-going COVID-19 pandemic, the microorganisms that are present in the built environments have significant public health implications. While the completed project focused on bacteria and fungi, the methodology and investigative framework can be extended to study viruses in air, surface and occupant skin in different built environments in Hong Kong, which have not been done before. The relationships between viruses and bacteria/fungi, and how different indoor factors such as ventilation rate, temperature and relative humidity affect the composition and concentration of viruses have been mostly unknown. The PI is now actively conducting preliminary work to refine the methods for studying viruses and preparing proposals to seek financial supports for the work.

11276116.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11276116.value: People on average spend over 90% of their time indoors, making it a key habitat that must be safeguarded to ensure occupants’ health. Understanding the microbial populations that are present and their metabolic activity are vital for assessing occupants’ microbial exposure and implementing the necessary control. In this study, we deployed state-of-the-art high-throughput sequencing methods to investigate the fungi that are present in air, surface and occupant skin in the indoor built environment and assess their relationships with bacteria. We found that the fungal populations are dynamics in a seasonal timescale and they are transferred between air, surface and occupant skin by various extent. The diversity and composition of fungal and bacterial communities are positively correlated, indicating that the two populations are not independent of each other. The microbial populations detected in the indoors are not merely present but some are metabolically active over a long period of time, especially those that are low in abundance. Overall, this study highlights the importance of both the fungal and bacterial members in the indoor built environment and indicates that taxa that are rare cannot be overlooked as their metabolic activity is disproportionately high.

11276616.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11276616.value: 回收利用钚和次锕系元素并把其置于快堆中已被发现是管理铀同位素配置的有效途径，如乏燃料中存在的钚，镅和镎等元素。钚和次锕系元素有较长的半衰期，并主导着与核废料排放相关的长期放射性毒性。钠冷快堆已成为三种第四代快堆类型中的主导堆型。钠冷快堆可以满足以下技术目标：可持续性，经济性，安全性，可靠性和防止核扩散性，减少核废料的总放射毒性，并大幅降低核废料的寿命。 氧化物核燃料已经由于其成熟性和易于加工被广泛应用于轻水堆和快堆。(U1-y, Puy)O2-x氧化物燃料则成为第四代钠冷快堆燃料的一个非常有吸引力的候选者，它能使长寿命的次锕系元素发生嬗变，并能建立具有很高防止核扩散的快中子增殖反应堆（FBR）循环。了解快堆燃料性能是快堆优化的关键一步，完全耦合的多物理建模将提供给钠冷快堆一个设计和优化的重要工具。 拟议的钠冷快堆(U1-y, Puy)O2-x氧化物燃料性能建模和仿真研究计划将预测燃料、包壳和装配结构部件在正常操作和反应器瞬变情况下的三维（3D）动态燃耗依赖行为和失效模式，以及进行灵敏度和不确定性的量化分析以确定感兴趣的建模和仿真的重要宏观参数，和改进材料性能和现象的物理模型。该项目将对(U1-y, Puy)O2-x混合氧化物燃料在钠冷快堆应用及辐射条件下的特性和性能进行基于COMSOL Multiphysics框架的自定义偏微分方程多物理建模和模拟。我们将采用多时间和长度尺度方法对快堆应用中稳态和瞬态条件下完全耦合的物理现象进行建模和仿真。材料特性将包括燃料，包壳和冷却剂的热物理，机械，化工，相图等性质，多物理场燃料性能将包括热能，机械，化学和组分重构，裂变气体的产生，扩散，释放和燃料肿胀，晶粒成长，燃料与包壳机械相互作用（FCMI），燃料与包壳化学作用（FCCI）和蠕变断裂。材料性质和物理现象的模型都将是动态燃耗依赖的来体现燃耗的历史及演变。拟议的研究还致力于在原子或分子尺度下确定材料性质，例如，热膨胀，比热，导热性和元素扩散系数，以及在原子或分子尺度下确定物理现象，例如，采用分子动力学进行燃料化学和组分重构分析，以改善材料性能和物理现象模型。分子动力学计算的燃料材料性能和物理现象的结果将与已有的实验数据和经验关系进行比较，然后作为多物理燃料性能软件的输入文件来预测燃料在快堆中的性能，以增加燃料的寿命，提高反应器的效率，并减少核废料的产生量。 该研究项目涉及在正常运行和反应堆瞬态条件下燃料材料性质和性能表现的先进物理建模和详细的分析研究。该项目将不仅将帮助我们预测(U1-y, Puy)O2-x混合氧化物燃料性能，理解在辐射、腐蚀和极端高温环境下具有挑战性的多物理场现象，还有利于其它的核能研究，例如，先进的下一代核反应堆研究和核能先进的建模和仿真。拟议的研究也将影响新燃料材料的开发和核反应堆的设计。

11276616.label: Realisation of objectives
11276616.value: During the fast reactor nuclear fuel fission reaction under Normal Operation and Reactor Transients, fission gases accumulate and form pores with the increase of fuel burnup, which decreases the fuel thermal conductivity, leading to overheating of the fuel element. The diffusion of plutonium and oxygen with high-temperature gradient is also one of the important fuel performance concerns as it will affect the fuel materials properties, power distribution and overall performance of the fuel pin. In order to investigate these important issues, the (U1-y, Puy)O2-x fuel pellet is studied by fully coupling thermal transport, deformation, oxygen diffusion, fission gas release and swelling, and plutonium redistribution to evaluate the effects on each other with burnup dependent models, accounting for the evolution of fuel porosity. The approach was developed using self-defined multiphysics models based on the framework of COMSOL Multiphysics to manage the nonlinearities associated with fast reactor mixed oxide fuels performance analysis. The modeling results showed a consistent fuel performance comparable with the previous results. Burnup degrades the fuel thermal conductivity, resulting in a significant fuel temperature increase. The fission gas release increased rapidly first and then steadily with the burnup increase. The fuel porosity increased dramatically at the beginning of the burnup and then kept constant as the fission gas released to the fuel free volume, causing the fuel temperature increase. Another important finding is that the deviation from stoichiometry of oxygen affects greatly not only the fuel properties, for example, thermal conductivity, but also the fuel performance, for example, temperature distribution, porosity evolution, grain size growth, fission gas release, deformation, and plutonium redistribution. Special attention needs to be paid to the deviation from stoichiometry of oxygen in fuel fabrication. Plutonium content will also affect the fuel material properties and performance. However, it’s not that significant compared to the deviation from stoichiometry of oxygen due to the similar material properties of UO2 and PuO2.

11276616.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11276616.value: In summary, the (U1-yPuy)O2-x mixed oxide fuel performance has been modelled in a fast reactor with fully coupled physics models based on the framework of COMSOL Multiphysics, and new burnup dependent models were adopted. The modeling results showed a consistent fuel performance comparable with the previous results. Burnup degrades the thermal conductivity of the fuel, and results in an increase in the fuel centerline temperature greatly. It was also found that the fuel porosity increased dramatically at the beginning of the fuel burnup and then kept constant as the fission gas released to the fuel free volume. The porosity is found to cause about 50K (50°C) increase in fuel centerline temperature. The fission gas release model results show good agreement with the previous work. Another important finding is that the deviation from stoichiometry of oxygen plays a significant role in fuel material properties and performance. Special attention needs to be paid to the deviation from stoichiometry of oxygen in the fuel fabrication. Overall, an effective approach was developed using self-defined multiphysics models based on the framework of COMSOL Multiphysics to manage the nonlinearities associated with fast reactor mixed oxide fuels performance analysis. The modelling results can be used to identify the important phenomena and parameters, to direct and design experiments and to assist in post analysis of expensive nuclear experiments for fast reactor nuclear fuel performance analysis.
