11612016.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11612016.value: Research related to social movements has paid little attention to urban movements and their long-term consequences. The proposed research project will fill this gap by focusing on how municipal governments respond to the demands of urban movements. In particular, it will distinguish between institutional and non-institutional outcomes and between intended and unintended outcomes to assess which are more effective and consistent with the social and political objectives of such movements. Furthermore, it will determine the extent to which local governments comprising former urban activists are able to meet the goals of such movements. Spain provides an exceptional setting for fulfilling the aims of this project. The mobilisations that took place in Spain beginning in May 2011, known as the 15M or Indignados movement, were internationally relevant and closely connected to other Occupy-like movements. The proposed project will assess the performance of various new municipal governments in Spanish cities to determine 1) how the institutional co-optation of former activists has contributed to fulfilling the goals of urban movements and 2) which of the institutional and non-institutional outcomes of urban movements have been most effective and persistent under the new local governance relations. The research design of the project will thus involve careful examination of the outcomes of urban movements during the cycle of mobilisations opened up by the 15M movement, four years before and two years after the municipal elections of May 2015 and in cities with different electoral results and governance arrangements. The project will hypothesise that urban movements were more successful where municipal governments shifted away from bi-partisan domination towards new electoral platforms with substantial activist input due to the continuing pressure of active movements. Therefore it will focus on four cities where the local government experienced such a shift in addition to examine two more cities that act as ‘control cases.’ The main information to be gathered will stem from interviews and documents. Afterwards, critical discourse analysis will be applied. This study may help social organisations and political authorities to consider the interplay between urban activism and local policies. Knowledge of citizen participation may make municipal governments more responsive and accountable. Urban activists and non-governmental organisations may use the findings of the project as either a basis for their negotiations with municipal authorities or as indicators for planning their own projects and campaigns. 社會運動的研究很少涉及到城市運動及其長期成果。這擬議研究項目將填補這片空白，集中在市政府如何回應城市運動的訴求。這研究會詳細辨別建制與非建制之間，以及預期與非預期的成果，從而評估它們在運動之中的社會和政治目標效益為更有效還是維持不變。此外，它將決定地方政府怎樣能夠滿足前城市運動者達到這些運動目標的程度。 西班牙為本研究項目的宗旨提供了一個特殊的環境。從2011年5月開始，西班牙發生了稱為15M或Indignados的社會運動動員。這次動員緊密連接到國際上其他相關的佔領運動。本研究項目將評估西班牙多個城市新市政府表現來決定: 1）前社會運動家如何在建制下的選舉為為履行城市運動的目標作出貢獻及；2）在新的地方治理關係下，城市運動中的建制與非建制性成果，哪個最有效、最持久的。這項目的研究設計將仔細檢查由15M運動發展出來的動員週期所帶來的城市運動成果，尤其是2015年5月市政選舉之前四年和之後兩年，以及擁有不同選舉結果的各城市和其治理安排。這研究將假設由於積極社運所帶來的持續壓力，市政府脫離兩黨統治，轉至大量的社會運人士進入新的選舉平台，城市運動將會更加成功。因此，這研究的重點將放在四個城市的地方政府的轉變經歷，並以另外兩個城市充當「控制變數例子」。研究資料主要從訪談和文獻收集信息。隨後，利用批評話語分析（CDA）方法研究。 這項研究將可以幫助社會團體和政治機關考慮城市行動和地方政策之間的相互作用。對公民參與的認識可使市政府增加回應和責感任。城市活動家和非政府組織可能會使用本項目的調查結果作為與市政當局談判的基礎，或作為規劃自己項目和運動的指標，。 關鍵詞：城市運動，運動的成果，地方治理，西班牙

11612016.label: Realisation of objectives
11612016.value: This project has not been totally smooth, especially due to the departure of the original PI, Miguel Martinez, from Hong Kong. However, in the end nonetheless, in terms of knowledge goals, we have collected enough information and conducted sufficient analyses in order to assure that our four research objectives were accomplished. This was especially possible due to additional outsourcing of research to a field work researcher, Evin Deniz, in Spain. As a result, the project has suffered delays, which explains that some of the publications are not yet accepted for publication. However, we have been able to collect significant information, and are very confident - also in view of the first review of these papers - that the papers will be published. Overall, the six cities under examination provided substantial material for the comparison in terms of intensive knowledge of every case and significant differences among them. It is remarkable to note that the housing issue led most of the cross-city comparisons due to the emphases given by the interviews and the political agenda of all these cases. Therefore, a great proportion of our focus and interpretation had the relationships between local governments and housing movements as the central matter. Community gardens and other social spaces were finally grouped under the category of ‘urban commons’, which was also a productive theoretical lens for understanding the main similarities and differences at play. The topics of health and education, despite the many representatives we interviewed about, were found not as key issues as we initially hypothesised, so we have not included them in our publications yet. All publications produced under the umbrella of this project have covered each of the research objectives. In addition, we have engaged with crucial international debates on ‘municipalism’, ‘urban commons’, housing movements and the impacts of urban movements in local governance. Hence, we kept developing a ‘contextual approach’ and also tested the role of key variables (such as the co-optation of former activists by local governments) and concepts (e.g. the notions of ‘influence’ and ‘responsiveness’) that contributed to the theories of social movements impacts and policy-making. The article submitted to Social Movement Studies is our main output of this analysis. Regarding the time-span of the project, our assessments have included the whole political cycle of 2015-2019, and not only the initial years of municipalist governments. Although most of the empirical work was done before 2019, the extension of the project allowed us to follow more in detail the developments of the relationships between local authorities and urban movements. In particular, regarding each objective, the following observations apply: 1) There was a clear positive relationship between the presence of former activists as members of the ‘municipalist’ local governments and policies in accordance to urban movements’ demands. However, the type of government coalition, the priority of the issues in the local political agenda, and the strength of the movements were identified as key features of the variability of outcomes in the four municipalist cities. As for the control cases, with non-municipalist governments but strong urban movements, no clear co-optation process was observed as well as local policies did not satisfy urban movements at all. 2) An important finding is that the even most progressive municipalist governments were, on the one hand, dependent on votes and support from traditional forces and, on the other, were in regular strains with urban movements despite their close ties. Governance networks and negotiations between municipalist governments and movements were more regular, institutionalised and positive in terms of policies, especially when compared with the control-cases. This explains that the protest activity of movements, both before and after the change of cabinets, was highly influential to modify some local policies, but very far away from any established partnership between movements, parties and governments. 3) The most significant argument we made here is that the local sphere of government was the most accessible one for the influence of anti-austerity movements that emerged in 2011 across Spain. It was only in 2019-2020 (beyond the time-span of our analysis) when the central state level, with the coalition between the parties PSOE and Podemos, experienced openness to urban movements. We have collected a great amount of evidence of the former influence, but our focus on its conflictual features (for instance, in issues such as residential squatting, as our article in the Journal of Urban Affairs shows) allowed us to understand the mismatch between the movements’ achievements and the unstable electoral support of the municipalist governments, as it was manifest after the local elections of 2019 (the cities of Cadiz and Barcelona were the only municipalist strongholds that remained in power. 4) As predicted, the complexity of the governance arrangements in Madrid and Barcelona was much higher than in the other cases. Capital pressures and party coalitions had more economic and political implications there, as well as symbolic visibility in the media, than the other medium-size cities. Nonetheless, we found specific policies (such as those against poverty and the municipalisation of public services) that drew a relevant spectrum of differences, similarities and potential actions for municipalist governments. This is more obvious in our analysis of the housing movement led by the PAH (a typical social movement organisation operating in many cities simultaneously). They managed to modify both local and regional regulations with different outcomes in each case but, importantly, by paving the way for incremental cases in the following negotiation or legal regulation they attempted to change. Our article in the journal Housing Studies reflects well these achievements, failures, unintended consequences and the contextual circumstances that explain them.

11612016.label: Major findings and research outcome
11612016.value: The same as mentioned above in 5.3. In short: 1) There was a clear positive relationship between the presence of former activists as members of the ‘municipalist’ local governments and policies in accordance to urban movements’ demands. However, the type of government coalition, the priority of the issues in the local political agenda, and the strength of the movements were identified as key features of the variability of outcomes in the four municipalist cities. 2) Even municipalist governments were, on the one hand, dependent on votes and support from traditional forces and, on the other, were in regular strains with urban movements despite their close ties. Governance networks and negotiations between municipalist governments and movements were more regular, institutionalised and positive in terms of policies, especially when compared with the control-cases. 3) The local sphere of government was the most accessible one for the influence of anti-austerity movements that emerged in 2011 across Spain. 4) We found specific policies (such as those against poverty and the municipalisation of public services) that drew a relevant spectrum of differences, similarities and potential actions for municipalist governments. This is more obvious in our analysis of the housing movement led by the PAH (a typical social movement organisation operating in many cities simultaneously). They managed to modify both local and regional regulations with different outcomes in each case but, importantly, by paving the way for incremental cases in the following negotiation or legal regulation they attempted to change.

11612016.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11612016.value: There are three promising research avenues based on the findings of this research that would deserve additional academic publications: 1) The analysis of social movements’ outcomes. Most theories and studies have focused on the influence of protest repertoires, organisational resources, political opportunity structures and policy impacts. Our research indicates that multi-level governance, historical and political economy contexts, long-term intended and unintended effects of social movements, and impacts on social and political spheres other than standard policies, represent a more fruitful approach. 2) The issue of ‘municipalism’ and the attention to movement-party relationships have been renewed based on the Spanish experiences. Our contribution to this topic has highlighted the conflicts in those negotiations, their weak electoral support and the role of ‘urban commons’. This is a matter of discussion worldwide, not only in Spain, but our findings could contribute to further envision how to assess in more effective ways the performance of such political approaches. 3) The rising strength of housing movements can illuminate how global speculative capital lands in local environments and the sort of social and political reactions it triggers. Spain is an extreme and dramatic example of this dynamic, which facilitates learning lessons to other contexts. In addition, our study has shown that a deep understanding of the structure-agency relationships (structures as enabling and constraining collective action) demands more focus on specific strategies by both powerholders and challengers, on the one hand, and intersectional relations at a macro and micro scales, on the other. More evidence and better interpretation of these aspects will certainly give us more scientific gains on the knowledge of housing struggles across spatial and political scales.

11612016.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11612016.value: We have studied the performance of six local governments in Spain between 2015 and 2019 according to their relationships with various urban movements. The movements started as part of an anti-austerity wave of protests in 2011. Among them, different housing struggles, protests and campaigns became the spearhead of those mobilisations. The rise of progressive ‘municipalist’ local governments in the period 2015-2019 represented a rare opportunity to explore to what extent movements influenced local authorities. We conducted research in four cities under municipalist rule and also in two cities with a more traditional type of government. Our comparisons yielded important findings. First of all, we confirmed that the housing movement across cities was quite effective in producing policy changes. This was partially facilitated by the inclusion of former housing activists in local governments but rarely appeared as the main mechanism at play. Instead, the deep scope of the housing crisis, the regular conflicts and intense negotiations between movements and governments, opened the ground for collaborative policy-making. Secondly, we have identified a significant spectrum of urban movements’ influences and city halls’ responsiveness. They become more visible when controversial issues are under dispute, but are dependent on local contexts as well.

11616216.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11616216.value: 在過去幾十年，香港由難民社區轉變為一個物質富裕的社會。香港市民的現代家居理想，已由50年代的基本住房需要，轉變為80年代要求優質與時尚的家居生活。學者認為，香港現代家居理想是建基於政府政策，以及私人發展商及媒體推廣，繼而被中產階級吸納及再建構的產物。 現代家居理想充斥著複雜的社會意義。家居既是一種經濟投資(物業)，亦是社會指標(顯示成就及身份象徵)，同時展示一個家庭的品味及氣質。報紙廣告如何建構香港現代理想家居？從1961 年至2011年間，廣告呈現的理想家居有否隨著香港城市人口，社會和政治改變而衍生變化？ 報紙廣告運用了哪種文化與視覺符碼推廣香港現代理想家居？這些文化與視覺表徵有否隨著房地產市場週期而改變？這些被推廣的香港現代家居理想，又促進著甚麼潛存的價值觀和隱藏的權力結構？雖然香港房屋研究文獻數量龐大，卻鮮有系統性研究香港房地產廣告，這項研究的主要目的就是填補這研究領域。 本研究將搜集過往的住宅物業報紙廣告(1961-2011)，並通過系統性的內容分析和文本分析，找出廣告中反覆出現的主題，文化與視覺符號，從而分析（ 1）香港現代家居理想的連貫性與轉變模式，（ 2）廣告商在不同時期以甚麼文化與視覺符碼銷售香港住宅物業，及（ 3）住宅物業廣告如何建立、再建構，或顛覆某種主體性及生活風格。

11616216.label: Realisation of objectives
11616216.value: Objective 1. To identify the cultural codes and visual expressions advertisers used during 1961 and 2011 to market Hong Kong’s residential properties. 100% achieved. To identify cultural codes and visual expressions of housing advertisements, we adopt content analysis and structural semiotics. Our sample covers residential property advertisements in Hong Kong’s Chinese newspapers from the population census years of 1961, 1971, 1981, 1991, 2001 and 2011. Our final sample contains 647 advertisements. For textual themes, we recorded the frequency of words used in property name and slogans, and categorised lexicons under ‘environment’, ‘view’, ‘property’, ‘dwelling’, ‘lifestyle’ and ‘aspirations’. Facilities described in the advertisements were coded into ‘leisure facilities’, ‘venues for domestic duties’, ‘children-related facilities’ and so on. Economic considerations and investment were coded as ‘property price’, ‘mortgage’, ‘instalments’, ‘discount’, ‘rate of return’ and so on. For the visuals, we focused on one main image and secondary images in each advertisement. We analysed items (e.g. maps and floorplans), perspective (e.g. outward views from the property), dominant colours, settings, props and models in the images. Our systemic textual analysis on slogans and property names aim to identify key messages and identities projected. We selected the three most prominent slogans in each sampled advertisement, based on font size, followed by positioning (higher over lower). These texts were then processed by an online tag cloud generator to produce a visual representation based on their frequency of appearance. The same process was used on property names. Words that appeared most often were analysed in relation to qualities associated with the property. To understand how developers produce, develop, and market housing as “luxury” between 1961 and 2011, we mainly used textual analysis only because the idea of “luxury” is changing across time and different between cultures and societies. When analysing these findings, we refer to corresponding socio-political and economic context of Hong Kong and the literature. Objective 2. To analyze the historical patterns of continuity and change of the advertisement-mediated Hong Kong domestic ideal in the 50 years between 1961 and 2011. 100% achieved. We identify three stages for HK housing advertisements, and the three stages indicate progression towards increased abstraction. In stage 1 (1961 and 1981), the ideal home in the 1960s is portrayed as a place around which residents go about their everyday life activities – they take public transport, shop for groceries, go to the cinema, use public sports facilities and relax in nearby parks; potential homeowners are assumed to care about a property’s location and its internal layout. Earlier advertisements positioned new private developments as superior versions of public housing estates, promising convenience and community. The integration of private housing and public (leisure) space between 1961 and 1981 suggested an inclination to reproduce a sociality centred on the relationship among living space, daily-life activities and community. This development was partly linked to the housing policies of the colonial government. These all contributed to the property market’s development and promoted the ‘pro-homeownership discourse’. In stage 2 (1991-2001), nature is increasingly privatised and leisure facilities become resort-like, through which use values and social distinction are constructed via a more abstract blend of connotations (‘relaxation’ and ‘healthy living’). References to sociality and community are replaced by inward-looking, experience-oriented quality living. Stage 2 coincided with a period of economic boom in Hong Kong. Between 1981 and 2006, an emerging middle-class became prime agents in constructing Hong Kong’s modern domestic ideal (Ng, 1995), as homeownership dramatically increased (Yip et al., 2007). In stage 3 (2011), where advertisements seemed to target not homeowner–occupants but non-local investors/speculators. The Closer Economic Partnership Arrangement (CEPA), launched in 2003, facilitates cross-border economic activities between Hong Kong and Mainland China and eases the inflow of capital. Today, Hong Kong is the world’s largest offshore investment hub for the Chinese currency renminbi. The proportion of Mainland purchasers of residential property rose from 8.5% in 2008 to 28.3% in 2011, and corresponding figures for their share of total amount invested in the housing market grew from 10.6% to 36.9% (Centaline Property, 2014). In stage 3, the intensified use of notional grandeur targets buyers who may not live inside the ‘home’ after all. Hyperbolic superlatives, stylised graphics and sexualised femininity sever shenghuo from ‘living’. We argue that from the late 1970s onwards, Hong Kong government policy actively promotes homeownership and a housing hierarchy discourse, as housing advertisements changed from emphasising functionalities and everyday living in 1961–1981 to privatised quality living in 1991–2001. Working in tandem with the government’s neoliberal policies in the 2000s, advertisement began to represent housing as a spectacle through distinction and abstraction. By 2011, housing advertisements have divorced from real living, promoting a specific ‘hyperindividualistic’ political subjectivity. This development reflects and accelerates the exclusion of those who cannot afford to participate in financial investment and speculation from accessing much needed living space. We also reveal the strategies of developers in creating and injecting variable expressions of ‘luxury’ housing to maximise profit. For instance, although luxury in Hong Kong’s high-priced housing has remained centred upon exclusivity, it has changed from scenic areas far from urbanity (1961), to high-rises, elevated podiums and gated communities (1971), to foreign charm and privatised leisurely lifestyles (1981 and 1991), aspirational exclusivity (2001), and arrived at the vulgar, imperial fantasies of excess in 2011. Luxury elements have extended beyond property-oriented material and immaterial qualities to include convenient transport, private clubhouses and elite school catchment areas. Presently high-priced housing has even converged upon representing unrestrained, excessive and wasteful vulgarity as desirable.

11616216.label: Major findings and research outcome
11616216.value: We published two journal articles for this research. In the first article, we analysed utilised insights from Baudrillard’s political economy of the sign and Lipovetsky’s concept of hypermodernity integrating temporality with the three modalities of housing consumption, that is, as living space, investment and financial speculation. By demonstrating the increased abstraction of living, the promotion of the hyperreal, and private housing as objects of financial speculation as evidenced in the construction of ideal homes, we illuminate key features of and inequalities associated with housing advertisements in a global city in neoliberal, late capitalism. The paper titled “The disappearance of community, work, and everyday life in late capitalism: Private housing advertisements from 1961 to 2011 in global Hong Kong” was published in Journal of Consumer Culture in 2019. DOI: 10.1177/1469540519846201. Journal of Consumer Culture is a A+ journal. Its 5-year Impact factor is 3.134, ranking 1/40 in Cultural Studies. Reviewer’s comments: “I enjoyed this article. It’s informative and well written; it covers an important topic that should be of interest to scholars working across several subfields; the research is sound; the findings are significant.” In the second paper, we build on insights from critical luxury studies and we examine how developers produce ‘luxury’ in Hong Kong’s high-priced housing from 1961 to 2011. Findings show how advertisers and developers actively injected new elements of luxury to maximise profits. We argue that Hong Kong’s property oligarchy has successfully created luxury housing in previously unremarkable locations by producing various exclusivist aspirations, thus promoting excess and reinforcing housing and socio-spatial inequalities. Our discussion deepens understanding of Hong Kong’s housing hierarchy by looking beyond location-based exclusivity and contributes to critical luxury studies by underscoring the strategies of property conglomerates in the production of luxury housing. The paper titled “Producing ‘luxury’ housing: Developers’ strategies and housing advertisements in Hong Kong (1961-2011)” was published in Urban Studies in 2020. DOI: 10.1177/0042098019896711. Urban Studies is a A+ journal; its 2-year Impact factor is 3.272, ranking 5/40 in Urban Studies. Reviewer’s comments: “This is an interesting paper that examines the discursive construction of 'luxury' housing advertisements in Hong Kong. To my mind, there are few in recent years that examines how real estate advertisements shapes and influence residents' perception of luxury housing.”

11616216.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11616216.value: The PI has collected overseas property sales leaflets for around 10 years. Although these leaflets market overseas properties as investment, the texts and graphics are not as hyperbolic as those appeared in HK housing advertisements in 2011. A cross-cultural study could be done. In this research, we successfully analysed how the private property developers marketed Hong Kong housing, how and why representations of the ideal home have changed, and how Hong Kong government’s unbalanced favouring of developers’ control of housing production contribute to the skyrocketing price of Hong Kong housing. Nevertheless, as Hong Kong has one of the least affordable housing markets in the world, we have not yet known how ordinary Hong Kong citizens, especially the young people who are lack of homeownership opportunities, view what means by ‘ideal home’. Although pro-establishment politicians have attributed recent anti-government protests to young people’s lack of homeownership opportunities, survey findings do not support this conjecture (Forrest and Xian, 2018). A follow-up research on Hong Kong people’s perception of ideal home should be done.

11616216.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11616216.value: This research, based on a longitudinal study of private housing advertisements from 1961 to 2011, reveals how and why representations of the ideal home have changed. We argue that from the late 1970s onwards, Hong Kong government policy actively promotes homeownership and a housing hierarchy discourse, as housing advertisements changed from emphasising functionalities and everyday living in 1961–1981, to privatised quality living in 1991–2001, and abstract living and ‘hyperindividualistic’ political subjectivity in 2011. We also reveal the strategies of developers in creating and injecting variable expressions of ‘luxury’ housing to maximise profits. Prestigious location, a prime determinant of housing price, is no longer restricted to traditionally privileged areas. The erosion of location-bound exclusivity means that ‘luxury’ housing has geographically spread but not democratised. By demonstrating the increased abstraction of living, private housing as objects of financial speculation, and the production of luxury in housing constructing exclusivity as desirable, we illuminate key features of and inequalities associated with housing advertisements in a global city in neoliberal, late capitalism.

11617116.value: 香港私立專上院校發展探微:1950-1970年代

11617116.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11617116.value: 1949年大批南來學人湧港興學施教，一時間私立專上院校(下稱私專)紛紛成立，為不少逃難到港難民提供教育機會。另一方面，人口激增帶來莫大教育需求。促使私專頓時如雨後春筍般迅速發展。大半個世紀後，部分院校已湮滅無聞，部份則獲得港府納入制度而轉型為公立大學，也有部份仍以私立大學/院校的身份、面貌繼續辦學施教。香港的私專發展史，不但構成香港教育史的重要一環，為香港培養數以十萬計的莘莘學子，同時也映照出香港文化、歷史乃至政治的複雜發展內容和社會變遷。然而，這段歷史至今仍未廣受學界深細探討。本計劃現階段將集中探討1950年至1970年代為止這三十年間私專教育事業發展的經過，特別是從東西方冷戰政局、中港社會變局、國共或左右兩翼對峙等等的多元互動中，探究相關教育事業從興起到轉型求存、從收編到反收編、從初創到式微乃至再發展，檢視英國政府、港英政府、國共雙方乃至辦學者自身如何通過高等教育(如課程設置、資歷認證)塑造香港/人的文化價值和身份認同，同時從中窺探殖民情境與民族主義在香港高等教育發展過程中產生的影響和作用。

11619816.value: 香港學童的閱讀困難：語言及認知基礎能力

11619816.label: Project Objectives
11619816.value: To investigate the cognitive and linguistic skills which explain individual differences in reading comprehension in Hong Kong Chinese children To investigate if different sets of cognitive and linguistic skills predict comprehension of texts with different genres in Chinese To elucidate the cognitive and linguistic deficits in reading comprehension difficulties in Hong Kong Chinese children To demonstrate the existence and the cognitive and linguistic markers of Chinese specific poor comprehenders

11619816.label: Realisation of objectives
11619816.value: The four objectives for this project have been achieved satisfactorily. This project aimed to investigate the cognitive and linguistic underpinnings of reading comprehension in Chinese children. Concerning objectives one and two, our team developed a battery of tests to assess reading comprehension and related cognitive and linguistic skills in Chinese children. A new Chinese reading comprehension test was developed, which allowed the examination of the effects of text genres on reading performance of children. Also, items of various reading-related cognitive and linguistic tests with difficulty level suitable to primary school children were constructed. They assessed word reading, vocabulary knowledge, phonological awareness, morphological awareness, working memory, syntactic awareness, inferencing skills, and nonverbal cognitive ability. They differentiated children with higher or lower ability in these cognitive and linguistic skills. These tests were administered on 353 primary school students in Hong Kong. The results showed that some cognitive and linguistic factors, such as vocabulary knowledge and working memory, were uniquely predictive of Chinese children's reading comprehension of texts with different genres. Performances in reading comprehension of texts with different genres were moderately and positively correlated. Concerning objectives three and four, this study identified children with poor reading comprehension based on their performance in the reading comprehension test developed in this study. Cognitive and linguistic abilities were compared between children with poor reading comprehension and their counterparts with good reading comprehension. Among children with poor reading comprehension, a group of Chinese poor comprehenders who had poor reading comprehension despite adequate word reading ability were identified. The poor comprehenders' performances on cognitive and linguistic tests were compared with a group of typically-developing readers matched on nonverbal reasoning and word reading ability with them. Weaker performances on some cognitive and linguistic tasks, including vocabulary knowledge and working memory, in the poor comprehenders than the typically-developing readers were observed. Overall, this project has provided valuable insights into reading development in Chinese children.

11619816.label: Major findings and research outcome
11619816.value: A number of important findings, leading to several journal publications and conference papers, have been obtained from this project. Major findings and research outcomes are summarized below. Firstly, this project developed a set of tests to assess reading comprehension and reading-related cognitive and linguistic skills in Chinese children, and identified cognitive and linguistic factors fundamental to children's Chinese reading ability. For example, the results showed that some cognitive and linguistic factors, such as vocabulary knowledge and nonverbal cognitive skills, were uniquely predictive of children's Chinese reading ability (Chow*, 2018a; Chow*, 2019; Dong, Tang, Chow*, Wang, Dong, 2020; Wong, Cheng, Chow* & Chung, 2019). Secondly, individual variations in Chinese reading comprehension were observed in Chinese primary students, and learning methods were found to play an important role in these variations (*Chow, 2018b; *Chow & Wong, 2020; Dong, Chow*, Wu, Zhou, & Zhao, 2020). Thirdly, the performances in reading comprehension of texts with different genres, including narrative and expository texts, were moderately and positively correlated. In general, similar sets of cognitive and linguistic skills predict reading comprehension of narrative and expository texts (Dong & *Chow, 2018). Fourthly, this study identified children with poor reading comprehension and the cognitive and linguistic markers of reading comprehension difficulties. Among children with poor reading comprehension, a group of Chinese poor comprehenders who had poor reading comprehension despite adequate word reading ability were identified. Weak performance on cognitive and linguistic tasks, including vocabulary knowledge and working memory, contributed to reading comprehension difficulties in Chinese children (Chow, 2018b; *Chow, under review; Dong, Chow*, Wu, Zhou, & Zhao, 2020). Overall, this project has unraveled cognitive and linguistic skills fundamental to the development of and difficulties in reading comprehension among Chinese children.

11619816.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11619816.value: Findings and outcomes of this project have laid an important ground for development of future research on reading development in children. This project has provided empirical evidence on the important roles of cognitive and linguistic skills in reading comprehension in Chinese children. While more is known about the roles of cognitive factors, the extent to which affective factors and the interaction between cognitive and affective factors contribute to reading in L1 Chinese and L2 English remains unclear. These research ideas were developed into grant proposals and are currently investigated in research projects, including a CityU Strategic Research Grant project and a GRF project funded in the 2019-20 exercise. Also, this project has indicated interesting results on reading comprehension difficulties in Chinese. Future research can examine if the findings are language-specific or language-universal by comparing the roles of cognitive and linguistic skills in reading comprehension in different languages.

11619816.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11619816.value: The ability to read is critical for knowledge acquisition and communication. Children who struggle with reading comprehension often encounter great challenges in learning. This study addressed important issues regarding the nature of reading comprehension and its difficulties in Chinese children. In this study, we indicated individual variations in Chinese reading comprehension in Chinese primary students and the contribution of cognitive and linguistic skills to these variations. Also, a group of Chinese poor comprehenders who had poor reading comprehension despite adequate word reading ability were identified. Weak performance on cognitive and linguistic tasks, including vocabulary knowledge and working memory, contributed to reading comprehension difficulties in Chinese children. The findings have offered important insights into the best methods to assess children's reading comprehension skills and develop effective interventions. Specifically, the findings have yielded important knowledge for guiding the selection of appropriate measures for assessment and diagnosis of reading comprehension difficulties, as well as the identification of cognitive and linguistic skills to be targeted for intervention. The findings from this study can potentially help parents, educators and practitioners better understand the needs of children who struggle with reading comprehension in Chinese.

11621016.label: Project Title(Chinese)
11621016.value: 如何提升外派人員績效：成年依附安全感對跨文化衝突及其威脅的緩解作用

11621016.label: Co - Investigator(s)
11621016.value: Prof Chao, Man Chi Dr Fu, Ho Ying

11621016.label: Project Objectives
11621016.value: Our prime objective is to test a new theory of expatriate intercultural conflict resolution and cultural adjustment. Specifically, we propose that an expatriate’s adult attachment security, a non-work factor, will ameliorate the psychological threats experienced in work-related intercultural conflicts. We will also explore conflict-related factors that attenuate the positive effect of adult attachment security. Our research findings will provide important, novel, and practical implications for managing expatriation and intercultural conflict. The findings will be disseminated through journal publications, conference presentations and workshops for business practitioners.

11621016.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11621016.value: As companies expand into foreign markets, there is an increasing need for expatriation activities to manage human resources, maintain consistency in business operations and align the work processes across different geographic locations. For instance, the percentage of companies with more than 1,000 expatriates worldwide increased from 12% in 2001 to 49% in 2013 (Cigna, 2013). Despite such growing trends, cultural adjustment remains a critical barrier to retaining expatriates and receiving effective performance. According to a survey by InterNations (2014), less than half of China’s expatriates indicated they were satisfied with their lives during their stay. In particular, many expatriates find settling in and family life difficult and this is evident in many other developing countries, such as China, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, as host countries. This finding is consistent with the academic literature that spousal and family adjustment plays a critical role in expatriate adjustment and retention (Black & Stephens, 1989). Past research on expatriate adjustment has primarily focused on the effects of personality, and job-related and organizational factors, and has not explored the challenges from the perspective of adult attachment security and intercultural conflict. This proposal draws on theories from social psychology and organizational behavior to understand the psychological conditions under which expatriates can adjust successfully in the host country. We theorize that a major challenge of expatriate performance and retention is the extent to which expatriates can constructively manage and resolve interpersonal conflicts with their peers and subordinates from the host country. While conflicts and disagreements are common in intercultural interactions, expatriates’ appraisal of the behaviors of the counterparts in terms of task-based differences instead of threats and intimidations would be conducive to constructive conflict management. Our major hypothesis is that an expatriate’s adult attachment security may ameliorate the psychological threats experienced by expatriates through intercultural conflicts and hence promote the use of cooperative and constructive conflict resolution strategies (Study 1). We suggest that such effects are results from less reliance on negative cultural stereotypes when expatriates have a strong sense of attachment security (Study 2). We further propose that the positive effect of attachment security will be pronounced in task conflicts (vs. relational conflicts) and in conflicts where cognition-based trust (vs. affect-based trust) is broken (Study 3 and 4). These propositions will be tested with different methodologies and samples of expatriates in four studies. Our research framework will provide important practical implications for managing expatriation and intercultural conflict. 隨著商業全球化下, 各地企業需要外派人員來處理公司在不同國家內人力資源體制上的差異, 而這外派趨勢持續增強 。在中國，外派員工人數於2007至2012年間跳增17%，多達240,000人(Durnin, 2014)。由於入息及購買力提升， 中國成為最受外派員工歡迎的目的地之一 (Yan, 2014)。儘管這些增長趨勢，文化適應力一直影响外派員工的工作表現及回歸意向。不少外派人員認為融入中國文化及建立家庭生活感困難，在中東及非洲等其他發展中地區工作的外派員工，亦面對類似的挑戰。學術研究亦指出配偶及家庭的文化適應力對外派員工的適應力和回歸意向，擔當著重要的角色 (Black and Stephens, 1989)。由於外派職務對公司和外派員工均帶來高昂的成本，我們必須有效地研究影響外派員工及其配偶或伴侶適應能力的心理因素及原理。 以往有關外派員工適應力的研究主要聚焦於個人性格和工作及組織的相關因素。少有研究以成年依附安全感的角度來探索文化衝突對外派員工的影響。文化衝突是外派經理在工作上遇到最困難的挑戰之一。來自經濟學人智庫(2010)的研究曾指出，一半的外派員工認為同事間發生之文化衝突是外派經理面對的最大困難，百分之四十二的受訪者則認為無法了解當地文化和不同的工作模式及辦公準則為最大困難。就此，有關如何能有建設性地去調解文化衝突的研究，對外派成功可是非常重要。 本研究的宗旨在於揉合社會心理學及組織行為學的理論，以提出一理論框架來探索外派員工的文化衝突調解方法。研究前提為外派員工的成年依附安全感，可改善他們在工作環境中經歷的文化衝突所帶來的心理威脅，從而促使他們運用建設性及合作性的調解策略。具體來說，當外派員工在與伴侶的關係上得到安全感，他們相對較少依賴認知捷徑，如文化刻板印象，來評估於辦公室內引起爭執的當地同事。相反，他們可能更有信心去與跟自己不同文化背景的爭執者互動。再者，本研究擬提議當衝突是任務性（相對於關係性）時，或是爭執者之間的認知性信任（相對於情感性信任）破裂時，依附安全感所帶來之正面效應會比較強烈。本提案會透過4個獨立研究項目，使用不同調查方法和樣本，來驗證這些假設。本研究框架會為管理外派職務及處理文化衝突，提供重要的應用含義。

11626616.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11626616.value: This project extends previous research on public opinion of energy security and energy policy in Japan. In April 2010, the PI of this proposal investigated public views on energy security. Specifically, the 2010 project sought to identify public views on which dimensions of energy security should be prioritized when formulating Japanese energy policy. The findings suggested that i) a high degree of agreement existed amongst citizens regarding which dimensions of energy security should be prioritized and ii) public perceptions of energy security did not differ significantly from existing government energy policy objectives. The study, which was published in Energy Policy, concluded that a radical shift in energy policy would be unlikely in the near future, given the cohesion between public expectations and existing energy policy. One year after the study, the Fukushima disaster occurred. Since March 2011, the cohesion that existed between public expectations of energy governance and government energy policy has eroded. Some polls now suggest that up to 70% of the Japanese population is opposed to a reintroduction of nuclear power. Conversely, Prime Minister Shinzo Abe has announced plans to reintroduce the nuclear power program, aiming to generate 20% of the nation’s electricity by 2020. This fragmentation of public perspectives and government policy raises an important question: “Is public opposition based on an altered perspective on energy security or is public opposition based on safety concerns over nuclear power governance?” If the answer is the former, then the government might face extreme opposition to its nuclear power reintroduction plans and could find energy policy becoming a central issue in the 2018 general election. If the answer is the latter, the government could attenuate public opposition and realize its nuclear power expansion ambitions by further bolstering the nuclear power governance regime. In order to ascertain how public energy security perspectives have changed, this research study will replicate the 2010 study, employing the 2010 results as a benchmark. The project will reveal whether or not a true paradigm shift has occurred in the minds of the electorate. To validate the survey results, the study will interview a group of 6-12 energy policy experts in Japan – asking them to analyze the results and assess the political significance of the survey findings. The findings will contribute to a better understanding of emergent Japanese energy policy and will contribute to enhanced academic insights regarding the nexus between public perceptions and policymaking. 11635116.label: Project Objectives
11635116.value: To trace the historical development of the SPC’s judicial interpretations, and to investigate the specific conditions under which such historical development occurred and such legislative function was established by the NPC in the amendment of Legislation Law in 2015. To investigate the models of the SPC’s judicial interpretations, and the differences of these models in practice. The SPC acts in the specific context of reform-era China, and the project focuses on the processes, mechanisms and conditions for the different models in the implementation of the SPC’s judicial interpretations in specific contexts. To explore the extent to which the SPC’s judicial interpretations are effective or sometimes perhaps ineffective in practice, in particular in comparison with the application of corresponding national laws, and the weight of judicial interpretations in the trial practice. To reveal the effectiveness of the SPC’s judicial documentations of a judicial interpretation nature in trial practice, and the conditions under which the SPC issue judicial documentations instead of formal judicial interpretations. In particular, the extent to which the judicial documentations can influence the adjudication of the courts is to be addressed in an empirical approach. To investigate the changing structure of the SPC’s legislative function after the adoption of the Guiding Cases System in 2010. This is because the guiding cases, as empirical research shows, play a significant legislative role in trial practice (Sichuan High People’s Court, 2013). The outcome of the objective is to discover the extent to which the internal structure of the SPC’s legislative function has been changed and its potential impact on the effectiveness of judicial interpretations in reality. To understand the weight of judicial interpretations in the Chinese legal system compared with other sources of laws, and their relationship with other categories of Chinese laws in trial practice.

11635116.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
11635116.value: Although it is generally assumed that the judiciary is not an organ set up primarily for the purpose of making law but for deciding disputes based on pre-existing laws, it is perceived in the context of China that the Supreme People’s Court (SPC) has been playing a primarily legislative role to great effect in reform-era China since the Standing Committee of National People’s Congress (NPCSC) delegated the power of judicial interpretation to the SPC in 1981. Despite the fact that this is often criticized as unconstitutional as it would appear that the SPC is encroaching on the legislative power according to the Constitution, the legislative function of the SPC in the form of judicial interpretations has been formally institutionalized by the NPC in its amendments of the Legislation Law in 2015. Nevertheless, in terms of the SPC’s judicial interpretations as clearly stipulated in the Provisions on the Judicial Interpretation Work 2007, very little empirical analysis has been carried out on the effectiveness of these judicial interpretations; for example, in what ways and under what conditions are different types of judicial interpretations applied effectively by local courts in comparison with corresponding national laws in trial practice. In addition, for those judicial documentations of a judicial interpretation nature, although they do not have the same legal force as judicial interpretations they do play a significant but distinctive role in the adjudication of local courts. Furthermore, after the adoption of the Guiding Case System in 2010 the SPC became able to interpret provisions of national laws relating to a case by attaching a part to the Guiding Case called “Main Points of Adjudication”. Nonetheless, it is unclear the extent to which this can influence the function of the SPC’s judicial interpretations. This project, therefore, will employ empirical methods beyond the literature review to collect and analyze resources on which we will build a conditional theory in the context of China. It will consider the mechanism and conditions through and under which the SPC’s judicial interpretations are effective in trial practice. Further, it will focus on the processes, mechanisms and conditions for the implementation of the SPC’s judicial interpretations in specific contexts rather than the grander theoretical claims which are merely based on normative views. Emphasis will be placed on the interactive relationship between empirical work and theoretical development in China. Abstract: This project is to employ empirical methods beyond the literature review to collect and analyze resources on which we will build a conditional theory of the effectiveness of the judicial interpretations of the Supreme People’s Court (SPC) in the context of China. It will consider the mechanism and conditions through and under which the SPC’s judicial interpretations are effective in trial practice. Further, it will focus on the processes, mechanisms and conditions for the implementation of the SPC’s judicial interpretations in specific contexts rather than the grander theoretical claims which are merely based on normative views. 摘要： 本課題將在現有研究的基礎上，結合經驗性的方法來研究中國最高人民法院所頒佈的司法解釋在審判實踐中的實效性，並嘗試構建一種中國語境下的理論，從而更有效地解釋司法解釋在審判實踐中的獨特功能和作用。其中，該研究不局限於一般的宏觀性及規範性論述，進一步具體研究最高人民法院在中國制度語境下頒佈司法解釋的具體機制和過程，以及在何種條件下所頒佈的司法解釋具有或者不具有實效性。

11635116.label: Realisation of objectives
11635116.value: This project has employed empirical methods to explore the effectiveness of judicial interpretation as a formal document with a legal status, and these informal judicial documents in China’s legal system. It has now achieved the specific objectives as listed in the original research plan. Specifically, this project used a combination of empirical methods in the form of ethnographic observations, the extensive interviews with the judges and lawyers, and the contextual analysis of the documents collected during the fieldwork. This research project was greatly facilitated by a group of senior Chinese judges attending the Supreme People’s Court (SPC)’s common law training program in Hong Kong, in which I was participating. Through my connections with these judges, I conducted fieldwork in the SPC, an Intermediate People’s Court (in FS city), and three grassroots level courts (in SZ, HZ, and FS cities). In order to better understand the role of judicial interpretations and documents in the process of adjudicating disputes, in particular the ways and the extent to which judges refer to these documents explicitly or implicitly when handling cases, I conducted fieldwork in the courts in FS city in June 2019 and was allowed to sit in the courtrooms to conduct ethnographic observation of 16 court hearings. As recording of court proceedings is not allowed, I took notes from the observation. I also conducted semi-structured interviews with 13 judges immediately after the court hearings and asked them how and why they used relevant judicial interpretations and documents when making a decision. I interviewed twenty judges and ten lawyers outside the courtroom. The interviews with the lawyers were conducted before or after hearings during my fieldwork. Given the sensitive nature of the topic, I only took notes during the interviews, with the consent of the interviewees, instead of recording them. As my field sites were located in Beijing and South China, in which there were regional differences, to verify the data collected during the fieldwork was not regionally unique I interviewed fifteen more judges from the provinces of Jiangsu, Guangxi, Hebei, Jilin, Chongqing, and Zhejiang by phone. Each interview took between 30 minutes and one hour, depending on the extent to which the interviewees had considered and applied judicial interpretations and documents in legal proceedings. During the fieldwork at the courts, I was able to access relevant unpublished judicial documents produced in SZ city and in HZ city. Primarily based on data analysis, it was found that the SPC’s judicial interpretation, in contrast to its other forms of interpretation through judicial documents, was legally institutionalized as a type of formal statutory law that can be cited, like other statutory laws, by judges during judicial decision-making. The SPC’s Provisions on the Work Concerning Judicial Interpretation 2007 关于司法解释工作的规定 (hereafter Provisions) clearly stipulate that judicial interpretation can be classified into four types—“Interpretation” 解释, “Provisions” 规定, “Reply” 批复 and “Decision” 决定. Specifically, on the issue of how to apply a particular law or how to apply judicial interpretation on a specific type of case or issue in the administration of justice, the Interpretation type shall be adopted. Regulations or opinions that need to be formulated in the administration of justice based on the legislative spirit shall adopt the Provisions format. With regard to judicial interpretation formulated to request the higher people’s courts or the military courts of the People’s Liberation Army for direction on the specific application of laws in a trial, the Reply format shall be adopted. Finally, with regard to the amendment or repeal of a judicial interpretation, the Decision format shall be adopted. In this regard, legally speaking, the SPC’s judicial interpretation has become a type of statutory law and, by its very nature, has been distinguished from other judicial documents that fall outside the scope of formal statutory laws. As a common practice since 1997, all formal judicial interpretations have been issued seriatim with a formal document number, “Fa Shi 法释 [Calendar Year] Number”, which is different to other judicial documents, “Fa Fa 法发 [Calendar Year] Number.” In accordance with the Provisions, the SPC has been able to perform a judicial lawmaking function in practice through the formal mechanism of judicial interpretations. Although the judicial document is by no means a legal basis for adjudication, it is still an essential tool for the adjudicative and administrative work of the courts. Despite the SPC’s judicial interpretation becoming a formal law, the SPC still retains its lawmaking practice of interpreting laws in the form of judicial documents, which are called “judicial interpretation documents” 司法解释性质文件 and have a similar lawmaking function to the SPC’s formal judicial interpretations. In fact, after decades of the SPC interpreting laws on the basis of the NPCSC’s delegation, in 2011, the NPCSC made wholesale changes to the legislation work plan to safeguard the uniformity of the legislative regime. Such action forced the SPC to conduct a systematic cleanup of all its formal judicial interpretations and informal judicial documents. In particular, the local courts, which had not been delegated any judicial lawmaking authority by the NPCSC, have been explicitly prohibited from creating documents that involve judicial lawmaking activities, such as interpreting statutory laws. Apart from judicial interpretations that had been effective, the SPC retained a large number of informal judicial documents. These were finalized and officially published by the SPC in the Compilation of the SPC’s Judicial Interpretations 最高人民法院司法解释汇编 (1949-2013). This retention of previous judicial documents was tacitly agreed to by the NPCSC, which indicates that the NPCSC, at that time, had endorsed the SPC’s judicial lawmaking practice through the mechanism of judicial documents. Moreover, the SPC’s informal judicial documents function as a bridge between law and politics. On the one hand, given that a judicial document is non-statutory, the SPC as the CCP’s political subordinate, is able to implement the will of higher political authorities through the flexible mechanism of judicial documents. On the other hand, given the higher adjudicative status of the SPC, it is understandable that the SPC’s judicial documents, which involve judicial lawmaking activities, will be observed by the lower courts when adjudicating relevant cases. However, judicial documents, though effectively implemented in trial, actually inhabit a twilight zone due to their lack of an explicit constitutional status. Furthermore, judicial documents have become a practical and effective way for local courts to engage in judicial lawmaking enterprises, to respond to dynamic local politics, and accommodate subnational diversity, as long as they do not obviously contravene the statutory laws and are not subject to populist pressure. Given the changing local conditions, in the cracks and joints of the SPC’s rule governing subordinate courts, we can find judicial documents developed by the local courts themselves.

11635116.label: Major findings and research outcome
11635116.value: It's found that, in Chinese law, constitutionally speaking, the courts must apply statutory laws, including the SPC’s judicial interpretations, as they are legally formalized for judicial decision-making. However, the SPC’s judicial interpretations and judicial documents play different roles in China’s adjudication. The case of China shows that, given the lack of case law and the existence of an instrumentalist legislative system composed of thousands of statutory laws covering almost all aspects of society, the judicial lawmaking function has been performed without cases and without congressional delegation. In this authoritarian society, given the political dominance of the ruling Party, the courts, as both an adjudicator and Party subordinate, must be able to meet the overarching legalistic requirements to adjudicate in accordance with statutory laws and efficiently and flexibly respond to authoritarian politics. Due to the lack of case law, judicial documents become informal state laws, which exist in a twilight zone with no congressional delegation. This has become the primary form of judicial lawmaking by the courts, apart from SPC’s formal judicial lawmaking in the form of judicial interpretation with congressional delegation. Due to the exclusive congressional delegation to the SPC to engage in judicial interpretation, local courts are prohibited by the SPC from creating judicial lawmaking documents. However, politically, the court, as the Party’s political subordinate, may produce relevant non-statutory internal documents for lower courts. It is a constitutional requirement that the superior court shall guide the trial work of lower level courts. As such, it is not surprising that local superior courts produce relevant non-statutory documents to guide the trial work of lower courts, performing a judicial lawmaking function in disguise. To distinguish these documents from those that are prohibited, local courts normally circumvent the rules and use different titles and forms, including the summary of minutes produced by court judicial committees (or subcommittees) or tribunals, often after a professional meeting attended by representative senior judges and professionals. Functionally, the judicial documents fill legal loopholes and reflect the practical social needs of localities where the relevant uniform statutory law is ambiguous or insufficient. The research outcome of this project has been finalized, and is forthcoming on the journal – Modern China.

11635116.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11635116.value: With the development of China’s legal system, in particular its various case law systems as emphasized recently by the SPC, the factors that influence the operation of judicial interpretations and documents may change further. This largely depends on the extent to which the courts could become independent, and the judges could make judicial decisions independently. Given that China has been attempting to build up an authoritarian legal system that fits with the leadership of the CCP, more empirical research will be needed in order to address the relevant new issues concerning the sources of law, that arise from the practice of Chinese law.

11635116.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11635116.value: The results of the project have provided a comprehensive view of the effectiveness of judicial interpretations and documents in China’s adjudication from comparative and empirical perspectives, which is beyond most of the literature whose focus has been on the grand theoretical claims associated with this subject. Furthermore, the project is of significant practical value and will help legal professionals to understand how various judicial interpretations and documents are employed in China. Moreover, it proposes a twilight theory of China’s judicial documents, explaining why this judicial lawmaking practice exists in a twilight zone between legal and illegal and why it is suitable for China’s authoritarian legal regime with political resilience. This has made a significant contribution to the literature on Chinese law, comparative law, and China studies.

11657816.value: 迷惘的移民歷程:年青三峽移民的社會記憶,雙重身份與求生策略

11657816.label: Realisation of objectives
11657816.value: The four stated objectives have been satisfactorily achieved. OBJECTIVE 1: To identify the changing social/political/economic/cultural experiences of young-adult migrants in Guangdong, Shanghai and Sichuan(or Hubei) over more than a decade of resettlement from 2000 to the present. FINDINGS: The present study finds that the context of Guangdong constitutes at least two peculiar features which complicate the young adults informants’ experiences of migration as compared to those relocated to the other areas, such as Shanghai and Hubei. First, the weather, language, and local culture (e.g., the cuisine and gender stereotypes) of Guangdong are starkly different from those of Chongqing, and second, the human geography in Guangdong is significantly more complex, due to rapid urbanization and improved railway links in this coastal province. As promised in the proposal that the PI would write a “working paper” to “highlight the need for further research on the changing social, political, economic and cultural contexts of young-adult migrants (aged 18-29) in Guangdong, Shanghai and Sichuan (or Hubei) over more than a decade of resettlement”. This promise is delivered in the PUBLICATION of “JCAD article”*. OBJECTIVE 2: To obtain oral histories and personal stories in general, and ‘lifescape’ narratives in particular, from interviews with young-adult migrants who are in Guangdong, Chongqing(the returnees), Shanghai and Sichuan(or Hubei). FINDINGS: Oral histories were solicited from a sample of TDG young adult migrants from different areas (48 from Guangdong, 22 from Shanghai and 18 from Hubei). Unlike, what were identified in the previous studies on TDG migrants which emphasized mainly the negative side of migration, and neglected the voice of returnees who had moved back to Chongqing, the present study finds that the young adult migrants manifest a strong sentiment of “ambivalence” towards migration. Such feeling usually comprises complex feelings that transcend simply maladjustment-induced negative sentiments. In the PUBLICATION of “China Review article”, the PI pioneers the discussion of the findings in a way to examine the deeper political implications of the existence of such an ambivalently mobile population to the authoritarian state. Emphasis is placed on the clandestine alignment of the subjectivities of the young-adult migrants and the state policies to facilitate urbanization and regulate economic development. OBJECTIVE 3: based on 2), to explore and compare the respondents’ social memories and experiences, perceptions of bicultural identity, and livelihood strategies. AND OBJECTIVE 4: based on 2) and 3), to examine the commonalities and differences in the displacement experiences of young-adult migrants in Guangdong, Chongqing, Shanghai and Sichuan(or Hubei); and draw implications in our current theoretical understanding of ‘project-induced forced migration. FINDINGS: Based on their testimonies of social memory, bicultural identity and livelihood strategy, the present study finds that the young-adult TGD migrants in Guangdong maintain an “ambivalence” about their migration experience, and are generally caught in-between being “a stranger and local”, “a Guangdonger and Chongqinger”, and “a sojourner and dweller”. These accounts are contradistinctive to those of the first-generation TGD migrants in Guangdong as well as in other areas. The older migrants generally feel that the migration was “forced”, and possess a strong self-identification as Chongqingers as they usually claim that their “roots” are not in Guangdong but Chongqing. Moreover, unlike their older counterparts, young-adult migrants’ post-migration dissatisfaction in Guangdong is said not to be a result of their exposure to the major impoverishment risks of landlessness, joblessness, homelessness, and marginalisation as widely reported during fieldwork and in the literature. Instead, their dissatisfaction (or satisfaction) is found to hinge upon the interaction of a different set of factors, including past discrimination in school; nostalgic links with their hometowns; relationship with local government officials; education quality; native origin of one’s courtship partner; quality of local connections; accent accuracy, or future career opportunities. Since all these factors are either subjective or subject to change in accordance with different times, contexts, and individual’s life-courses, the post-migration experience of young-adult migrants are always tainted with an “ambivalence”. They have yet to have a static viewpoint on whether the migration has brought about misfortunates or opportunities to the life of oneself and his/her family. One should note that one possible but not probable mobile route manifested by the young adult migrants in Guangdong – which was totally unexpected during the proposal stage – is their participation in and support of collective petitioning activities in Beijing. Thanks for the information I solicited from several young adult migrants I met in Guangdong, I managed to explore the processes whereby TGD migrants from all over the country selected and played out particular tactics and framings from societal “repertories of contention” to fight against the repressive state of Beijing in mid-2017 - see the PUBLICATION of “Mobilization article”. On the theoretical front, as suggested in the proposal, previous research on project-induced migration tends to be atheoretical, and scholars have complained that no systematic conceptual framework has been designed specifically to address forced migration driven by a development project. The present study thus provides a valuable conceptual framework of “ambivalent mobilities” to address the understudied topic of development-induced forced migration in the interdisciplinary field of migration/refugee studies. *Here the PI would like register an apologetic note that the acknowledgment note of this publication has not been published in a way to acknowledge the present GRF. The reason is that the first-and-corresponding author (PI’s student) made a mistake of missing to acknowledge the present GRF. The PI realized this mistake two months before the article published, and emailed the Chief Editor of JCAD immediately to request for a rectification. Unfortunately, due to the miscommunications between the first-and-corresponding author and the Chief Editor, the mistake was not rectified. It was really an unfortunate incident as the paper was explicitly promised in the proposal, and so DIRECTLY RELATED to the GRF project. I attached my letter of requesting change of the acknowledgment note to my publication in Part C. And, taking into account the PI's will and efforts to acknowledge the present GRF, the PI indicated “yes” in acknowledging the fund for this publication in Part C.

11657816.label: Major findings and research outcome
11657816.value: The major findings suggest that the feeling of “ambivalence” toward migration has made the young-adult migrants in Guangdong a partially uprooted population with more complex movement imaginaries than their first-generation counterparts; in other words, young-adult migrants express a higher uncertainty of their next destination. One should note that young-adult migrants in Guangdong have very different migration experiences than those conventionally defined as forced migrants as usually portrayed in migration/refugee studies. Comparatively speaking, young-adult TDG migrants in Guangdong feel less bitter than refugees or diaspora who excelled abroad because their return route “back home” is always a possibility. Some informants even express strong view of returning to Chongqing and consider their native home as having better air and water quality, social connections; and to some, even better welfare and supportive policies. However, these imaginaries of return are usually juxtaposed by certain upsides of staying in Guangdong such as “Guangdong is more [economically] open than our old native home”; or “Guangdong has more [economic] opportunities for the next generation”. Against such feeling of “ambivalence” it is common to hear non-high school informants express: “Everywhere is the same”; or, “Everywhere is a foreign place” (chuchu shi yixiang). Therefore, compared to older migrants, and probably the locals as well, young-adult migrants in Guangdong have richer movement imaginaries with a more “ready-to-move-on” inclination.

11657816.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11657816.value: - A more rigorous comparative analysis between the young adult migrants in Shanghai and Hubei can be conducted in the future. - The post-migration experiences of young adult migrants in areas beyond Guangdong, Shanghai and Hubei can be conducted in the future. - The present study has marked an important stepping stone for understanding the concept of “project-induced forced migration” in the interdisciplinary field of migration/refugee studies. Further theoretical deliberation of the concept can be conducted in the future.

11657816.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
11657816.value: The Three Gorges Dam project (1994–2009) in Chongqing of China created 1.35 million forced migrants. As the region next to the reservoir could not accept all the displaced, 96,000 were relocated to 11 provinces/cities. Among these “out-bound” (waiqian) migrants, 9,007 were moved 2,300 km away to coastal Guangdong during 2000–2004. Through soliciting testimonies from dozens of young-adult “dam migrants” (currently aged 18–39) in Guangdong, this study identifies a commonly shared ambivalence over the meaning of displacement such that the informants – after more than a decade of resettlement – still maintain different degrees of feeling both “a stranger and local”, both “a Guangdonger (Guangdong ren) and Chongqinger (Chongqing ren)”, and both “a sojourner and dweller”. It is argued that they possess more complex movement imaginaries than older, first-generation migrants, and experience a more complex mode of marginalization both in Guangdong and other areas such as Shanghai and Hubei. One important, political implication of the findings is that the existence of an ambivalently mobile population echoes the emerging governmentality scholarship on the migrant experience.

11658816.label: Project Objectives
11658816.value: To historicize the initiation, design, and construction of grand theaters in China. To investigate and evaluate the public space delivered by these grand theaters. To decode and summarize the architectural design language of the new generation of grand theaters in China.

11658816.label: Realisation of objectives
11658816.value: This research sets up three objectives. For Objective 1 'To historicize the initiation, design, and construction of grand theaters in China', we have written the history of performance building from the early 20th century to the 21st century. Those cities usually started with informal teahouse to a simple stage with audience. In the periods of National and Communist government, auditoriums for political gathering were built. In the 21st century, the performance buildings evolved to "grand theaters". Our targeted investigation focuses on 13 cities, first tier, second tier and third tier, from coastal to hinterland. More cities have been observed with the similar method. For Objective 2 'To investigate and evaluate the public space delivered by these grand theaters', we have investigated public space of grand theaters in all targeted cities. Their relationship with the theaters and cities are recorded and analyzed. We have also interviewed some managers of theaters, to see the challenges of using the public space by the members of public. For Objective 3 'To decode and summarize the architectural design language of the new generation of grand theaters in China' , we have collected drawings and visited the site of grand theaters in the targeted cities. Moreover, we have interviewed designers of some theaters, for example, gmp and East China Architectural Design Institute in Shanghai. We read the articles of designers and understand their design intentions and methods. These intentions are compared with the real effect on site.

11658816.label: Major findings and research outcome
11658816.value: This research has set up a database of grand theaters since 1998, when the first grand theater was completed through international design competition (Shanghai Grand Theater). We have collected total 105 grand theaters, each consisting of 2-3 halls, with one hall over 1200 seats. We carry on historical study of performance buildings from the early 20th century to the 21st century, and observe how performance buildings evolving from simple stage to a complicated complex of entertainment, social event and city brand nowadays. Studies of performance buildings and grand theaters are integrated with the viewpoints of social change, technological advancement and the growth of people's freedom and wealth. Through our investigation, the trend of grand theater construction and interaction between buildings and cultural production in China are illuminated with the theory of globalization, commercialization, consumerism and cross-border design. Building design language is linked with the symbolization the designers used to convey the meaning of the clients. In analyzing design languages, we particularly highlight the impact of international design and mechanism brought to the Chinese cities. We also study the effectiveness of grand theaters by making statistics of their performances, how many and what types of show in months and years. These data illustrate the popularity and degree of convenience of the theaters. They can somehow explain the cultural phenomenon of Chinese cities. One book "Grand Theater Urbanism – Chinese cities in the 21st century" and five papers are published. In this book, grand theater is linked with "urbanism", instead of conventional study of sightline, acoustics and interior theatrical design. The publications timely fill the gap of China's cultural mega-structure heat in the 21st century.

11658816.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
11658816.value: This topic is worth deepening in two direction. One is to enlarge the targets to more city types in the east and west, old prosperous and newly emerging cities. Another is to compare with cities in overseas, with similar ambitions and challenges. Through the further study, one can see how the cultural mega-structures influence the urban development and people's life. It will help the decision makers to use the tax-payers' money in a more effective and useful way.
