12622616.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12622616.value: Since the early 2000s, the creative industries in Hong Kong, and the cultural industries that depend on them, have found themselves at the centre of attention of socio-political and economic discussion, in both the public and academic spheres; they have become a major issue in governmental policy-making, and the bearers of much hope and many expectations. Nonetheless, little is actually known about the stakeholders at the core of this discussion, the individual creatives. What are the living conditions of visual artists working and living in Hong Kong? How do they go about their work, how do they earn money, how do they live their lives? In short: How do they ‘survive’? At this point, there are no comprehensive, systematic data available on the economic livelihood of the creative population in Hong Kong. For example, the traditional employment surveys conducted, e.g. by universities do not necessarily apply to the alternative modes of making a living prevalent in the visual arts. Similarly, other common key indicators inadequately reflect the professional reality of the creative and cultural sectors. This lack of comprehensive statistics is not merely a problem for policy-making and educational development in an area of significant market potential, but may also obscure more problematic socio-political developments. For example, arts programmes traditionally have a very high ratio of female students, yet the number of practicing female creatives in Hong Kong appears particularly low. This may be a sign of structural/systemic gender discrimination, yet no hard evidence of this is available. Accordingly, the proposed project ‘Creative Livelihoods’ aims first to produce a significant body of statistical data about the economic circumstances of creatives in Hong Kong, by means of a cross-sectional survey of graduates from tertiary creative undergraduate programmes since 2001. Its second stage will be a detailed look at the situation of female visual artists in Hong Kong, to determine their particular situation and contribution to the local creative ecology. The data, once evaluated and interpreted, will be the basis for a comprehensive report that will for the first time give a full picture of the livelihoods of the creative talent of Hong Kong. This academic and administrative research will provide much-needed resources to enhance planning and decision-making at the programme, university, and UGC levels, and by governmental, educational, professional, and cultural stakeholders. 從2000年代初開始，香港的創意產業以及與之唇齒相依的文化產業，不論在大眾輿論還是學術界，都逐漸成為社會政治及經濟討論中炙手可熱的議題，不但政府制定政策時會以此為考慮重點，外界亦對此寄予厚望。不過，各方對這些討論焦點所在的持分者──從事創意行業的個體，卻知之甚少。在香港工作並生活的視覺藝術家的生活條件如何？他們到底如何工作，收入多少，如何過活？簡而言之：他們如何｢生存」？ 至今為止，香港就創意藝術人群的經濟狀況尚未有全面、系統的調查數據。例如，各間大學等機構進行的傳統就業調查，不一定適用於視覺藝術圈常見的另類職涯模式，同樣，其他常見的重要指標，亦不足以反映創意及文化產業這門專業的現實就業狀況。 由於缺乏全面數據，當局制定政策以及發展相關教育時，不但無法充分發掘相關市場的潛力，甚至會引發社會政治發展的問題。例如，藝術課程向來女生比例甚高，但似乎香港從事創意工作的女性數目卻極少，當中也許涉及結構／系統性的性別歧視問題，但一直沒有實質證據支持。 因此，｢創意事業職涯」計劃以2001年後的專上院校創意學士學位課程畢業生為對象，開展跨界別調查，希望整理出有用的統計數據，藉此了解香港創意人士的經濟狀況。計劃第二階段會詳細研究香港女性視覺藝術人士的情況，以總結出她們獨有的狀況，以及對本地創意生態的貢獻。 計劃所得數據經過評估和詮釋後，將用作撰寫一份全面報告，首次把香港創意人才職涯的整體情況呈現出來。這個學術及行政研究將提供重要資源，讓政府、教育機構、專業人士、文化業界持分者在課程、大學、教資會三個層面上均能作出妥善規劃及明智決策。

12622616.label: Realisation of objectives
12622616.value: Objective 1: Through the efforts of the project team it could be established that between 2001 and 2015 a total of 4,953 students graduated from the six creative undergraduate programmes under study in this survey. Of those graduates, 3,432 valid contacts were collected through archival research from public sources, despite all best efforts the project team could not establish large proportions of the graduation cohorts of PolyU’s School of Design from the early years 2001 to 2007. In total, 585 eligible graduates from the programmes under study subsequently completed the full survey of more than 80 questions regarding their livelihoods, resulting in a response rate of 11.8%. Additionally, approx. 1,100 graduates submitted partial questionnaires. While these responses may not be considered systematically, they provided supporting insights nonetheless. Proportionally, the survey received the lowest feedback from graduates of PolyU School of Design with only 4% of the eligible population responding – or even having been contacted. Accordingly, any data on the BDes scheme must be interpreted with great caution as the sample size needs to generally be considered too small. Methodologically, the inclusion of the BA in Fine Arts programme of HKAS in the survey was intended as a control group for comparative purposes only, as in many ways – most notably for its funding – it’s distinct from the other programmes surveyed. Therefore, also the results of HKAS – if shown – are highlighted in light grey colour and will equally be considered for information/comparison only. With a response rate of 9.8% for that constituency, the numbers for HKAS should however be more representative than those of PolyU. Thus, if the responses for BDes (PolyU) and BAFA (HKAS) are taken out of the formal statistical considerations of the survey results, a total of 454 valid responses were received, representing a response rate of 17.8% of the eligible remaining population. This allows for a statistical significance of ±5% across the total population. However, as more responses were received from early career practitioners than from their more experienced counterparts, deductions especially on established career creatives generally were considered with more care. Objective 2: The initial data collected through an online data was carefully cleaned up, statistically analysed and interpreted for their possible meaning. The original research proposal suggested then to conduct a series of focus group interviews, which however turned out to not be feasible; in general graduates approached felt uneasy to openly talk about livelihood matters – including e.g. salary etc. – publicly., Thus, a series of 22 individual interviews with graduates from different programmes in various career stages, and further 12 individual interviews with other stakeholders from the industry (employers, gallerist, academics, etc.) subsequently helped to put the quantitative findings into perspective. All this information was compiled in a comprehensive report, which was subsequently sent directly to various government agencies, academic institutions and other stakeholders. The same report was also provided for download from a dedicated project website (creative-livelihoods.org) that – through its design – additionally encouraged interactive engagement with the data. Objective 3: In principle, also this objective was fully achieved, though – as is probably the nature of this kind of questions – the quantitative and qualitative findings from the project didn’t produce as clear a result as would’ve been desirable. Despite the ambition to find conclusive data for the existence – or absence – of gender-based discrimination in the creative and cultural sectors in Hong Kong, the findings turned out to complex. In terms of financial compensation female creative graduates on average earn 6% less to their male counterparts; while that’s obviously not desirable, it’s a comparatively little “salary gap” (e.g. according to HK’s Census Office women on average get more than 20% lower pay than their male colleagues) that may be the result of factors other than systemic discrimination. On the other hand, female visual artists are grossly under-represented in essentially all instances of public professional recognition, be it exhibitions, events, awards or else. Also, female graduates are twice as likely as their male counterparts to leave creative practice behind and to move on to either careers in teaching or in (arts) administration. There are more indicators that suggest that discriminatory mechanisms may be at work, but no ultimately conclusive correlation could be found. Thus, though the local creative and cultural sectors do certainly show signs of possible gender-related bias, it may not amount to full-fledged systemic discrimination. Objectives 4 & 5: The final two objectives were achieved in as much as their aims were to “stimulate new educational policies” and to “suggest areas for policy making for the improvement of Visual Arts in HK”; this the project did achieve, leading to a number of on going new policy developments, changes in educational programmes etc. by different stakeholders. E.g. following its completion the Creative Livelihoods report was widely disseminated to creative economies stakeholders. These submissions were followed up by in-person presentations and extensive explanatory discussions, and feedback from stakeholders was always very appreciative. Many parties subsequently took the report findings into particular consideration, though the exact degree of impact is often difficult to determine. In terms of educational development, HKBU's Academy of Visual Arts developed and got approved a substantial revision of its undergraduate programme in Visual Arts that took into consideration many of the research findings and was highly commended by reviewers during the accreditation and an Academic Consultation Panel, which scrutinised the programme's implementation this year. Other sister institutions have taken on board other recommendations from the report, though not always as comprehensively. For the sector beyond tertiary institutions, as a result of the report and its findings on visual arts education, the project PI was invited to serve on HKEAA’s HKDSE Visual Arts Subject Committee, which develops policies and standards for HK’s secondary school visual arts assessments. However, to what extent and/or effect this research in particular contributed to any discourse and/or new policies across the field in HK is difficult and probably too early to tell. In terms of the wider ecology the report e.g. very specifically pointed out that the results of the annual HK Artist of the Year awards were heavily skewed towards male artists. While HKADC officially insisted that the awards strictly only reflected the quality of the work submitted, in the year following the report’s circulation the cohort of recipients turned out to be gender-balanced. Similarly, the report criticised HKWKA for the selection of exclusively male representatives for the bi-annual Venice Biennale in recent years. In summer 2018 it was announced that a female artist was selected for the 2019 Biennale. Unofficial sources hinted that for public pressure (incl. this report) “the only un-negotiable criterion for selection was that it had to be a woman”, but neither have any publicly available selection criteria been formally amended, nor can our report alone claim to have had this impact. Despite these difficulties, we believe the project has significantly contributed to the local discourse, and supported a gradual on-going change in attitude and awareness. Various follow-up projects have come from it, and a follow-up report to systematically document any changes is planned for 2021 – five years after the first survey was conducted.

12622616.label: Major findings and research outcome
12622616.value: The ‘Creative Livelihoods’ project aimed at producing a significant body of statistical data about the economic circumstances of creatives in Hong Kong, by means of a cross-sectional survey of graduates from publicly funded tertiary creative undergraduate programmes since 2001. The data, once evaluated and interpreted, became the basis for a comprehensive report with three key findings: - while gender-based income inequality in the creative and cultural industries in HK is less articulated than in other fields locally and less than in comparable sectors abroad, female visual artists are significantly under-recognised in professional contexts; - while income levels of visual artists are on average better than commonly assumed, they are in general not high enough to support a reasonably comfortable professional career based on a creative practice; - creative education in Hong Kong before university-level has very little impact on career development of visual artists. After its completion the report was widely disseminated to creative economies stakeholders (governmental: the HKSAR’s Secretary of Finance, Home Affairs Bureau, Legco members, HKADC etc.; professional: M+, Tai Kwun, Art Basel HK, ARTHQ etc.; NGOs: AAA, Robert Ho Foundation, etc.; academic: local universities). These submissions were followed up by in-person presentations and extensive explanatory discussions. The report was additionally published on the project website where it has been viewed more than 2,900 times (30 June 2019). The report was cited repeatedly by different speakers at various events like the seminar “Art Labour – Middle-Aged Women and Neoliberalism” at Arts & Culture Outreach in December 2018, or Asia Art Archive’s “Women in Art” series all through early summer 2018, and was exhibited physically e.g. in the curated exhibition Show Art’s Hand: An Investigation on Art Labour (Oil Street Gallery Hong Kong from 12 October 2018 to 6 January 2019). It has also been cited locally – e.g. in Apple Daily on 29 January 2019 – and internationally – e.g. in Hergen Wöbke. Studio Berlin III. Berlin: Institute for Strategic Development, June 2018. Findings of the Creative Livelihoods project were the basis for the academic workshop Mapping Creativity, an associate programme of Art Basel Hong Kong in March 2019 which had the aim to outline new perspectives for governance at the intersections of policy making and creative economies.

12622616.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12622616.value: The previous findings – and activities following thereof – suggest three main paths for further research in the field: 1. Continued in-depth research on the background and mechanisms of gender-related representation in the creative and cultural sectors. The Livelihoods project team has already begun a follow-up project in association with Art Basel Hong Kong that uses big data from Art Basel’s institutional records to statistically analyse patterns in international artists’ representations by gender, age, and geographic origin. 2. Continued development of new policies for the creative and cultural sectors and continuous monitoring of their implementations and subsequent impact. Initial steps towards this direction were already during the workshop Mapping Creativity in March 2019, which resulted in a call to develop new definitions and measurements for the creative economies. A follow up conference and workshop will be held in Berlin in October 2019. 3. More specifically to advance new educational formats for creative practices at and beyond university-level. I’ve co-initiated an international consortium of art schools with this specific intention. A formal 5-years agreement for this purpose will be signed in December 2019 in Zurich, Switzerland.

12625716.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12625716.value: The proposed project aims at reconstructing the history of mass production of bronzes in China between 500 and 300 BC. Barbara Keyser and Robert Bagley have reconstructed the pattern-block method of bronze casting in approximately 500 BC, which lays the foundation of this study. However, there are various other methods of mass production unknown to scholars, including the component-model and multiple-transfer methods, altogether proposed as a new hypothesis established by the principal investigator’s (PI). Bronze casters in this period had adopted these methods in producing bronze mirrors, vessels, and sculptures. To prepare the clay models and molds for mass-producing these bronzes, casters had to manipulate multiple transfers between the models and molds formed by clay components, which were eventually shown as delicate componential surface decorations on the bronzes. Within these technological contexts, bronzes whose shapes and decorations are completely identical were cast, and the components of their surface decorations would be identical to those on other bronzes. The operation of their foundries also desired a higher efficiency of production, intelligent division of labor, and an assembly-line method. Active economic activities, a booming population, a convenient transportation system, and high social mobility are some of the reasons explaining the mass production and consumption of bronzes. Future scholars of this field cannot ignore the facts that mass production of bronzes had significantly shaped socio-economic activities during this period. However, it is very difficult to locate evidence of mass-produced bronzes since they had been scattered throughout the world after over 2,000 years. The PI has already identified thirteen groups of mass-produced mirrors but more evidence is needed to validate the hypothesis. The PI and two co-investigators (Co-I) propose to develop and improve four tools to efficiently collect more datasets of 3D models of bronzes to constitute the evidence. This study consequently requires an interdisciplinary approach by incorporating assistance from computer scientists. A portable 3D scanner, computer programs that automatically generate, superimpose, and match 3D models, and an online database are needed to enable experimentations to identify mass-produced bronzes and their identical components. We will make extensive research trips to museums and archaeological institutes to digitally record the bronzes of interest. Any 3D models of bronzes that superimpose perfectly during the experiments will prove that they were mass-produced in these foundries. The application of 3D technology to the field of mass production will inspire new methodologies in art historical and archaeological studies. 此研究計劃旨在重構公元前500-300年大規模生產中國青銅器的歷史。Barbara Keyser和Robert Bagley已重構了公元前500年青銅鑄造之模版生產法，為此研究計劃奠定基礎。但是，仍有許多大規模生產方法不為學界所知，包括塊模生產法、多次轉換法等，這些方法都是本計劃主要負責人新近提出的假設。於此期間(公元前500-300年)的青銅鑄匠採用了這些方法以生產銅鏡、銅容器、與其它銅像。大規模生產這些銅器需要先準備陶模與陶範，鑄匠要把塊模組合起來，製造大一點的模與範，也要控制在模與範之間的多次轉換。最後在銅器上的方塊紋表面裝飾就是由塊模組成的。於此技術背景下，形狀、紋飾完全相同的銅器就此鑄成，而其總體紋飾上的塊模紋飾亦可與其它銅器上的相同。其工場、熔爐的運作亦需要更有效率的生產、聰明絕頂的分工與流水線式系統。蓬勃的經濟，不斷膨脹的人口，更為便捷的交通系統，高度社會流動性，這些原因可解釋銅器的大規模生產與享用。將來的學者不能忽視銅器之大規模生產已深刻影響此期間的社會經濟活動。但是，要找出並證明大規模生產的銅器絕非易事，因為在這2000多年中，它們早已四散世界各地。本計劃主要負責人已找出13組大規模生產、一模一樣的銅鏡，但仍需更多證據去支持此假設。本計劃的三位負責人建議開發與改善4種工具去更有效率地搜集更多3D銅器模型以構成更多證據。故此研究需要跨學科的協助，猶其是電腦科學的協助。便攜式3D掃描器，可以自動生成、配對3D模型的電腦程式，加上網上數據庫，可以幫助進行試驗，從而找出大規模生產的銅器及其一模一樣的塊模。我們們會籌劃研究之旅，去博物館、考古所等去收集所需銅器的電子紀錄。試驗中若找到某銅器之3D模型與其它的完全吻合，即可證明它們是同一作坊、同一流水線生產出來的。3D技術之應用在大規模生產歷史研究中，將會揭示藝術史與考古研究的新路向。

12625716.label: Realisation of objectives
12625716.value: Thanks to the generous support of the RGC, our team has made a series of achievements, including technological invention, inviting museums and archaeological institutes to collaborate, conducting research travels and collecting data, and publication. We will report our accomplishments in this final report. Objectives 1 and 2 We have examined numerous artifacts which might have been mass-produced in ancient China. We generated 3D models of these artifacts when we accessed them and collected enough research data. After data collection, we studied how different bronze mass production methods developed in ancient times and how these products were disseminated. These fulfill objectives 1 and 2 by enriching the field of the history of mass production with the case study of ancient China and examining the distribution forms of bronzes in ancient East Asia. First of all, the PI devises two approaches to study the history of mass production. The first approach is to reconstruct the history of designs and manufacturing methods of ancient Chinese bronze mirrors and provide concrete examples for further discussion. The mirrors under consideration have been collected by a number of public and private museums and libraries interested in Chinese studies, and are the most actively exchanged items in the art market of ancient Chinese bronzes. They have not, however, received commensurate scholarly attention. No English scholarly monographs on the subject of Chinese mirrors exist. What the field has been lacking is both a greater level of detail in research that is based on concrete examples and a clearer theoretical underpinning, which the present study seeks to supply. The second approach is to examine the relationship between mass production and individual creativity. Through investigating every step of this phenomenon of the artistic mass production of mirrors, reconstructed from the concrete examples via the first approach, the PI discovered that the emphasis on efficiency and division of labor permitted every art producer who was involved in this process to creatively produce various designs and improve production steps through their expertise and experience accumulated from long-term training and professional practice. Producers were given opportunities to freely experiment with materials with which they were familiar. The production outcome, the mirrors, demonstrated their creativity and the freedom they enjoyed. Diversity and efficiency co-existed in the artistic mass production of mirrors, demonstrating that mass production commingled harmoniously with individual creativity and freedom in the case of ancient bronzes. These approaches have resulted in a number of publications. One of them is the monograph that the PI is preparing. He has also published another scholarly book, Universe within Inches: Bronze Mirrors Donated by Professor Mark Kai-keung with the Art Museum, Chinese University of Hong Kong. This book summarizes the approaches mentioned above and sheds light on how we can study the mass production methods of the mirror industry in the Eastern Zhou period China. Due to the limitation of the final approved funding, we could merely organize several research trips to collect data. We visited a number of museums in China, Japan, USA, and UK to collect research data and generate 3D models of the artifacts to enrich our database. We also conducted XRF tests of some of the mirrors stored in the Changsha and Yiyang museums, which share the same decorated models. We collaborated with the British Museum, Asian Art Museum of San Francisco, and Freer Gallery and they provided computer tomography (CT) scans and/or X-ray analysis data of the three identical quadrupeds. We will publish these findings in our upcoming publications. Objectives 3, 4, 5, and 6. As stated in the proposal, we will improve already-existing tools to enable us to efficiently locate and verify mass produced products. As the final report does not allow inserting any image/photo, reviewers please refer to the mid-term report: A. We have purchased some simple 3D scanners and experimented in improving their functions and performance. This enables us to efficiently 3D scan the desired artifacts into 3D models. Some of the 3D models have been uploaded to this website: http://www.makifit.com/BMBW/detail.html We will keep expanding this online database and display more 3D models of artifacts for public viewing. B. We have also explored using a precise computer-measuring method in the software called Meshlab to measure the length of the 3D model of a bronze quadruped. This quadruped is stored at the San Francisco Asian Art Museum, and there are two more quadrupeds, which may share the same decorated model but stored in two different museums, the British Museum and the Freer Gallery. If we want to compare whether they are identical, we can superimpose their 3D models into each other and measure them in the Meshlab to determine whether their length, height, width, and distance between corresponding patterns are exactly the same. We finally generated 3D models of the three quadrupeds and are preparing an article to publish our findings. C. In our online database, we have developed several functions to enable researchers to search for desired images and 3D models. These include searching artifacts by their accession numbers and/or website numbers within our website. For example, if researchers know the accession numbers of the artifacts, they can go to this page: http://www.makifit.com/BMBW/search.html to search for the corresponding numbers. Clicking into the numbers allows them to access the images and/or 3D models of the desired artifacts. D. We have also developed some 3D-printing technologies. Please refer to our article published in the journal Visual Computer. We can elaborate the 3D-printing technology to 3D print out artifacts to educate students. Problems encountered Originally we requested $1,783,735 HKD to conduct research travels and invent new tools, but the final approved amount is $770,480 HKD, though we obtained 4.5 points in the grading of our proposal. The significant reduction has seriously hindered our progress of technological development. Our team members have but to look for cheaper ways to accomplish our specified targets. When we were conducting our justified research trips, which have already been approved the RGC reviewers, the administrative unit suddenly rejected our reimbursement requests of about $100,000 HKD because they said that the trips were not included in the proposal. After we submitted the change-request application and the review committee said that they had already approved our requests in the proposal, the administrative unit had but to approve of our reimbursement requests. This has significantly hindered the research progress without any justified reason and threatened the researchers from conducting trips. We urge the administrative unit and RGC to review the process of reimbursement handling. Conclusion Our research findings have enriched the field of the history of mass production, as we have utilized numerous artifacts from ancient China to provide the evidence. These evidence will probably change some of our viewpoints towards the development of science and technology in ancient China, as mature mass production methods have been long readily available to bronze casters. We provide the interactive 3D models to serve as evidence, so that reviewers and eventually the general public can verify our observation results and findings. These constitute new methods in data collection and research result verification in art history. Art and museum professionals can also benefit from these trends of bridging art historical studies with computer science.

12625716.label: Major findings and research outcome
12625716.value: As stated in the article titled "The Component-Model Method of Mirror Manufacture in 300 BCE China,” published in Archives of Asian Art, the book chapter “Qingtongjing yanjiu de fansi yu fazhan” 青銅鏡研究的反思與發展 (Reflections on the field of bronze mirror studies and its development), and another book chapter “Chudi de daguimo shengchan – yi tongjing, sizhipin weili” 楚地的大規模生產——以銅鏡、絲織品為例 (Mass production in the Chu area – examples from bronze mirrors and textiles), we find out that in approximately 300 BCE, a new method was developed in the design and manufacturing technologies of the bronze mirror production industry in China that completely changed the ways in which producers cast mirrors. In 500 BCE, Shanxi Houma and numerous other places were undergoing a technical revolution in bronze casting. This revolution was a response to certain external economic factors, which had prompted the Houma producers to cast vessels much more efficiently and rapidly. As for mirrors, evidence indicates that producers started to decorate mirror models. They were no longer carving on a single mold for a single mirror. Instead, they replicated identical molds from the decorated model and cast several identical mirrors. Later in 300 BCE, producers referenced the previous methods, adopted the model replicating method, and also invented new techniques to efficiently produce multiple mirrors and simultaneously manage the diversity of decorations. We have discovered that this period’s mirrors could be categorized in multiple groups. There are mirrors that are completely identical, and partially identical but revealing individualized motifs. Certain mirrors possess decorative patterns that can be separated into two layers, the background pattern and main motifs. The motifs of each layer may possess identical counterparts on different mirrors. Such archaeologically excavated mirrors have been discovered across the East Asian continent, indicating an enormous output of the mirror industry during the 300 BCE era. We thus hypothesize the invention of the termed “component-model method” of mirror manufacturing. Our findings have been published in a number of scholarly book and journal articles and presented in various occasions. The scholarly book Universe within Inches: Bronze Mirrors Donated by Professor Mark Kai-keung provides a summary of the long-term development of the mirror designs and production technology. It also addresses the 3000-year history of mirrors in East Asia.

12625716.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12625716.value: 1. We propose at least three more approaches to investigate the history of mass production. First, mass production is not limited to the bronze industry. The textile, porcelain, bamboo and lacquer, and lapidary industries were all well-developed in ancient China and producers in each industry developed different mass production methods that catered to the concerns of design diversity and production efficiency. We can expand the history to cover a variety of materials. Second, we can study the history of mass production in different time periods. Third, we can compare the methods in China and outside China to generalize if there is any universality of mass production activities in human history. My scholarly book Universe within Inches indicates some of these approaches and we can further expand the studies. 2. The 3D technology can help with at least two more aspects. First, mass-produced products that may have shared the same size and shape can be proven by superimposing 3D models of the products together. This is an unprecedented investigation method and we can keep experimenting it. Second, other scholars can verify the results online and take further research actions when accessing the freely-rotatable 3D models of the artifacts.

12632816.label: Project Objectives
12632816.value: To study the most popular online discussion forums in mainland China and Hong Kong for theory-testing. Our empirical analysis of large-scale online data will shed light on the function of online discussion forums as integrators or polarizers of opinion expression. To examine how online discussion forums intervene in the developing tensions between Hong Kong and mainland China. To use combined methods of content analysis and network analysis in order to study the issue content of online discussions and the structure of users' reply networks, and the distribution of their attitudes. To examine the extent to which reply networks in these two forums are based on the bond of attitude-based homophily, and whether rates of homophily differ across different attitudes in online networks. From the policy perspective, this is particularly crucial for reducing opinion polarization and promoting political tolerance. To analyze the topical, source and linguistic characteristics of post content that may contribute to vibrant response from the online public. We will identify the "opinion leaders" both in terms of immediate impact and long-term, indirect influences. This will test classical public opinion and media theories in a new context of digital media. To investigate the online discussants' views on various approaches to ameliorate hostile speech, to reduce homophily, and to facilitate formation of crosscutting ties as a foundation of political tolerance. This has profound policy implications. To produce conference papers and journal articles.

12632816.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12632816.value: This study focuses on discursive struggles in online discussion forums over contentious issues that provoke major conflicts between Hong Kong and mainland China residents. While mass media rarely provide a space for individuals to express their views, computer-mediated discussion tools--above all, online discussion forums--serve not only as a platform for a wider range of actors to struggle over the conflicts, but also as an active agenda-setter and interpreter of such conflicts. Traditional survey methods and polls have not been able to grasp the general pattern and evolving dynamics of online conversation. This study will investigate two most important online forums (i.e. Hong Kong Golden Forum and the mainland's Tianya Club) to map out the structure of users' online networks and the distribution of their attitudes towards major conflictual issues. We will integrate network analysis and content analyses to examine previously inaccessible aspects of user interaction: particularly, the network structures that link online debaters to the heuristics of their attitudes. Grounded in a larger theoretical debate, we shall analyze what factors serve to consolidate group homophily that attracts people of the same opinions, and what factors serve to reduce the degree of group heterophily that presumably should promote exchanges between people of different opinions. How do netizens of distinct attitudes towards Hong Kong-mainland conflicts differ in their bond of homophily? To what extent are the users of a particular attitude hostile towards those holding a different attitude? This would help us better understand whether online discussion forums serve as integrators of opinion or as polarizing "echo chambers." Moreover, we will analyze topical and linguistic characteristics of root messages that contribute to vibrant response from the online public. To what extent do root messages cite media coverage or other sources to clarify, reinforce or develop their opinions and how does it affect netizen response? Moreover, we will trace how Hong Kong and mainland Chinese netizens present themselves and the "other side," normatively and descriptively. In their eyes, what are the causes and consequences of the conflicts? What are the facts or assumptions that undergird their arguments and presentation? This research will examine how the posts in online forums can be harnessed to estimate public sentiment, particularly those of socially active citizens. A series of recent mass protests in Hong Kong testify to an acute need for more enlightened and evidence-based policymaking. 近年來，多宗中港矛盾爭議性事件接連引發兩地民眾的激烈反應，在互聯網社區引起廣泛關注。 本研究通過檢視網路論壇上的民眾意見表達和互動方式，追溯和梳理兩地網民關於中港矛盾的論述和爭論。 在眾多電腦中介傳播形式之中，網路論壇是民意展現的重要場域之一。 大眾傳媒僅為少數人提供觀點表達空間，而網路論壇是存在於電腦網路中的虛擬公共空間，容納了形形色色的網路意見--從單純的發洩情緒的意見、公開自由的散佈訊息、交換意見到理性的時事議論和公共論述。 它不僅為更多人提供平臺來參與討論，更是一個積極的議題設置者。 研究者通過傳統的調查研究資料蒐集方法往往很難一窺線上互動的整體模式以及發展動態。 本研究結合社會網路分析法和內容分析法，對兩地網絡論壇上爭議性議題的形成、發酵與衰變進行個案研究，試圖勾勒網民的互動網路結構以及他們在中港矛盾議題上的態度立場分佈。 網路論壇的參與討論者是否構成虛擬社群？網絡論壇空間是否因為參與討論者的互動增加而提升政治間的對話，抑或由於網際網路的客製化與社會網路而加劇了群體極化現象？網絡論壇使用者具備易得之技術性和制度性的能力後，是否更加傾向於選擇接觸與自己看法一致的使用者，進而更強化原本已存在的態度和信條？在社交網絡興起後，研究者曾用美國的在線實證數據驗證了「迴聲室效應」的理論觀點，試圖辨明網路意見「愈辯愈對立」的形成機制。本研究將通過對中港兩地在線實證數據的分析來進一步探究網絡意見的表達和互動機制。此外，本研究會著眼於網絡論壇中的信息與情緒擴散。在網絡論壇空間中，參與討論者的社會經濟地位與背景不能直接決定其發帖的接受度和擴散度，而發貼者的影響力在一定程度上取決於其言論的內容與說理程度。

12632816.label: Realisation of objectives
12632816.value: This project has successfully addressed all seven objectives through a range of empirical studies. This project systematically analyzed massive datasets collected from popular online discussion platforms in Hong Kong and mainland China using a mixed-method design comprised of topic modeling, automated content analysis, discourse analysis, social network analysis and semi-structured in-depth interviews. On the one hand, our analysis identified a considerable level of homophily existing in the interaction networks, referring to the observed echo chamber effect. On the other hand, cross-cutting exchange was found to exist in all platforms studied, albeit to a lesser extent than like-minded exchange. Moreover, a considerable amount of cross-cutting interactions involved requesting or providing information which may attenuate the likelihood of opinion polarization. Findings suggested that online forums have not only helped promote public discourses and civic life as opinion integrators but also amplified incivility online, often leading to a greater degree of polarization and cynicism (objective 1). This project adopted a longitudinal study design which not only compared the pre-Umbrellra Movement (UM) period and post-UM period but also examined how online discussion forums intervened in the developing tensions between Hong Kong and mainland China in the aftermath of the UM. We found UM as a treatment variable had a significant effect on the sentiments, pro-social and anti-social behaviors manifested in Hong Kong Golden Forum (HKGolden) and mainland’s Tianya Club (Tianya). A series of political incidents took place in the immediate aftermath of UM which led to heated discussions over the intensifying bilateral conflicts in both forums. Aligning with the lower number of relevant posts and replies that we identified, no major political incidents took place in the first half of 2017. Since late July 2017 when the LEGCO announced that four more pro-democracy LEGCO members-elect were disqualified, the political tension had escalated into other aspects such as: the livelihood issues (e.g., public disputes over integration infrastructure projects), as well as cultural conflicts (e.g., public uproars against the downgrading of Cantonese in favour of Mandarin). Through quantifying the structural aspects of interactions, and analyzing the nature and content of the interactions, we identified an intensifying anti-outgroup and arguably radical sentiments in all platforms studied. It was particular the case for HKGolden, which reflected the rise of localism and radicalism in the post-UM Hong Kong (objective 2 & 3). Methodologically, this project utilized automated content analysis (e.g., topic modeling, dictionary-based approaches to sentiment classification and identification of pro-social/anti-social expressions), discourse analysis (which identified linguistic characteristics of the posts, and discursive strategies used to construct the in-group and out-group) and social network analysis (which measured the distribution of user attitudes) (objective 3). To measure the level of attitude-based homophily in the user interaction network, we constructed interaction networks with reference to reply-based relationships, repost-based relationships, comment-based relationships, and quote-based relationships. For all the platforms studied, users were substantially more likely to engage with like-minded others. Individuals on the extremes exhibited higher levels of homophily than those on the center. Our case study of HKGolden further testified to the partisan learning processes and the effect of ideological extremity on this process. The findings have implications for promoting political tolerance in that polarization in the network might be reduced by convincing individuals (e.g., through education, exposure to diverse viewpoints, or incentives) to adopt a more neutral stand towards the controversial issues that provoke bilateral conflicts (objective 4). To further explore the opinion dynamics, we analyzed the opinions of all users as well as opinion leaders that were identified with reference to three criteria (i.e., number of fans, number of replies one’s posts had received, and k-core members). We observed strong attitude homogeneity across the whole network and the subgroup defined by k-core in all online discussion forums. In the case of Weibo, more attitude heterogeneity surfaced among influential users who received more comments and had more fans. The two-step ﬂow model of communication emphasizes the role of influential individuals in disseminating information to a wider audience. Given the socio-technical affordances of online discussion tools, one- and multiple-step flow models were also considered in our project to distinguish direct communication with audiences (i.e., broadcast diffusion) and other intermediaries (i.e., viral diffusion). Our findings suggested that one-step, two-step and multiple-step flow phenomena coexisted in all the platforms studied, and also testified to substantial social influence pressures acting on people navigating online messages. Furthermore, this project also contributed to a more nuanced understanding of the linkage between post characteristics and message virality. Based on the content of the original post, we constructed several measures for post characteristics, including emotions and cognition displayed, anti-social and pro-social expressions used as well as topics discussed in the post. Using the case of HKGolden, we examined the contagion of online swearing as a type of linguistic mannerism of anti-social behavior and systematically tested multiple mechanisms (e.g., direct mimicry, third-person effect, and social reciprocation) through which online swearing became contagious. Using the case of Tianya, we examined how use of pro- and anti-social expressions in the posts were predicted by cognitive and reflective components and impulsive and automatic components in the proposed Dual System Theory model. We linked our analysis to a broader aim of testing classical public opinion and media theories in the digital contexts (objective 5). To investigate online forum users’ views on approaches to ameliorate hostile speech and facilitate cross-cutting exchange, semi-structured interviews were respectively conducted with Tianya users and HKGolden users. The interview questions targeted their perception of Hong Kong-Mainland China Conflict, their experiences of like-minded and cross-attitudinal exchange, and their suggestions to alleviate the incivility towards dissimilar opinions. The interviews yielded a diversity of viewpoints on the issue content of Hong Kong-mainland conflict as well as the causes and consequences of online incivility. Self-regulation was preferred as a solution to hostile speech. Tianya users showed less sensitivity the distinction between censorship and moderation, and whereas HKGolden users were alert to the forum’s core value as a defender of free speech and enabler of public debate. Although the system of moderation was perceived as inconsistent, both forums’ users looked to community policing as the solution to alleviate online incivility. Our findings laid the foundation for evidence-based policymaking. For example, swearing was shown to only generate short-term surges in popularity, especially among the first-generation adopters in the context of mainland China. In the context of Hong Kong, online forum users suggested that a platform provide more individualized tools to have control over what they see rather than banning consensual uncivil behaviors outright (objective 6). Thus far, we have published two journal papers, and another paper is under review of Communication Research, a top journal in the field of communication. This project has also led to six conference papers. Four of them were accepted by the top conferences in the field of communication, such as the ICA, AEJMC and NCA, and two were published as proceedings of Computer Science's top conference. Notably, one of the papers won the ICA Mass Communication Division's Top Faculty Paper Award. We are currently revising two conference papers and will send them to reputable top journals respectively in August and September (objective 7).

12632816.label: Major findings and research outcome
12632816.value: Using an approach integrating social network analysis, automatic text analytics, discourse analysis and in-depth interviews, this longitudinal project mapped the online public’s changing views of Hong Kong-Mainland China conflict in the digital space of both Hong Kong and mainland China. First, the network analysis identified a mixture of attitude-based homophily and heterophily in users’ discussions around conflictual issues in all internet platforms studied. The formation of conversational ties was found to be predominantly organized around attitude similarity. Meanwhile, cross-cutting exchange did occur, albeit to a lesser extent than like-minded exchange. Cross-cutting interactions generally contained a significantly greater amount of emotions—and more negative ones—as well as information and uncivil expressions than interactions among the like-minded or between users without a clear attitude. Moreover, the influential users in both regions’ online forums—indicated by number of fans—were largely those holding a moderate attitude, and whereas users active in online discussions of conflictual issues—either as activists or as skeptics—tended to exhibit strong attitudes. In addition to the user characteristics, this project also examined the post characteristics that affected users’ responsiveness. Users responded with strong emotion both to cognitive and emotional cues, and were more likely to express extreme emotions to posts with more replies. Political topics attracted more vibrant responses than other topical categories, and information-related posts were also more likely to go viral. An exhaustive discourse analysis identified the evolving targets of users’ posts on Tianya (e.g., student activists, protest organizers, and US government) and HKGolden (e.g., Chief Executive and the Beijing government), and examined the discursive strategies used to construct the out-group. The analysis pointed to an intensifying anti-outgroup and arguably radical sentiments in both regions’ online discussion forums. The post-Umbrella Movement period witnessed an increasing incidence of uncivil behaviors attacking dissimilar opinions. The in-depth interviews with Tianya and HKGolden users suggested that incivility use was more likely to be unconscious than conscious in that users merely followed their stereotypical understandings of certain issues, or were under peer pressure to act in certain ways. The analysis also identified a set of solutions to alleviate incivility from users’ perspective, such as setting up community-policing rules of conduct for all perspective members of the forum to follow, employing checkers who can dispute and correct abusive content in posted comments, and including prominently displayed threads where moderators can post information or topics that would increase heterophilous exposure.

12632816.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12632816.value: There is considerable potential to extend this project into a follow-up study investigating in-depth the phenomenon of political incivility in Hong Kong's digital space. From the 2014 Umbrella Movement to the recent anti-extradition bill movement, an increasing number of Hong Kong Internet users have adopted a style of behavior that is abusive and hostile, partially an expression of frustration with a series of contentious issues that provoked conflicts between Hong Kong and mainland China. This online incivility may possibly corrode reasoned discourse in cyberspace and fuel social climates of hate in public debate. To help address these analytical and empirical gaps in our scholarly and practical knowledge, the investigator has developed a proposal that sought to examine the social and behavioral mechanisms through which the instances of uncivil behaviors at the individual level might possibly generate a self-perpetuating process of ever-growing uncivil and aggressive group behaviors. Given the endogenous relationship between social network formation and political attitudes, it is difficult to establish whether social media networks shape political opinions, or vice versa. We are planning to conduct field experiments on online discussion platforms to test whether exposure to opposing political views will increase polarization in the context of Hong Kong-Mainland Conflict.

12632816.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12632816.value: This study focused on discursive struggles in online discussion forums over contentious issues that provoked major conflicts between Hong Kong and mainland China residents. Whereas mass media seldom provide a space for individuals to express their views, computer-mediated discussion tools provide a platform for a wider range of actors to voice their attitudes and opinions, and thus serve as an effective interpreter of such conflicts. This study systematically analyzed large-scale digital trace data collected from popular online discussion platforms in Hong Kong and mainland China using a mixed-method design. Grounded in a larger theoretical debate, this study showed that online forums not only helped promote cross-cutting exchange but also amplified incivility online, often leading to a greater degree of polarization and cynicism. Moreover, this study analyzed user-level and post-level characteristics that contributed to vibrant response from the online public, and traced how Hong Kong and mainland Chinese netizens presented themselves and the “out-group”, normatively and descriptively. In-depth semi-structured interviews were further conducted to understand their experience of cross-cutting and like-minded discussions and to explore the strategies for alleviating the incivility towards dissimilar opinions from users’ perspective. The findings have implications for more enlightened and evidence-based policymaking.

12638216.label: Project Title(Chinese)
12638216.value: 十八世紀植物學與其書籍運用

12638216.label: Project Objectives
12638216.value: To document that, in contrast to what is usually tacitly assumed, scholarly books were not available where they were needed, not just in exceptional cases, but on a regular basis. Based on correspondences of the eighteenth century it will be shown that complaints about urgently required books not being available, or, where they were, only at prohibitive prices, were ubiquitous, even in university cities and those which hosted a book fair, such as Paris, Göttingen, Leipzig, Vienna, and Oxford, not to mention more peripheral cities such as Montpellier, Verona, Turin, and Stockholm. To argue that, as work even on local and regional floras depended fundamentally on a wide and comparative use of literature, ways had to be found to make up for the deficiencies of the book market. The international botanical correspondence was used not only for the exchange of natural objects, as has often been pointed out, but also for obtaining relevant literature, which was equally important for the knowledge-making process of botany. The functioning of this system will be addressed, from initial contacts with potential exchange partners to the complicated logistics of shipping and finding reliable contacts. The exchange of botanical books, like that of plants, depended on the local and regional “capital” of correspondents. For scholars, books published locally were their main objects for exchange, especially their own works, which were rarely available elsewhere. To demonstrate with a focus on leading eighteenth-century botanists - Johann Jakob Dillenius, Nikolaus von Jacquin, and Carl Linnaeus - that the exchange of books was not only a part but a pillar of what I would like to call the collaborative publication system of botany. Scholars used the (sometimes not yet published) publications of others, incorporating material from them into their own works while making reference to the original author. Within the framework of this form of cooperation, each scholar sent his most recent writings to his partners as quickly as possible so that they could complete their own publications, which guaranteed him the same privilege in return. To highlight that these practices had a major impact on forms of co-authorship that emerged in eighteenth-century botany.

To argue that, as work even on local and regional floras depended fundamentally on a wide and comparative use of literature, ways had to be found to make up for the deficiencies of the book market. The international botanical correspondence was used not only for the exchange of natural objects, as has often been pointed out, but also for obtaining relevant literature, which was equally important for the knowledge-making process of botany.

The functioning of this system will be addressed, from initial contacts with potential exchange partners to the complicated logistics of shipping and finding reliable contacts. The exchange of botanical books, like that of plants, depended on the local and regional “capital” of correspondents. For scholars, books published locally were their main objects for exchange, especially their own works, which were rarely available elsewhere.

To demonstrate with a focus on leading eighteenth-century botanists - Johann Jakob Dillenius, Nikolaus von Jacquin, and Carl Linnaeus - that the exchange of books was not only a part but a pillar of what I would like to call the collaborative publication system of botany. Scholars used the (sometimes not yet published) publications of others, incorporating material from them into their own works while making reference to the original author. Within the framework of this form of cooperation, each scholar sent his most recent writings to his partners as quickly as possible so that they could complete their own publications, which guaranteed him the same privilege in return.
To highlight that these practices had a major impact on forms of co-authorship that emerged in eighteenth-century botany.

12638216.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12638216.value: This project will address the fact that the knowledge-making process of eighteenth-century natural history, botany in particular, was as dependent on books as on herbaria and botanical gardens and examine widely-used practices of procuring, exchanging and working with botanical books. It also intends to analyse the epistemological function of the use of books and therefore of second-hand experience in a knowledge culture that has so far been defined as predominantly empirical. But even a cursory reading of the botanical correspondences of the eighteenth century makes it clear that, as a rule, botanical books were not available where they were needed. As work even on local and regional floras depended fundamentally on a wide and comparative use of literature, ways had to be found to make up for the deficiencies of the book market. This situation forced scholars to resort to personal contacts and use their correspondences for the exchange and acquisition of books. The functioning of this system will be described, from initial contacts with potential partners and the complicated logistics of shipping to the fact that the exchange of locally available books propelled the dynamics of international exchange. On the basis of the correspondence of leading eighteenth-century botanists, including Johann Jakob Dillenius, Nikolaus von Jacquin, and Carl Linnaeus, it will then be demonstrated that the exchange of books was a pillar of what can be called the collaborative publication system of botany. Scholars used the publications of others, incorporating material from them into their own work while making reference to the original author. Within the framework of this type of cooperation, an author sent his most recent writings to his partners as quickly as possible so that they could complete their own publications, which guaranteed him the same privilege in return. The constant procurement of books was, like the exchange of plants, an indispensable part of botanical work. This is why establishing and maintaining exchange relationships was vitally important for every scholar. It will be shown that everyone who took part in this international system of exchange had to submit to a code of behaviour which sanctioned the symmetry of gift and return gift and punished violations, thus guaranteeing the long-term functioning of a mechanism that was essential for all involved. 此研究計劃將闡明十八世紀植物學的知識產生過程不僅依靠標本收藏與植物園，同時也依賴書籍的運用。此計劃亦檢視廣泛的植物學書籍購買、交換、使用之行為，進而分析在十八世紀知識文化中，使用書籍而生成知識之功能。學者一直以爲此知識文化主要依經驗而生成知識，然而此計劃會展示它同樣依靠二手經驗。

12638516.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12638516.value: Christian political participation is obvious in the Umbrella Movement of 2014. The role of Christianity in this area demands serious attention. Its root can be traced back to the colonial period. In previous studies, Christianity was usually considered as a “tool” of the colonial government. This research suggests that the interactions between religion, politics, and society are more complicated than we supposed. Since the colonial government implemented its localization policy and subsidized social services programs to cope with discontents among Hong Kong Chinese after the 1967 riot, Hong Kong Chinese Christians have become increasingly active in their participation of social and political issues. In these socio-political involvements, it might be that Chinese Christians emphasized their Chinese identity, but did not agree with left-wing patriot activism. Also, they criticized the government and its policies, while at the same time supporting its reforms. In order to have a better understanding of the decolonization process of Hong Kong and an understanding of what a good church–state relation might be, it is important for us to study the interrelations and conflicts between Christians’ religious, ethnic, and socio-political identities. This project focuses on studying the dynamics and interactions of religious discourses, identity construction, and social participation of Hong Kong Chinese Protestant Christians from 1970 to 1997. More specifically, it explores the reciprocal relation of religious belief and social identity construction of believers, and the religious-socio-political implications of this relation in a colonial context. The key research questions are: 1. What are the characteristics of the relationships between religious discourses, social participation, and socio-political identity of Christians? Is there any reciprocal relation? 2. What are the characteristics of these discourses compared with the general understanding of social participation and socio-political identity in Hong Kong of that period? 3. What are the strengths and weaknesses of this identity construction for coping with social change when comparing it with the general ethos of the Hong Kong society and other Christian decolonization experience? The major contribution of this research is providing information and an analytical angle for a framework of understanding decolonization and Christian political participation. The methodology of this research is oral and documentary history. This method is chosen because gathering primary sources and establishing a substantial data bank is important for an exploratory research on contemporary history. Two analytical articles, one monograph of oral history and historical documents with analysis, and one audio-visual archive will be generated. 在2014年的雨傘運動裡，基督徒的政治參與十分顯著。基督教在相關領域的角色，亦引起高度關注。但香港基督徒政治參與的根源，其實可追溯至殖民地時期。過往的研究常視基督教作殖民地政府的「工具」。此研究欲指出，宗教、政治，以及社會的互為影響，事實上遠比想像中複雜。自67暴動發生後，殖民地政府開始實施本地化政策，並大力資助社會服務項目，以紓緩華人之不滿。香港華人基督徒也因此對社會及政治的參與變得積極。華人基督徒在政治參與的過程中，他們雖然認同自身的中國人身分，但並不代表他們同時贊同左派的愛國激進主義。此外，他們一方面批評政府的政策，但同時又支持政府的改革。為了進一步認識香港的去殖民化過程，以及更多了解政教關係可如何良性互動，我們有必要進一步研究基督徒的宗教、道德，和政治社會身分的互動與張力。 此項目將集中研究1970至1997年間，香港華人基督徒的宗教論述、身分建構，以及社會參與之多元互動。更確切而言，此研究會探索信徒的宗教信仰與社會身分建構的相互關係，以及這些身分建構如何受在殖民地政府統治下的宗教、社會、政治層面影響。 本研究主要的研究問題如下：1. 宗教論述 、社會參與，以及基督徒的社會政治身分，三者之關係有何特點？當中有否互惠關係？ 2. 將上述三十年間的宗教社會參與論述，與一般公眾的社會運動以及社會政治身分認同作比較時，前者有何特點？ 3. 在應對社會轉變的能力層面而論，當時的基督徒身分建構與香港當時普遍的社會風氣，以及其他基督教去殖民化經驗作比較時，有何優點與缺點？ 此項目的主要貢獻在於提供相關資料以作參考，並分析探討去殖民化及基督徒之政治參與。 此項目會採用口述史及文獻史之方式進行，希望蒐集更多原始資料，同時建立一個可觀的資料庫。

12638516.label: Realisation of objectives
12638516.value: 1. To assemble oral histories and historical documents of the social participation of Hong Kong Chinese Christians from 1970 to 1997. The project collected oral histories of 19 interviewees from 11 Christian organizations that were active in socio-political participation from 1970-1997. 18 interviewees have done two rounds of oral history interviews according to the research design of the project. 1 interviewee has finished only one round of interview for emigration of the interviewee. All interviews have been video recorded and transcribed. The total volume of the transcriptions is over 200,000 words. The draft version of English translation of the verbatim has been done. Editing works will be continued after the completion of the project. The PI aims to provide a bilingual oral history collection to general public and researchers. The PI also has collected over 800 entries of historical documents of social participation of Hong Kong Chinese Christians from 1970 to 1997. For the copyrights issue, the PI cannot duplicate and publish the content of the documents. Thus, the PI has indicated the original source of the documents and provided a summary of the event and participants of the events. In the research proposal, the PI suggested to publish a monography of oral and documentary history. But, the recent development of digital humanities compels the PI to think otherwise. The PI finally decided to publish the oral histories and collected historical documents through digital scholarship program of HKBU library. The project collection is now available at https://digital.lib.hkbu.edu.hk/christianhistory/index.php . This new way of presenting the oral histories and the historical documents enables flexible cross data analysis and non-textual historical data capture. Also, the digital database can facilitate sophisticated factor analysis. In the website, the PI attempted to use keywords and interpersonal relationship to analyse the dynamic of Hong Kong Christian social participation. More importantly, the website can generate an impact that paper publications usually not able to achieve. The website has been published online since September 2019 and has more than 21,000 views. 2. To enumerate the characteristics of the discourses on social participation and identity construction of the involved Hong Kong Chinese Christians. The project employed narrative theory to capture the subjective experience and impression of social participation and identity construction of the interviewees. The semi-structured interviews of this project aimed to report the important moments of the interviewees’ social participation. Also, they probed the possible theological influences that the participants received and exerted. All interviews collected interviewees’ reflection of their identity construction. The initial characteristics of the discoursed are analyzed through the data analysis on the website. The PI provided analysis of the themes and affiliations of the social participation event, and interpersonal relationship of the interviewees. The data analysis showed that democracy, human rights and livelihood are the major themes of Christian social participation from 1970 to 1997. It also showed that how key leaders are connected with each other in the Christian social participation. The PI has completed 3 book chapters and 1 conference paper to analyze the national identity consciousness, the political identity, the mutual impact of internal and external social influences and the gender empowerment in Hong Kong Christian social participation. 3. To analyze the similarities and differences of these discourses with the ethos of general public in Hong Kong by that period of time. In the oral history interviews, the PI probed how the interviewees viewed the relationship between their social participation and the general public ethos. In “The Hybridization and Localization”, the PI found that the interviewees have gained access to Hong Kong’s political sphere for their education and profession help them become elites and social leaders of Hong Kong society. In other words, they have more resources and opportunities than general public of Hong Kong in engaging with socio-political issues. In “Religious Discourse, Social Participation, and Identity Construction”, the PI found that though the interviewees can be considered as political activists, they embraced both Hong Kong and Chinese identities. The democratic movement in the transitional period did not mean a rejection of China. China was always a family root that they could not deny, a context that they needed to respond to. Their political participation was mainly motivated by a heart of solidarity and a vision for Hong Kong’s future. In other words, the interviewees showed a strong affinity with the general public of the city. In the “’The West’ and the Formation of Hong Kong Christian Leaders”, the PI found that the overseas experience of interviewees enabled them to have innovative ideas in social participation and exported impacts to the overseas. With the international connection of Christian faith, the interviewees have a broader stage than the general public. But, their participation made Hong Kong and Hong Kong church known by the international audience. They have a contribution for developing international reputation of the city. 4. To scrutinize nuances of the interactions between Hong Kong Christianity, and the government and general public from 1970 to 1997. Through the semi-structured interviews, the PI probed how the interviewees understand their participation in relation to the governments (i.e., UK government, PRC government and HK government) and the general public. The transcriptions recorded how the interviewees engaged with the governments and mobilized the public. They showed the development of local administration policy adopted by the Hong Kong colonial government in 1970s and 1980s. In “The Hybridization and Localization”, the PI found that the interviewees have their agency in developing agenda and strategy of their participation. In “Religious Discourse, Social Participation, and Identity Construction”, the PI identified that though the interviewees can be considered as activists, their political identity consciousness is a “legitimate identity” that channels the political action into established political institutions and systems. 5. To critically assess the relative merits and shortcomings of these historical data sets about social participation and identity construction in terms of promoting a positive Church and State interaction in Hong Kong. The data analytics showed that the Christian social participation covered many aspects of life of Hong Kong people. Christian social participation from 1970 to 1997 can be considered as a voice for promoting wellbeing and quality of livelihood of Hong Kong people, rather than political activism for drastic political change. In “Religious Discourse, Social Participation, and Identity Construction”, the PI’s analysis pointed out that the Christian social participation before 1997 can work with the localization strategy of the colonial government. One can also find that the openness of the government officials to the actions and suggestions of the interviewees contributed to a healthy interaction between Christian social activists and the government. The PI is also aware that the interaction between the interviewees and the Chinese government is more positive before 1989 than after. In “’The West’ and the Formation of Hong Kong Christian Leaders”, the PI found that one of the interviewees emphasized the importance of exchange and mutual understanding. The interviewee recalled that he explained his understanding of the Basic Law to the mainland officials and pointed out the possible misunderstanding of the officials. The interviewee used the example as an evidence of the constructiveness of constant contact and exchange. The PI believed the example indicated the importance of the rule of law and the legitimacy of the law through public support.

12638516.label: Major findings and research outcome
12638516.value: Major Findings 1. National identity and local (Hong Kong) identity are not mutually exclusive among Christians joining social participation from 1970 to 1997. More importantly, identity of Christian faith always provides the interviewees resources to inspire their participation 2. Christian faith is not only a theological or ideological resource. It is also an institutional empowerment and interpersonal network that facilitate social participation. 3. The oral history showed that the interviewees can creatively integrate the Western Christian theology, Chinese culture and Hong Kong social needs and initiate meaningful social participation. 4. Christian social participation in Hong Kong does not only generate local impacts. It also brings impacts to the World Christianity. Social participation does not only generate upward social mobility locally but also globally. 5. Though the interviewees can be considered as activists, their political identity consciousness is a “legitimate identity” that channels the political action into established political institutions and systems. It also explains why the democratic movement in Hong Kong from 1980 to 1997 was very peaceful and non-violent. 6. The Christian social participation covered many aspects of life of Hong Kong people. Christian social participation from 1970 to 1997 can be considered as a voice for promoting wellbeing and quality of livelihood of Hong Kong people, rather than political activism for drastic political change. Research outcome 3 academic book chapters and 1 conference paper have been generated (Please refer to Part C for details. The original proposal suggested to produce 2 analytical articles). More importantly, a digital scholarship database that contains oral histories and sources of the historical documents has been created under HKBU library website. The website contains the verbatim of the oral histories (over 200,000 words) and a database of the historical documents (over 800 entries). The website also offers data analytics to visualise the categories of social participation and the interpersonal relationship of Christian participation. From September 2019 to 31 May 2021, there are over 21,200 views. The link of the website is: https://digital.lib.hkbu.edu.hk/christianhistory/

12638516.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12638516.value: The project has big potential for further development. It can be extended to cover more Christian leaders that the interviewees have mentioned. A wider scope of interview targets can help researchers and public to have a more comprehensive understanding of the Christian social participation in the colonial Hong Kong. Also, the project can be extended to cover the time period after 1997 and before 1970. The extension in time frame can help us to gain a sense of social and political change. The project should also collect more photos and audio-visual records. Finally, the PI is translating the interview verbatim into English and hope the translation can help non-Chinese researchers to access the valuable research resources of this project.

12638516.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12638516.value: The present project collected oral histories of 19 interviewees and over 800 entries of historical documents from 11 Christian organizations that were active in socio-political participation from 1970-1997. The project found that the Christian social participation covered many aspects of life of Hong Kong people. Christian social participation from 1970 to 1997 can be considered as a voice for promoting wellbeing and quality of livelihood of Hong Kong people, rather than political activism for drastic political change. The project also found that the national identity and local (Hong Kong) identity are not mutually exclusive among Christians joining social participation from 1970 to 1997. The identity of Christian faith always provides the interviewees resources to inspire their participation. Though the interviewees can be considered as activists, their political identity consciousness is a “legitimate identity” that channels the political action into established political institutions and systems. It also explains why the democratic movement in Hong Kong from 1980 to 1997 was very peaceful and non-violent.

12641016.label: Realisation of objectives
12641016.value: Objectives 1 and 2 were fully achieved by using stage 1 qualitative study of semi-structured interviews. Limited knowledge and low awareness of HPV-related issues, low perceived risk of HPV infection, perceived association between HPV vaccine and promiscuity, and lack of accessible official information on HPV-related topics were identified as the key barriers that had prevented the men participants from receiving HPV vaccination. In general, the male informants had low incentives in getting vaccinated because they perceived HPV as irrelevant to men. The only incentive that could motivate them to get vaccinated is that if they are informed about the clear relevance of HPV with men’s health. In addition, quite a number of male informants commented that they would consider about doing the vaccination if they are forced by their spouses and/or partners. For women informants, the following factors intertwined to influence their decision-making process: perceptions of HPV and HPV vaccine; perceived worthiness of HPV vaccine, which was affected by its cost, marriage plans, and experiences of sexual activities; history of experiencing gynecological conditions; stigma associated with HPV vaccination; acquisition of information on HPV vaccines; distrust on HPV vaccines; and absence of preventive care in the healthcare practice. Altering these barriers in addition to offering discount on the vaccination can serve as motivation for women participants. Social construction of the HPV vaccine as a women's thing and as a sex-related taboo has made HPV vaccine to become feminized and moralized. These social and cultural values can have remarkable effect on the informants' decision of whether getting vaccinated. Objective 4 was fully achieved by using stage 2 experiment study. Objectives 3 and 5 were fully achieved by using stage 1 qualitative study of semi-structured interviews and stage 2 experiment study. We completed two experimental studies to examine the promotional message effect on men and women population to see their attitude toward and behavioral intention of HPV prevention. 400 young women (aged 18 - 25) and 400 men (aged 18 - 45) were sampled from local universities and community to do the experiments. The focus of the first study was on male’s attitude toward and behavioral intention of HPV prevention. The purpose of the study was in twofold: (1) to examine the effect of framing the vaccine as either HPV vaccine or Cervical Cancer vaccine; and (2) to examine how the framing effect differed for those who currently have romantic partners and those who do not. Male participants in the first study were exposed to a promotional video in which the protagonist considered whether to get vaccinated or not. Four hundred males participated in a 2 (Vaccine framing: HPV vaccine vs. Cervical Cancer vaccine) by 2 (Relationship status: in a romantic relationship vs. single) between subject factorial experiment. The preliminary analyses indicated that, for male participants who are currently in a romantic relationship, those who were exposed to the promotional messages framed as “Cervical Cancer vaccine” showed more positive attitude and greater behavioral intention of getting vaccinated. On the contrary, for male participants who are currently single, those who were exposed to the promotional messages framed as “HPV vaccine” showed more positive attitude and greater behavioral intention of getting vaccinated. The other two names of 性器疣疫苗and 子宮頸癌及性器疣疫苗, however, showed the weakest sensitivity to men respondents. The focus of the second study was on female’s attitude toward and behavioral intention of HPV prevention. The purpose of the study was to examine the effect of story with upward/downward counterfactual thinking. Four hundred females participated in a single factor between-subject experiment (Counterfactual thinking: Upward counterfactuals vs. Downward counterfactuals). The preliminary analyses showed that narratives with upward counterfactuals elicited greater anticipated regret and mental simulation, and, in turn, influenced the female respondents’ attitude toward and intention of vaccination. On the contrary, narratives with downward counterfactuals elicited greater anticipated relieve and mental simulation, and, in turn, influenced the respondents’ attitude toward and intention of vaccination.
