12641016.value: Limited knowledge and low awareness of HPV-related issues, low perceived risk of HPV infection, perceived association between HPV vaccine and promiscuity, and lack of accessible official information on HPV-related topics were identified as the key barriers that had prevented the men participants from receiving HPV vaccination. In general, the male informants had low incentives in getting vaccinated because they perceived HPV as irrelevant to men. The only incentive that could motivate them to get vaccinated is that if they are informed about the clear relevance of HPV with men’s health. In addition, quite a number of male informants commented that they would consider about doing the vaccination if they are forced by their spouses and/or partners. Spouses and/or partners, thus, served as significant others that can motivate male informants’ vaccination. For women participants, perceptions of HPV and HPV vaccine; perceived worthiness of HPV vaccine, which was affected by its cost, marriage plans, and experiences of sexual activities; history of experiencing gynecological conditions; stigma associated with HPV vaccination; acquisition of information on HPV vaccines; distrust on HPV vaccines; and absence of preventive care in the healthcare practice, are all influential in their decision making. Social construction of HPV vaccination as a women’s concern of no consequence to men and as a sex-related taboo have feminized and moralized HPV vaccination. This has greatly affected the incentives of men to get vaccinated. Even for women informants, the moralization of HPV vaccine that has made HPV vaccine to relate to one's chastity is also key to prevent the women informants from getting vaccinated. Also, distrust on private healthcare in Hong Kong can demotivate informants to get vaccinated as well. In the experiment study, for male participants who are currently in a romantic relationship, those who were exposed to the promotional messages framed as “Cervical Cancer vaccine” showed more positive attitude and greater behavioral intention of getting vaccinated. On the contrary, for male participants who are currently single, those who were exposed to the promotional messages framed as “HPV vaccine” showed more positive attitude and greater behavioral intention of getting vaccinated. The preliminary analyses for women respondents showed that narratives with upward counterfactuals elicited greater anticipated regret and mental simulation, and, in turn, influenced the female respondents’ attitude toward and intention of vaccination. On the contrary, narratives with downward counterfactuals elicited greater anticipated relieve and mental simulation, and, in turn, influenced the respondents’ attitude toward and intention of vaccination.

12641016.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12641016.value: The findings of the study have strong practical implication for health authorities in Hong Kong in promoting HPV vaccination as a preventive health behavior. The barriers and incentives of receiving HPV vaccination identified in the study provide solid information to the health authorities when they are doing health promotion of HPV vaccination to men and women population. The cultural values serve as a remarkable barrier for vaccination, and thus using the most sensitive elements to men (eg. the best vaccine name to be used, partner/spouse impact) and women (eg. how to make the vaccine sounds worth for them, relieving the stigma attached, and providing more vaccine information etc.) that have the biggest impact to motivate them to do the vaccination will have significant implication in HPV vaccination promotion in future in order to reduce the disease burden of HPV-related diseases. Also, from the experiment study, men respondents with different marital relationship can have different response and sensitivity to the different names of the vaccine. Different portray and framing of communication approach can also have different impacts and sensitivities to women respondents. These will help the health authorities thinking about how they should frame HPV vaccine in their future health promotion.

12644516.label: Realisation of objectives
12644516.value: This study adopted the methodologies of participatory action research (PAR) to integrate community participation and engaged scholarship by developing partnerships involving a university, service providers and communities to building social capital and cohesion thorough a participatory process. The approach of Working from the Ground up (WFGU) which was adopted in Australia has informed the approach and methodologies of this study. The WFGU model followed three phases. This research project started in January 2017. After experiencing some delay due to the difficulties of recruiting a research staff who has background in community development, the Project managed to complete Phase One: ‘engaging the community’ by end of February 2018. Regarding Research Objective (RO)1 and RO2, pre- and post- community surveys were conducted in Kim Shin Lane of Shamshuipo, and a pre-survey in Sai Wan Estate and Tai Pak Terence of Kennedy Town. Measurement tools to assess the levels of social disadvantage, social cohesion, resident participation, perception of the physical environment, social network and community social capital were developed. During Phase One, there were interviews with five key informants from each community and also five and three resident feedback sessions organised in Kim Shin Lane and Tai Pak Terrence respectively. Partnerships were established with two community service units of Caritas-Hong Kong, which are key service providers in the communities. In addition, all local businesses, resident organisations and government departments were identified and initial contacts were established. Based on the principles of PAR that the findings of one stage will inform actions of the next, Phase Two: ‘developing and trialing initiatives’ was launched from mid-2018. Two resident groups were formed in Kim Shin Lane. There was a women caregivers’ group that met in the morning every two weeks focusing on women’s safety threats. Another group that met in the evening involved both women and men labourers who prioritized law and order issues. These residents, together with community workers, the research team and university students have initiated actions including organizing street activities for children and residents to collect views on community issues, co-researching with university students using community observations, Photovoice and group discussion. Both groups met with district counsellors and organized activities for the community to work for changes. During the pandemic, the concerns of the residents have shifted from the community environment to health protection and safety, and unemployment issues. Phase Two of this study, therefore, was characterised by residents’ collective actions to respond to COVID-19 since early 2020. The actions initiated by the residents included distributing personal protection equipment (PEP) and food to low-income families, and organising cleaning activities in buildings without building management services. The self-help practices also included fabricating cloth facemasks and coordinating community resources for the needy. The research team, following the principles of WFGU, has extended the research focus to cover residents’ responses to health crisis and effective community development strategies adopted by NGOs during the COVID-19. Both the Caritas projects at Shamshuipo and Kennedy Town joined the research team to collect the strategies through an online seminar. More than 13 community development projects including the two Caritas projects shared their work strategies which included the WFGU cum PAR. The Tai Pak Terrence of Kennedy Town, however, has not proceeded further beyond the first community survey and the feedback sessions organized for residents and service providers. The differences in the process and effect of the WFGU and PAR between the Kim Shin Lane and Tai Pak Terrence have served to highlight factors of effective community development strategies, that is, RO2. The comparisons yield fruitful findings regarding what make WFGU and PAR works and what does not. Factors not contributing to the effectiveness that were identified included the lower commitment of community workers to WFGU and PAR which are novel to the field of community work in the local context. Other factors included the structure of community participation in the neighbourhood that was characterized by various old resident groups and district counsellors who have been active in solving community problems. The extent of ethnic diversity among residents, and the resources of the residents and the community was higher in Tai Pak Terence. There were also changes of the Caritas team members. The resistance of the team and the community was amplified during the social protest and COVID-19. Instead of running one resident group in each district, the research team decided to conduct two resident groups from different background in Shamshuipo. The research study period was extended to end of 2020 allowing the research team to complete Phase Three of the WFGU model, that is, ‘enabling consolidation and sustainability’. During this phase, the Caritas project in Shamshuipo has solicited further funding to continue the research study in collaboration with the research team. Besides, the achievements of the research study were widely recognised by the professional social work community. The PI has successfully solicited a fund of HKD$1.00M from the HSBC Partnership Fund to apply community development approaches and strategies to innovate social services. RO3 was to identify effective strategies of universities-community engagement. Through the research process in collaboration with Caritas projects, university students and residents, strategies including engaging, educating, sustaining, advocating and ongoing evaluating were found effective. RO4 was to compare the community development strategies and their effectiveness in Hong Kong and in Sydney, Australian, which was realised. During the research process, more than ten meetings were conducted with Prof Susan Goodwin of University of Sydney via zoom. Reflecting on the differences between Hong Kong and Sydney, the Australian WFGU model was found relying heavily on volunteers rather than professional social workers. Since the Sydney project was funded by the local government while politicians played significant roles in influencing the allocation of public fund, the Sydney team had to work closely with the politicians and political changes have influenced the sustainability of the project. In the Hong Kong context, researchers had to actively liaise with NGOs instead. Changing personnel and the commitment of the team has resulted in the need to negotiate and re-negotiate for the intervention strategies. Besides, community workers in Hong Kong were less inclined to work closely with politicians. While the major concepts applied to Sydney were networking and volunteering, social capital was deliberately used in the Hong Kong study, which was proved to be effective in understanding the network and resources of individual resident and the community on the whole. The study of strategies was more systematic in Hong Kong following the three phases of the WFGU model developed by the Sydney research. Both projects mobilized students to participate and emphasized on university-community collaboration. In sum, this study has demonstrated that the WFGU model is best implemented together with the PAR approach such that social work interventions and scholarly work are well integrated. Adopting the WFGU model, the active participation of stakeholders is a necessary condition to achieve the objectives of this study. The condition, however, was hampered by the social protest and the pandemic. Turning to the focus of COVID-19 among residents and collecting data about community development strategies in the local context represented the great efforts of the team to actively respond to the situation. The adoption of PAR also means that data analysis and publishing the results is only possible at a later stage.

12644516.label: Major findings and research outcome
12644516.value: To address ROs 1 and RO2, three community surveys were conducted as pre-and post-studies in Kim Shin Lane and another community survey at Tai Pak Terrace during Phase One. The pre-study survey conducted at the community level in Kim Shin Lane targeted 10% of the population and 201 households completed an interview. Due to COVID-19 restrictions, the post-study survey was finally conducted in late 2020 with 105 residents who had participated in the WFGU project. In the pre-study survey, the mean of the general total score for social capital is 71.29 but increased to 72.67 in the post-study survey. Factor A ‘participation in the local community’ is significantly increased from 9.03 in 2018 to 10.83 in 2020. As for the Neighbourhood Cohesion Scale, ‘sense of community’ received the highest score in both the pre- and post-study surveys. The total neighbourhood cohesion score is 55.54 for 2020, which is a slight increase compared to that of 2018 (55.37). Factor A: ‘neighbourhood attraction’ is significantly increased for 2020 as opposed to 2018 (i.e., from 8.56 to 9.50, respectively). Factor C: ‘sense of community’ is also increased from 29.26 to 30.52 respectively. The higher scores reflect the good outcomes of the intervention. A 6-item Community Participation Scale was added to the 2020 survey. The core members of the project scored 10.08 which is significantly higher than the 2.23 of the non-core members. The qualitative data collected are very rich, particularly on the priorities of the residents around community needs and assessment of the various community problems that threaten their safety and health conditions. In the feedback sessions conducted at Kim Shin Lane, the women who participated agreed that the issues included in the survey are important, but disagreed that they are a top priority. Instead, they spoke at length about the threats to safety in the neighborhood, which they identified as the most pertinent issue of concern. These threats include security threats such as robbery, physical and sexual assault, and theft. They are extremely anxious about the safety of their living environment. They have developed different ways to protect themselves and their children. The qualitative findings informed Phase Two: ‘developing and trialing initiatives’ of the WFGU project. During the three phases, more than 30 group sessions with the two resident groups of Kim Shin Lane were audio-recorded, transcribed and analysed to identify effective strategies of WFGU.

12644516.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12644516.value: This study is the first of its kind in Hong Kong applying the Working from the Ground UP (WFGU) model of community development and Participatory Action Research (PAR) methodologies in old urban areas. Though the research study has been impeded greatly by the social protest and COVID-19, the active bottom-up responses of the residents particularly during the pandemic were evidence of the effectiveness of the models/methodologies. Drawing the research findings as support evidence, the research team has already assisted the Caritas project to solicit a funding of $3.0M to continue applying the models in Kim Shin Lane, Shamshuipo. The potential for further development of the research also lies in the strengthening of the depth and broadening of the scope. Future research study can be conducted to validate relevant measurement tools and set up a larger database. Comparing communities of different housing types such as public housing and private rental housing; disadvantaged groups such as new arrivals from mainland China, ethnic minorities, older adults and people with disabilities, etc., can be attempted. The research team will continue to solicit grants for research and/or community development in order to carry out the models in the future.

12644516.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12644516.value: This study is the first of its kind in Hong Kong applying the Working from the Ground UP (WFGU) model of community development and Participatory Action Research (PAR) methodologies in old urban areas. Though the research study has been impeded greatly by the social protest and COVID-19, the active bottom-up responses of the residents particularly during the pandemic were evidence of the effectiveness of the models/methodologies. The findings of the pre- and post- surveys conducted in Kim Shin Lane, Shamshuipo, revealed a significant increase in the total social capital score and in particular, the factor of ‘participation in the community’. The core members of the project achieved a mean neighbourhood cohesion score of 10.08 in the post-survey which was significantly higher than 2.23 of the non-core members. The rise and differences in scores reflected the outcomes of the intervention. The qualitative findings were collected by interviewing the key stakeholders. The contents of the feedback sessions and interviews conducted in Phase One has informed the community actions in Phase Two. Individual and group interviews were also conducted in Phase Three to study the experience of the residents in going through the WFGU and PAR process.

12644816.label: Project Title(Chinese)
12644816.value: 現實主義與先秦戰爭倫理：對《韓非子》的跨文化分析

12644816.label: Project Objectives
12644816.value: To conduct an in-depth scrutinity of the interstate as well as intrastate statecraft as advocated in the book of Hanfeizi. To analyze the convergence and divergence of various contemporary Western realist and neorealist schools of thought. To examine the thesis that the book of Hanfeizi embodies “realism”. If it does, what kind of realism or proto-realism does this treatise advocate? To assess the merits and shortcomings of this cross-cultural moral hermeneutics and critical dialogue.
rows: To conduct an in-depth scrutinity of the interstate as well as intrastate statecraft as advocated in the book of Hanfeizi.
To analyze the convergence and divergence of various contemporary Western realist and neorealist schools of thought.
To examine the thesis that the book of Hanfeizi embodies “realism”. If it does, what kind of realism or proto-realism does this treatise advocate?
To assess the merits and shortcomings of this cross-cultural moral hermeneutics and critical dialogue.

12644816.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12644816.value: Realism is a Western school of thought in statecraft which argues that, by virtue of anarchy in interstate relations, the best interests of the state are to be promoted by the relentless quest for its maximal power, to the exclusion of petty ethical considerations. The state would then be able to launch an “anticipated self-defense” military operation against another state, though others would condemn such an operation as aggression. For several decades, both Chinese and Western scholars have detected the presence of realist tenets in the book of Hanfeizi, an Early China (Pre-Qin) philosophical treatise. Very little follow-up, in-depth investigation on this thesis has been done and this proposed research is designed to fill this vacuum. Given that contemporary Western realism is not a monolithic ideology, we need to analyze the divergence and convergence of contemporary realism and neorealism, and to investigate what kind of realism is embodied in this treatise. The implications of realism to warfare ethics are enormous and this research will assess the warfare ethics in the Hanfeizi vis-à-vis the Confucian book of Mencius as well as contemporary Western discussions on warfare ethics. 現實主義是西方治國思想的一個重要流派。這學派認為，鑑於國際關係是一個無政府狀態，國家要採取行動不懈追求自己的最大利益， 而把一些倫理方面的考慮因素排除為微不足道。因此，國家可以針對另一國發動“預期的自我防衛”軍事行動，雖然其他國家會譴責這種操作為侵略。幾十年來，中國和西方學者皆發現先秦《韓非子》這部哲學著作內含有現實主義思想，但一直很少跟進的深入研究。所以，本研究計劃則填補這一學術空白。鑑於西方當代現實主義不是一個單一的意識形態，我們需要分析當代現實主義和新現實主義之間的共通及分歧點，並嘗試指出《韓非子》內蘊含的現實主義是屬於哪一種。現實主義涉及戰爭倫理的重大議題，本研究計劃將透過當代西方戰爭倫理及古代《孟子》蘊含的戰爭倫理討論，來評估《韓非子》的戰爭倫理。

12644816.label: Realisation of objectives
12644816.value: The objectives have been largely realized. But the result outputs have been delayed in publication because I was side-tracked by a related issue. To put in proper perspective, Han Fei’s realism in warfare ethics should be studied vis-a-vis Mengzi’s idealism in warfare ethics. Hence during this period I have more output on the latter than on the former.

12644816.label: Major findings and research outcome
12644816.value: Much work has been done to show that modern Western realism has its roots in Thucydides, Thomas Hobbes and Machiavelli. In a standard text on history of Western philosophy, Machiavelli would not be mentioned. In a standard text on the history of Western political thought, however, Machiavelli is always regarded as a pioneer of modern political thought. Similarly, Han Fei usually gets little attention in a standard text on the history of Chinese philosophy. In a standard text on the history of Chinese political thought, however, Han Fei usually gets a full chapter’s treatment. This research project argues that Han Fei is a brilliant international relations thinker. In terms of contemporary International Relations theories, Han Fei’s realism resembles neo-realism (rather than classical realism), structural realism (rather than human nature realism), and offensive realism (rather than defensive realism). The resemblance of Han Fei’s realism to the theory advanced by John J. Mearsheimer, of the University of Chicago, is stunning. It has been acknowledged that realism has been the guiding thought of modern China international politics. An in-depth appreciation of Han Fei’s proto-realism can help us to understand contemporary Chinese realism better.

12644816.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12644816.value: Han Fei’s construction of his realist political theory was meant to replace Confucian idealistic political thought. The relative merits and demerits of these two theories need more sophisticated assessment in the future.

12644816.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12644816.value: “Might makes right” is a layman’s tenet of realism in international relations. This amoral realism is advocated not only by Western thinkers, but also by Chinese philosophers as well. The book Hanfeizi contains the best example of realism in Chinese political thought. It was admired throughout Chinese history from the first Emperor of Qin to Mao Zedong. Realism has been used as an ideology to justify actively resorting to military violence for the defense of one’s country. But a realist can argue that the best defense is to run a good offense. Hence countries rising as great powers would actively use war as an instrument for pro-active self-defense. This leads to what John J. Mearsheimer calls “the tragedy of great power politics.” Han Fei’s legacy of offensive realism to China is similar to that of Thucydides, Thomas Hobbes and Machiavelli to the West.

12645816.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12645816.value: In western market economies, collective bargaining is voluntarily conducted between trade unions and employers, without government intervention. Union organizations represent workers and bargain with the workers’ employers for the terms and conditions of employment. The failure to reach an agreement is likely to lead to a strike. However, as Chinese trade unions are unable to represent workers, and workers themselves are virtually unorganized, who represents workers during bargaining with employers? How is bargaining actually conducted in the absence of union representation? Evidence shows that, in more and more factories in Guangdong, workers are electing their own representatives to negotiate with employers. These “worker representatives” (WRs) are becoming de facto “bargaining units” on labor’s behalf. Treating the WR as a new model of labor conflict resolution in China, this project aims to examine the context, formation, and processes of the WR and the effects it has had on both the labor movement and labor relations in China. Specifically, it seeks to address the following questions: How can the emergence of WRs be explained? What are the legal foundations of the WR? What role have WRs played in strikes and CB? How do WRs interact with employers? What are local governments’ and trade unions’ responses to WRs? To what extent have WRs affected the outcomes of collective bargaining? The proposed project aims to accomplish the following goals: To examine both the socioeconomic and legal contexts under which the WR emerges, and to explain why this new model of labor conflict resolution has spread in the PDR. To explore the formation and role of WRs—how WRs are elected, who are the people who stand out in order to become WRs, how WRs represent workers’ demands, and what consequences they may face as WRs. To explore what changes the WR has brought to the process of conflict resolution in workplaces and what new rules are generated with the entry of WRs in workplace labor relations. To investigate the attitudes of local governments and trade unions toward the WR and explain why their responses vary from endorsing and accommodating to suppressing WRs. The project is designed to contribute to our understanding of the new development of labor dispute resolutions, state-labor relations, and the labor movement in China. 在西方市場經濟，集體談判是勞資雙方的自願行為，政府一般不予干預。工會代表工人就僱用和工作條件與資方談判。談判失敗可能會觸發罷工。在中國，由於工會無法真正代表工人利益，工人事實上處於無組織狀態。那麼，當工人罷工並與資方進行談判時，誰來代表他們？在缺乏工會代表的情況下，集體談判如何進行？廣東地區的初步證據顯示，在越來越多的工廠裡，工人自己選舉代表同資方談判。這些工人代表成為集體談判中代表工人的談判主體。此項研究將“工人代表制”視為中國解決集體勞動爭議的新模式，探討這一模式的背景，形成，過程以及對工人運動和勞動關係的影響。本項研究回答如下問題：如何解釋工人代表制的出現？這一制度法律基礎是什麼？工人代表在罷工和集體談判中發揮了什麼作用？工人代表如何與資方互動？地方政府和工會對工人代表的做法有和反應？工人代表制在多大程度上影響集體談判結果？具體來說，本項研究有如下目標：（1）分析工人代表制出現的社會經濟及法律背景，解釋為何這種衝突處理模式在珠三角地區得到傳播。（2） 探索工人代表制的形成和角色──工人代表是如何選舉的，什麼樣的人會站出來當工人代表，他們如何代表工人訴求，他們的行為會面臨什麼後果，等等。(3) 探索工人代表制為工廠的勞動爭議解決帶來了什麼變化，是否創造出任何新的、具有長遠意義的遊戲規則。（4）調查地方政府和工會對工人代表做法的態度，解釋他們對工人代表制反應的差異性──為何有時認可、有時支持、有時壓制。這一研究項目將對深入瞭解中國勞動爭議解決制度、國家與勞工的關係以及工人運動的發展作出貢獻。

12645816.label: Realisation of objectives
12645816.value: In western market economies, collective bargaining is conducted between trade unions and employers voluntarily with less government intervention. Union organizations represent workers to bargain with employers for the terms and conditions of employment. However, as Chinese trade unions are unable to represent workers and workers are de facto unorganized, who stands for workers at the bargaining table? Evidence shows that, in more and more factories in Guangdong, workers have elected their own representatives during collective disputes. These representatives have organized workers, pressed their demands at the bargaining table, and sought social support as well as the endorsement of local authorities and official trade unions—they have become de facto ‘bargaining units’ for the benefit of the labor force in many labor disputes cases. The practice has been termed as ‘Worker Representation. This project has sought to understand this new practice in labor relations. I adopted the following methods to realize the objectives of the project. First, an extensive literature review on labor relations, labor disputes settlement, worker representation in the West in general and in China in particular, with an aim to locate the research question in the larger intellectual context. Second, I conducted fieldwork in the Guangdong Province and collected more than 30 cases in which striking workers elected their representatives to negotiate with employers. Some cases were collected through interviews by myself and my students, while others were provided by my research collaborators in Guangdong. The cases covered some notable strikes that happened in 廣東諾基亚, 哥士比鞋厂，广 東聯盛磨具公司，深圳威迪信，勝美達廠，永隆玩具廠，佛山工藝总廠，番禺恆宝厂，深圳IBM, etc. I explored how the practice of worker representation, which was not officially recognized by local authorities, was justified, what roles worker representatives performed in the process of strikes and collective bargaining, and how local governments responded to worker representation without trade unions. I also tried to look into workers’ motivations of choosing to become a representative and the difficulties they met in the performing of their role. The interviews were conducted in open-ended and semi-structured format. Prepared questions were used, though modified and new questions were added during the interview process. Most interviews were transcribed. I conducted a series of in-depth interviews with the members of Laowei, a Shenzhen-based law firm also operating as a NGO that initiated and promoted the idea and the practice of worker representation. I visited the firm several times and also invited its members to come to our campus to have informal talks. My interview with the members of Laowei focused on their strategies to turn worker representation as a spontaneous action in some factories into a somewhat regularized practice and how they attempted to legitimize the practice of worker representation, which does not have legal status in Chinese labor laws. In the meantime, I also interviewed some NGO members who followed the model established by Laowei to practice worker representation. Based on the research on what Laowei and other NGO did in advancing worker representation, I developed the conceptual categories to understand the strategy to legitimate worker representation in normative, pragmatic and cognitive terms. I also interviewed local officials of Nanshan Township in Shenzhen about their practices to deal with labor strikes and disputes. Third, supporting research students was an important way of realizing the objectives of the project. Two of my doctorate students were partially financed by the research grant in their research. They all conducted extensive fieldwork in the Guangdong area. One student did research on NGOs in Guangzhou and Shenzhen, with the role of NGOs in assisting worker representation as one of the important issues of her dissertation. Another student investigated worker representative-led strikes in two factories and compared their strategies and the outcomes. Her paper was published in China Review. Fourth, I held a half-day workshop to discuss the current labor situation in the Guangdong area. The purpose of this event was to share the views with scholars from the mainland on the new development of labor conflict resolution and worker representation. Participants included labor scholars who happened to be visiting Hong Kong and NGO members from Shenzhen as well as scholars from local universities. They came from the following universities and organizations: Capital University of Economics and Trade (two scholars), Chinese Institute of Labor Relations (one scholar), City University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong Baptist University (2 scholars and 2 PhD students), NGO activists (three) and a few local postdoc and postgraduate students. In the workshop, Prof. Jiao from Chinese Institute of Labor Relations talked about the recent changes in the government’s policy toward labor relations, trade unions and NGOs. Prof. Meng Quan from Capital University of Economics and Trade presented his research on labor dispute settlements. Mr. Wang and Mr. He from Laowei in Shenzhen introduced the practice of worker representation In a Summer School on "Labor and Rights in an Era of Global Precarity: Views from China," organized by Australian National University and co-organized by several European Universities in 2017, I was invited to give two talks, one of which is entitled on “Representation without Trade Unions: Worker Representatives in Labor Strikes in South China,” based on the preliminary findings of this research project. More than 30 researchers, graduate students and unionists from Europe and China attended this event. Although many of its objectives have been realized, I have to say that some unexpected occurrence snice mid-2018 hindered the research process at the late stage. First, since 2018, local governments’ control over labor activism has intensified. A few NGOs which once promoted worker representation were forcibly closed and their leaders detained. The atmosphere turned unfriendly for fieldwork. Second, the outburst of Covid-19 pandemic further impeded the research, not only because field visits were impossible, but also because RAs and research collaborators could not carry out their duties. Both first and second reasons to some extent influenced the scheduled interviews with local officials, which is the fourth objective of the project. Third, my full-time senior RA, who is my PhD student, had to quit the post in the summer of 2018, as she received an offer of assistant professorship from Nanjing University. I tried to find another full-time RA since then but was not successful for various reasons. I could only hire some part-time assistants. This is the reason why a portion of the budget for staffing was unspent

12645816.label: Major findings and research outcome
12645816.value: 1) A paper entitled “Contesting for Legitimacy: Worker Representation in Collective Bargaining in Guangdong” was published in Journal of Contemporary China. This is the first paper dealing with the topic in the English literature. The paper shows that to promote worker representation (WR), NOG activists have tried to legitimize the practice in pragmatic, normative, and cognitive terms. Nevertheless, WR poses a dilemma to the government, as it brings two divergent outcomes: it provides solution to labor disputes and it inspires labor activism. As a result, the government’s response to WR has oscillated between accommodation and suppression. 2) A co-authored paper entitled “Movement-oriented Labor NGOs in South China: Exit with Voice and Displaced Unionism” published in China Information examines the role of labor NGOs in assisting worker representation in strikes. It defines this type of labor NGOs as movement-oriented NGOs and demonstrates that performing a union-like role, these NGOs are instrumental to promote WR in factories. 3) In the field work on labor issues, I came cross the problems regarding how local governments manage social conflict through institutional innovation. The interest in this issue led to a paper entitled “Local State Adhocracy: Infrastructural Power and Stability Maintenance in Grassroots China” that appeared in Problems of Post-Communism. This study explores a new format of infrastructural power, termed the “local state adhocracy,” by using China’s stability maintenance apparatuses as a case. It argues that uch an adhocracy generates new capability of the state but also weakens the rule of law and institutionalization. 4) In the meantime, co-authored one book chapter entitled “Seeking Solutions: How Local Governments Handle Collective Labor Disputes” in Handbook on Urban Development in China, Ray Yep, June Wang and Thomas Johnson, eds. My book on state-labor relations in contemporary China （當代中國的國家與勞工：制度、衝突與變遷）was published by Chinese University Press in January 2020. This book is the product of six GRF-financed projects in the past two decades. Sponsored by this research fund, my student, Dr Chen Wei, published a paper in China Review. Her paper examines how worker representatives set up informal strike organizations and explores the factors that led to success or failure of strikes.

12645816.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12645816.value: During the execution of this project, I found that several issues are worth a further exploration: 1) the networks of worker representatives to mobilize their fellow workers in collective action; 2) the ideological context in which the idea of worker representation is formed. I found that WP represents a liberal alternative for labor conflict resolution, in contrast with other two types of activism: moderate and leftist, both of which have different ideological orientations and strategies. It would be interesting to understand the ideological underpinning of each activism and compare their strategies and outcomes; and 3) the relationship between trade unions and worker representatives. The official trade union has tried to keep distance from the practice of worker representation. However, some local union cadres have showed accommodative attitudes towards worker representation. A further investigation into unions’ perception of WR, to what extent WR affects unions’ view on their role in labor disputes, and how unions interact with WP, etc., will help deepen our understanding of the impact of WR in labor relations.

12645816.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12645816.value: Worker representation (WR) has emerged from Chinese workers’ collective struggles for economic betterment. WR activists have attempted to turn this spontaneous practice into a substitute dispute settlement arrangement. This research has found that WR constitutes an alternative way of labor organizing without trade unions in labor conflicts. Substituting for some roles that trade unions have failed to fulfil, WR allows workers to confront employers and make claims in a more organized manner. It has provided a format for organization and enhanced workers’ position as a ‘party’ in labor conflict. It forces employers to face a more organized labor force with one voice for its demands as well as bargaining power backed by collective action. Electing representatives has provided workers with opportunities to practice ‘democracy’ in workplaces, while debates on demands and tactics, along with concerted actions, have enhanced their consciousness and solidarity. Thus, it can be argued that the practice of WR has to some extent helped nurture organized labor activism in factories.

12646116.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12646116.value: Background: Children with intellectual disabilities (ID) are more vulnerable to obesity when compared to the normal children (Getchell et al., 2012; Maiano, 2011). Active video games (AVGs) on physical activity (PA) behavior have attracted academic interest and exploration since 2000. It has been demonstrated that an intervention with AVGs is compatible with the school setting and behavioral change in health and PA (Lau, et al., 2015). However, special populations such as ID children and their needs have been neglected in this area (Martins, Carvalho & Soares, 2011). ID children’s PA behavior, motor ability and physical fitness is still an under-explored area. Aims: To determine the effect of a prescribed AVG intervention on ID children’s PA levels (sedentary, light, moderate, and vigorous), motor ability, and physical fitness. The intervention effects in children with different intellectual disability categories (i.e., mild, moderate, severe and profound) will be also explored. Design: A standard two-arm parallel, single-blinded, randomized control cluster trial. Schools: Participants will be recruited from six special schools in Hong Kong (two mild, two moderate and two severe & profound categories). Schools with same intellectual disability categories will be randomly assigned into intervention group and control group. Participants: 360 Children aged 9~16 years old (180 in each group) with intellectual disabilities will be recruited. Intervention: ID children randomized to the intervention group will participate in an AVG intervention 60 minutes per week for 16 weeks in their PE class, in addition to their usual activity levels. The research team will prescribe updated AVG consistent with moderate-vigorous intensity. Control: The control group will continue with usual PA alone and will not receive the AVG intervention. Analysis: Repeated measures mixed model (2 groups X 2 time points (16-week post- test and 8-week follow up test)) by SPSS 23.0 will be used to investigate the intervention effect on primary and secondary outcomes, adjusting for baseline characteristics and correlation between repeated observations. Significance: This will be the pioneering study to provide definitive evidence for the impact of a prescribed AVG intervention on ID children’s PA level, motor ability and physical fitness. If effective, this research will provide significant evidence from the innovative method to inform health professionals and PE teachers how to incorporate AVG to enhance physical active behaviors, motor ability and physical fitness in ID children. Finally they may be able to enjoy a better quality of life. 研究摘要 研究背景 與正常兒童相比，智力障礙兒童更容易罹患肥胖症(Getchell et al., 2012; Maiano, 2011)。自2000年起，體感遊戲中的身體活動行為已經引起相應的學術興趣和探索。應用體感遊戲的干預研究已經證明其在學校環境中的可適性，及其對身體活動和健康行為改變的效果(Lau, et al., 2015)。但是，此領域在智力障礙等特殊人群及其需求中的應用是被忽視的(Martins, Carvalho & Soares, 2011)。智力障礙兒童的身體活動行為、運動能力及體適能仍未有充分研究。 研究目的 研究應用體感遊戲對智力障礙兒童的身體活動量（靜坐及輕度、中度、重度強度）、運動能力和體適能的干預效果。并探討其對不同智力障礙水平（輕度、中度、重度及深度）的干預效果區別。 研究設計 兩個組別、單盲的隨機對照試驗。 學校選取 本研究擬選取香港6所特殊學校，其中輕度、中度、重度及深度智力障礙學校各2所，并將相同智力障礙分類的學校隨機分配為干預組和對照組。 研究對象 360名9~16歲的智力障礙兒童，每組各180名。 干預措施 隨機分配為干預組的智力障礙兒童將接受體感遊戲干預措施。除學生正常的身體活動外，干預組兒童每週在體育課中使用體感遊戲60分鐘，共16周。體感遊戲中的分類遊戲將選取中至高強度身體活動量的遊戲（如、乒乓球、拳擊、跳繩等）。對照組不接受體感遊戲干預，僅進行常規日常生活的身體活動。 研究分析 學生的身體活動水平、運動能力及體適能將在研究開始前、體感遊戲結束后（第16周）、干預結束后8周（第24周）分別測量三次。數據分析將應用SPSS中重複測量的混合模型（2組*2個時間點）分析體感遊戲干預措施對主要和次要結局變量的效果，并在分析中調整基線特征值和重複測量值間的相關性。 研究意義 本研究將開創性的為體感遊戲對智力障礙兒童身體活動量、運動能力及體適能的干預提供研究證據。如果干預研究有效，本研究也將為健康專業人士和體育教師針對如何整合體感遊戲增加智力障礙兒童的健康提供依據。并幫助智力障礙兒童享受更好的生活質量。

12646116.label: Realisation of objectives
12646116.value: A two-arm cluster trail was conducted in 203 children with intellectual disability (ID) in Hong Kong. The intervention group was provided with AVG (bowling, soccer, boxing, table tennis etc.) at two 30-min sessions per week, with a total of 12 weeks. The control group continued with usual physical activity (PA). In this intervention study, results indicated that significant increases in BMI and body fat percentage were observed at post-test within both groups. The same trend existed for motor proficiency. Children’s BOT-2 (motor proficiency) score increased from 52.06 (standard deviation (SD): 21.80) at baseline to 55.27 (SD: 16.32) after intervention in the intervention group, while it increased from 58.01 (SD: 14.74) at baseline to 60.46 (SD: 14.20) at post-test in the control group. However, the intervention effect with adjusted changes in the intervention group relative to the control group was not statistically significant for children’s body composition, PA levels, and motor proficiency. Although AVG interventions have been successful in enhancing PA behaviour among typically developing children, the present study provides a different finding. A more in-depth understanding of why the AVG intervention was ineffective regarding body composition, PA and motor proficiency in students with ID was discussed. Specific considerations in AVG intervention research among students with ID: Howie and colleagues (2017) found that the quantity of game exposure (i.e. game time, pattern of exposure) does not lead into the ineffective outcome. The ineffectiveness of the AVG intervention is because of the quality of play (i.e. game selection, facilitators and barriers to play). Below are the recommendations that may explain why the intervention was ineffective in the children with ID and how the future intervention may adopt the recommendations to modify and produce significant intervention effects in students with ID. (1) Program dosage Based on the majority of the AVG intervention studies with typically developing children, the minimum effective dosage regarding the exercise frequency, intensity, time and type were two 1-hour sessions/week for 12 weeks. In the present study, exercise frequency, intensity and type were the same, but the exercise time was significantly less, i.e., half the time compared to similar studies. In the study of Howie and colleagues (2017), they specified that 80 minutes per week was the minimum time of AVG intervention for disabled children. Therefore, at least 40-minute per session is recommended to produce significant effects in the future study. The meta-analysis conducted by Hocking and colleagues (2019) showed that variable dosages has produced inconsistent effects of AVG on disabled children’s motor function. Hickman et al., (2017) also proposed that further researches in the dosage is imperative to maximize the potential benefits of AVG on children with movement disorders after they conducted a systematic review. (2) Game selection ID students seldom played multiple games or tried new games even though they were provided. This behavioural characteristic might reduce their adherence and increase boredom when intervention progressed. To tackle this behavioural characteristic of children with ID, tailored game play should be deliberately matched and delivered by the researchers or teachers to them in future interventions to relate the player’s behaviour and the AVG narrative. At the same time, AVG with dramatic tension, humor and optimal challenges should be selected to continuously produce fun element in the game (Thompson, 2012). Supervised play by game instructors with varieties of AVGs should be implemented to ensure the relatedness and fun of the AVG to the players. (3) Game competitiveness During the AVG play, students with ID were significantly frustrated when they played sport games with winners and losers. On the contrary, they demonstrated much more pleasant emotions when playing adventure games. Staiano and colleagues (2012) suggested that cooperative games is a better approach to engage the children in AVG play. For the adventure games, students with ID experienced progression and advancement through scoring, and they could self-pace themselves. This self-paced content and scoring could provide students with a feeling of success and accomplishment. This phenomenon echoed what Thompson (2012) claimed that self-monitor, problem solving opportunity and exploration are effective game features to AVG design. To conclude, AVGs with win-lose games should be minimized or avoided and self-paced game should be installed in ID student interventions in the future because game competitiveness might induce lower motivation and emotional fluctuations. (4) Game difficulty Physically too hard or cognitively too complicated are reported as the major barriers for disabled children to play the AVG (Howie, et al., 2017). Students with ID were found to be less active when playing more demanding sport-specific skills in AVGs since these sport skills could be too challenging for them and caused failure, that caused them frustration, and they might have stopped playing. Students with ID also showed much more preference towards games liked the real-world background such as trees, forests, waterfalls, etc., and less sport-specific skills were required. Therefore, simple sport skills and realistic backgrounds are preferred in future interventions. (5) Efficiency of the AVG setting It was discovered that the school spent significant time to set up training, change the games and explain the AVG instructions during the 30-minute intervention. This inefficiency of the AVG setting should be reduced in the intervention of AVGs on students with ID. (6) Transfer of motor proficiency According to the Challenge Point Framework (Guadagnoli and Lee, 2004), and OPTIMAL Theory (Wulf & Lewthwaite, 2016), to find out the optimal challenge point and link up the expectancy effect, learner autonomy and external focus of the participants in motor ability improvement should be considered in the future intervention study in children with ID. (7) Social interactive AVGs During the intervention, students with ID demonstrated difficulty with playing when the AVG requested them to interact with other students either in cooperative or competitive play. It is understandable that students with ID, especially those with ASD symptoms, have problems with interacting and cooperating with others. Therefore, individual AVGs are more appropriate for this population. Feltz et al., (2012) and Thompson (2012) suggested an alternative that an avatar can be an ideal approach to motivate the adoption and sustainability on AVG play. On one hand, avatar can avoid the interactive or communication problems of the children with ID. On the other hand, avatar can achieve the effect of modelling, cooperation and interactivity. Since players may identify with the avatar, it can be a reinforcing effect to them. (8) Role of the PE teacher and teacher/student ratio In the intervention, students with ID demanded that their PE teachers be with them and helped start the AVGs, especially those with ASD symptoms. This process was not only related to the technical issues (i.e., instructions and knowledge) of the AVG play, but was also linked with trust, security, social support and provided positive social experience to overcome the barriers to play (Howie et al., 2017). In the present study, PE teacher was not planned to act as a facilitator in the intervention. But based upon the participant’s response, PE teachers’ facilitation should be added into the intervention and hence student’s adoption and sustainability in AVG could be better. Individual assistance from teachers to students with ID is a significant factor for ensuring the quality of the AVG delivery and producing effective intervention outcomes.

12646116.label: Major findings and research outcome
12646116.value: Major findings are: (1) Overall intervention effects Significant increases in BMI, body fat percentage and motor proficiency were observed at post-test within both groups. Children’s BOT-2 score increased from 52.06 to 55.27 after intervention in the intervention group, while it increased from 58.01 to 60.46 in the control group. However, the intervention effect with adjusted changes in the intervention group relative to the control group was not statistically significant for children’s body composition, PA levels, and motor proficiency. (2) Age group difference Among the younger children, significant increases in adiposity-related outcomes (BMI, body fat percentage), were detected after intervention within the intervention group (BMI: 17.80 kg/m2 at baseline vs. 18.04 kg/m2 at post-test, p=0.008; body fat percentage: 17.75% at base line vs. 19.06% at post-test, p=0.025) but not within the control group. The BOT-2 score significantly increased from 50.29 to 53.43 in the intervention group (p<0.001) and increased from 54.21 to 58.33 within the control group (p<0.001). No significant group intervention effect difference was found for all of the outcomes in the intervention group compared with the control group (mean (95%CI) of adjust change: -1.50 (-4.34, 1.35)). For the older children, participants in the intervention group had a decrease in MVPA and an increase in BOT-2 score after intervention compared to the control group. No significant difference was detected for any outcome within the control group at post-test. (3) Body weight group difference Among non-overweight groups, BMI in the intervention group increased at post-test (17.77 kg/m2 at baseline vs. 17.97 kg/m2 at post-test, p=0.004), while MVPA decreased after the intervention (56.07 min/day at baseline vs. 45.83 min/day at post-test, p=0.001). The BOT-2 score significantly increased from 55.13 to 59.43 within the intervention group (p<0.001) but not within the control group. However, no significant intervention effect was found across the intervention and control groups. Among the children with overweight, an increase in BOT-2 score was obtained within both the intervention and control groups after intervention, while the adjusted change was not significant. (4) ID group difference During the data collection, most of the severe/profound and moderate participants could not finish the testing items due to their emotion disturbance. Therefore, the present study only had 202 students with mild ID and 17 students with moderate ID, analysis power was inefficient to compare the intervention effect. From the test values, there seems no obvious improvements on variables across group after intervention.

12646116.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12646116.value: Based upon the present findings and the discussion, intervention guidelines are developed for future AVG interventions for children with ID. To maximize the AVG technology for this special population, the quality of the AVGs and the special behavioural/emotion characteristics of the children with ID should be considered and matched as these factors are very different from their typically developing counterparts. The recommendations and guidelines can be used to apply for the 2nd stage of the intervention to increase the motivation and minimize barriers to play AVGs and enhance PA, motor proficiency and health among children with ID.

12646116.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12646116.value: Background: Active video games (AVGs) intervention is compatible with the school setting and behavioural change in physical activity (PA) and health. However, children with intellectual disability (ID) and their needs have been neglected in this area. Methods: A two-arm cluster trail was conducted in 203 students with ID. The intervention group was provided a 12-week intervention with AVG. The control group continued with usual PA. Children’s body composition, PA level, and motor proficiency were measured by Tanita BC-418, ActiGraph GT3X+ and Bruininks-Oseretsky Test of Motor Proficiency™ - Second Edition (BOT-2), respectively. The differences of the intervention group relative to control group were calculated by univariate analysis in general linear model adjusted for participants’ demographic characteristics and baseline assessment of the variable. Results: Children’s BOT-2 score increased in both intervention and control group after the study. However, the intervention effect was not statistically significant for children’s body composition, PA levels, and motor proficiency. Subgroup analyses in different age and body weight status groups did not find the significant intervention effects. Conclusion: The rationales of why such intervention was ineffective in this population was discussed. These explanations may provide better guidelines for future AVG intervention for children with ID.

12646716.label: Project Title(Chinese)
12646716.value: 一種全新政治視野的出現：中國人對盧梭社會契約論的接受，1895-1925

12646716.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12646716.value: This project explores the rise of a new political horizon through the case study of Chinese intellectuals’ reception of Rousseau’s Of the Social Contract, 1895-1925. Compared with all other Western classics, Rousseau’s work was most popular among the first generation of Chinese intelligentsia. Its reception decisively changed their political horizon. According to Gadamer, “The horizon is the range of vision that includes everything that can be seen from a particular vantage point.” People use their own horizons to imagine others’ to overcome the boundaries between present and past (Gadamer, 2004). While Gadamer focuses on the “fusion of horizons” within one tradition, the project uses his theory to frame dialogues between two traditions of political thought. Rather than focusing on an individual thinker’s response to Western political thought, this project studies how a group of influential intellectuals interacted with each other as critics of Rousseau’s work. Rather than concentrating on prestigious figures, this project also scrutinizes less well-known intellectuals’ writings in newspapers and journals. The project reveals that Chinese intellectuals’ reception of Western political thought was facilitated by at least four different horizons, whereas previous studies focus on only one or two of them. More importantly, the project shows how these horizons interplayed, contradicted, compromised and eventually fused into one unique horizon, whose formation accompanied the rise of the Chinese intelligentsia as both agents and products of modernization. It is the synthesis of the four horizons but not particular concepts or doctrines that characterized modern Chinese political thought. The research outputs, which include a monograph and three articles, will advance understanding of the resources the Chinese intelligentsia have been mobilizing to reflect upon their past, to confront the problems of the present and to imagine a brighter future. Furthermore, while previous studies focus on Rousseau’s influence on liberalism and statism in China, this project sheds light on a neglected aspect of the story, namely the connection between the Chinese reception of Rousseau and the origin of radical movements. Finally, the project helps understand Rousseau’s legacy in Chinese politics by uncovering various political visions evident in the Chinese writings on Rousseau. The project combines the methods of intellectual history and political philosophy. Rather than focusing on a few concepts and phrases or paragraphs, the project performs close readings and contextual analyses of a text from beginning to end to grasp its overall arguments and the line of reasoning. 本計劃通過中國知識分子於1895到1925年間對盧梭《社會契約論》的翻譯和詮釋，考察一種新的政治視野在中國的出現。加德瑪 (Gadamer) 認為人們總是通過他們自己的視野想像別人的視野，以消除過去與當下之間的隔膜。他強調的是一個傳統內部當下和過去不同視野的融合。本計劃則借用他的理論討論中西兩個政治思想傳統的對話。 本計劃揭示中國知識分子對西方政治哲學的接受，至少受到至少四種不同視野的影響，包括中國傳統政治思想、中國近代的經驗、日本明治以來的反思和圍繞盧梭理論而傳入中國的西方哲學的視野。以往的研究往往只注意其中一到兩種視野。更重要的是本計劃展示了所有這些視野互動、衝突、妥協和最終融合成一種全新的、獨特視野的全過程。正是這四種視野的融合而不是特定的概念或主張構成了現代中國思想的特色。 本研究幫助我們深入了解中國知識分子用來反省過去、面對現實問題和想像未來的思想資源，其中一個重點是揭示中國人接受盧梭理論與現代激進思潮興起的聯繫。最後，本研究也希望通過分析早期中國人對盧梭理論的描述和討論，考察盧梭在中國政治中的遺產。

12646816.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12646816.value: 從三大都市 ：香港 丶 亞特蘭大和比勒陀利亞看移民人仕的住房安全 住房是人類基本的必需品 。透過住房這鑰匙 ，能改善人們在醫療 ，福利及増加他們對某地方的歸屬感 。在迅速都市化下 ，全球超過十億人面對房屋缺乏或對居住環境感到不安 。因此 ，聯合國近日將新都市權益事項作為焦點 。然而 ，大眾對住房安全沒有一個統一國際的定義 ，也對自身常推動都市化的移民人仕怎樣經驗其住房危機 ，缺乏深層的認識 。例如 ，合法身份或基於信仰機構（FBOs）的延伸角色 ，它們兩者如何影響移民人仕的住房安全感 ？因此 ，我們三大國際合作伙伴包括香港（中國）丶 亞特蘭大（美國）和比勒陀利亞（南非）一致定義移民人仕為一羣非本土出生和在該城市居住少於一年 。我們會透過這羣組分別在以上指定三個城市的生活經驗從而建構住房安全的知識 。 本研究項目有四大目標 。第一 ，考察以下關係 ：（甲）移民人仕的合化身份 ，歸屬感及不安感（乙）基於信仰機構的做法和實踐 ，歸屬感及不安感 ；從而深化我們對移民人仕其住房安全的認識 。本研究籍著釐清住房安全在不同場景的重要性 ；從而進一步發展有關危機的學術研究 。第二 ，透過相關人仕建立一個基於鄰舍其住房安全的指標 。第三 ，轉化我們優質的理論概念與實踐經驗成為更理想的政策 。第四 ，增進公眾就移民人仕住房的參與 。 本研究項目為期三十個月 。我們會在香港丶亞特蘭大和比勒陀利亞當中 ，每兩個城市進行住房安全對比分析 ，共六個對比 。這三個城市是研究重點 ，因為它們有嚴竣的住房問題 ，對於移民人仕合法身份有著截然不同的定義及擁有形形式式 ，有影響力的基於信仰機構（FBOs） 。我們將會採用參與行動研究方法 ，在每一個研究城市中組成一個指導小組來收集政府 丶 基於信仰機構（FBOs）丶 房地產 丶 舊居民和移民人仕的資料 。本研究項目會採用半結構性訪問 ，收集三十個移民人仕及六個基於信仰機構（FBOs）的第一手資料 。然後我們會運用紮根理論進行分析及計算初步住房安全指標數值 。進一步 ，我們會基於移民人仕 丶基於信仰機構（FBOs）和政府代表成立焦點小組進行復校和統一住房安全指標 。 本硏究計劃成果包括有學術文章 ，政策概要及評價文章 。我們將透過加入本地相關人仕共同參與及其表達的意見 ，提升社會與公眾在移民人仕及其住房權利方面的關注 ，和相關的討論 。本計劃還帶給本科生一些研究經驗 ，藉著他們的學習反映出新的參與式研究方法作為課程材料 。在這持續都市化的鄒勢下 ，本硏究將會令國際間 ，對移民人仕其住房問題有著深遠的影響 。

12646816.label: Realisation of objectives
12646816.value: Objective 1 This objective has been fully achieved. We followed and, in one area, enhanced the originally proposed research design. Adopting a Participatory Action Research (PAR) method, we established Steering Groups (SGs) in each city location, i.e. Hong Kong, Atlanta and Tshwane. The Terms of Reference covered: survey and question design; case-study profiles; assistance in accessing newcomer migrants; interpreting empirical findings; partnership in changing public understandings of housing security issues. We recruited 5-7 members from amongst Government and Non-Government Organisations (NGOs), the property sector, permanent residents, and migrants. To identify suitable case study communities we collated relevant census, secondary survey, and other data relating to migration, housing, and employment. Drawing on these data and SG input we selected two areas per city that could represent diverse experiences of migrants: To Kwa Wan and Yuen Long in Hong Kong; Sunnyside and Mamelodi East in Tshwane; Clarkston and Stone Mountain in Atlanta. The detailed pilot study among newcomer migrants in Hong Kong was completed during the summer and fall of 2017. Following extant literature we explored: vulnerability and precarity in key domains such as economy, housing, social relations, and legal status, and access to NGO support. A total of 22 newcomers completed long interviews. Based on analysis of transcripts and triangulation with literature, particularly on migrant wellbeing, we drafted common long interview prompts for all sites and shared these with each SG. After sustained and productive cross-national discussion and negotiation, we enhanced our original research design by doubling the target number of interviews from 30 to 60 per city. This we did to see more diversity in the data. To compare results we devised common nomenclature across the sites. We defined “newcomer migrants” are those persons who have been living in a community for less than a year, and were born outside this area. “Community” refers to a locally and officially recognized place that is home to about 100,000 persons. “Area” refers to the Hong Kong SAR, the USA, and the Gauteng region in South Africa. “Housing” covers the range of habitations recognized by the UN, including sleeping rough, squatting, renting, owning, and staying in temporary quarters. We established a common Google Drive protocol for securely storing, updating, and sharing all project materials from all sites. Collecting double the number of interviews incurred extra time, and we appreciate the support of HKBU and RGC in granting a no-cost six month extension to the project timeline. Each interview format and protocol was approved by the relevant national IRB authority. SGs suggested key contacts in each community who could make introductions to newcomer migrants, and we further snowballed from these multiple seeds. The PI travelled to the Atlanta site twice and Tshwane site three times during the project to ensure consistency of methodology, and to better understand the field conditions. Between March 2018 and April 2019 we completed and transcribed target interviews (Hong Kong and Tshwane 60 each, Atlanta 112, total 232). Over the same period we also completed and transcribed 18 interviews with six NGOs in each city. The interviews generated a range of nominal, ordinal, ratio, and ethnographic data. We followed standard methods of analysis, notably cross-tabulations, correlations, and grounded theory). Our preliminary findings were discussed, interpreted, and clarified by each SG independently, and at a project team meeting in Tshwane in August 2019. Overall findings and policy recommendations were discussed at the culminating Virtual SG in November 2019. Our dissemination strategy also follows the original proposal. We have prioritised the release of policy findings (see Objective 3 and 4 below), submitted three manuscripts (at the time of writing) to Q1 journals and are drafting a fourth, and have prepared the data archive. Objective 2 Our SGs affirmed the relevance of what we had proposed in Objective 2 (i.e. to produce a summary measure of “migrant housing security” in local areas that can inform policy). However, analysis of our pilot data led us to re-formulate how we operationalized this. Our data suggested that a single measure of “housing security” would not capture the interdependent and diverse experiences of migrant vulnerability. To best represent what these data showed, we re-formulated our index using research on migrant Subjective Wellbeing (SWB). SWB is widely recognized in the migration literature as being a meaningful and accessible summary of complex social processes that can be compared from one location to another, over time, and across different groups. Our migrant interviews thus included a series of items on SWB. To date, we have submitted one paper that discusses variations in SWB (see output 4 in section C below) and we are drafting a second paper linking SWB with declining self rated health for the journal Cities & Health. Objective 3 and Objective 4 We have achieved these objectives through active dissemination and by building capacity for sustaining public engagements. Our empirical data supports five specific policy recommendations: (1) Increase locally sourced social and cultural capital to enhance belongingness and home; (2) Increase educational access for migrant children; (3) Increase NGO support for newcomers; (4) Promote physical and mental health (wellbeing) of arriving migrants; (5) Increase the effectiveness of communications between migrants and partners in urban prosperity. Taken together, these interventions are examples of how to build “platform communities” that enable and empower migrants and non-migrants to be partners in sustainable urban development. Our dissemination efforts therefore included a holistic message about the concept of platform communities, and more targeted content concerning particular policy examples. To increase access to these findings in a timely manner we produced a 16 page glossy Policy Brief booklet. This is available on-line through the HKBU Institutional Repository. We have sent hard copies to over 60 Government Departments and NGOs in the three cities. In December 2019 we contributed to a “Platform Communities” press event that involved other social science research from HKBU. This attracted journalists and editors from leading media organisations in Hong Kong, including SCMP, TVB, Cable TV, Commercial Radio, RTHK, Ming Pao, HK Economic Times, Sing Tao Daily, HK Economic Journal, and AM730. It generated subsequent press coverage (see section 11 below). We are disseminating the research through in-house publications, including HKBU Horizons which reaches 6,000 current and recent students. Outputs 2, 3 and 4 make reference to policy implications. The PAR design seeks to embed training, mentorship, and partnership relations into the research process. Our “research practice” team includes 12 students and 15 steering group members. By “training the trainers” the findings and recommendations of the research can sustain. For example, the research funded a PhD student who is now working at a local HK University and has incorporated research methodology into her curriculum materials. A Research Assistant is now enrolled as a PhD student at a leading South African University. Two of the three HKBU Undergraduate Research Fellows have been accepted onto Masters programmes (one in Canada, one in the UK).

12646816.label: Major findings and research outcome
12646816.value: The major empirical findings: (a) show that migrants experience structural vulnerabilities interdependently across the domains of everyday life (output 2); and (b), support the hypotheses that precarity (output 2, 3) and wellbeing (output 4) are contextual and relational. While migrants did report common experiences of precarity across the cities, particularly in regard to their employment and financial arrangements and socio-legal status, our analysis found differences in the experiences of housing, social relations, and belonging. While housing conditions expose migrants to vulnerability in Hong Kong, they are viewed more equivocally in Atlanta and Tshwane. For example, the sense of feeling “at home” varied widely, and we conceptualise this as a process of dwelling (output 1) involving distinct life course strategies (output 2). Migrants make differential use of government and NGO support. We found that selected NGOs play a strong mediating role in how migrants experience the material and symbolic precarities associated with housing (output 1). We report that one in five migrants had declining levels of self-rated health since moving, but this rose to one in three in To Kwa Wan (under preparation). The outcomes of the research advance theory in two directions. We extend life course transition theory by showing how linked lives and projects of belonging and dwelling are impacted by the conditions and affective relations of precarity in the first year of living in a new city (output 2). The dual aspect of precarity delays/accelerates transitions, de-links and re-links lives, and re-orients belonging (outputs 2 and 3). Initial evidence also identifies how family and institutional contexts may embed and reproduce precarity over the life course (output 3). Second, we contribute to wellbeing theory by linking life course with housing-specific contextual variations in SWB (output 4), and by exploring how measures of wellbeing and precarity account for variations in changes in self-rated health. The comparative and cross-national research design led us to make policy recommendations that address relevant international frameworks, namely the 2016 UN Healthy Cities and 2018 UN Global Compact on Safe, Regular, and Orderly Migration processes. While specific programmes addressing, for example, the education of migrant children need to be developed city by city, we advanced the cross-cutting concept of “platform communities” as a way to enable migrant resourcefulness to flourish. Undertaking cross-national research using PAR is still somewhat pioneering, and our research processes and protocols may serve as guides for other teams.

12646816.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12646816.value: The variations in patterns of declining health we found are consistent with “the salmon hypothesis” of selective return migration, and need more detailed and longitudinal tracing of how life course processes unfold comparatively across places and cohorts. More generally, further analysis is needed of how life course processes impact vulnerabilities that all city dwellers face (i.e. not just migrants, output 2). We have begun to consider the precarities of urban young adult cohorts who experience transitions in living arrangements, adulthood, education, and employment. We also see potential to enhance wellbeing theory by jointly considering objective, subjective, and affective factors. In our research, the latter included dynamic spatial and temporal meanings which have been traditionally hard to measure. We will use smart data to open up these inquiries because they are dynamic, offer greater spatial granularity, and expand the range of population scale analyses. Third, we are exploring ways to operationalise our understanding of dwelling processes into a deliverable policy framework. Two of the research team have long standing experience in their local communities embedding participatory methods, and we have obtained support from the Misereor Foundation Grant (MFG) “Urban Studio-Advancing Community Based Urban Praxis”) as follow-on funding.

12646816.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12646816.value: The objective of this research is to understand how housing conditions affect the physical and mental wellbeing of newly arriving migrants in cities. Our research team was the first to compare the housing and living conditions of newcomer migrants across three major cities: Hong Kong, Atlanta (USA), and Tshwane (South Africa). Analysis of 232 interviews with migrants and 18 interviews with NGOs revealed that, in each city, migrants face a common cocktail of financial, employment, and socio-legal vulnerabilities. However, health status, satisfaction with housing, and sense of home vary from city to city. We connect these variations with conditions of structural precarity, and with how migrants manage subjective factors in relation to their life plans. The findings are significant because they suggest that key development frameworks – including the 2018 UN Orderly Migration process – should address objective (including conditions of work, housing, and legal status) and subjective (including life planning and sense of belonging) factors holistically. The research is valuable because migration will be responsible for much of the rapid urbanization forecast over the next thirty years, and enhanced policy enabling migrants to contribute to sustainable development has to be based on empirical understandings.

12653416.label: Project Objectives
12653416.value: 從舞蹈美學、身體理論及脈絡研究(contextual studies)，評介六位香港當代舞編舞家的代表作。 梳理一九八Ｏ至二Ｏ一Ｏ年間香港當代舞蹈的多元發展。 評讀及闡述六位本地編舞家於此期間塑造的「香港身體」 與社會文化場境的關係。 分析六位編舞家作品所呈現的豐富文化意涵，以及作品內容對香港特殊文化環境的態度及回應。 邀請兩岸三地舞評人，透過共同閱讀及討論，撰寫對六位編舞家作品的觀賞角度、比較舞蹈美學及文化分析。 以跨學科（身體理論、舞蹈美學、舞蹈史、文化研究）方法，探討香港當代舞蹈創作中的藝術實踐及文化身份。

12653416.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12653416.value: This proposed project aims to conduct an in- depth study and provide critical perspectives to contemporary dance composition in Hong Kong from 1980 to 2010. It is the first systematic attempt to integrate fragmented information and critical writings of local contemporary dance choreography and its multi-developments. It reviews artistic attempts under the perspectives of dance history, aesthetics, social and cultural contexts. It focuses on six contemporary dance choreographers Helen Lai, Mui Cheuk Yin, Poon Siu Fai, Daniel Yeung, Uri Ng and Chin Sau Lin, who share same artistic background and dance resources in Hong Kong during the last three decades. They are all active choreographers introducing various dance forms and ideas of aesthetic bodies to the Hong Kong dance forum. More importantly, their works concern with the making of Hong Kong bodies under the post-colonial context and capitalistic consumption environment. This project will study representative works of these choreographers and analysis the dance forms and contents in details before providing overview and remarks. The project is also the first one to involve collaborative efforts of Hong Kong, Taiwan and PRC dance critics via interactive discussion to produce writings regarding the artistic achievements of the six individual choreographers. Dance theories spelt by Susan Sontag, Amelia Jones, Pina Bausch and Lin hwai-min which have direct influences on the representative work of the six choreographers are reviewed, as well as post-colonial art theories and body aesthetics. The findings result in academic research publications help to provide artistic recognition to contemporary dance scene in Hong Kong. They can also work as references for government’s sponsorship, presentation and assessment of the local dance art.

12653416.label: Realisation of objectives
12653416.value: 計劃目的，除去第五點未能邀請中國大陸舞評人以外，皆與最初計劃目的一致。未能邀請中國大陸舞評人的主要原因，是由於研究對象皆為香港當代編舞家，港、台舞評家最為熟悉，他們的研究亦最為深入。不過本研究曾舉辦研討交流，研討會上不乏中國大陸舞評人參與，他們的觀察與提問亦豐富了港、台藝評人彼此閱讀的角度，平衡了論點。 本計劃選出六位同期活躍於本港當代舞壇的編舞家，探討他們從一九八〇年代以還，近三十年的舞蹈藝術風格、美學變化與發展。此六位編舞家為錢秀蓮、黎海寧、梅卓燕、伍宇烈、潘少輝及楊春江。他們有著相近的背景，在香港生活及成長，接受專業的舞蹈教育，曾與國際編舞作出交流，並在本地當代舞壇別樹一幟，於舞蹈教育、編舞創作、藝術性舞蹈表演等方面富有影響力。他們的作品均展現了豐富的舞蹈議題， 拓闊了地道生活與藝術舞蹈的互動，並尋找及塑造了香港的藝術性身體。 計劃關注編舞家於作品中如何展示對香港社會及政治議題的知覺與態度；並特別著眼於編舞者彼此所曾經受到的共同影響，以及在香港互動及互相參詳的關係。 他們其中曾在香港生活及成長，於同一平台上創作(如城市當代舞蹈團)，但各放異彩。他們或從個人生活出發(如梅卓燕的《日記》系列)，或與傳統中國名著接軌(如黎海寧之《九歌》、《女書》)，或響應西方現當代藝術及中西文化的交融(如錢秀蓮的「武極」系列)，或思考舞蹈創作與香港社會場域的關係 (如潘少輝之《後獅子山下的遊園荊夢》)，或呈現身體與性別的議題(如楊春江之《灵灵性性天體樂園》)，或探索舞蹈作品所能「體現」的「香港性」(如伍宇烈的《糊塗爆竹賀新年》)。 計劃對黎海寧及梅卓燕的編舞閱讀，參考Pina Baush (包殊) 的舞蹈劇場理論。包殊善用劇場表現手法，呈現各種身體互動的可能，並把舞蹈作為有意味的生活關係論述。本計劃亦以環境美學中人與自然及社會的主客互動，闡述潘少輝如何在香港倡導環境舞蹈。關於楊春江作品的身體議題，研究參考包括東方的身體觀以及凝視 (gaze)理論中的主客體關係張力，如何在他的舞蹈中得以重整及消解。至於伍宇烈舞蹈的「香港性」，解讀參考包括後殖民理論以及箇中的文化身分策略。 錢秀蓮的中西舞蹈觀，部分可總結為道家陰陽關係的閱讀，此點觸及香港當代舞蹈裡的「中國性」，本計劃從比較美學及文化研究的考慮作出了補充。 計劃匯聚了港、台藝評人，共同對六位編舞家的作品進行研讀及展開對話，並透過研究報告交流會，豐富彼此閱讀的角度，平衡論點，並藉比較方法，見出香港當代舞蹈的發展進程於身份探求。交流後的書寫。經由編者的回應及總結，把焦點集中於文化脈絡及舞蹈美學的分析。 計畫所秉持的舞蹈哲學，是依美國美學家蘇珊.朗格(Susanne Langer)的提示，即任何一位觀賞者在與作品的邂逅裡感受興奮，是整體人類精神所可能達到的一種深度；包括作品中的社會意涵帶來的震撼和影響。那是透過創作或欣賞者在美感直覺的過程中，掌握到表現力的形式。

12653416.label: Major findings and research outcome
12653416.value: 香港舞壇於一九八〇年代，遇上港英政府引入現代舞蹈，為舞蹈思維帶來了衝擊。但影響香港當代舞的還不是一窩蜂的西方藝術與思潮。 本計劃中的編舞家對中國舞蹈、書法、音樂、文學及哲學的涉獵敏銳過人。楊春江便應用了他所認識的中國音樂與醫學，梅卓燕的舞袖亦沿依中國書法的筆觸; 錢秀蓮的「武極」系列等舞出篆、隸、楷、行、草，同時經營舞蹈的意、氣、形、韻。 黎海寧舞蹈熱愛香港作家的文字，沉浸於當中的女性書寫，內維情感濃重，外維則是「容積」編舞。潘少輝早期接受中國傳統舞蹈訓練，但創作題材和環境離不開香港，以舞蹈留住對中國和香港的歷史記憶。伍宇烈以生活的小趣味，回應香港環境正在進行的大論述，包括性別政治，同時採用反嚴肅的調子，其態度是研究「香港性」的上佳材料。研究計劃成書: 【香港當代編舞家作品研究（1980-2010）——身體：歷史、美學及身份探求】。香港: IATC。2019年9月。共頁256。(香港藝術發展局出版資助項目。)

12653416.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12653416.value: 計劃對六位香港編舞家的研究，乃基於他們成熟的表現力與舞蹈的「虛幻力」。其中共通的亦中亦西，非中非西，此消彼長，或離邏各斯中心，挑戰主流大論述的不同嘗試，是否正在轉化為愈趨個人化、私密化與瑣碎化，反歷史大論述的香港情懷? 舞台上的身體，正在怎樣伸展、扭曲、蜷縮、吶喊？怎樣呼應文字？還依然是完整、有機的整體呈現？ 這些問題有待繼續觀察並研究香港編舞新章中的表現力與生命力。

12653416.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12653416.value: 本計劃是一項系統性的研究工作，透過舞蹈、身體及文化理論等思考，深入研讀個別香港編舞家的舞蹈美學，連繫至創作間的共同社會文化背景， 以及創作中與「香港身體」有關的呈現及社會意涵，作出整理、陳述及反思。本計劃將直接促進香港當代舞蹈的藝術探索，使香港編舞家在國際上具文化及美學定位，有助制定評估準則以及對作品意涵的理解，包括創作的動機及藝術成就等；亦可成為政府文康部門策劃及資助本地當代舞蹈節目的參考。
