12656516.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12656516.value: This research project explores the dynamics and complexity of the relationship between the state, nationalism and globalisation in music teacher education in Hong Kong and Taipei. Hong Kong and Taiwan have long been crucibles of cross-cultural encounters between Chinese and Western cultures. They have different political ecologies (in terms of level of democracy), and have different relationships with Mainland China. These two factors have affected the meaning of “home country”, and therefore the promotion of national identity and nationalism in education and music education in both Chinese societies. In this project, nationalism is an important social and political phenomenon that involves creating, for Hong Kong and Taiwan, a definable identity through participation in singing and listening to both national anthems, and by developing Chinese and/or Taiwanese traditional and folk music in school music education. The dynamic effects of globalisation on teacher education are found in the integration of world music and popular music in both in-service and pre-service teacher education. To date, no studies examining the similarities and differences in music teacher education in Hong Kong and Taiwan have been found in relation to the double paradigm of nationalism and globalisation. The research methods will involve a survey questionnaire to a significant number of students (in the hundreds) attending a music education programme, as well as in-depth interviews with music teacher trainers, and pre- and in-service primary and secondary school teachers in the two localities. The core question for each of the different sectors of informants is the extent of their response to cultural shifts in the educational policies and music practices involved in the double process of nationalism and globalisation. This research will advance our understanding of the concepts of nationalism and globalisation in music education, not only by comparing Chinese localities with different socio-political contexts, but also by contrasting these experiences with those in other parts of the world. By reframing the major concerns of comparative education around the dynamics of national and global forces, the theoretical significance of this study is to provide insight into, and new explanations for, how changes in national and international systems and relations result in changes in the values and musical cultures of music teacher education. Why, and to what extent, education systems in different parts of the world are similar to and/or different from one another are major questions for scholars in the field of comparative music education. 本研究探索國家、民族主義、全球化和音樂教師教育之間的動態和複雜的關係性。香港和台灣是中國文化和西方文化交匯的地方。它們有不同的政治生態和民主水平，並與中國大陸有不同的關係。這兩個因素已影響這兩個華人社會，對“家國”有不同的含義，並因而在教育和音樂教育上促進民族認同和民族主義有所不同。 在這個香港和台灣研究中，民族主義是一個重要的社會和政治現象，涉及透過唱和聆聽國歌，並在學校音樂中推動中國和/或台灣的傳統和民間音樂，來創建一個可定義的國民身份和民族主義。全球化對教師教育的動態效果，已體現於在職和職前音樂教師教育中世界音樂和流行音樂之結合。迄今為止，還沒有研究探討民族主義和全球化對香港和台灣的音樂教師教育，有什麼相同和不相同之影響。 本研究的研究方法包括一份有關兩地學生參與音樂教育計劃的學生問卷調查，深入訪談音樂教師培訓者及在職和職前中小學音樂教師。我們問不同的研究對象一個共同核心問題，是有關他們對在教育政策和音樂實踐上民族主義和全球化文化轉變的反應程度。 這項研究將不僅通過比較香港和台灣不同的社會和政治背景，與它們跟世界其他地區的對比，使我們對音樂教育中的民族主義和全球化有進一步的概念理解。本研究重要理論意義是，通過重新界定在比較教育中國家和全球因素的重大關注點，對有關國家和國際體系的變化如何改變音樂教師教育的價值觀與音樂文化，提供新的洞見和解釋。

12656516.label: Realisation of objectives
12656516.value: The question of the link between nationalism and globalisation in education has puzzled many scholars and has generated numerous arguments that have dominated the debate in both Western and non-Western contexts in recent decades. This research project explored the dynamics and complexity of the relationship between the state, nationalism, and globalisation in music teacher education in Hong Kong (HK) and Taiwan (TW). These two Chinese territories have long been crucibles of cross-cultural encounters between Chinese and Western cultures. They have different political ecologies (in terms of level of democracy) and have different relationships with Mainland China. These two factors have affected the meaning of “home country”, and therefore the promotion of national identity and nationalism in education and music education in both Chinese societies. Granted that political education is now part of the school curriculum, the question of how to cultivate students’ national and cultural values through the curriculum will continue to be contentious. In order to realise the objectives of the research project, the research methods involved a survey questionnaire distributed to pre-service and in-service primary and secondary school teachers in HK and TW, as well as interviews with teachers who agreed to participate, conducted between winter 2017 and February 2019. The findings of the study revealed that there are fundamental gaps between overt and operational curricula, as well as the background of the teachers’ training and professional development. Towards the end of the data collection in HK and TW, the project also included the participation of music teachers from Mainland China. Given the current tumultuous political unrest between China and the regions of TW and HK, this project sought to illuminate the tensions facing school music education and teacher education in the selection of music cultures and knowledge not only to be taught in HK and TW but also in Mainland China in 2019. These challenges have prompted music teachers, education authorities, and policymakers to rethink and reconsider music cultures, cultural and national values, and delivery strategies in both the contents and methods of school music education. At the moment of finishing the research project, the current centralisation policy in Mainland China’s and Hong Kong’s school education and the decentralization policy (or intended to be) in Taiwan’s school education might result in a different but interesting and challenging scene between political and cultural impositions of music education in these Chinese territories’ future. How to balance the cultural dimensions of the teaching and learning of local, national, and global music cultures in contemporary HK’s and TW’s school music education will remain an issue in the future political and cultural developments of the two societies. Due to the two China factors mentioned above, it is also equally important for the respective governments to develop a long-term policy for teachers’ professional development to facilitate them in coping with the demands of the incessantly changing contexts in which they serve. This research project will advance readers’ understanding of the concepts of nationalism and globalisation in music education, not only by summarising these Chinese localities’ different sociopolitical contexts but also contrasting these experiences with those in other parts of the world. Based on the survey findings, the research project argues that preparation for globalization and multiculturalism not only poses a challenge or a threat but also creates an opportunity for the development of the teaching profession, and that this depends to a large extent on how governments translate these global and national essentials into demands or requirements on teachers. At present, the availability of the vast range of local, national, and global cultures throughout the world goes hand in hand with the associated tendencies of globalisation. Reframing the major concerns of comparative education around the dynamics of national and global forces to provide insight into, and new explanations for, how changes in national and international systems and relations result in changes in values and music cultures in school education and teacher education is the theoretical significance of this project. The broader significance of the dynamics and tensions discussed in this research project are obvious: instead of withering, national sovereignty, national identity, and local identities and cultures are still significant factors in understanding cultural influences on music education and, consequently, the values and practices of music education in schools as well as teacher education in these Chinese localities. The study of school music education in Greater China further highlights the emergence of new tensions resulting from different music experiences and types to be taught or not taught, to be highly valued or less valued, regarding cultural and national values. In this time of great need for mutual cooperation between nations and cultures, this research project will without doubt increase communication and collaboration between these Chinese regions. It also considers a number of complex issues that inform social transformations and cultural and national values in school education. Many aspects of social change, school music education, nationalism, and globalisation are the same worldwide, while each country has individual and unique challenges to face and overcome. There are some limitations to this study, the foremost of which is the representativeness of the pre-service and in-service teachers, as well as the sample of music teacher trainers from Taiwan as a whole. This challenge was compounded by the distribution limitations of the online survey. As a result of the online format, this study was unable to randomise the sample population, which might have resulted in reduced variation in the data. Thus, the teacher interviewees could not be treated as representative of the teacher sample in this study. In addition, the teacher trainers from Taiwan were not willing to participate in the interviews (despite numerous follow-ups in 2019), so the story of professional development in response to global, national, and cultural developments may have some limitations in providing a more comprehensive view to explore theoretical issues and empirical knowledge about the relationships between multiculturalism, nationalism, school music education, and social change in an increasingly globalised world.

12656516.label: Major findings and research outcome
12656516.value: The participants of the survey questionnaire in Hong Kong (HK) and Taiwan (TW) were comprised of 102 and 53 student teachers from respective local universities, and 124 and 74 teachers from local primary and secondary school sectors, correspondingly. The interviewees in this study included 24 HK teachers (13 teaching in primary schools, 10 in secondary schools, and one in both a primary and a secondary school) and 12 female TW teachers (six teaching in primary schools and six in secondary schools). Their musical and educational training was basically on Western musical instruments (mainly the piano) and Western classical music. As findings shown in both HK and TW, traditional Western classical music and other world music were the most popular music types in their classroom music lessons, respectively. Though multicultural music education was perceived as very important in the respective school curricula, some HK and TW teachers in the interviews related that teaching world music was not welcomed or was not properly placed in the school curriculum. Based on the survey questionnaire and interview findings, many respondents in HK and TW were reluctant to teach and sing their national anthems and other patriotic songs, and they had no intention of introducing nationalistic or patriotic education through song singing and other music activities in the curriculum. The t-test analysis of the HK teachers’ responses demonstrated that there was a significant difference (p < 0.05) in rating their interest in teaching patriotic music between the pre-service teachers and the in-service teachers [t(215) = 2.50; p = 0.01]. However, for the TW teachers, there was no significant difference (p > 0.05) in rating their interest in teaching patriotic music between the pre-service teachers and the in-service teachers [t(108) = -0.835; p > 0.10]. Teachers in both HK and TW were conflicted not only by the issue of the relationship with Mainland China in the introduction of the national anthem and other patriotic songs in the curriculum, but also their professional education and training to provide a facilitating environment for global, national and cultural development. To some extent, the student teachers and teachers who participated in the study had different experiences with and understandings of culture and knowledge, as well as the dynamics of music classrooms, in ways that inculcated the cultural and national values in their teaching.

12656516.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12656516.value: The conclusion of the research project suggests that an understanding of social-cultural models and values in music and music education in the Chinese territories can be enhanced by seeing music as a sociopolitical construction between nationalism and multiculturalism. This study, the first of its kind to focus on teachers’ perspectives, represents a new perspective on school music education in response to nationalism and globalisation in the Chinese communities. Little empirical research has been conducted regarding the effects of globalisation and nationalism on school music education and teacher education. Research into this area could illuminate how music teachers have affected students’ music and non-music learning in classroom music lessons. The conceptual structure of music education and teacher education is shaped by the social context in which the political ideologies of all countries/regions function. China, Hong Kong, Taiwan, as well as other Asian countries such as Japan, Indonesia, India, Singapore, South Korea, and Thailand, all of which have built cultural traditions over a long history, have made great efforts towards maintaining their cultural assets and national identities while facing the changes of globalisation in their teacher education and music practice in schools.

12656516.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12656516.value: This research project examined the recent developments in school education and music education in Hong Kong and Taiwan and the relationship between the integration of national cultural identity and globalisation in the respective school curriculums. Regardless of their common history and cultural backgrounds, in recent decades, these localities have experienced divergent political, cultural, and educational structures. Through a literature review, official curriculum documents, approved music textbooks, and a survey questionnaire and in-depth interviews with music teachers, this project also examined the ways in which policies for national identity formation and globalisation interact to complement and contradict each other in the context of music education in respect to national and cultural values in these Chinese territories. Many aspects of social change, school music education, nationalism, and globalisation are the same worldwide, while each country has individual and unique challenges to face and overcome. This research will advance readers’ understanding of the concepts of nationalism and globalisation in music education, not only by summarising these Chinese localities’ different sociopolitical contexts but also contrasting these experiences with those in other parts of the world. More generally, this research project will make a valuable contribution to music education, comparative educational studies, and Asian studies.

12656716.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12656716.value: Transport demand and travel behavior may vary not only from day to day but from generation to generation. Until recently travel behavior research has been more concerned about short-term travel behavior variations than long-term changes and trends in travel demand. While study on day-to-day variations of travel demand is important for designing policies for managing the daily operations of transport systems, investigation into the long-term trends in travel behavior is crucial for strategic development of transport systems and decisions about investment in transport infrastructures. This is particularly important for countries like China, which are rapidly developing and uncertain about future transport growth and its environmental implications. A better understanding of past and possible future trends in car ownership, car usage and long-term transport developments are vital so that transport demand can be assessed and catered for in an efficient and environmentally sustainable way This research will investigate the possible changes in travel behavior between generations in Hong Kong and Shenzhen. The Shenzhen case will provide evidence on the change patterns in car ownership, car usage and travel demand in a newly and fast motorized society; the Hong Kong case will serve to answer the question if individuals’ demand for daily travel in a public-transport dominated developed society has stabilized and why. The study of both cases will contribute to the emerging literature concerning the possible saturation of travel demand and the so-called ‘peak car’ or ‘peak travel’ debate in travel behavior research, by widening the existing study scope and applying a new analytical and modeling approach through conducting empirical studies in two neighboring cities at different development stages. Overall, this research will advance knowledge of long-term changes in activity-travel behavior. The outcomes of this research should be highly relevant for developing transport policies that can accommodate long-term changes in travel behavior and transport demand.

12656716.label: Realisation of objectives
12656716.value: All the objectives of the research project had been fully realized and addressed: 1. We collected data on four waves of the Household Travel Survey of Shenzhen (from 2000 onwards) from the Urban Planning, Land & Resources Commission of Shenzhen Municipality (深圳市规划和国土资源委员会); we also collected data on two waves of Hong Kong’s Travel Characteristics Surveys (2001 and 2011). Empirical analyses were carried out for both the cases of Hong Kong and Shenzhen in terms of the inter-generational changes in activity-travel behavior and car ownership. 2. We developed an analytical approach that employs propensity score matching to distinguish changes in activity-travel behavior caused by socio-economic changes from that by preference, attitude or lifestyle changes 3. Research findings on inter-generational changes in daily travel behavior in Hong Kong and Shenzhen were presented and shared with officials of the Urban Planning, Land & Resources Commission of Shenzhen Municipality; 4. A paper entitled ‘Long-term Trend of Automobile Ownership and Usage in a Chinese Metropolis’ was presented the Annual Meeting of American Association of Geographers (AAG) on April 6, 2017 in Boston, the US; 5. A paper entitled ‘Inter-generational changes in activity-travel behavior in Hong Kong: An exploratory study’ was presented at the 2017 World Symposium on Transport and Land Use Research’, which was held in July, 2017, in Brisbane, Australia. 6. A paper entitled ‘Generational differences in the attitudes towards private cars: evidence from a less car-dependent megacity’ was presented at the 15th International Conference on Travel Behavior Research organized by the International Association for Travel Behaviour Research (IATBR) and held in Santa Barbara, the US, July 15-20, 2018; 7. Six peer-reviewed papers were published in top journals in the fields of geography and transportation including Transportation, Transportation Research Part A; Part C; Part D; and Annals of the American Association of Geographers. These papers document the research findings concerning the inter-generational changes in activity-travel behavior and the causes of these changes related to travel attitudes, the built environment, weather, etc. In addition, we also explored the use of big data in addressing the research questions. 8. a new GRF proposal entitled ‘Urban expansion and travel behavior evolution in Shenzhen: the role of travel time budget’ was developed on the basis of research findings of this project. The proposal was submitted to RGC for possible funding.

12656716.label: Major findings and research outcome
12656716.value: Overall, this research project has so far generated six publications in top international journals of the research field and five presentations in international academic conferences. The major research findings of the project can be summarized as follows: Car ownership and travel demand might have reached a saturation level in Hong Kong, which echoed the trend observed in the developed and private car prevalent societies (Zhou and Wang, 2018, Transportation); There were significant differences among different Chinese generations in terms of attitudes towards cars and their influences on car ownership, holding a driver’s license, and trips by cars (Zhou and Wang, 2019, Transportation Research Part D); A growing trend of car ownership in Shenzhen attributable to economic growth (Zhou and Wang, 2017, presentation at AAG Meeting in Boston); Differences in activity-travel behavior between Hong Kong’s private and public housing residents (Wang and Cao, 2017, Transportation Research Part A); How weather influences public transport ridership in Shenzhen (Zhou, Wang and others, 2017, Transportation Research Part C); Distinct features in travel and activity patterns between males and females in Hong Kong and at different time periods (Zhou and Wang, 2017, presentation at conference in Harbin, China); and the impacts of mobility on accessibility in Shenzhen (Chen, et al., 2018, Annals of the American Association of Geographers)

12656716.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12656716.value: Based on research findings of this project, a new GRF proposal entitled ‘Urban expansion and travel behavior evolution in Shenzhen: the role of travel time budget’ was developed and submitted to RGC for possible funding. This research proposes to extend from examining the long-term trends of activity-travel behavior of the current project to investigate the interactions between the built environment and activity-travel behavior and identify the long-term dynamics of land use impacts on travel behavior. If funded, the new project will contribute to the literature on the built environment and travel behavior with a dynamic and long-term perspectives. The project also inspired the development of an initial proposal on 'Mobility and travel behavior in hyper-dense cities', which intends to investigate travel and transport issues in hyper-dense cities including Seoul, Hong Kong, Bangkok, Manila, and Shenzhen, which are common in terms of high population and development density, but different in culture, development stage, urban structure, social norm, etc. The initial proposal was submitted to the Collaborative Research Fund (CRF) earlier, but unfortunately was not successful. We would like to improve the proposal and apply for funding again in future.

12656716.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12656716.value: This research developed methods to identify real changes in daily travel and investigated the long-term trends in activity-travel behavior in Hong Kong and Shenzhen. Our study found that the peak car or peak travel phenomenon, which was observed in the Western and private car dominated context, was also evident in Hong Kong, a public-transport dominated society. On the other hand, this project also revealed that car ownership and willingness to own cars were still on the rise in Shenzhen and other Chinese cities. Nevertheless, we further revealed that the attitudes towards owning and using private cars changed from generation to generation in Chinese cities. The research methodology developed in this project is useful for isolating the effects of different type of factors including attitudes and lifestyle on travel behavior changes. Overall, this research advanced knowledge concerning the long-term changes in activity-travel behavior. The outcomes of this research are highly relevant for developing transport policies to accommodate long-term changes in travel behavior and transport demand.

12660516.label: Project Objectives
12660516.value: To survey the local popular arts infrastructures (hard and soft) and practices for and by EM youth over the past five years; To develop a set of qualitative cultural indicators appropriate to EM youth social formation in HK, for evaluating and interpreting participation through an international “right to culture” framework; To use the cultural indicators to perform a “critical cultural mapping” toward policy planning.
rows: To survey the local popular arts infrastructures (hard and soft) and practices for and by EM youth over the past five years;

To develop a set of qualitative cultural indicators appropriate to EM youth social formation in HK, for evaluating and interpreting participation through an international “right to culture” framework;
To use the cultural indicators to perform a “critical cultural mapping” toward policy planning.

12660516.label: Realisation of objectives
12660516.value: For objective 1, we successfully conducted a detailed capacity analysis – the first of its kind in Hong Kong – to pave the way for a more formal cultural indicator survey development. Our capacity analysis bears important implications for understanding ethnic minorities’ habitus and cultural dispositions, which in turn sheds light on whether migrant ethnic marginalization can or cannot be ameliorated by participatory practices, especially enjoyment and creative participation in popular arts. Specifically, in order to look at what the user-oriented cultural resources in popular arts are being provided in the city, we conducted a survey of the local popular arts infrastructures (hard and soft) for and by EM youth and discovered a total of 36 organizations that have provided 756 programs over the study period. We then capture the scale, tendency, pattern, and distribution of a variety of local organizations and venues providing arts participation for EM. Our analysis focuses on the landscape in terms of numbers, level of growth, types and clusters of local organizations and venues, and the kinds of activities on offer. Important themes and tendencies were identified and discussed to form a baseline understanding of the capacity for EM cultural participation. This kind of cultural archive or inventory does not exist in Hong Kong, when an empirically-driven grounding of the stakeholder-participation approach is much needed. In short, the survey tasks set out for objective 1 had been successfully accomplished, and incorporated into various outputs stated later in this completion report. (Detailed tables and charts are available upon request). For objective 2, our capacity analysis above generates at least four priority areas of concern. The various typologies, patterns, and tendencies identified indicate the need to reconsider the visions in our various types of organizations and to redeploy public and private resources. Our findings show four types of indicators that should be rigorously developed for surveying the organizations and the EM participants: 1. Tier 1 indicators: EM youth community capacity (e.g. skills/education attainment; self-organizing capacity for cultural, arts, and leisure activities; capacity for cultural initiatives (e.g. dance, music, websites); cosmopolitan/ liberal capacities; civic engagement); 2. Tier 2 indicators: EM youth social and cultural capital (e.g. resources and networks embodied in life domains (school, family, friendship, work); bonding, bridging, and linking forms of capital; capacities to engage social agencies that hold power (media, cultural organizations, industry); ethnic community cohesion, belonging, confidence, ownership; 3. Tier 3 indicators: Cultural identity (e.g. heritage; struggle for self-recognition/ respect; paths of maturation; intra- and inter-ethnic identity negotiation and development); 4. Tier 4 indicators: Access and participation (e.g. frequency; resource expenditure; locations; sense of availability and variety; physical and symbolic aspects of access; self-narration of a “participation continuum” (active, passive, creative, interpretive, critical); place-making (sense of belonging, artistic aspirations, defense of community spaces); assessment of responsiveness of social agencies and government). They are conceived of as tiers because of the way EM community capacity, social and cultural capital, and cultural identity impinge on their relation with cultural activities. Drawing on Bourdieu, the provision of access and participation in a well-coordinated cultural infrastructure would help to produce a habitus conducive to positive self-confidence, which in turn impinges on how organizations (such as the 36 organizations we identified) re-chart their visions and operations. In short, the task set out for objective 2 had been successfully accomplished, and incorporated into various outputs stated later in this completion report. (A scientifically tested measurement instrument that incorporates the 4 tiers of indicators is available upon request). For objective 3, we raise a critical discussion of the relation of cultural planning for minority cultural participation to what French social theorist Pierre Bourdieu called “habitus” – the site of interplay between structure and practice. While structure and practice can be observed directly, habitus cannot because, habitus can be understood as a person’s mental and inner processes formulated as a result of cultural disposition. In this way, we recommend that cultural planning considers the interwoven aspects of cultural resources (cultural infrastructure and cultural capital on the one hand, and habitus and cultural disposition on the other) ultimately inform human agency. This is commensurate with a famous argument made by Australian Aboriginal scholar Langton: “Through cultural mapping, communities and their constituent interest groups can record their cultural practices and resources, as well as other intangibles such as their sense of place and social value. Subjective experiences, varied social values and multiple readings and interpretations can be accommodated in cultural maps” (Council for Aboriginal Reconciliation, 1994). Critical cultural-mapping studies take the analysis of cultural access and capacity-building to establish indicators to explore in greater depth the reality of the “subjective experiences, varied social values and multiple readings and interpretations” of the communities, that is, “measuring” human agency. The mapping also requires consultation with the cultural sectors of schools, NGOs, groups formed by EM themselves, government agencies, etc., which can in turn take the results of a continuous cycle of capacity mapping as a basis for considering resource allocation and program implementation (i.e. the cycle of capacity mapping -> community-derived indicators -> cultural planning). Such a mapping is operationalized through a continuous feedback loop across constituent interest groups, forming cultural portfolios/inventories consisting of the interplay between cultural infrastructure inventories and cultural narratives of agency qua participation. In short, the task set out for objective 3 had been largely accomplished by way of a set of recommendations to organizations and relevant government agencies. The actual implementation of the cultural planning exercise can and should continue after the completion of this project (see the potential for further development described below).

12660516.label: Major findings and research outcome
12660516.value: The two major findings in this project include (a) a detailed inventory of cultural resources in the limited infrastructure provided by and for the EM community in Hong Kong, and (b) an 11-page cultural indicator survey that is the first scientific instrument developed in HK to measure cultural participation of EM youth. For (a), NGO-run community centres outperform the other 4 types of organizations for providing both “hard” and “soft” cultural programming to cultivate EM youth’s interest in the arts. Most outstanding exemplar in our findings is the “All About Us” annual filmmaking program organized under the Hong Kong Arts Centre’s “ifva Community Tour.” A related finding concerns a number of distinct “clusters” of cultural activities formed by the different nature of organizations involved. Our findings point to the “minority interests cluster,” defined as those organizations who mainly target EM young persons of the same ethnic background in order to help nurture them with particular ethnic cultural activities; the “cultural intermediary cluster” of organizations that set out a unique strategy to promote inter- and intra-ethnic interaction, hoping to draw vital energy by EM youth of different ethnic backgrounds interacting with each other and doing creative projects together; the “community service cluster,” which are place-based organizations that plan all-round programs to develop the cultural capacity of EM youth residents in a particular district, through language classes, talent training, arts competition, and local cultural festivals; and finally the “public education cluster,” which focus mainly on anti-discrimination education project via cultural messages. For (b), the 11-page cultural indicator survey we devised was culled from qualitative and quantitative data used for testing item validity and clarity of meaning. The focus-group and survey research were conducted for the largest minority populations by ethnic groups in Hong Kong, namely Pakistanis, Indians, Filipinos, and Nepalese. Ultimately, our findings show four types of indicators that should be rigorously developed for surveying the organizations and the EM participants: EM youth community capacity; EM youth social and cultural capital; Cultural identity; and Access and participation. We consider this instrument to be a major research outcome of knowledge-transfer value, alongside the publications and conference disseminations we produced.

12660516.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12660516.value: According to our analytical model, the cycle of capacity mapping -> community-derived indicators -> cultural planning should be followed. These 3 aspects should be incorporated into a long-term strategy for cultural development for minority youth in Hong Kong. In other words, the analysis of cultural access and capacity-building should be conducted periodically (say every 5 years), while the indicators we established (and the survey instrument we developed) to explore in greater depth the reality of the “subjective experiences, varied social values and multiple readings and interpretations” of the communities, should be re-tested and further refined through periodic measurement (say, every 2 years). Finally, a robust cultural planning or cultural mapping policy should be developed using the empirical bases of the inventory analysis and indicator measurement. The planning or mapping, which requires consultation with the cultural sectors of schools, NGOs, groups formed by EM themselves, government agencies, etc., should be made public for a wide discussion.

12660516.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12660516.value: This project fills the gap in the minority cultural participation scholarship developed in accordance with the “right to culture” framework espoused by the UN. It joins the international scholarship underway that interrogates a much-discussed dimension in anti-racist work today, namely the role of “cultural participation” in developing strong social capital and resilient cultural identity for ethnic minority groups. The infrastructure survey, the cultural indicator survey, and the recommendations for cultural planning that we develop in this project are all “firsts,” never been attempted in Hong Kong. Hopefully, it sets an important intellectual and practical basis for advancing our understanding of the relationship between the needs of ethnic and linguistic minorities in HK and the role of arts.

12661016.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12661016.value: This project will research the cultural phenomenon of camp in Hong Kong from the 1960s into the 2000s. Admittedly one of the most elusive ideas in modern culture, camp has a close affiliation with Western gay subculture, but it is not confined to it. While much of current English-language scholarship on camp tends to focus on what camp is and who has access to it (thus the debate over gay camp versus straight/mass camp), these studies, nonetheless, generally foreclose the legitimacy of camp appreciation in non-Western cultures. To initiate a productive discussion on camp in a transcultural framework, my project proposes a discursive approach to camp in both Western and non-Western cultures. I consider camp as a discourse: a descriptive and analytic implement that does not belong to a particular culture, and that travels around and can be adapted to different cultural settings. The kernel of this formulation lies in the different contexts in which camp takes form and effect, as well as the different uses of camp associated with their particular contexts. To proceed with this project, my research will be conducted in three main directions. Firstly, it will emphasize the socio-historical context particular to Hong Kong from the 1960s onwards. By way of an expansive survey on Hong Kong mass culture that ranges from the rise of youth culture to the impact of television culture, I mean to provide an explanation of the diffusion of the mass camp impulse in the Hong Kong populace, increasingly characterized by a self-conscious, often parodic attitude toward the artifice of conventions, particularly those associated with art, dress, gender behavior, and media representation. This socio-historical context, in my formulation, serves as the material basis of an articulation of camp in modern Hong Kong. Secondly, my research will trace this articulation: the emergence of camp as a discourse in Hong Kong and its changing meaning since the mid-1970s. It will involve an extensive survey of the relevant archival materials, ranging from popular magazines to newspapers, and to academic publications. I will also interview a number of veteran cultural critics on this subject. Thirdly, this project will investigate the particular ways in which mass camp has found expression in Hong Kong mainstream cinema from the 1970s onwards. In so doing, this project serves as an alternative historiography of Hong Kong cinema from the perspective of the mass camp impulse and camp discourse. 這項研究計畫將以香港1960年代至本世紀初的camp文化現象作為主題。Camp 可謂當代文化裡最曖昧難解的概念之一，它雖與西方的男同志次文化密切相關，但卻不宥限於此。目前英語學界有關camp的文獻多聚焦於camp的定義和進用權（此證諸同志 camp vs. 異性戀/大眾 camp的爭辯），然而這些研究卻多以排除camp在非西方文化之合法存在作為前提。為了開啟一個在跨文化脈絡中對於camp的正向討論，我的研究計畫提議以「論述模式」探討西方以及非西方文化中的camp。我視camp為一種論述：它是一個描述和分析的工具，不獨屬於特定文化，而是會漂移、並在不同文化情境中作出調適。這個提議讓本研究計畫聚焦於讓camp成形與生效的不同脈絡，以及關乎這些特定脈絡之不同的camp用法。 這項研究計畫將主要從三方面著手。首先，它強調香港自1960年代以降的社會歷史脈絡。藉由廣泛檢視香港大眾文化，包括從青少年文化的興起以至電視文化的影響，我將提出一個大眾camp脈動在香港民眾間擴散的詮釋，該脈動表現在民眾對於各種慣例，特別是有關藝術、服裝、性別表現和媒體再現等慣例之人為性，逐漸表現出一種自覺和嘲諷的態度。這個社會歷史脈絡在我的討論中亦是camp於現代香港接合(articulation)的物質基礎。其次，我的研究將會追溯camp於現代香港接合的軌跡：亦即它作為一種論述，從1970年代中期的出現，以至其後的意義轉變。這項研究將廣泛檢視資料館相關文獻，從流行雜誌到報紙，乃至學術出版。我也將訪談諸多資深文化評論者對這個議題的看法。第三，這項研究將探討大眾camp在1970年代以降的香港主流電影中之特殊表現方式。藉此，這個研究計畫也可視為透過大眾camp脈動和camp論述這個特殊的視角，書寫出的另類香港電影史。

12661016.label: Realisation of objectives
12661016.value: 1. This project on the expressions of "camp" in Hong Kong has supplemented current studies on modern Hong Kong popular culture with crucial missing information. a) With wide-ranging archival research, this project has successfully traced the historical formation and evolution of the discourse on camp from the mid-to-late 1970s into early 2000s. b) Corresponding to this discursive trajectory, this project has simultaneously identified crucial and abundant evidence of camp expressions in Hong Kong mass culture, which manifested camp sensitivity as an expanding, widespread social impulse in the local society. c) The local Hong Kong society, as detailed in my analysis, notably underwent a series of significant structural changes since the 1960s. These structural changes, I maintain, not only involved cross-cultural transactions, but they provided the material basis for the shaping and dissemination of camp sensibility, alongside the emerging camp expressions and camp discourse from the 1970s onwards. This project is the very first comprehensive and systematic endeavour to approach the important idea of “camp” and its varied expressions in Hong Kong popular culture. It provides current studies on modern Hong Kong popular culture with fundamental missing knowledge. 2. This project sets an example for the research on camp discourse and camp expressions in a transcultural framework. Although the term and notion of camp originated from the Western societies, my project foregrounds the articulation of camp (as a discourse and expressions) in Hong Kong in a historically grounded manner. It challenges the bias that sees “camp” as an exclusive property of the West, shedding fresh new light on understanding camp in a transnational paradigm. My presentation of mass camp in Hong Kong pop culture at the top-notch SCMS conference last year (with the Hui-styled comedy as my prime example) was very well received by several international scholars, including Professors Chris Berry, Victor Fan, and Earl Jackson in the audience. I am confident that my forthcoming publication based on this extensive project (see attached document) will further draw productive conversations between Western and non-Western scholars working on camp and transnational pop culture in general. 3. This project analyses camp in Hong Kong pop culture in a more general manner, before it zooms in onto Hong Kong cinema, tracing the particular articulation and processes of camp sensibility/impulse in Hong Kong mainstream cinema. This project indeed provides an alternative historiography of modern Hong Kong cinema that has not been done previously. 4. So far I have written a very extensive and in-depth analysis based on my research for this project. The long and detailed article (please see enclosed document) is 90 pages long, with over 280 footnotes. In terms of its length and rich content, this article is equivalent to two-to-three separate articles. Although my original objective was to produce two articles based on this research project, this long article as it is, I feel, provides the most complete and coherent account of my whole research findings all at once. This detailed piece will be published as one chapter in my monograph titled Queer Representations in Chinese-language Film and Media. Under contract with Amsterdam University Press, the whole book manuscript has recently gone through peer review with very positive feedback (and is expected to be in print next year). The relevant chapter, titled “Mass Camp in Contemporary Hong Kong Cinema”, has been highly praised by the two peer reviewers. At this point, I think it makes more sense to keep this long piece as it is, instead of cutting and repackaging it into two separate articles. Still, I will consider the possibility of generating another piece based on my findings and analysis.

12661016.label: Major findings and research outcome
12661016.value: As the first comprehensive and the most systematic study on the expressions of mass camp in Hong Kong, this projects provides current studies on modern Hong Kong popular culture with crucial findings. a) With extensive archival research, this project has successfully traced the historical formation and evolution of the discourse on camp from the mid-to-late 1970s into early 2000s. b) Corresponding to this discursive trajectory, this project has simultaneously identified crucial and abundant evidence of camp expressions in Hong Kong mass culture, which manifested camp sensitivity as an expanding, widespread social impulse in the local society, as manifested in film, television, music, fashion, and performance arts since the 1970s. c) The local Hong Kong society, according to my research, notably underwent a series of significant events and structural changes from the 1960s into late 1990s. These findings and in-depth analyses comprise the very first study of Hong Kong camp in a transnational framework.

12661016.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
12661016.value: Further investigation can be followed by research and comparative analysis of the discourse and expressions of "camp" in Taiwan. There are discursive intersections and interactions of camp discourses in Hong Kong and Taiwan since the 1990s. A comprehensive investigation of this area can shed fresh new light on "camp" in the larger Sinophone (queer) culture. I have proposed this as an extension of my current GRF project.

12668516.value: 摘要 這項擬定的研究的範圍是全球性，不論是自傳式，檔案式，及跨文化式的，包含了知識資產的研究以至不同形式的探究。這些資料是由一眾扎根於中國及日本的學者所提供。威廉．燕卜蓀，英國詩人，分別於1931年及1952年在以上兩個國家授學及居住。這是一項綜合的研究，目的在於紀錄燕卜蓀如何以他的評論和詩詞建構 “亞洲” ，一個西方的幻象，並帶出他的一套論說。本來這是由羅賓德拉納特．泰戈爾所掀起的潮流。處於第二次世界大戰後，全球一體化萌芽的時期，泛亞的價值觀成為了歐洲英語系了解全球趨勢及政治的中心思想，即使當時此等世界觀與一般的政治理念，不論在實際內容，地域與人脈均有所差異，而且與社會主義者、共和主義者及君主體制主義者的關係不是十分明確。相對而言，燕卜蓀對於職場政治明顯的冷感，加上他對於詩詞的幻想，批判性的銳覺和親身的經驗，令“亞洲”這主題更受歡迎，而且他的教學對於當時處身於中國革命時期的知識分子帶來重大的影響。除了文學傳記外，我們的研究希望紀錄邁向全球化的戰後英國文學及亞洲於當時的政治架構上，文化及審美觀去領土化的關係，並了解此題目對於中國人及日本人的價值。燕卜蓀不但是其中一名最早提出地方主義文學的倡議者（其中他也懷疑過帝國和國家是全球化自覺的一種手段），他同樣是其中首批的學者去肯定其中國學生是這項多邊文化知識傳遞的重要持份者 。因此，燕卜蓀的教學方式為傳統的東方理論學者 帶來了有益的改變，令未來領袖在全球的舞台上能使用這種生機蓬勃的“亞洲”慨念作為提述。在“亞洲”的土地，配合日本及中國演員，於這個值得關注的社會過渡時期，地域性設計實踐的出現，實在地呈現了這幻想中，又富有彈性的“亞洲”。這項研究利用了現今的資料管理系統，資料模型工具及影像實現的技巧，體現及傳播用英語集合燕卜蓀以日語和中文撰寫的文學作品的第一套綜合參考書目。完成後，受到管理的燕卜蓀資料庫會同時在網上平台公開以供網上瀏覽。希望不同地域的學者 ，能透過英文翻譯與全球不同的學者同儕進行交流。我們希望這項合作研究能在關於學習燕卜蓀的分支研究討論中，建立西方與不同地域觀點之間一條實在，國際化的溝通渠道。

12670716.value: To contribute to the ongoing scholarly literature on music and exoticism by looking at exoticism not only as a system of representation but also as contextually constructed. To organize a symposium on Chinese music exoticism in early 2018. To produce two scholarly articles and one single-authored book manuscript on the topic. 12670716.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
12670716.value: Musical exoticism refers broadly to the evocation of foreign peoples and places in musical works and performances, often with recognizable stylistic devices or contextual tropes that invite exotic imaginations. China’s extensive musical encounters with its neighboring peoples and cultures in the modern time have resulted in a sizable oeuvre of exotic-styled compositions that begs questions of power and representation against circuits of majority-minority relations. The current project proposes to conduct a thorough examination of minority exoticism in Chinese music in the twentieth century and beyond. Research will be conducted through archival and ethnographic approaches to consult manuscripts, written records, audiovisual materials, as well as composers and musicians involve in the emergence of minority exotic styles in modern Chinese music. A major hypothesis is that the emergence of contemporary techniques and styles in Chinese music is intimately linked to the aestheticizing of foreign musical elements appropriated from minority music traditions as Chinese musicians work to represent their exotic minority subjects. Such adaptation of real or imagined minority styles has not only enriched the expressive capacity of Chinese instruments; it has also expanded the musical vocabularies and the range of compositional options for modern Chinese music. This research seeks not to approach exoticism as a mere act of representation (although I propose, as a part of the project, to construct a small-scale database of Chinese musical works with exotic and/or minority themes composed since the early twentieth century inside and outside China). Rather, it suggests that the exotic attributes of minority-themed musical works are contingent, acquired contextually rather than reflective of any intrinsic exotic quality. One major theme of the research is to examine how the European musical languages borrowed from nineteenth-century Romanticism have allowed for a new conception of minority otherness, on which the modern Chinese self is predicated and simultaneously constructed. As such, I suggest that minority exoticism should be approached as one about how a modernizing Chinese nation has sought to domesticate its neighboring peoples and cultures on its way to becoming modern. The broader contribution of this project lies in the fresh framework it offers to look at exoticism, while tied to Eurocentrism in origin, not as a unilateral procedure but one that is both reciprocal and generative, acquired simultaneously by peoples and cultures that have long been cast as exotic in Orientalist Euro-American representations to fashion their own forms of cultural modernity. 古今中外有不少音樂作品以異域為題材，以特殊的音樂素材，呈現異域的人物和景觀，為聽眾提供無限幻想。近現代中國與周邊的少數民族接觸緊密，五十年代以降，不少中國作曲家嘗試以少數民族音樂為題材，創作了大量現代中國音樂作品。本計劃重點研究二十世紀中國音樂當中以周邊少數民族為題材的作品。當中一個重要的假設，是當代中國音樂的風格和演奏技巧，與中國作曲家挪用少數民族音樂風格有十分密切的關係，大大豐富了現代中國音樂的風格和技巧。本研究認為，對於音樂的異域風格和元素的分析，必須從作品原本的風格脈絡出發。因此，其中一個研究的主題，是現代中國音樂如何在異化少數民族音樂的同時，亦為自身提供一個現代化的契機。

12670716.label: Major findings and research outcome
12670716.value: This research has looked at the roles musical exoticism has played in China’s becoming of a modern musical nation. What might these self-fashioned and largely concocted “minority” styles tell us about China’s modern national music, and how is modern Chinese musical creativity related to its representation of minority otherness? It approaches exoticism not only through the critiques of misrepresentation and cultural exploitation, but also as an aesthetic trope, which explores new techniques and means of expressivity for a modern tradition that considers itself deficient and in dire need of both. The research has demonstrated that devices, techniques, and gestures that are perceived as exotic in modern Chinese music operate in a web of ideological and cultural contexts that are contingent upon the changing Chinese conception of otherness in the modern time. In addition, it is crucial to understand minority exoticism not merely as an outcome of some broader ideological processes but also as important means through which some of the difficult aesthetic goals may be achieved in modern Chinese music. As the original PI have written in one recent publication, “[to] listen to China as a modern musical nation is not to focus our aural attention exclusively on how European art music procedures and techniques have been installed—successfully or otherwise—in Chinese music under the disguise of “modernization” or “development.” Rather, it is also through the intersections between modernity and otherness, progress and alterity that many of these creative endeavors are enabled.”

12670716.value: The original PI is continuing to work to on the remaining part of the book manuscript.

12670716.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
12670716.value: This project studies the roles of musical exoticism in modern Chinese instrumental musical. The major research question is: what might these self-fashioned minority styles tell us about China’s modern national music, and how is modern Chinese musical creativity related to its representation of minority otherness? The significance of this research is that it refutes ongoing claims about modern Chinese music as shaped solely through its interaction with Western European traditions. Rather, this research demonstrates that the modern Chinese musical self is as much a construct with its internal ethnic others.

13629816.label: Project Objectives
13629816.value: To identify the motivations and contexts behind non-single professionals’ transient transnational migration to Hong Kong, and the problems they face. 13629816.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
13629816.value: Intensified transnational circulations of capital, technologies, cultures and populations increasingly impact a vast array of social processes and formations, and are generally summarized as the phenomenon of globalization. Voluntary transient transnational migration, often understood as economically motivated, is increasingly common across social and geographical locations. Such movements often have significant impact on individuals’ personal, family and social lives, and can result in local as well as global meso- and macro-level social changes. Research on transnational migration tends to focus on migrants in the lower echelons of the social hierarchy and those migrating from less to more developed countries. The situations of transnational professional workers are under-studied by comparison, particularly that of female non-single (i.e. married, partnered, and/or with dependent children) transnational professionals who are ‘lead migrants’ – i.e. initiators of the migration. In addition, existing studies rarely differentiate between transient and settler transnational migrants in their analyses. The proposed study stems from the recognition that transnational migration is an important site for personal and social transformation, and aims to further our understanding of this phenomenon by asking questions such as: how do transnational contexts shape professional men and women’s subjectivities and everyday lives? How do family and marital status affect the life choices and strategies of transient transnational professionals? What are the constraints and possibilities for personal and social change arising out of such contexts? To what extent and under what circumstances can transnationalism offer transformatory possibilities for the personal and the social? How do intersections of gender, class, ethnicity and family status affect such possibilities? Specifically, we are interested in exploring emerging intimacy and family formations that may be found in transnational contexts, and practices and strategies used in their negotiation. Using a variety of qualitative methods, we aim to conduct an in-depth study on the experiences of 50 non-single, transient transnational professionals in Hong Kong. The findings of this study will contribute to existing scholarship by engaging with three broad themes, namely (1) the transnational flows of transient professionals and their consequences, (2) personal lives and family processes in transnational contexts, and (3) the intersections of class, ethnicity and gender in transnational contexts; the study will also deepen our understanding of the problems and issues faced by such migrants in Hong Kong, and will offer insight as to how they may be addressed. 全球化下，資本、科技、文化和人口的跨國流動對社會造成的影響越趨多樣化和深遠。跨國的、短暫的移居人口（通常理解為移民工）在全球多個地區都越來越普遍。這些人口流動對個人的家庭和社交生活必定有所影響，同時也會導致本地和更廣闊的全球性社會影響。有關跨國移民的研究較多關注那些處於較低社會階層或從發展水平較低地區移往發展水平較高地方的移民。有關跨國專業人士的移民情況甚少受到關注，特別是這批人士中非單身女性（即已婚、有親密伴侶和/或有未成年子女者）而又是移居主導者（即發起移居者）的狀況。現有研究亦甚少在分析中把短暫跨國移居和跨國定居類移民作出區別。本研究嘗試提出以下問題：跨國移居狀況怎樣影響男性和女性專業人士的主體性和日常生活？非定居跨國移民專業人士的家庭和婚姻狀況如何影響他們在生活和工作上所作出的選擇和策略？在這處境中，個人生活和社會轉變有什麼限制和可能性？性別、社會階級、族群和家庭身份的交織如何影響這些可能性？我們特別有興趣探討於跨國狀況中會否有新的親密關係和家庭模式的出現，以及在商討過程中當事人採用些什麼做法和策略。我們採用質性研究，跟五十名在香港生活的非單身跨國移居專業人士進行深入訪談。此研究的結果將對下列範疇有所貢獻：（1）跨國移居專業人士的狀況和後果（2）個人生活及家庭於跨國狀況下的情況（3）跨國狀況中性別、社會階級、族群和家庭身份的交織的情況。本研究也可加深我們對這類移居人士在香港說面對的問題，從而對如何應對有所啟發。

13629816.label: Realisation of objectives
13629816.value: Objective 1: To identify the motivations and contexts behind non-single professionals’ transient transnational migration to Hong Kong, and the problems they face. Three main motivations underlie informants’ decisions to move to Hong Kong – (1) socio-economic advancement opportunities, (2) to experience foreign cultures, and (3) to re-connect with family/ethnic roots. These three motivations are not exclusive, but the first dominates and often works in tandem with ‘push’ factors related to the places or personal life situations prior to the move. Hong Kong’s much lower taxation, considerably higher salaries, widespread use of English as well as the affordability and availability of domestic workers were all highly attractive. For many of the informants who prioiritise the second motivation – desire to experience foreign cultures (‘see the world’) – they did not specifically search for opportunities in Hong Kong; in some cases they came only because Hong Kong was the first or the only place that offered them an opportunity. But Hong Kong’s location in Asia is attractive as a hub for regional travel. Finally, informants with Hong Kong, Chinese or Asian family connections see moving to Hong Kong as a means to re-connect with what they consider to be important parts of their self-identities; it was also important for these informants to be physically closer to their Asian families by virtue of being in Hong Kong. Informants’ ages ranged from early 30s to early 60s, but most lie in the age range of ‘prime’ adulthood in terms of career development and family formation. During the data collection period, Hong Kong was very much an attractive destination. Since the interviews took place, social unrest in 2019 began. We tried to contact all the informants to ask if the situation affected their thoughts about staying in Hong Kong. Most who replied said the events at the time made no difference to them. As most informants had their job offers secured prior to coming to Hong Kong or were able to very quickly find work soon after, the problems they encountered were mostly NOT related to their work lives. Most of the difficulties they described were relatively minor and have to do with initial adjustment to any new place one moves to. For female informants (and that is the vast majority), their major difficulty has been to adjust to the new roles and new dynamics in their relationships with their partners. Some of their partners also experienced such difficulties, some to severe extend. Objective 2: To identify the constraints and possibilities for personal and social change arising out of transnational contexts for these individuals. The intersecting complexities of informants’ (and their partners’) transnational lives are constrained primarily by adherence to traditional gender roles by themselves and also by others. These constraints can give rise to discontent, anxieties and conflicts. Many informants got married after coming to Hong Kong in order to enable their partners to be able to stay in Hong Kong as their dependent. The case of an informant and her same sex partner illustrates the grave importance for access to the dependent visa for transnational movements. This couple suffered many and often serious difficulties because the informant was not entitled to the dependent spouse status at the time of the study, and the relationship eventually disintegrated. The case of one male informant went through a complete role reversal and became a full-time home maker; this relationship was on the verge of breaking point at the time of the study. Many female informants struggled to come to terms with the various contingencies arising out of changes in division of labour in the relationship. Those who are more comfortable with a traditional division of labour, AND have partners who were able to fulfil expectations arising from it, were able to find greater satisfaction. However, there are many more informants who were not able to do so, whether due to their own or their partners’ adherence to the traditional gendered division of labour. By insisting on the value of this arrangement as ideal, deviations from it easily lead to misunderstandings, conflicts and distrust. A few couples are able to find satisfaction in novel arrangements by limiting the requirements of a ‘good’ relationship to their bare minimal, and making accommodations in terms of co-residence, intimacy and finances. For example, two informants (one male, one female), both lived apart from their spouses and children on a semi-permanent basis, whilst maintaining their relationships making full use of technologies and novel ‘family rules’. While some women were happy with the opportunity to be the main breadwinner, their male partners and their family and friends often have great difficulties accepting the arrangement. In short, the transnational context provides plenty of opportunities for genuine transformations, although only a few are taken up and utilised with success. Objective 3: To explore how transnationalism may offer transformatory possibilities for personal and family lives (e.g. reconfigurations of marital and familial relations, strategies involved in the negotiation of ideal family formations and related gender norms). Following on from the findings to objective 2, transnationalism does offer many opportunities for the transformation of personal and family lives. Individuals who are motivated to take up these opportunities and can find value and satisfaction in such transformations, however, typically have privileged access to a range of resources, including socio-economic, cultural and social capitals. They are also privileged in terms of their positioning in Hong Kong’s racial/ethnic hierarchy, giving Hong Kong’s colonial past and its current status as a Special Administrative Region of the People’s Republic of China. In short, these transformatory possibilities are not equally accessed. Nevertheless, there are a few informants who are able to get the most of transnationalism by actively disregarding normative expectations and prioritising what ‘works’ for them given the transnational context. The latter category of informants are, however, few and far between. In short, the possibilities offered for genuine transformation do exist but informants have to overcome personal, relational and broader societal hurdles before these can be realised. Relationships are stripped to their core components in order for them to ‘work’, and in some cases they are made stronger despite time space inconveniences and challenges to socially-defined roles. Objective 4: To analyze how intersections of gender, age, social class, ethnicity and family status shape the above issues. Gender, class, ethnicity and marital status are found to have significant intersectional effects on how transnationalism plays out in informants’ lives in Hong Kong. Following on from the findings to objective 3 above, heterosexual married couples with equally high incomes or male partners with much higher incomes were more able to find satisfaction in their transnational lives. Those with a Hong Kong or Chinese connection (and this is not necessarily related to race or ethnicity) also find it easier than those without, as the value of these ‘assets’ emerge only in Hong Kong’s transnational context. The advantages offered by transnational corporations for transnationals, as conventionally understood, continue to be self-evident in this study. Apart from this well-known pattern of transnational professionals, in our sample, higher education and lifestyle (fitness and well-being) are also important occupational fields that create opportunities outside of the transnational corporation route.

13629816.label: Major findings and research outcome
13629816.value: Non-single professional transient transnational migrants face many more difficulties than their single counterparts. They are mostly motivated to move to Hong Kong by socio-economic factors, often in conjunction with the desire to ‘see the world’ or to be closer to their ethnic and/or familial roots. The transnational context often dramatically alters the pre-existing balance and dynamics in informants’ relationships, particularly regarding gender roles and financial contributions. In many cases, getting married is needed for the couple to stay together in Hong Kong. Such challenges create transformatory opportunities to reconfigure relational arrangements, but gender role expectations continue to produce hurdles, sometimes leading to serious conflicts and even relationship dissolution. Being situated in privileged positions in the occupational, racial/ethnic and cultural hierarchies in the Hong Kong context allows some informants to minimise difficulties or challenges. Only in a few cases can novel arrangements ‘work’ to the satisfaction of both partners in the relationship. Even so, these arrangements are unlikely to persist, as informants view them as temporary; if and when they cease to live transnational lives, they foresee and in some cases look forward to a resumption to ‘normal’. Whether or not their experiences in this transitory phase may affect their future relational and family configurations, remains to be seen. An important finding is the toll of ‘role reversal’ (i.e. women as major breadwinner) on men and also to a lesser extent on women in heterosexual relationships. Although this reversal may seen initially as exciting and potentially rewarding, the lack of social and personal resources to support it tends to result in relationship conflicts and even breakdown. These findings contribute to the existing literature on transnationalism by firstly, drawing attention to the persistence of class, race and gender divides which affect not only migrants from low to higher income destinations, but also highly educated professionals from one high income country to another. Secondly, despite the increasing numbers of highly educated female transnationals, gendered norms and role expectations continue to affect them as well as their partners negatively.

13629816.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
13629816.value: Firstly, we need to further examine whether and how transformations to relational configurations and practices develop over time for transnationals. As the current study is a cross-sectional one, we are unable to confirm whether informants’ anticipation of a ‘return to normal’ (i.e. gendered norms and practices conforming to traditional division of labour) would materialize. Second, the COVID-19 pandemic has taken a huge and unprecedented toll on what it means to live and work as transnationals. Media reports and casual observations suggest that flight bans and quarantine requirements have seriously affected the well-being of many transnationals and their families. Research suggests that the pandemic has taken a much greater toll on women than men because of increased and intensified care responsibilities. What are the implications for professional transnational migrants? And to what extent do the attractions of Hong Kong as a destination fare compared to the costs incurred by its pandemic policies? Further research focusing on these two areas could deepen our understanding of transnational migrants in the 21st century.

13629816.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
13629816.value: Highly educated, non-single professional women who come to Hong Kong to live and to work face many more issues than their single counterparts. As lead migrants, the women we interviewed often become the main bread winner, while their male partners become the one who is ‘trailing’ or ‘dependent’. This role reversal creates many challenges as well as opportunities for changes in how their relationship and family lives are practiced. However, within this relatively privileged group, some are more able to have a positive transnational experience, such as those who are employed by transnational corporations, those with family or cultural connections to Hong Kong and China, and those not excluded from marriage (i.e. same-sex couples). Others were less fortunate, and in some cases their relationships suffer greatly. What are the factors that could help transnational women succeed without compromising their relationships and family lives? We find that couples who are willing to focus on the core features of their relationship, rather than becoming overwhelmed by challenges to preconceived ideals, are more likely to succeed. Transnationalism can create valuable opportunities for transformation, but not everybody can make the most of them.

13643616.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
13643616.value: This is a revised grant application. The GRF panel encouraged us to resubmit our application, which received 17 top (“excellent”, “high” and “appropriate”) and 7 “very good” scores from three anonymous reviewers. The comments of the reviewers and the panel were constructive and we have made every effort to address them. The historical injustices committed by Japan continue to significantly affect its relations with South Korea. From 1910 to 1945, Japan colonised/occupied the Korean peninsula and it has been unable to unequivocally deal with this past. Although political scientists have studied the effects of these historical legacies on interstate relations, very little is known about the grassroots perceptions of Japan in Korea. These grassroots perceptions are critical for business and cultural contacts, and political reconciliation between the two democracies. This project examines the effect of transitional justice, or its absence, on ordinary Koreans’ perceptions of Japan and the Japanese. It draws on insights from sociology, political science and psychology to further our understanding of reconciliation from the perspective of the victim nation. This project benefits conceptually and methodologically from its interdisciplinary approach. Conceptually, it draws on insights from research in transitional justice, social psychology and Korean studies. Methodologically, a qualitative inquiry into the meanings of critical concepts (i.e. justice, reconciliation, apology) is combined with quantitative research (i.e. survey experiments, a social survey). The project builds on the PI’s twenty years of research in the area of transitional justice, his experience in managing research projects in six countries, and his publication record in leading social science outlets. He also conducted three experiments in Korea, which resulted in three research papers. The investigative team consists of two Lingnan-based Co-Is: a Korean-speaking political scientist and a psychologist with experience in conducting cross-cultural experiments in Hong Kong, Japan and Korea. Significance: First, although most existing studies focus on interstate reconciliation, this interdisciplinary project examines reconciliation at the individual and group levels. Second, this study combines qualitative and quantitative approaches, including the relatively novel and powerful method of survey experiments. Third, the project will provide basis for policy recommendations for fostering reconciliation initiatives at the governmental and non-governmental levels. Fourth, its insights could be useful for reconciliation between Japan and China. The project will result in a book monograph, three research papers, six conference presentations, and a conference. It will also provide mentoring for two junior professorial co-investigators, and training for an MPhil student and two undergraduate students. 歷史上日本對韓國作出的不公義的事情深遠地影響著兩國關係。從1910年到1945年，日本佔據著朝鮮半島/於朝鮮半島建立殖民地，而日本一直無法明確地處理這過去。雖然政治學家研究過這歷史遺留下來的問題對日韓關係的影響，但韓國草根階層對日本的看法仍有待探討。這些草根階層的看法對於兩民主政體間的經貿關係﹑文化交往﹑政治上的和解都有關鍵的作用。 本研究計劃探討在轉型正義(Transitional justice)，或缺乏轉型正義的影響下，韓國大眾對日本和日本人的看法。研究計劃借鑒社會學﹑政治學﹑和心理學的知識，加深我們對於從受害國角度看和解的認識。在概念上和研究方法上計劃得益於跨學科的研究方法。在概念上，計劃借鑒在轉型正義﹑社會心理學﹑和韓國研究領域內的研究結果。在研究方法方面，質性上對於一些關鍵概念(如正義﹑和解﹑道歉)的意義探究會與量性的調查方法(如問卷調查﹑問卷實驗﹑社區問卷調查)結合。 研究計劃建基於 在二十年間於轉型正義領域內的研究成果，於六個國家推行研究計劃的經驗，和他於著名社會科學學術期刊的出版記錄。他亦於韓國進行三次實驗，結果亦於三份研究報告上匯報。 調查團隊由兩名嶺南大學的協作調查員組成，一名懂韓語的政治學者和一名有於香港﹑日本﹑和韓國進行跨文化實驗經驗的心理學家。 研究意義: 首先，雖然大部分出色的研究集中於國家層面上的和解，本次跨學科的研究計劃探討在個人和社區群組層面上與他國的和解。另外，本研究結合了質性和量性的研究方法，包括較新穎和有效的問卷實驗方法。第三，本研究為於政府和非政府層面上加強推動和解提供政策建議的基礎。最後，研究結果可對日中和解提供深刻見解。本研究計劃的成果將會是一本專題著作﹑三份研究報告﹑三次研討會上的匯報及一個研討會。

13662816.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
13662816.value: 在《繪製成圖：當代小說及文化中的地圖使用》中，我探索了當代後殖民文學和文化中所呈現的地圖。對後現代主義的空間修辭、全球化話語、以及後殖民意義下位置和身份掙扎的研究，成果已經相當豐碩。然而，把文本中確實存在的地圖作為一種可寫可讀的文本來闡釋，還鮮有人嘗試。我試圖論証：當下地圖描寫的激增，表明「繪圖或者被圖繪」已經成為當代後殖民生活的一個重要元素；後殖民經驗的製圖過程中，種族、階級和性別被持續隱沒；以及後殖民空間如何被並存的隱沒和當中的衝突所構築。我所採用的批評方法是把後殖民與全球化理論、以及關於地圖的文本分析融為一爐，把文學研究中的空間轉向擴展至一系列新的文本，從而開啟更多文化及文學批評的可能性。 本研究項目的目的在於通過對文學研究與批判地理學進行跨學科研究，從而開拓新的閱讀空間。本研究以地理批評為開端，聚焦於作家們如何運用文學製圖法去呈現社會空間、增強文本的現實主義質感，或如何擾亂既有的穩定模式及人們識別地點的固有方法，以及如何打破既有的空間經驗。第一部旨在審視傳統地理批評，通過探討當代小說中以城市、疆界、旅程、和空間性為主題的敘事、或者作為敘事本身的地圖的文本中，識別當中有意識地推進地圖邊界的嘗試，從而研究地圖在地域性的理論化過程中所做的貢獻。具體來說，「繪製成圖」指的文本中那些用地圖去創造製圖，在實踐的進程中可揭示具危險性且先前不可見的地理權力。 第二部分把「繪製成圖」中涉及到的批評方法論闡釋為一種有意識的製圖實踐，探究了地圖與漫畫之間共享的視覺詞彙和形式上的技巧、兩者的虛構性、以及它們在「建構世界」中的投入。本研究的後面章節以香港作為「繪製成圖」的個案研究對象。我認為，香港特殊的後殖民性可以用地圖這種「新型的」類型來闡述，並以此代替那些更為傳統的表現形式。總而言之，通過探索文學理論、文化研究與批判地理學之間的可視性，對拓寬文學研究、後殖民理論與全球化理論的研究範圍有着無可估量的價值，有力地回應了「空間轉向」的時代趨勢。

13662816.label: Realisation of objectives
13662816.value: During the grant period, I have completed the project objectives fully. In drafting three articles for publication and numerous talks, I developed “map-ability” as a viable methodology and mode of critique that draws from an interdisciplinary array of sources (obj. 1). I have discussed my methodology and case studies with peers in my field at various conferences and talks I have been invited to give. Reading widely to identify patterns and commonalities, I successfully identified an archive of map-able texts, focusing on literary and visual texts contain within them actual maps that contribute in significant ways to the plot or interpretation of the text (obj. 2). To fulfill objectives 3 and 4, I read widely within the developing and interdisciplinary field of geo-humanities isolating the ‘spatial turn’ in literary studies, human geography, urban studies, to name a few. I grounded my research by exploring canonical writers on spatiality such as Henri Lefebvre, Edward Soja, and Doreen Massey, for example, then, with each draft article, I moved on to studying case studies and specific questions and issues raised by my research. This project has allowed me to form a coherent, original and useful narrative for how geo-criticism intersects with map-ability and will eventually form the theoretical foundation of my second monograph. Finally, I drafted two articles that are currently under review at top-tier journals (Cultural Critique and the International Journal of Comic Art); a third article is currently being drafted and will be completed in June 2019. Due to the long peer review time for top-tier journals in the humanities (6-9 months), I cannot estimate when these articles will finally be published. I attended three international conferences and gave several invited talks locally and internationally. Of note, one talk was a keynote presentation at a symposium at the Singapore University of Technology and Design and the second, a special research seminar for the English Department at King’s College London.

To investigate, determine and evaluate the shared theories from literary studies, critical geographies, spatial studies and geo-criticism. Again, as this project represents a new direction in my research trajectory, I am seeking time to master an interdisciplinary set of existing scholarship.

To produce at least two conference papers at international venues and a series of three articles to be published in peer-reviewed, scholarly outlets. These articles will be incorporated into my second monograph.

13662816.label: Major findings and research outcome
13662816.value: This project has helped me define the contours and characteristics of map-ability within the context of the geo-humanities. Geo-humanities is defined as the creative and scholarly co-mingling of geography, with its emphasis on place and spatiality, and the humanities. In literary studies, this collaboration has long been dominated by geo-criticism: the study of the importance of place to narrative. However, my project intervenes in such an approach by being the first to explore the deliberate integration of maps and cartographic practices into contemporary fiction as part of the political repertoire of reclaiming space. Through careful research, drafting three articles and receiving feedback from reviewers and my peers at interdisciplinary conferences and talks, I have also identified what is original about my argument and methodology. Specifically, this project’s innovations lie in its articulation of a prefigurative politics that require the participation of the reader in multiple acts of interpretative; its revelation of previously invisible geographies of power and how, through map-ability, literary studies can participate in the discourse of post-representational cartography.

13662816.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
13662816.value: Having identified the major gaps and interventions I can make in the field of geo-humanities, the logical next step of this project is to complete the draft of my second monograph. The second monograph will offer a cohesive and timely study of the proliferation of physical maps in contemporary literary texts. The introduction of the second monograph will pull together the research I have done for this current GRF and define the contours of the methodology and phenomenon I have termed map-ability. Each chapter will engage with a new facet of map-ability’s problematics not covered by the current GRF. In these chapters I will explore map-ability’s affordances to diverse but inter-related questions of gender, affect, island studies, neo-colonialism, and carceral geographies, to name a few. To prepare this draft and bring it to publication, I applied for a GRF in 2019.

13662816.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
13662816.value: In this project, “Map-able: The turn to the map in contemporary fiction and culture”, I explored the representations of maps as they appear in examples of contemporary postcolonial literature and culture. I defined and deployed an innovative and interdisciplinary critical approach I term “map-ability” to interpret the impetus to map in contemporary fiction. My project argues for how ‘map-able’ fiction pushes the boundaries of what maps and literature can contribute to the definition of territory. The viability of map-ability as a methodology was realized in three case studies. The first argued that Hong Kong’s anomalous postcoloniality can best be understood via the genre of maps. The proliferation of maps across Hong Kong demonstrates the impetus of ‘map or be mapped’ in the current political landscape. My second example explores the travelogues of graphic novelist, Guy Deslisle, whose cartoon maps and illustrations reveal the complexities of borderscapes. My final example focuses on novelists, Xiaolu Guo and Kamila Shamsie, who use maps to illustrate the geographies of power that structure women’s lives in a postcolonial context. At stake in this project is how maps collaborate with literature to invent and generate counter-authoritative versions of place and territory.
