14119516.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14119516.value: 胚胎幹細胞（ESC）是獨特的細胞類型，它們具有自我更新和全能性，能分化成任何細胞類型。胚胎幹細胞自我更新和分化之間的平衡受到細胞外環境和固有轉錄因子網絡信號的複雜調控。胚胎幹細胞可以作為一個極好的體外模型用於研究早期胚胎發育過程中的關鍵分子機制。 近年來有研究報導胚胎幹細胞中有多種離子通道的表達，然而，離子通道在幹細胞生物學和胚胎發育中的作用在很大程度上是未知的。囊性纖維化跨膜電導調節因子（CFTR）是能夠調節氯離子和HCO3-的陰離子通道。編碼CFTR基因突變可導致囊性纖維化（CF），該疾病是在高加索人群中常見的常染色體隱性遺傳病。雖然CF患者有不同程度的發育問題，我們對CFTR在胚胎發育過程中的生物學作用卻一無所知。有趣的是，我們最近的研究發現，CFTR在小鼠ESC（mESCs）中不僅表達，而且具有離子通道功能。 CFTR基因敲除的mESCs在胚層分化中有缺陷。另外，CFTR缺失抑制眾所周知的調節mESCs命運的Wnt 、β-catenin信號通路。這些發現促使我們推測CFTR通過Wnt /β-catenin信號通路調控胚胎幹細胞分化和胚胎發育。為了檢驗這一假設，該課題特設一下研究內容1）進一步明確CFTR在mESCs分化中的作用; 2）了解CFTR如何鏈接到mESCs分化過程中Wnt信號/β-catenin的途徑; 3）使用非洲爪蟾模型系統，評估CFTR的早期胚胎發育過程中的作用和信號機制。 該研究將有助於揭示CFTR在控制干細胞分化和胚胎發育的生物學功能。

14119516.label: Realisation of objectives
14119516.value: AIM1: To determine the role of CFTR in mESC self-renewal/differentiation To study the function of CFTR in mESCs, we crossed the CFTRtm1unc +/- mice to establish CFTR wild type and knockout (KO) mESC lines, and CFTRF508+/- mice to establish CFTR wild type and F508 mutant mESC lines. Two pairs of wild type (WT1 and WT2) and CFTR-/- double knockout (KO1 and KO2) (Figure 1a). One pair of wild type (WT1) and F508 mESC lines were selected for further study. Both CFTR WT and KO cells maintained the typical mESCs morphology under LIF+2i (Figure 1b). Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP) and SSEA-1 staining of CFTR WT and KO mESCs revealed that CFTR deficiency resulted in mild reduction of self-renewal capacity (Figure 1b). In contrast to the KO mESCs, the self-renewal and growth capability of F508 mESCs showed no difference compared to WT mESCs (Figure 1c&d). In addition, the colony formation analysis also indicated no difference between WT and F508 mESCs (Figure 1e). Western blot analysis further confirmed that the expression levels of pluripotency markers Oct-4, Sox-2 and Nanog were similar between WT and F508 mESCs (Figure 1f) in LIF+2i. Taken together, these data suggest that CFTR mutation F508 does not affect the self-renewal and pluripotency of the mouse ESCs. While we did not find any morphological difference between WT and F508 EB from day 1 to 7, the expression of mesoderm/mesendoderm (T, Mixl1, Gsc, Eomes) and endoderm (Gata4, Gata6, Sox17, Foxa2) markers showed differences. As shown in Figure 2a, the expression of the early mesendoderm markers examined, such as T, and Eomes, was significantly down-regulated in F508 mEBs compared to WT mEBs, starting from day 4. Following that, the expression of endoderm markers (Gata4, Gata6, Sox17, Foxa2) was prominently downregulated at day 7. In contrast, the expression of ectoderm (Pax6, Fgf5) markers did not show difference between WT and F508 mEBs. Both WT and F508 mESCs formed teratomas after 4 to 6 weeks of inoculation. Our real-time PCR analysis showed that in consistent with the in vitro data, the expression levels of Mixl1, T and Foxa2 were significantly decreased in the teratomas generated from F508 mESCs compared to that generated from WT mESCs. In summary, we have found that CFTR mutation at F508 impairs mesoendoderm differentiation, but not ectoderm differentiation of mESCs. AIM 2: To elucidate molecular mechanisms underlying CFTR-mediated regulation of mESC function The mRNA expression levels of β-catenin target genes, such as Lef1, c-Jun, and Axin2 were significantly decreased in F508 mESCs compared to that in WT mESCs (Figure 3a). Western blot analysis indicated that the expression level of active -catenin, TCF1 and LEF1 were significantly downregulated in the F508 mESCs (Figure 3b). Given that β-catenin signaling is activated and essential during mesendoderm differentiation in mESCs, we further investigated the regulatory role of CFTR in β-catenin signaling during mEB formation. Our western blot results showed that while the expression level of total β-catenin was similar between WT and F508 mEBs, the activated form of β-catenin, which is destined for nuclear translocation, was significantly decreased in F508 mEBs compared to WT mEBs (Figure 3d). In addition, we found that the expression levels of Lef1, Axin2, Cdx1 and T were significantly decreased in F508 mEBs at day 4 (Figure 3c). We also used a luciferase-based -catenin activated reporter and found that when treated with Wnt3a, the transcriptional activation of -catenin was significantly reduced in the F508 mESCs compared to the WT mESCs (Figure 3e). The regulatory effect of CFTR on β-catenin pathway was further validated in teratomas. The expression levels of active β-catenin were significantly reduced in F508 mESC-inoculated teratomas compared to that of WT teratomas (Figure 3f). We used a protein synthesis inhibitor, cycloheximide (CHX), to block the de novo synthesis of β-catenin, so that degradation process could be detected. Our results showed that the protein degradation of β-catenin in F508 mESCs was significantly faster than that in WT mESCs (Figure 4a&b), suggesting that the loss of CFTR results in increased β-catenin degradation. Then we used co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) to further test if CFTR physically interacted with β-catenin in mESCs. As shown in Figure 4c, CFTR interacted with β-catenin in mESCs. We then attempted to rescue the differentiation defect in F508 mEBs with CHIR99021, which inhibits Gsk3β and thus prevents β-catenin phosphorylation and degradation. After incubation with CHIR99021 (2 μM) for 4 days, both WT and F508 mEBs showed significantly elevated expression of Wnt/β-catenin targets (T, Cdx1) with no significant difference detected between WT and F508 mEBs (Figure 4d). Additionally, we overexpressed β-catenin in F508 mESCs using pT3-N90 (constitutively active form of β-catenin) and determined the expression of mesendoderm markers. The result showed that overexpression of β-catenin completely rescued the repressed mesendoderm markers in F508 mEBs (Figure 4e). These results indicate that CFTR regulates mesendoderm differentiation in mESCs via β-catenin pathway. AIM 3: To evaluate the role of CFTR in stem cell pluripotency and embryo development in vivo To determine the role of CFTR in embryo development, we performed loss-of-function of CFTR in Xenopus Laevis embryos using CFTR antisense morpholino (MO) nucleotide. Injection of 25 ng CFTR MO into both blastomeres of two-cell stage embryos resulted in an increase in the number of embryos exhibiting gastrulation defect and the number of death. Moreover, those embryos that survived exhibited various abnormal features including eye defects, head malformations, and curved body axis (Figure 5a). The quantification results showed that 72.9.4% of embryos were dead, 27.1% showed abnormal phenotype and none was normal in CFTR MO group (Figure 5b). In contrast, 4.0% of embryos were dead, 7.9% showed abnormal phenotype and 88.1% was normal in control group. Consistent with the results from mESC in vitro differentiation data, the expression of the mesoderm and endoderm marker genes examined was significantly down-regulated in CFTR morphants compared with that expressed in control embryos (Figure 5c). These results suggest that CFTR is crucial for early embryonic development in the Xenopus Laevis in vivo. RA signaling plays board roles in development and organogenesis. We next asked if the CFTR-mediates RA signaling in development. Injection of RA receptor RARα MO decreased the percentage of normal embryo while markedly increased the percentage of embryo showing the anterior truncation phenotype. Importantly, co-injection of Cftr mRNA with RARα MO partially rescued the percentage of normal embryo and prevented the anterior truncation phenotype (Figure 5d). The rescue effect of CFTR on RA signaling was further supported by the gene expression profiling of stage 10 embryos showing the decreased expression of markers of the mesoendoderm in RARα MO injected group can be restored by co-injection of Cftr mRNA (Figure 5e&f). These results suggest that CFTR and its downstream β-catenin signaling is involved, at least in part, in mediating the effect of RA signaling during embryo development in Xenopus laevis.

14119516.label: Major findings and research outcome
14119516.value: The present study has revealed a previously unrecognized role of CFTR in ESC differentiation, which is fundamentally important for embryonic development. Using CFTR mutant mESC lines, we have clearly demonstrated that deltaF508 affects mesendoderm commitment and endoderm differentiation. In light of the present finding that mesendoderm differentiation is significantly affected by CFTR mutation, it is likely that some of the developmental problems observed in CF patients in the lung, bone, pancreas, heart and intestine, may stem from defective mesendoderm differentiation during embryonic development due to CFTR mutation. On the other hand, in view of the importance of Wnt/β-catenin pathway in embryonic development, stem cell maintenance and cancer development, the presently demonstrated critical role of CFTR in regulating β-catenin signaling provides novel insights into the molecular mechanism underlying embryonic development and cancer development. Indeed, with the captured funding, we have also found that CFTR is involved in fibrosis and cancer development (Zhang JT et al., Sci Rep. 2017; Zhang J et al., Cell Mol Life Sci. 2018, Zhang JT et al., J Cell Mol Med, 2020). Altogether, we have revealed that CFTR is not merely an ion channel but also an important regulator of cancer development and progression with multiple signaling pathways identified. Apart from that, RA has been shown to promote the differentiation of ESC and embryonic development. Thus, we also assessed the transcriptional activation of CFTR by RA in ESC. In line with the differentiation of ESC, the expression of Cftr was modestly increased in vehicle control group and markedly increased by RA treatment. ChIP assay also demonstrated the binding of RARα to the two RAREs proximal to the promoter of Cftr gene in ESC. Additionally, as shown in Figure 5, CFTR and its downstream β-catenin signaling is also involved, at least in part, in mediating the effect of RA signaling during embryo development in Xenopus laevis. Together, these results suggest that CFTR mediates RA’s effect on ESC differentiation and development. These results have been published recently (Li XF et al., BBA Mol. Cell. Res. 2018).

14119516.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14119516.value: Defective CFTR ion channel function due to the most common mutation of CFTR, ΔF508 mutation, has been shown to underline the pathogenesis of some of the disease conditions in CF, such as obstructive lung disease, pancreas exocrine deficiency, CF-related diabetes, abnormal gonad function, and infertility. However, the biological role of CFTR in development is unknown. Our study reveals a previously undefined role of CFTR in controlling ESC differentiation and b-catenin pathway which advance our understanding of the biological role of CFTR in embryonic development. Based on these findings, we have already initiated further research to investigate the role of CFTR on specific lineage differentiation in endoderm. For instance, we have found that CFTR regulates hematopoiesis via channel-independent role, providing an explanation for the anemic phenotype of CF patients. In addition, by using ESC-cardiomyocyte differentiation model, we are studying whether and how CFTR would affect heart development. Finally, CFTR has been considered ideal targets for highly selective drugs due to their membrane localization and complex structures. As such, CFTR could be exploited as therapeutic targets for the control and optimization of stem cell-based regenerative medicine.

14119516.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14119516.value: CFTR is a cAMP-regulated anion channel capable of conducting both Cl- and HCO3-. Mutations in the gene encoding CFTR cause cystic fibrosis (CF), a common autosomal recessive disease in Caucasian populations. Although CF patients are known to have a varied degree of developmental problems, the biological role of CFTR in development is unknown. Here, we have found that CFTR is functionally expressed in mouse ESCs. deltaF508 mutated mESCs exhibit significant defect in mesendoderm differentiation. In addition, CFTR physically interacts with β-catenin, defect of which leads to premature degradation of β-catenin and suppressed activation of β-catenin signaling. Furthermore, knockdown of CFTR retards the early development of Xenopus laevis with impaired mesoderm/endoderm differentiation. In addition, RA transcriptionally up-regulates CFTR by promoting the direct binding of its receptor RARα to Cftr promoter. Ectopic overexpression of CFTR restores the developmental defects, as well as Wnt/β-catenin signalling, induced by the knockdown of RARα in Xenopus laevis. Our study reveals a previously undefined role of CFTR in controlling ESC differentiation and early embryonic development via its interaction with β-catenin, and provides novel insights into the understanding of embryonic development and pathogenesis of CF-related diseases.

14120516.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14120516.value: 這項研究的目的是確立血漿胎盤生長因子（PGF）作為新生血管性年齡相關性黃斑退化（AMD）的新生物標誌，並研究由我們新檢測到的AMD相關PGF突變的生物學效應。 新生血管性AMD是老齡人口中不可逆失明的主要原因。目前新生血管性AMD的主流治療方法是在玻璃體內注射抗血管內皮生長因子（VEGF）製劑，主要包括雷珠單抗和一種新的藥物aflibercept。其中雷珠單抗只結合VEGFA，而aflibercept則結合VEGFA，VEGFB和PGF等三種蛋白。近期等報道指出，aflibercept所需的注射頻率較低，並具有与雷珠單抗可比擬的治療效果，並且其對雷珠單抗耐受的患者也有作用。這些使得aflibercept在AMD治療上具有相當的優勢。 最近，我們發現在PGF基因中的2個單核苷酸多態性（SNP, rs2268615和rs2268614）與新生血管性AMD有顯著的統計學關聯。我們還通過基因測序檢測到一個PGF啟動子缺失突變（C.-486_-469del18），其增加了AMD的相對危險性達7.3倍之多。另外，我們還檢測到一個新的保護性剪接位點突變（c.393-2_393delAGG）。因此，我們的研究結果表明PGF是AMD的一個相關生物學因素。值得注意的是，SNP rs2268614的風險基因型在先前的報導中已被證明与較低的血漿PGF水平相關。因此血漿PGF水平可能是新生血管性AMD的生物標誌物。在我們的研究計劃中，我們將收集500名新生血管性AMD患者和500名年齡和性別匹配的對照組受試者的血液樣本，并對其PGF的基因型及血漿PGF水平進行檢測。 然後對PGF基因型與新生血管性AMD的發病以及治療效果進行關聯分析。我們將通過各種細胞生物學方法確定PGF突變（C-486_-469del18及c.393-2_393delAGG）的生物效應。 本研究計劃的結果將有利於我們確認血漿PGF作為新生血管性AMD一個新的生物標誌物，並且為PGF在血管生成中的生物學作用提供新的信息。

14120516.label: Realisation of objectives
14120516.value: The project was conducted based on the five objectives to test the key hypothesis that the placental growth factor (PGF) and related genes in the same pathway are potential biomarkers of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and/or polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy (PCV). 1. We first sequenced the promoter region, coding sequences and splicing regions of the PGF gene in a Hong Kong Chinese cohort of 235 neovascular AMD patients and 435 controls. A novel 18-base-pair deletion mutation in the promoter region of PGF was identified in 3 (1.28%) patients and 1 (0.23%) control subject (OR = 5.61; 95% CI 0.58-54.26). The 18 base-pair deletion was then analyzed in a Shantou Chinese cohort of 189 neovascular AMD patients and 846 controls. It was found in 2 (1.06%) patients and 2 (0.24%) controls (OR = 4.51; 95% CI: 0.63-32.25). In the combined Chinese sample, this deletion had a significant association with neovascular AMD (P = 0.026; OR = 5.08, 95% CI: 1.21-21.36). The transcription activity of this disease-associated promoter variant was determined in human ARPE-19 cells by promoter-luciferase analysis. The deletion was predicted to alter the transcription factor binding sites in the PGF promoter, and higher luciferase expression was detected in ARPE-19 cells transfected with the deletion variant plasmid than those transfected with wild type plasmid. In contrast, another mutation c.393-2_393delAGG detected in our prelim study was found not to be associated with AMD or PCV in the Hong Kong cohort; therefore, it was not carried to the replication study. This part of study confirmed a rare, functional promoter variant in the PGF gene that increases PGF transcription activity and confers a 5-fold risk to neovascular AMD. The objective #4 was achieved. Meanwhile, we validated the association of PGF with AMD, partly achieving objective #2. (published data) 2. In view of the role of PGF in the genetic susceptibility of AMD and PCV, we tested other genes in the related pathway, including ANGPT2 and TIE2, as new candidate genes for the diseases. By using haplotype-tagging SNP analysis, we confirmed that these two genes are also susceptibility genes for AMD and PCV. Thus, the objective #5 was achieved. (published data) 3. To test the hypothesis underlying the objectives #1-3, we recruited new AMD (n=250) and PCV (n=200) patients and controls (n=300), and tested their plasma level of PGF using ELISA assay and electrochemiluminescence immunoassay as proposed in the study. We found that the plasma level of PGF was not different between patients and control (P>0.3). Also, the plasma level of PGF was not correlated with the treatment response of anti-VEGF agents (Lucentis / Eylea) in neovascular AMD or PCV (P>0.5). Finally, we tested the correlation of the PGF genotypes with plasma level of PGF, and no significant correlation was identified (P>0.1). Therefore, we confirmed that plasma level of PGF is less likely to be a biomarker for AMD or PCV (unpublished data).

14120516.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14120516.value: Based on the findings in this project, we have conducted/planned the following research projects. 1. We have tested the association of PGF, ANGPT2 and TIE2 genes with central serous Chorioretinopathy (CSCR), which is a major maculopathy affecting working-age population. We found that these genes were not associated with CSCR, suggesting the genetic profiles of AMD, CSCR and PCV are different (manuscript under preparation). 2. We also tested the association of PGF, ANGPT2 and TIE2 variants with diabetic retinopathy (DR), which is a major ocular complication in diabetes and characterized by retinal hemorrhage in the early stage and new vessel formation in the advance stage. We found that the TIE2 gene is associated with DR, suggesting that AM) and DR may share some genetic components (manuscript in preparation). 3. We will continue to test other candidate genes in the pathway of PGF, ANGPT2 and TIE2, with a view to identify new associated genes for AMD and PCV (lab work ongoing). 4. In another study, we found that the level of ANGPT2 in the aqueous humor was significantly higher in AMD patients than in normal controls. We will test whether plasma ANGPT2 and TIE2 are potential biomarkers for AMD.

14120516.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14120516.value: Neovascular age-related macular degeneration (nAMD) is a leading cause of central vision loss in elderly. nAMD is a complex disease resulted from the interaction of multiple inherent (e.g., aging), environmental (e.g., smoking) and genetic risk factors. The identification of genetic risk factors may enable us to better understand the disease and provide potential biomarkers for earlier detection. In our previous study, we have identified single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in the placental growth factor (PGF) gene to be associated with nAMD. In this study, we first sequenced the promoter and coding regions of the PGF gene in nAMD patients and controls, and identified a novel 18-base-pair deletion mutation in the promoter region to be associated with nAMD. Patients carrying this mutation had about 5 folds of increased risk of nAMD. Subsequent biological analysis showed that this mutation could affect transcription efficiency of the gene. We also tested the plasma level of PGF, but we found no significant difference between nAMD patients and controls. In addition, we evaluated other genes in the pathway related to PGF, and identified ANGPT2 and TIE2 as new susceptibility genes for nAMD. These findings altogether suggested PGF, ANGPT2 and TIE2 as new genetic biomarkers for nAMD.

14120816.label: Realisation of objectives
14120816.value: Both project objectives 1 & 2 have been successfully completed. For Objective 1, we have determined the crosstalk of IL-6-STAT3 and AR-CCRK axes in HCC, based on the experimental data that 1) knockdown of STAT3 downregulated AR and CCRK, which could be rescued by ectopic AR expression; 2) overexpression of constitutively-active STAT3, but not dominant negative STAT3, upregulated AR and CCRK, and such stimulatory effects could be abolished by AR knockdown; 3) CCRK auto-regulation was disrupted following knockdown of STAT3 and AR; and 4) the physical association of AR and phosphorylated STAT3 was confirmed by coimmunoprecipitation, and their binding at ARE of CCRK promoter was verified by ChIP-reChIP assay. Moreover, we also confirmed the activation effect of CCRK-EZH2-NF-κB signaling on IL-6 transcription, by showing that 1) the expression levels of CCRK, EZH2, NFκB and IL-6 were all positively associated; and 2) there was physical association between EZH2 and phosphorylated p65, and both proteins were enriched at IL-6 promoter with concurrent transcriptional upregulation. These consistent data obtained from multiple cell models corroborated the positive feedback regulations in the IL-6-STAT3-AR-CCRK and CCRK-EZH2-NF-κB-IL-6 pathways. In addition, we validated the overexpression of IL-6, STAT3, AR, CCRK, GSK-3β, β-catenin, EZH2 and phosphorylated p65 in HCC clinical specimens by either Western or ELISA analysis. Collectively, all three tasks listed under Objective 1 in our proposal have been addressed. For Objective 2, we have determined that CCRK/GSK-3β kinase cascade indeed drives the mTOR signaling, as 1) overexpression of CCRK induced the maturation of SREBP1 and the phosphorylation of mTOR, 4E-BP1 and other downstream molecules, which could be abolished by co-expression of constitutively-active S9A-GSK3β mutant; and 2) knockdown of TSC2 could abolish the GSK3β-dependent inhibitory effect on mTOR signaling molecules. Moreover, we validated the functional relationship of CCRK/GSK-3β and mTOR signaling in both NASH and NASH-HCC mouse models. Furthermore, we have investigated the functional roles of this new signaling cascade in cell survival, lipogenesis and tumorigenesis using new inducible CCRK cell lines and CCRK transgenic mouse model. Our results showed that CCRK/GSK-3β/mTORC1 activation induces metabolic and immunosuppressive reprogramming to promote NASH-associated hepatocarcinogenesis.

14120816.label: Major findings and research outcome
14120816.value: As obesity and diabetes reach global epidemics, non-alcoholic-fatty-liver-disease (NAFLD) increases as a drastic health problem and emerges as a major risk factor for HCC. Based on our previous findings, we hypothesized that the pro-inflammatory signals in NAFLD induce a self-reinforcing CCRK circuitry to drive lipogenesis and tumorigenesis through mTORC1 activation. To address this hypothesis, we have developed and utilized complementary genetically-engineered cells and NAFLD-related HCC models in this project (Tian et al., Nat Commun 2019). The major findings are described below: CRISPR/Cas9 knockout of Ccrk significantly reduced HCC tumorigenesis, accompanied by reduced polymorphonuclear myeloid-derived suppressor cell (PMN-MDSC) expansion. Mechanistically, hepatoma CCRK stimulated immunosuppressive CD11b+CD33+HLA-DR−MDSC expansion through upregulating IL-6. At molecular level, CCRK activated NF-κB via EZH2 and facilitated NF-κB-EZH2 co-binding to IL-6 promoter. Consistently, hepatic CCRK induction in transgenic mice activated the EZH2/NF-κB/IL-6 cascade, leading to accumulation of PMN-MDSCs with potent T-cell suppressive-activity. In contrast, inhibiting tumorous CCRK or hepatic IL-6 increased IFN-γ+TNF-α+CD8+T-cell infiltration and impaired tumorigenicity, which was rescued by restoring PMN-MDSCs. Furthermore, deletion of hepatic Ccrk expression therefore breaks the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment and enhances the therapeutic efficacy of immunotherapy (Zhou et al., Gut 2018). Furthermore, we used a carcinogen-dietary induced NAFLD spontaneous HCC mouse model to further determine the relationship of CCRK and immunometabolic regulation in HCC development. Using lentivirus-mediated knockdown strategy, our data confirmed a critical role of CCRK in NAFLD-associated HCC. Mechanistic and functional analyses in CCRK-inducible and CRISPR/Cas9 cell models elucidated an inflammatory-CCRK circuitry that promotes lipid accumulation, glucose intolerance, insulin resistance and HCC tumorigenicity via mTORC1/4EBP1/S6K/SREBP1 cascades. Moreover, hepatic CCRK induction in liver-specific transgenic mice stimulates mTORC1-dependent immunosuppressive reprogramming via PMN-MDSC recruitment. As the CCRK-mTORC1 pathway components are concordantly over-expressed in human NASH-associated HCCs, our findings unveil a new mechanism driving the pro-tumorigenic microenvironment for HCC development (Sun et al., Nat Commun 2018). By integrating both tumor cell biology and immunology, the results from this project demonstrated that CCRK is an exploitable druggable target for cancer therapy (Mok et al., Pharmacol & Ther 2018).

14120816.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14120816.value: In spite of the anticipated therapeutic value of CCRK inhibition, there is currently no CCRK-specific inhibitor available, and no development of such reagent has been reported. A major reason for this is the unresolved 3-D structure of CCRK protein, with or without its cyclin partner, which is indispensable for designing and screening compatible inhibitors. In 2017, we have initiated a collaborative effort together with medicinal chemists and structural biologists from Oxford University, Sussex University and Cardiff University in the Structural Genomics Consortium to accelerate CCRK structural characterization and drug discovery. We have also installed an X-ray diffraction facility in CUHK with hybrid photon counting detector, which dramatically speeds up the screening of protein-drug complexes. The continual delineation of the functions and structure of CCRK will provide pharmacological proof-of-concept for the development of new combination immunotherapeutic strategies against HCC.

14120816.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14120816.value: Recent large-scale prospective and population-based studies have underscored obesity and diabetes, which induce non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), as important causes of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) especially in male. Approximately 1.4 billion people are now living with obesity and diabetes. As the number is expected to grow especially in developing countries including China, there is a compelling need to understand the molecular mechanisms underlying hepatocarcinogenesis in NAFLD. Cell cycle related kinase (CCRK) is the latest member in the cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK) family. Similar to other CDKs, CCRK plays important roles in the regulation of cell proliferation, and is thus associated with tumor development. In this project, we have delineated a positive feedback loop between inflammatory (IL-6-STAT3) and male (AR-CCRK) signaling pathways in HCC, and the subsequent activation of EZH2-NF-κB and GSK-3β-mTORC1 cascades in mediating CCRK-induced metabolic and immunosuppressive reprogramming. As we also showed activation of this signaling network in human NAFLD-related HCCs, our mechanistic and functional studies have unveiled a central role of the inflammatory-CCRK in establishing a pro-tumorigenic microenvironment for HCC development and offered therapeutic strategies to combat this dreadful disease in an era of global obesity and diabetes.

14121116.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14121116.value: Acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding (AUGIB) is a common medical emergency. In an ageing population, antiplatelet drugs are increasingly being prescribed for treatment and prophylaxis against cardiovascular thrombo-embolic events. In many patients, platelet dysfunction mostly acquired is the principal cause of bleeding. To clinicians, the management of patients on antiplatelet drugs or anticoagulants is a challenge. One has to carefully balance the bleeding against thrombo-embolic risks. Therefore measuring platelet function should be integral in the management plan. A quantitative measurement allows titration of platelet function in accordance with bleeding or thromboembolic risk. To our knowledge, platelet function has not been studied in a large cohort of patients with acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding. As a first step, we sought to determine if platelet dysfunction is associated with clinical outcome. In this prospective, observational single centre cohort study of consecutive patients with overt signs of acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding, we measure their platelet function by point of care tests (light transmittance aggregometry, verify now p2y12,the platelet function analysis system (PFA-100) upon their admissions. We then follow up patients for 30 days after trial enrollment. The primary endpoint is defined as significant bleeding that requires interventions (endoscopic, radiologic or surgery). Secondary end points include cardio- and cerebrovascular thrombo-embolic events and all cause deaths. A receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis is calculated for each point-of-care test to evaluate if individual test can distinguish between patients with and without primary end point. We aim to evaluate the capability of platelet function tests to predict clinical outcome in patients with AUGIB. Logistic regression models will then be built in search for independent correlates to the primary and secondary endpoints and to adjust for confounding variables.

14121116.label: Realisation of objectives
14121116.value: 1. We measured platelet function in 3.2% citrated whole blood taken peri-endoscopy among 476 patients admitted with acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding. We used the platelet function analyzer-100 system (PFA-100, Siemens Health Diagnostic, Germany) with citrated blood in collagen/ epinephrine (CEPI) cartridges. The prevalence of platelet dysfunction defined by aperture closure time of 197 seconds. The prevalence of platelet dysfunction was 124/476 (26.1%). The prevalence of dysfunction was significantly higher in those with a history of gastrointestinal bleeding (18.5% vs. 11.1%, p-0.034), with thrombocytopenia (platelet count <150× 109 /L( (33.8% vs 13.4% ,p<0.001), with Glasgow-Blatchford score > 12 (13.7% vs. 5.6%, p=0.016), with chronic renal disease (10.5% vs. 4%, P=0.007) and use of aspirin (29.8% vs. 12.8%, p<0.001). 2. Our primary endpoint was the need for hemostatic intervention in 30 days. The rate of hemostatic intervention was (110 of 352, 31.3%) in the normal platelet function group and (46 of 124, 37.1%) in the platelet dysfunction group (difference 5.8%, 95% CI, -3.9 to 15.6; adjusted OR 1.18, 95%CI 0.71 to 1.85). 3. We were not allocated with a sufficient budget to use other platforms. A comparison was therefore not possible. 4. None of the patients in this cohort had an thrombotic event. 5. Secondary endpoints of further bleeds(10 vs. 4; adjusted OR 0.80, 95%CI 0.21 to 3.07) and deaths (7 vs. 5; adjusted OR 1.18, 95%CI 0.31 to 4.51) were similar between groups.

14121116.label: Major findings and research outcome
14121116.value: There are several findings that are potentially practice changing 1. Platelet dysfunction is more commonly found in patients as expected on antiplatelet therapy, with thrombocytopenia, with renal impairment and with more severe bleeding probably related to dilutional coagulopathy from resuscitation. 2. Platelet dysfunction in patients with acute upper GIB does not appear to correlate with their clinical outcomes. 3. Withholding antiplatelet medication is probably unnecessary in the majority of patients with AUGIB.

14121116.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14121116.value: In a large cohort of patients hospitalised with acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding, platelet dysfunction is seen in about a quarter of them. Platelet dysfunction is more seen in patients with a history of prior bleeding, with a low platelet count, with more severe bleeding as indicated by a high Glasgow Blatchford Score, with renal impairment or using anti platelet medication of aspirin. The occurrence of platelet dysfunction is not significantly associated with adverse outcomes (the need for interventions, further bleeds and deaths).

14121816.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14121816.value: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a common and severe complication in the critically ill patients with poor clinical outcomes. It has been shown that activation of the intrarenal inflammatory cascades contributes to the overall acute renal damage where inflammatory macrophages are a key player in AKI. However, mechanisms whereby macrophages mediate AKI remain unclear, which limits the development of effective therapy for AKI. We have previously demonstrated that macrophage migration inhibitory factor (MIF) is a proinflammatory cytokine largely produced by inflammatory macrophages and plays a pivotal role in immunologically-mediated kidney diseases. However, the role of MIF in AKI remains unexplored. To examine the functional importance of MIF in AKI, we performed preliminary study in ischemia–reperfusion injury (IRI) and cisplatin-induced mouse models of AKI in MIF knockout (KO) mice. We found that mice lacking MIF were protected from AKI, which was completely reversed by adoptive transfer with MIF wild-type, but not MIF KO macrophages, suggesting a critical role for MIF, particularly macrophage-derived MIF, in the pathogenesis of AKI. Our preliminary data also found that MIF promoted AKI by activating the inflammatory M1 macrophages via the CD74-NF-kB-Clec4e mechanism and blockade of the MIF-CD74 interaction with a novel MIF inhibitor RPS19 protected against cisplstin-induced AKI. All these preliminary findings lead us to hypothesize that macrophages may mediate AKI via a MIF-dependent mechanism and targeting MIF may represent as a novel therapy for AKI. We plan to test this hypothesis in IRI and cisplatin –induced AKI in MIF knockout (KO) mice. Furthermore, the specific role of macrophage-derived MIF in AKI will be determined by adoptive transfer of MIF KO or WT macrophages and by specific deletion of MIF from macrophages in macrophage-specific MIF KO mice (LysM-Cre/MIF flox/flox). Mechanisms whereby MIF activates inflammatory macrophages via the CD74-NF-kB –Clec4e pathway will be elucidated in vitro and in vivo. Finally, we will develop a novel and effective therapy for AKI by blocking the MIF-CD74 interaction with a novel MIF inhibitor (RPS19). Ultimately, this study will identify the pathogenic role of MIF, specifically macrophage-derived MIF, in AKI. We will also define the underlying mechanism by which MIF mediates AKI by activating inflammatory macrophages via the CD74-NF-kB-Clec4e pathway. Identification of this novel role for MIF in AKI will result in the development of a specific therapy for AKI by targeting MIF with a novel MIF inhibitor. Thus, outcomes from this study will be highly significant both scientifically and clinically. 急性腎損傷（AKI）是一常見，伴有嚴重臨床結果的急性病。目前研究顯示腎內炎反應如炎性巨噬細胞是在AKI的發生起了重要關鍵角色。然而，其機制仍不清楚，這限制了有效治療AKI的發展。我們前期研究表明，巨噬細胞遷移抑制因子（MIF）主要是由炎性巨噬細胞產生，導致腎臟疾病。然而，MIF在AKI的作用仍然未知。根據我們的前期研究初步數據，我們推測巨噬細胞可經由MIF依賴性機制介導的AKI。 所以，本研究擬應用MIF基因敲除（KO）小鼠， 在缺血再灌注損傷（IRI）和順鉑藥物誘導的小鼠模型進行MIF在AKI的作用與致病機制；通過應用MIF KO或WT巨噬細胞轉移實驗研究巨噬細胞源性MIF在AKI的具體作用；並通過巨噬細胞特異性MIF KO小鼠確定巨噬細胞來源MIF在AKI的特異功能；對MIF經由CD74-NF-kB的-Clec4e途徑激活炎性巨噬細胞在體外和體內進行闡述。最後，我們將通過應用一種新穎的MIF抑製劑（RPS19）阻斷MIF-CD74相互作用，探討對AKI的新的有效治療方法。 這項研究將確定MIF的致病作用，特別是巨噬細胞源性MIF在AKI的作用與機制。此外， 本研究將探討抗MIF靶向治療AKI的新方法。因此，這項研究成果將有非常顯著的科學和臨床意義。

14121816.label: Realisation of objectives
14121816.value: The grant has been successfully completed with all objectives obtained. 1. We have extended the Specific Aim 1 to measure MIF levels in patients with AKI. We believed that this is important because the new expensed study is clinically relevant and provides strongly rationale for the experimental studies. In collaborating with Prof Anping Xu and Dr Tang Ying from Sun Yat-Sen Memorial Hospital in Guangzhou, we have collected more than 40 patients with AKI and found that in patients with AKI, both plasma and urinary MIF levels are largely elevated at the onset of AKI, declined to normal levels when AKI is resolved and correlated tightly with the severity of AKI clinically. As stated in the Specific Aim 1, we have completed both IRI and cisplatin-induced AKI mouse model in MIF KO mice and found that deletion of MIF was capable of protecting against both RIR and cisplatin-induced AKI by suppressing the MIF-CD74-NF-kB signaling pathway. These data were presented in the 9th World Congress of Nephrology, Mexico City (April 21-25, 2017) and published in J Cell Mol Med (2019;23:3867-3877) and Mol Ther (2018; 26:2523-2532). As stated in the Specific Aim 1, we have also successfully generated the macrophage-specific MIF KO mice by crossing MIFflox/flox mice to the LysM-Cre mice. We have uncovered the pathogenetic role of macrophage-derived MIF in AKI as adoptive transfer of MIF KO, but not MIF WT macrophages, can attenuate AKI and specific deletion of MIF from macrophages in macrophage-specific MIF KO mice (LysM-Cre/MIF flox/flox) is also capable of suppressing AKI. All these studies have been completed and the results are fully support our hypothesis that macrophages are a rich source of MIF and macrophage-derived MIF plays a critical role in AKI. A new manuscript is under preparation (a draft is attached in Part C). 2. As stated in the Specific Aim 2, we have completed the regulatory mechanisms whereby MIF activates macrophages to promote AKI via the CD74-NF-kB –Clec4e pathway. We found that MIF is induced by a LRNA9884 as silencing LRNA9884 is able to block MIF-mediated AKI (Front Physiol 2020;11:590027). MIF KO mice adoptively transferring with MIF-producing macrophages is associated with a significant increase in CD68+Clec4e+ M1 macrophages in the AKI kidney. We also found that addition of MIF is able to upregulate Clec4e and iNOS (two M1 markers) on macrophages in a time- and dose-dependent manner, which was associated with upregulation of MIF receptor CD74 and activation of NF-kB signaling in vivo and in vitro. Blockade of the MIF-CD74 interaction with a novel MIF inhibitor RPS19 and NF-kB signaling with an inhibitor Bay11-7085 is able to inhibit MIF-induced Clec4e, MCP-1, and TNFa expression on bone marrow-derived macrophages. These results fully support our hypothesis that MIF may promote AKI by activating the inflammatory macrophage phenotype via a CD74-NF-kB-Clec4e-dependent mechanism. These data have partly published in J Cell Mol Med 2019;23:3867-3877; Mol Ther 2018; 26:2523-2532; and Front Physiol 2020;11:590027. In addition, a new manuscript is under preparation (a draft is attached in Part C). 3. Importantly, as described in Specific Aim 3, in collaborating with Prof Jörg Klug and Andreas Meinhard from, Justus-Liebig-University, Germany, we have successfully developed a new effective MIF-targeted therapy for AKI. We found that the treatment with RPS19, but not the mutant control protein, largely suppressed AKI as demonstrated by dramatically reducing serum levels of creatinine, tubular necrosis, and macrophage infiltration. These results revealed RPS19 as a novel therapeutic agent for AKI and also demonstrated that targeting MIF may represent as a new effective therapy for AKI. These data were presented in the 9th World Congress of Nephrology, Mexico City (April 21-25, 2017) and have been published in Mol Ther 2018; 26:2523-2532. In summary, we have successfully completed all 3 objective studies with expected achievements. In addition, we have also expensed and added a new approach to study MIF as a biomarker in patients with AKI. The new results are beyond the original scope and have largely enhanced the impact of this study. However, due to the COVID-19, two research staff who are engaging in this grant are unable to come to Hong Kong, a new manuscript remains in the draft stage as attached in the Part C. Hopefully we are able to complete it within 3 months.

14121816.label: Major findings and research outcome
14121816.value: We have completed all 3 Specific Aim studies as originally described. There were several major findings. 1) In patients with AKI, plasma and urinary MIF levels are largely elevated at the onset of AKI, declined to normal levels when AKI is resolved and correlated tightly with the severity of AKI clinically . Importantly, we also uncovered that MIF is pathogenic in AKI as mice lacking MIF are protected against AKI induced by IRI- and cisplatin (J Cell Mol Med 2019 Jun;23:3867-3877; Mol Ther 2018; 26:2523-2532). 2) We also uncovered the pathogenetic role of macrophage-derived MIF in AKI as adoptive transfer of MIF KO, but not MIF WT macrophages, can attenuate AKI and specific deletion of MIF from macrophages in macrophage-specific MIF KO mice (LysM-Cre/MIF flox/flox) is also capable of suppressing AKI. All these studies have been completed, and a manuscript is in preparation. 3) Mechanistically, MIF is induced by a LRNA9884 and is capable of mediating AKI via the CD74/TLR4-NF-κB signalling as silencing LNRA9884 blocks MIF-mediated AKI and mice lacking MIF are protected from AKI by largely suppressing CD74/TLR-4-NF-κB associated renal inflammation. These data were presented in the 9th World Congress of Nephrology, Mexico City (April 21-25, 2017) and have been published in J Cell Mol Med (2019 Jun;23(6):3867-3877) and in Front Physiol (2020;11:590027). Further studies also found that MIF can activate M1 macrophages specifically via the CD74-Mincle (Cle4e)-NF-kB signaling pathway to mediate AKI and MIF KO mice transferring with MIF-producing macrophages with silencing Mincle are protected from MIF-induced AKI in vivo and in vitro. A new manuscript is in preparation as shown in Part C. 4) As described in Specific Aim 3: we have successfully developed a new and effective MIF-targeted therapy for AKI by treating AKI mice with a MIF inhibitor RPS19. Thus, targeting MIF may represent as a new effective therapy for AKI. These data were presented in the 9th World Congress of Nephrology, Mexico City (April 21-25, 2017) and a manuscript has been published in Mol Ther (2018;26:2523-2532). With this grant support, a PhD student LI Jinhong has been successfully trained (See Thesis copy) and importantly, 6 international collaborative studies have been established to investigate inflammatory mediators including CRP in AKI. These studies have been extremely active and productive with total of 24 joint publications (See Part C).

14121816.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14121816.value: In this study, we have uncovered the pathogenic role of MIF in AKI. We first find that plasma and urinary MIF is high in patients with AKI and correlated with the severity of AKI. Second, we have revealed a pathogenic role of MIF in AKI as mice lacking MIF are protected against AKI. Third, we also detect that macrophages are a rich source of MIF and specific deletion MIF from macrophages can inhibit AKI. Fourth, MIF is induced by a LRNA9884 and is capable of activating the inflammatory macrophages to mediate AKI specifically via the CD74-Mincle (Cle4e)-NF-kB signaling pathway. Finally, we have successfully developed a new and effective MIF-targeted therapy for AKI by treating AKI mice with a MIF inhibitor RPS19. Thus, targeting MIF may represent as a new effective therapy for AKI.

14124216.label: Project Title(Chinese)
14124216.value: 激活TFEB及誘導自噬反應而改善糖尿病小鼠的內皮細胞功能的機理研究

14124216.label: Project Objectives

To investigate the functional role of TFEB in regulation of autophagy and preservation of endothelial function in diabetes.

14124216.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14124216.value: 內皮功能障礙是常見的二型糖尿病血管併發症，會大大增加動脈粥樣硬化和高血壓等血管疾病的發病機會。自噬是哺乳動物細胞一種高度保守的穩定內環境的機制，通過在自噬溶酶體中降解受損的蛋白質和細胞器以滿足细胞自身的代谢和更新细胞器的需要。越來越多的實驗和臨床證據表明，自噬活動在心血管代謝性疾病中有所改變。例如一項最近的研究證明，伴隨衰老發生的自噬受損會導致動脈內皮功能障礙。然而，在糖尿病的病程中自噬受損是否與內皮細胞功能障礙相關還不清楚。此外，誘導自噬是否用利於糖尿病血管內皮功能的改善尚待闡明。 TFEB是調控細胞自噬和溶酶體生成的關鍵轉錄因子。我們的實驗初步表明，TFEB可以在人內皮細胞內調控自噬基因的表達，而增高TFEB表達可以改善糖尿病血管內皮功能。進一步研究TFEB在代謝疾病中內皮細胞生理和病理中的功能和重要性將十分有意義。為此目的，我們將採用糖尿病小鼠（db / db）和高脂飲食誘導的肥胖小鼠模型，具體研究（1）正常自噬活動是否有助於維持內皮功能，以及增強細胞自噬是否能改善db/db小鼠的內皮功能;（2）TFEB和自噬在糖尿病中如何被調節，以及TFEB對糖尿病小鼠血管內皮功能的的保護作用。

14124216.label: Realisation of objectives
14124216.value: Objective one: TFEB (transcription factor EB) was induced by atheroprotective laminar flow and play an anti-atherosclerotic role by inhibiting inflammation in endothelial cells (ECs). This study aims to investigate whether TFEB regulates endothelial inflammation in diabetic mice. Endothelial denudation shows that TFEB is mainly expressed in ECs in mouse aortas. Adenoviral TFEB overexpression reduces endothelial inflammation as evidenced by decreased expression of vascular inflammatory markers in db/db mouse aortas, and reduced expression of a wide range of adhesion molecules and chemokines in human umbilical vein ECs. RNA sequencing of TFEB-overexpressed human umbilical vein ECs suggested TFEB inhibits NF-κB (nuclear factor-kappa B) signaling. Indeed, luciferase assay shows TFEB suppresses NF-κB transcriptional activity. Mechanistically, TFEB suppresses IKK (IκB kinase) activity to protect IκB-α from degradation, leading to reduced p65 nuclear translocation. Inhibition of IKK by PS-1145 abolished TFEB silencing-induced inflammation in human umbilical vein ECs. Lastly, we identified KLF2 (Krüppel-like factor 2) upregulates TFEB expression and promoter activity. Laminar flow experiment showed that KLF2 is required for TFEB induction by laminar flow and TFEB is an anti-inflammatory effector downstream of laminar flow-KLF2 signaling in ECs. TFEB exerts anti-inflammatory effects in diabetic mice and such function in ECs is achieved by inhibiting IKK activity and increasing IκBα level to suppress NF-κB activity. KLF2 mediates TFEB upregulation by laminar flow. Thi study was published in ATVB in 2019 (SONG W, ZHANG CL, GOU L, HE L, GONG YY, QU D, ZHAO L, JIN N, CHAN TF, WANG L, TIAN XY, *LUO JY & *HUANG Y (2019) Endothelial TFEB (Transcription Factor EB) Restrains IKK (IκB Kinase)-p65 Pathway to Attenuate Vascular Inflammation in Diabetic db/db Mice. Arteriosclerosis, Thrombosis and Vascular Biology 39(4):719-730. doi: 10.1161/ATVBAHA.119.312316. April 2019). Please also see the attached paper in PDF format. Objective two: Endothelial dysfunction contributes to development of vascular complications in diabetes. Growing evidence implicates that autophagic dysregulation is involved in the pathogenesis of diabetes. However, the role of autophagy in endothelial cells (ECs) in diabetes remains unclear. The present study aims to investigate the role of autophagic dysregulation in mediating endothelial dysfunction in diabetes. We found that autophagic flux was impaired in aortic endothelium from diabetic db/db mice and in renal arteries from diabetic patients. Impaired autophagic flux was also observed in ECs exposed to AGEs and ox-LDL. Defective autophagic flux contributed to overproduction of mitochondrial ROS, reduction in NO production, and impairment of endothelium-dependent relaxations. In addition, we found that the nuclear localization of TFEB, a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagic flux, was reduced in the endothelium of db/db mice. Adenoviral TFEB overexpression reversed the autophagic dysfunction, attenuated mtROS overproduction and restored endothelial function in db/db mice. The present results reveal that impaired autophagic flux contributes to endothelial dysfunction in DM, and restoration of TFEB-mediated autophagic flux may represent a potential therapeutic strategy for treating diabetic vasculopathy.

14124216.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14124216.value: We have set up a drug screen platform targeting TFEB in human endothelial cells aiming to identify activators of TFEB for further development into anti-diabetic and anti-atherosclerotic drugs.

14124216.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14124216.value: Our research clearly demonstrate that TFEB exerts anti-inflammatory effects in diabetic mice and such function in vascular endothelial cells is achieved by inhibiting IKK activity and increasing IκBα level to suppress NF-κB activity. In addition, KLF2 mediates TFEB upregulation in response to laminar flow, thus we established a functional link between KLF2 and TFEB. Furthermore, we reveal that impaired autophagic flux contributes to endothelial dysfunction in diabetes, and restoration of TFEB-mediated autophagic flux may represent a potential therapeutic strategy for treating diabetic vasculopathy. We are currently screening FDA-approved drug library hoping to identify some drugs which can activate TFEB in endothelial cells for further investigation of the potential drugs against diabetic vasculopathy and atherosclerotic vascular diseases.

14126016.label: Realisation of objectives
14126016.value: Objective one: To determine migration defects of Dom mutant sacral neural crest cells in vitro and during their pre-enteric migration in situ This objective has been fully achieved with the following experimental methods: (a) Neural tube explant culture coupled with time-lapse live cell phase-contrast microscopic imaging for studies of sacral neural crest cell (SNCC) migration in vitro: We successfully explanted intact and clean neural tubes at the sacral level (caudal to somite 24) from wild-type (Sox10+/+) and homozygous (Sox10Dom/Dom) mutant mouse embryos at Embryonic day (E) 9.5. The neural tube explants were cultured ex vivo with a specific medium containing EGF and FGF. After 24 hours, sacral neural crest cells (SNCCs) which were positive to neural crest cell markers Sox10, p75, Ednrb and Ret were found to emigrate from the explants and form an outgrowth area adjacent to each explant. With phase-contrast microscopic techniques, specific double or triple immunofluorescence staining, BrdU labelling, TUNEL staining and morphometric analyses, we were able to compare the numbers of emigrated SNCCs, the average SNCC migration distances, proliferation rates and apoptotic activities within the outgrowth areas derived from the wild-type (Sox10+/+) and homozygous Dom (Sox10Dom/Dom) neural tube explants. We then developed a time-lapse live cell imaging technique using a phase-contrast microscope and computer software to reconstruct 3-dimensional images. With this technique, we were able to determine the migration defects of SNCCs in vitro by recording and comparing in real time the migration morphology, speed, displacement and directionality of live wild-type and homozygous Dom SNCCs. (b) Whole mouse embryo culture coupled with specific cell labelling for studies of SNCC migration in situ: To determine the migration defects of SNCCs in situ, we used whole embryo culture after specific cell labelling of SNCCs. We first isolated intact whole mouse embryos with intact yolk sac and amniotic membranes from wild-type, heterozygous and homozygous Dom pregnant mice at E9.5, and then labelled the pre-migratory SNCCs (i.e. SNCCs prior to their emigration from the neural tube) with a vital dye (i.e. wheat germ agglutinin conjugated with gold particles or WGA-Au) by microinjection of the dye into the neural tube lumen. The whole mouse embryos with SNCCs labelled were cultured ex vivo for one to three days in a special culture medium consisting of rat serum. The embryos were then fixed and serially sectioned for immunofluorescence staining. The serial sections were examined under a confocal microscope, and the migration pathways of SNCCs were reconstructed in 3-dimensions with in-house computer software based on the spatiotemporal distribution of WGA-Au-labelled cells in the serial sections. With these methods, we were able to compare the pre-enteric migration (i.e. migration prior to entering the gut) of SNCCs in the wild-type, heterozygous and homozygous Dom mouse embryos at E9.5 to E13.5. To determine the proliferation and apoptotic activities of SNCCs in situ, we performed BrdU pulse labelling of SNCCs by injecting the label into pregnant mice at E9.5 and E10.5, and TUNEL staining with the serial transverse sections through the sacral region of mouse embryos at E9.5 and E10.5. (c) Specific triple immunofluorescence staining with confocal microscopy for studies of SNCC migration in the hindgut: To determine the migration defects of SNCCs in the hindgut of Dom embryos, we made use of triple immunofluorescence staining with whole mount preparations and serial sections using specific antibodies against neural crest cell markers p75, Sox10, Ret and Ednrb followed by confocal microscopy. Objective two: To determine the role of cadherin-19 in the defective migration of Dom mutant sacral neural crest cells With genome-wide microarray profiling and transcriptomic analysis, we found that the expression of cadherin-19 (Cdh19) was markedly down-regulated in Sox10Dom/Dom SNCCs as compared to their wild-type counterpart. In this part, we aimed to determine the role of Cdh19 in the defective migration of Dom mutant SNCCs. This objective has been fully achieved with the following experimental methods: (a) Luciferase reporter assay: To investigate whether Cdh19 is a direct downstream target of Sox10, we used the standard luciferase reporter assay. The potential Sox10 binding sites in the promoter of Cdh19 were cloned into pGL3-Basic plasmids carrying the luciferase sequence, which were then co-transfected with Sox10 plasmids into 293T cells. We found that Cdh19 could directly activate Sox10 expression. (b) Site-directed mutagenesis: To confirm the regulator-target relationship and to find out the critical binding sequences in the Cdh19 promoter, site-directed mutagenesis was used to construct a series of shortened promoters after deleting sequences of varying lengths from the distal end (5’ end) of the promoter. These deletion mutants were cloned into pGL3-Basic plasmids, which were then co-transfected with Sox10 plasmids into 293T cells to determine the luciferase activities of the deletion mutants. We identified the critical binding sequences for Sox10 in the Cdh19 promoter. (c) Chromatin Immunoprecipitation (ChIP) assay: To further confirm the relationship between Cdh19 and Sox10, we made use of ChIP. We first expressed Sox10-Flag fusion protein in NIH3T3 cells and then precipitated DNA-protein complexes with an anti-Flag antibody. The successful expression of the fusion protein 24 and 48 hours post-transfection was demonstrated by Western blot with an antibody against Flag and immunofluorescence staining with another antibody against Sox10. Once again, we confirmed that Sox10 was able to bind directly to the Cdh19 promoter. (d) Dual fluorescence in situ hybridization: As a specific anti-Cdh19 antibody has not been available yet due to the high homology of cadherin proteins, we used fluorescence in situ hybridization with whole mount preparations and serial sections using Alexa Fluor 488- and 555-labelled RNA probes to determine the spatiotemporal localization of Cdh19 expression. (e) Gain- and loss-of-function assays on SNCC primary culture: To determine whether Cdh19 is involved in regulating SNCC migration, we knocked down the expression of Cdh19 with lentiviral transfection of shRNAs into wild-type SNCCs in vitro (i.e. loss-of-function assay). We also re-expressed Cdh19 by transfecting the full-length Cdh19 into homozygous Dom SNCCs in vitro (i.e. gain-of-function assay). The knockdown and re-expression of Cdh19 were confirmed by real-time PCR and Western blot. With the Boyden transwell assay, we found that the migration abilities of SNCCs with Cdh19 knockdown was reduced whereas re-expression of Cdh19 partially restored the Dom SNCC migration ability. (f) Novel ex vivo electroporation with live mouse embryos: To determine the role of Cdh19 in regulating SNCC migration in situ, we knocked down the Cdh19 expression in SNCCs by electroporating siRNA oligos to live mouse embryos ex vivo. Normal mouse embryos at E9.5 were first isolated with intact extraembryonic membranes, and were then gently pulled out from the yolk sac through a small hole on the membranes without damaging major blood vessels. Two siRNA oligos targeting Cdh19, mixed with GFP plasmids which served as an indicator of successful transfection, were microinjected into the lumen of the neural tube at the sacral level (caudal to somite 24). Electroporation pulses were delivered, and the embryos were cultured for 24 hours. With this novel method, we successfully knocked down Cdh19 expression in SNCCs ex vivo. (g) Liquid chromatography and tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS): To ascertain molecularly how Cdh19 regulates SNCC migration, we used immunoprecipitation and proteomic analysis. Cdh19-Myc fusion proteins were expressed in NIH3T3 cells, and the proteins immunoprecipitated with an anti-Myc antibody were separated by SDS-PAGE, silver stained, determined by liquid chromatography and tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS), and then analyzed by Gene Ontology (GO).

14126016.label: Major findings and research outcome
14126016.value: The present study aimed to (1) determine the migration defects of sacral neural crest cells (SNCCs) in Dom mutant mice, an animal model of Hirschsprung’s disease where Sox10 is mutated, and also (2) identify downstream targets of Sox10 during SNCC migration. We found that SNCCs emigrated from the neural tube explant of Dom embryos showed tendency to aggregate with a reduced migration speed in vitro comparing to their wild-type counterparts. SNCCs in heterozygous and homozygous Dom embryos cultured ex vivo also showed a reduced ability to migrate. With genome-wide microarray profiling and transcriptomic analysis, we identified an adhesion molecule, namely cadherin-19 (Cdh19), which was markedly down-regulated in Dom SNCCs. We then demonstrated with in situ hybridization that Cdh19 expression was localized to normal migrating SNCCs where Sox10 was also expressed. Concomitant with the reduced migration of SNCCs in the Dom mutant with a Sox10 mutation, Cdh19 expression was down-regulated. In the primary culture of normal SNCCs, knockdown of Cdh19 expression led to a reduced ability of SNCCs to migrate. When siRNAs were electroporated to SNCCs to knock down Cdh19 expression in normal mouse embryos cultured ex vivo, SNCC migration was also reduced. Conversely, when a full length of Cdh19 was transfected to Dom SNCCs, their migration ability was partially restored. Hence our gain- and loss-of-function studies clearly indicated that Cdh19 regulated SNCC migration in vitro and ex vivo. To ascertain molecularly the relationship between Sox10 and Cdh19, we first used the dual luciferase reporter assay, and found that Sox10 activated directly Cdh19 expression. We then constructed different mutant Cdh19 promoters using site-directed mutagenesis, and successfully identified critical sequences for the binding of Sox10 to the Cdh19 promoter, indicating that Cdh19 was a direct target of Sox10. To determine the downstream molecular events after activation of Cdh19 expression by Sox10, we employed immunoprecipitation and LC-MS/MS to show that Cdh19 formed cadherin-catenin complexes which then interacted with β-actin, the most abundant protein in the filamentous actin (F-actin) of the cytoskeleton. In summary, this study demonstrated that Cdh19, a direct target of Sox10, modulated SNCC migration by forming cadherin-catenin complexes which in turn regulated the dynamic changes of the cytoskeleton during cell migration (see first publication in Part C.8). In the genome-wide search of migration-related molecules, we accidentally identified an adapter protein, namely Disabled-2, which was found to be a positive regular of early myoblast differentiation (see second publication in Part C.8).

14126016.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14126016.value: The following studies for further development of the research are suggested: (a) The availability of a specific anti-Cdh19 antibody is very crucial to further functional studies. We have tried to produce a specific antibody but in vain. A more specific amino acid sequence using computer software may be designed for the production of a specific monoclonal antibody by myeloma cells. (b) To study the roles of Cdh19 in the neural crest cell migration in vivo, a Cdh19 conditional knockout mouse line may be generated by crossing Sox10Cre/- and Cdh19flox/- transgenic mice. The phenotypes of the knockout mice and the knockdown effects on sacral NCCs can then be characterized. (c) Like sacral NCCs, vagal NCCs are also able to migrate long distances from the neural tube to the developing gut. It has been known that vagal NCCs are more able to colonize the developing gut as compared to sacral NCCs in the hindgut region, implying that vagal and sacral NCCs may have some intrinsic differences in their migration characteristics. Hence, it would be of interest to compare the roles of Cdh19 in migrating vagal and sacral NCCs using similar experimental approaches described in the present study.

14126016.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14126016.value: During early embryonic development, a special type of embryonic cells known as sacral neural crest cells (SNCCs) migrate into the developing gut and form enteric neurons and glia of the gastrointestinal tract. Defective migration of SNCCs may lead to deficiency of neurons in the gut, resulting in congenital gastrointestinal motility disorders such as Hirschsprung’s disease in humans. The present study aimed to determine the migration defects of SNCCs in the Dominant megacolon mutant (Dom), a mouse model of Hirschsprung’s disease with a Sox10 mutation, and identify important molecules that are involved in the normal migration of SNCCs in mouse embryos. We found that SNCCs in Dom embryos were less able to migrate to the gut as compared to normal SNCCs, although they could still migrate along the same pathway. Our genome-wide microarray profiling identified an adhesion molecule, namely cadherin-19 (Cdh19), the expression of which was down-regulated during the defective migration of Dom SNCCs. Alterations of Cdh19 expression and subsequent molecular analyses showed that Cdh19 regulated the SNCC migration by the direct binding of Sox10 to the promoter of Cdh19 to activate Cdh19 expression. Cdh19 then formed cadherin-catenin complexes to modulate the dynamic changes of the cytoskeleton during SNCC migration.

14126116.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14126116.value: The chloroplast is a type of plastids responsible for photosynthesis. Chloroplasts use solar energy to produce molecular oxygen and reduced carbon molecules that are critical for the survival of aerobic heterotrophs. The light energy is captured and converted into chemical energy by proteins and pigments localized in the thylakoid. The thylakoid consists of stacks of flat discs, the grana, and tubules that interconnect the stacks. This complex membrane system is assembled from proplastids in germinating seedlings or from etioplasts in greening tissue in response to light. Although the thylakoid is the defining structure of the chloroplast, we still do not understand how the elaborate membranous system is assembled in the stroma and what proteins are involved in the process. C4 plants concentrate carbon dioxide to cells capable of Calvin Cycle to suppress photorespiration. C4 species are especially suited to dry, hot climates and some of them, such as maize (corn), are important crop plants. Photosynthetic cells of C4 plants have two different types of chloroplasts in which thylakoids are differentially organized. Changes in mRNA and protein levels in developing maize leaf samples have been monitored. However, the structural intermediates that appear during the process of dimorphic chloroplast establishment in the maize leaf have not yet been investigated. In this proposed research, we will address these fundamental questions of chloroplast development by conducting three-dimensional (3D) electron microscopy. Our specific aims are to dissect the mechanism of thylakoid assembly in proplastids and etioplasts in Arabidopsis (C3 plant) and maize (C4 plant) using electron tomography (ET) and immuno-ET. Our comparative analysis of Arabidopsis and maize will allow us to unveil characteristics unique to C3 and C4 plants. The PI's lab has carried out ET analysis to characterize the macromolecular organizations of secretory organelles and their reorganizations in plant cells. In preparation for this chloroplast research, we have optimized electron microscopy protocols to determine the 3D chloroplast structure and to localize proteins with nanometer-level resolutions. Our research will uncover novel aspects related to how the photosynthetic compartment self-assembles in the chloroplast. Once completed, our study will provide stepping-stones for manipulating the photosynthetic activity machinery at the seedling stage, which may prove useful for weed control or for generating breeding markers. It is of interest to confer a C4 pathway to C3 plants to improve their photosynthetic efficiency. 14126116.label: Realisation of objectives
14126116.value: For Objective 1, we carried out electron tomography analysis of proplastids and etioplasts after the onset of their conversion to chloroplasts at multiple time points. In parallel, correlative transcriptomic analysis and immunogold labeling of proteins critical for the thylakoid assembly were performed. Using high-resolution 3D electron microscopy methods, we characterized macromolecular complexes and organelle membranes quantitatively at the nanometer level resolutions. For example, we measured ribosome densities from the thylakoid membrane to prove that ribosome binding is associated with membrane flattening. Locations of proteins were determined by immunogold labeling to propose a molecular mechanism of thylakoid morphogenesis. A diagram illustrating the mechanism was included in one of our papers. Our primary discovery was that photosystem to insertion in the membrane elements in proplastids transforms the tubular compartments into planar pre-granal thylakoids from which stacked membrane disks and interconnecting helical tubules are derived. We also have demonstrated that a dynamin-related protein, FZL, is required for the thylakoid membrane fusion to construct an organelle-wide network of the photosynthetic membranes. For objective 2, we performed similar electron tomography characterization of maize leaves from their basal zone where new leaf cells arise and to the tip where mature leaf cells accumulate. We monitored the diversification of bundle sheath and mesophyll chloroplast along the developmental gradient from the base to the tip and determined macromolecular compositions in the two types of chloroplasts. We delineated the process of dimorphic chloroplasts in the maize Kranz anatomy and operation of its dual cell C4 system from the results. Interestingly, the cytoplasmic conduit connecting the mesophyll and bundle sheath undergoes remodeling for stringent control of C4 metabolite movements. Since the C4 cycle runs in the direction and the concentration differences between the mesophyll and bundle sheath, it is critical to gate the channel to prevent reverse flow. This notion was tested with maize mutant lines in which enzymes mediating reactions of the C4 cycle are inactivated. During the leaf greening, chloroplasts grow and divide. As expected from their bacterial origin, chloroplasts proliferate by fission into two daughters. It is not understood how thylakoids are bisected in dividing chloroplasts. Proteins account for ~70% of the thylakoid membrane in which photosystem proteins and light-harvesting complexes constitute 2-dimensional crystals, and grana stacks comprise tall piles of membrane disks. These protein-rich membrane stacks pose obstacles in partitioning the thylakoid. However, almost nothing is known about the thylakoid division. While we were examining the chloroplast biogenesis, we stumbled upon dividing chloroplasts to capture thylakoids being severed before the envelope membranes were pinched in. The thylakoids located at the division plane were sharply kinked as if they were pre-processed for severing, and photosystem proteins retreated from the sites. We suppose that conventional TEM approaches did not uncover the division intermediates because the intricate membrane structures were degraded by harsh chemical fixation. Our samples were prepared by high-pressure freezing that immobilizes all types of molecules in the cell within milliseconds.

14126116.label: Major findings and research outcome
14126116.value: Objective 1 was to investigate chloroplast biogenesis in Arabidopsis. We elucidated the structural dynamics involved in the thylakoid assembly in cotyledon cells during germination. Molecular factors playing roles in the transformation of prothylakoids into granal thylakoids and thylakoid membrane fusion were identified. Objective 2 was for characterizing the development of dimorphic chloroplasts in the C4 maize Kranz anatomy. We determined the developmental gradient of the chloroplast in bundle sheath and mesophyll cells and delineated remodeling of the boundary between the two cell types that mediate transport of C4 metabolites. We published papers on the chloroplast biogenesis in C3 and C4 plants in the Plant Cell (Impact factor: 9.618), Scientific Reports (Impact factor: 3.998), and Frontiers in Plant Science (Impact factor: 4.407). One manuscript on the development of the maize leaf C4 system is under revision at the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America (Impact factor: 9.412), and another manuscript on image processing of 3D analysis for thylakoid membrane is under review at IEEE Transactions on Image Processing (Impact factor: 6.790). We have presented research outputs at the annual meetings of the American Society of Plant Biologists (2017 and 2019), international conferences (International Congress on Arabidopsis Research, The 3rd East-Asia Microscopy Conference), and domestic meetings (National Plant Cell Biology Congress, 3D electron microscopy conference on organelles and macromolecules, and so on). Two post-graduate students finished their Ph.D. program with the support from this grant. Besides, we had several visiting students from overseas under the summer undergraduate research program. We had five students from 2016 to 2019, who contributed to this chloroplast project. Furthermore, three students from the Chinese Agricultural University (Supervisor: Yongliang Zhang) came to my lab to characterize viral replication in the chloroplasts using the 3D electron microscopy setting on the CUHK campus.

14126116.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14126116.value: We described the membrane dynamics of chloroplast biogenesis and key factors playing roles in the assembly. However, there is much to be learned about its molecular mechanisms. The most intriguing part of chloroplast biogenesis is how thylakoids are severed. To bisect the protein-ridden membrane, it will take a large amount of energy and force-generating proteins. We do not have any information on the thylakoid cutting machinery. Another exciting aspect is the intergenomic coupling between the chloroplast and the nucleus. It turns out that photosystem II (PSII) is expressed and inserted into the thylakoid membrane before photosystem I (PSI). When we have carried out RNA-seq analysis of transcripts in the chloroplast and originated from the nucleus, transcripts for PSII from the two genomes appear simultaneously at earlier time points, and those for PSI became abundant later together, indicating that they are coregulated. This stepwise activation suggests more than one signaling molecules produce multiple sets of transcripts according to sequential gene expression. There have been several candidate molecules for the coupling, but almost nothing is known about their regulation by developmental stages. We will pursue these research directions in the future.

14126116.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14126116.value: The chloroplast does photosynthesis, capturing energy from the sun. Chemical energy stored in organic molecules, including food and fossil fuels, originates from photosynthesis. Chloroplasts have a specialized membrane compartment called thylakoid in which proteins and pigment for photosynthesis are embedded. The thylakoid is an intricate membrane network comprising stacks of membrane disks and interconnecting tubules. Chloroplasts arise from small and simple organelles in the seed termed proplastids during germination. It is not understood how the photosynthetic membranes assemble when proplastids mature into chloroplasts. With support from the GRF grant, we determined the key steps in the thylakoid assembly and identified crucial players. Corn plants have two types of chloroplasts to enhance photosynthetic yields and resist drought stress. They arise from a single type of chloroplasts. We have delineated the process involved in developing distinct chloroplasts and characterized the interface between leaf cells containing the chloroplasts. Using state-of-the-art three-dimensional electron microscopy methods, We documented previously unknown structures in growing chloroplasts with unprecedented accuracy. The information from our research provides insight into the membrane dynamics in eukaryotic organelle biogenesis. It will contribute to engineering chloroplasts in crop plants to prepare for climate change and global warming.
