14503416.label: Realisation of objectives
14503416.value: This project has successfully achieved the proposed objectives. First, this project has collected and constructed for Chinese firms including the Chinese customs trade data (2000-2011), the Annual Surveys of Manufacturing Enterprises (1998-2007), and the GIS geo-referenced information of firm address and highway routes (2000-2006). This database is not only useful for the current project, but also generates spillovers to several other ongoing projects and for PhD student thesis study. Second, this project has investigated the impact of highway networks on firms' exports by constructing two firm-level measures of highway access using GIS information on firm locations and highway routes: one is the shortest distance from each firm to the highway system, and the other is highway density around each firm. We find that improvement in highway access during 2000 and 2006 significantly promotes firms' exports, after controlling for firm characteristics in addition to unobservable city and industry time-varying factors. Highway access promotes Chinese firms’ exports to the global market, and also helps firms to expand the export scope and export intensity. More interestingly, the positive effects of highway access on exports are stronger for less productive firms. With greater highway access, less productive firms lower their markup, but more productive firms increase their markup. Firms in the inland regions or non-port cities benefit more from access to highways than other firms that are less dependent on highway transportation. Moreover, we also find that highway access helps firm to increase import scope but not import intensity. We did not find highway access has significant effects on firms’ TFP thus it is not the focus in the current paper. This project provides empirical evidence that infrastructure in particularly the highway transportation system is an important force of comparative advantage for Chinese firms in the global market. China’s experience in infrastructure investment and export growth provides an example for other developing countries, particular for countries along the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI). Based on this project, we are currently working on another project to evaluate the effect of the BRI on China’s trade and investment along countries along the Belt and Road. This project also suggests that infrastructure investment has significant spillover effects on firm exports, supporting the argument that public investment in infrastructure is one of the important channels that fiscal stimulus could boost the economy. As the infrastructure investment in China is largely from public finance, our project provides micro evidence for a significant government spending multiplier for infrastructure investment.

This data set can be the foundation for many other important topics such as how infrastructure reshapes industrial agglomeration, inter-regional trade, city growth, and pattern of migration.

The project will conduct the first systematic analysis on the impact of the massive investment in infrastructure in China on firm performance. In particular, we will study how the transportation network in China helps domestic firms to export and import, and also improves firm productivity.

We will explore the heterogeneous effect of transportation infrastructure on different types of firms. One particular question is which types firms benefit more from the improvement of transportation network.

Our analysis will have important policy implications, particular for the government new initiative for globalization: “One Belt and One Road”. Our analysis can cast the light on the question how infrastructure improves market integration within China and thus helps firms go globally.

This project also provides micro evidence for the government spending multiplier. Public investment in infrastructure is one of the important channels that fiscal stimulus could boost the economy. However, most of studies focus on macro level analysis and our study can provide micro-evidence for the effect of infrastructure investment on firms output and productivity.

14503416.label: Major findings and research outcome
14503416.value: This project shows that the improvement in highway access promotes Chinese firms’ performance in global market. We find that improvement in highway access during 2000 and 2006 significantly promotes firms' exports, after controlling for firm characteristics in addition to unobservable city and industry time-varying factors. Highway access promotes firms’ exports to the global market, and also helps firms to expand the export scope and export intensity. More interestingly, the positive effects of highway access on exports are stronger for less productive firms. With greater highway access, less productive firms lower their markup, but more productive firms increase their markup. Moreover, we also find that highway access helps firm to increase import scope but not import intensity. Based on those results, we have finished a working paper titled with “Highways and Firms’ Exports: Evidence from China”. We have presented this paper in many prestigious international conference such as SAET 2018 and FREIT 2018 in Japan, and this paper is under preparation for journal submission. More importantly, this project constructed a database for Chinese firms including the Chinese customs trade data (2000-2011) , the Annual Surveys of Manufacturing Enterprises (1998-2007), and the GIS geo-referenced information of firm address and highway routes (2000-2006). Based on the Chinese customs trade data, we have finished another working paper “Did the Rising Labor Cost Erode China's Global Competitiveness?” which examines the effect of rising labor cost (from the minimum wage) on China’s export competitiveness and the country’s attraction for multinational production. This paper currently is revised and resubmitted to Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization. Moreover, one of my PhD student Shi-Ting He is also using this dataset for her dissertation, in which she tried to evaluate the effect of the opening of new China’s international air routes on firms’ exports and imports. This is also part of my research agenda on evaluating the impact of infrastructure improvement on Chinese firms’ performance in the global market. She has successfully shown that air access helps firms to export more, particularly for those products that use air shipping intensively. Moreover, air access also helps firms to acquire information of market demand. Currently we have done most of empirical analysis and we will be able to finish a working paper soon.

14503416.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14503416.value: For further development, we will first try to publish the two working papers: “Highways and Firms’ Exports: Evidence from China”, and “Did the Rising Labor Cost Erode China's Global Competitiveness?”. Meanwhile, we will continue the project on air routes and firm export and import performance. Based on this project, currently I am also working on the project titled with “Investment and Trade Along the Belt and Road,” with Prof. Zheng Huanhuan in NUS and Prof. Jing Zhao in Wuhan University. This project aims to examine the effectiveness of One Belt One Road Initiatives (BRI), with a focus on China’s outward direct investment (ODI) and international trade. We conduct a difference in difference (DID) analysis on both Chinese ODI and trade using the classic gravity equation. We collect detailed data on Chinese ODI (both greenfield and M&A) at the project level as well as Chinese export and import at the HS8 product level for 15 years (2003-2017). We find the BRI has a positive effect in boosting Chinese greenfield ODI to countries involved in BRI (BR countries), especially in the infrastructure sector, and it also promotes Chinese exports to BR countries.

14503416.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14503416.value: Transportation infrastructure plays a key role in economic growth. The poor transportation network in less developed countries has been a major barrier for trade expansion and economic development. Business leaders, policy makers, and academics all consider transportation infrastructure as a critical stimulus for firm growth and economic development. However, much less is known about how transportation networks affect firms' performance in the global market. This paper provided new firm-level evidence on how highways promote firms' exports, drawing experience from a fast-growing economy, China, during the episode of rapid trade expansion and dramatic improvement of transportation infrastructure in the country. The paper's main empirical innovation is to construct a measure of highway access at the firm level, by using GIS information on firms' addresses and highway routes during 2000-06 in China, measured as the highway density in the area centered at each firm with the baseline radius of 20 kilometers (km). We find that better access to highways helps firms to expand the scope of their exports and imports. More interestingly, we find that less productive firms benefit more in promoting exports from the improvement of highway access than more productive firms.

14504716.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14504716.value: 隨著團隊合作日益興盛，理解團隊有效運作的關鍵要求變得十分重要。儘管有效的團隊協作取決於很多因素，其中一個因素是團隊斷裂帶的力量。斷裂帶是一種團隊的組成模式，指由於成員的特質互相重合，團隊中傾向于產生由相似成員組成的子團隊(Lau & Murnighan, 1998; 2005)。團隊斷裂帶很強時，子團隊的自我認同很可能變得顯著；尤其當出現與子團隊差異有關的問題時，子團隊之間的衝突就會頻繁發生。結果導致團隊協作變得效率低下，並伴隨著低水平的團隊績效和成員滿意度。 強團隊斷裂帶的不利影響已經得到一致廣泛的證實(Thatcher & Patel, 2011)。它能夠作用與一系列不同類型的團隊，包括特定實驗團隊，固定組織團隊，高層管理團隊，全球虛擬團隊，國際合資企業，以及戰略聯盟。大量的不利影響顯示需找到一些解決辦法，即使不能完全消除，但是至少能夠減弱這些不良效應。現有文獻已發現一些有效措施，但是這些措施都是基於不同視角的特定方法，因此需要對斷裂帶的解決方法進行系統研究。 爲了回應這一問題，我們考查團隊結構和團隊文化在減弱團隊斷裂帶力量不利影響中所起的作用。基於近期形成的團隊類型分類(Hollenbeck, Beersma, & Schouten, 2012)，我們提出權力分化和臨時穩定性是兩個潛在的減弱因素。當團隊的權力出現高度分化，一個人（經理）做出大部分決策時，子團隊的重要性就會降低。不穩定的臨時團隊，由於團隊成員頻繁變化的特點，子團隊的界限被持續打破，因此斷裂帶的影響傾向與被減弱。除了團隊類型，另外一個潛在的因素是工作相互依賴，即成員的工作輸入對其他成員工作產出的依賴程度。當工作互相獨立時，我們不認爲斷裂帶會產生作用，因爲工作績效和決策不依賴與同事，成員不需要從其他人那裏獲得支持來成功地完成工作。子團隊儘管存在，但是傾向于不明顯。 文化，“人類思維的集體運作” (Hofstede, 1980, p. 25)，設定了團隊運作的情境以及對團隊成員可接受行爲的期望。匹配團隊結構和文化將使相應的解決方法得到合法化和強化。特別地，我們提出集體主義文化能夠促進工作相互依賴，而高權力距離文化能夠使權力分化合法化。 我們通過在實驗和在工作場所中進行調查，來理解這三個結構性解決方案，即高權力分化，低暫時穩定性和工作互相依賴對團隊斷裂帶不利影響的潛在減弱效果。實驗將會在香港、中國和美國三個具有不同集體主義和權力距離水平的地區展開。研究發現將會指引我們找到更有效的管理工具。當強團隊斷裂帶不可避免出現時，管理人員能夠運用這些工具來處理團隊問題。

14504716.label: Realisation of objectives
14504716.value: In the proposal, we suggest to study the stated research objectives through two methods: surveys in two cities in China where diverse cultural settings are expected and experiments to be conducted in three different places, including Hong Kong, China, and USA. Based on our proposed theoretical model, we collected time-lagged and multi-source survey data from three companies in different provinces and cities in China, including Shandong, Shanghai, and Shenzhen throughout 2017 and 2018. These organizations varied in terms of ownership (state-owned vs. private), size (1,000 to over 60,000 employees), and industries. We collected survey data from a total of over 400 employees in about 90 teams. In the first phase of the survey, the respondents reported their personal information, including demographics, personality and values, and group structure, including authority differentiation, temporal stability, and task interdependence. In the second phase, respondents reported their perceptions of group processes, including group conflict. Finally, leaders were invited to report team performance in the third phase. In general, the time lag between each phase was about 1 month. Besides collection survey data, we have designed and conducted experiments since 2017. We made several attempts to design and operationalize the three team structure constructs – authority differentiation, temporal stability, and task interdependence. Through many trials, we have finally decided on the manipulation of each team structure construct and pilot tested them in Hong Kong. We have also written a detailed protocol for subsequent sharing with our potential partner schools in US and China. The co-I applied for IRB approval at her school in USA. Until now, we have collected a total of 100 trials in Hong Kong. Our target was 120 trials and we were 20 trials short of our original target. The co-I conducted the same experiment in US after receiving the IRB approval. In US, the co-I has collected 84 trials and we were 36 trials short of our target of 120. Our biggest challenge was the COVID-19 situation which prevented us from conducting face-to-face experiments. In particular, our participants were required to work closely with each other in building the lego products. Social distancing requirements in both Hong Kong and USA has stopped us from conducting more experiments. We have considered other options such as changing the data collection method and the research sites. However, these options had their challenges. The purpose of the experiments was to establish causal relationship between our predictors and dependent variables. Other methodologies would not serve this purpose. In addition, we have considered changing our research site from US to another country with an individualistic culture. This option is challenging as the COVID-19 situation was similar across many countries in the world and re-establishing all the experiment protocols and hiring appropriate RAs to run the experiments would be costly. The remaining amount of money left in the grant did not allow us to do so. Consequently, we chose to go with our original plan while waiting for the COVID situation to become better. Up to now, we are not able to conduct any more experiment and we have already started to clean and analyze the data, submit our findings to conferences and journals. Although we are not able to collect the expected number of experimental trials, we are able to complete the research objectives, as originally planned. The survey data allowed us to examine the relationship between group structure, including task interdependence, authority differentiation, and temporal stability, group faultline strength, and various group processes and outcomes in a field setting. In addition, our experimental trials in Hong Kong and USA provided us with data covering the effects of group structure, including task interdependence, authority differentiation, and temporal stability in a controlled setting. With the data collected from these two complementary methods, we realized objective 1 in understanding the relationship between group structure, group faultline, and group processes and outcomes. In realizing objective #2, we learnt from our survey data as we have measured various cultural factors, including power distance and collectivism. Although the survey data was only collected from organizations in China, we found some variance among these cultural variables so that we were able to study their impact on groups with various faultline strength and group processes and outcomes. Our experimental data provided a direct comparison between teams in two different cultures: Hong Kong and USA. We measured respondents’ perception of cultural backgrounds and studied whether the group faultline effects were different in these two places. Although the sample size in both places was short of expectation, we were able to conduct the necessary analyses with limited power. In realizing objective #3, we also relied on the data collected from the survey and the experiments in Hong Kong and USA. From the survey data, we conducted interaction analyses between group structure and cultural variables in understanding their impact on group processes and outcomes. From the experimental data, we compared the effects of group structural factors between the Hong Kong and USA data. Because we have 3 structural factors, we used a 2x2x2 factorial design. Unfortunately, our data were not evenly distributed among 8 cells and our analyses focused on the cells where we had sufficient data. Besides the survey and experimental data, we also examined other datasets that were collected in other contexts to enrich our exploration of the 3 stated objectives. For instance, we have gained access to a sample of start-up teams in the Hong Kong setting where it reflected some unique group structural characteristics and the Chinese setting. We were able to examine some group structure and cultural effects in this particular sample. In addition, my previous PhD student, Su Qin, was trained using the funding from this grant. She developed her doctoral thesis regarding power-based faultline in China. In China, the power distance is large and power is a salient characteristic. She found that power was a relevant faultline attribute but the faultline compositional patterns was different from the demographic attribute-based faultline. This finding reflected the unique manifestations of faultline composition and effects in particular cultures. Finally, we conducted qualitative analyses of a dataset of interview scripts to gain deeper understanding of the effects of cultural factors in faultline effects. Given the limitation in our sample size in the experimental study, we would like to complement the findings with our learnings from some interview data from a diverse list of Chinese organizations. In this study, we asked why Chinese scholars and practitioners did not view diversity or faultline as important factors in managing team processes and outcomes while North American and European organizations often identified diversity and / or faultline as essential predictors of group conflict, information elaboration, and team performance. Building on foundations of the survey and the experimental datasets and adding on the findings from the data sets mentioned above, we were able to complete the proposed objectives. While it will be better if we could collect more experimental data, given the COVID situation, we tried our best to collect as much data as we could to complete the proposed studies.

14504716.label: Major findings and research outcome
14504716.value: Consistent faultline effects were found among various types of Chinese organizations (Part C 8.1-8.4; 9.1-9.4). We studied new venture teams (8.1), teams from state-owned companies (8.3) and private companies (8.2, 8.3, 9.3), and student teams (8.4 & 9.4) This finding demonstrates the relevance of studying faultline in China, regardless of its unique cultural characteristics when compared to North America and Europe. In terms of faultline attributes, Chinese employees recognize many of the demographic attributes as relevant components of faultlines, including gender, age, education level, tenure, and personality. In addition, they reported that provincial origin, work experience in international corporations and school location (local vs. overseas) as relevant faultline attributes (8.2). This findings suggest that whether employees have prior experience or exposure to the western influence, education or work, is an important characteristic in identifying similar or different others in terms of work values and cultures. In addition, we found that power is a relevant faultline attribute in China (9.2). This is an interesting finding as Chinese culture can be described as one with high power distance and it is not surprising that employees view power as a salient faultline attribute. Different from the demographic-based faultline, the composition of power faultline is different. Instead of forming faultline on a similar attraction basis, power faultline aligns with power centers, i.e., each subgroup has a high-power leader and some low-power followers. Power faultline strength depends on the divergence of power within subgroups (rather than similarity among subgroup member attributes) and the similarity of power between subgroup leaders (rather than differences between subgroup members). Among the various proposed group structure effects, we found that temporal stability has intriguing effects in faultline groups. We found that unstable groups actually benefitted new and strong faultline teams by reducing conflict and increasing performance growth (8.4 & 9.4). However, this was not found among established faultline teams. Instead, temporally unstable teams with strong faultline experienced a stronger and negative relationship of team conflict and performance. In terms of work cultures, we found that Chinese employees were usually conflict avoiding (9.2). As faultline was prone to conflict, employees were not comfortable discussing diversity or faultline. In addition, faultline-related conflict tend to be resolved by strong and powerful leaders, rather than among team members. These findings enhance our understanding of the salience of faultline discussions, or lack of, in China, despite of its consistent effects (as discussed earlier).

14504716.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14504716.value: Our findings suggest a few potential directions for further research. First, our sample size, especially the experimental studies, was limited given the COVID challenges. We are not sure whether our lack of results regarding some structural factors, such as task interdependence or authority differentiation, was due to an irrelevant choice of variables or a lack of statistical power in our analyses. When face-to-face experiments become available, it will be helpful to replicate these studies and verify. Second, our effects of temporal stability are intriguing and worth replicating. Our findings suggest that temporal instability may be helpful in new teams while detrimental in established teams. This finding opens up a new line of enquiry about the effects of member compositional change in teams which can be both interesting and relevant in team-oriented work settings. Finally, power-based faultline is a newly developed idea. We identified its existence and effects in China but were not sure about its corresponding effects in low power distance cultures. Also, in addition, to power-based faultlines, there may be other culture-related faultline attributes which are worth exploring.

14504716.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14504716.value: Group faultline refers to a special group compositional pattern where members align based on one or more personal attributes so that subgroups tend to evolve in the group processes. Thus, groups with strong faultline are prone to within-group conflict and thus worse group performance. Although this relatively new concept was introduced in the North American context, we found consistent evidence that its effects also exists in China. With different cultural values, Chinese faultline groups are found to be characterized in terms of demographic attributes, which are similar to those in the western context, as well as unique Chinese attributes such as province, overseas experience, and power. Special cultural background, such as conflict avoidance and the importance of leadership, play an important role in understanding faultline effects. Moreover, we also found that special group structure, such as temporal stability (whether group memberships are stable throughout time), will also affect faultline effects, depending on whether the teams are new or established. Our findings shed light on group compositional effects beyond the western context, including North America and Europe and enable researchers and practitioners in understanding how to manage teams in a more effective manner.

14505416.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14505416.value: An experience good or a service can only after purchase and use be judged by consumers as to whether it meets their needs and is worth the price. Hence the usage experience greatly affects consumer purchase (and repurchase) decisions. Meanwhile, advertising that helps diffuse product information also plays a pivotal role in the consumer purchase decision of an experience good or a service. In this project, we develop dynamic advertising competition models where firms (brands) sell an experience good (or a service) with heterogeneous price and quality. The exact product quality is not observable by consumers. Consumers make purchase decisions based on their past usage experience of the product and the advertising outlays of the firms. In particular, they exhibit the following switching behavior: buy another brand when experiencing dissatisfaction with the present brand. So we call them {it switching consumers}. We develop the firms' decision model that integrates such purchase behavior. We then characterize the steady-state equilibrium advertising strategies and market shares of the firms under two market structures: duopoly market and fragmented market (a large number of firms). We examine how each firm's equilibrium advertising strategy and market share are affected by the switching behavior of consumers as well as its price and product quality. Comparisons of equilibrium solutions between these two types of market are conducted to unveil the impact of market structure. We also study another type of consumers, those who react to satisfactory experience ({it brand-loyal consumers}) and analyze the firms' advertising strategies. The equilibrium outcomes under brand-loyal consumers are expected to differ from those under switching consumers and so insights about the impact of different consumer switching behaviors can be investigated. In particular, we identify scenarios when the firms prefer selling to one type of consumer rather than the other. Finally, the model and analysis are extended to cases where consumer experience has a longer reinforcement effect. 消費者對於後驗品或者服務是否滿意，往往需要購買並且使用之後才能確定。因此，消費者對產品的使用體驗將大大影響消費者的購買（和再次購買）行爲。與此同時，企業對其產品的廣告投放，因爲有助於產品信息的傳播和擴散，同樣對消費者的購買決策有著很重要的影響。 本項目致力於研究後驗品（或服務）市場的企業閒的廣告競爭。市場上的企業銷售不同品牌的同一後驗品。這些品牌的質量和價格各不相同，但是消費者對這些品牌的質量不能進行準確的評估。消費者基於自己對產品過去的使用體驗以及企業的廣告投入做出購買選擇。特別地，消費者有如下的選擇行爲：如果對於當前使用的品牌不滿意，下個階段她將轉換到另一品牌；否則她會基於商傢的廣告投入決定購買哪個品牌。我們稱有此類行爲的消費者為轉換型消費者。我們構建了考慮上述消費者行爲的動態廣告競爭模型，刻畫了商傢的穩態均衡廣告策略及它們相應的市場份額。我們重點考慮兩種市場結構：雙寡頭壟斷市場和分散型市場（商傢的數量大，市場份額分散）。我們研究消費者的轉換行爲對商傢的均衡廣告投入和市場份額的影響，以及品牌的質量和價格對其均衡廣告投入和市場份額的影響。通過比較這兩個市場結構下的結果，我們給出了市場結構對商傢廣告競爭的影響。 我們還進一步考慮了另外一種類型的消費者，她們的選擇更多的被她們對產品的滿意的體驗而不是不滿意的體驗所影響（我們稱其為品牌忠實消費者）。同樣，我們將刻畫在面對該種消費者下企業的穩態均衡廣告策略。 儅企業面對品牌忠實消費者，我們預期其廣告競爭的均衡結果將和轉換型消費者的結果有所不同。因此，我們從中可以研究不同的消費者轉換行爲對於企業廣告競爭的影響。特別地，我們將研究在何種情況下，商傢更願意面對轉換型消費者，而何種情況下更願意面對品牌忠實消費者。最後，我們將把模型和分析拓展到消費者的選擇行爲受到其以往多期的產品體驗所影響的情形。

14505416.label: Realisation of objectives
14505416.value: All the objectives listed above about the project have been achieved. In particular, we model how consumers react to their purchase experience at stores and the resulting consumer choice behavior among multiple competing stores. Building on the behavior models, we further developed advertising competition models where the stores decide their advertising outlays to compete in the market. By solving equilibrium advertising strategies and market shares of the stores under different consumer switching behaviors, we examined the effects of consumer satisfaction under different market structures and consumer behaviors. In the duopoly, we show that the store with a higher profit margin spends more on advertising; a store's profit is not necessarily increasing in its own satisfaction probability; and the store with higher satisfaction probability prefers more loyals whereas the store with lower satisfaction probability prefers more switchers. We also investigate the existence of the perverse equilibrium by incorporating the service quality levels of the stores into the model parameters. We then studied the case with more than two competing stores under two market structures---the symmetric market and the fragmented market. One interesting finding for the symmetric market is that the switchers are always preferred. Meanwhile, for the fragmented market, we showed that the effect of customer satisfaction on the equilibrium outcomes is negligible for the switchers, and thus, similar as the duopoly, the stores with higher (lower) satisfaction probability prefer more loyals (switchers). We also conducted numerical studies to illustrate our main findings and discuss additional insights. In another related paper, we study a multilocation newsvendor model with a retailer owning multiple retail stores, each of which is operated by a manager who decides the order quantity for filling random customer demand of a product. The store managers and the retailer are all risk-averse while the managers are more risk-averse than the retailer. We adopt conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) as the performance measure and consider two alternative strategies to improve the performance of the system. First, the retailer centralizes the ordering decisions. Second, the managers still decide the order quantity for their own store whereas their inventories are pooled together. We analyze and compare the optimal order quantities and the resulting CVaR values of the systems and study their comparative statistics. For centralization, we find that each store has a higher inventory level in the centralized system than in the decentralized system, and centralization brings positive benefits to the retailer as long as some store manager(s) is strictly more risk-averse than the retailer. When there is inventory pooling, the ordering decisions in the decentralized system depend on how the additional profit from pooling is allocated among the stores. We consider a weighted proportional allocation rule and characterize the Nash equilibrium of the resulting ordering game among the store managers. Our key finding is that as long as the store managers are sufficiently more risk-averse than the retailer or the demands are very heavy-tailed, inventory pooling brings less benefit than centralization. We further derive a lower bound on the value of centralization and two upper bounds on the value of inventory pooling. Finally, our analytical results are illustrated using a data set from an online retailer in China and various comparative statics are further examined via extensive numerical experiments.

14505416.label: Major findings and research outcome
14505416.value: This project generates three papers, one under revision, two accepted. The one under revision is titled” Customer Satisfaction, Advertising Competition, and Store Performance.” In this paper, we study how customer satisfaction affects stores' advertising competition and their equilibrium market shares and profits. In the duopoly, we show that the store with a higher profit margin spends more on advertising; a store's profit is not necessarily increasing in the probability that customers would be satisfied with their experience of the store; and the store with higher satisfaction probability prefers more loyals whereas the store with lower satisfaction probability prefers more switchers. We then study the case with more than two competing stores under two market structures---the symmetric market and the fragmented market. One interesting finding for the symmetric market is that the switchers are always preferred. Meanwhile, for the fragmented market, we show that the effect of customer satisfaction on the equilibrium outcomes is negligible for the switchers, and thus, similar as the duopoly, the stores with higher (lower) satisfaction probability prefer more loyals (switchers). The paper titled “Multilocation Newsvendor Problem: Centralization and Inventory Pooling” is recently accepted by Management Science. In this paper, we study a multilocation newsvendor model with a retailer owning multiple retail stores, each of which is operated by a risk-averse manager who decides the order quantity for filling random customer demand of a product. We use CVaR as the risk measure and examine two alternative strategies: centralization and inventory pooling, which could help improve the system performance. Our key finding is that as long as the store managers are sufficiently more risk-averse than the retailer or the demands are very heavy-tailed, inventory pooling brings less benefit than centralization. We further derive a lower bound on the value of centralization and two upper bounds on the value of inventory pooling. Finally, our analytical results are illustrated using a data set from an online retailer in China and various comparative statics are further examined via extensive numerical experiments. The third paper titled “Trade-in for Cash or for Upgrade? Dynamic Pricing with Customer Choice” is accepted by POMS. In this paper, we consider a firm who offers both trade-in for cash and trade-in for upgrade options to acquire old products, then refurbishes and resells them, together with new product over a finite selling horizon. When the selling price of new product is exogenous, we derive the optimal trade-in prices of old product and resale price of refurbished product. We show that the optimal trade-in and resale policies are of a threshold-type and trade-in-for-upgrade should be offered with a premium refund (compared to trade-in-for-cash) only in early periods of the selling horizon. We further consider two variants of the above base model.

14505416.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14505416.value: We investigate how customer satisfaction affects stores' advertising competition and their equilibrium market shares and profits. We examine a market with multiple competing online stores. A customer chooses the store that gives him or her the highest utility which depends on his or her experience of the last purchase and on the advertising outlays of the stores. There are two types of customers in the market: loyals and switchers, who react differently to their past purchasing experience. Each store sets its advertising outlay to maximize its long-term average profit per period. In the duopoly, we show that the store with a higher profit margin spends more on advertising; a store's profit is not necessarily increasing in its own satisfaction probability; and the store with higher (lower) satisfaction probability prefers more loyals (switchers). We then study the case with more than two competing stores under two market structures---the symmetric market and the fragmented market. One interesting finding for the symmetric market is that the switchers are always preferred. Meanwhile, for the fragmented market, we show that the effect of customer satisfaction on the equilibrium outcomes is negligible for the switchers, and thus, similar as the duopoly, the stores with higher (lower) satisfaction probability prefer more loyals (switchers). As nowadays consumers are harder to please and place more reliance on their experience with the good/service when making purchase decisions than before, gaining deeper knowledge about their purchasing behavior so as to make decisions effectively would certainly be a competitive advantage for firms. The findings of the project can help advance the understanding of the impact of consumer satisfaction and switching behavior on stores’ advertising strategies.

14507416.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14507416.value: A fundamental question concerning shareholder activism is whether it improves firm value. Since 1942, when the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) changed its rules to allow institutional investors, particularly mutual funds and pension funds, to submit proposals, shareholder activism has become a widely adopted corporate governance mechanism. Prior studies in this area have been conducted under the assumption that shareholders’ utility-maximizing decisions coincide with firm value maximization, which is the essence of the Fisher Separation Theorem (Fisher, 1929; Fama and Miller, 1972; DeAngelo, 1981). For example, Brav et al. (2008) find an abnormal return around the announcement of hedge fund activism of around 7%, suggesting that activist hedge funds are informed monitors that can create value. We explore shareholder activism when the Fisher Separation Theorem is violated. That is, when activism generates private benefits to the activist but costs that are borne by all shareholders. Specifically, we examine whether the activism of “customer shareholders” — investors that simultaneously hold equities in, and purchasing products from, the same company — influence the actions of the company in the product market. We are specifically interested in how U.S. public pension funds that provide health care to their beneficiaries take actions to reduce drug prices, and therefore their own liabilities, through forcing brand-name pharmaceutical companies not to preclude generic manufacturers from the market. Since the Hatch-Waxman Act in 1984, generic drug approvals from the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) have been expedited and streamlined. In this increasingly competitive environment, to prevent their revenues from “falling off a patent cliff,” brand manufacturers leverage various instruments to deter, or delay, the entry of generic manufacturers. The higher drug prices resulting from blocked generic entries increases the liabilities of public pension funds. However, these pension funds often holding significant equity stakes, thereby allowing them to exert influence on brand companies. We use unique datasets and novel empirical strategies to answer the following questions. First, to what event can the brand’s exploitation of current legal and patent systems to deter generic entry be blocked by pension fund activism? Second, through which explicit channels do pension funds influence the management team of brand drug manufacturers? Third, how do pension funds hedge cash flow risks of brand stocks if a generic entry is successful? Addressing these questions will contribute to a better understanding of the value implication of shareholder activism in the presence of a conflict of interest among shareholders. 增加投資者的活躍度是否提高了公司價值？在投資者效用最大化和公司價值最大化一致的假設前提下， 前人的研究認為投資者的活躍度提高了公司價值。本課題提出以下問題：如果提高某些投資者效用的成本需要所有股東承擔，以上結論是否成立？一個例子是投資者同時購買本公司的商品。作為公司客戶，此類投資者可能用其投票權降低公司產品的價格。比如，養老保險基金是美國專利藥公司的客戶。這些基金是如果通過對專利藥公司的干預來促進仿製藥公司進入市場，從而降低藥品價格的？養老基金要為基金收益人的醫藥費買單，它們理所應當希望通過價低藥價來減輕自己的財務負擔。 本研究利用獨特的數據來回答以下問題。第一，專利藥公司是如何利用法律和專利體系的漏洞來抵禦仿製藥的進入的？養老保險基金是如何來抵禦專利藥的入侵？第二，養老保險基金通過哪些手段來干預專利藥公司的管理層？第三，因為專利藥在仿製藥的入侵後利潤會下滑，養老保險公司如何對沖此類風險的？回答這些問題可以幫助我們更好地理解當投資者之間存在利益衝突時投資者活躍度和公司價值是怎樣的關係。

14507416.label: Major findings and research outcome
14507416.value: Brand-name pharmaceutical companies often file lawsuits against generic drug manufacturers that challenge the monopoly status of patent-protected drugs. Institutional horizontal shareholdings, measured by the generic shareholders' ownership in the brand-name company relative to their ownership in the generic manufacturer, are significantly positively associated with the likelihood that the two parties enter into a settlement agreement in which the brand pays the generic manufacturer to stay out of the market. Horizontal shareholdings are also positively associated with the brand's daily abnormal stock returns around the settlement agreement. Generic manufacturers who settle with the brand-name company are more likely to delay the sale of generic substitutes if they have higher horizontal shareholdings with the brand-name firm. These delays preclude other generic firms from entering the market.

14508616.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14508616.value: The capital misallocation among firms has been an important issue during the China’s economic growth. Especially, after the 2008 financial crises, capital misallocations between sectors with government support and market-oriented private sectors are amplified by massive stimulate package. In this project, we intend to investigate two important questions. First, how this structural problem affects the transmission mechanism and the effeteness of China’s monetary policy, and capital flow and the choice of exchange rate policy; Secondly, if Chinese economy continues to slow down, is there any room for fiscal simulation again? If so, what should the monetary policy do? To address these issues, we will develop a two-sector sticky price small open economy model with capital misallocation, which is driven mainly by uneven fiscal policy between sectors. We will conduct rigorous quantitative analysis under this framework and provide possible policy suggestion. Our preliminary results show that expansionary monetary policy may have adverse effect, depending on the degree of capital misallocation or fiscal distortion and the across-border capital flow. This implies that stimulating effects of fiscal policy might be exaggerated, which is at the expense of the ineffectiveness of monetary policy.

14508616.label: Realisation of objectives
14508616.value: In view of the increasing importance of China in the global economy, the global policy circle and market paid more attention to China macro policy, especially monetary policy. However, there are very few studies on Chinese monetary policy. For instance, Chang, Liu, and Spiegel (2015) study optimal monetary policy in a dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) model that incorporates Chinese characteristics. They highlight a trade-off between domestic policy stability and costly sterilization. Chen, Ren and Zhan (2018) study how monetary policy in China influences banks' shadow banking activities. These studies examine China's monetary policy from the angle of financial system. In addition to the frictions in financial system, capital misallocation among firms, especially, between SOE and private firms is crucial to the conduct of monetary policy and its effectiveness. Capital misallocation among firms have been important issues during the China's economic growth. Hsieh and Klenow (2009) find that the aggregate TFP (total factor productivity) loss in China due to resource misallocation is of an magnitude from 30 to 50 percent. Following their work, Song and Wu (2014) estimate that capital misallocation alone may reduce aggregate TFP in China by 20 percent in late 2000s. In this paper, we intend to investigate how the existing capital misallocation problem affect the transmission mechanism of monetary shock in China, and in particular, the effectiveness of monetary policy. Furthermore, we would like to explore what the monetary policy would be in face of financial shocks that affect capital allocation among firms. To address these issues, we develop a full-fledged DSGE sticky-price model featured capital misallocation to investigate the transmission mechanism of monetary shock and the choice of monetary policy. To make our model better characterize Chinese economy, we document several stylized facts that related to monetary policy in China, including excess money supply, indirect financing (bank loan), ineffective monetary simulation, and mixed monetary policy. Based on these facts, we build a full-fledged DSGE monetary model with banking's portfolio choice, capital misallocation among firms, and endogenous entry of FDI flow. We use real financial assets (money supply, loan, bond ) data to calibrate the model. The are two major findings in our quantitative model. First, we show that capital misallocation does reduce the response of output to a cut in policy rate, and this effect is quantitatively substantial if the technology difference between SOE and private firms are considered.Secondly, we find that even with productivity shock and endogenous monetary policy such as inflation targeting, capital misallocation among firms can still have nontrivial negative impact on output. Overall, results in our paper can help to explain the excess liquidity and the ineffectiveness of monetary policy in China. Overall, this project has fully achieved the first objective in the original proposal. However, for the second objective that explore the interaction between fiscal policy and monetary policy, we only partially achieved this object. There are two reasons for under-achievement along this dimension. First, when we discuss the project with experts in the field, all the feedback suggests us focus on monetary policy first. Our current model has incorporated rich Chinese characteristics, including bank sectors, state-owned enterprise, and foreign direct investors. Therefore, we should no consider endogenous fiscal policy. Instead, we should take the fiscal policy as exogenous institutional arrangement. Secondly, as discussed in Wu (2015), both policy distortion including fiscal policy and financial frictions are important for capital misallocations. In our project, we consider a shock to financing cost of private firms. This shock represents all the distortion in the economy that may affect capital allocation. Therefore, our project has some results on how monetary policy responds to fiscal distortion; The limitation is that we did not consider endogenous fiscal policy.

14508616.value: There are several major findings in this project. (1) we document several stylized facts that related to monetary policy in China, including excess money supply, indirect financing (bank loan), ineffective monetary simulation, and mixed monetary policy. (2) Based on these facts, we build a full-fledged DSGE monetary model with banking's portfolio choice, capital misallocation among firms, and endogenous entry of FDI flow. We use real financial assets (money supply, loan, bond ) data to calibrate the model. (3) The are two quantitative results that have importat policy implication. First, we show that capital misallocation does reduce the response of output to a cut in policy rate, and this effect is quantitatively substantial if the technology difference between SOE and private firms are considered. Secondly, we find that if there is a financial shock that amply the capital misallocation among firms, the central bank has incentives to use money supply rule to respond to the shock. (4) Our results can help to explain the excess liquidity and the ineffectiveness of monetary policy in China. There is a working paper for this project, which will be submitted to referred academic journal. Part results will be also summarized for policy report for central banks.

14508616.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14508616.value: 1.The current model is calibrate to match some financial data, therefore, for some parameters, we are still lack of empirical evidence. For further development, we will consider to estimate the model using more available macro and micro data so that we can provide a useful model for policy analysis. 2. Our model can also be used to analyze other types of shocks, such as export demand shock. Hence, we can use the model to investigate the impact of the China-US trade war on Chinese economy and the role of monetary policy in dealing with these shocks.

14508616.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14508616.value: This paper documents some stylized facts on Chinese economy and constructs a full-fledged DSGE model to investigate how frictions in capital allocation affect the transmission mechanism of monetary shock in China. The model has rich Chinese characteristics, including banking system, State-own enterprises, and FDI flow. Our calibration results show that capital misallocation between SOE and private firms substantially reduce the effectiveness of monetary in stimulating output. Furthermore, we find that, in face of productivity shock, even with endogenous monetary policy, capital misallocation still has substantial negative impact on the output.

14514416.label: Realisation of objectives
14514416.value: Objectives 1 and 2 have been 100% achieved. Objective 3 is almost fully achieved. The first objective of this project is to to study the interaction among vertical accountability, horizontal accountability, and legislative checks and balances. This objective is achieved in my paper "Vertical vs Horizontal Accountability" (joint with SUN Yufeng and SUN Yumeng). In that paper, we construct an encompassing model that can accommodate vertical accountability, horizontal accountability, and legislative checks and balances all at the same time. The model has the nice feature that these different elements of a successful democracy all play a different roles, and in an inter-related manner instead of independently of each other. The second objective of this project is to enhance our understanding of why some new democracies succeed while others fail. This objective is achieved in my paper "Vertical vs Horizontal Accountability" (joint with SUN Yufeng and SUN Yumeng). In that paper, we explain that some new democracies fail because they merely introduce vertical accountability without building professional oversight. As a result, opposition parties not only do not have adequate incentives to exercise diligent legislative checks and balances, but instead become overzealous in engaging in disruptive behavior in legislatures. Introducing delegative democracy in these countries end up lower instead of enhancing welfare. The third objective of this project is to shed light on how to implement welfare-improving (instead of destabilizing) political reforms in democratizing societies such as China and Hong Kong. This objective is almost fully achieved in my paper "Career Concerns: Beijing Style" (joint with CHE Jiahua and QIAO Xue; second Revise & Resubmit at the Journal of Public Economics). In that paper, we explain how checks and balances can be possible without vertical accountability, notwithstanding many examples of failure in the under-developed world. We explain how career concerns, Beijing style, can be a substitute for vertical accountability, and provide checks and balances that discipline the ruling parties. My paper, however, does not discuss the case of Hong Kong, where the political environment has changed too fast, to an extent unexpected at the time of the proposal of this project. As such, Objective 3 is slight shy of 100% achieved.

14514416.label: Major findings and research outcome
14514416.value: In this project, we construct an encompassing model that can accommodate vertical accountability, horizontal accountability, and legislative checks and balances all at the same time. The model has the nice feature that these different elements of a successful democracy all play a different roles, and in an inter-related manner instead of independently of each other. We use this framework to explain that some new democracies fail because they merely introduce vertical accountability without building professional oversight. As a result, opposition parties not only do not have adequate incentives to exercise diligent legislative checks and balances, but instead become overzealous in engaging in disruptive behavior in legislatures. Introducing delegative democracy in these countries end up lower instead of enhancing welfare. We also explain how checks and balances can be possible without vertical accountability, notwithstanding many examples of failure in the under-developed world. We explain how career concerns, Beijing style, can be a substitute for vertical accountability, and provide checks and balances that discipline the ruling parties. These results are documented in two papers of mine. The first is "Vertical vs Horizontal Accountability" (joint with SUN Yufeng and SUN Yumeng), and the second is "Career Concerns: Beijing Style" (joint with CHE Jiahua and QIAO Xue; second Revise & Resubmit at the Journal of Public Economics).

14514416.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14514416.value: This project is theoretical in nature. The natural next step is to take its theoretical predictions to the data. The prediction that vertical accountability can surprisingly lower welfare when professional accountability is weak is especially worth testing empirically. If this prediction is confirmed empirically, then the next step is to examine whether the underlying mechanism is actually as postulated in this project. In this project, I postulate that legislative checks and balances as the key channel through which vertical accountability can lower welfare when professional oversight is weak. A serious empirical study should be conducted to investigate whether this is exactly the true mechanism.

14514416.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14514416.value: When most of us think about democracy, what we have in mind are often merely elections. Therefore, when we see some newly democratized countries slide into chaos after introudcing elections, many of us start to lose faith in democracy. We start to wonder whether we may be different from those living in mature democracies, and whether we may actually belong to a different kind for whom democracy simply does not work. In this project, we explain that democracy actually has many different components, and election is only one of them. When we do not pay adequate attention to the other components, introducing election will predictably backfire. This phenomenon can be readily explained within a political economy we constructed in this project, and does not resort to arguments of "cultural differences". This project lifts us from the fatalistic feeling of "democracy simply would not work for people like us", and points us to what we should pay attention to in order to reap the benefits of democracy.

14519116.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14519116.value: We aim to understand how policy credibility is established and evolves over time in emerging markets or transitional economies. We will develop a new theoretical framework that has a rich expectations structure and allows credibility to be determined by the interactions between individual heterogeneous expectations and policy actions. There, the extent to which a policy is credible evolves via a "natural selection" process. The proposed evolutionary theory may deliver two main results. First, an abrupt change in policy can cause disproportionately large movements in asset prices and a rapid loss of credibility. In this regard, our theory favors gradualism as opposed to "big bang" regime changes. Second, the dynamics during the transition to the new steady state depend crucially on how agents interact. Credibility is harder to lose when interactions occur within segmented markets. We will then take this framework to the data to identify how expectations are formed and how credibility is built. In particular, we will look into the recent RMB devaluation since August 11, 2015, and use the interactions between the onshore and offshore markets to test our theory. Some preliminary work suggests that the recent patterns observed from the Chinese foreign exchanges are all in line with our theory. Finally, our model also delivers important normative implications on the optimal sequence of policy actions in various environments. 我們將研究政策可信性是如何在新興市場和轉型經濟中演進和形成的。一個重要的案例將基於2015年8月開始的中國匯率政策改革。

14519116.label: Realisation of objectives
14519116.value: We have developed a case study for policy credibility in China’s financial sector (Objective 1). The details can be seen from "Liquidity Rules and Unintended Financial Transformation in China", coauthored with Kinda Hachem from University of Virginia (Co-PI). Motivated by the case study, we have also developed a new theoretical framework that has a rich expectations structure and allows credibility to be determined by the feedback between individual expectations and policy actions (Objective 1). The details can be seen from "Liquidity Rules and Credit Booms" (again, coauthored with Kinda Hachem), which was released as NBER Working Paper 21880 and is currently under R&R at Journal of Political Economy. We are confident that Objective 1 has been fully achieved. We eventually decided to give up "national selection process" we put into the proposal. Instead, we adopt a game-theoretic approach to formalize the interactions among the policymaker, the market monopoly (the big four banks in China) and followers (the other commercial banks). The details can be seen from "Liquidity Rules and Credit Booms", which was released as NBER Working Paper 21880. We think 80% of Objective 2 has been achieved in the sense that "national selection process" was not pursued as planned in the proposal. However, Objective 2 is achieved through an alternative venue, in which policy credibility is investigated in subgame perfect equilibrium (government/big banks move first and small banks follow). We encountered some difficulties in studying China’s onshore and offshore foreign exchange markets (Objective 3). The main reason is that the gap between CNY and CHN, which was an important policy issue when we prepared the proposal, has stopped being significant since 2017 as speculation essentially disappeared. As stated in the mid-term report, we decided to focus on more on the dynamic interaction between regulations and the development of shadow banking in China. There, we have found very interesting observations from rich transaction-level data to shed light on policy credibility and its implications. We think 80% of Objective 3, with some reasonable revisions, has been achieved. That said, in terms of the more general theme, the objective has been fully achieved through the venue that is different but spiritually similar to that planned in the proposal. We studied policy implications in both of the papers mentioned above. Moreover, we published a review article "Risks in China's Financial System" (coauthored with Wei Xiong from Princeton) on Annual Review of Financial Economics in 2018. We are confident that Objective 4 has been fully achieved.

14519116.label: Major findings and research outcome
14519116.value: In the paper "Liquidity Rules and Credit Booms" (coauthored with Kinda Hachem from University of Virginia), we show that stricter liquidity standards can trigger unintended credit booms. Attempts to arbitrage the regulation change the allocation of savings across banks, eliciting strategic responses that also change the allocation of lending across markets. More credit is generated per unit of savings in the new equilibrium. Applying our model to China, we find that a move to stricter liquidity standards in the late 2000s accounts for one-third of the unprecedented credit boom that followed. A quantitative extension allowing for other, non-regulatory shocks also identifies variation in liquidity rules as the dominant force behind observed co-movements in market-determined interest rates. In the paper "Liquidity Rules and Unintended Financial Transformation in China" (coauthored with Kinda Hachem from University of Virginia), we trace the origins of China's rapidly developing shadow banking sector to the adoption of stricter liquidity rules by Chinese regulators in the late 2000s. Our analysis exploits cross-sectional differences in the bindingness of these rules along with time variation in product characteristics. We also discuss alternative hypotheses for the rise of shadow banking in China and explain why these hypotheses cannot account for the origins of the system. In the review article "Risks in China's Financial System" (coauthored with Wei Xiong from Princeton) on Annual Review of Financial Economics in 2018, we review several commonly perceived financial risks and discusses their roots in China’s politico-economic institutions. We emphasize the need to evaluate these risks within China’s unique economic and financial systems, in which the state and non-state sectors coexist and the financial system serves as a key tool of the government to fund its economic policies. Overall, we argue that (a) a financial crisis is unlikely to happen in the near future and (b) the ultimate risk lies with China’s economic growth, as a vicious circle of distortions in the financial system lowers the efficiency of capital allocation and economic growth and will eventually exacerbate financial risks in the long run.

14519116.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14519116.value: We will continue to study the interactions between the policymaker and market in China and other emerging markets.

14519116.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14519116.value: We have developed three papers from this project. The main contributions are two-fold. First, we developed a theoretical framework to study the endogenous response of the market (banking sector) to policy (liquidity regulation) and the implications for the aggregate economy. Specifically, we showed that stricter liquidity standards can generate unintended credit booms. Second, applying our framework to China, we found that a regulatory push to increase bank liquidity and cap loan-to-deposit ratios in the late 2000s accounts for one-third of China's unprecedented credit boom between 2007 and 2014. A quantitative extension that allowed for other, non-regulatory shocks also identified variation in liquidity rules as the dominant force behind observed co-movements in market-determined interest rates.

14519516.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14519516.value: Literature in the field of strategic management has identified a variety of conditions, including competitive structure, organizational resources and capabilities, and institutions, that explain variations in firm performance. This study considers firms’ age structure, which is defined in terms of firm age, birth cohorts, and periods of observations, as an additional predictor of performance variation. The association between age structure and performance variation can be examined through two approaches. The first approach, called the Beta model, focuses on between-group variation (changes in performance mean over age). The second approach, called the Lambda model, focuses on within-group variation (changes in performance disparity over age). While a growing, albeit still limited, number of studies examine the Beta model, this study examines the Lambda model, which has received even less attention in prior research. We propose and examine the performance convergence hypothesis that performance disparity becomes smaller as age grows (age effects) and varies across founding conditions (cohort effects) and ongoing conditions (period effects). We investigate this prediction using an Age-Cohort-Period (ACP) analysis of a panel of the data constructed from firm-level data across countries in Asia. 戰略管理領域的文獻區分了一系列的條件以解釋公司業績差異，包括競爭結構、組織資源與能力、制度等。本研究將公司的年齡結構作為公司業績的一個新的預測量。公司年齡結構以公司的年齡、出生佇列和觀察週期為定義。年齡結構與業績差距之間的關係可以通過兩種方法進行檢測。第一種方法，稱為貝塔模型，側重於組間變異（隨著年齡變化，業績均值的變化）。第二種方法，稱為拉姆達模型，側重於組內變異（隨著年齡變化，業績差距的變化）。有越來越多的研究檢測貝塔模型，但是依然有限。本研究將檢測先前研究較少關注的拉姆達模型。我們提出並檢驗業績收斂假說：業績差距隨著年齡的增長而變小（年齡效應），並且因成立條件（佇列效應）和持續條件（時期效應）的不同而變化。我們通過對一組構建于多個亞洲國家的公司層面的面板資料進行年齡-佇列-時期（ACP）分析，以審查該預測。

14519516.label: Major findings and research outcome
14519516.value: The project resulted in three on-going studies. These studies are built on my earlier work (Makino S & Chan CM. 2017. Skew and heavy-tail effects on firm performance. Strategic Management Journal, 38(8):1721-1740), which proposed the "Positive skew hypothesis" that predicts a positive association between the mean and skewness of a firm's performance distribution. This study laid the conceptual foundations of the following three ongoing studies, funded by the current GRF. 1. Examined the "Performance Convergence Hypothesis" Drawing on the organizational learning theory, the variance-centered view, and the random walk model of organizational evolution, my co-author and I proposed the Performance Convergence Hypothesis in which the mean, variance, and skewness of firm performance distributions become lower, smaller, and more negative as firm age increases, but these measures vary across founding conditions and ongoing conditions. We tested this hypothesis using a sample of 3,089 Japanese listed firms (in 89 birth cohorts) for the period of 1980–2015, which projects an unbalanced panel of 59,380 firm-year observations. Our analyses provide strong support for the hypothesis. This study is under the 1st R&R at Organization Science. 2. Examined the inequality in firm performance distribution across the world This project attempted to explain why firms perform differently across countries and time. Using publicly available data on listed companies from more than 60 countries between 2000 and 2015, my co-author and I report four patterns of performance distribution during regular economic periods and one pattern for economic recessions. We found that economic development tends to be associated with an increase in firm inequality and a convergence in firm inequalities across countries. This paper is currently under review at Industrial and Corporate Change, a journal in economics. 3. Examined the "Learning-across-generation Hypothesis" The project also examined the association between the age structure of firms in a country/region and the growth of the economy across the world. Drawing on the organizational learning theory, we argue that new and young firms are a key driving force of the economic growth; and a wide range of age groups will create opportunities for learning among firms across generations, which makes additional contributions to the growth. The results suggest that countries/regions with a greater proportion of young firms (high positive skew) and those with the firms that are dispersed across age groups (low kurtosis) are more likely to achieve high economic growth. These results remain consistent even after controlling for firm size and country heterogeneity. This study is to be submitted to Administrative Science Quarterly.

14519516.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14519516.value: The first paper is currently under R&R at Organization Science. My co-author and I have been working hard on revision. Luckily, we received very comprehensive and constructive comments from the Editor and the reviewers, which we found very useful. We plan to resubmit the paper by the end of March 2020. The second paper is currently under review at Industrial and Corporate Change, a journal in economics. We have received many positive and constructive comments from renowned scholars in both business studies and economics, although earlier versions of this paper have been rejected by a few journals. We hope to receive a positive feedback from the journal. The third paper, which is to be submitted to Administrative Science Quarterly, is almost completed. We are now proofreading the paper. I have been invited to present the study in multiple schools in Korea, Japan, and China, and many scholars found the findings of the study interesting.

14519516.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14519516.value: The first study examines whether corporate "aging" affects corporate productivity. Our research has revealed that the answer is yes. Specifically, the study found that profitability declined as firms grew older, and that variance in profitability between firms of the same age cohort got smaller. The second study looks at the uneven distribution of wealth created by firms around the world. We found that inequality exists and varies greatly by country / region. It was also revealed that this inequality is closely related to the level of economic development of the country / region and is promoted by economic globalization. The third study examines the age distribution of firms around the world and how they affect economic growth. The age structure was found to have a unique relationship with economic growth. Specifically, the study found that countries / regions with a good balance of young and old firms are more likely to achieve higher economic growth.

14519816.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14519816.value: Firms choose an optimal level of debt by making a tradeoff between benefits of tax shelter and expected costs of distress and bankruptcy. High costs of distress and bankruptcy deter firms taking more debt. The expected cost of distress is different from the cost of bankruptcy, but does not receive enough attention in the literature of studying corporate decisions to borrow. First, the cost of distress occurs when the firm is entering distress, but well before it officially files for bankruptcy, at which bankruptcy costs occur. Second, the cost of distress is borne by equity holders before bankruptcy, while the cost of bankruptcy is borne by debt holders at bankruptcy. Before bankruptcy, equity holders of distressed firms suffer from the cost of distress themselves because the loss of productive workers decreases their firms’ productivity and operating profits. At bankruptcy, it is the debt holders who take over the assets and pay all the liquidation and bankruptcy costs. Therefore, compared with the cost of default, the cost of distress has more direct impacts on the wealth of a firm’s owners, equity holders, and their decision to borrow. The lack of sufficient attention on the expected cost of distress could be attributed to the difficulties to measure it. First, most of the distress costs (the loss of reputation to customers and workers) are much larger but unobservable. Second, it is hard to precisely define the timing of when the firm starts to become distressed. This study aims to overcome these two problems and provide an accurate estimate of expected cost of distress for a large sample of U.S. firms, and then empirically determine impacts of various firm characteristics on the expected cost of distress, such as growth opportunities, product uniqueness and labor mobility. We emphasize labor mobility in this study. Workers who are more experienced and capable have more opportunities to find new jobs and therefore have greater job mobility. Troubled firms are likely to lose their capable workers with greater mobility, which in turn lowers these firms' productivities and profits further. Hence, labor mobility will significantly increase the cost of distress. When making a financing decision, firms with high mobility workers expect this high cost in the future bad times and choose to borrow less today. 財務困境成本不同與破產成本。當研究一個公司的借債決定，財務困境成本沒有得到足夠的重視。首先，財務困境成本在公司申請破產之前出現。 一旦公司正在進入財務困境，困境成本產生。困境中的企業可能會失去信譽，失去客戶和材料供應商，並難以吸引和留住有才華的員工。二，財務困境成本由股票持有人承擔，而破產成本由債權人在破產承擔。 一旦公司破產, 債權人接管的資產，並支付所有的清算和破產成本。而因為有限責任，股權持有人一分錢不花。相反，股權持有人支付財務困境成本。因為生產工人的流失降低了企業的生產效率和經營利潤受損，與違約的成本相比，財務困境的成本對企業的所有者，股權持有人，以及他們的借債決定的更直接的影響。當想到在未來更大的財務困境成本，股權持有人會選擇減少今天的借貸。 財務困境成本缺乏足夠的重視可以歸因於困難來衡量它。首先，財務困境成本（即訴訟成本）的直接成本小，而間接成本（信譽的客戶和員工的損失）大得多，但無法觀察到。其次，很難界定的什麼時候公司開始有財務困境。 這項研究的目的是克服這些問題，研究財務困境成本。我們使用美國公司的大樣本，提供財務困境的預期成本的精確估計，然後確定不同企業特徵對財務困境成本的的影響，如成長機會，產品獨特性和勞動力流動性。在這項研究中我們強調勞動力流動性。有經驗工人的能夠有更多的機會找到新的就業機會，因此具有較大的工作流動性。陷入困境的公司可能會失去這些有更大的流動性工人，從而進一步降低其生產率和利潤。因此，量化由於勞動力的損失促使的財務困境成本是重要的。

14519816.label: Realisation of objectives
14519816.value: Realization of Objectives 1. Evolution of Project Objectives The objectives of this project have been evolving along the progress of research. 1.1. Original Objectives The first objective in our original proposal is to show that the expected distress cost is underestimated via structural estimation. In our last report, we have confirmed our conjecture: by overcoming the endogeneity issue in our structural model, the expected distress cost is larger than we expected. The intuition is as follows. The firms with a low distress cost choose a high level of debt and financial leverage. Those firms with a low distress cost but a high leverage will be more likely to become distressed and enter the distress firm sample. If we estimate the distress cost using this endogenous sample, we will end up estimate the distress cost from a sample of firms with a low distress cost. That is why we underestimate the distress cost in the previous literature. Our structural model overcomes this problem. The second objective in our original proposal is to identify a number of important sources of the cost of distress and determine the main driver of the expected cost of distress, particularly labor mobility. 1.2 Objectives and Tasks Our first objective remains the same: estimate the distress cost. We extend the objective to estimate the distress cost separately in the bad and good states, because we expect the distress cost is countercyclical. That is, it is greater in the bad state than in the good state. For example, it is more costly to fire-sell assets in recessions than in expansions. Our second objective has been revised in our extension request on Sept 14, 2018, and has been approved by the panel members. The reason for us to revise our second objective is that we want to downplay the lability mobility in this research, because our competitors have a unique dataset on the detailed information of labor force. Additionally, we want to focus on systematic distress cost, which allows us to understand two empirical puzzles: the negative failure probability-return relation (Campbell, Hilscher, and Szilagyi, 2008, Journal of Finance) and the positive distress risk premium-return relation (Friewald, Wagner, and Zechner, 2014, Journal of Finance). 2. Completions of the Objectives In this section, we elaborate the completion of objectives. 2.1. First Objective We use the simulated method of moments (SMM) to estimate the model. The key to structural estimation is to choose the right target moments that are informative about the parameters to be estimated. We discipline our model mainly using the moments of financial leverage, because debt is our important choice variable. Moreover, we match the average earnings growth rates from the NIPA table from 1974 to 2015. The estimated distress cost in the bad state is 1.50 %, greater than the 1.01% in the good state, confirming our intuition that distress cost is countercyclical Section 4 of the attached paper. 2.2. Second Objective To achieve our second, revised objective, i.e., connecting the negative failure probability-return relation (Campbell, Hilscher, and Szilagyi, 2008) with the positive distress risk premium-return relation (Friewald, Wagner, and Zechner, 2014), we need to show the ranking variables, failure probability and implied distress risk premium, are two negatively correlated. 2.2.1. Intuition Endogenous distress status helps connect the two puzzling observations or ranking variables. Following Andrade and Kaplan (1998), we define a firm as ``distressed'' when its cash flow level falls below its contractual interest payment. Higher coupon payments imply an earlier time of entering distress. Hence, the distress threshold and therefore distress status are endogenously chosen in our model, because debt levels are endogenously chosen over the business cycle. That is, firms with low exposure to aggregate distress risk (cash flow betas), more systematic distress costs, choose higher leverage ex ante. When hit by a large market-wide shock, those firms are more likely to become distressed relative to their counterparts. In other words, firms with a low distress risk premium are more likely to be highly distressed ex post and hence earn low stock returns, explaining the findings in Friewald et al. (2014). Thus, distress risk premium and distress status are negatively related. 2.2.2 Closed-Form Solution To facilitate our understanding of the negative relation between failure probability and stock returns, we first simplify the model and derive closed-form solutions to show that the negative relation between failure probability and return is due to the negative covariance between the equity beta and the market risk premium in Section 3 of the attached paper. Then, we take advantage of the dynamic model and demonstrate that it can generate a sizable failure risk premium, quantitatively, in Section 4. Following Campbell, Hilscher, and Szilagyi (2008), we perform logit regressions and construct failure probabilities using our simulated panels. When sorting firms on failure probability, highly distressed firms exhibit high leverage and default probabilities, but have low returns and negative CAPM alphas. Lastly, we provide empirical evidence to confirm the novel economic channel in our model. We first show that the debt-to-equity ratios of distressed firms are more negatively associated with the market risk premium than are those of healthy firms. Then, we follow Lewellen and Nagel (2006) and construct time-varying equity betas, and confirm that levered equity betas are negatively (positively) correlated with the expected market risk premium in distressed (healthy) firms. Finally, the negative covariance between the levered equity beta and the market risk premium helps explain about 50% of the distress risk premium in the conditional CAPM. 3. Outcomes This project has been successfully executed. We produce a paper of “a unified model of distress risk puzzles”. This paper has been well received and has been presented in the top finance conferences, namely, the 2020 American Financial Association meetings (San Diego), the 2019 European Financial Association meetings (Lisbon), and the 2009 SFS Cavalcade North America. I also presented in some small but prestigious conferences, such as the 2019 Corporate Finance Theory Symposium (Cambridge), the 2019 COAP finance conference (CASS and Inquiry UK), 2nd World Symposium on Investment Research, the 2019 Great Bay Area Finance Conference , CAFIN Finance Workshop, and Shanghai University of Finance and Economics. We will submit the paper to the Journal of Finance by the end of Feb, 2020. I very much appreciate financial support from the GRF and has acknowledged this funding in the paper.
