14613516.label: Major findings and research outcome
14613516.value: The research project directly results in a number of articles and conference presentations, including two publications in top journals: “Intervention, Fixation, and Supervenient Causation” (forthcoming in Journal of Philosophy) and “Taking Emergentism Seriously” (published in Australasian Journal of Philosophy). There are three major research findings. First, the research project offers an original solution to the exclusion problem by reviving and developing the tradition of parallelism. Second, the project puts forward a sophisticated counterfactual theory of causation that is suitable for the analysis of supervenient causation. Third, the project forcefully refutes a popular approach to mental causation that proposes mental-physical overdetermination.

14613516.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14613516.value: The causal closure of physics is widely accepted in contemporary philosophy of mind. My previous work on mental causation also presupposed this doctrine. However, in the final stage of the research project, I started reflecting on this presupposition. In the article “Taking Emergentism Seriously”, I preliminarily suggest that the non-reductive physicalist should reject the causal closure of physics in solving the exclusion problem. I plan to conduct further research on this topic in the future. If denying physical causal closure is physicalistically acceptable, this would make significant progress on mental causation and physicalism.

14613516.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14613516.value: It is widely believed that regardless of how closely the mental is related to the physical, mental states remain irreducible to, or nonidentical with, physical states. However, the notorious Exclusion Problem seems to imply that if mental states are distinct from physical states, then mental states are causally impotent—the putative causal powers of the mental would be excluded by those of the physical. In this research project, I aim to solve the exclusion problem by reviving and developing the tradition of parallelism. On the parallelist approach I propose, even if mental states do not cause fundamental physical states, they can still cause higher-level states (such as behavioral, mental, and social states). The parallelist approach enjoys significant theoretical advantages over alternative approaches. For example, a parallelist approach to mental causation does not have to reject the causal closure of physics; this approach also need not postulate controversial metaphysical doctrines like mental-physical overdetermination.

14613616.label: Project Title(Chinese)
14613616.value: 中國股東表決制度研究

14613616.label: Project Objectives
14613616.value: To articulate the historical, economic and political contexts in which the legal and regulatory framework for shareholder voting rights has evolved in China; To examine empirically the manner in which shareholders in Chinese listed companies exercise their voting rights; To discern empirically the determinants, as well as the impact, of shareholder voting in Chinese listed firms; and To propose a more grounded theory for understanding the role that shareholder voting plays in the development of national securities markets, with particular reference to China but also more generally.
rows: To articulate the historical, economic and political contexts in which the legal and regulatory framework for shareholder voting rights has evolved in China;
To examine empirically the manner in which shareholders in Chinese listed companies exercise their voting rights;
To discern empirically the determinants, as well as the impact, of shareholder voting in Chinese listed firms; and

To propose a more grounded theory for understanding the role that shareholder voting plays in the development of national securities markets, with particular reference to China but also more generally.

14613616.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14613616.value: The aim of this project is to explore empirically the important issue of how shareholders in Chinese listed companies exercise their rights to vote. The power of the shareholders to vote on the affairs of the firm in which they invest is a fundamental concern in corporate governance. Shareholders’ voting rights empower them to elect and remove directors, and to participate in various decision making processes in the firm’s affairs. The conventional wisdom holds that, in the firms where ownership is widely dispersed, minority shareholders are likely to be apathetic in their approach to voting. More recent studies suggest, however, that minority shareholders, in particular, institutional investors, have taken an increasingly activist approach to their voting rights and shown a greater interest in the governance of their invested firms. Although the comparative literature on shareholder voting is rapidly expanding, the manner in which Chinese shareholders vote their shares remains understudied and under-theorized. This project aims to fill this important gap, and to thereby significantly enhance our understanding of corporate governance both in China and more generally. The project’s particular focus is on non-controlling shareholders in Chinese listed firms, including both individual minority shareholders and institutional investors. Drawing on two unique, hand-collected datasets on shareholder voting in Chinese listed firms, as well as qualitative data on the voting strategies of institutional investors to be obtained with the support a network of collaborating PRC securities regulators, this project will present new insights into, among other things, the patterns in shareholder voting, the determinants of shareholders’ voting behavior, and the impact of shareholder voting on the governance of Chinese listed firms. It is anticipated that the systematic, empirical and comparative analysis of shareholder voting in China, which this project offers, will inform and help to generate a more grounded theory for understanding the role that shareholder voting plays in the development of national securities markets, with particular reference to China but also more generally. The theoretical and empirical findings of this project will also contribute to better minority shareholder protection in China, as the potential effectiveness of the legal and regulatory reforms aimed at strengthening shareholder rights depends critically on the manner in which shareholders actually exercise those rights. 本課題旨在使用實證方法，研究中國上市公司股東如何行使表決權。 股東通過行使表決權參與公司決策，是公司治理中的重大議題。表決權賦予了股東選舉和罷免董事、參與公司事務決策過程的權利。傳統理論認為，在股權結構分散的公司中，小股東對於表決權的行使往往漠然置之。然而，近來的多項研究表明，以機構投資者為代表的小股東已經越來越積極地行使表決權，並越來越重視公司的治理。儘管對於股東表決制度的比較研究方興未艾，對於中國上市公司股東如何行使表決權的研究尚付諸闕如。本課題嘗試彌補這個領域的研究空白，並希冀從該視角加深對於中國和比較公司治理的研究。 本課題的研究關注重點是中國上市公司的非控股股東，既包括個人中小股東，也包括機構投資者。本課題將通過手動收集資料的方式，構建兩個中國上市公司股東表決資料庫，並且通過與監管機構協作，瞭解機構投資者的表決策略。基於此，本課題嘗試研究股東表決的模式和特徵、股東表決的影響因素、以及股東表決對於中國上市公司治理的影響等重要問題。 本課題將通過對於中國股東表決制度的系統化、實證和比較研究，試圖加深對股東表決制度與股票市場發展之間關係的理論研究。本課題的研究成果還將有助於提升中國上市公司中小股東的法律保護水準。

14613616.label: Realisation of objectives
14613616.value: Quantitative and qualitative investigation undertaken under the project has been guided by, and directed to fulfill, its four objectives. All four objectives have been successfully and fully achieved. Objective 1: To articulate the historical, economic and political contexts in which the legal and regulatory framework for shareholder voting rights has evolved in China This component of the project has relied primarily on materials derived from secondary sources. Thus, a unique documentary archive has been created that traces the evolution and functioning of shareholders’ voting rights under Chinese law. This archive collects not only published materials that are more readily accessible (such as monographs, yearbooks, journal articles, and newspaper entries), but also materials that are ‘internal’ in nature, yet are not classified or otherwise confidential. The latter include ‘internal’ policy reports, ‘internal’ policy addresses, as well as ‘internal’ meeting minutes. They are particularly useful for gaining an insight into the academic and policy debates on the case for empowering shareholders by way of enhancing shareholder voting power. These secondary materials are supplemented, importantly, by elite interviews. Interviews have been conducted with senior and rank-and-file officials, both serving and former, at the regulatory bodies who were involved in the development of China’ shareholder voting rights regime. These interviews have shed light on the underlying, often times undocumented, considerations that account for the regulatory initiatives taken on shareholder voting rights, as well as their institutional constraints. Objective 2: To examine empirically the manner in which shareholders in Chinese listed companies exercise their voting rights; and Objective 3: To discern empirically the determinants, as well as the impact, of shareholder voting in Chinese listed firms In order to achieve Objectives 2 and 3, two separate, albeit related, datasets have been constructed, with one focusing on the shareholder voting outcomes at the shareholders’ meetings as disclosed by all Chinese listed firms during the period from 2002 through 2016 (‘Shareholder Voting Dataset’), and the other on the voting records of institutional investors during the course of the so-called “Split-share Structure Reform” that was unfolded from 2005 to 2007 (‘Institutional Investor Dataset’). Elite interviews have also been undertaken to achieve the objectives. The Shareholder Voting Dataset The Shareholder Voting Dataset consists of the voting results on the agenda items that require a vote of the shareholders at the shareholders’ meeting in all Chinese listed firms during the period from 2002 through 2017. It is of note that the period of investigation has been extended by one year to 2017 from 2016 as stated in the approved GRF proposal, in order to more fully capture the recent developments in China’s shareholder voting regime. The Dataset is constructed based on the company disclosures of the shareholder voting results at the shareholders’ meeting. These have been collected from CNInfo, an officially recognised source of information on Chinse listed firms. It provides a broad, near-inclusive coverage of company releases on shareholder voting outcomes. Nevertheless, firms that at the time of data collection are already delisted would no longer have their disclosures available on the website of CNInfo. The absent releases are manually collected from leading Chinese financial news outlets, including the Shanghai Securities Daily and the China Securities Daily, to which the CUHK Library has ready access. The Institutional Investor Dataset The Institutional Investor Dataset contains the proxy voting records of institutional investors from 2005 through 2007, during which time the so-called “Split-share Structure Reform” (“Reform”) was rolled out with a view to transforming the Chinese securities market. During the course of the Reform, Chinese listed companies were required to disclose the identity of their top ten non-controlling shareholders (which were almost invariably institutional investors) and, more importantly, the specific voting records of these shareholders at the special shareholders’ meeting that approved the firm’s reform proposal. The Dataset is constructed based on the company disclosures of those special shareholders meetings, using the same quantitative methods used to create the Shareholder Voting Dataset. It includes additional key quantitative data for the purpose of the research, in particular, the identity of the institutional investors involved, the percentage of share capital each of them represented, and the voting records of each of them. It also contains data on a similar cohort of selected independent variables, including a selected number of portfolio firm and board characteristics that the existing literature has identified as associated with the voting preferences of institutional investors. Elite Interviews Prior empirical research has convincingly documented the institutional investors’ strong preferences for behind-the-scenes, private engagements over public activism. Evidence further suggests that institutional investors engage with their portfolio firms predominantly through private interventions, and that they take public actions only after the behind-the-scenes engagements have not succeeded. The private, confidential nature of the behind-the-scenes interventions means that they usually are unobservable in studies that rely purely on company disclosures. Therefore, in addition to the quantitative data described above, elite interviews have also been carried out to acquire valuable qualitative data that help achieve the objectives 2 and 3. I have interviewed various types of institutional investor, including securities investment funds, private equity funds, pension funds, securities firms, and QDIIs. Interviewees include senior executives of these institutional investors. Lines of questioning include: how, and at what level, are voting policies identified and determined; how are these turned into specific voting decisions; (c) how are target firms for activist engagement and intervention identified and selected; so on and so forth. Interviews have also been conducted to gain a greater understanding of how listed firms have been affected by and have reacted to institutional investor activism, and how they have attempted to influence the voting decision-making of the institutional investors that intend to engage with them on governance issues. The interviewees include not only senior executives of the target firms, but also rank-and-file bureaucrats of the government agency controlling the listed firms concerned (in the case of state-owned firms). Moreover, interviews have been carried out with the CSRC officials, as well the officials of the Shanghai Stock Exchange and the Shenzhen Stock Exchange, who are responsible for the making and enforcement of rules and regulations on shareholder voting. Objective 4: To propose a more grounded theory for understanding the role that shareholder voting plays in the development of national securities markets, with particular reference to China but also more generally. Building on the quantitative and qualitative findings described above, I have been successfully engaged in conceptualization and generalization, and developing a theoretical framework for understanding the institutional constraints for shareholder activism in China and beyond. This endeavour has resulted in: Harpreet Kaur, Chao Xi, Christoph Van del Elst, and Anne Lafarre, Cambridge Handbook on Shareholder Voting and Engagement (Cambridge University Press, 2022 June expected). I co-author the Handbook’s introductory chapter and author its concluding chapter, in addition to my chapter contribution in the Handbook on shareholder voting and engagement in China.

14613616.label: Major findings and research outcome
14613616.value: Research outputs of the present project include: • A co-edited volume entitled Cambridge Handbook on Shareholder Voting and Engagement (Cambridge University Press, 2022 June expected), covering shareholder voting and engagement in 19 jurisdictions; • Five authored/co-authored chapter contributions to edited volumes published by the Cambridge University Press or Edward Elgar; • Three authored/co-authored articles published in leading/respectable peer-reviewed journals; • Four authored/co-authored articles currently under review by top-ranked/leading peer-reviewed journals; and • 16 conference/seminar presentations and public lectures delivered at international or regional academic events. In addition, two international conferences have been organized under the present project. The major findings of the present project include: • Empowerment of minority shareholders has been a central theme of China’s corporate governance movements in the past two decades. • The practical effect of China’s reforms to strengthen shareholders’ rights to vote needs to be evaluated in the context of China’s path-dependent conditions, notably the prevalence of concentrated share ownership, the relatively weaker presence of institutional investors, and the approach to allocating corporate power which centers on the shareholders meeting. • Empirically, shareholder dissent in China’s listed sector was infrequent, with a large percentage of the resolutions winning the unanimous support of the shareholders who attended. Shareholders seem to have differentiated among different resolution types when casting their votes, lending some support to the thesis that Chinese shareholders are not invariably passive and indifferent. • Empirically, there is a heterogeneity of institutional investors in respect of their stewardship effect. The general restrictions on share transferability had unintended counter-productive effect on investor stewardship in China. • A three-layered conceptual framework might be useful for future comparative research on shareholder voting and engagement. At the center lies the body of shareholder voting laws, essentially a jurisdiction’s web of laws, regulations and rules setting the parameters of shareholders’ voting rights and the ways in which they can exercise these rights. The second layer of the framework relates to engagement tools that transcend the formal, if not mechanical, act of casting votes at the shareholders meeting. The outer right of the framework entails a jurisdiction’s broader ecosystem for voting and engagement. The three layers are closely intertwined, and interact dynamically to shape the way in which laws and corporate practices of shareholder voting and engagement in a given jurisdiction have evolved.

14613616.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14613616.value: An international network of collaboration is being formed on the basis of the team of leading international experts covering shareholder voting and engagement in 19 jurisdictions who have contributed to the Cambridge Handbook on Shareholder Voting and Engagement (which I co-edit). With necessary institutional and funding support, I plan to take lead in exploring the potential of a multi-jurisdiction, data-driven project on shareholder voting in order to yield new jurisdictional, as well as international and comparative, insights, to supplement the more traditional, doctrinal and anecdotal approaches.

14613616.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14613616.value: This project explores empirically the important issue of how shareholders in Chinese listed companies exercise their rights to vote. The power of the shareholders to vote on the affairs of the firm in which they invest is a fundamental concern in corporate governance. The project’s particular focus is on non-controlling shareholders in Chinese listed firms, including both individual minority shareholders and institutional investors. Drawing on two unique, hand-collected datasets on shareholder voting in Chinese listed firms, as well as qualitative data on the voting strategies of institutional investors to be obtained with the support a network of collaborating PRC securities regulators, this project presents new insights into, among other things, the patterns in shareholder voting, the determinants of shareholders’ voting behavior, and the impact of shareholder voting on the governance of Chinese listed firms. The systematic, empirical and comparative analysis of shareholder voting in China, which this project offers, generates a more evidence-based theory for understanding the role that shareholder voting plays in the development of national securities markets, with particular reference to China but also more generally. The theoretical and empirical findings of this project also contribute to better minority shareholder protection in China.

14614416.label: Project Objectives

14614416.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14614416.value: 青少年特發性脊柱側彎症(Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis, AIS)是現時兒童到青少年轉化時期最普遍的脊柱畸形疾病. 估計受影響的兒童約佔十至十六歲人口的2-4%。 症狀會於兒童踏入青春期時影響其身體發展. 若側彎角度大於45度，更會長期嚴重影響健康。 對於骨骼未完全成熟而側彎角度又在20-40度之間度的青少年而言，穿戴矯形腰架為最首選的治療方法。有新的研究指出合規地穿戴矯形腰架能顯著地避免脊柱側彎的情況惡化，進而減低需要進行矯正手術的風險。然而，穿戴矯形腰架 是一個不舒適的經驗。矯形腰架的建議穿戴時間為每天20小時，持續四到五年，直到骨骼成熟；而該時段的青少年對自身體態形象非常敏感。因此，穿戴矯形腰架的青少年反應生活質量較同齡健康同輩更低，且穿戴矯形腰架的合規性普遍較低（約50%）。 過去幾十年間，大量的國際研究表明靜觀治療對於慢性疼痛、抑鬱、焦慮癥及情感障礙等有所益處。靜觀可以被形容為「有意識地、不武斷地、集中當下此刻而升起的覺察」。本研究假設靜觀治療能夠對自律機制產生正面影響，從而改善AIS患者穿戴矯形腰架的合規性和生活質素。 我們將進行雙項干預的隨機對照試驗，以評估靜觀治療（mindfulness-based intervention，MBI）對矯形腰架穿戴合規性和AIS患者的生活質素的影響。本研究將招募120名年齡在10至15歲的AIS患者，並將他們隨機分配至干預組或對照組。這項研究的結果有機會為未來的AIS治療帶來極大的變化, 亦很可能成為第一份以改善AIS患者腰架合規性作目標的干預心理社會研究。

14614416.label: Realisation of objectives
14614416.value: All of the four proposed objectives were completed and achieved. A total of 122 participants were recruited. Before the randomisation, we contacted the recruited subjects about their confirmation to participate the interventions, and 39 of them could not find time to participate the interventions. The final randomised participants were 83, less than our targeted sample of 120. However, as reported in our interim report, once they joint the interventions the observed drop-out rate (8.4%) was much lower than the anticipated drop-out rate (20%). Thus, our recruited sample size is comparable to the effective sample size (N=80). The primary outcome was bracing compliance at 6-month post-intervention. We modify the 14-days Timeline Followback for exercise inventory to measure compliance of bracing. Participants are also required to do a self-report of their average bracing hours per day in the past two weeks. The minimum number of 14-days average values of sensors record and the self-report value was recorded as the compliance at each timepoint. The secondary outcome measure included The Scoliosis Research Society 22-item questionnaire(SRS-22), Chinese version Quality of Life–5 Dimensions 5-level questionnaire (EQ5D-5L), the Brace Questionnaire (BrQ), the Self-Compassion Scale (SCS), Chinese Adaptation of the Emotion Regulation Questionnaire for Children and Adolescents (ERQ-CCA), The General Self Efficacy Scale (GSE), Five Facet Mindfulness Questionnaire (FFMQ),and the Perceived Stress Scale (PSS). Intent-to-treat analysis was performed on all of the data. For objective 1, we conducted ANCOVA with bracing compliance measured at post-intervention as the primary outcome, baseline compliance measures and treatment group covariates. For objective 2, we conducted ANCOVA with quality of life related measures (QALY, SRS, BrQ) at post-intervention as the primary outcome, baseline values and treatment group covariates. For objective 3, we conducted linear mixed model with bracing compliance measures at different timepoints as outcome, time-points (baseline, post-intervention, and 6 months post intervention), treatment group, and their interaction as covariates. For objective 4, we conducted mediation analyses using Baron and Kenny's approach, to assess the direct and indirect effect of intervention effect through mediator self-efficacy.

14614416.label: Major findings and research outcome
14614416.value: For details regarding study design, subject recruitment, data collection, statistical analysis, and sample size calculation, we are referring to our published trial protocol (Output 1 in Part C). Our systematic review revealed that that there are very few high-quality RCT with intervention aiming to improve bracing compliance (Output 2 in Part C). The most promising intervention so far is brace embedded temperature sensor that monitor patients' compliance. Participants' awarenesses of being monitored had psychosocial impact and caused a higher compliance. For the primary outcome, the bracing compliance improved marginally significantly for participants randomly assigned to MBI at the end-intervention and decrease significantly for patients in the PE group at 6-month post-intervention. Compared with the control group, 8 weeks of MBI intervention induced a significant increase of around 2 hours in participants’ bracing compliance ( month 2: 1.89 h/day, 95%CI: 0.36 to 3.41; month 8: 2.15 h/day, 95%CI: 0.37 to 3.93) in comparisons at each timepoint and this superiority still existed in LMM analysis with random effect (month 2: 1.80 h/day, 95%CI: 0.19 to 3.40; month 8: 1.97 h/day, 95%CI: 0.33 to 3.61). For secondary outcomes, MBI induced a significant improvement in the quality of life at 6-month post-intervention as measured by SRS-22(d=0.08, p<0.05) while at this timepoint PE also lead to a significant improvement in the body function of patients (d=0.09, p<0.05) which was measured by a subscale of SRS-22. However, there is no significant between-group difference for the quality of life of the two groups. The emotion regulation strategy (Cognitive Reappraisal) as reported by the ERQ-CCA among patients in the MBI group were significantly improved at 2-month (d=0.28, p<0.05) and 8 months (d=0.28, p<0.05) compared with baseline value and the participants of the MBI group showed greater improvement in than that of the control group at the end-intervention in ANCOVA analysis(d=0.22, p=0.047), but this difference was not statistically significant at 6 months post-intervention or at neither timepoints when considering the time effect in LMM analysis. No significant between-group differences were found in measurements of quality of life, the expressive suppression component of ERQ-CCA, GSE, PSS, and other components of FFMQ and SCS at the end of the intervention and at 6 months post-intervention in both ANCOVA and LMM analysis. For more details, please see output 3 in Part C. No significant mediation effect of any secondary outcomes was found on bracing compliance.

14614416.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14614416.value: Though the sample size of this study was small, we found a significant positive effect of MBI in improving bracing compliance for AIS patients. Participants were all teenagers. Busy home-work or after school activities made the subject recruitment challenging. Many of the participants could not attend the intervention, even after providing consent to join the study. We conducted a preliminary analysis to assess whether MBI also benefit the clinical outcome, Cobb Angle, when the follow up time was beyond the original RCT study period (up to 30 months follow-up of the earliest batch). The result is very promising. Thus, we are planning to apply new fundings for a new RCT to evaluate the effectiveness of an online MBI program for AIS subjects. Since the online version will facilitate participants' participation we are aiming a much larger sample size of 200 vs 200.

14614416.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14614416.value: Bracing is the primary treatment in preventing spine curve progression for Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) patients. Poor compliance to bracing therapy is a major factor limiting treatment outcomes in AIS patients. Despite its importance, compliance to brace treatment is well known to be poor. Still, very few interventions were suggested to improve bracing compliance. To meet the research gap, we evaluated the effectiveness of a 8-week mindfulness-based intervention (MBI) program on bracing compliance, with physical exercise (PE) as the comparison group. Eligible subjects were AIS patients with poor bracing compliance, which was assessed by temperature sensor embedded to the brace and by self-report. We recruited and randomly assigned 83 subjects into MBI and PE group. Brace compliance data were assessed at baseline, 2 month and 8 months. We found participants in the MBI group wore, on average per day, significantly two hours more than the PE group (2month and 8month). There is indication that MBI might enhanced emotion regulation strategy which thereby improve bracing compliance as a potential mechanism explanation. Noteworthy, many participants (mostly secondary school children) could not join our study due to their busy schedule. Future study should evaluate the effectiveness of an online MBI to facilitate participation.

14617716.value: 是次研究將以被視為日本動漫畫活躍群組的中國讀者作為研究核心，探討他們運用甚麼閱讀策略及規律以享用合法或非法跨國輸入的文化產品，從中延申至探索中國動漫畫粉絲群組形成的過程。研究最主要目的是評價日本動漫畫對中國年青一代在文化消費上可造成甚麼程度的潛在文化衝擊。以下為是次研究三項主要研究範疇。 首先，是次研究沿用文化研究的綱領，探討不同模式的閱讀及資訊接收中的文化本質。例如一部份的讀者以享樂為閱讀日本漫畫的主要動力，讀者在文化接收上處於較被動的位置；另一邊廂一部份主動受眾及粉絲則在這些外來文化載體上加上個人或群體的解讀，這些主動解讀將固有的文化載體意義從新改寫，成為只屬於主動解讀者獨特的文化文本。本研究將會探討中國讀者在此方面的閱讀策略及規律。 其次，就著網上粉絲群組的形成，是次研究探究讀者們作為粉絲群組一份子時如何主動地參與發佈及二次創作既有的文化載體。在現今的日本動漫畫網上群組中，主動受眾主要參與的「分工」包括漢化（則指將動漫畫中的日文原文翻譯為中文，並將譯文放於適當位置上，作為字幕供其他較被動的讀者使用）、作品評鑑或資料搜集及整理、衍生創作（包括同人誌、同人小說、改圖、改對白、繪畫等等）。這些「分工」在建構粉絲群組以及粉絲個人身份形成上扮演著重要的角色，而本次研究將會對此加以探索。 最後，本次研究會站在文化全球化的學術立場上提出疑問：當中國受眾消費日本文化產品時，他們是如何消化這些針對全球市場及文化的文化產品﹖這些文化產品中涵括不少全球普世價值及日本文化，包括自由（日本漫畫例子為《進擊之巨人》）、和平共存（日本漫畫例子為《火影忍者》）、正義及武士道 （日本漫畫例子為《銀魂》）、伙伴之間的羈絆（日本漫畫例子為《海賊王》）、人道及倫理（日本漫畫例子為《鋼之鍊金術師》。予此，中國讀者會如何解讀、理解及想像日本及上述的日本文化及全球普世價值，這些文化價值對讀者根深蒂固的中國文化及價值會有甚麼相勃／相同之處﹖這會為中國讀者帶來甚麼文化衝擊﹖在現今中日關係緊張的情況，這些對日本文化的解讀會否影響中國年青人對日本的看法﹖ 當中國受眾在遠離日本情境下接觸日本文化文本， 他們對日本文化的想像、解讀及了解相信與日本當地受眾的有很大落差。這個情況對中國年青人特別有影響性。由於中國網絡實行政治監控及資訊過濾，大部份的國營媒體及國內論述均偏向以負面描述日本，這些內容顯然與中國年青人從動漫中想像的日本有著根本上的矛盾。在這種資訊及意識上的矛盾中，中國年青人面對著中日關係國情時晴時雨，以及社會監控時嚴時寛，他們會在社會及政治價值上有著何種的表述﹖這種表述在不同的情況下如何和日本動漫畫中的普世價值相附及相勃﹖ 為了解答上述的學術問題，以及探索中國受眾特性及中國粉絲群組的形成，是次研究將會以質性研究方法中的核心小組討論及深入訪問收集數據。是次研究會同時針對日本動漫畫進行文本分析，藉此探究中國城市年青人的閱讀習慣、粉絲群組形成以及日本外來文化產品對中國的文化衝擊。在收集上述數據之後，這項研究將會探索一套嶄新的理論模組，用以解構主動閱讀、粉絲形成過程及衍生文化輸出（如粉絲創作），並就文化消費對青少年身份及價值的影響建立理論論據。同時，基於國家資訊監控此一特殊性，是次研究除了可以顯示外來文化產品及粉絲形成如何轉變、改變及淡化中國國族意識形態，其結論亦可應用於同樣進行資訊監控的國家。這項研究展現世界公民概念如何藉文化全球化產品，經跨國文化輸入得以打破當地國家資訊監控的局面、改變當地年青人現存的國族意識形態及文化偏見。在全球傳理理論中，這項研究能為日後相關研究及社會與全球的文化角力中帶來長遠的啟示。

14617716.label: Realisation of objectives
14617716.value: All the three research objectives have been accomplished under the proposed time frame (in the proposed three phrases). There is no difficulty in accomplishing all the fieldwork in China. Fieldwork in China has been assisted (in terms of coordination and arrangement) by Beijing Normal University where the PI is now also affiliated with, and by Jinan University in Guangzhou where the PI used to serve as the Pearl River Chair Professor. Fieldwork in Japan is all arranged by co-I and his Ph.D. students and helpers recruited from Tokyo University of Arts, Tokyo University and Waseda University. The entire project is also facilitated by a Ph.D. student and another Ph.D. student that PI co-supervise in Communication University of China (with each Ph.D. leading to publications with PI and Co-I as seen in Part C). First Objective With an interdisciplinary perspective and based on empirical studies, the research team has examined the youth’s models of interpretation and ways of reading comic/anime in different research sites. Multiple methodologies were applied to tackle the research questions. We conducted 10 focus group interviews in Beijing, Shanghai, Hong Kong, Guangzhou and Tokyo. The entire focus group study involved recruitment and participation of more than 100 animation-comic-game (ACG) fans (mainly young generation below age of 25). Guidelines of the focus groups were developed. The PI and co-I travelled together to serve as moderator of focus groups in Beijing and Tokyo, while the RA hired and Ph.D. students conducted focus groups in Shanghai and Guangzhou. Questions about their reception of Japanese comic/anime (in comparison with China’s own production), their interpretation, cross-border consumption, and fandom formation were asked. After the focus group study, interpretation strategies of the three groups were compared and analyzed. Subsequently, after formulating specific thesis and hypotheses about the pattern of readings and models of interpretation, we conducted 9 more follow-up interviews with ACG fans as comic artists, as member of doujin groups (meaning those who engage in secondary production or reproduction based on the original anime) (Studio Realistic, Edogawa Fire, Seven Lives, ForestFire, 0.5 fuyuka, NeoGod and Fingerfish) and as those who participate in ACG festivals in Hong Kong and ComicUp (ACG festival) in Shanghai. The research team accomplished these fieldwork through informal and formal means. For individual fans, we spent time to join, discuss and gain trust with these doujin fandom before they accepted our interviews. Through the formal channel of Hong Kong’s ACG Festival 2018/ 2019, the research team also went to Hong Kong Conventional Centre where ACG Festival took place for observations and interviews. Second Objective: To investigate the process of fandom formation, fan labor (meaning that fans contribute for secondary production or the user generated content (UGC)) and consumption in relation to fan activities, after the focus group interviews, specific participants in relation to fandom organization were selected for interviews. In addition, through snowball sampling and referral, we also interviewed (1) active comic reader involved in various fandom activities, (2) members in fan club, (3) those who hold important position in the fan club, and (4) other key opinion leaders/ readers among Hong Kong and China’s fandom communities. Altogether, we conducted more than over 100 formal and informal in-depth interviews. Based on these interviews and discussion on Chinese blogs (e.g. Baidu Tieba and other animation discussion platforms), we assessed the popularity of these anime and selected around 15 specific Japanese animation and comics for textual analysis. For some anime (e.g. Naruto, Fullmetal Alchemist, Deathnote, etc.), selected episodes were analyzed (with some specific fans’ comments and analysis appearing on publications); for some cases such as Attack on Titans that was significant enough to be developed for an independent publication, the whole narrative was systematically analyzed. In this textual analysis, we extracted values, ideologies and themes embedded in these titles and, more important, examined potential alignment or contradiction with existing values of the fans and the social context. Third Objective To shed light on the cultural impact of the anime consumption, in particular on youth identities and culture in China, apart from probing into values of consumption and fans’ production, the PI also did multiple interviews with Chinese creative industries that are relevant for the production, dissemination and circulation of youth culture, including Tencent and Douyin (the largest short video platform). These producers should be the most informed frontline workers who understand the tastes and needs of these young audience. Their production experience and interactions with the Chinese fandom enabled them to develop insight about the cultural impact of these cultural production. The analysis involved not only evaluating the specific impact of Japanese content on Chinese youth under the complicated history of the Sino-Japanese diplomatic relationship (which is a reception study), but also how Japanese product as a regional or global product that could affect and shape the imaginaries (e.g. imagination, perception, values, symbolic meanings, etc.) of youth in China, and hence the youth culture. This is a theoretical question of cultural globalization, and this part involved more discussion and analysis among members of the research team. In general, the habits of comic/ anime consumption, together with the existing Chinese mainstream culture and popular culture, have shaped Chinese youth’s identity, values and sense of citizenship for the generation. In general, instead of finding a strong incompatibility among values of Japanese (global) cultural product and that of Chinese culture, in fact, Chinese youth are able to harmonize well the global and local cultures, and eventually, develop their own youth culture and create new ones through UGC on various social media platforms. In sum, the entire research team accomplished all research objectives in that the PI, co-I, the RA employed and the Ph.D. student of the PI collaborated and conducted the fieldwork in different research sites and published the findings found with coauthorship. During the end of the research, in particular, the PI, together with his Ph.D. students, attempted to publish all major findings of the study (see section 6).

14617716.label: Major findings and research outcome
14617716.value: First, there are differential patterns of reading strategies and interpretation of audience in the three places examined. In short, Japanese audience more often treat animation as mere entertainment. Rarely do they overinterpret the relationship between societal context and animation content. Hong Kong youth reading Japanese animation (and even local ones) tend to focus on universal values such as justice, equality and freedom embedded in these animations. Chinese audience display more diverse and complicated ways of interpretation: while some audience appropriate the ideological parcels more flexibly and contingently, some have strong reflection over their society based on the imagination that derives from the animation. Output described in Part C 8(1-3, 8) and 9(1) are all publications describing these findings in details. The second outcome is about how specific imported cultural products (e.g. Attack in Titans) and secondary production (or reproduction) of fans, transform youth culture, drive social change, and represent the incompatibility or reconciliation with the ideologies of the state or nationalism. In the publications, we mainly explicate the new and alternative imaginings of values and global citizenship of youth in China due to such border-crossing or global consumption. This research area is an enduring area in international communication studies. One of the academic papers is now in review in an SSCI-listed international communication journal and the other is published as a book chapter under University of Amsterdam Press, as seen in outputs in Part C 8(4-5). The third outcome, that is, the cultural effect of fandom, is the most unexplored area in the field globally and in China. Under the digital era, fandom formation in fact empowers youth, for example, in actively selecting their animation choice, resisting and even detesting contents—sometimes in collective action--that are contradictory to their aesthetics and values. Besides, fandom nowadays has concrete buying power, thereby, creating a big online fandom economy. In order to cater to tastes and preferences of the new generation, we have seen creative industries have an about-change of their strategy: from listening to monitoring fandom before production. Such important findings (which is also related to new media) enable the team to publish in top SSCI and CSSCI-listed journal as seen in outputs in Part C 8(6-7). Moreover, this study trains up and provides a rich data support to PI’s Ph.D. student Boris Pun for his dissertation on Chinese ACG fandom, which, mainly examines how fans as labor acquire skills and knowledge about production of animation.

14617716.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14617716.value: One of the prominent findings is that, apart from cultural differences, audience reception and digital fandom formation in Chinese and Asian societies display observable collective behaviors. As said, facilitated by social media (e.g. TikTok, Tencent, etc.), there is a strong connection between ACG fandom and other fandoms (e.g. fandom of all online content, including video, novel, and UGC). What is worth further investigating is the pattern of connections, its social consequences and youth culture formation. Second, on the business side, instead of producing content by estimating individual taste and needs of audience, creative industries can now be informed by the increasingly crisscrossing fandom, their preferences and behaviors. Future studies could focus on how creative industries have to depend on fandom economy for maximizing impact and profit. Third, the interconnection/ inseparability of entertainment content among various forms (e.g. among novel, animation and games) manifests the convergence of value-chain of creative industries enhanced by the IP (intellectual property) in that, for example, animation can be easily translated to games to target the same fans group in the market/ across regions. The study of IP trade, popular culture, globalization/ localization is an important area for further policy and academic research.

14617716.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14617716.value: This project focuses on Chinese readers who are identified as an active community reading and interpreting Japanese comics/anime. The findings and conclusions contain both cultural and commercial implications. First, what has been found is that there is a strong cultural difference between young generation audience at different cities, implying that, on the aspect of cultural impact, hardly is there any global/ regional/ universal impact or values (e.g. equality, justice, humanity, etc.) interpreted across communities, and therefore, creative industries have to devise and identify diverse strategies so as to target and satisfy their audience. Second, strategies of creative industries and content studied are not just about modifying, localizing or creating appropriate cultural content. In the process of fans’ consumption (and sometimes reproduction as in UGC), online fandom as a “cultural intermediary” has become the crucial factor that not only shapes fans’ attitudes and worldview. From the point of view of creative industries, understanding or co-opting fandom can also help market/ sell their comic/anime, develop their production, and maximize their interest. Third, while border-crossing reading does not necessarily lead to cultural homogenization, availability of global/ regional cultural product for consumption has become the basis for connection among global youth.

To develop a practice model to guide and promote sexuality nursing care in clinical practice in Hong Kong.

14620316.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14620316.value: Gynaecological cancer (GC) refers to cancer involving the female reproductive tract, i.e. cervix, uterus, ovaries, vulva, vagina and fallopian tubes. A diagnosis of GC and the effects of related treatment have devastating effects on sexual functioning. According to the National Cancer Institute, sexual dysfunction affects 50% of GC survivors, and such problems may last for prolonged periods. Despite the profound impacts of impaired sexual functioning and the problems prevalent among GC patients, both care and interventions in this area are still neglected in Hong Kong. In current local clinical settings, no routine nursing care is provided to address sexuality needs. Limited information is available only when specifically requested, and its quality depends on the individual experience of nurses. Using a concept mapping approach, the research aims to develop a practice model that will guide and promote the provision of sexuality nursing care to Hong Kong GC patients. The proposed study will be implemented in three phases. In Phase I, a qualitative method will be used to explore and elicit perceptions of sexual functioning and ideas about good nursing practice in sexuality care from the perspectives of GC patients, their spouses/partners, registered nurses and physicians working in the gynaecological oncology unit. Statements generated in Phase I will be returned to the same participants for them to rate the perceived level of importance as to how each statement will affect the acceptability, appropriateness and feasibility of providing sexuality care. Based on these ratings, statistical techniques will be used to produce a concept map illustrating the relationships and clustering between the statements. Finally, in Phase III, the concept map will be used to inform the development of a practice model and local protocol to guide nurses and promote the provision of timely, effective and economical nursing care in the area of sexuality. A better understanding of GC patients and their spouses/partners, nurses and physicians’ opinions and concerns about sexuality care will have long-term impacts on healthcare services. An empirical practice model will help nurses to render more effective assistance to GC patients, their spouses/partners in adapting to the changes in sexuality after diagnosis and treatment. It is hoped in this way to open up a neglected area of nursing, to improve patients’ quality of life, and in some needy cases to bring timely medical consultation or professional care to bear, thus having a considerable humanitarian impact on individuals and families in Hong Kong.

14620316.label: Realisation of objectives
14620316.value: All objectives have been successfully achieved. To achieve objective 1, individual interviews was conducted to generate statements about opinions, perceptions, attitudes and experiences in the sexuality care area in Phase I. A total of 30 GC patients, 30 spouses/partner, 20 registered nurses and physicians from the gynaecological oncology unit of two acute hospitals in Hong Kong were interviewed. Each interview lasted for 30 to 40 minutes. Interview topics included factors contributing to the viability of sexuality care measures for GC patients, opinions towards the provision of such care by nurses and physicians’ perception on the role of nurses in providing sexuality care. All interviews were audio-taped and transcribed verbatim by a research assistant. From the interviews, 50 statements were generated which were consistent to the themes and statements obtained from the literature review. To achieve objective 2, the 50 statements generated in Phase I were ranked importance and sorted similarity by 76 participants. Multidimensional scaling was used to generate a two-dimensional point map of the statements. The goodness-of-fit indices, S-stress = 0.10 and RSQ = 0.95, indicate the statement map is good fit to the data. Hierarchical cluster analysis was then performed to partition the statement map into clusters and a seven-cluster solution was identified with the smallest and greatest clusters comprising four and nine statements respectively. The clusters in the concept map include (1) information giving, (2) discussion about sexual impact of treatment, (3) organisational support, (4) attitude towards sexuality care provision, (5) personnel involved in sexuality care delivery, (6) mode of sexuality care delivery and (7) timing of sexuality care delivery. With regard to the results of importance rating, among the seven clusters, discussion about sexual impact of treatment was rated as the highest importance (mean = 5.9±0.9), whereas mode of sexuality care delivery was rated as the least importance (mean = 5.1±0.9). To achieve objective 3, the concept map was used to inform the development of a practice model and local protocol that would guide nurses in how to provide timely, effective and economical sexuality nursing care for GC patients. The outline of the protocol is shown below: Standard Statement All GC patients’ needs for sexuality care are assessed, and appropriate intervention and support are provided to address these sexual healthcare needs. Expected Outcomes 1. GC patients will receive sexuality care in clinical setting. 2. Healthcare professionals will proactively deliver individualised sexuality care to GC patients. Structure Standard The gynae-oncology care team includes: - Protocol introducer# - Healthcare professional# - Organisational support# Process Standard This process standard was guided by the Extended PLISSIT (Ex-PLISSIT) model (Taylor & Davis, 2006), which has five phases. Findings from the study were incorporated into each phase of the Ex-PLISSIT model to guide sexuality nursing care for Hong Kong GC patients. 1. Permission-giving stage# All healthcare professionals should take the initiative in discussing sexual issues with GC patients. Sexuality care should be provided to all patients, irrespective of their age, type or severity of cancer, treatment modality and availability of sexual partner. 2. Limited Information stage# During this stage, healthcare professionals should provide information about the impact of GC and its treatment on sexuality and sexual functioning, clarify misconceptions and dispel myths (Taylor & Davis, 2006). 3. Specific Suggestions stage# This stage aims to address the patient’s particular problem using a problem-solving approach. Suggestions have to be tailored to address individual needs (Taylor & Davis, 2006). 4. Intensive Therapy stage# For issues that are beyond the competence of healthcare professionals, patients should be referred to other professional sources: sexual therapist, clinical psychologist or psychosexual counsellor (Taylor & Davis, 2006). 5. Reflection and review# To ensure the sexuality care provided meets patient needs, it is important to reassess sexual healthcare needs regularly or during medical follow-up with patients and adjust the content accordingly. For healthcare professionals, clinical supervision should provide opportunities to reflect on current practice, explore feelings and challenge any assumptions (Taylor & Davis, 2006). Outcome Standard 1. GC patients receive sexuality care in clinical setting. 2. Healthcare professionals proactively deliver sexuality care to GC patients. #Details not shown here Reference: Taylor, B., & Davis, S. (2006). Using the extended PLISSIT model to address sexual healthcare needs. Nursing Standard (Royal College of Nursing (Great Britain): 1987), 21(11), 35-40. The newly developed protocol was returned to 17 healthcare professionals in Phase I for further validation using a survey with open-ended questions. The appropriateness and acceptability of the protocol were assessed on a five-point Likert scale ranging from “very appropriate/ acceptable” to “very inappropriate/ unacceptable”. Among the 17 respondents, 88.2% of them found the protocol to be acceptable or very acceptable while 82.4% of them found the protocol as appropriate or very appropriate. Qualitative comments on the protocol was also gathered. Some participants raised concerns about readiness of nurses to provide sexuality care, insufficient resources and training. There were also a few suggestions on the topic (onco-fertility), format (group format not appropriate), timing of provision (post-surgery not appropriate) and priority setting (low priority for those with older age or those without a partner).

14620316.label: Major findings and research outcome
14620316.value: This study was implemented in three phases. In Phase I, a qualitative method was used to explore and elicit perceptions of sexual functioning and ideas about good nursing practice in sexuality care from the perspectives of different stakeholders. A total of 30 GC patients, 30 spouses/partners, 20 registered nurses and physicians working in the gynaecological oncology unit were recruited for individual interviews. Each interview lasted for 30 to 40 minutes. After analysis, 50 statements were generated. The 50 statements were then returned to the same participants for them to rate the level of similarities and perceived level of importance in good sexuality care. Based on these ratings, we applied statistical techniques to produce a concept map illustrating the relationships and clustering between the statements. The map depicted seven clusters of statements grouped under seven themes in descending order of importance: discussion about sexual impact of treatment, organisational support, information giving, attitude towards sexuality care provision, personnel involved in sexuality care delivery, timing of sexuality care delivery and mode of sexuality care delivery. Finally, in Phase III, the concept map was used to inform the development of local protocol to guide nurses and promote the provision of timely, effective and economical nursing care in the area of sexuality. The newly developed protocol was returned to 17 healthcare professionals for further validation using a survey with open-ended questions. Among the 17 respondents, 88.2% of them found the protocol to be acceptable or very acceptable while 82.4% of them found the protocol as appropriate or very appropriate. Some participants raised concerns about readiness of nurses to provide sexuality care, insufficient resources and training. There were also a few suggestions on the topic, format, timing of provision and priority setting.

14620316.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14620316.value: With the positive feedback from the healthcare professionals of the study regarding the acceptability and appropriateness of the newly developed protocol on sexuality nursing care in the local clinical context, further study should explore the feasibility of territory-wide dissemination of this protocol in clinical setting. The feasibility study should explore the views and opinions towards the protocol among clinical and management staff in all clinical setting that provides GC care. In particular, the barriers of implementing the protocol and strategies to overcome such barriers should be explored. For example, the availability of culturally sensitive sexual health training resources and referral options for healthcare professionals. At the government level, the findings of the feasibility study could be used to inform health policy. On the other hand, the protocol may also be used to produce clinical indicators of practice standards and alert stakeholders the aspects of care that need to be reviewed and improved.

14620316.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14620316.value: The diagnosis and treatment of GC can have significant impacts on sexual well-being. To date, such area of assessment and care have been surrounded by silence, especially in Chinese societies. A detailed understanding of patient needs – and of the quality of existing sexuality care services – is a crucial step in promoting patient-centred sexuality care. Using a concept mapping approach, this research aimed to develop a practice model that would guide and promote the provision of sexuality nursing care to GC patients in clinical setting. To our knowledge, this is the first study that explored the views of a variety of stakeholders on sexuality care in Hong Kong. A better understanding of GC patients and their spouses/partners, nurses and physicians’ opinions and concerns about sexuality care could have long-term impacts on healthcare services. The findings helped to inform the development of a protocol that could help nurses to render more effective assistance to patients, their spouses/partners in adapting to the changes in sexuality after diagnosis and treatment. Notably, the feedback from nurses supported the acceptability and appropriateness of the newly developed protocol in the local context, implying that there is a potential for territory-wide dissemination of this protocol.

14621516.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14621516.value: Republican period of Shanghai has been perceived as a modern world of vibrant urban culture with a mixture of traditional Chinese and Western features of aesthetics. How to understand “modernization” and “modernity” in the art world has been one core issue in the field of twentieth century Chinese art history. The recent two decades have witnessed a transition in the theoretical approach from interpreting the aesthetic features of artworks to examining the social context of cultural institutions and urban environment with advanced technologies, managerial style and urbanism. However, the connection between the geographic distribution of artists and the urban context is a yet unexplored issue. The geographic accessibility of cultural institutions/facilities to artists reflects the probability of using the cultural facilities and communicating with cultural organizations. The emergence of clusters of artists, if any, would be an important indicator of dense cultural exchange and co-learning activities within a certain geographic scope in Shanghai. If clusters existed, what were the urban conditions that triggered the agglomeration, open and tolerant cultural policies, dynamic art market, affordable rents, convenient traffic and others? A literature review of Shanghai urban history confirms this as a missing piece of knowledge. This research innovatively introduces the hot concept of “creative milieu” in the bourgeoning literature of human geography and economic geography to tentatively interpret modernity of urban art scene in Republican Shanghai. It aims to find out whether the modern urban art scene in Republican Shanghai can be conceptualized as “creative milieu” that catered to the artists’ activities, which had the potential leading to the prosperity of art and culture in Shanghai. This research will 1) develop a database of the locations of artists’ residences and workplaces, the locations of business services and cultural organizations and facilities in Republican Shanghai; 2) use historic GIS approach to analyze the spatial features of artists’ geographic distribution and their relationships with the organizations and infrastructure; 3) generate a geographically weighted regression (GWR) model to quantitatively explain the variables that led to the emergence of clusters; 4) qualitatively explore the feature of the urban environment that fostered the clusters, e.g., cultural policies and cultural ambience; and finally 5) explore the internal features of the art clusters, if any, e.g., cooperation and competition in the inter-artist networks. Methodologically, this research will be based on rich primary sources of data and innovatively apply historical GIS technologies to the geographies of artists in Shanghai. 民國時期的上海，常被視為一個具有活躍文化、混合傳統中國及西方審美元素的摩登城市。如何理解藝術領域中的“現代化”及“現代性”為二十世紀中國畫史中的一個核心議題。近二十年中國近代畫史的理論取向出現了從解釋藝術作品的美學特徵向關注文化機構及社會環境的轉變，尤其關注技術進步、管理風格，以及城市特徵所帶來的影響。然而，藝術家的地理分佈與城市環境之間的關係，卻尚未被學者研究。文化機構的可及性反映了使用文化設施，以及參與文化組織的條件。藝術家社群的存在與否，則表明一定地理範圍內可能存在的較為密集的文化交流，以及共同學習的活動。進而言之，如若藝術家社群果真存在，那是什麼樣的城市及社會條件使然？民國上海是否具有開放及具有容忍性的文化政策、活躍的藝術市場、可負擔的房價、方便的交通？上海城市歷史的文獻回顧顯示此為未知之知識。 本研究創造性地將人文地理以及經濟地理中熱議之概念：“創意環境”，引入民國上海近代城市藝術風景之研究。其目的在於探索當時上海是否存在我們今天討論之適合藝術家活動之“創意環境”，並由此帶來民國上海文化及藝術之繁榮。 本研究將 1）建立一個上海藝術家居住及工作地點的數據庫；2）應用歷史地理信息系統分析藝術家地理分佈的空間特徵，以及他們與文化組織及設施的空間關係；3）建立一個地理權重的關聯模型，以量化地解釋變量與集聚效果之間的關係；4）定性地探索集聚形成之條件，如文化政策、文化氛圍等，及其與城市環境之間的關係；最後，如果藝術家的聚落存在，5）將探索聚落內部的特徵，如合作、競爭，以及藝術家之間的人際脈絡。 研究方法上，本研究將基於豐富的第一手資料，創造性地運用歷史地理信息系統技術，分析民國上海藝術家的地理分佈特徵。

14621516.label: Realisation of objectives
14621516.value: 1, To build a database of artists’ locations of residence and workplaces in Republican Shanghai. We collected both first-hand and second-hand historic data from 156 biographies, 22 auto-biographies, 9 types of Republican-period newspapers, 33 types of magazines, 652 academic books, 288 academic papers, 94 memories, and 57 volumes of archives housed in the Shanghai Archive House. A database of artists’ locations of residence and workplaces in Republican Shanghai was built, including 1368 artists’ residential addresses (valid historical period specified). We were aware of the deficiency of one single database: due to the incompleteness of historical data, the data stored in the database are insufficient to illustrate a full picture of transforming pattern (artists’ spatial distribution). Thus, we built the second database that concentrates on 48 artists drawing on complete residential addresses across the historical span of 36 years. Moreover, to identify the relationship between the spatial pattern and the surrounding causal factors, e.g., schools, libraries, bookstore, exhibition halls, we built the third database of cultural facilities locations, which comprises three types of data, i.e., social facilities (e.g., restaurants, bars, coffee shops, entertainment venues), cultural facilities (e.g., exhibition halls, museums, stationary stores), and cultural organizations (e.g., art societies, book stores). We collected data for the identified variables from 18 types of Republican period business guides, e.g., Da Shanghai Zhinan (Shanghai Business Guide), which contain (1) 591 addresses of food and beverage venues (e.g., restaurant, teahouse, dim sum shop, coffee shop); (2) 445 addresses of leisure and recreational venues (e.g., theatre, cinema, private garden, park); and (3) 1,116 addresses of cultural facilities and art shops (e.g., library, museum, archive house, publishing house, fan shop, photoshop, antique shop). 2. To produce maps of artists’ geographical distribution and reveal the transformations of the pattern across years. We selected eight years for spatial analysis, attempting to capture historical transitions in Republican Shanghai, i.e., 1912, 1920, 1925, 1928, 1933, 1936, 1942 and 1948. To prepare spatial data, we selected two Shanghai maps, ‘Zuixin Shanghai Jieshi Tu’ (The Latest Shanghai Neighborhood Map) (1937 and 1947) on the scale of 1:20,000, from the virtual Shanghai website due to their high resolution. The datum that we used is based on the Open Street Map coordinate system. With ArcGIS 10.2, we performed heads-up digitizing and geo-registered our base maps using 50 control points each. In this process, rubber sheeting and spline transformation were used to improve the precision. Our digitalized map of 1937 comprises 1087 streets, and the 1947 map comprises 675 streets. We used the K function to identify the spatial clusters of artists, located art clusters in urban districts with social and political meanings, analyzing the district density of artists, hot spots and the social connections of each cluster. We identified 4-14 functional clusters in each of the selected years, which reveals the dynamics of the spatial distribution pattern during the course of the Republican period of history. 3. To build a regression model that explains how a number of variables affected the spatial clustering of artists. We selected three years to build regression models, Year 1920, Year 1930 and Year 1948. We built one multiple linear regression model, one spatial lag model, one spatial error model and one GWR model for each of the three years. For Year 1920, we tested six combinations of 14 independent variables and chose the combination of seven independent variables according to the statistical significance (90% confidence level or above), the multicollinearity and heteroscedasticity issues, and the R square value of the model. 59.25% of the variation of the density of artists about its mean can be explained by the combination of the density of restaurants, private gardens, art schools, art organizations and art intermediaries (positive correlation) and the density of museums and antique shops (negative correlation). To explore how qualitative conditions, e.g., policies and cultural ambiences, affected the clustering of artists. Our research project shows that policies, cultural policies in particular, had positive impact on artists’ location selection. Both of the French Concession and the International Concession attained an evident higher degree of concentration compared with the district under the governance of the Chinese authority. Evidence shows tolerance for diverse lifestyles and freedom of speech was an important contributing factor towards spatial agglomeration of artists. 5. To study the features of the artists’ clusters, e.g., inter-actor networks, in the clusters. To understand the characteristics of our identified major functional clusters with respect to social networks. The key issue is to determine whether short linkages or long-distance pipelines were the major type of social networks. We first computed the ‘mean nearest neighbor distance’ which is the average distance from one point to its nearest neighboring point (Getis, 1992; Griffith, 1987). This number provides a reference value for evaluating the mean geodesic distance of all the pairwise social connections. In theory, if all networks existed within geographic clusters, the average geodesic distance should not be much longer than the mean nearest neighbor distance. We set up a threshold for tolerating cross-cluster linkages. We ran one Z test and two t-tests in this sub-section to meet the second objective. The Z test was used to compare the average geodesic distance of all the pairwise social connections and the threshold based on one-tailed probabilities. The second and third t-tests are two-sample difference-of-Means test for μ_(1 - ) μ_(2 ). We compared the mean geodesic distance of all pairwise social contacts in the key functional clusters with that of all networks (year specific). The same mechanism was applied the first-tier artists of popularity living in the major clusters and the major clusters. We conclude that long-distance pipelines were the major type of social connections in the major art clusters.

14621516.label: Major findings and research outcome
14621516.value: There are four main findings of this research. First, from 1912 to 1948, the overall spatial distribution pattern of artists in transformation was gravitated from the Chinese City into the foreign settlements. This process, however, was disrupted by the Sino-Japanese War outbreak (1937) and the Civil War outbreak (1945), when some artists moved out of the city taking asylum in other Chinese cities and overseas. Foreign concessions have achieved higher degrees of concentrations compared with the Chinese authority governed district. We used the K function to identify the spatial clusters of artists and also used hot spot analysis to determine the urban districts surrounded by areas of similar densities. We identified 4-14 clusters in each of the selected years, which reveals the dynamics of the spatial distribution pattern through the course of the Republican period of history. Further, we considered artists’ social networks and identified the major functional clusters that balanced the density of artists and the quantity of their social connections. Second, we explored ten categories of independent variables and discussed the nuances on the qualitative and quantitative dimensions. Through this effort, we developed more sophisticated understanding about the factors that contributed to a creative milieu. In line with the literature, art school, art organization and transportation are found to be the crucial factors that led to the spatial clustering of artists. Different from the literature, individual art intermediaries, instead of gallery or art shop, have been confirmed to be a significant factor. Other important factors include library, private garden and restaurant. Publishing house, park, ballroom and theatre were relevant only to particular groups of artists or historical period, yet less generalizable to the whole population. Third, cultural policy was a critical factor that influenced the spatial congregation of artists. The French Concession enacted two key policies during the period of 1912 – 1931, open to diverse lifestyles, being tolerant with critical views and revolutionary activities. A tolerant and open cultural atmosphere – produced by cultural policies – was concerned by the artists. Finally, vibrant inter-actor networks played an important role in attracting artists to conglomerate. This also contributed to the formation of functional clustering of artists in the foreign concessions in Shanghai. We have identified six centers of the artists’ networks and their intensive communications in support of teaching, learning and socializing activities. These constructive inter-actor networking stimulated mutual learning and characterized the clusters with functional features.

14621516.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14621516.value: This research has developed an understanding about the broad social and urban context underlying the transformation of the art landscape during the Republican period of Shanghai. Our research has rich implications to both research fields of twentieth century Chinese art history and Chinese urban history. For future researchers of modern Chinese art history, they may take into account the urban environment and the artists’ networks when researching the modernization of Chinese art. This new perspective may guide the researchers to discover the new meanings of modern Chinese art, such as the integration of the urban imagery based on individual artists’ perceptions on the cultural facilities, urban public spaces and restaurants and bars. Also, socializing activities taking advantage of geographic proximity boosted collaborative artistic practices, resulting in a sense of modernity. To researchers of modern Chinese urban history, the landscape of artists as well as their artistic activities should constitute one dimension of urban modernity, which goes beyond the built environment. This means that researchers may further explore how the presence and activities of artists in groups at some urban venues (e.g., restaurants, bars, book stores, publishing houses, art schools and organizations) created a modern sense of place.

14621516.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14621516.value: This research maps the residential locations of visual artists who were active in the Republican period Shanghai art world from 1912 to 1948 using Historical Geographic Information System (HGIS), R and pgadmin4 (database management software). We created three databases. The first database stores the locational information of 1,368 artists, which reveals their spatial distribution pattern. The second database focuses on 48 artists with a complete set of addresses. Mapping the two datasets reveals the track of artists’ relocation from the Chinese City into the foreign settlements. The factors that contributed to the spatial concentration of artists include art intermediaries, art schools, art organizations, cultural facilities (i.e., libraries and archive houses), recreational venues (i.e., ball rooms), food and beverage venues (i.e., restaurants), transportation and private gardens. Other factors were relevant to some particular groups of artists but not the entire population of artists. Such factors can be exemplified by newspaper and magazine offices, parks and theatres. Factors with little significance in creating artists’ spatial congregation include art shops, coffee shops and tea houses. Moreover, flexible cultural policy in the foreign concessions attracted artists. In addition, intensive and vibrant inter-act networks, contributing to the mutual learning, knowledge sharing and synergies among artists.

14623416.label: Project Title(Chinese)
14623416.value: 苦痛現象學：歷史、方法學及意義

14623416.label: Project Objectives
14623416.value: Demonstrate that phenomenology of pain offers a distinctive methodological approach to pain research and that this approach is to be understood as an alternative to naturalism and social constructionism, which are often conceived as the only possible methodological standpoints in pain research. Facilitate a cross-disciplinary dialogue between different human and social sciences of pain (especially philosophical, anthropological, psychoanalytic and neuroscientific studies of pain). Open a dialogue between phenomenology and cognitive science, especially with regard to various pain syndromes, such as pain asymbolia, threat hypersymbolia, and congenital analegia. Demonstrate how such a dialogue enables phenomenology to clarify the experiential structures of lobotomized, cingulotomized and morphinized patients. Demonstrate that phenomenology of pain has a history that is no shorter than the history of phenomenology itself. The goal is to establish a historic tie that binds classical phenomenological studies of pain to contemporary phenomenological pain research. Offer a critique of the exclusively neurophysiological approach to pain, which suggests that the subject of pain is the body, conceived neurophysiologically, and that only a feeling derived from organic causes is to be identified as pain. Demonstrate that the subject of pain is not the body, conceived neurophysiologically, but the person, conceived phenomenologically, i.e., as a subject with a unique history, who holds a unique relation to the surrounding world and a distinctive communicative relation to others. Offer a phenomenological description of chronic pain as a temporally extended process, marked not only by depersonalization, but also repersonalisation, and show that as a temporally extended process, chronic pain necessarily provokes the subject’s responses to pain, which are essentially of three types: bodily, emotive, and cognitive. In their own turn, these three types of responses to pain constitute the phenomenological basis that underlies the processes of somatization and psychologization.
