14623416.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14623416.value: A GRF grant would enable me to spend the next three years writing a book manuscript on the phenomenology of chronic pain. To this day, in the English-speaking philosophical world, there is not a single book-length phenomenological study of chronic pain. My goal is to fill this gap by offering a cross-disciplinary investigation, which brings phenomenology into conversation with analytical philosophy, anthropology, cognitive science, psychoanalysis, psychology and sociology. The available literature on the phenomenology of pain suffers from three fundamental deficiencies. First, there is a methodological flaw. No study has demonstrated what is distinctive about the phenomenological research on pain. My goal is to show that only insofar as it relies on the phenomenological method (the phenomenological and eidetic reductions in particular) can pain research be qualified as phenomenological. Most importantly, insofar as it proceeds in accordance with its own methodology, phenomenology offers a third and much needed alternative to two established methodological standpoints in pain research, viz., naturalism and social constructionism. Secondly, there is a historical deficiency. Current phenomenological studies of pain are disconnected from their own heritage. My goal is to offer a historically oriented analysis, which builds a phenomenological account on the basis of F. Brentano’s, C. Stumpf’s, E. Husserl’s, M. Scheler’s, E. Stein’s, F.J.J. Buytendijk’s and J.P. Sartre’s works. Thirdly, one can also speak of a “deficiency of relevance.” It remains unclear why phenomenological studies of pain are significant for philosophy, pain research, and medicine. With the aim of counteracting this deficiency, I will aim to demonstrate that: 1) Phenomenology of pain clarifies a number of central conceptual distinctions in philosophy of medicine (especially between such fundamental concepts as suffering, pain, illness and sickness). 2) By providing an eidetic point of access to pain experience and showing that pain is a highly stratified phenomenon, it dispels some fundamental equivocations that surround pain research (especially between pain conceived as a natural, sociocultural and psychological). 3) By recognizing that the subject of pain is the person, and not the body (Körper), phenomenological investigations lead to the recognition of the ethical and therapeutic significance of dialogue in pain research. 迄今為止，在英語哲學界，還沒出版過一本關於慢性苦痛的現象學研究書籍。為此，我希望用跨領域的研究方法，以現象學為經，跟分折哲學、人類學、認知科學、精神分析學、心理學和社會學等學科互為比較和切磋。優配研究金的撥款使我在往後三年有能力寫這本書。 現有的苦痛現象學研究有三大缺失。首先是方法學的問題 —— 沒有研究能清楚說明用現象學來研究苦痛有何獨特之處。我希望能說明，只要以現象學的方法來研究苦痛 (特別是現象學和本質還原方法)，這個研究就算得上苦痛現象學的研究。更為重要的是，從關於苦痛經驗的方法學而言，除自然主義和社會建構主義兩個研究方法之外，現象學堪足第三個研究苦痛的方法。 第二個缺失是沒有歷史淵源。現今的苦痛現象學研究都跟歷史斷裂。我的研究則會加入歷史向度，借鏡於貝倫塔諾、史普夫、胡塞爾、舍勒、史坦茵、拜腾狄克、沙特等前人的研究成果，建立一個關於苦痛的現象學解釋。 直到現在，大家還不清楚用現象學法來研究苦痛，對哲學、苦痛研究和醫學有何重要，這亦是痛苦現象的第三個缺失 —— 相干性的缺失。為解決這個問題，我這個研究希望能說明三件事：一、苦痛現象學能闡明醫療哲學裏一些重要概念的毫釐分別 (特別是受傷、苦痛、病患和病症的分別)。二、提供一個討論苦痛經驗本質的觀點以及證明苦痛是個多層次的現象，掃除苦痛研究裏一些概念含糊的問題 (特別是自然的苦痛、社會文化的苦痛和心理的苦痛之間的分別)。三、當明白感受苦痛的是人而不是肉體，現象學研究令我們明白苦痛研究中道德和治療之間互為表裏這個重要之處。

14623416.label: Realisation of objectives
14623416.value: The GRF grant has enabled me to write a book, The Phenomenology of Pain (Ohio UP, Series in Continental Thought, publication date: February 20, 2020). I have met the central objectives in different chapters of this study. 1st Objective: Chapter 1, “Methodological Considerations,” demonstrates that phenomenology of pain offers a distinctive methodology for pain research, which must be conceived as an alternative to naturalism and social constructionism. Here I show that the methods of the epoché, the reduction and eidetic variation are the three principles that make up the methodological core of phenomenologically oriented pain research. I argue that the three fundamental phenomenological methods are necessary, yet not sufficient, and that they need to be supplemented with the method of factual variation. This opens phenomenology to the developments in other sciences—natural, social, and human—as well as to the advances in literature, poetry, cinema and fine arts. I further qualify the four methods outlined above as the methodological commitments of static phenomenology and I further argue that they need to be supplemented with the methodological principles of genetic phenomenology. 2nd Objective: it is met in different chapters of my study. Chapter 2, entitled “Pain and Intentionality: A Stratified Conception of Pain Experience,” opens the question concerning the relationship between the phenomenological conception of pain and the one that is prevalent in neurology, which suggests that pain is composed of sensory, emotive and cognitive components. Chapter 3, entitled “Phenomenology of Pain Dissociation Syndromes,” engages in a dialogue between phenomenology and those studies of pain, which rely on pain neurology. Chapters 6 and 7, entitled respectively “Phenomenology of Embodied Personhood: De-Personalization and Re-Personalization” and “Pain and the Life-World: Somatization and Psychologization,” open up a dialogue between phenomenology, psychoanalysis, cultural anthropology and cultural psychopathology. Throughout the study, I also engage in historical studies of pain as well as those that we come in fiction. 3rd Objective: it is met in the third chapter of my book. This chapter engages in a dialogue between phenomenology and cognitive science. Here I argue that a stratified conception of pain experience, as presented in Chapter II, can clarify the structure of a number of pain dissociation syndromes. I pay close attention to congenital insensitivity to pain, threat hypersymbolia, pain asymbolia as well as the so-called “pain affect without pain sensation.” Here I also address the experiential structures that are modified through lobotomy, cingulotomy and morphine. My task is to demonstrate that these highly perplexing pain syndromes can be rendered comprehensible not only neurologically, but also phenomenologically. My task is to show how the analysis of these pain syndromes can enrich our understanding of the fundamental structures of pain experience. 4th Objective: The second chapter of my study meets this objective. Here I turn to those reflections of pain that we come across in classical phenomenology, and especially in the works of Brentano, Stumpf, Husserl and Sartre. Firstly, I give an account of the central reasons that underlie the Stumpfian view that pain is a non-intentional feeling-sensation. Secondly, I turn to the Brentanian position and clarify the different ways in which one can understand pain as an intentional emotion. Thirdly, argue that there are good reasons to preserve both views and suggest that Husserl’s schema of apprehension — content of apprehension enables one to do just that. Fourthly, I further contend that such a standpoint clarifies what it means to claim that pain can only be given in first-hand experience. I maintain that the proposed resolution leads to the realization that pain is an irreducible stratified phenomenon. The stage is thereby set to clarify the experiential structures of various pain syndromes, which are then addressed in Chapter III. 5th and 6th Objectives: The sixth chapter meets both objectives. According to my central claim in this chapter, the subject of pain is not the body, conceived neurophysiologically, but the person, conceived phenomenologically. After showing why this claim is polemically set against some entrenched assumptions in biomedicine, I turn to three implications that affect medical praxis. Firstly, drawing on psychoanalytic and anthropological studies, I argue that biomedicine’s indifference to the person’s unique relation to pain often renders physiological treatments of pain ineffective. Secondly, I show that even when physiological treatments are successful, they carry adverse consequences: they threaten to rob the patient of autonomy by making her dependent on those analgesics that were supposed to alleviate her suffering. Thirdly, I argue that medicine is an irreducibly ethical profession, whose primary responsibility is not to alleviate pain, but to help the patient confront the effects pain has upon the person’s self-relation, relation to the body, relation to others, and relation to the world at large. 7th Objective: The fifth and the seventh chapters meet this objective. Chapter V focuses on the temporal structures characteristic of pain experience. Firstly, the chapter demonstrates that the field of presence constitutes the exhaustive horizon within which chronic pain is lived. Secondly, it further show that chronic pain should be conceived as a form of de-personalization in that it cuts the field of presence from the past and the future. Thirdly, drawing on some recent findings in phenomenology, psychiatry and neurology, I show that the past and the future, despite their apparent irreality, continue to affect the present either through implicit bodily memory, or through implicit bodily anticipation. This means that, despite its de-personalizing effects, chronic pain is a deeply personal experience. The chapter also addresses the therapeutic significance of such a phenomenology of temporality. I maintain that if chronic pain is nested in implicit temporality, then to confront it, one must become conscious of its effects and, if possible, neutralize their meaning. Chapter 7 focuses on somatization and psychologization. These processes bring to light that pain is fundamentally a mosaic of physiological, psychic, cultural and social factors, for only so can pain be conceived as an indirect expression of social conflicts, as a defense mechanism against stigmatization, or as a help-seeking behavior. The person, I here maintain, is a fundamentally expressive being, while the life-world constitutes the general framework within which any expression can reach its fulfillment. However, the person’s immersion in the life-world is deeply paradoxical in that the life-world is not only the medium of expression, but also the framework that proscribes the expression of particular feelings, emotional dispositions and thoughts. Nonetheless, no matter how restrictive the concrete structures of the life-world might be, they cannot transmute the person’s fundamentally expressive nature. Insofar as direct modes of expression are forbidden, the person turns to the only possible alternative: she devises indirect modes of expression, transforming his body into a symbolic medium of coded messages. Pain, in this regard, is to be understood as a specific experience of separation: to be in pain is to feel separated from the life-world while at the same time being at home in the life-world. In the final analysis, the processes of somatization and psychologization teach us that the fundamental imperative inscribed in the experience of pain is not “stop,” but “listen,” and that the listening in question calls for attentive decoding and interpretation. In light of these details, I hold the view that I have met all the research objectives as stated in my objectives.

14623416.label: Major findings and research outcome
14623416.value: The major findings of this study fall into three categories: 1) methodological, 2) conceptual and 3) anthropological. 1) According to the view defended in this study, the methods of the phenomenological epoché, the phenomenological reduction and eidetic variation constitute the three fundamental and indispensable principles of phenomenologically oriented pain research. These principles are necessary, although not sufficient. The method of eidetic variation must be supplemented with factual variations. Such a supplementation provides the reasons needed to identify phenomenology as a dialogically oriented discipline. Besides that, static phenomenology, conceived as a methodological outlook that is based on the three fundamental methods mentioned above, must be supplemented with the fundamental principles of genetic phenomenology. Such, then, are the fundamental principles of phenomenological research. According to the view defended in this study, an investigation has the right to call itself phenomenological insofar as it subscribes to such a methodological orientation. 2) The goal was to provide the concept of pain with a definition that would be grounded in phenomenological principles. I argued that the established definition of pain, endorsed by the International Association for the Study of Pain (IASP), and which suggests that “pain is an unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with actual or potential tissue damage, or described in terms of such damage” (Merskey and Bogduk 1994, 209), is for various reasons unacceptable. Building on the basis of the methodological orientation as presented above, I argued that pain is an aversive bodily feeling with a distinct experiential quality, which can only be given in original first-hand experience, either as a feeling-sensation or as an emotion. This definition of pain, taken along with the justification that I have provided it with, is the most important finding of this study. 3) My goal was to demonstrate that the phenomenological concept of the person not only provides us with the possibility to conceptualize the embodied subjectivity as the subject of pain, but it also enables us to analyze the de-personalizing and re-personalizing nature of pain experience. Moreover, still within the framework of a philosophical anthropology, my goal was to demonstrate that a phenomenological approach, which considers the life-world as the ultimate horizon of pain experience, enables us to conceptualize such processes as somatization and psychologization, which so often affect the human experience of chronic pain.

14623416.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14623416.value: This study provides the basis to address some further important questions that were not tackled in this study directly. First, the pain of non-human animals: According to the view here defended, phenomenology should not be confused with any kind of autobiography, “pain narratives,” introspectionism, or psychologism. There are therefore no good reasons to claim that reflections on the pain of non-human animals take us beyond the limits of phenomenological research. The methodological framework developed in my study provides the basis to study animal pain from a phenomenological point of view. Ethical implications. They were not addressed in this study. One of the reasons is that here I was concerned with pain, as it is given in original first-person experience. I therefore left the ethical questions concerning the pain of others out of consideration. The reasons behind this omission are methodological. Nonetheless, this study should provide a strong methodological and conceptual basis to carry out an analysis that focuses on the ethical dimensions of pain experience from a phenomenological standpoint. My plan is to address both issues in separate publications.

14623416.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14623416.value: The Phenomenology of Pain is the first book-length investigation of its topic to appear in English. Groundbreaking, systematic, and illuminating, it opens a dialogue between phenomenology and such disciplines as cognitive science and cultural anthropology to argue that science alone cannot clarify the nature of pain experience without incorporating a phenomenological approach. Building on this premise, the study develops a novel conception of pain grounded in phenomenological principles: pain is an aversive bodily feeling with a distinct experiential quality, which can only be given in original first-hand experience, either as a feeling-sensation or as an emotion. The book crystallizes the fundamental methodological principles that underlie phenomenological research. On the basis of those principles, it offers a phenomenological clarification of the fundamental structures of pain experience and contests the common conflation of phenomenology with introspectionism. It further analyzes numerous pain dissociation syndromes, brings into focus the de-personalizing and re-personalizing nature of chronic pain experience, and demonstrates what role somatization and psychologization play in pain experience. In the process, the book advances Husserlian phenomenology in a direction that is not explicitly worked out in Husserl’s own writings.

14626416.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14626416.value: The global and local expansion of higher education systems starting from the twentieth century has a profound effect on youth transition from secondary school to higher education and work. In particular, nowadays it is common for youths to delay the transition until their early twenties (OECD, 2000). The life after upper secondary education from age 20 to 22 has become more important than ever before, and has been a stage when young adults make critical educational and/or career decisions. This project aims to investigate the complexity, stability and flexibility in Hong Kong young adults’ transition at this post-secondary stage. It attempts to identify the possible factors at individual, family, school and community levels which facilitate or hinder young adults’ transition after secondary education. Since 2000, the expansion in higher education in Hong Kong has taken place rapidly and mainly in the sub-degree sector, which has absorbed a large proportion of secondary graduates (EDB, 2013). While past research studies mainly focused on the employability and productivity of sub-degree graduates, little has been done to investigate “how” and “why” they are so. Besides, not much has been known about the relations between various background and contextual factors and young adults’ participation in higher education. Given that the Hong Kong higher education has entered into the post-massification period, there is an apparent need for an updated and comprehensive picture of Hong Kong young adults’ post-secondary transition. This study will be a continuation of the research endeavor started from the HKPISA 2012 and HKLSA studies. While these two studies have tracked the patterns of transition of a sample of young adults from 2013 to 2015, the present two-year study will continue to trace their pathways for two years from 2016 to 2018 after their graduation from secondary school. It will adopt a mixed-methods design, with an interview study and a questionnaire survey in the first year (2016-2017), and another questionnaire survey in the second year (2017-2018). While the quantitative part will collect information about young adults’ choices of education and/or occupation and the related factors, the qualitative part will provide interpretations of young adults’ choices from their own perspectives. It is expected that this study will provide insights on how the higher education policy and New Academic Structure have worked so far, and what appropriate educational and life planning policies can be formulated for our new generations. 自二十世紀開始，全球和本地高等教育體系擴展，對青少年從中學到高等教育或工作的歷程帶來重大影響。時至今日，青年人二十多歲才就業的情況漸趨普遍（經濟合作與發展組織，2000），由20至22歲高中教育後的階段變得更為重要，青年人往往須要在這階段作出重要的升學及／或就業抉擇。本計劃旨在探討香港青年人在完成中學階段後，其歷程的複雜性、穩定性及彈性，並識別能協助或阻礙青年人中學畢業後升學或就業的種種個人、家庭、學校及社區層面因素。 自2000年以來，香港的高等教育迅速發展，尤其集中在副學位界別上，此界別吸納了大量中學畢業生（教育局，2013）。以往研究主要探討副學位畢業生的就業能力和生產力，卻鮮有探討青年人升學就業選擇的過程及原因，以及他們接受高等教育與各種背景因素之間的關係。鑑於香港高等教育已步入擴張後期，實有需要掌握香港青年人中學畢業後歷程的整體面貌和最新情況。 本研究將建基於「香港學生能力國際評估計劃」（HKPISA 2012）及「香港青少年之追蹤研究」（HKLSA）所取得的研究成果。該兩項研究自2013至2015年追蹤一組青年人樣本的歷程模式，本研究將繼續追蹤這組青年人自中學畢業後兩年間（2016至2018年）的路向。研究將採用混合研究法：第一年（2016-2017年）將進行訪談研究及問卷調查，第二年（2017-2018年）將進行另一輪問卷調查。量化部分將收集有關青年人升學及就業的選擇及相關因素，質化部分則從青年人自身的角度來闡釋他們作出抉擇的歷程。預期本研究將為高等教育政策及新學制的成效提供參考數據，並為香港青年人的升學就業及生涯規劃政策提供啟示。

14626416.label: Realisation of objectives
14626416.value: The four objectives stipulated in the proposal have been achieved to the full extent. They are accomplished by the two waves of survey for young adults in accordance with the project proposal. The Wave 4 Questionnaire Survey was completed from June to August 2017. There were 847 young adults who completed the online survey and an additional 202 young adults who provided their current educational or occupational status only via telephone calls or instant messages, totaling 1049. The Wave 5 Questionnaire Survey was completed from January to May 2019. There were 760 young adults who completed the online survey and an additional 228 young adults who provided their current educational or occupational status only via telephone calls or instant messages, totaling 988. Compared with the previous waves of survey (Wave 1 to 3), the participating young adults in Wave 4 and Wave 5 surveys have a similar distribution of socio-economic background and gender, showing that the sample continues to be representative of the young adult population in Hong Kong. As for the first objective, the transition outcomes of young adults at the age of 20 and 22 have been examined in both waves of survey. These include their realization of higher education (HE) and occupation (Ho & Sum, 2021), adaptive or autonomous choice of HE programme or job (Ho & Sum, 2018a), completion or dropout from HE programme, job experience and income, educational and occupational expectation (Ho & Sum, 2019; Keung & Ho, 2019, 2020), satisfaction with HE programme or job, hope (Ho, 2019; Ho, Chiu, Sum, Cheung & Lee, 2021; Ho, Li & Lee, 2018), life satisfaction (Ho & Sum, 2021), career search competencies (Keung & Ho, 2020), career adaptability (Ho & Sum, 2018b; Ho, Sum & Lee, 2021) and perceived employability (Ho, Sum & Lee, 2021). These transition outcomes were analyzed with individual factors, including young adults’ gender, socio-economic background and immigrant status, which were collected in the previous waves of survey. This study has shown that a vast majority of sampled young adults (over 90%) are in employment or HE at age 22. About a half (55.1%) of sampled young adults are working either full-time or part-time only, and 27.7% are studying in either a local or non-local HE programme full-time or part-time only. Besides, there are 11.2% of young adults who are in both employment and HE. Young adults in local HE are mostly studying in a bachelor programme (75.8%). The major occupations of employed young adults are professionals (34.0%), technician and associate professionals (23.6%) and service and sales workers (21.3%). Finally, there are 5.2% of young adults who are not in education or employment. Regarding the second objective, a number of family factors have been identified as contributors to young adults’ transition outcomes. These include family resources (Keung & Ho, 2020), cultural communication with parents, career encouragement from parents, parental emotional support (Ho, 2019; Ho, Chiu, Sum, Cheung & Lee, 2021; Ho & Sum, 2018a, 2018b; Ho, Sum & Lee, 2020), social communication with parents, perceived parental expectation, actual parental expectation, living up to parental expectation (Ho, Li & Lee, 2018; Keung & Ho, 2020), and perceived career-related parental support (Ho, Li & Lee, 2018). In general, young adults at age 20 and 22 perceive a moderate level of support from their parents in terms of career encouragement, career guidance, and emotional support. Besides, they perceive more career encouragement than career guidance from parents, which may indicate a shift in parents’ role from being career advisors and information providers to encouragers and supporters in young adulthood (Ho & Sum, 2018b). Objective three is to examine the effect of institutional factors on the patterns of young adult’s transition after secondary education. The following conversion factors/ constraints have been assessed: sense of belonging to HE institution, attitudes towards HE institution, truancy, types of career guidance activities participated (Ho, Li & Lee, 2018; Keung & Ho, 2020), and institutional habitus of HE institutions perceived by young adults (Ho & Sum, 2017; Ho, Tse & Sum, 2020). This study has shown that young adults in HE are in general moderately engaged in their HE institutions, which is indicated by their moderate to high sense of belonging and attitudes towards institutions, and a low to moderate truancy. Among the various educational and career exploration activities, education and career talks are found to have a positive association with young adults’ expectations of pursuing a bachelor degree (Keung & Ho, 2020). Besides, the institutional habitus of HE institutions has shaped the HE decisions of young adults from different socio-economic backgrounds (Ho, Tse & Sum, 2020). For the fourth objective, the relative contributions of various family, school and community factors to young adults’ transitional outcomes have been studied and compared by means of different statistical methods. Specifically, comparisons have been made on young adults’ educational expectations, hope and career adaptability, to name but a few. By using logistic regression analysis, the different effects of family-level, school-level and individual’s capability factors on young adults’ expectations of pursuing a bachelor degree have been examined (Keung & Ho, 2020). Besides, by using latent growth model analysis, the relative contributions of individual and family background and academic achievements on the growth of young adults’ educational expectation have been investigated (Ho & Sum, 2019). By using mediation model analysis, the mediating effects of three types of parental support on the relationship between family socioeconomic status and young adults’ hope, which include cultural and academic communication and career encouragement from parents in early years, and current parental emotional support, have been investigated (Ho, Chiu, Sum, Cheung & Lee, 2021). Furthermore, the effects of parental support and peer support on the social disparity in young adults’ hope have been examined by mediation and moderation model analysis (Ho, Sum & Lee, 2020). Finally, by using multiple regression models, the relative contributions of three types of parental support, namely career guidance, career encouragement and emotional support, on young adults’ career adaptability have been compared (Ho & Sum, 2018b). Overall, this study has collected and analyzed data on the “achieved functionings at age 20-22”, “conversion factors/ constraints” and “capability set at age 20-22” according to the proposed Capability Approach Framework. It has provided evidence which generally supports that young adults from different backgrounds and prior achieved functionings mobilize different forms of capital from different fields including family, peers, HE institutions and workplace to a different extent, depending on the individual and institutional habitus. This affects their capability set, that is, their freedom of choice towards future education and career that they have reason to value, which in turn determines the achieved functionings in their subsequent life stages. It echoes the perspectives of Coleman, Bourdieu and Sen that whether and how social, cultural and economic capital can be converted into capability sets depends on internal (personal) and external (social and environmental) conversion factors in different fields. While this study has put an emphasis on young adults’ education and career, it is suggested that future investigation can be extended to other life domains including intimate and social relationships, health and well-being so as to gain a more comprehensive picture of young adults’ transition to adulthood.

14626416.label: Major findings and research outcome
14626416.value: (1) Educational expectations: There is a continuous decelerated growth in educational expectation from adolescence to young adulthood in Hong Kong (Ho & Sum, 2019). Specifically, at age 15, the percentage of participants who expect a bachelor degree is 54.8%, which increases to 68.3% at age 16 and 83.0% at age 18, then levels off at 83.5% at age 20. Students’ capability (in terms of their academic ability, self-study effort, and information search skills) can strengthen one’s education expectation of pursuing a bachelor degree even after family socio-economic background and parental expectation have been taken into account (Keung & Ho, 2020). (2) HE choices: There is a similar proportion of young adults who reported that they had made an adaptive HE choice (51.4%) and those who reported an autonomous choice (48.6%) (Ho & Sum, 2018a). It reveals that family resources, particularly home educational resources, and parental emotional support may be contributing to young adults’ autonomous HE choice. Besides, the HE decisions of young adults are also shaped by the institutional habitus of HE institutions, which manifests itself in three forms: infrastructure, prestige, and culture. (Ho, Tse & Sum, 2020). (3) Hope: HK young adults perceive an above-average level of hope in terms of both pathway and agency thinking (Ho, 2019). Family socioeconomic status is a significant factor of young adults’ hope; yet, this social disparity is fully mediated by three types of parental support. (Ho, et al, 2021) Among them, parental emotional support is the strongest mediator. Besides, it is also found that peer support has a moderating effect on the social disparity in young adults’ hope (Ho, Sum & Lee, 2020). The effect of peer support appears to be stronger than that of parental support and is relatively stronger on the hope of low-SES young adults. (4) Career-related outcomes: HK young adults have above-average career adaptability and perceived employability. A social disparity is found among young adults in perceived employability but is no longer significant when career decision self-efficacy and career adaptability are included (Ho, Sum & Lee, 2021). Cultural possessions have a significant effect on career adaptability (Ho & Sum, 2018b). Besides, parental career encouragement and emotional support have significant positive effects on career adaptability. This implies that there is a shift in parents’ role from being career advisor and information provider to encourager and supporter when young adults step into adulthood.

14626416.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14626416.value: The PI of this study and a scholar from the Education University of Hong Kong have prepared a research proposal for the Fourth Phase of HKLSA study, and it was funded by the Research Grants Council (RGC) in the 2019/20 General Research Fund (GRF) (see Section 11). This new Phase of HKLSA will continue to trace the transition patterns of the sampled young adults until their eighth post-secondary year, i.e. age 25. By adopting a mixed-methods design, it attempts to explore the lived experiences of Hong Kong young adults in five domains, namely hopes and dreams, education experiences, employment experiences, intimate and social relationships, health, and well-being. It also attempts to identify the transition pathways and the possible factors at the individual, family and institutional levels contributing to their transition outcomes at age 25. It is hoped that together with the previous phases of HKLSA study, this study will provide a comprehensive picture of a ten-year trajectory of the post-colonial generation of Hong Kong young people from adolescence to young adulthood.

14626416.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14626416.value: This study is a continuation of the research endeavor started from the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) 2012 and the Longitudinal Study of Adolescents in Hong Kong (HKLSA). While these two studies have tracked the patterns of transition of a representative sample of young adults from 2012 to 2015, the present study continues to trace their pathways until 2019, that is, during the third and fifth year after their graduation from secondary education. Being a first-of-its-kind longitudinal study in Hong Kong, this study has not only given a comprehensive picture of the transition pathways of Hong Kong youths from the entry point of senior secondary education to post-secondary education but also identified important factors at the individual, family and institutional levels which affect young adults’ transition outcomes. On one hand, the social disparity has been found in transition outcomes including educational expectations, hope and perceived employability. On the other hand, individual agency including academic ability, career search competencies and career adaptability, and parental and peer support have been found to be important factors for supporting young adults’ transition and mitigating the adverse effect of disadvantaged backgrounds.

14629516.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14629516.value: In tropical cities, urban spaces are one’s extended living spaces. Pedestrianization promotes a healthier and more sustainable urban environment, improves the well-being of urban dwellers, and save transport energy. This study intends to understand and quantify the dynamic and transient human comfort of city dwellers so as to provide insights to the planning and design of more pedestrian friendly urban spaces in high density sub-tropical cities. Outdoor thermal comfort studies have proved that urban design has a great influence on pedestrians’ thermal comfort; its assessment helps to understand the quality and usage of the pedestrian environment. However, the majority of outdoor thermal comfort studies perceive pedestrian thermal comfort as “static”. The dynamic multiple-use of urban spaces and the highly inhomogeneous urban morphology in high-density cities of the tropics are seldom considered. The transient nature of human thermal comfort has been discussed in some indoor studies. Transient conditions are experienced when people move between spaces with a wide range of microclimatic conditions. In high-density outdoor environment like Hong Kong, pedestrians experience highly variable microclimatic conditions within short distances. However, the application of the concept of transient thermal comfort in outdoor environment is rather limited and the use of longitudinal field surveys is relatively rare, which leads to a lack of understanding about how pedestrians respond to the changes of the outdoor environment. The proposed study aims to contribute by: (A) conducting longitudinal field measurements and surveys in order to establish a better understanding of pedestrian thermal comfort in the summer months of sub-tropical high-density urban conditions; (B) determining the dynamic thresholds of microclimatic conditions which pedestrians may find comfort when they travel through different urban settings; (C) based on the above findings, developing a dynamic human thermal comfort model that relates human thermal sensation and the built environment; and (D) establishing urban design guidelines for urban planning and design practitioners. Linking urban meteorology, urban design and outdoor thermal comfort, this study aims to provide a comprehensive understanding and quantification of the transient nature of pedestrian thermal comfort. Findings will, for example, inform the Hong Kong Planning Standards and Guidelines (HKPSG), and the current Hong Kong Government planning efforts of “HK2030+” towards a more livable environment. The study findings will also be useful for urban planners and designers in other sub-tropical high-density cities experiencing increasing urbanization. 在熱帶城市，城市空間是個人生活空間的延伸。本研究擬了解與量化市民的“動態人體舒適度”，從而就高密度的亞熱帶城市中，規劃和設計更多有利行人的城市空間提出見解。 室外熱舒適度研究證明，城市設計對行人的熱舒適度有重大影響；行人熱舒適的評估有助理解行人環境的質素和運用。然而，大部分的室外熱舒適研究將行人熱舒適視為「靜態的」。在熱帶高密度城市裡，城市空間的動態多用途特性和高度不同質的城市形態甚少被提及。 “動態人體舒適度”在一些室內研究有所討論。當人們在微氣候條件甚為廣泛的空間之中移動，就會經歷動態情況。在香港這樣的高密度室外環境，行人在短距離就經歷到高度變化的微氣候環境。然而，對於室外環境，“動態人體舒適度”的概念甚少被應用，而且縱向的實地測量亦較為罕見，因而導致難以理解行人如何應對室外環境的改變。 本研究的目的在於：(一) 進行縱向實地測量和調查，對亞熱帶高密度的城市環境中，夏季的行人熱舒適度有更透徹的理解；(二) 測定微氣候條件的“動態人體舒適度”閾值，即行人在不同城市環境下遊走時可能感到舒適的條件；(三) 根據上述調查結果，建立一個“動態人體舒適度”模型，聯繫人體熱感覺和建築環境；以及(四) 為城市規劃和設計人員建立城市設計準則。 結合城市氣象學、城市設計和室外熱舒適度，本研究旨在全面理解和量化行人“動態人體舒適度”性質。研究結果將會，舉例而言，有助於完善香港規劃標準與準則，及現時香港政府規劃工作的《香港2030+》，邁向更宜居的環境。對於其他日益城市化的亞熱帶高密度城市，本研究結果對其城市規劃人員和設計人員亦有所幫助。

14629516.label: Realisation of objectives
14629516.value: Walking studies were conducted in three study areas covering public housing estates, central business areas, and urban parks in summer 2016 and 2017. A total of 40 participants (20 males and females) were involved in the walking studies. In each study area, two walking routes were performed to cover different exposures to microclimatic conditions and urban geometry, with the same starting and destination. Route 1 generally consists of narrow street canyons with occasionally open spots at street intersections and open spaces, while route 2 basically follows the two main roads along the E-W orientation and then the N-S orientation. It takes approximately 60 min to complete each of the two walking routes (approximately 1.5 km), and they were instantaneously conducted in order to avoid temporal differences of the background meteorological conditions. Fifteen survey points were designated to conduct the thermal comfort survey. At each survey point, the subjects were asked for their thermal sensation vote (TSV) for the environment; they were situated according to the ASHRAE seven-point scale with cold (−3), cool (−2), slightly cool (−1), neutral (0), slightly warm (+1), warm (+2), and hot (+3). Fifteen TSV values were obtained for each subject during each walking route. Sky view factor (SVF) was used to represent the compactness of the urban geometry, and the SVF values were calculated for each survey point using the Rayman model based on fisheye photos taken during the survey. The surveys were conducted during four late summer days to capture three types of weather conditions, namely, clear, partially cloudy, and overcast skies. Six male and eight female university students with ages ranging from 19 to 21 participated in the survey. The survey campaigns were conducted from 2 p.m. to 4 p.m. to represent the critical summer conditions in Hong Kong. A backpack-type of mobile meteorological station was developed for the micro-meteorological measurements during the survey campaigns. It consists of a set of microclimatic sensors for the measurements of air temperature, relative humidity, and wind speed. Globe temperature was measured using a tailor-made globe thermometer composed of a thermocouple wire held in the middle of a 38-mm black table tennis ball, which is designed for the purpose of decreasing the response time during mobile measurements. Mean radiant temperature was then estimated using air temperature, relative humidity, wind speed, and globe temperature. Autocorrelation analysis was used to investigate the possible time-lag effect of thermal sensation, i.e., the immediate thermal experience of participants. Average thermal senstiton votes obtained at survey points served as the inputs of the autocorrelation analysis. TSV was used as the dependent variable for the cross-correlations with meteorological variables as well as thermal comfort indicator, PET, in order to determine the time lag(s) of the effect of the meteorological variables preceding the thermal sensation reported by subjects. The dynamic thresholds for thermal comfort were determined based on the results of autocorrelation and cross-correlation.

14629516.label: Major findings and research outcome
14629516.value: The walking studies showed that there were considerable variations in the meteorological conditions and the corresponding thermal sensation reported by subjects. Openness is one of the predominant factors influencing pedestrians’ thermal comfort. It was also shown that subjects felt more comfortable when moving from sunlit to shaded places. The improvement to thermal comfort is greater when the difference in PET is higher. It implies that more careful geometry design is important to pedestrian-level thermal comfort, taking into account the level of tolerance to thermal discomfort. The longitudinal survey provided a comprehensive understanding of the dynamic thermal comfort on how thermal sensation changes throughout the walking route and how it is affected by micro-meteorological conditions and the urban geometry. The large variations in micro-meteorological conditions throughout the walking routes are predominantly influenced by the urban geometry. Additionally, the spatial pattern of thermal sensation varies based on the weather conditions, emphasizing the need to account for such variations in the assessment of pedestrian thermal comfort. The results also show that thermal sensation was associated with participants’ short-term thermal experience (2–3 min) and that the urban geometry plays an important role in the time-lag effect of meteorological variables on thermal sensation. Results also showed that TSV and TPV showed remarkable differences under partially cloudy and clear sky conditions. Their relationship also showed the possible effect of thermal alliesthesia due to the higher magnitude of response of TPV. Results of the autocorrelation analysis implied the existence of potential thresholds for the level of tolerance to unfavourable thermal conditions. The methodology of the present study was also applied in Genova, Italy. The results were published in Journal of Building Engineering. Moreover, a comparative study between Hong Kong and Singapore was also conducted in July 2018. Data were incorporated into subsequent analysis and the thermal comfort thresholds were considerably different from those obtained in Hong Kong. The tolerance to unfavourable conditions was slightly higher, especially in prolonged period of exposure. Findings were documented in a manuscript under preparation and it is expected to be submitted to International Journal of Biometeorology in early 2021.

14629516.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14629516.value: This study is based on the field measurements and questionnaire surveys. Data acquired from the thermal studies were subsequently analysed to determine the thresholds of dynamic thermal comfort. This contributes to better design of urban geometry to create a more thermally comfortable pedestrian environment. Further studies can employ numerical modelling techniques such as agent-based modelling to take into account both subjective perception and observed microclimatic conditions for route-finding purposes. Such information can be incorporated into online map platform for suggesting routes that are optimized for human thermal comfort. Potential collaborations with the Hong Kong Observatory can be established to provide real-time meteorological conditions for instantaneous route-finding purposes. Another research direction can be oriented to scenario- or case-based studies that evaluate different design options for optimizing human thermal comfort. Such micro-scale information can contribute to fine details of site-level building design or provision of small open spaces that are typical in high-density cities.

14629516.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14629516.value: This project explored how people’s thermal perception changes during their walks in the outdoor environment. It adopted a combination of questionnaire surveys and field measurements to obtain subjective perception and observed microclimatic conditions respectively. As shown by the data, there are large variations in microclimatic conditions within short distances in the complex urban geometry in high-density cities. People’s thermal perception also corresponds to such changes in microclimatic conditions. Statistical analyses showed that there is a possible threshold of 3-5 minutes for pedestrian to tolerate unfavourable thermal conditions, e.g. heat stress, hot weather, direct sun exposure, during their walks in cities. It implies that diversity in the thermal environment is important to maintain comfortable conditions in pedestrian environment, especially in high-density cities where land resources are scarce. Urban designers can therefore optimize their design by providing “cool spots” in the pedestrian environment without compromising people’s thermal comfort.

14631816.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14631816.value: Mutual aid is a valuable source of assistance in the rehabilitation of young people with chronic mental illness. It prolongs and consolidates the contribution of social work services, which makes it essential to clarify how these benefits can be maximized. This clarification is also necessary to verify untested theories about the relationship between social workers’ inputs and mutual aid. Moreover, research pertaining to mutual aid among young people with chronic illness is particularly lacking. The proposed project aims to demonstrate the relevance of theoretically based factors in the mutual aid and rehabilitation of young people with chronic illness. The type and specificity of aid is one such factor. Balanced coordination between social workers and mutual aid groups is also important in ensuring the optimal use of resources. This requires that social workers do not intervene excessively in the operation of mutual aid groups. The proposed project will use a panel study design to examine factors that are conducive to effective mutual aid, and will contribute to sustained rehabilitation by encouraging efficient social workers’ inputs. Young people with chronic illness and their social workers will provide information for the proposed research project through surveys and focus groups. We will conduct a panel study involving baseline and follow-up surveys of 400 young people (aged 12 to 24) and 50 social workers, followed by five focus groups involving young people and social workers concerned with the development of mutual aid among young people. The proposed project will provide useful data for the long-term development of mutual aid for youths with chronic illness. Free and voluntary aid is an essential form of support for social work services, which generally cannot be provided for any great length of time due to their high cost. Mutual aid helps to maintain the benefits of social work services, which would otherwise diminish over time and thus waste early inputs and resources. Accordingly, the proposed project will help maximize the benefits of social work by emphasizing social workers’ ability to engender mutual aid among disadvantaged groups while providing individual and temporary care to these populations. The project will also facilitate the social work sector in meeting the long-term challenge of sustainable development, and advance it beyond the delivery of subsidiary individual-based services.

14631816.label: Realisation of objectives
14631816.value: 1. To investigate how mutual aid contributes to the rehabilitation of youths with chronic illness in such areas as problem alleviation, function enhancement, improved illness management, and continued support for the mutual aid group. The data collected from our panel study of 391 participants (aged 12-45), recruited from 50 mutual aid groups in Hong Kong, have provided empirical evidence on the positive influence of mutual aid on the rehabilitation of young people with chronic illness (YPCI). Of particular concern are the relationships between mutual aid related factors—supportive group interaction, facilitator input (e.g., support from social workers or healthcare professionals), trust among group members, emotional support reception, and emotional support provision—with rehabilitation outcomes—problem alleviation (e.g., depression), function enhancement (e.g., life satisfaction, purpose in life, personal growth, accomplishment, and social connectedness), and improved illness management (e.g., coping with stigma, health maintenance efficacy, and treatment adherence). The results show that supportive group interaction, facilitator input variety (i.e., the number of different topics that are raised and discussed by facilitators in mutual aid groups to provide support for issues faced by YPCI in different areas of their lives) and trust among group members contribute to better treatment adherence of YPCI (please refer to Attachments 1 and 2 in Section 8 of Part C: Research Output). In addition, emotional support provision positively affects YPCI’s life satisfaction, purpose in life, and personal growth. Nonetheless, the results do not support the positive direct effect of emotional support reception on those rehabilitation outcomes of YPCI (please refer to Attachment 3 in Section 8 of Part C: Research Output). 2. To examine how input from facilitators (e.g., support from social workers or healthcare professionals) enhances mutual aid among youths with chronic illness by developing trust in the reciprocated or unconditional aid of group members, maintaining balanced coordination of tasks between the facilitator and group members, and promoting group cohesion and group interaction. Based on data collected from 391 YPCI, our findings support the hypothesis that facilitator input variety promotes the rehabilitation of YPCI, signifying that a more holistic and comprehensive approach to facilitator input could lead to better rehabilitation. Moreover, the results partially support the hypothesis on balanced coordination of tasks between the facilitator and group members. Our findings indicate that YPCI who receive a higher level of facilitator input variety during the early stages of mutual aid groups are more likely to have a higher level of supportive interaction in later stages, supporting that high facilitator input during the initial stages of mutual aid groups facilitate effective mutual aid. Nevertheless, our findings on the positive influence of supportive interaction in the early stages of mutual aid groups on facilitator input variety in later stages do not support the hypothesis that effective mutual aid requires the facilitator to gradually retreat from the group as the group’s mutual aid matures (please refer to Attachment 1 in Section 8 of Part C: Research Output). Furthermore, trust among mutual aid group members positively influences YPCI’s chronic illness self-management—treatment adherence (i.e., the ability to follow treatment plans as advised by healthcare professionals), health maintenance efficacy (i.e., the ability to execute courses of action required to manage their health effectively), and coping with stigma (i.e., the ability to adopt strategies to deal with the stress of stigmatization)—which subsequent promotes their rehabilitation outcomes. Specifically, trust significantly contributes to YPCI’s health maintenance efficacy, which in turn increases their sense of accomplishment and social connectedness while decreasing their level of depression. Similarly, trust significantly reduces YPCI’s level of depression through treatment adherence (please refer to Attachment 2 in Section 8 of Part C: Research Output). In addition, our results show that supportive group interaction positively affects YPCI’s emotional support reception, which in turn results in their higher levels of emotional support provision, thereby ultimately facilitating various psychological well-being outcomes including life satisfaction, purpose in life, and personal growth (please refer to Attachment 3 in Section 8 of Part C: Research Output). 3. To provide empirical data that help identify key success factors for effective mutual aid among youths with chronic illness in Hong Kong. Our findings reveal the following five key success factors contributing to the effective mutual aid among YPCI in Hong Kong: (1) Supportive group interaction: Supportive group interaction can help boost mutual aid among YPCI. Our findings indicate that interacting with others who have endured similar experiences and difficulties first induces emotional support reception, which further triggers emotional support provision, which subsequently leads to the enhancement of psychological well-being (please refer to Attachment 3 in Section 8 of Part C: Research Output). Moreover, supportive group interaction facilitates YPCI’s chronic illness self-management in terms of treatment adherence. Through supportive group interaction, YPCI are encouraged to acquire more effective ways of coping with one’s difficulties and thus, in turn, improve their ability to follow treatment plans as advised by healthcare professionals (please refer to Attachment 1 in Section 8 of Part C: Research Output). (2) Emotional support provision: The act of emotional support provision is therapeutic for YPCI, as it positively affects their psychological well-being. Being a helper can improve one’s self-image and well-being as a result of the act of doing something deemed worthwhile, and they can also inadvertently encourage themselves when attempting to encourage other group members. Furthermore, as a by-product, support providers lighten their stress when they shift their focus away from their own suffering as they attempt to help others, while also simultaneously gaining a sense of purpose from their acts of helping (please refer to Attachment 3 in Section 8 of Part C: Research Output). (3) Trust among mutual aid group members: Trust plays a vital role in improved illness management and psychological well-being of YPCI. Trust among mutual aid group members facilitates the exchange of informational, practical, and emotional support with each other. The transmission of different kinds of support and health-related information and resources can help YPCI improve illness management, which in turn promotes their psychological well-being, such as gaining accomplishment, nurturing social connectedness, and reducing depression (please refer to Attachment 2 in Section 8 of Part C: Research Output). (4) Facilitator input variety: This study provides strong evidence that facilitator input variety of mutual aid groups also plays a critical role in the rehabilitation of YPCI. Our findings suggest that a holistic approach to facilitator input can lead to better treatment adherence of YPCI. This input would address a wide range of difficulties encountered by members in mutual aid groups in different areas of their lives (e.g., work, education, finance, emotional and behavioral problems, physical health, and family) (please refer to Attachment 1 in Section 8 of Part C: Research Output). (5) Chronic illness self-management: YPCI’s effective chronic illness self-management is crucial for their rehabilitation outcomes. Our findings suggest that coping with stigma and health maintenance efficacy positively affect YPCI’s sense of accomplishment and social connectedness. Moreover, treatment adherence helps reduce depression (please refer to Attachment 2 in Section 8 of Part C: Research Output). Given the importance of chronic illness self-management, this study has also developed and validated a holistic measurement instrument for assessing self-management of YPCI aged 12-45 years across a wide range of chronic health conditions in Hong Kong (please refer to Attachment 4 in Section 8 of Part C: Research Output).

14631816.label: Major findings and research outcome
14631816.value: Time is a vital factor for effective mutual aid groups, as it takes time for members to build trust. Our results show that although supportive group interaction and facilitator input variety are not associated with the treatment adherence of YPCI at the beginning of mutual aid groups, they can lead to improvements in treatment adherence after YPCI have participated in the groups for approximately one year. The findings suggest that the impacts of mutual aid groups take time to develop. Moreover, our findings on the positive relationship between facilitator input variety and treatment adherence suggest that facilitators should cover diverse topics (e.g., work, physical health, and family) in group meetings for better rehabilitation. Furthermore, chronic illness self-management significantly contributes to YPCI’s psychological well-being. Specifically, coping with stigma and health maintenance efficacy positively influence accomplishment and social connectedness. Meanwhile, treatment adherence and health maintenance efficacy can lead to reduced depression. The findings indicate that enhancing YPCI’s chronic illness self-management could be a useful strategy for improving their psychological well-being. In addition, given the critical role of chronic illness self-management in YPCI’s rehabilitation, this study has developed and validated a holistic measurement instrument for assessing YPCI’s chronic illness self-management. Our findings also show that trust among mutual aid group members positively predicts YPCI’s chronic illness self-management, which in turn promotes their accomplishment and social connectedness while decreasing their level of depression. Moreover, emotional support reception and emotional support provision sequentially mediate the relationship between supportive group interaction and YPCI’s psychological well-being, suggesting that it is sequential reciprocity (i.e., repaying the helper or a third party in the future after receiving help) instead of equitable reciprocity (i.e., a balance of receiving and providing emotional support, where no party over-benefits or under-benefits) that explains how supportive group interaction benefits the rehabilitation of YPCI in the Hong Kong Chinese context. Different from the individual-oriented and equity-driven social networks in Western cultures, Chinese social networks are guided by mutual sharing. Due to the influence of Confucianism, Chinese people typically strive for communal harmony and favor reciprocal relationships. People feel that it is obligatory to repay favors, but they do not demand the other party to repay immediately nor return an equivalent amount of favor. The discrepancies reflect how culture may affect people’s mindsets about returning favors in mutual aid groups.

14631816.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14631816.value: Further development of the research includes: (1) This study employed the self-report method, which may be subject to social desirability bias and recall bias. Future studies could adopt a combination of different measurements, such as medical records and information from family members to address the limitations of self-report; (2) We focused on YPCI in a Chinese society. To ensure the generalization of the research results, further studies may consider focusing on YPCI from diverse cultural backgrounds; (3) This study collected data at baseline and follow-up surveys a year apart. Future research could collect intermediate measurements to examine whether change happens at an earlier time; (4) Ten types of chronic health conditions were included in the study. As the subsample size for each type of illness was small, further moderation analysis examining the effect of the type of illness was not feasible. Future studies should investigate how the type of illness interacts with the relationships among group dynamics, facilitator input, trust, mutual aid, and rehabilitation of YPCI.

14631816.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14631816.value: Current research shows that young people with chronic illness (YPCI) can benefit from mutual aid groups. Nevertheless, research pertaining to the influential mechanisms of mutual aid groups, particularly relationships among facilitator input, mutual aid, and rehabilitation is lacking. Accordingly, this study examines factors that are conducive to mutual aid and rehabilitation of YPCI. Data came from a two-wave panel study of 391 YPCI (aged 12-45) recruited from 50 mutual aid groups in Hong Kong. The results reveal that facilitator input variety (e.g., number of topics discussed by facilitators with members), supportive group interaction, trust, chronic illness self-management, and emotional support provision are success factors for effective mutual aid. Moreover, this study supports sequential reciprocity (i.e., repaying the helper or a third party in the future after receiving help) instead of equitable reciprocity (i.e., a balance of receiving and providing support, where no party over-benefits or under-benefits) in mutual aid, owing to the Chinese culture wherein people do not demand recipients to repay immediately nor return an equivalent amount of favor. Our findings also indicate that facilitators should cover diverse topics in group meetings. In addition, enhancing YPCI’s chronic illness self-management is a vital strategy for improving their rehabilitation.

14632016.label: Realisation of objectives
14632016.value: Objective 1. Conduct a longitudinal study of 2 groups of Mandarin-English bilingual children from 1;6 to 5; 4 children from Hong Kong and 4 from North America (total no=8) will be selected to participate in the study. The children's interactions with parents and research assistants in the home setting will be video and audio-recorded on a biweekly basis over a period of twenty-four months. This objective was fully realized. We recruited two groups of Mandarin-English bilingual children: (1) 4 from North America (US group) (2) 4 from Hong Kong (HK group) The US group were heritage children who are second generation born to first generation immigrant parents who speak Mandarin as native language. They grew up with varying degrees of exposure to English which is the language of the community. The HK group grew up in households where Mandarin is the home language with some exposure to English from parents and the community. The Hong Kong children’s parents are native speakers of Mandarin who speak English as second language. The children’s interactions with parents and other adult speakers (research assistants) were recorded in recording sessions where the child produced English and Mandarin as the target language each for about 20-30 minutes. Some recording sessions were conducted via Skype call which we pioneered as an innovative method that allows our research team to collect data successfully. Video as well as audio files are available for most if not all of the sessions. The spontaneous naturalistic speech data in Mandarin and English will be transcribed in a standard format, digitized and linked with video/audio files. A new multimedia bilingual child language corpus containing heritage bilingual data will be created. The objective was realized fully to the extent that the parents allow the research team to keep the video data for internal use but not released to the public due to privacy issues. The children’s speech data were transcribed in standard CHAT format. A total of 218 files (223 Mandarin and 174 Cantonese files) have been transcribed (see Table 1). While recordings were made on a biweekly basis, initially they have been transcribed on a monthly basis. There are more recordings than we can transcribe due to lack of continuity in engaging the same transcribers. Different student transcribers were engaged in transcribing the speech data at different stages during the project and the trained ones who had mastered transcription were unable to continue the task once they graduated. As a result a portion of the recordings remain untranscribed. We have targetted at least one transcription per month for each child and in some cases two transcriptions per month are available. Privacy issues have been a major concern for the parents who are increasingly cautious about releasing their child’s images and information and their family life in the public domain. Some parents especially those in the US had reservations about releasing the videos and would not want us to release the transcripts linked to the videos. Efforts were made to reassure the parents that without their permission the videos will definitely not be released to the public and they will only be used for internal purposes by our research team. After some negotiation, they were willing to give permission to release the audio files for research purposes while preserving the privacy of the child, parents and family caretakers. 3. Comparison of the developmental milestones and trajectories: 1) between the 8 Mandarin-English bilingual children and their monolingual peers and 2) between the HK group and the North American group. The objective was realized in the analysis of core aspects of grammatical development in the two groups of children (please 6.1 for further information). There are a number of limitations in the present study. First, the sample size (N=8) remains relatively small and the language input conditions are more variable than anticipated, even though the families are from similar SES backgrounds in the Hong Kong community. Second, the measures used to assess children's dominance are limited and further measures can be used. To further assess the validity of these measures for other samples, as well as the generalizability of our approach, future research should investigate different language dominance patterns for different age groups and with different outcome measures.

14632016.label: Major findings and research outcome
14632016.value: Overall, both groups of bilingual children were able to achieve developmental milestones and show trajectories on a par with monolinguals and succeeded in developing bilingualism in Mandarin and English from 1;07-6;11. Development of Mandarin: The Mandarin of the bilingual children in both heritage and homeland contexts shows age-appropriate developmental patterns compared to their monolingual peers. Heritage children’s Mandarin develops the core aspects of grammar and phonology largely on schedule like their monolingual peers, with only slight delay in certain domains. Decline in some Mandarin structures reflects the shift of dominance from Mandarin to English. Development of English: The development of English shows slight delay in a few heritage children and in the Hong Kong group. Heritage children have an advantage in English compared to the Hong Kong group, but their English shows some differences from the monolingual baseline, such as a higher rate of uninflected verbs. Input and crosslinguistic influence: Differences between the heritage grammar and homeland variety are attributable to the heritage children receiving less input in Mandarin than the homeland group, qualitative differences in the input, cross-linguistic influence from the societal majority language and attrition of previously acquired properties. Bidirectional cross-linguistic influence is found in the development of the heritage children’s two languages. The heritage children omit subjects in Mandarin less frequently than the baseline monolinguals (reflecting influence from English) but omit subjects in their English more than monolinguals (reflecting influence from Chinese). In English verb-particle constructions, both groups of children show a preference for the non-split order (“pick up Sophie”) unlike monolinguals who prefer the split order (“pick Sophie up”) suggesting influence from the children’s Mandarin. Influenced by English, the heritage children’s Mandarin is less syllable-timed than the monolinguals and homeland bilinguals. The heritage children produced Mandarin BA constructions to varying degrees compared with the monolingual baseline. Variation is found among the heritage children who show different patterns: L initially under-produces BA but catches up by age 4. A overproduces BA compared to the baseline (consistent with high frequency in the input), while W does not use it until age 3 but then shows explosive development, followed by a decline attributed to increased English input once enrollment in school started. To summarize, the children’s bilingual development reflects influences of the dual input and specific experiential factors. The observed developmental differences are likely to be the product of multiple linguistic and environmental factors that jointly shape the development of the target languages.

14632016.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14632016.value: The corpus has potential for further development. Further qualitative and quantitative analysis of individual children’s developmental data and the input can be conducted, for example, to determine the extent of individual variation and input effects: whether there are correlations between input and output in specific grammatical domains such as subject/object omission and the BA construction. Phonetic and phonological properties of heritage language development remain largely uncharted territory. To tap the new databases more fully and provide a comprehensive picture of how heritage and Hong Kong children develop bilingualism in Mandarin and English, it is essential to analyze their phonological development in detail. The proposed course of action to examine input effects in bilingual development is as follows: Apart from coarse-grained measures such as MLU, apply more fine grained measures to determine the children’s developmental milestones and language dominance patterns; To complement the present study on the role of input from home, investigate input from school, e.g. the distribution of input in the school curriculum. Experimental studies of heritage and bilingual children can be conducted to address the issue of generalizability of the findings. The natural course of action is to conduct cross-sectional experiments engaging many more subjects at different ages.

14632016.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14632016.value: The project investigated the bilingual development of Mandarin-English preschool children in Hong Kong (N=4) and US (N=4) over 24 months covering the age range from 1;07-6;11. Childhood bilingualism involving Mandarin and English is likely to become the most prevalent form of bilingualism around the world, given that the two languages are internationally prestigious and highly sought after by parents and educators. For many overseas communities, Chinese is a heritage language: children hear Chinese at home, English outside. This project focused on a newly recognized form of bilingualism, “heritage bilingualism” by comparing Mandarin-English bilingual children growing up in the United States with those in Hong Kong. The development of Mandarin-English bilingual children across the two contexts was systematically documented and compared with that of monolingual peers. The project breaks new ground in the study of childhood bilingualism by documenting the development of two groups of Mandarin-English bilingual children under different input conditions and contributing to the emerging field of heritage bilingualism. A new multimedia bilingual child language corpus was created involving Mandarin and English which is the first heritage child language corpus available to the international research community. This is an innovative project on both theoretical and empirical grounds. Theoretically, it contributes to our understanding of how children achieve bilingual competence in Mandarin and English and how their competence changes under different input conditions. Empirically, it significantly enriches the existing database by including an important language pair in the child language corpora in CHILDES. The project is highly relevant to the local community in view of the Hong Kong SAR Government’s language policy which promotes 兩文三語 “biliteracy and trilingualism”.
