14650816.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14650816.value: This project is a study of the narrative poems in “song form” (gexingti 歌行體) by the celebrated poet Wu Weiye 吳偉業 (1609-1671) of the Ming-Qing dynastic transition. Wu’s poetry has been substantially studied, but revisiting Wu’s narrative poems from the perspectives of literary culture and cultural history promises to shed innovative light on Wu’s long-lasting literary legacy. I will explore Wu’s poems along the themes of Garden, History and Love. Famous gardens in Ming-Qing times were both private and public spaces, infused with individual, cultural and historical memories. Wu’s poems “Pipa xing” 琵琶行, “Hou Donggaocaotang ge” 後東皋草堂歌, and “Yong Zhuozhengyuan shanchahua” 詠拙政園山茶花 concern the gardens of Wang Shimin 王時敏, Chen Zhilin 陳之遴, and Qu Shisi 瞿式耜. Wu, Wang, Chen and Qu were Jingnan natives, good friends, and Ming officials. After the fall of the Ming, both Wu and Wang lived as recluses, Qu embraced martyrdom defending the fugitive Ming court, and Chen served the Qing court. I will discuss how these gardens, as a form of material culture, mirrored the lives of their owners. Wu’s “Yuanyuan qu” 圓圓曲 and “Songshan ai” 松山哀 about Wu Sangui 吳三桂 and Hong Chengchou 洪承疇 will be discussed along the theme of History. Wu and Hong were positioned in Manchuria to resist the Qing invasion. They deflected to the Qing after tragic battles and massacres. Understandably, Chinese historians have passed harsh judgement on them, and literary critics followed suit. I beg to differ. I shall argue that besides criticism, Wu was sympathetic to them—he rooted ethics in human condition. The love story between Wu and the courtesan Bian Yujing 卡玉京 is engaging. Wu declined the proposal of marriage by Bian in late Ming. Their romance, nevertheless, continued. Focusing on “Ting nǚdaoshi Bian Yujing tanqin qu” 聽女道士卞玉京彈琴曲 and a series of texts by Wu on Bian, I will discuss how they intimate Bian’s change in emotion and physiological constraints over time. More importantly, I will explore Wu’s senses of identity, power, desire, taste, gender, positioning, and subjectivity. His roles as lover, the ungrateful, the heart-broken, confessor, oral history chronicler/versifier, and reminiscent will also be fully discussed.

14650816.label: Realisation of objectives
14650816.value: The objectives of this research project have been realized in the following areas: Scholars in the past have paid particular attention to either the relationship between history and poetry in Wu’s poetry or the artistic value of his works. This project, at once a literary and cultural history one, opens up new horizons for the study of Wu Weiye. It yields new insights into Wu Weiye’s narrative poems by expanding its horizon to include ideas of literary culture and cultural history. For instances, in my paper “「仙源」與「劫灰」——吳梅村詩中的「礬清湖敘事」” (Paradise and Its Loss: Wu Weiye’s Narrative Poems on Lake Fanqing) (forthcoming in Journal of Chinese Literature 中國文學學報, Vol. 10 [Dec. 2019]), I explore the idea of “home and paradise in refuge” against the backdrop of chaos and wars during the Ming-Qing dynastic changeover of seventeenth century China. Wu Weiye’s thirteen poems (along with a long preface) on Lake Fanqing constitute what can be called “a narrative of Lake Fanqing.” Wu was celebrated for his long narrative song-form poems in his own “Meicun Style”; these poems engage and represent historical events and figures. The poems discussed in this paper are narrative poems in “Old Style,” not in the Meicun Style. Yet, Wu’s poems on Lake Fanqing hold a special interest for us because they are much more personal and private. Firstly, these poems include some autobiographical moments through which we can see the mind of the sensitive, fragile poet and the ways in which he employs the poetic form to bemoan his sad fate and to configure the chaotic world of the Ming-Qing dynastic changeover. Secondly, reading the poems of the Lake Fanqing narrative, we can understand how some particular memories—pleasure, pain, shame, guilt, fear—take shape, persist and transform, and how narration and metaphor, as literary devices, interact with and embody and give form to them. In another paper, “明清易鼎之際江南太倉之南園與梅村” (The Gardens Nanyuan and Meicun in Taicang of the Ming-Qing Dynastic Changeover) (under preparation for publication), I suggest that garden building by Wu Weiye after the fall of the Ming dynasty is both an endeavor to create an ideal dwelling and a nuanced manner of self-constitution amidst historical turmoil and personal crisis. In a book manuscript tentatively titled《一曲琵琶說到今》, I am looking at how a musical instrument, pipa 琵琶 or the lute, serves as a metaphorical trope for Wu Weiye to understand his own life and the historical and political new world brought about by the dynastic changeover. All the above-mentioned studies are also underpinned by the conceptual framework of “Three Contextualizations,” namely, literary contextualization, biographical contextualization, and historical contextualization, that I advocate for the study of Ming-Qing literature. In the course of carrying out this research project, I presented papers in quite a few international conferences in Hong Kong, Mainland China and Taiwan (at the Chinese University of Hong Kong; Taiwan’s Academia Sinica; Mainland China’s Huanan Normal University, etc.), to share my findings and to exchange ideas with colleagues in the field. I also delivered public lectures in various localities (such as the Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong University, Nanjing University, Fudan University, Huadong Normal University, etc.), of which one is worthy of special note. In May 2017, Taiwan’s Center for Chinese Studies 漢學研究中心 (under National Central Library 國家圖書館) invited me to deliver the prestigious Taiwan Lectures on Chinese Studies 臺灣漢學講座. My lecture entitled “Wu Weiye’s (1609-72) ‘Song of the Lute’: A Mourning Song for the Fallen Country 吳偉業〈琵琶行〉中之哀悼亡明與自我懺悔” was delivered in Jagiellonian University, Krakow, Poland. The reception was enthusiastic. For this occasion, I also prepared an English translation (the first of its kind) of Wu’s celebrated long poem “Pipa xing” (Song of the Lute), which I plan to publish after some revision and expansion. All these scholarly activities, be they local or overseas, helped promote the study of Wu Weiye in particular, and Ming-Qing literature in general. For the purpose of encouraging and training more graduate students to conduct research on Wu Weiye and Ming-Qing literature, I also offered a graduate seminar on Wu Weiye’s poetry through the Department of Chinese Language and Literature (CUHK). It was a great success. The class generated 16 wonderful term papers, among which two were already published in academic journals in Taiwan. All in all, the five stated objectives of the project were pursued and achieved successfully.

14650816.label: Major findings and research outcome
14650816.value: The major findings are: 1) The theme “Paradise and Its Loss” can be employed to study a group of Wu’s biographical poems spanning 1645 to 1659, in which Wu reflects on his life experiences and the new strange world unfolding before him; 2) A study of Wu’s garden, the Meicun, from the perspective of cultural history can expose human and cultural dynamics that bear on self-identification, self-constitution, community bonding, and regional culture and history; and 3) The musical instrument pipa (the lute) is a metaphorical trope for representing personal and historical memories, figuring importantly in Wu’s poetry and plays. This project generated two papers and one book manuscript. The papers are: “「仙源」與「劫灰」——吳梅村詩中的「礬清湖敘事」” (forthcoming in Journal of Chinese Literature); “明清易鼎之際江南太倉之南園與梅村” (under preparation). In the book manuscript tentatively titled《一曲琵琶說到今》(under preparation), I look at how a musical instrument, pipa, serves as a metaphorical trope for Wu to understand his own life and the new world brought about by the dynastic changeover. What follows is an account of “Paradise and Its Loss.” In 1645, Wu took refuge in Lake Fanqing and wrote “Taking Refuge, Six Poems.” Wu likens Lake Fanqing to Peach Blossom Spring. After the Manchu conquest, Wu led a quiet life until 1653, when he was summoned to serve the Qing court. He served until 1657. That same year, when he learned of the gloomy news of the lake, he composed “Lake Fanqing, with a Preface.” In 1659, Zheng Chenggong led his navy into Jiangnan in an attempt to revive the fallen Ming dynasty. Wu composed “To Dispel Anguish, Six Poems,” in which Lake Fanqing appears again. These thirteen poems (with one preface) constitute “a narrative of Lake Fanqing.” They hold a special interest for us because they are personal and private, including autobiographical moments through which we can see the mind of the sensitive poet and the ways in which he employs the poetic form to bemoan his fate and to configure the chaotic world. Through them, we can also understand how some particular memories take shape, persist and transform, and how narration and metaphor interact with and give form to them.

14650816.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14650816.value: This project differs from most other studies of Wu Weiye in the field in that it is a literary project but it expands its horizon by including ideas of literary culture and cultural history. This brings Wu’s poems and prose writings into the larger cultural and historical contexts of seventeenth century China on the one hand, and to the particular life experiences of the person on the other. The success of the current project inspires us to further our study of Wu in the conceptual and theoretical frameworks of New Cultural History developed in the West since the 1980s. This approach will yield new insights into Wu Weiye’s narrative poems and enlighten us on the following issues: the author’s self-recognition and self-constitution through poetic texts; narrative poems as a source of public and historical knowledge; the intricate relationship between metaphor and historical analogy; textual constructs and the larger cultural and social energies of the time; circulation of texts and the formation of public opinion; the act of writing as a social practice, participated by like-minded communities with a particular regional interest, etc.

14650816.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14650816.value: Classical Chinese poetry is a wealth of wonderful language and cultural and historical memories. Wu Weiye, Qian Qianyi, and Gong Dingzi were venerated as “The Three Masters of Jiangnan” of the Ming-Qing dynastic changeover of seventeenth century China. Among the three, Wu Weiye was celebrated for his long song-form narrative poems that engage and represent momentous historical events and figures. Scholars in the past have paid particular attention to either the relationship between poetry and history in Wu’s poetry or the artistic value of his works. This project opens up a new horizon for the study of Wu Weiye and yields new insights into Wu Weiye’s narrative poems. It brings Wu’s poems and prose writings into the larger aesthetic, cultural and historical contexts of the time on the one hand, and to the particular life experiences of the person on the other. This project enhances our understanding of Wu Weiye’s poetry in particular, and of Qing literature in general. Students of literature and history alike will find the results of the project stimulating and useful.

14652016.label: Realisation of objectives
14652016.value: The implementation of this project has adhered closely to the proposed five interrelated objectives. Specifically, a theoretical framework was first proposed for Particulate Matter (PM) concentration estimation, which integrates all the components contained in the project. The components include the retrieval of Aerosol Optical Depth (AOD) from satellite imagery, the retrieval of Aerosol Optical Properties (AOPs) from mobile phone photos, an interpolation model to incorporate multi-source data, prototype system implementation, and a case study. An improved AOD retrieval algorithm from satellite images has been designed and implemented. In this study, 3 km AOD data generated through fusion using the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) Collection 6 AOD products were used to estimate ground PM2.5 concentrations. We considered the seasonal characteristics of AOD distribution and incorporated them in an improved geographically and temporally weighted regression (GTWR) model, which achieved a better performance than other spatiotemporal regression models. Although the aforementioned algorithms have largely improved the estimation accuracy of PM2.5 concentration on the spatial dimension, the low update frequency of satellite sensors still limits the possibility of acquiring air quality information in real time. Smartphone photos that can be taken at any time, any location were, therefore, attempted to measure outdoor PM2.5. Such photos, similar to satellite imagery, were viewed as an important source of big data that can contribute to real-time estimate of PM2.5 concentrations of a surrounding environment. An image-based retrieval algorithm for extracting AOPs from smartphone photos was designed and implemented. We first estimated the transmission map and the extinction coefficient using visual features (i.e., sky, depth map, and segmented scenes) that are extracted from a smartphone photo. As the scene structure is an essential factor that influences the estimation accuracy in urban areas, we designed a selection criterion based on scene structures to choose an appropriate optical property. Finally, the PM concentration can be estimated from the selected AOP. In this way, we can monitor the ambient PM2.5 by simply taking a photo using a smartphone. To achieve this, we developed a prototype system named “PhotoAir” that incorporates the proposed image-based algorithm. The PhotoAir app can turn users’ mobile photos into an air quality sensor without either manual input or additional information. With PhotoAir, we have constructed a large-scale dataset consisting of more than 4,000 photos taken in Hong Kong and mainland China from 2018 to 2021. Their corresponding PM2.5 concentrations were estimated and validated. Considering the asynchronous update frequency and disparate spatial coverage of the satellite imagery and smartphone photos, an interpolation model that fuse multi-source data is required. Traditional methods faced challenges in generating high spatial and temporal resolution images and capturing complex land surface changes. To overcome these problems, a two-stage fusion model namely robust adaptive spatial and temporal satellite image fusion model (RASTFM) was designed and implemented. The non-shape change and shape change were first predicted through a non-local linear regression of the subject pixel’s similar neighbors. Then, a post-processing step was followed through residual correction. Combining these two steps we have successfully applied this model to fuse spatial and temporal images with complementary resolutions. Meanwhile, we further proposed an improved fusion algorithm for covering large geographical areas (e.g., national or global scale), namely sparse representation-based gap filling model (SPGF). We employed a machine learning approach, sparse representation, to help reconstruct high-resolution images from prior low-resolution images. We first developed a method of multi-spatial resolution AOD dictionary-pair learning in order to enforce data to be represented by the same sparse coefficients. Then, the high spatial resolution AOD was reconstructed with sparse coding. To sum up, we presented a theoretical framework that uses both smartphone photos and satellite images for PM concentration estimation in urban areas. Under this framework, we first designed the visual feature extraction algorithm from smartphone photos and an improved AOD retrieval algorithm for PM concentration estimation from satellite images. Then, a data fusion approach was developed to incorporate multi-source data. To facilitate the testing of the proposed framework, a prototype system was developed and tested in Hong Kong which achieved an average accuracy of 80% in comparison with the actual measurement by a portable air quality monitor. Overall, all the proposed objectives have been realized as expected and research findings reported in publications. We still have more research articles about the proposed methods and applications in the pipeline.

14652016.label: Major findings and research outcome
14652016.value: Traditional methods for acquiring air pollution concentrations may directly use the observations from sparsely distributed ground monitoring stations and then apply a spatiotemporal interpolation method. Despite varying levels of success, there is clearly a need to improve the accuracy, frequency and coverage of observations such that users can access PM2.5 concentrations at any time any location. To generate high-resolution PM concentrations, a combined 3 km Aerosol Optical Depth (AOD) dataset was produced and fused using the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) Collection 6 AOD products. Based on this dataset, PM concentrations with fine granularity were estimated through the improved geographically and temporally weighted regression (GTWR). Therefore, it becomes possible to capture the variations of air pollution in a large urban area. Compared to satellite imagery, smartphone photos can reveal more local variations. We considered the photos as an alternative data source as it can provide Aerosol Optical Properties (AOPs) of the ambient environment and hence more accessible fine-grained PM concentrations. To achieve this goal, we devised a two-stage algorithm for retrieving AOPs from smartphone photos to measure PM concentrations. In the first stage, the proposed algorithm learns the visual features of smartphone photos to estimate AOPs, while in the second stage it exploits the importance of urban scenes in determining a suitable AOP, thereby rendering the proposed algorithm applicable in various urban scenes. The proposed algorithm was implemented into a prototype system, PhotoAir, which turns users’ mobile phones into portable air quality monitoring devices. With PhotoAir, users can sense the surrounding environment in real-time. By using this app, a large PM2.5 dataset can be generated in higher accuracy. Nonetheless, to cover a large area, PhotoAir measurements may not be sufficient. Thus, we also made use of the powerful ability of fusion methods to blend multiple AOD sources and proposed a novel framework for incorporating different AOD products. We devised a fusion model to generate AODs with both high spatial and temporal resolution through a sparse representation-based method. In this way, both AOD products can provide complementary information leading to more accurate and frequent PM2.5 concentration distribution. In summary, this project has successfully delivered a methodology and an associated prototype app for estimating outdoor PM2.5 concentration in real time and made it possible for large area PM2.5 mapping with high accuracy and frequency. [Note: Zhao, Huang*, Liu & He (2021) did not acknowledge the support of this funding due to negligence.]

14652016.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14652016.value: Accurate PM concentration estimation is vital for monitoring air pollution and measuring individual exposure in an urban area. Complex urban microclimate makes the PM distribution heterogeneous and the air quality estimation extremely challenging. In particular, the problem becomes more complicated when intending to acquire data with both large spatial coverage and fine granularity. The proposed theoretical framework has successfully generated fine-grained PM concentrations and obtained satisfactory results. However, a more robust platform should be developed using parallel computing and cloud computing techniques. This way a more powerful platform can be built to cater to the need of more simultaneous users. As such, more photos can be collected, which will, in turn, improve the estimation models. Another aspect that deserves further investigation is the indoor PM2.5 monitoring, which might be more important than outdoor PM monitoring as people stay more time indoors than outdoors. However, the visual features on a photo to be extracted to derive indoor PM concentration may be totally different from those for outdoor scenes. This adds challenge to the extension of this project. Nevertheless, deriving indoor PM2.5 concentrations definitely merits further exploration. If successful, an app for measuring both indoor and outdoor PM2.5 concentration can be developed, which will be of higher value to the researchers and the public.

14652016.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14652016.value: Hong Kong and other cities in China are suffering from a serious air pollution problem. Public awareness of polluted air has been growing and there is an increasing demand for access to more accurate and timely air pollution data so as to reduce the population’s exposure to unhealthy air. Providing such data has proven to be a great challenge to air quality monitoring services trying to meet people’s demands. However, due to high set-up and operation costs, ground monitoring stations are usually limited in number and often sparsely distributed, rendering them insufficient to capture the large spatial variation of urban air quality. This project has developed a framework for PM2.5 concentration estimation using smartphone photos and a prototype app has been implemented to fulfill this purpose. The methodology arising from this project has greatly contributed to the exploration of big data for real-time monitoring of urban air environments. The generation of accurate and timely air quality data has significant value for estimating an individual’s exposure to air pollutants and for other public health studies. The Hong Kong case study also showcase an example for other cities in China or other countries fighting air pollution.

14652516.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14652516.value: The aims of this project are two-fold: - to conceptualise Asian models of strategic spatial planning in Hong Kong, Singapore and Shenzhen with reference to a synthesised study framework. - to identify from the three cities specific examples of more effective planning practices in the context of global, regional and local environmental uncertainties, socio-political complexities, economic competition and institutional challenges and opportunities. Most of the literature on strategic spatial planning comes out of the European context and there has been a dearth of research work on strategic spatial planning in Asia. While Asian cities have practised their versions of strategic spatial planning, these practices have not been thoroughly researched and theorised. In Hong Kong, strategic spatial planning started in the post-WWII years and the latest version is Hong Kong 2030 published in 2007. However, subsequent developments and proposals either did not relate to their recommendations (such as Hong Kong’s Climate Change Strategy and Action Agenda) or the proposed actions have caused widespread societal controversies (such as reclamation in the central Harbour areas and the development of rural New Territories). Strategic spatial planning in Singapore and Shenzhen, however, seems to have been much more effective in spurring their respective socio-economic and spatial transformations in the past decades. To generalise the Asian models of strategic spatial planning, a comparative study of Hong Kong, Singapore and Shenzhen will be carried out. Singapore is an often-cited ‘more successful’ international competitor of Hong Kong while Shenzhen is a fast-catching up domestic contender as a sustainable global city. A synthesised study framework that charts strategic spatial planning between responsive (pro-status quo) and transformative (pro-radical changes) practices will be used to analyse, evaluate and theorise the history, driving forces, processes (institutional set-up, actors, visions and agenda, methodologies and outcomes), as well as implementation and consequences of strategic spatial planning in the three cities. Theoretically, historical strategic spatial planning practices in growth-oriented Asian cities would give varied answers to current research questions raised by European scholars as their cities are moving towards a more entrepreneurial style of strategy making. Studies of strategic spatial planning approaches and practices in Hong Kong, Singapore and Shenzhen are long overdue and the research results will introduce the modes of Asian strategic spatial planning to the world. More importantly, this comparative study will help Hong Kong identify transformative strategic spatial planning approaches and practices in the face of global and regional challenges, competition and opportunities.

14652516.label: Realisation of objectives
14652516.value: All the four objectives have been accomplished. The research has synthesised a research framework to examine if historical evolution, driving forces, the processes, contents and implementation of strategic spatial planning in a place represent reactive or transformative strategic spatial planning practices. The former means strategic spatial planning is just a tool to reproduce the status quo and does not activate institutional changes towards a more desirable direction. The latter means strategic spatial planning leads to institutional changes that moves a place towards a more resilient and sustainable future. The investigation into the planning histories of the three cities quickly pointed to a need to examine also their political economies and governance cultures. My sabbatical leave spent in Singapore and Shenzhen was particularly helpful for me to not only conduct interviews, observe the cities but also experience the city as a local resident. Strategic spatial planning in Hong Kong focuses on land use planning and cannot be called strategic. This nature is probably a legacy of the colonial government that, unfortunately, seems to have continued in the current administration. Unlike the ‘thinking-ahead, thinking-again and thinking-across’ culture of the Singaporean government, the government of Hong Kong has adopted a rather path-dependent trajectory to carry out spatial planning. It seems that spatial plans, often involving reclamation and mega-infrastructure development, becomes a tool to legitimise options to raise the government’s sources of revenue, that is, land sales and related development. Implementation of these plans, however, was often triggered by political crises. Cases in point are the development of new towns after the riots in the 1960s and the ten airport-related core projects after the 1989 June Fourth Incident in Beijing and the exodus of Hong Kongers before 1997 when the city returned to Chinese rule. The way strategic spatial planning unfolds is totally different in Singapore. Eager to be a successful city-state, the People’s Action Party (PAP) led government carries out scenario building at the highest level every three to five years to develop a research-informed and deliberation-oriented scenario to facilitate the review of every policy area and to develop strategies and policies to address the agreed scenario. Hence their planning authority, the Urban Redevelopment Authority, just need to satisfy the spatial needs of the agreed policy actions. Unlike Hong Kong, their SSPs, the Concept Plan and its implementation tool, the Master Plan, have become important platforms to meet the spatial needs of different policy areas to achieve their identified strategies. It is also a collaborative stage to negotiate and harmonise spatial needs of various policy domains. While plans are made/synthesised by the Planning Department alone in Hong Kong, plans are made through a ‘whole-of-government’ approach at strategic and practical levels in Singapore. Strategic spatial planning is done differently in Shenzhen. Unlike Singapore where the political negotiations are done at the scenario building level by the president and the cabinet, the strategic spatial plans produced in Shenzhen incorporate a comprehensive and holistic review of the socio-economic and environmental dimensions of development in the city within the regional and national contexts. As Shenzhen was indeed built by a number of strong state-owned enterprises in its early days when external investment was scarce and former farmers (indigenous villagers) still own a large stretch of collective land that has not be acquired for urban development by the government (due to lack of resources), strategic spatial plans not only needs to steer and control these powerful landed interests, it also has to formulate strategies for the city to become a truly pioneering and progressive Special Economic Zone. Strategic spatial planning in Shenzhen, therefore, is full of reflexivity and experimentalism. Their plan is also an important document for guiding the development of other strategies and plans. It can be argued that strategic spatial planning in the three Asian cities has been primarily formulated by the elites though the models are different. One may argue that Hong Kong takes a more reactive and path-dependent trajectory, with little reflection on its vision and does not proactively involve a lot of stakeholders within and outside the administration. HK2030 and HK2030+ are documents that synthesise and reflect existing and planned projects by different government departments, rather than a strategic process that critically review existing practices in order to do things differently to steer the place towards a more desirable direction. The situation in Singapore is completely different. The PAP-led city-state is keen to identify possible trends, eager to blunt uncertainties and is determined to mobilise the whole government to move the country towards a strategic future. The government also allows people to monitor their performance through consultation and ultimately democratic votes. Shenzhen’s master planning represents a third model. Like Singapore, it has defied a path-dependent trajectory, constantly experimenting with transformative actions in order to live up to its position as China’s first Special Economic Zone and a model and pioneer to become a global sustainable, low-carbon and high-tech city. However, unlike Singapore, the government has to counteract forces that may thwart good planning practices on the ground due to lucrative returns for land related interests. Strategic spatial plans in Shenzhen can, therefore, be argued as products of political negotiations and technical quality. There are a lot of good practices that Hong Kong can learn from both Singapore and Shenzhen: • There is a need to revisit the government’s strong reliance on land related income to sustain government operations. In Singapore, land revenue goes into a reserve for investment and only 50% of the income generated can be allocated as government revenue. The principle is to have a diversity of income. • Learn from both Singapore and Shenzhen their long-term sustainability perspectives in mapping pathways towards the uncertain future, towards people and place resilience. • Both Singapore and Shenzhen have engaged the general public throughout the planning process, from envisioning to implementation. However, consultation of the most recent spatial plan, HK2030+, was released after the government formulated the detailed plan, and massive reclamation (the East Lantau Metropolis), has led to much controversies. • Singapore and Shenzhen produce strategic plans for the city as a whole. Singapore’s spatial transformation includes reclamation and turning the rural areas into a constellation of self-contained and well-connected towns. Shenzhen is actively trying to equalise the quality of planning and service standards between the SEZ and the rest of the city. Hong Kong should plan the New Territories strategically with its rich history, natural and cultural heritage and most important of all, land resources, to search for alternative spaces for housing and creative economic activities. • Plans are useless if they are not implemented. Past plans were implemented only when crises arose. The government announced Lantau Tomorrow Vision before the finalisation of HK2030+, proving once again that strategic spatial plans is not meant to be taken too seriously in implementation. • Resource commitment is very important for strategic spatial planning. This can only be done right when a long-term and sustainable development perspective is adopted. A breakthrough in the financial structure of the government may free it from controlling land supply to sustain a high land price policy, allowing more land, especially brownfield or ecologically damaged sites, to be restored to enliven the economy and to improve people’s quality of life.

14652516.label: Major findings and research outcome
14652516.value: The research has contributed to a deepened understanding of the theory and practice of strategic spatial planning (SSP) in Asia. The research substantiates theoretical discussions of SSP, arguing for a kind of ecological and humane urbanism that strives to ‘leave no one, no place and no ecology behind’ (papers 1, 4). Indeed, SSP is directly related not only to place prosperity and planet sustainability, it is also fundamental to our multi-faceted well-being (paper 6). Based on this theoretical understanding, a framework is developed to compare and contrast strategic spatial planning practices in the three cities (paper 10). The realisation of an ecological and humane urbanism through SSP is not an easy task as history, political economy and governance culture in a place often determine how SSP is institutionalised, formulated and implemented (Papers 3, 4 and 10). The three cities represent three models of SSP. In Hong Kong, SSP has no legal status and the plan is often formulated by the Planning Department. The plan tends to be reactive and path-dependent, focusing on reclamation and infrastructure-led developments that would lead to land sales and related income to the government (papers 1, 3 and 4). Some of the consequences are socio-economic and spatial disparities (papers 7, 8 and 9). The model found in Singapore is much more transformative. Singaporean government takes strategic thinking seriously and carries out scenario building every three to five years. Ministers are required to review their policies and strategies, as well as resource commitment in order to address issues embedded in the adopted scenario. As a result, SSP becomes a platform for different policy domains to identify the best spatial locations to realise their policies and strategies. This whole-of-government approach allows Singapore to always ‘thinking ahead, thinking again and thinking across’ in the development of the city-state (papers 5 and 10). SSP in Shenzhen is the most complicated because the city is embedded in a hierarchical political and administrative structure, with a special role to become a pioneer and model of ecological, sustainable, low-carbon and high-tech development for the country. Also due to historical reasons, substantial amount of land in the city is controlled by the early ‘zone builders’ from the Central or Provincial Governments, and previous farmers who collectively owned the farmlands. Urban planners have to use strategic spatial plans as a tool to control powerful interests while steering developments towards a desirable direction (papers 2 and 10).

14652516.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14652516.value: There are many directions that this research can further take: Hong Kong • Research on possibilities of revamping the urban planning system in Hong Kong so that genuine strategic spatial planning can be carried out. • Research on diversifying sources of revenue in Hong Kong for urban development so that the city can break away from a reliance on land sales and related development. Singapore • Singapore’s state capitalism and ways of managing government finance have a lot of implications on sustainable spatial development and can be further studied. • Singapore’s experience in whole-of-government approach and its exploration towards a whole-of-nation approach serve valuable lessons for government administration in the 21st century. Shenzhen • Shenzhen’s strategic spatial planning exhibits political shrewdness and technical merit and definitely deserves more research to investigate its contributions to planning theories and practices • Shenzhen’s ways of integrating its once rural county into the city may provide some insights for Hong Kong to reconsider the territorial relationships between the urban and the rural spaces. The PI will be vigilant to explore funding opportunities to carry out the above research works.

14652516.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14652516.value: The research has made contributions to the theory and practice of strategic spatial planning (SSP). Theoretically, SSP should be an inclusive and participatory process led by the government to carry out internal and external assessments to produce strategic plans for a city towards a more resilient and sustainable future for human flourishing. However, actually practised SSP is influenced by the history, political and economic development as well as governance culture of a place, rendering some practices reactionary and others transformative. The research has identified three different models of SSP in Hong Kong, Singapore and Shenzhen. In Hong Kong, strategic spatial plans are reproducing the status quo, involving reclamation and infrastructure-led developments, providing avenues to boost land sales and related income for the government. In Singapore, SSP is preceded with a whole-of-government exercise of scenario building about the future. The job of spatial planning is to help identify the most suitable sites for different policies to realise their strategies tailored-made for a desirable future scenario. In Shenzhen, SSP is an important tool to help China’s first Special Economic Zone to overcome powerful local interests while simultaneously experimenting with various urban reforms to move the city towards a more sustainable, low-carbon and high-tech future.

14652616.label: Project Objectives
14652616.value: Construction of a digital archive covering ritual texts and performance practiced in 125 Daoist and local temples in Hong Kong, including construction of a searchable database on their historical development, geo-spatial distribution, stele inscriptions, and other religious features, based upon a Web-GIS platform already achieved in the previous GRF project. Digitization of collected ritual texts and the related video clips will be achieved. Two new functional modes of browsing on the Digital Museum will be developed: the first, image-text parallel browsing and the second, text-video browsing. With image-text parallel browsing, researchers can study the original scanned copied manuscripts in various versions and the edited and proof-read textual version on a parallel window. With manuscript-video browsing, researchers can watch the specific part of textual manuscripts with the matching video clip of ritual archive recorded in 360 degree/multi-dimension on a parallel window. Publication of a volume of analytical work on temple ritual studies with a new approach focusing upon the multi-dimensional ritual processes related to ritual objects, actions, masters, participants, environment, and texts. The book will cover popular liturgies such as the auspicious communal offerings, hungry ghost festivals, exorcistic rites, and spirit-writing still practiced in Daoist and popular temples in Hong Kong over the years.

14652616.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14652616.value: The proposed project aims at a new phase of developing the Daoist Digital Museum (DDM) (http://dao.crs.cuhk.edu.hk/digitalmuseum) by using the Geographic Information System (GIS) tools to provide not only historical, epigraphic and geographical data but also a new digital archive on rituals related to a selection of 125 Chinese temples (called miao 廟or guan 觀, except for Buddhist monasteries or nunneries) in Hong Kong today. These temples are dedicated to specific patron deities of whom there are a great many, among them Tianhou, 天后, Guanyin 觀音, Guandi 關帝, Hongseng 洪聖, Beidi 北帝, Huaguang 華光, Wenchang 文昌, and Lüzu 呂祖. The proposed Digital Ritual Archive of the DDM aims to develop a new and specialized function on ritual’s presentation on the established platform. One of the most innovative and outstanding development of this new multimedia archive on ritual studies will be the production and presentation of ritual video and textual scripts by employing the up-to-date novel technologies of 360 degree video-recording and video-text browsing. Differing from the previously adopted method of single angle recording, 360 degree recording can capture the overview of ritual performance conducted by ritual masters within the whole temple environment, including ritual space and altars, participants, and the ritual master’s symbolic actions. As a result, scholars can visually research on ritual performance not only from one single angle but covering its multi-dimensional ritual processes. Secondly, the proposed project will aim at a digitization of the related ritual texts preformed in Daoist and popular temples in Hong Kong. It is our belief that the digital ritual archive of the DDM will be able to provide researchers with not only a video clip of ritual performance in multi-dimensional way, but also a new methodological approach toward analyzing ritual texts. The proposed digital archive will provide original and scanned ritual texts in different versions, and an annotated and proof-read textual version. As a new and useful functionality implemented on the DDM platform for the research purpose of ritual studies, researchers can now search the keywords of specific ritual texts. With the construction of the new Phase of DDM, scholars of Chinese temple religions, Daoism, ethnography, and social history who are interested in studying temple history and rituals in Hong Kong (as well as in South China in general) will sufficiently be able to conduct extensive quantitative analyses of the geographical and ritual distribution of local temples across the region.

14652616.label: Realisation of objectives
14652616.value: This GRF project’s objectives are realized in the following ways: 1. On-site investigation of religious ceremonies in Chinese temples in Hong Kong This project has specifically investigated 26 ceremonial activities involved in 15 Chinese temples in Hong Kong. Among those ceremonies, the ceremonies of Lantern Festival and Ghost Festival always get the attention of people, for example, the Lantern Festival ceremony in Pak Tai Temple in Wanchai (灣仔北帝廟上元法會), Ghost Festival held by Nam On Fong Resident Association and Sai Wan Ho Cumunity in Shau Kei Wan (南安坊坊眾會盂蘭勝會、西灣河盂蘭勝會), Ghost Festival in the Tin Hau Temple in Stanley (赤柱天后廟盂蘭建醮勝會), Ghost Festival held by Hong Kong Chiu Chau Overseas Public Welfare Advancement Association (柴灣潮僑盂蘭勝會), etc. This project has also inspected 9 celebration ceremony of deities' birthday, such as birthday ceremonies of the North Emperor of Pat Tai Temple in Wanchai (灣仔北帝廟北帝誕), Empress of Heaven of Tin Hau Temple in Ping Chou (坪洲天后廟天后誕), Master Lo Pan in Lo Pan Temple in West Point (西環魯班廟魯班先師誕), Sea God Lord Tam in Tam Kung Temple in Sao Kei Wan (筲箕灣譚公廟譚公誕), Empress of Heaven in Fat Tong Mun (佛堂門天后寶誕), Kwun Yum of Kwun Yum Temple in Hong Hum (紅磡觀音廟觀音誕), Kwan Tai in Mo Tai Temple of Sham Shui Po (深水埗武帝廟關聖帝君寶誕), Zhang Fei in Temple administrated by Nam On Fong Resident Association (南安坊廟張飛誕), Hung Shing in Hung Shing Temple in Po Toi O (西貢布袋澳村洪聖廟洪聖寶誕). The PI has recorded live ceremonies conducted in these Hong Kong temples, through which we can investigate the changes of ritual practices taken place over years, as well as relationships with their surrounding communities. 2 Documenting temple ritual ceremonies This project has selected 14 ceremonies related to gods’ birthdays and ghost festival in 8 Hong Kong temples. The recorded rituals include “rite of repentance” (懺儀), “worshiping the star of the Dipper” (禮斗), “audiences and celebration of gods’ birthdays” (朝賀), “destroying the infernos” (破獄), “summoning the souls of the deceased” (攝召), “distributing flowers in order to dissolve ties” (散花), “feeding the hungry ghosts” (施食), “refining” (煉度), etc. These ritual records are valuable in studying Chinese temple ceremonies, but also provide us the chance to analyze different functions and responsibilities of ritual priests, temple attendants (廟祝), local community organizations in the ceremony, to get to know their liturgical roles in building a religious community of believes in these temples. 3 Conducting orals interviews The PI conducted 12 interviews with temple attendants and the Daoist priests that host the ceremony. Interviewees include Master Ip Yuen Ho (葉緣皓道長), Master Wong Yuen Hang (黃緣嫻道長), Master Chan Chun Fan (陳鎮藩道長), Master Wan Lai Sheung (尹麗嫦道長), Master Lam Tat Cheung (林達章道長), Master Luk Pang (陸鵬道長) and Mr Cheng Hing (鄭興先生). We get to know the details of the ritual services provided by local temples, and the roles and responsibilities of temple leaders, attendants, devotees, ritual priests, and musicians in rituals, as well as the cooperation mode of the group in temple ceremonies. 4 Digitalization of temple Ritual Texts and establishment of a digital archive covering ritual texts This project has digitized all the Hong Kong temple ritual texts collected by the PI for all these years. All the ritual texts have been scanned, proofread, edited, punctuated and annotated again. Moreover, the PI also conducts textual analysis and explanation of all the sources and the applications of these ritual texts. The 37 ritual texts include some of those used in pure and auspicious services (吉祥), for the purpose of praying for blessing (祈福), expressing gratitude for favor (謝恩), worshipping the stars (讚星), pay ritual homage to the God of the Dipper (禮斗), rewarding the gods (酬神), celebration of the deities' birthday (賀誕), consecration (開光), morning and evening ritual services (早晚功課), etc. At the same time, there are also some ritual used in meritorious ritual services with the goal of saving the deceased ones, such as those rituals of summoning the souls of the deceased (攝召), destroying the infernos (破獄), distributing flowers in order to dissolve ties (散花), feeding the hungry ghosts (施食), performing salvation by means of sublimation (煉度). Some of these ritual documents belongs to the ritual text of Hong Kong Quanzhen Daoist temples, such as Lüzu wuji baochan呂祖無極寶懺 and The Xiantian hushi jilian youke先天斛食濟煉幽科；and some are from the Zhengyi Daoist ritual traditions, such as Yingdou keyi迎斗科儀and The Qingxuan jiyao liandu shishi keyi青玄集要煉度施食科儀, etc. 5. Collecting Stele Inscriptions from Hong Kong Temples This project has finished the field investigation of 55 temples (mainly including the temples in Hong Kong island and Kowloon district), collecting 214 inscriptions. The PI has photographed all the original inscriptions, and finished the proofreading and annotation of the inscription, and in addition, added extra information to the introductions of these temples to further analyze the temple history, geographic information, community economy, religious groups, etc. A book manuscript covered all the collections, introductions, and integrations of the Hong Kong temple inscriptions has been completed and is going to be published by the title as Supplement of Hong Kong Temple Inscriptions香港廟宇碑刻彙集補編. 6. Construction of digital platform for management and display of Hong Kong temple ritual texts The PI has successfully cooperated with China Digital Corporation Limited (中國大數據集團) from Mainland China to develop a digital platform for Daoist Digital Museum (http://daoddm2.crs.cuhk.edu.hk). This platform consists of a page for material input and management per the usage of convenient storage, arrangement and categorization of the proof read ritual texts and inscriptions of Hong Kong temples. Besides, theme tags, multi-text indexes searching engine based on different searching conditions are adapted to cope with the future connections among text and geo-space information, images, videos etc. And this platform even supports various reading modes such as original text scan version, original inscription image, image-text parallel reading, even appended with text annotations and explanations. "Hong Kong Temple Ritual Texts Series" has already been officially launched around mid-March 2020, we would also bring "Hong Kong Temple Inscription Texts Series" to public test and usage very soon.

14653316.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14653316.value: 對於地理現象的測量，一般用地面站點進行監測，這些站點在空間中以點的形式存在，該方法的優勢在於我們可以在監測儀器所在的位置獲得相對精確的觀測值。城市區域中的氣候條件，例如溫度、風速、噪聲等級，以及大氣污染物的表面濃度，它們是非常典型的地理特徵，常規來講，關於這些信息的收集與傳播都是由相關單位來負責，得到它們的精確分布對於規劃我們的生存環境至關重要。盡管我們可以獲得這些變量在一些特定地面站點的相當精確的數據，但是這些站點數量較少，空間分布稀疏。在這種情況下，一類簡單的方法是利用插值來估計那些沒有地面觀測值的時空中的點，但因為已有站點但不足，時空觀測值比較少，導致在此基礎上得到的插值結果遠遠達不到我們的精度要求，尤其是當這些地理現象的分布在空間上變化比較大並且城市形態複雜的時候，結果不甚理想。近年來，隨著傳感器網絡的發展，其應用在那些沒有地面站點處的地理信息的測量與監測越來越廣。人們可以隨身攜帶移動傳感器將其安裝到車上，沿著他們的行進軌跡測量數據，從而在一定程度上彌補了地面監測網絡的不足。然而，移動傳感器雖然相對空間上密集但在時間上稀疏，因為它們只是測量經過某個固定點處的該時刻的現象，所以說如果我們可以有效地結合這兩者的信息來進行插值，便可大大提高結果的完整性，使之更為精確。因此，如何將空間稀疏但時間密集但地面監測數據與空間密集時間稀疏的移動傳感器數據結合起來，這是一個非常有挑戰的研究問題，無論是在基礎還是應用研究領域都有待解決。在這裡，我們所提出的研究便是要解決這個問題，其目的是制定一個綜合並且嚴謹的研究框架用以融合地面觀測站點與移動傳感器數據來全面剖析地理信息，這將對地理現象的監測與分析至關重要。作為已有地面觀測網的補充，我們會充分利用強有力的數據集成與插值方法，生成一個覆蓋面更廣的多目標傳感器網，該網絡可以實現對任一種地理現象進行精確的時空預測。具體來講，對於一個特定的地理現象，我們的方法是先將插值結果作為先驗信息，通過結合其它對該現象有影響的次要因素，例如影響城市溫度的通風設備、建築佈局等，以及影響城市空氣污染等交通流量、風向等因素，來最終生成其後驗分布，從而得以提高插值結果的質量。最後，該方法會被用於解決實際問題來檢驗其有效性以及對於結果是否有所提高。總而言之，地理現象與我們的生活息息相關，而我們所提出的研究將會從理論與方法層面推進對於地理現象的時空剖面研究。

14653316.label: Realisation of objectives
14653316.value: Objective 1 of this proposed research is to develop a general and rigorous Bayesian framework for the integrated use of ground-based stations, mobile sensors and contributing factors to perform profiling of geographical phenomena crucial to their monitoring and analysis. Through this project, we have formulated a flexible hierarchical Bayesian (HBM) framework for the construction of the spatio-temporal profile of a geographical phenomenon, e.g. air pollutant concentrations. Within this framework, spatial temporal Kriging (STK) is employed for interpolation based on available observations of a phenomenon, and the obtained results are used as priors in the HBM. To improve the STK results, the likelihood in the form of a nonlinear regression (NLR) with skewed normal residuals is employed to take into account the effect of impact factors, e.g. meteorological factors, to derive the posterior distribution of the geographical phenomenon, e.g. air pollutant concentrations. Due to high dimensionality and complexity, the formulation of the posterior distribution is nonanalytic. We thus need to draw samples from the estimated parameters of the posterior distribution with Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method, and approximate the population characteristics with the sample characteristics. The HBM model has been shown to be theoretically sound and empirically efficient, accurate and robust in a real-life application. Our additional contribution to the Bayesian approach is to get around the conventional Gaussianity assumption on the prior distribution and the likelihood function, which are often invalid presumption about the reality, and introduce the skew normal distribution, which better approximates the real world, with derived parameters and associated statistical tests. So, we have achieved Objective 1 of the project. To effectively and efficiently collect data by mobile sensors, we, building on previous research, have further developed a multi-target sensor network that complements the station-based network to provide a large enough basis for the reliable space-time interpolation of a phenomenon. We have extended the probability hypothesis density (PHD) approach to construct the multi-target mobile-sensor network to track a time-varying number of targets/sensors to make measurements of geographical phenomena in space and time. It is a two-level fusion scheme with a cluster-based hierarchical architecture comprising a position-aware central base station and multiple source sensors. The local censor heads collect sensor data within their area and perform the first level fusions. The fused data are then sent to the central base station for the second level fusion. Simulation results demonstrate its capability and effectiveness in balancing energy-efficiency and accuracy in the tracking of a time-varying number of sensors. Therefore, Objective 2 is satisfactorily achieved. For Objective 3, we have employed the spatio-temporal kriging methodology for interpolation with station-based spatio-temporal information within the HBM framework. During the research, we have discovered that a two-step local smoothing model is also an effective method in synchronizing and integrating station-based and mobile-sensor-based data of various spatial and temporal scales, and then using them to interpolate the spatio-temporal profile of geographical phenomena. Thus, not only we have accomplished what Objective 3 targets at, we have made further methodological contribution to spatio-temporal interpolation via the two-step local smoothing model when data are of various spatial and temporal scales. We have also explored the way remote sensing, ground-based and mobile sensor data can be integrated to perform spatio-temporal profiling of geographical phenomena. So, objective 3 is well achieved. For real-life application, we have applied the HBM model to perform spatio-temporal profiling of air pollutant concentrations in Northern China. We evaluate the HBM with the concentrations of air pollutants and the meteorological variables from Northern China. The empirical results show that the proposed HBM generally outperforms the nonlinear regression and STK in terms of efficiency, accuracy and robustness. The Framework is general enough to be applied to the profiling of air pollutant concentrations in other areas. For the two-step local smoothing model, we have applied it to the profiling of air pollutant concentrations in Daegu, South Korea, with high level of accuracy. Thus, we have achieved Objective 4. Throughout the data integration and profiling processes, we have also investigated errors and uncertainties involved and their propagations. Besides the Bayesian approach, we have also made an initial attempt to use machine learning as an alternative to estimate air pollutant concentrations. We have constructed a novel long short-term memory (LSTM) with a spatial attention mechanism that can effectively obtain the spatio-temporal profile of air pollutant concentrations. Furthermore, in order to have a powerful platform for the implementation of the proposed approaches and methods for the integration of multi-source, multi-scale and multi-type data for spatiotemporal profiling, we, extending on previous work, have constructed a prototype of an integrated air pollution decision support system for real-life applications.

14653316.label: Major findings and research outcome
14653316.value: We have formulated a flexible hierarchical Bayesian (HBM) framework for the construction of spatio-temporal profiles of geographical phenomena, e.g. air pollutant concentrations. Within this framework, spatial temporal Kriging (STK) is employed for interpolation, and the obtained results are used as priors in the HBM. To improve the STK results, the likelihood in the form of nonlinear regression with skewed normal residuals is employed to account for the effect of impact factors, e.g. meteorological factors, to derive the posterior distribution of the geographical phenomenon. Since the posterior distribution is nonanalytic, we need to draw samples from the estimated parameters of the posterior distribution with Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method to approximate the population characteristics. The HBM model has been shown to be theoretically sound and empirically accurate in real-life applications (see C2). Extending on the previous work, we have further developed the probability hypothesis density (PHD) approach to construct a multi-target mobile-sensor network to track time-varying number of mobile sensors making measurements in space and time. It is a cluster-based hierarchical architecture comprising a position-aware central base station and multiple source sensors. The system has been proved to be accurate in sensor tracking with minimum energy consumption (see C5). For spatio-temporal interpolation, we have applied spatial-temporal Kriging (see C2) and have also developed a two-step local smoothing model to integrate spatial and temporal data from different sources. The two-step local smoothing model is more flexible in synchronizing and integrating station-based and mobile-sensor-based data of various spatial and temporal scales, and in interpolating accurate spatio-temporal profiles of geographical phenomena. The model is supported by real-life applications (see C1). To explore alternative framework, we have developed a novel machine learning method, called spatial attention-based long short-term memory (SA-LSTM), that combines LSTM and a spatial attention mechanism to adaptively utilize the spatio-temporal information of multiple factors for forecasting air pollutant concentrations. The SA-LSTM employs gated recurrent connections to extract temporal information of multiple factors at individual locations, and the spatial attention mechanism to spatially fuse the temporal information extracted at these locations. This method is effective in forecasting air pollutant concentrations (see C3). To have a powerful platform for the implementation of the proposed approaches and methods for the integration of multi-source, multi-scale and multi-type data for spatiotemporal profiling, we have, as an extra undertaking, further extended a previous prototype of an integrated air pollution decision support system for real-life applications (see C4).

14653316.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14653316.value: To further improve the hierarchical Bayesian model for spatio-temporal profiling, we can search for an even more appropriate prior model and posterior distribution. The slash power normal distribution might be a good candidate. Moreover, a more sophisticated spatio-temporal Kriging interpolation can also be considered. For further research, we can consider integrating more data sources, such as land cover/land use data and real-time traffic condition, into the model to perform more robust and accurate spatio-temporal profiling and forecasting. To give further empirical support, we can apply the methodology to more real-life geographical phenomena for evaluation and improvement. Based on the capability and performance of the spatial attention-based long short-term memory (SA-LSTM) in considering multiple factors, we can integrate new multisource information into the model for spatio-temporal profiling of geographical phenomena. It will be beneficial to further explore the effectiveness of the deep learning approach to perform spatio-temporal profiling of geographical phenomena in places with highly complex morphology.

14653316.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14653316.value: Measurement of geographical phenomena has conventionally been made by ground-based stations located at specific points in space. Climatic conditions and surface concentration of air pollutants are typical measurements made at specific ground-based stations. However, the measurements are relatively sparse in space because of the limited number of located stations. Although interpolation methods can be employed to estimate values of a phenomenon at points in space and time at which no measurements can be made, profiles obtained by such process are generally far from desirable because we do not have large enough number of stations to serve as the reference points to make reliable interpolations. However, recent development of sensor network technologies has enabled us to deploy mobile sensors to measure geographical phenomena at places with no measurement stations. Nevertheless, mobile sensors are relatively sparse in time but dense in space. This study constructs a novel and powerful Bayesian framework and associated methodologies with which we can effectively integrate both of the information collected by the ground-based stations and the mobile sensors to derive complete and accurate profiles of geographical phenomena. The theoretical construct is supported by real-life applications in the profiling of air pollutant concentrations.

14654016.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14654016.value: China tops the world in the emissions of most major air pollutants as well as greenhouse gases. Policy enforcement is a serious challenge facing China's environmental governance to demand accurate, reliable data for catching non-compliance and issuing penalty. The current compliance monitoring system in China is largely bottom-up. Data from emitting firms should generally pass through, and inspected by, multiple levels of local governments and their environmental agencies before reaching the central government. The path may invite subjective distortions for the benefits of various entities. Facing immense pressure, the easiest way of compliance for local governments and firms could be to twist the numbers. Another shortcoming of the bottom-up compliance monitoring is the high costs. Because of China’s sheer size, the large system involves numerous personnel and occupies substantial resources. Top-down satellite remote sensing technologies have the potential to alleviate the above two shortcomings. First, remote sensing technologies could circumvent various levels of local governments and emission sources to provide objective data without subjective distortions. Second, they could potentially provide a relatively low-cost means to monitor emission sources. Although each satellite observing the Earth could cost a few hundred million US dollars, its wide spatial and regular coverage could substantially reduce the average costs per emission source. However, the technologies also have two major drawbacks. The spatial resolution on pollutant concentrations is coarse and the data accuracy does not satisfy the need to punish non-compliance. The research aims to explore a novel strategy to integrate top-down satellite data into the current compliance monitoring system, accommodating the advantages and disadvantages of bottom-up and top-down methods. Industrial parks are selected for in-depth examination, which concentrate many significant energy-intensive factories within geographically approximate regions to become emission hotspots. Bottom-up compliance monitoring in industrial parks could be especially problematic. They often act as semi-independent local governments with concrete administrative and legal jurisdictions. With a primary focus on industrial development, the balance between development and environment could be even more pushed toward the development side. The Ningdong Energy and Chemical Industry Base in Ningxia, China will be particularly chosen for a case study. Insights from this project could help China, as well as the international society, to integrate remote sensing technologies into current systems for more effective and efficient environmental enforcement to alleviate domestic environmental crises and mitigate climate change.

14654016.label: Realisation of objectives
14654016.value: The three inter-linked research objectives have been successfully completed. For realizing the first research objective to examine the bottom-up compliance monitoring system, we examined China’s national environmental governance and compliance monitoring system and conducted a case study in the Ningdong Energy and Chemical Industrial Base in Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region. We assessed the evolution and reforms of China’s environmental governance and explained that environmental compliance monitoring is not only on emitters but also on local governments. The relationships between the central and local governments were examined from the perspectives of chain of command and division of labour. Policy making is the primary function of central and provincial governments, while municipality and county governments shoulder primary implementation tasks. Environmental policy making and implementation have been significantly decentralized. China’s weak rule of law also strengthened such decentralization. Furthermore, we explored how the entire Chinese government, from the central to local levels, is mobilized for environmental protection via environmental goals, which heavily relies on effective environmental compliance monitoring. Ningdong Energy and Chemical Industrial Base is an emission hotspot as an industrial park. Besides publicly available official documents, regulations and reports, we collected first-hand data from in-depth multi-phase fieldwork through semi-structured interviews and participant observation. We analyzed how its environmental compliance monitoring system is structured and how its administrative leaders and emitters are incentivized. The climate governance reform in 2018 was also tracked to understand the impacts on CO2 compliance monitoring and climate policy implementation. Corresponding to the second research objective, top-down satellite data were examined in depth on their capacity for monitoring large emission sources and local governments. We assessed the capabilities of CO2 satellites as objective, independent, potentially low-cost and external data sources for monitoring energy-related anthropogenic CO2 emissions at regional/national, megacity and point-source geographical scales. After overviewing all major CO2 satellites, SCIAMACHY, GOSAT and OCO-2 were focused on due to their wider research applications and higher CO2 sensitivity in total column measurements that include near surface emissions. Nighttime light satellite data for proxy CO2 monitoring were also brought into comparison to distinguish the importance of direct CO2 satellite monitoring. We explored from the perspectives of spatial and temporal capability and accuracy to comprehend the current statuses of applications, assess the strengths and weaknesses of research methods, investigate major challenges and propose suggestions for future progress. We concluded that CO2 satellite monitoring can strengthen the data foundation for implementing international climate treaties and domestic climate policies. Furthermore, satellite observations, specifically OCO-2 XCO2 measurements, were utilized to develop an independent and objective approach to evaluate the attainment of national and subnational CO2 mitigation goals in China’s 13th Five-Year Plan (FYP, 2016-2020). We established three estimation models at both pixel and provincial levels to estimate China’s subnational CO2 emissions with OCO-2 observations. CO2 emissions of prefecture-level municipalities were interpolated based on pixel-level model. In 2019, approximately 65% had accomplished FYP mitigation goals assigned by provincial governments. Our provincial-level estimation indicates that 22 out of 31 provinces had accomplished their individual FYP goals in 2019. National aggregate absolute emissions showed 8.0%~18.4% reduction in 2019 across the three models from the 2015 level. The drop of CO2 emission intensity ranged from 29.7% to 37.7%, indicating that the national FYP goal of 18% reduction should have been overachieved. To regulate SO2 and NOx emissions, environmental compliance monitoring also plays a key role in effective and efficient policy implementation. With satellite data from Aura Ozone Monitoring Instrument (OMI) level 2 sulphur dioxide total column product (OMSO2 v003), we studied the implementation of two crucial policies, being “management on desulfurization electricity price of coal-fired generating units and the operation for desulfurization facilities (Trial)” and “upgrading and retrofitting action plan for energy conservation and pollution mitigation in the coal-fired power sector”, that entered into effect in 2007 and 2014, respectively, for deep mitigation in coal-fired power plants as emission hotspots. We examined the divergence of provinces in implementing these policies, particularly on whether, when and to what extent they witnessed a reduction of emissions in their coal-fired power plants. For achieving the third research objective, we examined the evolution of China’s environmental compliance monitoring system and explained its improvement trajectory in the past two decades. For improving the effectiveness and efficiency of environmental compliance monitoring, multiple measures were taken sequentially to reflect their relative difficulties. Various environmental compliance monitoring technologies have clear tradeoffs to offer potential cooperative opportunities for reaching better outcomes than anyone can achieve individually. The rapidly evolving new technologies like satellites could potentially reform the current environmental compliance monitoring system. They tend to be much cheaper in monitoring one polluter (in terms of average and especially marginal costs) but less accurate for legally confirming compliance statuses and issuing penalties, while conventional technologies are much more expensive but, if working smoothly, can meet the legal accuracy requirements. For exploring possible ways of integrating new compliance monitoring technologies and achieving high environmental compliance rates without demanding more compliance monitoring resources, we constructed a conceptual, computable model that simulates how influential factors in three categories – pollution abatement costs, noncompliance penalty and compliance monitoring effectiveness – affect compliance decisions of polluters and thus the compliance rate. Specifically, new and cheaper technologies are proposed to screen polluters and pick out those with higher probabilities of noncompliance, while conventional technologies will be employed to verify the compliance statuses of those polluters and issue penalties. This study calls the compliance monitoring system with systematic screening as the screening system and the conventional one as the diagnosing system. The screening system in general does show significantly better performance than the diagnosing system to achieve higher compliance rates. At the 2015 level of inspection staff in China, the screening system would be able to yield nearly full compliance for the 809,500 polluting sources as covered under the “double randomness, one publicization” scheme. However, the diagnosing system that is closer to reality would only bring about half of those polluters under compliance. For the screening system to prevail over the diagnosing system, sensitivity analysis suggests that the average cost of screening technologies should be no less than 65% cheaper than that of diagnosing technologies. Screening technologies should especially not wrongly recognize more than 40% compliant cases into the high-risk group, while diagnosing technologies should successfully convict at least 60% of noncompliant polluters in the high-risk group for penalties. For the 68,121 polluting sources under the central government’s special supervisory monitoring in 2015, generally being large or hazardous polluters, the diagnosing system should have already achieved nearly full compliance, but for the 5,925,576 polluting sources in the 2007 census, neither compliance monitoring system would work. Environmental campaigns with temporary increase of inspection staff or shocks with their temporary reduction could destabilize the equilibrium rates in the screening system with longer-term impacts, while the impacts in the diagnosing system would be short-lived as seen in empirical cases. Environmental campaigns might be especially utilized to pull the system out of a possible noncompliance trap. If polluters have longer memories and their current compliance rate is directly determined by those in the past multiple periods, the screening system will demonstrate more resilience against the short-term campaigns and shocks.

14654016.label: Major findings and research outcome
14654016.value: Major findings and outcome correspond to the research objectives. First, environmental compliance monitoring in China targets both polluters and local governments. CO2, SO2 and NOx mitigation is beyond the authority of environmental administrations alone to demand wider governmental cooperation (Kwok, et al., 2018; Xu, 2020). Although goal setting is centralized, goal attainment, policy making and implementation are heavily decentralized to require effective compliance monitoring on local governments (Xu, 2020). Chronic noncompliance of polluters could be explained by low probability of catching noncompliance and/or insufficient penalty upon conviction (Peng, et al., 2018). Technologies could facilitate the solution to environmental problems (Guo & Xu, 2018), but their adoption requires policy intervention. Leaders of China’s industrial parks are assessed primarily with economic targets and much less with environmental performance (Ma, 2021 (expected). Environmental governance and policy in industrial parks: A case study in western China. Ph.D. thesis. CUHK). Nevertheless, goals on electricity companies with effective compliance monitoring can lead to desirable outcomes (Chung & Xu, 2020). Second, satellite data can act as objective, independent, potentially low-cost and external data sources. SCIAMACHY, GOSAT and OCO-2 have higher CO2 sensitivity in total column measurements, while night-time light satellite data are mainly for proxy, thus indirect, CO2 monitoring (Pan, Xu & Ma., 2021). OCO-2 XCO2 measurements indicate that in 2019, approximately 65% of prefecture-level municipalities and 22 out of 31 provinces had accomplished goals in the 13th Five-Year Plan (2016-2020), while the national goal of 18% reduction should have been overachieved (Pan, Xu & Huang, Under Review). Satellite data can also monitor the implementation of air pollution mitigation policies, such as SO2 and NOx. SO2 VCD enhancements of coal-fired power plants decreased by 94 % from 2006 to 2020, while most of the reduction took place in 2008 and 2014-2015, relating to the “desulfurization electricity tariff” and “ultra-low emission” policies, respectively (Yan & Xu, Under Review). Third, a conceptual, computable model is constructed to simulate how pollution abatement costs, noncompliance penalty and compliance monitoring effectiveness affect compliance decisions of polluters (Xu, 2020). Satellite data are proposed to screen polluters and pick out those with higher probabilities of noncompliance, while conventional technologies will be employed to verify their compliance statuses (Xu, 2020). The reformed environmental compliance monitoring system could more efficiently utilize resources for more effective compliance, under which environmental campaigns might be used to pull the system out of a possible noncompliance trap (Xu, 2020).

14654016.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14654016.value: This research will be extended on two fronts. First, we will continue exploring the integration of satellite data, and more broadly Big Data, into environmental and climate compliance monitoring system. Compliance of large point sources has improved significantly over the past decade, while small sources with much weaker signals, or enhancements against backgrounds, should be better targeted for achieving fundamental environmental clean-up. China just announced to achieve carbon neutrality in 2060, merely 30 years past the planned peak in 2030 to indicate mounting challenges. These new developments significantly raise the demand for environmental compliance monitoring. This study has established a firm foundation to make further progress from these two aspects. Second, India and Belt-and-Road countries are rapidly developing to experience serious environmental degradation and rising CO2 emissions. Constrained by institutions, budgets and skills, many of them have not established sound environmental compliance monitoring system to ensure the implementation of relevant domestic policies and international treaties. Satellite data could provide such opportunities and enhance compliance with greater efficiency and effectiveness. Their economic development could thus cause less environmental damages and climate change.

14654016.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14654016.value: Pollution and climate mitigation in China would not be possible if emitters and local governments did not comply with relevant policies. Environmental compliance monitoring conventionally follows the monitoring, reporting and verification (MRV) procedure, in which polluters self-monitor their own emissions, report the data to authorities, and then receive verification especially when discrepancies are suspected. However, this system is costly and subject to data manipulation in China’s context. Ineffective compliance monitoring has been a key cause of China’s weak environmental policy implementation and serious pollution. This study first understands how the conventional system is organized in China’s institutional setting, especially in emission hotspots like industrial parks and coal-fired power plants. Then we utilize data from several satellites to monitor CO2, SO2 and NOx. The costs are much lower on a per source basis and they are external and objective to prevent possible manipulation, but the accuracy has not been high enough to replace bottom-up compliance monitoring. We established a computer model to simulate and explore the integration of satellite data for enhancing efficiency and effectiveness. This study could contribute to reforming the conventional system, enhancing its effectiveness and efficiency, and thus lifting the compliance rates of emitters and local governments.
