14654116.label: Project Objectives
14654116.value: To understand how different cognitive and linguistic skills contribute developmentally to the process of learning to spell and read words in Chinese. To understand how behavioral measures obtained in kindergarten might predict processing ability (as measured by ERP and eye movement studies) related to writing in primary school. To determine the extent to which performance (using ERP and eye movement studies) on character identification distinguishes good and poor spellers in second grade. To examine how early errors in spelling predict subsequent spelling performance in Chinese. To explore how behavioral, eye movement, and ERP performances correlate with each other and whether it is more reliable and effective to diagnose children’s risk for spelling/writing difficulties by using markers at both the behavioral and neural levels.

14654116.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14654116.value: How do children learn to “spell” in Chinese? Around the world, abilities to read and write are the basis for most subsequent learning. However, although there are many studies on how Chinese children learn to read, there are few on how children learn to write and spell. In the present study, children in kindergarten will be tested on linguistic and cognitive tasks once per year across three years (through second grade). Cognitive/linguistic measures and errors made in spelling each year will be used concurrently and longitudinally to explain spelling performance and to categorize developmental writing errors. In the final year of the study, we will test 50 of those who show, respectively, the highest and lowest behavioral spelling skills on ERP and eye tracking experiments related to character processing in order to understand whether how children process and prepare for writing characters at an early stage (i.e., behavioral measures) explains future writing skills (i.e., efficiency of writing knowledge measured via anticipation of strokes and eye movements at the millisecond level). Writing a character in Chinese is different from the process of sequencing letters to write a word in an alphabetic orthography. Chinese characters comprise radicals, which are made up of strokes. Strokes are written in a prescribed order, standard in Chinese pedagogy. We view Chinese “spelling” broadly as encompassing all processes through which writing a character or a word comprised of two or more characters correctly is accomplished, including a broad range of visual-motor and cognitive skills. That is, learning to spell likely involves not only linguistic skills such as phonological, morphological, and orthographic processing, but also pure copying and motor skills. Our lab-based behavioral and electrophysiological testing will help to reveal early markers of stable Chinese writing facility, including character structure awareness, anticipation of stroke order, and sensitivity to individual strokes within characters. Theoretically, this research will provide a comprehensive model of how Chinese character spelling develops. Practically, analyses will have educational implications for children learning to write Chinese, and allow an exploration of the earliest indicators of writing difficulties in Chinese. Targeting behavioral and neuropsychological indicators of early writing variability can facilitate early identification and remediation of writing skills for those at-risk for writing difficulties.

14654116.label: Realisation of objectives
14654116.value: During the reporting period, we recruited and conducted behavioral assessments on 325 Hong Kong Chinese kindergartners at the K3 level from 9 kindergartens in different districts including Hong Kong Island, Kowloon, and New Territories in Year 1. Year 1 behavioral assessment comprised the following tasks: Raven’s Standard Progressive Matrices, rapid automatized naming, phonological awareness, morphological awareness, orthographic knowledge in Chinese, vocabulary test in Chinese, fine motor skills, visual-motor integration skills, delayed copying in Chinese, pure copying in Korean and Hebrew, spelling/dictation test in Chinese, and word reading test in Chinese. This battery was very broad and allowed us to explore a variety of behavioral skills. In Year 2, we reached out for the same group of participants. As 58 participants dropped out from the study, there were 267 remained in the study. Year 2 behavioral assessment comprised the following tasks: delayed copying in Chinese, delayed copying in English, spelling/dictation test in Chinese and in English, word reading test in Chinese and in English, invented spelling in English, and silent word reading in English. We included tests on English because comparisons between Chinese and English literacy performance helped us to understand Chinese spelling acquisition better. In the final year of the reporting period, we continued to measure 215 participants from the original group with the same behavioral assessments used in Year 2. After collecting the behavioral data around August of 2019, we started to schedule some of the participants so as to perform the EEG experiment. In the EEG experiment, children were required to complete a stroke order task while their EEG were collected. We had collected EEG data with 26 children at the end of 2019. Due to the COVID-19 situation, schools were suspended for most of the time in 2020. We attempted to recruit participants once in a while when the pandemic seemed to be contained but this pandemic has obstructed our project progress mainly in two ways: Parents and children were hesitant to participate in recruitment, particularly for EEG work, and face-to-face data collection posed potential health risks both to experimenters and participants. In addition, some of the parents cancelled the appointments even they agreed to participate previously. As a result, we only managed to collect EEG data from 26 children. Therefore, Objectives 3 and 5 could not be 100% complete. However, even though the sample size is not large, we still have obtained some interesting findings with these data. With our behavioural data in hand, we noticed that, both concurrently and longitudinally, children’s performances on the delayed copying task explained a significant amount of variance in their spelling performance. In addition, pure copying emerged as a strong correlate of Chinese reading and spelling but not of English reading and spelling. The EEG data from our 26 participants also highlighted consistent ERP effects from the stroke order task, showing that our experimental design was reliable. This was the first time that any such a design was attempted with children, at least to the best of our knowledge. We also found that these ERP effects were correlated with Chinese word dictation and word reading performance, suggesting that Chinese children’s word reading and spelling performance is related to early visual processing of the writing sequence of Chinese characters.

14654116.label: Major findings and research outcome
14654116.value: First, based on the dataset, we found that rapid automatized naming, phonological awareness, orthographic awareness, morphological awareness, motor coordination, and delayed copying were all unique contributors to Chinese spelling performance among Hong Kong kindergartners after statistically controlling for other cognitive-linguistic related skills (Ye, McBride, Yin, Cheang, & Tse, 2020). Second, handwriting fluency and Vietnamese copying were unique correlates of spelling even after considering all well-established cognitive measures, including morphological awareness, orthographic awareness, and phonological awareness (Lam & McBride, 2018). Third, delayed copying was the strongest correlate of Chinese written spelling concurrently (Mo et al., 2018; Ye et al., 2020) and longitudinally (Ye, Tong, McBride, Li, & Tse, 2021; this study arose directly from this GRF project. But the journal forgot to put down the acknowlegdement and we did not notice this). Fourth, by comparing Chinese and English spelling development, we found that pure copying skill was a critical predictor of Chinese reading and spelling, whereas it was not a significant longitudinal correlate of English reading and spelling. In addition, Chinese phonological awareness was a unique correlate of subsequent English, but not Chinese, word reading and spelling (Ye, Yan, Ruan, McBride, & Yeung, 2020). In addition, Chinese word reading performance at kindergarten and first grade predicted Chinese spelling performance at first grade and second grade, respectively. However, the relations were not bidirectional (Ye, Yan, Ruan, McBride, Zheng, & Yin, 2021). Regarding the EEG study, the ERP N2 effect on the left and right central areas of the scalp were associated with Chinese word spelling and Chinese word reading, suggesting that Chinese children’s literacy performance is related to semantic and visual processing (Lui et al., in preparation). Together, these findings highlight the importance of delayed copying and pure copying: Both sensitivities to Chinese character structure and understanding of the function of semantic radicals are crucial to children’s early spelling abilities. In addition, the findings highlight the unique features of literacy learning in two different writing systems and suggest the importance of using somewhat different strategies according to the unique features of different writing systems during literacy learning and teaching.

14654116.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14654116.value: Our work inspired research in Korean kids and adults demonstrating that delayed copying explained unique variance in Korean spelling (Cho & McBride, 2020), suggesting that delayed copying may represent an important pathway between traditional literacy-related skills and spelling in Chinese and maybe in other writing systems. Future longitudinal studies in other writing systems and studies comparing children with and without spelling difficulties on delayed copying skill will be important to conduct to reaffirm the potential importance of delayed copying for the detection of early spelling difficulties. In addition, a focus for future studies can be intervention effects of systematic copying practice on struggling spellers. Also, as a relatively new task (skill), the design of this research limited us in understanding of the precise nature of delayed copying. Future studies should focus more on exploring the underlying mechanisms of delayed copying and how it may relate to spelling in Chinese and other writing systems.

14654116.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14654116.value: The abilities to read and write are the basis for most subsequent learning and academic achievement. Although there are many studies on how Chinese children learn to read, there are few on how children learn to write and spell. Writing a character in Chinese is different from the process of sequencing letters to write a word in an alphabetic orthography. We view Chinese “spelling” broadly as encompassing all processes through which writing a character or a word comprised of two or more characters correctly is accomplished, including a broad range of visual-motor and cognitive skills. Our behavioral and electrophysiological testing help to reveal early markers of stable Chinese writing facility, including character structure awareness, anticipation of stroke order, and sensitivity to individual strokes within characters. Theoretically, given our relatively comprehensive battery of cognitive-linguistic tasks included in this study, these results give us a clearer understanding of how these skills are related to Chinese spelling and provide a comprehensive model of how Chinese character spelling develops. Practically, analyses have important educational implications for children learning to write Chinese, and allow an exploration of the earliest indicators of writing difficulties in Chinese.

14654716.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14654716.value: This project aims to investigate complex nominal groups (traditionally known as noun phrases) in the written English of Hong Kong secondary students. It plans to analyse students’ argumentative writing for their use of embedding in nominal groups, and investigate the relationship between these embeddings and the ratings the texts receive. The ability to construct complex nominal groups has been identified in first language (L1) and English as a Second Language (ESL) contexts as crucial to the development of written English in adolescence. Expanding the nominal group enables the abstraction and generalization which is increasingly required as students progress through secondary education (Christie 2002; Fang, Schleppegrell & Cox 2006). In recent years, a small number of studies have included some consideration of the role of the nominal group in the writing of less experienced users of English, such as primary age L1 writers, university EFL (English as a Foreign Language) students, and even EFL students in secondary education (Lewis 2014; Liardét 2013; Maxwell-Reid 2015a; Maxwell-Reid & Coniam 2015; Whittaker, Llinares & McCabe 2012). However, despite these signs of interest, the nominal group is still generally neglected in EFL contexts, particularly with students below university age. Little is known as to how this group of learners uses expanded nominal groups, or whether being able to manipulate this language area is as central to their meaning making as it is for other users of English. Similarly, there is a lack of guidance for teachers on how to approach this type of language use. In order to address these issues, this project plans to collect argumentative writing from secondary school students in five schools. The texts will be graded, and analysed for genre and for one key aspect of nominal group expansion: embedding. The embeddings will be analysed for their textual function, and also for type of embedding used, the language resources involved, and the difficulties in control of those resources. The analytical framework employs tools from systemic functional linguistics (SFL) (Halliday & Matthiessen 2014). Relationships between the nominal groups and grade will be investigated. Differences between texts will be further considered using interview and questionnaire data detailing the English teachers’ and students’ experiences teaching and learning written argument. This research would have both theoretical and practical significance. It would contribute to understandings of L2 English writing development, and inform guidance for secondary school teachers in their teaching of L2 English writing. 香港中學生英語議論文中名詞片語的嵌入使用 摘要 本研究課題目的在於調查香港中學生英文書面語中複雜名詞片語（通常稱為名詞短語）之使用情況。本研究計畫通過分析學生的議論文來揭示他們在名詞片語中嵌入的使用情況，並且調查這些嵌入與文本評分間之相關關係。 構建複雜名詞片語的能力在母語（L1）語境及英語作為第二語言（ESL）語境中均被發現對青少年書面英語發展起至關重要的作用。擴展名詞片語能夠發展抽象和概括能力，這也逐漸被認為是中學教育中學生所需發展的能力（Christie 2002; Fang, Schleppegrell & Cox 2006）。近年來，少量研究已涉及到名詞片語在初級英語使用者之寫作中的作用，包括小學階段的母語使用者，英語作為外語的大學生，乃至英語作為外語（EFL）的中學生（Lewis 2014; Liardét 2013; Maxwell-Reid 2015a; Maxwell-Reid & Coniam 2015; Whittaker, Llinares & McCabe 2012）。然而，儘管既往研究已呈現了以上之種種研究興趣，名詞片語在英語作為外語的語境中仍受到普遍忽視，特別是針對大學階段以下的英語學習者。此階段的英語學習者怎樣使用擴展的名詞片語，亦或是對這些英語學習者而言能夠熟練使用這一語言領域是否跟其他英語使用者一樣是意義建構的核心，學界對此都不甚瞭解。同樣，既往研究缺乏對教師如何處理此類語言使用進行指導。 為解決這些問題，本研究課題計畫從五所中學收集學生的議論文文本。這些文本將被評分，並且從體裁及拓展名詞片語的一個關鍵方面—嵌入—進行分析。研究者將分析這些嵌入的文本功能，嵌入類型，包含的語言資源，及控制這些語言資源的難點。分析框架將採用系統功能語言學（SFL）的分析工具（Halliday & Matthiessen 2014）。名詞片語與文本評分間之關係也將被研究。文本之間的差異將通過訪談和問卷資料進一步研究，以期詳細揭示英語教師和學生教授和學習書面論證的經驗。 本研究兼具理論及實踐意義。它將促進對英語作為第二語言寫作發展的瞭解，並為中學教師二語寫作教學提供指導。

14654716.label: Realisation of objectives
14654716.value: The objectives were realized through collection and analysis of data, both of which followed the plan outlined in the research proposal. Data collection Data were collected from three schools, with one participatory class and teacher per school (plus one back-up class and teacher in case of drop out, which was not required). The three schools were all typical Hong Kong schools at the mid-to-high range (schools in Hong Kong are categorized, principally by the results of incoming first year students). The students wrote three argumentative texts (the main data used to address the objectives), and completed questionnaires on their experience of writing and of each writing topic. These provided supporting data, to check for issues that might affect the main data (student texts) and their interpretation. A subgroup of students in each class was interviewed to probe the questionnaire questions further, and the three teachers were interviewed on their experience of teaching writing generally, and also for each topic. The data collected matched the expectations of the proposal and enabled the research objectives to be addressed satisfactorily. In an ideal world we would perhaps have had more student texts at the higher levels of proficiency. However, elite schools were less willing to commit to the research schedule, and the advantage of using more typical schools is greater relevance to the school community overall. The prompts for the writing (Figure 1) were agreed with the teachers beforehand, and the questionnaires and student interviews indicated that they were acceptable topics for these students. One prompt was discovered to include a somewhat ambiguous element, but this did not prevent the students from writing on it, and the range of texts from this prompt were similar overall to the texts from the other two prompts. Round 1: Litter You are a team member of The Hong Kong Cleanup. During cleanup tasks, your team has observed piles of litter in country parks and at picnic spots. Your team captain has asked you to write an article for the school magazine to raise students’ awareness. In your article, describe the litter problem and its negative effects, and also give some suggestions for students. Round 2: Whole Person Development (WPD) You have recently read an article in the Hong Kong Post which suggested that Hong Kong students spend most of their time studying. The article argued that students should be encouraged to develop in other ways too, and not only focus on academic achievement. Write a letter to the editor of the Hong Kong Post stating your point of view with reasons and suggestions. Round 3: Pokémon Go (P Go) Your school magazine is going to include a special feature on leisure and technology. You have decided to write about the recent Pokémon Go craze in Hong Kong. Some people emphasise the benefits of Pokémon Go, but other people highlight possible negative effects. Write an article for your school magazine giving your opinion on Pokémon Go and including reasons for your view. Figure 1: The three prompts Data analysis. Objective one, to advance understanding of students’ use of nominal group embedding in their argumentative writing, was realized through analysis of all the student texts for use of embedding in nominal clauses. The embedding was identified and categorized following Halliday and Matthiessen (2014), as illustrated in Table 1, and also categorized for accuracy (considered as full or partial realization of the embedding). From this analysis we could see how much the students were using the various types of embedding, where they were using it, and if they were having trouble using it. 14654716.label: Major findings and research outcome
14654716.value: 1. Senior secondary writers of EFL use nominal embedding in argumentative writing. The resource is not restricted to the older and/or more expert users of English previously studied. The data included all four types of clausal embedding, plus phrasal post-modification. The less commonly-used phrasal embedding as Head of the nominal group was not found. 2. Students had problems in the control of language resources involved in the embedding, with overall more intermediate than fully realized examples. The errors were found in all types of nominal embedding, but were relatively less associated with non-finite clause as Head. Finite clauses as post-modifier displayed the greatest difficulties for the students. 3. The texts awarded higher grades were more likely to display greater use of embedding in nominal groups, and greater accuracy in the embedding. The difference was more marked in the fully-realized than the intermediate realizations, and the correlations between embedding and grade were stronger for phrasal embedding than for clausal embedding. 4. Embedding in nominal groups was used for text development and organization, contributing to the force of the writer’s argument. Highly graded texts were organized hierarchically, predicting material to come, and summarising that material. The predictions included macroTheme and hyperTheme, with the summarising or condensing macroNew and hyperNew used to a lesser extent. The embedding facilitated the development of these waves of information, as has been found elsewhere (Martin, 2013). Other uses of the embedding included presentation of points as ‘things’, connecting types of experience, and managing information flow in a chain of reasoning. 5. Students’ intermediate realisations of embeddings displayed a number of strategies which departed from the target language use. These strategies included the placement of modification before the noun (‘front-loading’), chaining of nouns together (‘back-to-back loading’), and cut and paste without using grammar (‘freeloading’). See 5.3 for examples. These findings have been reported at major international conferences in the field. One paper (detailing findings for clausal embedding) is under review with a key journal in the field, and another paper (on phrasal embeddings) is in preparation. These outcomes are listed in Part C. References Martin, J. R. (2013). Embedded literacy: Knowledge as meaning. Linguistics and Education 24, 23-37.

14654716.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14654716.value: Further research can be carried out with the current data, and also in related projects. With the current data, there is more to discover about the students’ use of embedding. Distinctions between the various types of clausal embedding are needed, and strategies to avoid embedding can also be investigated. Further research is also now needed into the teaching of embedding in nominal groups, particularly in senior secondary EFL contexts such as Hong Kong. Research is needed both to ascertain the current support for the development of this important area of language, and also to try out further support. The former would involve textbook analysis, and the second would be quasi-experimental research with the teaching of language resources required for the embedding and of the possibilities of using embedding in argumentative writing. The PI and the research staff intend to continue investigating these areas, as well as to work further with the data obtained so far.

14654716.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14654716.value: The project collected and analysed argumentative texts written in English by senior secondary students. The texts were analysed for expanded nominal groups (noun phrases in more traditional grammar terms), which have have been associated with successful academic writing from older students, or students in English-speaking countries. Nominal groups are expanded through a range of grammatical devices. This project focused on ‘embedding’, as this is considered to precede other devices, but has received little research or curricula attention, particularly for sub-university students. With embedding, a clause or phrase is used within or instead of the noun phrase. The project found that secondary students’ texts with more, and more accurate, embedding tended to be awarded higher grades. The embeddings were used for organizing the texts, and for developing the writer’s argument. The embeddings frequently contained inaccuracies (‘intermediate realizations’), and the inaccuracies were also analysed and categorized, providing new insights into developing writers’ strategies. The research provides support for curriculum change (the addition of nominal group expansion to the syllabus), and indicates where teachers can help their students improve their writing. It contributes to the understanding of the use of embedding in the argumentative texts of developing writers beyond those of this study.

14655416.label: Project Objectives
14655416.value: As noted, Levine, et al. (2014) demonstrated that ethnic diversity in markets prevents price inflation in the financial market, reasoning that ethnic homogeneity causes traders to place undue trust in the decisions of others. Anchoring bias is also a well-established phenomenon. Our first objective is to examine the effects of ethnic diversity on anchoring bias in financial decision-making. Second, the contents of information (high vs. low anchor) should be more focal than the source of information (e.g., ethnic diversity of the other traders). Individuals with local processing style should be affected by the more focal (anchor) information than their counterparts with global processing style, who in turn should be more affected by peripheral (diversity) information. Our second objective is to test this link. Third, research suggests that Chinese are more likely to engage in global (or holistic) processing than North Americans, who in turn are more likely to engage in local (analytic) processing. Therefore, our third objective is to examine how cultural origin of the traders affects their investment decisions. We will also test the causal influence of culture by experimentally prime cultural knowledge on Chinese-American bicultural individuals. 14655416.label: Realisation of objectives
14655416.value: We have realized all the objectives of the current research project. Specifically, we have conducted 16 studies in total and reported the findings in 8 journal articles, 1 handbook chapter, and 4 talks at international conferences. Below, we will first elaborate the details of how each objective was addressed; then we will discuss the practical and academic impacts of the current project. To elaborate, our first two objectives were to investigate anchoring biases, such as sunk cost fallacy, in financial decision-making, and its link with processing styles. To this end, we have performed five studies, examining the processes and mechanism underlying sunk cost fallacy. Specifically, continuing investing in a failing plan (i.e., the sunk-cost fallacy) is a common error that people are inclined to make. It is impossible to get resources back that already have been invested. Economic theory implies that decision makers’ decisions should only be guided by future gains and losses. According to the literature, sunk-cost decisions are driven by negative affect. Previous studies focused on negative incidental affect. In contrast, we investigated whether sunk-cost decision-making may be caused by integral affect, elicited by the specific decision context. Our findings were reported in Dijkstra & Hong (2019), as listed in Part C: Research Output. To address the second objective at a local (micro-) level, we conducted two behavioral games to examine how social norms and gender affect individuals’ decision making. We used bribing as a context for analysis because it bridges between ethics and economic investment decision. Previous research has suggested that bribery is more normative in some countries than in others. To understand the underlying process, our studies examined the effects of social norm and gender on bribe-giving behavior. We argue that social norms provide information for strategic planning and impression management, and thus would impact participants’ bribe amount. To test our ideas, we conducted two studies using a competitive game. In each game, we asked three participants to compete in five rounds of creative tasks, and the winner was determined by a referee’s subjective judgment of the participants’ performance on the tasks. Participants were allowed to give bribes to the referee. We used a latent growth curve model (LGCM) to depict the development of bribe-giving behaviors during five rounds of competition. The results showed that gender, creative performance, and norm level all influenced the trajectory of bribe-giving behavior. These findings were reported in Lan & Hong (2017), as listed in Part C. Our third objective was to examine how culture affects global versus local processing. To address this objective, we have conducted a cross-cultural study that examined the link between culture, global vs. local processing, and decision-making of affect under time limit. We systematically varied the ethnicity of the individual and group targets, and found that Chinese participants were more accurate than Americans in discerning the emotion shown in a group under time limit. At the same time, in an independent test, Chinese participants also showed quicker decisions than did Americans in identifying global (vs. local) visual stimuli, whereas American participants showed the opposite tendency. This cross-cultural difference in global versus local processing was found to mediate the observed cross-cultural differences in collective emotion detection. These findings were the first to show the link between culture, processing styles, and decision-making under time limit. We reported these findings in Yang, Hong, and Sanchez-Burks (2019), as listed in Part C. To further address our third objective, we examined how culture affects investment decision-making, and how participants’ bi- or multi-cultural experiences make a difference. We have addressed this question taking a global (macro-) approach by analyzing individuals’ responses when they encounter information/stimuli from multiple cultural background. Specifically, globalization has made exposure to multiple cultures not only possible, but often necessary and unavoidable. In our analysis, we focused on how people react and adapt to increasing globalization and multiculturalism. We posit that reactions to multiculturalism and intercultural contact are not universal, and are themselves shaped by cultural experiences. That is, culture provides a frame of reference for reconciling and negotiating the inflow of foreign cultures and peoples. Although exposure to foreign cultures can widen one’s worldview, thereby enhancing creativity and reducing prejudice, intercultural contact can also bring about negative exclusionary responses such as aversion, disgust, and defensiveness. We explored how the interplays between cultures, situational factors, and individual factors critically shape reactions to intercultural contact. In particular, we have conducted eight empirical experiments and reported the findings in two empirical papers (Tadmor, Hong, Chao, & Cohen, 2018; Cheon & Hong, 2020, see Part C). Based on our findings, we have also derived a theoretical paper and a handbook chapter (Hong & Cheon, 2017; Hong & Zhan, 2019, see Part C). Finally, for the last objective, we have formulated training programs to reduce biases of individuals in decision-making. Specifically, we adapted a computational approach and argued that it is important to understand how attachment to culture would affect people’s information processing style. This is especially important for people who face investment uncertainty and/or threats. Under such circumstances, the training programs can help individuals to use culture as a secure base upon which informative decision making can be made. This theoretical framework is very much informed by computational neuroscience. We have published a paper using this approach (Yap, Cheon, Hong, & Christopoulos, 2019, see listed in Part C). Taken as a whole, the current research project has achieved both practical and academic impacts. For practical impacts, we have applied our findings to understand consumer decision making, especially those decisions pertaining to ethical issues. We have explored how some specific, current social phenomena in China that may influence consumers’ ethical beliefs and practices, focusing on how some top-down, social and political changes could shape consumer behavior that needs to be understood in the Chinese context. In a nutshell, we examined how changes in both local-level factors (e.g., cultural beliefs and cognitive processing styles) and global-level factors (socio-political reforms in China) can impact consumers’ (un)ethical practices. Our analysis was published in Chen, Wang, Gao, & Hong (2019), see listed in Part C. This paper gives practitioners a better understanding of the ethical rationale behind consumers’ changing lifestyles especially in the Chinese context. For academic impacts, this research project has resulted in 9 publications (8 journal articles and 1 handbook chapter). Some of the journal articles were published in top-tier journals, including Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (impact factor=6.34), and Perspectives on Psychological Science (impact factor=8.19). Although all of the papers were published within the last three years, many have already been cited by other researchers in the field. For example, Hong & Cheon (2017) has been cited 31 times (according to Google Scholar). All 8 journal articles have been cited 49 times in total already. Copies of these publications are attached in Part C: Research Output.

14655416.label: Major findings and research outcome
14655416.value: The major findings included: 1. Continuing investing in a failing plan (i.e., the sunk-cost fallacy) is a common error that people are inclined to make. We found that sunk cost fallacy was affected by negative integral affect elicited by the specific decision context, rather than negative incidental affect as argued in previous literature. 2. Bribe giving is a decision based on ethical consideration and economic return calculation. Previous research has suggested that bribery is more normative in some countries than in others. We conducted two studies using behavioral (bribery) games in China and found that social norms and gender both influenced the trajectory of bribe-giving behavior across multiple rounds. 3. To examine the link between culture, global vs. local processing, and decision-making of affect, we conducted a cross-cultural study recruiting Chinese and North American participants. We found that Chinese participants were more accurate than Americans in discerning the emotion quickly. At the same time, in another test, Chinese participants also showed quicker decisions than did Americans in identifying global (vs. local) visual stimuli, whereas American participants showed the opposite tendency. We found that this cross-cultural difference in global versus local processing mediated the observed cross-cultural differences in collective emotion detection. 4. Culture provides a frame of reference for reconciling and negotiating the inflow of foreign cultures and peoples. Although exposure to foreign cultures can widen one’s worldview, intercultural contact can also bring about negative responses such as disgust or outgroup prejudice. We found that both situational factor (i.e., fusing one’s own culture and a negatively perceived foreign culture) and cognitive factor (i.e., mental resources depletion) contributed to disgust and prejudice, thereby affecting decision making. These findings were reported in 9 publications (8 journal articles and 1 handbook chapter). Copies of these publications are attached in Part C: Research Output. Some of the journal articles were published in top-tier journals, including Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (impact factor=6.34), and Perspectives on Psychological Science (impact factor=8.19). The rest of the papers were published in journals with impact factors above 2.0 in general. For example, two papers were published in Journal of Cross-Cultural Psychology, a top domain specific journal. Although all of the papers were published within the last three years, they have been cited 49 times in total already. This attests to the high values and impacts of the findings resulting from this research project.

14655416.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14655416.value: Our findings on decision biases, such as sunk cost fallacy, were based on responses from college students and lay persons. In future research, it would be useful to replicate the experiments on professional stock traders or seasoned financial consultants. As such, we can discern how investment experience plays a role in affecting financial decision biases. I am trying to find participants from the bank and financial industries with the help from colleagues in the Finance Department, and to inform the industries about my findings. In addition, we have examined global versus local processing style closely. As global processing also enhances a perception of interconnected among social events, it may also promote conspiracy mentality (i.e., a belief that many social happenings, such as the COVID-19 pandemic, were orchestrated by powerful entities in order to fulfil their secret goals). Therefore, it would be useful to examine how processing style is linked to conspiracy beliefs and how this link is moderated by culture. Based on this idea, I have submitted a new GRF grant proposal, which has just received funding. I will embark on this new project to investigate the cognitive underpinnings of conspiracy beliefs in the coming two years.

14655416.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14655416.value: Financial markets are central to modern society, so their failures can be devastating. In this research project, we have conducted 16 empirical studies to examine how culture, affect, and global versus local cognitive processing tendency can affect people’s economic decision making. In particular, we examined decision making in a wide range of domains and contexts, including financial and social investments, bribery, and collective affect detection. We have identified specific cultural, situational, and individual factors that contribute to accurate decision making under threats and time pressure. For instance, Chinese participants were more accurate than did North American participants in identifying the emotion of a group of people quickly. This higher performance was contributed by Chinese participants’ greater global (vs. local) processing tendency and American participants’ greater local (vs. global) processing tendency. This finding and other major findings were reported in 8 journal articles, 1 handbook chapter, and 4 talks at international conferences. Taken as a whole, our research findings shed light on understanding of financial decision making in Chinese and North American cultural contexts, and help practitioners to formulate interventions.

14659716.label: Project Objectives
14659716.value: To identify Hong Kong Chinese parents’ emotion socialization practices with their early adolescent children, specifically, how frequently they use supportive vs. nonsupportive reactions to adolescents’ negative emotions, and validating vs. invalidating reactions to adolescents’ positive emotions. To examine how parents’ emotion socialization practices may affect adolescents’ emotion regulation and in turn adjustment (beyond the effects of general parental autonomy support and psychological control, and parental educational attainment), specifically, whether parents’ supportive reactions to adolescents’ negative emotions and validating reactions to adolescents’ positive emotions predict adolescents’ heightened reappraisal and dampened suppression emotion regulation six months later, which then predict adolescents’ dampened depressive symptoms, problem behavior, social withdrawal, and heightened social initiative six more months later, whereas parents’ nonsupportive reactions to adolescents’ negative emotions and invalidating reactions to adolescents’ positive emotions predict adolescents’ dampened reappraisal and heightened suppression emotion regulation six months later, which then predict adolescents’ heightened depressive symptoms, problem behavior, social withdrawal, and dampened social initiative six more months later. To examine how parents’ socialization goals may relate to their emotion socialization practices (beyond the effect of parental educational attainment), specifically, whether self-development goals are associated with more frequent supportive reactions to adolescents’ negative emotions and validating reactions to adolescents’ positive emotions, whereas filial piety goals are associated with more frequent nonsupportive reactions to adolescents’ negative emotions and invalidating reactions to adolescents’ positive emotions. To explore the role of gender, specifically, how mothers’ vs. fathers’ emotion socialization practices and socialization goals may differ for girls vs. boys, how mothers’ vs. fathers’ practices may predict girls’ vs. boys’ emotion regulation and then adjustment differently, and how mothers’ vs. fathers’ goals may relate to their practices with girls vs. boys differently.

14659716.label: Realisation of objectives
14659716.value: Data from a relatively large sample of Chinese early adolescents (N=1434) and their parents in Hong Kong (132 girls and 228 boys), Shanghai (137 girls and 150 boys), and Shenzhen (393 girls and 394 boys) were obtained, addressing the four project objectives as detailed below. Regarding Objective 1, it was reported that 1) both mothers and fathers used more supportive and more nonsupportive reactions to adolescents’ negative emotions with boys (vs. girls), and similarly more validating and more invalidating reactions to adolescents’ positive emotions with boys (vs. girls), suggesting that both mothers and fathers tend to be more reactive to boys’ (vs. girls’) emotions; 2) for both girls and boys, both mothers and fathers used more supportive than nonsupportive reactions to adolescents’ negative emotions, and similarly more validating than invalidating reactions to adolescents’ positive emotions, suggesting that Chinese parents generally are supportive/validating in response to their adolescent children’s emotions; 3) for both girls and boys, mothers (vs. fathers) used more supportive and nonsupportive reactions to adolescents’ negative emotions, and similarly more validating and more invalidating reactions to adolescents’ positive emotions, suggesting that mothers (vs. fathers) tend to be more reactive to adolescents’ emotions. Regarding Objective 2, largely similar findings regardless of either adolescents’ or parents’ gender emerged: as expected, 1) the more autonomy support parents used with their adolescent children, the more reappraisal adolescents used to regulate their emotions six months later (whereas parental autonomy support did not predict adolescents’ use of suppression emotion regulation, and parental psychological control did not predict adolescents’ use of either reappraisal or suppression); 2) beyond the effect of parental autonomy support on adolescents’ use of reappraisal, the more supportive reactions to adolescents’ negative emotions and the more validating reactions to adolescents’ positive emotions parents used, the more reappraisal emotion regulation adolescents used six months later (whereas these reactions did not predict adolescents’ use of suppression), while the more nonsupportive reactions to adolescents’ negative emotions and the more invalidating reactions to adolescents’ positive emotions parents used, the more suppression emotion regulation adolescents used six months later (whereas these reactions did not predict adolescents’ use of reappraisal); in turn, the more reappraisal and the less suppression adolescents used to regulate their emotions, the greater social initiative while the less social withdrawal and depression adolescents experienced six more months later, and moreover, whereas adolescents’ use of suppression predicted their greater engagement in problem behavior six more months later among both girls and boys, adolescents’ use of reappraisal predicted less engagement in problem behavior among boys only and was unrelated to girls’ engagement in problem behavior. Regarding Objective 3, it was found that 1) for both mothers and fathers, the higher their educational attainment, the more supportive reactions to adolescents’ negative emotions and the more validating reactions to adolescents’ positive emotions they used, while the less nonsupportive reactions to adolescents’ negative emotions and the less invalidating reactions to adolescents’ positive emotions they used, regardless of adolescents’ gender, consistent with prior theory and research in showing promoting effects of parental educational attainment on optimal parenting practices; 2) beyond the effects of their educational attainment on their reactions to adolescents’ emotions, as expected, the greater mothers endorsed self-development socialization goals for their adolescent children, the more supportive reactions to adolescents’ negative emotions and the more validating reactions to adolescents’ positive emotions they used, with these effects being stronger for girls than for boys, and at the same time, the less nonsupportive reactions to adolescents’ negative emotions and the less invalidating reactions to adolescents’ positive emotions they used, with these effects being of similar strength for girls and boys, and in contrast, the greater mothers endorsed filial piety socialization goals, the less supportive reactions to adolescents’ negative emotions and the less validating reactions to adolescents’ positive emotions they used, with these effects being stronger for girls than for boys, and at the same time, the more nonsupportive reactions to adolescents’ negative emotions and the more invalidating reactions to adolescents’ positive emotions they used, with these effects being of similar strength for girls and boys; 3) beyond the effects of their educational attainment on their reactions to adolescents’ emotions, as expected, the greater fathers endorsed self-development socialization goals, the more supportive reactions to adolescents’ negative emotions and the more validating reactions to adolescents’ positive emotions they used, with the former effect being of similar strength for girls and boys while the latter effect being stronger for girls than for boys, and at the same time, the less nonsupportive reactions to adolescents’ negative emotions and the less invalidating reactions to adolescents’ positive emotions they used, with these effects being of similar strength for girls and boys, and in contrast, the greater fathers endorsed filial piety socialization goals, the less supportive reactions to adolescents’ negative emotions and the less validating reactions to adolescents’ positive emotions they used, with these effects being stronger for girls than for boys, and at the same time, the more nonsupportive reactions to adolescents’ negative emotions and the more invalidating reactions to adolescents’ positive emotions they used, with these effects being of similar strength for girls and boys. Regarding Objective 4, as described above, in exploring the role of gender, quite some similarities were observed with several notable differences among girls versus boys and/or mothers versus fathers: 1) for both girls and boys, both mothers and fathers generally are more supportive/validating (vs. nonsupportive/invalidating) in response to their adolescent children’s negative/positive emotions, while both mothers and fathers tend to be generally more reactive to boys’ (vs. girls’) emotions, and mothers (vs. fathers) tend to be generally more reactive to both girls’ and boys’ emotions; 2) the expected developmental pathways of parents’ supportive reactions to adolescents’ negative emotions and validating reactions to adolescents’ positive emotions predicting adolescents’ heightened reappraisal emotion regulation whereas of parents’ nonsupportive reactions to adolescents’ negative emotions and invalidating reactions to adolescents’ positive emotions predicting adolescents’ heightened suppression emotion regulation, and in turn of adolescents’ heightened reappraisal favorably predicting whereas heightened suppression unfavorably predicting their socioemotional adjustment (i.e. experience of social initiative vs. social withdrawal and depression, and engagement in problem behavior) largely held regardless of adolescents’ and parents’ gender, with the exception that while boys’ heightened reappraisal seemed to protect them from engaging in problem behavior, there was no such an effect for girls; 3) the expected links from parents’ self-development socialization goals to their more use of supportive reactions to adolescents’ negative emotions and more use of validating reactions to adolescents’ positive emotions while less use of nonsupportive reactions to adolescents’ negative emotions and less use of invalidating reactions to adolescents’ positive emotions, as well as those from parents’ filial piety socialization goals to their less use of supportive reactions to adolescents’ negative emotions and less use of validating reactions to adolescents’ positive emotions while more use of nonsupportive reactions to adolescents’ negative emotions and more use of invalidating reactions to adolescents’ positive emotions, also largely held, with some intriguing gender differences such that the links from parents’ self-development socialization goals to their more use of supportive and validating reactions as well as those from parents’ filial piety socialization goals to their less use of supportive and validating reactions were generally stronger for girls than for boys.

14659716.label: Major findings and research outcome
14659716.value: The project has yielded findings of important contribution both scholastically and practically. To the research team’s best knowledge, this is the first multi-wave longitudinal study quite comprehensively investigating the prevalence and the functional relevance of parents’ different types of reactions to adolescents’ emotions (negative and positive emotions, respectively) in Chinese culture. Chinese mothers and fathers in urban settings (i.e., in three metropolises – Hong Kong, Shanghai, and Shenzhen) are shown to use distinguishably supportive/validating versus nonsupportive/invalidating reactions to their adolescent female and male children’s negative/positive emotions, with notably greater use of supportive/validating reactions than nonsupportive/invalidating reactions. Significant implications of these reactions for salient aspects of adolescents’ socioemotional functioning (e.g., reappraisal and suppression emotion regulation as well as approach and avoidance coping, and in turn social initiative, social withdrawal, problem behavior, depression and anxiety as well as self-esteem and vitality) are also evidenced (Shi et al., 2019; Shi & Wang, 2021; Yan et al., 2019; see Part C). Furthermore, antecedents of parents’ reactions are identified in terms of parents’ cognition regarding child-rearing and child development (e.g., parents’ self-development versus filial piety socialization goals for their children, and parents’ beliefs about children’s emotions; Shi et al., 2019; Shi et al., under preparation; Yan et al., 2019; see Part C). And moving beyond much extant research on parenting, this study systematically examined the role of both adolescents’ and parents’ gender in the prevalence and the functional relevance of parents’ reactions to adolescents’ emotions, revealing a generally gender-similar picture with several interesting gender differences (e.g., mothers tend to be more reactive than fathers to both adolescent girls’ and boys’ emotions, while both mothers and fathers tend to be more reactive to boys’ than girls’ emotions; the facilitating effects of parents’ self-development socialization goals and the hindering effects of parents’ filial piety socialization goals on their use of supportive/validating reactions to adolescents’ emotions seem stronger for girls than for boys). Scholastically, the findings expand Western-originated theory and research on parental emotion socialization to Chinese culture and refine the understanding of the role of both children’s and parents’ gender, contributing to an increasingly socio-culturally sensitive perspective on parenting and adolescent development. Practically, the findings point to viable directions for education and intervention programs for parents and adolescents to cultivate optimal parental emotion socialization practices as well as effective individual emotion regulation strategies, thereby promoting family and youth well-being (e.g., Shi & Wang, 2021; see Part C).

14659716.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14659716.value: In addition to parents’ reactions to adolescents’ emotions, parents’ communication with adolescents about emotions in terms of discussing adolescents’ emotional experience is worth investigation (e.g., Ding et al., 2022; Ruyi Ding’s thesis; see Part C). Also, to better understand the consequences and the antecedents of parents’ reactions to adolescents’ emotions, it is critical to examine both adolescents’ and parents’ interpretations of different reactions – for instance, when a reaction is interpreted by adolescents as being out of parental care (vs. intrusion), it is more likely to benefit (vs. harm) adolescents' development, and when a reaction is interpreted by parents as training children to cope independently (vs. being uncaring), it is more likely to be adopted (vs. avoided) by parents; moreover, interpretations may vary across different socio-ecologies such as urban versus rural settings (e.g., Ding et al., under preparation; see Part C). Education and intervention programs for parents and adolescents employing online workshops and discussion groups as well as online daily reflection and feedback have been (e.g., Zeyi Shi’s thesis focusing on parental emotion socialization practices in the process of parents being involved in children’s homework; see Part C) and will be further developed (see collaborations in Part C).

14659716.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14659716.value: This project surveyed 1434 Chinese early adolescents and their parents in Hong Kong, Shanghai, and Shenzhen. It was found that when parents’ used supportive reactions to adolescents’ negative emotions and validating reactions to adolescents’ positive emotions, six months later, adolescents would use more reappraisal to regulate their emotions, and in contrast, when parents’ used nonsupportive reactions to adolescents’ negative emotions and invalidating reactions to adolescents’ positive emotions, six months later, adolescents would use more suppression to regulate their emotions; in turn, adolescents who used more reappraisal and adolescents who used less suppression would have better adjustment six more months later, taking greater initiative and being less withdrawn socially, suffering less from depressive symptoms, and engaging in less problem behavior. Also, the more parents considered self-development as important and the less they considered filial piety as important for their children, the more they would use supportive and validating reactions and the less they would use nonsupportive and invalidating reactions to their children’s emotions. The findings highlight directions for concerted efforts among parents, education and mental health professionals and the society at large to foster adolescent well-being, that is, to value adolescents’ self-development and to support and validate their experience of emotions.

14660716.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14660716.value: It is often thought that when acting in their official capacity, legislators, judges, and policy-makers in a pluralist society should not be influenced by their own personal views, in particular their religious convictions and controversial metaphysical beliefs. John Rawls argues that “constitutional essentials and matters of basic justice” in such a society should be settled by means of “public reasons,” reasons that do not depend on controversial religious, metaphysical or philosophical doctrines. If bioethical issues are subject to the same condition, this would be an important first step toward the resolution of some of them, because opinions from the religious sectors are intense and (at least among themselves) influential. This project investigates whether bioethical issues can legitimately be decided in the same way. The first issue to address, however, must be whether the idea of public reason can be grounded and defended. On one view, if we require our institutions to be justified in these public terms, the resulting agreement will be more just, fair, or reasonable. However, the idea of public reason in general, and Rawls’s version in particular, has come under attack. One criticism is that the theory merely reflects one particular culture - liberal secularism - and not as a culturally neutral background. Moreover, Natural Law Theorists have criticized the Rawlsian idea of public reason for being too thin and hostile to ideas of human flourishing. Confucians, on the other hand, argue that reason is itself a culturally embedded phenomenon and lacks the universality which public reasons theorists require of it. In addition to exploring critiques from these two perspectives, this project will explore a contractualist version of Public Reason Theory, based on the works of T.M. Scanlon. The researchers comprise bioethicists from three diverse perspectives, and will explore critiques to, and alternatives of, the Rawlsian account of public reason. Over two years the research team will hold a series of seminars and several workshops on the project's theme, under the auspices of the Chinese University of Hong Kong's newly inaugurated CUHK Centre for Bioethics. At the start of the second year a major international conference will be held on the research theme. At the end of the project a book will be published entitled: Public Reason and Bioethics: Three Approaches.

15105216.label: Project Objectives
15105216.value: Characterization of the oligomeric state of full-length NRBF2 and its direct interaction with Atg14L As a first step to test our hypothesis, we will carry out biochemical characterization of full-length NRBF2. Its oligomeric state will be characterized by both in vitro SEC-LS measurements and in vivo co-IP assay. The interaction between NRBF2 and Atg14L will be assessed by in vitro pull-down assay. Our preliminary data has confirmed that the full-length NRBF2 is indeed a homodimer and has direct physical interaction with Atg14L. Biochemical and structural study of the NRBF2 coiled coil region to investigate the molecular mechanism of self-oligomerization We aim to confirm that the coiled coil region is required and sufficient for self-oligomerization of NRBF2. A series of constructs representing different parts of the putative coiled coil region will be generated. Their oligomeric states will be assessed by SEC-LS measurements and compared to that of the full-length NRBF2. We also plan to solve the crystal structure of the coiled coil region to identify the key residues for NRBF2 self-oligomerization. Biochemical mapping of MIT-binding motifs in Atg14L and structural investigation of the NRBF2-Atg14L interaction A two-stage systematic mapping will be carried out to identify MIT-binding motifs in Atg14L. For the first stage, a library of Atg14L constructs systematically scanning through the full-length sequence will be generated and their binding to NRBF2 MIT domain will be tested by in vitro pull-down assay. For the second stage, shorter peptides within each suitable construct identified from the first stage will be further characterized by Isothermal Titration Calorimetry to measure their binding affinities. Lastly the structure of NRBF2 MIT domain in complex with its cognate Atg14L binding motifs will be determined to reveal the molecular details of the NRBF2-Atg14L interaction. Structure-based functional study to delineate the molecular mechanism of NRBF2-mediated autophagy regulation Using the biochemical and structural data of Objective 2 and 3 as guidance, we will generate NRBF2 mutations that either disrupt self-oligomerization or abolish Atg14L binding. The impact of these mutations on the architectural integrity of the Atg14L-containing Beclin1-Vps34 complex I will be probed by co-IP. Their effect on Vps34 activity and autophagy execution will be characterized by standard autophagy and lipid kinase assays. With these studies, we aim to confirm that both the self-oligomerization and the Atg14L-binding activities are required for NRBF2-mediated autophagy regulation.

15105216.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15105216.value: Autophagy is a cellular catabolic process that degrades and recycles a variety of cytoplasmic material through the lysosomal pathway. In the past few years rapid development in autophagy research has linked this process to diverse physiological and pathological events including glucose metabolism, tumorigenesis, innate immunity and neurodegeneration. The Beclin1-Vps34 complex is an essential module of the autophagy molecular machinery. Vps34 is the only mammalian Class III phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase (PI3K) and its activity is crucial for many vesicle-mediated trafficking processes including autophagy. Beclin1 is a scaffolding protein that recruits many modulating factors to form biochemically and functionally distinct Beclin1-Vps34 complexes so that the activity of Vps34 can be tightly regulated in response to specific cellular context. However, little is known about the regulation mechanism of these Beclin1-Vps34 modulators despite extensive studies. NRBF2 is a newly identified member of the Atg14L-containing Beclin1-Vps34 complex I, and a critical regulator of autophagy with an implicated physiological role in liver protection. Previous studies have found that NRBF2 is essential for maintaining the architectural integrity of complex I as loss of NRBF2 leads to its disassembly. We hypothesize that NRBF2 stabilizes the highly dynamic complex I by serving as a "link" molecule that bridges between the mobile elements like Vps34 and steady scaffolding members like Atg14L. Specifically we propose that NRBF2 forms a homodimer through its C-terminal coiled coil region and utilizes its N-terminal MIT domain for specific interaction with Atg14L. Such stabilization leads to a steady Beclin1-Vps34 complex with enhanced activity to promote autophagy. We will carry out biochemical and structural studies of NRBF2 to confirm our hypothesis and delineate the molecular mechanism of NRBF2-mediated autophagy regulation. As a first step we will characterize the oligomeric state of the full-length NRBF2 and confirm its direct physical interaction with Atg14L. We will then proceed to determine the structure of the NRBF2 coiled coil region and identify key residues responsible for NRBF2 homodimerization. Furthermore we will conduct systematic biochemical mapping to identify the MIT-binding motifs within Atg14L and determine the structure of NRBF2 MIT domain in complex with these motifs. Lastly cell-based functional studies will be conducted to confirm our structural findings. The findings from this project will provide valuable information on the molecular mechanism of NRBF2-mediated autophagy regulation. The “stabilizing” effect exerted by NRBF2 may be applicable to other autophagy modulators that target the Beclin1-Vps34 complex and may serve as a promising strategy to manipulate autophagy for disease-modifying therapies. 自噬是一個細胞分解代謝過程，通過將各種細胞質材料收集並運送到溶酶體以達到降解和回收的目的。在過去的幾年中，自噬研究領域快速發展，自噬過程被發現在許多生理過程中擔當著極為重要的角色。自噬功能的紊亂與多種疾病的發生關係密切，包括腫瘤、糖尿病和神經退行性疾病等。 Beclin1-Vps34複合體是執行自噬過程的複雜分子機器中的一個關鍵模塊。 Vps34是哺乳動物唯一的類磷脂酰肌醇3-激酶（PI3K），其活性對自噬過程中“自噬小體”的形成至關重要。 Beclin1是一個支架蛋白，它通過與許多自噬調製因子相互作用形成多種生化和功能上有特異性的Beclin1-Vps34複合體，以便依據細胞的新陳代謝信號來調節Vps34活性和自噬過程。然而，關於這些靶向Beclin1-Vps34複合體的自噬調製分子的調節機制我們卻所知甚少。 NRBF2是一個新發現的針對含Atg14L的Beclin1-Vps34複合體的調製因子，在自噬與肝功能方面起重要作用。先前的研究已經發現，NRBF2對維持複合體的架構完整性必不可少， NRBF2的損失會導致複合物的分解。我們的假設是NRBF2作為“橋梁”分子，通過將復合體中如VPS34的活動元素和如Atg14L的穩定成員連接起來，以增強複合體的結構穩定性。具體來說，我們認為NRBF2通過其C-端捲曲螺旋區域形成同型二聚體，並利用與Atg14L有特異性相互作用的N-端MIT功能域促成一個穩定的含Atg14L的Beclin1-Vps34複合體，以達到增強Vps34活性，促進細胞自噬的功效。 我們將通過開展針對NRBF2的生化和結構的研究來證實我們的假設，並希望從中了解NRBF2介導的自噬調控的分子機制。作為第一步，我們將表徵全長NRBF2蛋白，並研究其自我聚和狀態和與Atg14L的直接相互作用。然後，我們將解析NRBF2捲曲螺旋區域的結構，並確定負責形成其同源二聚體的關鍵殘基。此外，我們將進行系統化的生化分析，以確定MIT功能域內結合Atg14L的序列，並解析NRBF2-MIT功能域的複合體結構。最後我們將進行基於細胞的功能研究以確認我們從NRBF2的結構中獲得的信息。 這個項目的數據和結果將提供關於NRBF2介導的自噬調控分子機制的關鍵信息。如果我們確認NRBF2通過 “穩定” 含Atg14L的Beclin1-Vps34複合體的結構來調控細胞自噬過程，我們可以針對此機制設計小分子，為自噬相關疾病提供新型治療策略。

15105216.label: Realisation of objectives
15105216.value: The project has progressed very well through the 42-month period and is now completed with all objectives realized to 100%. We would like to report our activities and results obtained according to the four proposed objectives. Objective 1. Characterization of the oligomeric state of full-length NRBF2 and its direct interaction with Atg14L NRBF2 contains an N-terminal MIT (Microtubule Interacting and Trafficking) domain, a flexible linker of ~100 residues and a C-terminal coiled coil (CC) domain. In our original proposal, we hypothesized that the MIT domain would be responsible for interaction with Atg14L while the CC region should be sufficient to render the full-length NRBF2 molecule dimeric. We assessed the oligomeric state of NRBF2 by Size Exclusion Chromatography-Light Scattering (SEC-LS) system. Both full-length NRBF2 and its CC domain were confirmed to be a dimer in solution while the MIT domain alone was monomeric. We also used co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP) to confirm the self-association of NRBF2 in vivo, in which FLAG-tagged NRBF2 pulled down detectable amount of GFP-NRBF2. To characterize the direct interaction between NRBF2 and Atg14L, we expressed and purified multiple fragments of Atg14L including Atg14L-N, Atg14L-CC and Atg14L-BARA that covered the N-terminal region, the central CC domain and the C-terminal BARA-like domain respectively. However, none of these Atg14L fragments showed any detectable binding to NRBF2 as measured by Isothermal Titration Calorimetry (ITC) assay. In summary, Objective 1 is 100% accomplished with the dimeric state of full-length NRBF2 confirmed both in vitro and in vivo. On the other hand, direct physical interaction between NRBF2 and Atg14L has been ruled out by in vitro ITC results. Objective 2. Biochemical and structural study of the NRBF2 coiled coil region to investigate the molecular mechanism of self-oligomerization We solved the crystal structure of NRBF2 CC domain at 2.2 Å resolution using the Single Isomorphous Replacement Anomalous Diffraction (SIRAD) method. The structure reveals a parallel coiled coil homodimer with each alpha helix consisting of 6 heptad repeats with the abcdefg sequence motif to form 12 a-a’ and a-d’ pairings at the dimer interface. Eight pairings are the canonical hydrophobic type with leucine zipper pairs while the remaining four are the non-canonical type involving polar or charged residues. A previous study reported the crystal structure of the C-terminal homodimerization domain of Atg38, a yeast homolog of NRBF2. This Atg38 structure reveals an asymmetric dimer, with the second alpha helix being straight in one monomer but kinked almost 40 degrees midway in the other. In contrast, the structure of NRBF2 CC domain is highly symmetric. The dimer interface of NRBF2 is also longer by one heptad repeat as compared to Atg38 and contains two additional hydrophobic a-a’ and d-d’ pairings. In summary, Objective 2 is 100% accomplished with the dimeric state of NRBF2 CC domain confirmed in vitro and its structure determined at 2.2 Å resolution. The structure reveals a symmetric parallel coiled coil homodimer with multiple hydrophobic leucine zipper pairs at the dimer interface. Objective 3. Biochemical mapping of MIT-binding motifs in Atg14L and structural investigation of the NRBF2-Atg14L interaction NRBF2 is an accessary modulator of the Class III Phosphoinositol-3-kinase (PI3KC3) complex and positively regulates PI3KC3-mediated autophagy. NRBF2 only associates with the Atg14L-containing PI3KC3 Complex I (PI3KC3-C1) but not the UVRAG-containing PI3KC3 Complex II (PI3KC3-C2). The molecular mechanism of such selectivity is not well understood. At the time of initial proposal submission (in November 2015), we proposed that NRBF2 might interact with Atg14L directly to ensure selective association with PI3KC3-C1. Furthermore, we reasoned that the NRBF2-Atg14L interaction might rely on the NRBF2 MIT domain, a well-known protein interaction module. However, our in vitro ITC studies in Objective 1 showed that NRBF2 did not bind to Atg14L fragments directly. We then investigated whether NRBF2 would interact with other members of PI3KC3, i.e. Vps34, Vps15 and Beclin 1. During the course of this project, two cryo-EM studies reported structures of PI3KC3-C1 in complex with NRBF2 at the moderate resolution of ~10 Å. While no atomic details were available from these structures, one of the two MIT domains of the NRBF2 dimer was seen to dock onto Vps15 at a site that overlapped with the C2 domain of UVRAG in PI3KC3-C2. Taking this lead, we carried out Co-IP studies and confirmed that NRBF2 could pull down Vps15 directly, together with its endogenous partner Vps34. The MIT domain is most critical for Vps15 binding because NRBF2 with this domain deleted did not pull down any detectable amount of Vps15 or Vps34. We also used mutational scanning through the MIT domain to map the region most critical for Vps15 binding. The first two helical turns (aa 52-59) on the third helix were found to be most essential. Furthermore, our competitive Co-IP studies showed that over-expression of UVRAG reduced the amount of Vps15 or Vps34 pulled down by NRBF2, confirming that indeed UVRAG competes against NRBF2 for Vps15 binding. Removal of the UVRAG C2 domain relieved such effect, suggesting that the competition is between the NRBF2 MIT domain and the UVRAG C2 domain. In summary, Objective 3 is 100% accomplished with Vps15 confirmed as the direct binding partner for NRBF2, instead of Atg14L as previously thought. The Vps15 binding site in NRBF2 has been mapped to the first two helical turns of the third helix in the MIT domain. Furthermore, our data confirms that NRBF2 only associates with PI3KC3-C1 because it is incompatible with UVRAG in PI3KC3-C2. Objective 4. Structure-based functional study to delineate the molecular mechanism of NRBF2- mediated autophagy regulation Guided by the structure of the NRBF2 CC domain, we generated a series of monomeric mutants in which two, three or five of the critical leucine residues at the dimer interface were mutated to alanine (NRBF2_2A, _3A and _5A). We also replaced the CC domain in NRBF2 with dimeric and tetrameric GCN4 leucine zipper domain to generate NRBF2_GCN4_Dimer and _Tetramer constructs. The oligomeric states of these constructs were all confirmed by SEC-LS. We then carried out Co-IP studies to assess the impact of different oligomeric states on the NRBF2-Vps15 interaction. Our data shows that in presence of over-expressed UVRAG as competitor, monomeric NRBF2_2A, _3A and _5A mutants all pulled down less Vps15 as compared to wild-type NRBF2. In contrast, NRBF2_GCN4_Dimer pulled down similar amount of Vps15 as compared to wild-type NRBF2 while NRBF2_GCN4_Tetramer pulled down noticeably more. This result suggests that the oligomeric state of NRBF2 is essential for enhancing its binding to Vps15. We also assessed the functional significance of the oligomeric state of NRBF2 in promoting autophagy. Our data shows that NRBF2_GCN4_Dimer and _Tetramer co-localized with LC3, an important autophagosome marker, and rescued the autophagy deficiency phenotype in neuroblastoma N2a cell line with NRBF2 knockout. In contrast, monomeric mutants failed to do so. These results suggest that the oligomeric state of NRBF2 is critical for its cytosolic co-localization with autophagosome markers and for promoting autophagy. In summary, Objective 4 is 100% accomplished, with the oligomeric state of NRBF2 mediated by its CC domain confirmed to be critical to ensure full association with PI3KC3-C1 and to promote autophagy.

15105216.label: Major findings and research outcome
15105216.value: During this project period, we used in vitro binding assays and in vivo Co-IP studies to demonstrate that NRBF2 had no direct interaction with Atg14L, the unique member of PI3KC3-C1. Instead, NRBF2 binds to Vps15 directly through the third helix of its MIT domain. This NRBF2-Vps15 interaction is incompatible with PI3KC3-C2 due to competition between the NRBF2 MIT domain and the UVRAG C2 domain, thus explaining why NRBF2 only selectively associates with PI3KC3-C1 but not PI3KC3-C2. We also solved the crystal structure of the NRBF2 CC domain and showed that it formed a symmetric parallel coiled coil homodimer in contrast to the asymmetric dimer observed in yeast homolog Atg38. Our cell-based studies reveal that the oligomeric state of NRBF2 mediated by its CC domain is essential for strengthening the moderate NRBF2-Vps15 interaction to promote autophagy. A manuscript reporting these findings is under review in Autophagy (Part C, item 8[6]). A link to this manuscript is attached in this report, which contains all the data referred to in this completion report. As part of our on-going research on PI3KC3, we also determined the crystal structure of Beclin 1-UVRAG coiled coil complex and designed Beclin 1-targeting stapled peptides that increased autophagic flux and enhanced endolysosomal degradation of EGFR. A manuscript reporting these findings have been published in PNAS in 2018 (Part C, item 8[2]). A US patent for our designed peptides was awarded in April 2021 (Part C, item 11[2]). In collaboration with Prof. Zhenyu Yue in Icahn School of Medicine at Mt. Sinai (New York, U.S.A.), we investigated how ALS-FTLD-linked mutations in the autophagy receptor protein p62 disrupted selective autophagy. A manuscript reporting our findings has been published in Autophagy in 2020 (Part C, item 8[3]). In collaboration with Prof. Renxiao Wang in School of Pharmacy, Fudan University (Shanghai, P.R.China), we optimized the Beclin 1-targeting stapled peptides by staple scanning and enhanced their binding affinity to Beclin 1 by ~10-30 fold. These newly designed peptides showed potent anti-proliferative efficacy in multiple cancer cells. A manuscript reporting these findings is under minor revision in J. Med. Chem. (Part C, item 8[5]). A patent application for these newly designed peptides has been filed in China (Part C, item 11[3]). Three additional research output items, including two published manuscripts on antibiotic resistance (Part C, item 8[1] and 8[4]) and one autophagy-related manuscript under review (Part C, item 8[7]), are also included in this completion report.

15105216.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15105216.value: Our research team is interested in pursuing the following two initiatives in our future study. First of all, we plan to map the NRBF2 binding site on Vps15. While our Co-IP studies have identified the third helix within the NRBF2 MIT domain as most critical for Vps15 binding, the corresponding NRBF2 binding site on Vps15 is not known. Previous cryo-EM studies suggested that helix 12, 14 and 16 within the solenoid domain of Vps15 were involved but the molecular details were not clear. It is also unknown how two MIT domains of the dimeric NRBF2 dock onto PI3KC3-C1 simultaneously. We plan to use mutational scanning to search through the helices in Vps15 and assess their importance for NRBF2-Vps15 interaction by competitive Co-IP. The second initiative we plan to pursue is to test the translational potential of our engineered NRBF2_GCN4_Dimer and _Tetramer constructs in cell- and animal-based model of Alzheimer’s Disease (AD). Studies have shown that NRBF2 promotes the degradation of Aβ in cultured cells and NRBF2 expression was reduced in the hippocampus of AD mice. We hope to test whether our engineered NRBF2 constructs with higher oligomeric state may alleviate the accumulation of proteotoxic Aβ by promoting its autophagic degradation.

15105216.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15105216.value: Autophagy is a cellular process that packs cytosolic content into autophagosomes and delivers them to lysosomes for degradation. Autophagy has been functionally implicated in many processes ranging from glucose metabolism and innate immunity to neurodegeneration. The Class III phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3KC3) complex is essential for autophagy. In mammals, PI3KC3 exists in two biochemically and functionally distinct forms termed Complex I (PI3KC3-C1) and Complex II (PI3KC3-C2). These two complexes share the same three core members of Vps34, Vps15 and Beclin 1 but differ on the fourth modulatory member, with Atg14L in PI3KC3-C1 and UVRAG in PI3KC3-C2. NRBF2 is a proautophagic modulator that specifically associates with PI3KC3-C1 to enhance its activity. Here we report that NRBF2 binds to Vps15 directly through its MIT domain. This NRBF2-Vps15 interaction is only compatible for PI3KC3-C1 but not PI3KC3-C2 because the NRBF2 MIT domain and the UVRAG C2 domain compete for similar binding sites on Vps15. Furthermore, the dimeric state of NRBF2 mediated by its coiled coil domain is critical for strengthening the moderate NRBF2-Vps15 interaction to promote autophagy. Our work contributes to better understanding of NRBF2 and may offer insight on how to target NRBF2 to tackle autophagy-related diseases like cancer and neurodegeneration.
