15327216.label: Major findings and research outcome
15327216.value: The completed project has led to fruitful research results, including ten peer-reviewed papers, one book chapter, two papers under review, and one Ph.D. student trained to have obtained Ph.D. in statistics. The research project focuses on exploration on complicated data arising from epigenetic studies. The major findings are realization of the objectives and extensions when adapt to various data types or motivated from the unprecedented coronavirus disease 2019.

15327216.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15327216.value: There are still wide space to make new development. For example, in objective 3, we addressed the dimension reduction for challenging recurrent event data setting. For panel count data, it is also a quite general data setting that the researchers needs to address the dimension reduction. For objective 4, we solved some local and omnibus tests problems. However, for the multiple sample data that contains density ratio structure and are failure time outcome, the inference task is still tough.

15327216.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15327216.value: In 2015, when PI drafted the proposal and learned the word epigenetic from the Co-I, there was no much google searching information and no formal definition yet. Several years later, the epigenetic studies become pretty much popular. The complexity of the data poses series of problems for statisticians to solve. The completion of the project are strongly data-driven and have fulfilled all the objectives and beyond. It covers various survival outcomes not limited to univariate right censored, but more complicated recurrent event data, semi-competing risks. New modeling or inference are present when the responses are repeated measured and possess hierachy. For versatile covariates, the project addresses a series of statistical inference, analysis and algorithms, covering high-dimensional, ultrahigh dimensional, error-in-variables, latent variables, and etc. Causal inference automatically are involved for censored or complete data, or the covariates are unbalanced. Bayesian analysis is employed to alleviate computing burden when random effects are parametric whereas there is distribution unspecified model errors. The popular public GWAS data are naturally analyzed to verify presented methodology and inference. In a word, the results of the project fill out gaps in statistical inference, new modeling, methodology, and computing feasibility.

15327516.label: Realisation of objectives
15327516.value: There are four objectives in this project and their realisation are illustrated as below. 1. To formulate dynamic optimization of large-scale system with admissibility constraints. We realize this objective by formulating the large scaled system with input or admissibility constraint. These constraints are practical and realistic for various real applications and we provide the necessary background and motivations. We also address the necessary financial and economical illustrations with admissibility constraint. Specifically, the positive constraint with no-shorting constraint and convex cone constraint, and linear segment constraint are all addressed under suitable context. We also formulate the more general convex cone constraint that maybe well posed under projection mapping. 2. Based on (1), to study (LQ) mean-field game (MG) of large-scale system, on the special but important ``positive control" (MG-P), and in homogeneous setting. For objective 2, we continue to introduce the input constraint into the large-scale system with weakly-coupled agents, and highly interactive correlations. As the benchmark case, we introduce the homogeneous case where all agents are of the same parameters thus they are identical in statistical distribution. This homogeneous case connects to the symmetric game in game-theoretic analysis. 3. Based on (2), to further study (LQ) MG with general admissibility constraint (MG-C), in heterogeneous setting. In particular, (convex, closed set) constraints. We completely solve the LQ MG with input constraint in homogeneous case. The related consistency condition and Hamiltonian system for auxiliary control problem are all derived and their wellposedness are also investigated under rather mild general conditions. In particular, we use the discounting method to establish the wellposendess of related FBSDE with nonlinear projections. 4. Based on theoretical results of MG-P and MG-C from (1)-(3), to discuss some practical applications of them. We apply the theoretical results to some real and practical applications such as financial portfolio investment with relative performance, and habit formation; the leader-follower LQ game with weak-coupling in large-scaled market mechanism.

15327516.label: Major findings and research outcome
15327516.value: We derive the distributed strategy of large-scaled system with input or admissibility constraint. The strategy performance also analyzed. We derive the mean-field game with homogeneous agents, as well as heterogenous with finite subclasses. We also derive the strategy with mean-field team co-operations and social optima with input constraints can also be analyzed. In addition, we study the other game patterns with constraints such as leader-follower game and some other interesting and practical variants such as time-delay or robust soft constraint.

15327516.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15327516.value: The current project opens some new research frontiers for further development. We plan to study more involved case where the agents may be of continuum heterogenous setup, and are of different input constraints.

15327516.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15327516.value: Weakly-coupled large-scaled systems are very popular in considerable real applications. Usually, the decision input of agents may be subject to various constraints such as positive input (this is very common for economic analysis in which the economic factors are always assumed to take positive quantity). Thus, we analyze the linear-quadratic optimization of large-scaled system where all agents have input constraints in a convex closed set. This includes the positive or linear sub-space as their special cases. We derive the related distributed strategy that needs only the local information from agents. This may avoid the possible curse of dimensionality for such highly interactive system. We also apply our theoretical results into some practical applications.

15327716.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15327716.value: Many organisms undergo major changes in size and resource use over their life period in different demographic stages. Take mosquitoes for example, adult individuals lay eggs on water surface or its adjacent sites and these eggs stay in the aquatic environment until developing to adults and flying away. Therefore, immature and adult individuals live in totally different environments and are subject to distinct factors regulating their growth. To understand the dynamical properties of such growth, theoretical age-structured models should be developed with various types, such as difference systems, differential systems and integral models. In the meanwhile, species growth rates at different stages may also be largely dependent on the environmental conditions, in particular the weather condition for some mosquito species. It has been shown that the development time is markedly prolonged at cold temperatures above freezing and then declines rapidly with increasing temperatures, and the development is halted or greatly retarded when in winter (refer to as diapause). In this scenario, the development duration changes periodically, driven by the seasonality of temperature conditions and as a result, the relevant coefficients in a theoretical model take periodic functions. In this project, we propose models with both age structure and seasonality, with special reference to mosquito growth, which are applicable to various population growth settings. However, the modeling process, requiring a delicate balance between biological realism and mathematical tractability, is challenging. The resultant models turn out to be differential systems with time dependent delay or switched differential systems with time delay, which are different from previously formulated models without seasonal effects. All terms in the growth models will be interpreted from a biological point of view in this project. These theoretical models with novel features also pose new challenges to the mathematical analysis. To solve these challenges, we will adapt the theory of periodic semiflows and employ the dynamical system approach. The issue of well-posedness of the models will be considered, and the basic reproduction number of the population under different biological assumptions, defined as the average number of offspring per individual during an entire life, will be formulated and its role in determining population persistence and extinction will be investigated for each model. Furthermore, the global stability for the positive periodic state will be derived with suitable conditions by extending the current theories of monotone dynamical systems. 許多物種在不同的發育階段會受到不同的環境和營養要素的影響。以蚊子為例，幼年階段最主要在水中生長直至成年後飛走。由此蚊子的幼年和成年階段生長在不同的環境之中，從而所受到的環境制約因素不盡相同。基於此，需要用階段結構模型來刻畫蚊子的生長動力學。常見的階段結構模型包括微分方程模型和積分方程模型。此外，環境因素由於受到氣候等的季節性變化而呈現季節性波動。譬如，低溫將極大地延長蚊子的成熟期，甚至使蚊子的發育停止（休眠）。由於溫度是以一年為周期變化的，在這種情況下，成熟期和其它的一些生長發育率就具有周期性。在此研究計劃中，受蚊子生長的啟發，我們將研究具有季節性影響和階段結構的種群動力學。但是，該計劃從以下幾個方面具有極高的挑戰性：（1）數學模型的建立比較困難，因為這類模型將聯合考慮季節性和階段結構；（2）模型的分析也變得相對比較困難，因為模型將涉及周期變化的參數。具體地，我們期望建立具有周期時滯的微分方程模型和周期性的切換系統。在構建這些模型過程中，我們計劃從生物和數學角度來闡述模型的合理性。 這些模型將具有全新的形式，同時帶來新的數學分析上的挑戰。我們計劃拓展現有的動力系統理論中關於周期半流和單調動力系統的相關結論。同時估算這些模型的基本再生數用來刻畫一個個體在一生中能產生幾個下一代（如果基本再生數小於1，說明下一代會越來越少導致種群最終滅絕，反之，下一代會越來越多導致種群入侵）。期望該課題能發展現有的數學理論，同時該研究能深化我們對種群生長入侵的理解。

15327716.label: Major findings and research outcome
15327716.value: Motivated by the modeling framework we developed in Objective 2, we formulate a deterministic model with the consideration of various factors regulating population growth (Objective 3). The model takes the form of two coupled reaction-diffusion equations with time-dependent delays, which bring novel challenges to the theoretical analysis. The basic reproduction number is defined and shown to determine the global attractivity of either the zero equilibrium or a positive periodic solution by using the dynamical system approach on an appropriate phase space. Motivated by the diapause, a period of arrested development due to harsh environment conditions, we formulate a new mechanistic model in the form of a switch system (Objective 1), where the time instances of switching is carefully incorporated, which divide a one-year into three intervals: normal developmental interval, diapausing interval and post-diapause period. Two models of delay differential equations (DDE) to explicitly describe mosquito population growth with a single diapausing stage, either immature or adult. The seasonal population abundances of two temperate mosquito species with different diapausing stages are simulated to identify the essential role on population persistence that diapause plays and predict that killing mosquitoes during the diapause period can lower but fail to prevent the occurrence of peak abundance in the following season. The above modeling idea is extended to a reaction-diffusion system, involving (a) seasonal succession to distinguish the normal growth period, diapause period, and post diapause period; (b) diffusion term to represent the random movement of species; and (c) maturation delay term to describe the developmental duration of species (Objective 3 and Objective 4). We first study the model in a bounded domain for the survival and establishment of a species. Then we investigate the model in an unbounded domain for the spreading of the species. Our results show that the minimal wave speed for periodic traveling wave is equal to the spreading speed. All theoretical results are validated with numerical simulations. Numerical computations are also performed to other aspects quantitatively. Further studies are performed beyond these objectives to extend the population growth dynamics to the disease transmission models.

15327716.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15327716.value: The main contributions we have developed in this project, with spatial structure or without spatial movements, are the model formulation and analysis for population growth with seasonal development duration, which involve a delay which is a periodic function of time. However, this delay function in Models 1 and 3 are non-continuous function, while this function is a differentiable function of time in Models 2 and 4. In the future, we would like to unify these two modeling approaches by using an integral equation to characterize this time-dependent delay. In this case, the system will become a delay differential equation equipped with an integral equation. This would be an interesting extension of the current project, from both mathematical and ecological points of view.

15327816.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15327816.value: It is an accepted fact that mathematical modeling and numerical simulations in modern science play a key role in current time. The numerical simulation of wave propagation in metamaterials by using Maxwell type equations (local or nonlocal or with integrals) offers many challenges in terms of mathematical and numerical issues. The lossy Drude model describing the negative refractive index metamaterials may be considered as one of examples due to its some kind nonlocal nature or with memory effects. The modeling of pulse propagation in biological tissues plays an important role in dealing with electromagnetic wave interaction with human body. The famous Cole-Cole model containing a time fractional derivative is often used as a standard model in biomedical engineering, which in fact is a Maxwell system in time domain with fractional time integral. In this project PI proposes to study fast and reliable numerical schemes which may potentially provide physicists and engineers with efficient numerical tools in modern material and biological sciences. These may include constructions of new immersed finite/volume elements, a priori and posteriori error estimates, convergence and stability analysis, and local DG method with partially penalized techniques in numerical simulations. 一個公認的事實是數學建模和現代數字模擬學在當前起到關鍵的 作用。波傳播的數值模擬通過使用麥克斯韋方程類型超材料提供 了數學和數值方面的問題很多挑戰。有損德魯德模型描述負折 射率超材料可以被視為一次由於它的某種非局部性質或具有記 憶效應的例子。 脈衝傳播在生物組織造型, 處理與人體的電磁波相互作用中起著 重要的作用。著名的科爾 - 科爾 包含時間分數導數模型經常被 用來作為生物醫學工程一個標準模型，這實際上是一個麥克斯韋 系統的時域與小數時間積分。 在這個項目中PI提出要研究快速，可靠的數值方法, 在材料和生物 科學可能提供物理學家和工程師在現代高效的數值工具。 這些可能包括新的結構,沉浸有限/體積元素方法，先驗和後驗誤差估計， 收斂性和穩定性分析，並在數值部分局部DG方法模擬。

15327816.label: Realisation of objectives
15327816.value: We have worked on our objectives of this project. We addressed all questions, for instance, using for the Maxwell–Schrodinger system with rapidly oscillating coefficients (nonlinear coupled systems) and elliptic systems with interfaces as examples. Our focuses are on error estimates, interpolation errors, convergences and stabilities or first the second order numerical schemes. In addition the extensive numerical simulations are carried out, which are the essential parts in all publications. The immersed element spaces are used for detecting material shape in shape optimization, which is key part for engineering designs. The main difficulty is for 3D shape optimization that is very challenging topic. We are continuing work on, hopefully, it can be solved soon. In all multiscale numerical techniques all coefficients are assumed to be smooth. Recently we begin investigate the multiscale numerical methods for Maxwell type systems with piece-wise rapidly oscillating coefficients. This case is close to the real smart material design and simulation that have never been considered before mathematically. Some preliminary results have been obtained using domain decomposition techniques and boundary layered expansions.

15327816.label: Major findings and research outcome
15327816.value: The time-dependent Maxwell’s type equations used to modelling new smart material designs and wave propagations in dispersive lossy bi-isotropic media and related problems are investigated. Existence and uniqueness of the modelling equations are demonstrated. Also numerical schemes with multiscale expansions and second order in time algorithms are proposed and studied. The error estimates, stability and convergence are investigated, and their practical implementation and stability are discussed. The related inverse problems by detecting material property problems are also considered. We consider a posteriori error estimates for time-dependent Maxwell’s equations discretized by variable time steps in time domain and edge elements in spatial domain. The stability and optimal a priori error estimate are proved for both semi and fully discrete schemes. We study the multiscale computations for the Maxwell–Schrodinger system with rapidly oscillating coefficients under the dipole approximation that describes light-matter interaction in heterogeneous nanostructures. The multiscale asymptotic method and an associated numerical algorithm for the system are presented. We propose an alternating Crank–Nicolson finite element method for solving the homogenized Maxwell–Schrodinger system and prove the existence of solutions to the discrete system. Numerical examples are given to validate the efficiency and accuracy of the algorithm. We discuss the multiscale computations of the time-dependent Maxwell-- Schrodinger system with rapidly oscillating discontinuous coefficients. The multiscale asymptotic method for the system is presented. We propose a novel multiscale asymptotic expansion for the vector potential to capture the oscillations caused by the quantum current density. To solve the homogenized Maxwell--Schrodinger system, we present an alternating Crank--Nicolson finite element method. The stability estimates and the solvability of the discrete system are established. An iteration algorithm together with its convergence analysis is given. Numerical examples are carried out to demonstrate the efficiency and accuracy of the multiscale algorithms. In additional Some immersed finite element methods (with material interfaces) and finite volume element methods, some with two grid versions, are studied for related time-independent problems, which can serve as the first step for finding more proper and efficient numerical methods for Maxwell systems in time domains. We present finite element methods on a fixed mesh for solving a group of inverse geometric problems for recovering the material interface of a linear elasticity system. A partially penalized immersed finite element method is used to discretize both the elasticity interface problems and the objective shape functionals accurately regardless of the shape and location of the interface. Explicit formulas for both the velocity fields and the shape derivatives of IFE shape functions are derived on a fixed mesh and they are employed in the shape sensitivity framework through the discretized adjoint method for accurately and efficiently computing the gradients of objective shape functions with respect to the parameters of the interface curve. The shape optimization for solving an inverse geometric problem is therefore accurately reduced to a constrained optimization that can be implemented efficiently within the IFE framework together with a standard optimization algorithm. We demonstrate features and advantages of the proposed IFE-based shape optimization method by several typical inverse geometric problems for linear elasticity systems.

15327816.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15327816.value: We have developed the multiscale asymptotic method for the Maxwell– Schrodinger system with the rapidly oscillating effective mass and magnetic permeability under the dipole approximation. We have proposed an alternating Crank–Nicolson finite element method for solving the homogenized Maxwell–Schrodinger system. The existence of solutions to the discrete Schrodinger equations is investigated. The results of numerical simulations demonstrate the effectiveness and accuracy of the algorithms. This work is an elementary study of the multiscale asymptotic method for the Maxwell– Schrodinger system. Future works will be concerned with the Maxwell–Schrodinger system in which the vector potential and the scalar potential are incorporated; the rapidly oscillating electric permittivity and magnetic permeability are both included; the open boundary conditions are used. The proposed IFE method for the inverse geometric problems has additional advantages. Because it is based on an interface independent fixed mesh in the shape optimization process, the issues caused by the mesh regeneration/movement, the mesh distortion caused by large geometry changes, as well as some practical and theoretical issues for the construction of the velocity field are circumvented. We highlight that almost all the computations in the sensitivity calculation in the proposed IFE method are concentrated only on the interface elements. These benefits together with the fact that no need to remesh again and again in the shape optimization process suggest a strong potential of the proposed IFE method.

15327816.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15327816.value: Numerical analysis and simulation of Maxwell type equations offer many challenges in terms of mathematical and numerical issues. For example the multiscale computations for the Maxwell–Schrodinger system with rapidly oscillating coefficients under the dipole approximation that describes light-matter interaction in heterogeneous nanostructures. The immersed finite element methods are to be used to for saving many intermediate calculations at adaptive refinements along the material interfaces. In this proposal PI to study efficient and higher order numerical schemes for Maxwell type equations which may potentially provide engineers with better numerical tools in new smart material designs. In recent years, the study on the interaction of electromagnetic fields with two incompressible, immiscible and electrically conducting fluids is of great signification in the engineering, such as the Aluminum electrolysis cells, metallurgical industry, pump accelerators, MHD generators and fusion reactors. The results generated from this project can be the starting point for the new directions.

15328116.label: Project Objectives
15328116.value: To introduce lanthanide ions (Er, Tm, etc.) into layered semiconductor nanosheets, such as MX2 (M: Mo, W; X: S, Se) and form novel lanthanide-doped two-dimensional (2D) layered structures. To observe up- and down-conversion near-infrared (NIR) luminescence and extend the emission wavelength of 2D semiconductors to a wide range of NIR spectrum, including optical communication band at 1550 nm under the excitation of a single-wavelength diode laser. To gain an in-depth understanding on the luminescent mechanism of lanthanide ions in an unexplored form of 2D hosts by combining theoretical calculations. To demonstrate some proof-of-concept devices based on the synthesized lanthanide-doped 2D materials.

15328116.label: Realisation of objectives
15328116.value: 1. In order to achieve the project objective 1, some synthesis methods have been developed in this project to form novel lanthanide-doped two-dimensional (2D) layered structures since there is lack of lanthanide (Ln)-doped bulk semiconductor crystal with layered structure up to now and mechanical exfoliation method is not applicable. We have overcome the problem and realized general schemes for the synthesis of Ln-embedded layered semiconductor nanosheets mainly by using the two-step chemical vapor deposition (CVD) method and pulsed laser deposition (PLD). In the two-step CVD, as an example of MoS2: Er, prior to the growth, the Mo:Er metal precursor, named as “seeds” was deposited on the substrate using magnetron sputtering. The evaporated Mo and Er atoms from the seeds reacted with the injected high concentration sulfur vapor and were carried to the self-assembly field to form highly crystalline triangular domains. To fabricate the Ln-doped heterostructure such as WS2/MoS2, the seed layers (2.5 nm Yb doped Mo and 2.5 nm Er-doped W) were pre-deposited in sequence. Then the Ln-doped heterostructure was obtained after the subsequent sulfurization. Regarding PLD, The layered samples were deposited with a polycrystalline target at a 10 Hz laser frequency and a substrate temperature. Before the deposition, the chamber was evacuated to a base pressure of around 1×10-5 Pa. The bulk polycrystalline target was placed 4 cm in front of the substrates and ablated by a KrF pulsed laser with a 320 mJ output energy. The thickness of the as-fabricated thin film can be controlled by the number of laser pulses, which permits the in situ specific modulation of the number of WSe2:Yb/Er layers. Based on the above two methods, lanthanide ions are successfully doped into layered nanosheets according to careful characterizations described subsequently. 2. To achieve the objective 2, the near-infrared (NIR) photoluminescence (PL) spectra were recorded using an Edinburgh FLSP920 spectrophotometer equipped with a commercial 980 nm diode laser. Among the Er3+ PL emissions, the NIR emission band at 1550 nm is the most important one for NIR laser applications and broadband optical amplifiers at the telecommunication window. In order to evaluate spectroscopic parameters of the 1550 nm luminescence on 2D layers with different Er3+ ion concentrations, the emissions were recorded by exciting the samples with the single-wavelength NIR diode laser. The normalized spectra are presented as evidence of the intense NIR fluorescence emission. The broad emission band consists of two peaks, which originate from the stark splitting induced by the surrounding chemical environment on the crystal field of Ln ions. Besides, the pump power (P) dependence at 980 nm of the luminescence intensity was measured. The slope is fitted to be 1.08 according to the dependence of emission intensity on the pump power, indicating that the downconversion emissions mainly originate from the one-photon process. For the Ln-doped semiconductor nanosheets, the upconversion emission at about 800 nm was also observed with an appropriate excitation density. 3. To achieve the objective 3, we have combined the results of structural and luminescence measurements to recognize some correlations relevant to the luminescent mechanism of lanthanide ions. The structural information and chemical composition of the synthesized materials were characterized by optical microscopy, atomic force microscopy (AFM), energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). EDS analysis was performed with scanning electron microscopy (SEM) system. Raman spectra and bandgap emission spectra were recorded in a confocal Raman microscopic system with a 532 nm laser. The incorporation of Ln is evidenced by the XPS analysis. In order to provide an in-depth insight into the growth mechanism and impact of lanthanide doping on the semiconductor nanosheet host, density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed on both pristine and Ln-doped nanosheets such as Er-doped MoS2 monolayers with the DFT+U formalism. Quantum Espresso was employed using Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof pseudo-potentials on a 4×6×1 super cell containing 72 atoms. Parameters of the well relaxed crystal structures are presented. The incorporation of Ln ions introduces extra energy states within the semiconductor nanosheet bandgap, enabling the energy transitions in the NIR spectral range. Upon NIR laser pumping, electrons are populated from the ground state manifold and rapidly nonradiatively relax to the metastable level where the radiative transitions then take place. Our theoretical calculation is in good accordance with our experiment to gain an in-depth understanding on the luminescent mechanism of lanthanide ions in an unexplored form of 2D hosts. Our combined studies of experimental and theoretical investigations imply that the 2D host is an appropriate candidate for promoting the NIR emission when incorporating Ln luminescent ions. 4. To achieve the objective 4, we have made use of the capacities of tunable NIR emissions and wavelength conversion from the developed Ln-doped 2D materials in this project. We have designed and fabricated Ln-doped 2D stacked heterostructure devices. The Ln-doped heterostructure produces efficient NIR emission as a result of energy transfer between WS2:Er and MoS2:Yb layers, presenting proof-of-concept photonic device applications based on novel Ln-doped heterostructures. The corresponding energy level scheme and energy transfer mechanism of the fabricated Ln-doped heterostructure are investigated. Compared with the WS2: Er thin film, the WS2:Er/MoS2:Yb heterostructure presents more intensive NIR emission around 1550 nm, and the emission intensity is effectively improved, implying an enhanced device performance. Furthermore, the prepared composite films of Ln-doped 2D semiconductor materials have been made to demonstrate proof-of-concept Ln-doped nanosheet-based devices including tunable display devices and temperature sensors. The display exhibits a diversity of color variation from 77 K to room temperature. Under NIR (980 nm) and UV (365 nm) excitations, the color changes of the devices can be obviously observed from green to red, and yellow to weak white, respectively. Utilizing the distinct sublevel transitions of Ln ions, the developed 2D optical temperature sensor shows attractive device performances. 5. In summary, we have realized the three objectives of the project. Particularly, 8 high-quality papers are published with acknowledgements of this project. Among them, 3 papers are published in the journals with impact factor >12, including 2 ACS Nano (IF~14.588) and 1 Small Method (IF~12.130). Others are published in SCI international journals such as Adv. Opt. Mater, Nanoscale, Appl. Phys. Lett. and so on. One postgraduate student Lyu Yongxin financially supported by the GRF grant has been trained in the project period. The student has published international journal paper in Appl. Phys. Lett as the first author, and ACS Nano, Sci. China Mater. as co-authors. The PI was invited to contribute review articles in prominent journals such as Adv. Opt. Mater. (paper entitled “Luminescence in 2D Materials and van der Waals Heterostructures” included in Hall of Fame Article) due to our research impact on the research area. To disseminate our results, the PI has given 5 plenary or keynote or invited talks in several recognized international conferences, including prominent MRS Spring Meeting.

15328116.label: Major findings and research outcome
15328116.value: 1. We found that highly crystalline lanthanide-doped nanosheets can be formed by high concentration vapor induced transfer in the self-assembly region. Our developed two-step CVD method is promising for developing lanthanide dopants to form stable doping into 2D materials. The processing parameters, such as flow rate, temperature and growth time can greatly affect the properties of the lanthanide-doped nanosheets. Moreover, we develop the fast deposition of wafer-scale layered single lanthanide ion or co-doped lanthanides (e.g., Yb/Er) semiconductor nanosheets using pulsed laser deposition (PLD). The obtained 2D layers incorporated with lanthanides are found to exhibit high uniformity and crystallinity. (see: Part C: Journal 2,6,7, Conference 3,4). 2. We found that a proper selection of lanthanide dopants and layered structures of host lattices can enable one to tune near-infrared (NIR) emission of the system. The strategy of co-doping lanthanides such as Yb3+ and Er3+ ions serving as the sensitizer and activator is found to improve the absorption of excitation energy and enhance emission considering the large absorption cross-section of Yb3+ ions around 980 nm. Up- and down-conversion luminescence properties of lanthanide doped nanosheets are found in our measurements. More importantly, the luminescence of the nanosheets simply excited by a single diode laser can be extended to the telecommunication range at around 1550 nm, even when the film is as thin as atomic layer. We demonstrate the significantly extended and tunable luminescence of 2D semiconductors to a wide range of NIR spectrum. (see: Part C: Journal 2,4,6,7,8, Conference 1,2,5). 3. Through theoretical calculation, we found that the majority of the density of state structure remains unchanged since the electronic bands are mainly composed of the host states after lanthanide doping. The lanthanide impurity states give rise to the maximum of electron density distribution emerging at the edge of valence band, resulting in slight narrowing of host bandgap. Importantly, the lanthanide substitution can introduce energy levels within the bandgap of nanosheets, which can induce additional energy transition leading to near-infrared luminescence. Our theoretical results have been verified in our experimental findings. (see: Part C: Journal 5,6,8, Conference 2,3). 4. We found that the introduction of various lanthanides into nanosheets can offer a distinct class of materials with great technological potential in developing NIR emission devices, tunable display and optical temperature sensor for photonics and cutting-edge nanomaterials-based bioimaging, which is superior to conventional lanthanide-activated upconversion luminescent nanothermometers. (see: Part C: Journal 1,2,3,5,8, Conference: 1,2,5).

15328116.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15328116.value: We have developed facile methods to make semiconductor nanosheets and heterostructures doped with various lanthanide dopants. More types of 2D materials and heterostructures with different hosts and dopants can be developed by referring to our design and fabrication methods. The strategy can be further universalized to other dopants or 2D hosts on arbitrary substrates since the deposition of precursors in CVD and targets in PLD can be easily modulated by sputtering or doping for most metal elements. The theoretical modelling and calculations employed in this project can be expanded to various lanthanide-doped 2D systems. In the future theoretical studies, more types of van der Walls heterostructures can be constructed by considering that lanthanide energy transitions, host factors and defects. It is well-known that the low loss window around 1550 nm has been extensively utilized in optical communication and photonic technologies. The ultimate goal of creating atomically ultrathin photonic devices will further prompt the present studies on the lanthanide-doped 2D layered devices. In particular, further development of device is suggested to focus on the doping lanthanides into hosts with direct and wide band gap, which will be very attractive for applications in the future photonic devices at the 2D limit.

15328116.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15328116.value: Two-dimensional (2D) materials have received widespread attention for constructing next-generation functional devices. Lanthanide ions possess abundant energy levels and fascinating optical properties, presenting high-technology applications. In this project, we have developed techniques to prepare lanthanide nanosheets and heterostructures by using both chemical and physical vapor deposition methods. Furthermore, we take advantage of lanthanide ions to observe intriguing luminescence extended to a wide range of near-infrared spectrum, particularly emitting in optical communication range. Theoretical analysis is performed to further understand the growth mechanism and observed luminescence phenomena ascribed to the electronic structures of lanthanide-doped nanosheets, which is in good accordance with our experimental results. The demonstrated proof-of-concept devices based on lanthanide-doped nanosheet and heterostructure are highly favourable for constructing 2D near-infrared photonic applications. The results have offered a method to prepare wafer-scale lanthanide doped 2D materials and widely tune the luminescence of layered structures by introducing lanthanide ions. Our work offers the possibility to develop doping strategies in the 2D limit and provides an in-depth understanding of the lanthanide doping in atomically thin materials. Consequently, the results achieved in this project will significantly benefit for the investigations of the two research fields in 2D material and lanthanide luminescence.

Study the asymptotic behavior of solutions of the prey-taxis system for various predator-prey interactions, identify the predator-prey competition outcomes, find what kinds of predator-prey dynamics under prey-taxis will lead to biologically desired outcomes and show that the role of prey-taxis is closely corelated to the local predator and prey interactions. 15329816.label: Major findings and research outcome
15329816.value: In our research results, we not only mathematically improve the existing results on the predator-prey system with preytaxis by removing some technical assumptions imposed in the literature, but also we at the first explore the effect of density-dependent dispersal which is more biologically realistic for the predator-prey system. We find that the density-dependent dispersal may bring significant different dynamics compared to random dispersal in the pattern formation. Many systems, which can not generate spatial patterns with random dispersal, are able to produce interesting rich patterns once the dispersal become non-random (i.e. density-dependent). These novel research results have been published in prestigious journals (see research output) and received a number of citations although most of them are just published online.

15329816.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15329816.value: The density-dependent dispersal is a common strategy used by biological species to achieve various goals， but very few mathematical works have been developed due to the complexity of analysis that it brought. In this research project, we develop several new ideas to settle the analytical difficulties to greatly advance the understanding of this important dispersal strategy in the biological system. Our work opens a new direction for mathematical researches and will promote interests in other different areas of mathematical biology. For example, we have already successfully used some ideas to study the disease transmission models, see the item 4 in the research output.

15329816.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15329816.value: All the existing works on predator-prey systems ideally assumed that the dispersal of the predator is constant irrelevant of the distribution of prey population to avoid the mathematical challenges. In this project, we study predator-prey systems with density-dependent dispersal where the dispersal of the predator depend on the distribution of prey population. This is more realistic in real world. The density-dependent dispersal will generate cross-diffusion and degenerate diffusion, which raises enormous challenge for mathematical analysis. In the project, we face these challenges and find some new ideas to explore the global dynamics and find conditions under which the competitive exclusion and co-existence steady states are achieved. These results may be able to help biologist understand the complex dynamics in a realistic but completed biological system.

15330516.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15330516.value: Structural glasses, such as common silicate glasses, glassy polymers, and amorphous metals, are supercooled liquids with atomic or molecular motions dramatically slowed down upon cooling towards the glass transition temperature. The fundamental mechanism responsible for the corresponding glass transition is one of the most fundamental and long-standing puzzles in condensed matter physics. Besides being studied in bulk form, glasses in confined geometries including glassy polymer films of thickness in the nanometer regime have provided much further information. Their studies are also important technologically as polymer nanostructures are widely used in advanced electronic packaging, photoresist structures, battery matrix, lubrication, and adhesive applications. Experiments on short-chain unentangled polystyrene nanofilms have shown that a highly mobile surface layer exists on the free film surface and this mobile layer is believed to be responsible for many confinement effects including enhanced flow mobility and reduced glass transition temperature commonly observed. Computer simulations also show that particles in glasses in general move via intermittent hopping motions each over a distance comparable to the particle diameter. Moreover, hopping events typically occur in small groups of particles in a correlated form called string-like motion in which neighboring particles arranged in a line displace one another from head to tail. Recently, we observe from molecular dynamics simulations of bulk polymers that string-like motions become highly reversible and repetitive close to the glass transition temperature and this can be the major cause of the slow down of the dynamics. Our simulations of polymer films also indicate that the mobile surface layer may be induced by the propagation of strings to and from the free surface throughout the layer. We propose to study glassy polymer films using large-scale molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and analytical calculations. We will quantitatively measure using MD simulations of short-chain polymer films various statistical properties of string-like motions in the surface mobile layer. A mathematical explanation of the mobile layer based on string propagation will be attempted. We will also refine the definition of strings to better describe the logical sequence of particle motions and to better generalize its application to film geometry. Moreover, starting from a unified set of measured or calculated particle hopping probabilities, we will derive and relate the diverse behaviors of confinement effects exhibited in viscous flow, thermal expansion, and other phenomena.

15330516.label: Realisation of objectives
15330516.value: All project objectives are completed. We have studied surface mobile layers in glassy polymer films. Using molecular dynamics simulations of a bead-spring model, we measure a wide variety of layer-resolved structural and dynamic properties of polymer films at a low temperature. Surface enhancement on particle hopping rate is found to terminate abruptly only about 5 particle diameters from the free surface, while surface induced reduction of dynamic heterogeneity associated with a reduced hopping anti-correlation penetrate at least 2 particle diameters deeper. The diverse penetration depths imply the existence of a peculiar sublayer, referred to as the inner surface layer, in which surface enhanced mobility is caused by a reduced dynamic heterogeneity rather than more frequent particle hops. This layer is expected to dominate the flow dynamics in thin films for certain polymer chain lengths. It also provides a unique mechanism for varying the dynamic heterogeneity while keeping the particle hopping rate constant and this imposes important constraints on fundamental theories of glass. This is a significant progress both in understanding the surface mobile layer and glass in general. We have also investigated interfacial slippage of entangled polystyrene films on an adsorbed layer of another polymer called PDMS on silicon by studying spontaneous surface capillary excitations in the films. For films with a large molecular weight, substantial surface dynamics was found even at times shorter than 1/1000 times the reptation time of the films. For films with thicknesses above 100 nm, the dynamics was attributable to conventional plug flow. For the thinner films, a distinctly different dynamics was found. A model assuming the films to be dynamically pinned to the substrate surface in a stick-slip manner is able to describe the data. The model gives a general description of confinement effects based on particle hopping and related dynamics. These complete objectives 1 and 4. A new type of quasi-particle dominating particle dynamics in glasses has now been identified and is named quasivoid. For glassy materials such as window glasses and glassy polymers, what limits their viscosities has been puzzling scientists for decades. By performing week-long experiments on glasses modeled by colloidal solutions, particle motions are observed to be induced by tightly-bounded free spaces behaving as pseudo-particles called quasivoids. As a direct evidence of their existence, a quasivoid is seen to diffuse reversibly across a glass-crystal interface and unambiguously manifests itself in the crystal phase as a vacancy, a well-established quasi-particle. Contrary to common belief, particle dynamics in glasses and in crystals are therefore intimately related. The identification of quasivoid is likely to pave the way for a fundamental understanding of the physics of glasses. These and quantitative measurements involved complete objectives 2 and 3. Volume and enthalpy relaxation of glasses after a sudden temperature change has been extensively studied since Kovacs’ seminal work. One observes an asymmetric approach to equilibrium upon cooling versus heating and, more counterintuitively, the expansion gap paradox, i.e., a dependence on the initial temperature of the effective relaxation time even close to equilibrium when heating. Here, we show that a distinguishable-particle lattice model can capture both the asymmetry and the paradox. We quantitatively characterize the energetic states of the particle configurations using a physical realization of the fictive temperature called the structural temperature, which, in the heating case, displays a strong spatial heterogeneity. The system relaxes by nucleation and expansion of warmer mobile domains having attained the final temperature, against cooler immobile domains maintained at the initial temperature. A small population of these cooler regions persists close to equilibrium, thus explaining the paradox. The viscosities of some glasses upon cooling shoot up more dramatically within a narrower temperature range than others. Such a dramatic slowdown is now found to occur hand in hand with a dramatic drop of the system entropy, resulting at severely constrained particle kinetics. We perform kinetic Monte Carlo simulations of a distinguishable-particle lattice model of structural glasses with random particle interactions. By varying the interaction distribution and the average particle hopping energy barrier, we obtain an extraordinary wide range of kinetic fragility. A stretching exponent, characterizing structural relaxation, is found to decrease with the kinetic fragility in agreement with experiments. The most fragile glasses are those exhibiting low hopping barriers and, more importantly, dramatic drops of entropies upon cooling towards the glass transition temperatures. The entropy drops reduce possible kinetic pathways and lead to dramatic slowdowns in the dynamics. In addition, the kinetic fragility is shown to correlate with a thermodynamic fragility. These consequences of particle hopping events in glasses further contribute to objectives 2 and 3.

15330516.label: Major findings and research outcome
15330516.value: We have studied surface mobile layers in glassy polymer films using molecular dynamics simulations. Results show that surface enhanced mobility is caused by a reduced dynamic heterogeneity rather than more frequent particle hops. This is a significant progress both in understanding the surface mobile layer and glass in general. We have investigated interfacial slippage of entangled polystyrene films on an adsorbed layer of another polymer called PDMS on silicon by studying spontaneous surface capillary excitations in the films. For the films with a large molecular weight, substantial surface dynamics was found even at times shorter than 1/1000 times the reptation times of the films. For the films with thicknesses above 100 nm, the dynamics was attributable to conventional plug flow. This gives a general description of confinement effects based on particle hopping and related dynamics. (See Publications 1 and 2.) We experimentally study microscopic particle dynamics in colloidal glass formers at high packing fractions. With a small polydispersity leading to glass-crystal coexistence, a void in the form of a vacancy in the crystal can diffuse reversibly into the glass and further induces stringlike motions. In the glass, a void takes the form of a quasivoid consisting of a few neighboring free volumes and is transported by the stringlike motions it induces. In fully glassy systems with a large polydispersity, similar quasivoid actions are observed. The mobile particles cluster into stringlike or compact geometries, but the compact ones can be further broken down into connected sequences of strings, establishing their general importance. (See Publication 5.) The void-induced stringlike particle hopping motions supported by our experiments are studied using a distinguishable-particle lattice model. First, for volume and enthalpy relaxation of glasses after a sudden temperature change, a long-standing expansion gap paradox is studied and explained based on spatial heterogeneity. Second, by varying the interaction distribution and the average particle hopping energy barrier, we obtain an extraordinary wide range of kinetic fragility. The most fragile glasses are those exhibiting low hopping barriers and dramatic drops of entropies upon cooling towards the glass transition temperatures. Finally, we have performed an analytical evaluation of the mean-squared displacement (MSD) of the particles in glasses based on their coarse grained trajectories. Results are compared with the numerical simulations of a lattice glass model, and satisfactory agreement has been obtained. (See Publications 3, 4, and 6)

15330516.value: The void-induced particle motions found and supported via various methods in this project have motived us to submit further proposals, including one funded in 2020. We will continue to work on these projects for an eventual solution of the problem of glass transition.

15330516.value: For glassy materials such as window glasses and glassy polymers, what limits their viscosities has been puzzling scientists for decades. Glassy polymer films are known to possess a surface mobile layer which dominates dynamics. We have shown that it is caused by a reduced heterogeneity of the dynamics in the surface. The slippage dynamics of entangled polystyrene thin films is also characterized. A new type of quasi-particle dominating particle dynamics in glasses has now been identified and is named quasivoid. Contrary to common belief, particle dynamics in glasses and in crystals are therefore intimately related. Using a new type of lattice model based on void-induced particle hopping dynamics, we have resolved a decades-old paradox on the aging of glassy polymers. In addition, the viscosities of some glasses upon cooling shoot up more dramatically within a narrower temperature range than others. Such a dramatic slowdown is now found to occur hand in hand with a dramatic drop of the system entropy, resulting at severely constrained particle kinetics.

15333816.label: Realisation of objectives
15333816.value: Objective 1 is to develop new inhibitors for bacterial glycosyltransferase as antibacterial agents. A series of new inhibitors for bacterial glycosyltransferase based on the isatin structure were designed with reference to the binding pose revealed by the GT crystal structure (PDB ID 2OLV). Over 30 of such derivatives with the aminoguanidinyl group conserved were synthesized and their antibacterial activities against both Gram negative (E. coli) and Gram positive bacteria (S. aureus including methicillin resistant S. aureus) were studied. The minimum inhibitory concentration of these inhibitors against the different bacterial strains were obtained. The Structure-Activity Relationship (SAR) of these compounds as PGT inhibitors was also analyzed. So objective 1 is 100 % achieved. Objective 2 is to validate the PGT target of isatin derivatives by STD-NMR study. The interaction between all the inhibitors synthesized with GT was studied by saturation-transfer difference (STD)-NMR experiments to confirm that PGT is the binding target. However, as the STD-NMR experiment is based on the NMR signal of the inhibitors, it only proved that the compound interacts with the PGT protein but doesn’t show where it binds. Therefore we have developed a new target validation assay based on the consumption of the PGT substrate lipid II by the bi-functional bacterial cell wall synthesis enzyme PBP2a (which contains the PGT domain) to give peptidoglycan in the presence of different concentrations of the inhibitors. The amount of lipid II consumed is measured by HPLC. The lipid II is labeled with a fluorophore so that its amount can be measured by a fluorescence detector in the HPLC. This new assay was applied to our subsequent studies. So objective 2 is also 100 % achieved. Objective 3 is to perform backbone assignments of C-13/N-15 labeled PGT domain by triple resonance NMR experiments. The original purpose was to label all the amino acids of the PGT domain with C-13/N-15, and assign the NMR signals corresponding to each amino acid in the protein so that we can study the real time interaction of the inhibitors with the PGT protein by NMR spectroscopy. Unfortunately this work is very labour intensive and challenging for large proteins. After discussion with Dr. Sze Kong Hung, we were advised to trim down the size of the protein to ~ 20 kDa. The size of E. coli PBP1b is 95.4 kDa and the PGT domain is 28 kDa. We have tried very hard to reduce the size of the PGT domain by removing some of its loops. Quite a number of PGT domains with part of its amino acids removed were expressed. Unfortunately, all such proteins were very unstable. Due to the instability of the reduced size PGT proteins the backbone assignment of the PGT domain by NMR was not further studied.

15333816.label: Major findings and research outcome
15333816.value: Moenomycin A, the well-known natural product inhibitor of peptidoglycan glycosyltransferase (PGT), is a large amphiphilic molecule of molecular mass of 1583 g/mol and its bioavailablity as a drug is relatively poor. In searching for small-molecule ligands with high inhibition ability targeting the enzyme, we found in this study that the addition of hydrophobic groups to an isatin-based inhibitor of bacterial PGT significantly improves its inhibition against the enzyme, as well as its antibacterial activity. The improvement in enzymatic inhibition can be attributed to a better binding of the small molecule inhibitor to the hydrophobic region of the membrane-bound bacterial cell wall synthesis enzyme and the plasma membrane. In the present study, a total of 20 new amphiphilic compounds were systematically designed and the relationship between molecular hydrophobicity and the antibacterial activity by targeting at PGT was demonstrated. The in vitro lipid II transglycosylation inhibitory effects (IC50) against E. coli PBP1b and MICs of the compounds were investigated. MIC values for MSSA, MRSA, B. subtilis and E. coli were obtained. (Research output no. 1 under section 8 of part C) In addition to above, another series of 10 isatin derivatives bearing three different substituent groups at N-1, C-3 and C-5 positions of the isatin scaffold were systematically designed and synthesized to study the structure-activity relationship of their inhibition on bacterial peptidoglycan glycosyltransferase (PGT) activity and antimicrobial susceptibility against S. aureus and E. coli including methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA (BAA41)) strain. The substituents at these sites are pointing towards three different directions from the isatin scaffold to interact with the amino acid residues in the binding pocket of PGT. By comparing their structure-activity relationship, we could understand at which direction of the substituent may contribute critical interaction that may provide significant inhibition ability against the enzyme. Our results demonstrated that the modification on these sites is able to maximize the antimicrobial potency and enzyme inhibition ability. The results of this study will be reported in a subsequent paper. We have also developed a new assay for PGT target validation based on the consumption of the PGT substrate lipid II by the bi-functional bacterial cell wall synthesis enzyme PBP1b (which contains the PGT domain) in the presence of inhibitors. After years of effort, the total synthesis of lipid II, a very complicated biomolecule, has been achieved in our laboratory by a chemoenzymatic approach. The availability of lipid II always limits the study related to bacterial cell wall synthesis because it is difficult to prepare and very expensive. Only a few laboratories in the world can prepare lipid II in milligram level, we are now among one of these laboratories. The assay reported in output 1 under section 8 part C was based on this new method.

15333816.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15333816.value: Potential inhibitors for PGT can be further developed based on other natural products that are less toxic than isatin. For example, rosmarinic acid is a potential candidate for further modification into a PGT inhibitor as docking result indicated that it can bind to the pocket of the PGT domain quite well. Based on the information obtained in this study, a direction for modifying rosmarinic acid into an effective PGT inhibitor is the addition a hydrophobic group to its core so as to enhance its binding to the hydrophobic region of the membrane-bound PBP enzyme and the plasma membrane. Our research group is working towards this direction by synthesizing rosmarinic acid derivatives and testing their antibacterial susceptibility and inhibitory effect towards PGT

15333816.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15333816.value: Antibiotic resistance is a serious worldwide health threatening problem. There is an urgent need to develop new antibiotics based on new chemical structures and new drug targets. The bacterial peptidoglycan glycosyltransferase (PGT), which plays an important role in bacterial cell wall synthesis, is considered an important target in the development of antibiotics for the next generation. The PGT inhibitors developed in this study, though not yet ready for use as antibiotics, do give insight and assist the development of the next generation new antibiotics to overcome the multidrug resistance problem. We will further develop the PGT inhibitors based on the information obtained in this study. Hopefully when a compound is identified as a potential antibiotic drug candidate, we will be able to partner with a pharmaceutical company to further develop it for preclinical and clinical trials.

15333916.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15333916.value: Irradiation of a molecule with ultraviolet (UV) light creates electronic excited state that may undergo excited state intramolecular charge transfer (ESICT) and proton transfer (ESIPT). The ESICT and ESIPT, which occur generally in extremely rapid timescale, are at the core of many processes in chemistry and biology, and they play a central role in a wide variety of practical areas such as energy storage, lighting materials, fluorescence probe in biology, and the photo-stability of media exposed to high-intensity optical irradiation. Two types of aromatic carbonyls (ACs), the para-substituted aminobenzoate derivatives (p-ABZs) and ortho-substituted hydroxyl aromatic carbonyls (OHACs) are, respectively, the archetype system showing the ESICT and ESIPT. The two apparently different ACs are however related to a common category of compounds known as UV photo-stabilizers, or more specifically those used as active ingredient in topical sunscreen or UV absorber in polymers. This application requires the compounds having high degree of photostability after irradiation by UV light. Despite the intense interest and the extensive previous studies on ESICT and ESIPT, the precise connection between them and the property of photo-stabilization, in particular the molecular mechanisms and the elementary steps as well as major factors responsible for such a connection have remained largely unexplored. Herein we propose to employ a combination of the state-of-the-art femtosecond time-resolved spectroscopy including time-resolved fluorescence, transient absorption, and time-resolved resonance Raman with ultrafast time resolution to study a series of selected p-ABZs and OHACs with a purpose to directly probe the dynamics of ESICT and ESIPT, the protective excitation elimination channels initiated by or occurring in parallel to the ESICT and ESIPT, as well as to examine how these are affected by the microscopic solvation condition. The proposed research will provide direct evidence for achieving a comprehensive and yet detailed molecular-level description for excited state dynamics. The results are also essential for revealing the structure-property relationship and for indentifying key factor dictating the photostability and probable photo-degradation of the related UV photo-stabilizer compounds. The proposed work will advance dramatically our understanding of not only the ESICT and ESIPT reactions themselves but also the dynamic consequence that are caused by these fundamentally important processes. 分子吸收紫外光產生電子激發態，激發態可進行分子內電荷傳遞（ESICT）和質子傳遞（ESIPT）反應。 ESICT和ESIPT通常發生在很短的時間尺度，是許多光化學和光生物學過程的核心步驟，在各種應用領域（如儲能、照明材料、生物熒光探針、以及物質被高強度光照射後的穩定性）也起著關鍵作用。作為芳香族羰基（ACs）衍生物，對位取代的氨基苯甲酸（p-ABZs）及鄰位取代的羥基芳族羰基（OHACs）分別是ESICT和ESIPT的原型系統。這兩種ACs衍生物同時也屬於一類被稱作紫外光穩定劑的化合物，是應用在防曬霜和聚合物中吸收紫外光的活性成分。這類化合物具有很高的抗紫外光穩定性。儘管人們以往對ESICT和ESIPT進行了大量的研究，但這些過程與光穩定性之間的關係尚屬未知，而且其分子機制、基元步驟、及影響這些過程的主要因素還未被充分探索過。為此我們建議採用尖端的組合飛秒時間分辨光譜，包括時間分辨熒光、瞬態吸收、和皮秒時間分辨共振拉曼光譜技術，通過研究一系列的p-ABZs及OHACs化合物，直接探測並跟踪ESICT和ESIPT的動態過程，以確定與ESICT和ESIPT相關的激發態去反應通道，並考察微觀溶劑化對這些過程的影響。本研究將提供直接的證據，以在分子水平上描述激發態的演化過程。研究結果將會揭示導致紫外光穩定劑光穩定性的分子機理及光穩定性與結構之間的內在關係，並指認調控光穩定性及光損傷的主要因素。本研究工作將深化我們對ESICT和ESIPT反應的認識，並為了解這些反應所能導致的各種動力學過程及潛在應用提供重要信息。

15333916.label: Realisation of objectives
15333916.value: For objective 1: 100% achieved We have performed an integrated spectroscopic investigation where we combined steady-state absorption and fluorescence, femtosecond time-resolved fluorescence (fs-TRF) and femtosecond transient absorption (fs-TA) experiments on selected para-substituted aminobenzoate derivative (p-ABZ) compounds. The dynamics and reactivity properties of the excited-states involved in the UV initiated processes as well as solvent and substitution effects are studied. For objective 2: 100% achieved The results from objective (1) have been used to develop an overall mechanism to account for the photostability of the selected p-ABZ compounds. These results have also been used to evaluate role of excited state intramolecular charge transfer (ESICT) in the excited state decays and its relevance to photostability as well as to assess efficiency of particular transient excited state that may lead to photodegradation of the compounds. For objective 3: 90% achieved We have performed the combined fs-TRF and fs-TA experiments on selected ortho-substituted hydroxyl aromatic carbonyl (OHAC) model compounds and some related UV photo-stabilizers in current use. The dynamics and electronic feature of the transient states involved in the excited state processes of these compounds are explored. The microscopic solvent condition and substitution in the selected OHAC compounds are studied. For objective 4: 90% achieved The results from objective (3) have been used to develop an overall mechanism to account for the photostability of the selected OHACs as well as to evaluate role of excited state intramolecular proton transfer (ESIPT) in the excited state deactivation and its relevance to the photostability. The key factors governing the course of excited state decays and regulating efficiencies of the varied involved deactivation channels of selected OHACs are studied. For objective 5: 95% achieved By performing the investigations to achieve the objectives 1 to 4 above, we have obtained useful information on the photophysics and photochemistry of the selected aromatic carbonyl compounds in general and the specific roles of ESICT and ESIPT and their affected by microscopic solvation in particular.

15333916.label: Major findings and research outcome
15333916.value: We have conducted most of the experiments planned in this project. Through these measurements, expected evidences have been obtained for addressing most of the questions posed in the proposal. Our study provides direct observation of photo-excited methyl dimethylaminobenzoate (MDMABA) in a water solvent revealed a rapid intramolecular charge transfer (ICT) reaction occurring with a time constant of ~0.7 ps from an initial locally excited (LE) state identified to have the La-pipi* character; this produced a weakly emissive ICT state featuring radiative rate constant decreased by more than two orders of magnitude. The fluorescence of the ICT state is strongly quenched exhibiting a decay time of ~49.7 ps, unusually faster than the nanosecond range lifetime in a polar aprotic solvent when intersystem crossing (ISC) is the major deactivation channel. The results contain an important insight for the in-depth understanding of the excited state H-bonding dynamics, and also have significant implication for clarifying the ‘‘sunscreen controversy’’ of the DMABA type of UVB sunscreen molecule. Our study also unveils the excited state cascades for 2-ethylhexyl 4-dimethylaminobenzoate (EHDMABA) and two of its derivatives in solvents of varied properties. The results provide direct evidence for a nearly solvent independent inner sphere ICT reaction occurring on the sub-picosecond time scale, and an ensuing solvent dictated deactivation of the ICT state. The findings of this work demonstrate the pivotal role of the microenvironment and the direct participation of solvent molecules through H-bonding in drastically altering the nonradiative dynamics and promoting or inhibiting photostability and photoprotection. This may assist in developing next-generation UV filters and help in improving formulation design for the optimal efficacy of sunscreen products. Our study also provides evidence at the molecular level for the detrimental effect of 4-aminobenzoic acid (PABA) if used as a sunscreen ingredient. In contrast, our investigation on 4-dimethylaminoacetophenone (DMAAP) and 4-dimethylaminobenzaldehyde (DMABA) unveils an unusual solvent controlled deactivation dynamics rendered by the participation of the carbonyl oxygen associated no-pi* state featuring energy and structure strongly responsive to solvent properties. The revelation of highly solvent sensitive fluorescence emission from DMABA and DMAAP implies the potential application of these molecules as the functional element in the design of sensory materials for probing the polarity and hydrogen bonding character of the surrounding environment.

15333916.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15333916.value: Based on the outcome of this project, further research will be attempted to perform more combined fs-TRF and fs-TA experiments to directly probe the dynamics and spectra of the excited-states for more selected p-ABZ and OHAC compounds.

15333916.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15333916.value: Following the research plan suggested in the proposal, some selected para-substituted aminobenzoate derivative (p-ABZ) and ortho-substituted hydroxyl aromatic carbonyl (OHACs) compounds were investigated using femtosecond time-resolved fluorescence, femtosecond transient absorption spectroscopy. The spectra and dynamics signatures for intrinsic excited-states and associated emission pathways were obtained. The results also bring important new insight into role of microscopic solvation in affecting the excited state intramolecular charge transfer (ESICT) and proton transfer (ESIPT) and modulating the course and relative efficiencies of elementary steps for the photostability and probable photo-damages. The outcomes of this project have led to several publications in top international journals. The research grant allows training of several students, at both the undergraduate and post graduated levels.

15334316.label: Project Objectives
15334316.value: Study the formation and characterization of targeting ligand-conjugated prodrug self-assembled nanoparticle (TPSN). (i) Synthesis. Selected biopolymer will be used to make the TPSN. One anticancer drug, doxorubicin (DOX), will be selected as the drug model. The biopolymer and drug will be synthesized through selected pathway to obtain the prodrug. (ii) Self-assembly. Because of the amphiphilicity of the selected biopolymer, the prodrug will self-assemble into nanoparticle (PSN), which has the anti-multidrug resistance property because of its endocytosis pathway, size, and surface properties. (iii) Targeting ligands (TL) conjugation. For targeted delivery, selected TL will be conjugated onto the surface of the PSN to make TPSN. Study the in vitro targeted release and stimuli-responsive triggered release of TPSN. TPSN has the advantages of both targeted release and triggered release. The in vitro targeted release will be studied by evaluating the effect of the TL and comparing the cellular uptake of TPSN and PSN on various cancer cells. The stimuli-responsive triggered release will also be studied and the triggered release profiles will be built. Study the in vitro cytotoxicity, and cellular uptake and intracellular trafficking mechanism of TPSN on various cancer cells. The effect of TPSN on cancer cell killing will be studied using human cancer cell lines and human normal cell lines. The cellular uptake and intracellular trafficking mechanism of TPSN and prodrug, as a comparison, will be investigated, which will help to understand the improved cytotoxicity and anti-multidrug resistance effects of TPSN. To localize the intracellular drug release point of TPSN, various pathway inhibitors and compartment markers will be selected. In vivo study of the pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, and anticancer activity of TPSN using tumor xenografted animal models. To understand the pharmacokinetics of the TPSN in vivo, SD rats model will be selected. The TPSN as well as prodrug will be administered and blood samples will be collected. Tumor xenografted animal models will be used for the in vivo biodistribution and anticancer activity studies of TPSN. The TPSN as well as the prodrug will be administered. The weight of the mice and the size of the tumor will be measured daily. At certain times, the animal will be sacrificed and the tumor as well as the blood and organs, including liver, spleen, kidney, lung, heart, and brain, will be collected. The drug content in the blood and organ samples will be measured. The evaluations of the therapeutic effects, including tumor weight index and tumor volume, will be conducted.

15334316.label: Realisation of objectives
15334316.value: 1). Study the formation and characterization of targeting ligand-conjugated prodrug self-assembled nanoparticle (TPSN). The original objectives were completely achieved. (i) Synthesis. Zein was used to make the prodrug self-assembled nanoparticles. Anticancer drug paclitaxel (PTX) and doxorubicin (DOX) was selected as the drug model. Disulfide bonds, which can be cleaved by glutathione (GSH) that is overexpressed in most cancer cells, was used as the linkage of zein and the drug. Various concentrations and ratios of zein, selected drug, and disulfide was tried to obtain the zein-S-S-PTX prodrug (Z-prodrug). FTIR and NMR was used to characterize and evaluate the synthesized Z-prodrug. (ii) Self-assembly. The prodrug, zein-S-S-PTX was self-assemble into nanoparticle using evaporation induced self-assembly and phase separation methods. The SEM image showed a homogeneous spherical structure of zein-S-S-PTX_NP. (iii) Targeting ligands (TL) conjugation. Selected TL, folic acid (FA), was conjugated onto the surface of the zein nanoencapsulation of DOX (FA-NP-DOX). The formation of the TL conjugation was evaluated using DLS, FTIR, and UV-vis spectroscopy. The structure of FA-NP-DOX was characterized using SEM. FA-NP-DOX was found to be uniformly spherical in shape with a particle size of around 200 nm. The drug EE was 88% and the FA conjugation yield was higher than 90%, which indicated successful encapsulation and conjugation. 2). Study the in vitro targeted release and stimuli-responsive triggered release of TPSN. TPSN has the advantages of both targeted release and triggered release. The original objectives were completely achieved. The original objectives were completely achieved. Sprague Dawley (SD) rats were used to study the pharmacokinetics. At selected time points (0.5, 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, and 24 h), blood samples (100 μL) were collected from the orbital cavity. The DOX content in the blood samples was determined using fluorescence spectrometry. The longer controlled release of DOX from NP-DOX than pure DOX is because the protection of the DOX by the single layer of zein. While the much longer controlled release of DOX from FA-NP-DOX than NP-DOX or pure DOX is because of the bilayer encapsulation of zein and FA as well as the hydrogen bond interaction between FA and zein. The weight of the mice and the size of the tumor were measured daily. At certain times, the animal was sacrificed and the tumor as well as the blood and organs, including liver, spleen, kidney, lung, heart, and brain, were collected. 15334316.label: Major findings and research outcome
15334316.value: In this study, a novel prodrug was synthesized using paclitaxel (PTX), zein, and a disulfide linker, and nanoparticles were formed by self-assembly of the prodrug. The SEM image showed a homogeneous spherical structure of zein-S-S-PTX_NP.An effective in vitro triggered release, 80−90% in 5 min of the prodrug based nanoparticles (zein-S-S-PTX_NP) was successfully approached. Folic acid (FA), was conjugated onto the surface of the zein nanoencapsulation of DOX (FA-NP-DOX). FA-NP-DOX was found to be uniformly spherical in shape with a particle size of around 200 nm. The drug EE was 88% and the FA conjugation yield was higher than 90%, which indicated successful encapsulation and conjugation. The in vitro control release of FA-NP-DOX, NP-DOX, and pure DOX was also studied. It took only 8 h for pure DOX to have 100% release in PBS medium, while, at 100 h, about 80 and 60% of DOX was released from NP-DOX and FA-NP-DOX, respectively. The controlled release of DOX was highly improved by NP-DOX and even more by FA-NP-DOX. The cytotoxicity of zein-S-S-PTX_NP as well as the zein encapsulation of PTX (zein_PTX_NP) and pure PTX on HeLa cells and NIH/3T3 fibroblast cells was tested using MTS assay. The in vitro cytotoxicity study revealed that zein-S-S-PTX_NP had similar cytotoxicity to HeLa cells as pure PTX. To NIH/3T3 fibroblast cells, zein-SS-PTX_NP showed zero toxicity at the equivalent PTX concentrations of 0.1, 0.5, 1, and 5 μg/mL while pure PTX decreased the cell viability to 63.6%, 45.9%, 40.2%, and 39.8% at the same concentrations, respectively. At higher equivalent PTX concentrations of 10, 20, and 40 μg/mL, zein-S-SPTX_NP started to show toxicity to the NIH/3T3 cells and decreased the cell viability to 78.7%, 77.2%, and 71.6%, respectively. However, pure PTX decreased the NIH/3T3 cell viability to 37.2%, 34.02%, and 28.6%, respectively. It indicated that zein-S-S-PTX_NP had a good selectivity of cancer cells over normal cells compared to pure PTX, which can highly reduce the side effects. In the animal study, the tumor was 50% of the original size after the treatment of zein-S-S-PTX_NP for 9 days with 3 doses. Zein-S-S-PTX_NP showed a well improved antitumor activity compared to pure PTX in the animal model study. This study suggested that the novel prodrug based nanoparticle zein-S-S-PTX_NP could be a promising approach in chemotherapy with targeted delivery, improved efficacy, and reduced side effects.

15334316.value: In this study, the zein based nanoparticles showed high potential for the formation of multifunctional drug carriers, including prodrug. As a protein, zein showed great potential in conjugating with targeting ligands as well as forming special chemical bonds with trigger release properties. Various conjugations with different targeting ligand and trigger release connections are expected in our future study. In this study, zein based nanoparticles showed low cytotoxicity to normal cells while kept the same cytotoxicity to cancer cells as the pure drugs. It also showed great selectivity in the in vivo studies. The good selectivity will enable zein nanoparticles to apply on different organs and tissues for target delivery with low immunogenicity. In the study, it was shown that, as an amphiphile, zein has the potential property of cell penetration and body barrier penetration. In the future study, zein based nanoparticle will be conjugated with brain-targeting ligand and applied for the treatment of glioblastoma, which so far has difficulties in the current therapies and brain targeting delivery of drugs shows great potential to bring in new treatment method.

15334616.label: Project Objectives
15334616.value: Develop the convergence theory of randomized Kaczmarz algorithms in separable Hilbert spaces. The strong assumption of positive lower bound of eigenvalues of covariance matrix in literature will be removed. The noise-free situation will be studied as an ideal scenario. Polynomial convergence rate will be derived which marks the significant difference between infinite dimensional spaces and Euclidean spaces (where exponential decay is proved in literature). Then the noisy setting will be studied, and the corresponding learning rates will be derived. The obtained theory of Kaczmarz algorithms in Hilbert spaces will be extended to online learning algorithms. For both noise-free and noisy settings, learning rates will be derived. Tikhonov regularization usually used in literature will be removed, and the regularization effect of step-size control will be studied.
