16140216.label: Major findings and research outcome
16140216.value: A manuscript has been prepared pending submission. In this manuscript, we used imaging and biochemical approaches to demonstrate that fasting-induced degradation of DGAT-2 is dependent on AUP-1 and the ERAD pathway in C. elegans. We propose a model that DGAT-2 and AUP-1 interact directly or indirectly on the LD surface, which is a pre-requisite for the delivery of DGAT-2 to the ER, prior to its degradation. Accordingly, the dual localization of AUP-1 in the ER and LD surface in C. elegans and other experimental models reflect its role in shuttling protein cargoes from LDs to the ER. The broad expression pattern of AUP-1 suggests that DGAT-2, which is only expressed in the intestine, is not its sole cargo. DGAT-2 and AUP-1 also show divergent requirement of individual ERAD E3 enzymes for their degradation, once they reach the ER. Therefore, it is plausible that DGAT-2 disassociates with AUP-1 in the ER, prior to their engagement with the ERAD pathway. We used CRISPR/Cas9 mediated genome editing to generate a suite of new transgenic strains in this project, which will benefit other researchers in the field. A major innovation is the demonstration of robust photo-conversion of the mKikGR::DGAT-2 fusion protein. For the first time, pre-existing proteins could be labeled and their localization and stability monitored simultaneously in vivo. This is an attractive alternative to the traditional approach of using cycloheximide to halt protein synthesis, prior to the detection of protein level by Western blotting, which does not provide the localization of the target protein. In addition, our method can be generalized for studying the trafficking of additional proteins between the ER and LDs. This is important because the gating mechanism that prevents the exchange of proteins between LDs and the ER is not well-defined. It has been suggested that proteins compete for their retention on the LD surface under lipolytic condition, as LDs shrink. As a result, abundant proteins with high-affinity domains for phospholipid monolayer association are preferentially retained. In addition to physical constraints, our work is the first to suggest that the turnover of LD associated proteins can also be linked to their function during lipolysis. Specifically, neutral lipid synthesis enzymes are targeted for degradation since their activities are counter-productive when nutrients are lacking. Our work points to an integrated fasting-induced response that firmly tips the balance from fat storage to fat mobilization.

16140216.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16140216.value: We have sought to determine the mechanisms that mark DGAT-2 for degradation in fasted worms. We hypothesized that post-translational modification of DGAT-2 may be necessary, prior to its recognition by AUP-1 and translocation to the ER for degradation. To this end, we focused on the potential role of phosphorylation in modulating DGAT-2 degradation. Bioinformatics analysis indicates that there are 32 potential phosphorylation sites in C. elegans DGAT-2. To determine if DGAT-2 turnover is regulated by phosphorylation, we have conducted an RNAi screen on 86 predicted serine/threonine or tyrosine phosphatases in C. elegans. The expression of each phosphatase was knocked down either ubiquitously or specifically in the intestine, and the level of mRuby::DGAT-2, expressed from its endogenous locus, was examined by confocal microscopy. From this screen, we have tentatively identified four phosphatases that either increase or decrease mRuby::DGAT-2 level. Our immediate goal is to replicate our observations in genetic mutants that lack these phosphatases. We also plan to extend our studies on OP9 pre-adipocytes that stably expressed mRuby::DGAT2 and AUP1::GFP. We propose to demonstrate the proximity of DGAT2 and AUP1 under lipid-loading and serum-starvation conditions by Fluorescence Resonance Energy Transfer (FRET) assays.

16140216.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16140216.value: Our body has to decide between storing or using fat, depending on whether we have eaten sufficient amount of food. Inside each cell, similar decision on fat storage or mobilization is made at conserved organelles called lipid droplets (LDs). For example, fasting coordinately triggers the release of fatty acids and the cessation of neutral lipids such as triacylglycerol. In this project, we report the selective degradation of diacylglycerol acyltransferase DGAT-2, which is essential for triacylglycerol synthesis, in fasted C. elegans. We came to this conclusion in part by monitoring DGAT-2 that was fused to fluorescent proteins in live animals, as they became progressively starved after food withdrawal. First, Ancient Ubiquitous Protein 1 (AUP-1) promotes the movement of DGAT-2 from LDs to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). The degradation of DGAT-2 then relies on the ER-associated degradation (ERAD) pathway. Our imaging results was confirmed by further genetic and biochemical analyses, which suggest that three ERAD protein-modification enzymes contribute redundantly to DGAT-2 degradation. We propose a model in which AUP-1 dependent degradation of DGAT-2 by ERAD forms part of an integral response to fasting that prevents inappropriate fat synthesis.

16140616.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16140616.value: In Southern China (including Hong Kong), estuaries have been extensively exploited for their rich resources. They are home to numerous shellfish aquaculture activities due to their abundant food supplies and close proximity to human activity. However, estuaries are extremely dynamic with their physico-chemical conditions influenced by tidal action, including salinity, dissolved organic carbon (DOC), dissolved oxygen, redox conditions, and total suspended solids. Concomitantly, estuaries are often the most contaminated coastal systems due to the uncontrolled releases of industrial effluents. These dynamic coastal environments coupled with increasing metal pollution in estuaries have presented great challenges to shellfish living in the estuary. The estuarine oyster, namely Crassostrea hongkongensis, has been widely farmed in Southern China estuaries. In recent years, the oysters have been found to be contaminated with different metals due to their hyper-accumulating capacity for many toxic metals. However, we know very little about how oysters handle the metal challenges in such dynamic and turbid estuarine environments. In the present project, I propose to study the bioaccumulation and toxicity of metals in oysters under fluctuating conditions typical of estuarine environments. Specifically, we will 1) study metal bioaccumulation and toxicity in oysters under intermittent exposure; 2) study metal bioaccumulation in oysters under high suspended sediment loads and illustrate the exposure of metals in the highly dynamic food environments that vary both in quality and quantity; and 3) study metal bioaccumulation and toxicity in oysters under varying exposures in the field using a transplantation approach. The impact and significance of this project are threefold. First, it will help us understand the bioaccumulation and toxicity of metals in oysters under highly dynamic estuarine environments. Traditional ecotoxicological studies tend to focus on constant exposure, but exposure can be very dynamic and fluctuating in estuarine environments. A study of intermittent exposure may provide important information for our understanding of the basic ecotoxicology of oysters in a real estuarine environment setting, as well as for better refinement of water quality criteria. Second, the project can provide information on the adaptation of oysters to estuarine environments. Very little knowledge is currently available on the relationship between oyster physiology (e.g., particle selection and feeding physiology) and metal bioaccumulation and toxicity. Third, results generated from this study can be important for managers and governments in developing strategies to reduce the toxic metal levels in oysters. 16143016.value: 真核細胞DNA複製起始開始於pre-RC在複製起始位點的組裝。 在以往，pre-RC組裝的過程已經有了廣泛的研究，其具體的組裝步驟也已經比較清楚。簡要的過程可以概況如下：ORC最先結合在複製起始位點，做為一個平台，在Cdc6和Cdt1的協助下，將MCM2-7複合物組裝到雙鏈DNA上，形成MCM2-7雙複合物。體外重組研究發現，這兩個MCM的組裝有一個時間先後順序。在ATP水解被抑制的情況下，組裝過程會形成一個包含ORC-Cdc6-Cdt1-MCM2-7(OCCM)的中間複合物。而在ATP水解之後，Cdt1會首先被釋放出來，從而形成另一個中間複合物ORC-Cdc6-MCM2-7(OCM)。最後，第二個MCM2-7被組裝到OCM上，形成MCM雙複合物。 以往的生化研究，已經使我們對於pre-RC組裝的大概過程有了比較清楚的認識。但是，許多其中的分子機制是如何協調運作而完成pre-RC的組裝，對我們還是未知之迷。為了更好了解這些分子機制，我們已經成功運用最先進的冷凍電子顯微鏡，解構了MCM雙複合物3.8埃分辨率的蛋白質構象。本研究，我們會進一步解構pre-RC組裝過程中的中間複製起始複合物對構象，並應用計算機模擬來解析其中精細的構象變化。本項研究的成果，旨在理解DNA複製起始的調控機理，以及對於癌症治療和早期檢查，提供重要的理論支持。

16143016.label: Major findings and research outcome
16143016.value: DNA replication in eukaryotes is strictly regulated to ensure the integrity of the genome. To ensure that each replication origin is activated no more than once per cell division, the initiation of DNA replication is carried out in two temporally separated steps: replication licensing, and origin activation. Replication licensing begins in early G1 phase with the sequence-specific binding of origin DNA by the ORC to first recruit Cdc6 and then other factors. Escorted by Cdt1, the MCM single hexamer (SH) is loaded onto the ORC–Cdc6-bound origin DNA to form an ORC–Cdc6–Cdt1–MCM2–7 (OCCM) complex. Subsequently an ordered release of Cdc6 and then Cdt1 occurs, leading to the formation of an ORC–Mcm2–7 complex. The loading of a second Mcm2–7 involves the incorporation of Cdt1, Cdc6 and ORC to complete the assembly of a head-to-head Mcm2–7 DH known as the pre-replication complex (pre-RC). Although the events leading to pre-RC assembly has been largely falling into place, the detailed mechanism underlying MCM loading is not well understood at a molecular level. In this period period, we determined the cryo-EM structures of Cdt1-Mcm2-7 and Mcm2-7 complexes, which are the precursors of DH. Both complexes form left-handed coil structures with a 10–15-Å gap between Mcm5 and Mcm2, and a central channel that is occluded by the C-terminal domain winged-helix motif of Mcm5. Cdt1 wraps around the N-terminal regions of Mcm2, Mcm6 and Mcm4 to stabilize the whole complex. The intrinsic coiled structures of the precursors provide insights into the DH formation, and suggest a spring-action model for the MCM during the initial origin melting and the subsequent DNA unwinding. This work was published in Nat Struct Mol Biol 2017. We further analyzed the structures of each Mcm2-7 subunit to reveal their unique roles in replication licensing. It turns out that the individual C-terminal extensions (CTEs) of Mcm2-7 complex have defined roles during helicase loading. The flexible NT insertions (NTIs) of Mcm2-7 are crucial for DH formation. These analyses are documented in Mol Cell in 2017.

16143016.value: The techniques and knowledge developed in this project allowed us to work on other replication related protein complexes. This have led to the determination of ORC-DNA structures published in Nature 2018.

16143016.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16143016.value: DNA replication is one of the most fundamental cellular processes that govern the billions of cell divisions from a single fertilized egg to develop into a full-grown human. Every single step of the DNA replication process is strictly controlled, ensuring the genome is faithfully duplicated once and only once per cell division. When errors occur, catastrophic consequences are expected because the mistakes would be amplified and accumulated through DNA replication during the development process. Cancer development often results from the accumulation of mutations due to unrepaired DNA damage, and a major source of DNA damage is introduced during DNA replication. Therefore, basic research in DNA replication is an integral part of cancer research. The fundamental knowledge of DNA replication can be applied to identify targets against cancer whether in early detection, prevention, or therapeutics. In this project, we made use of cryo electron microscopy to visualise the key factors which act as the core of the machine to unzip our DNA duplex. Our discovery provides a structural framework and knowledge for our campaign against cancer.

16144416.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16144416.value: The unicellular cyanobacteria Prochlorococcus and Synechococcus are the most abundant photosynthetic organisms in the oceans. They are responsible for as much as 50% of total primary production in oligotrophic regions. Viruses (cyanophages) that infect cyanobacteria are also abundant. Adsorption of cyanophages to the host cells is the first step of infection. During adsorption, cyanophage tails recognize specific receptors on the host cell. For cyanophages infecting Synechococcus, it has been shown that their adsorption to the host cells can be light-dependent or light-independent. However, it is unknown why cyanophages have different adsorption strategies, and whether the fitness of a cyanophage is affected by its adsorption strategy. We found that these two adsorption strategies are also used by cyanophages infecting Prochlorococcus. Our preliminary experiments suggested that cyanophages with light-dependent adsorption had a fitness advantage when the infection was initiated during the daytime, and cyanophages with light-independent adsorption had a fitness advantage when the infection was initiated at night. We showed for the first time that the daily light-dark cycle provides a temporal niche for viruses. We hypothesize that different adsorption strategies allow cyanophages to reduce their competition by infecting the host cells at different times of the day, which may promote their coexistence and diversity. In our proposed work, we plan to study how adsorption strategies affect the fitness of cyanophages from three aspects: lab cultures, field samples, and host receptors. We will first use the lab cultures to compare the diel infection patterns of cyanophages with different adsorption strategies to understand how their fitness changes at different times of the day. Next, we will measure the diel abundances of cyanophages with different adsorption strategies at different depths in the South China Sea. We hypothesize that cyanophages with light-dependent adsorption should be relatively more abundant in the surface ocean than those in the deeper ocean, since the light period in the surface ocean is longer. Finally, we will map the host receptor genes for cyanophage adsorption, which may help study the molecular mechanism of different adsorption strategies in the future. Our work will give us valuable insight into the intrinsic role of light in shaping cyanophage and cyanobacteria interactions. Cyanophage infection eventually results in the death of their cyanobacterial host through burst, which releases dissolved organic matter into the marine ecosystem. Therefore, the research proposed here will deepen our understanding of the role of viruses in nutrient cycling in aquatic environments. 做為世界上數量最多的光合作用生物，藍細菌固定了全球大約四分之一的二氧化碳。感染藍細菌的病毒（噬菌體）也在海洋中廣泛存在。噬菌體侵染宿主的第一步是吸附。有的噬菌體只能在白天吸附，而有的噬菌體可以在白天和晚上都吸附。我們認為這兩種不同的吸附方式可以讓噬菌體在不同的時間侵染宿主，從而促進海洋中病毒的共存和多樣性。本項目將研究不同吸附方式的分子機制，已經其對噬菌體的益處。研究成果將有助於我們理解噬菌體和藍細菌在海洋中的相互作用，以及對全球碳循環的影響。

16144416.label: Realisation of objectives
16144416.value: We have been able to fully achieve all the three objectives of the proposal. In Objective 1, we compared the relative fitness of cyanophages with different dark infection strategies. We competed equal numbers of two cyanophage strains under continuous light or at different times of a light-dark cycle. First, we competed a phage that does not replicate in the dark (P-HM2) with a phage that does (P-SSP7 or P-GSP1). In the competition of P-HM2 and P-SSP7, P-SSP7 became the dominant phage under continuous light. However, P-HM2 became the dominant phage at most times under light-dark cycles, suggesting that P-HM2 had a fitness advantage over P-SSP7 under light-dark cycles. P-SSP7 can only defeat P-HM2 under light-dark cycles when the competition was initiated shortly after lights off. This might be because P-SSP7 replicated in the dark while P-HM2 cannot, and after lights on P-SSP7 already had more progeny phages than P-HM2. Similar results were also observed when P-HM2 competed with P-GSP1 under light-dark cycles. We noticed that P-GSP1 did not outnumber P-HM2 under continuous light, although the burst sizes of P-GSP1 (66 phages/cell) and P-SSP7 (40 phages/cell) are both larger than that of P-HM2 (28 phages/cell). This suggested that the burst size is not the only factor that determines the competition between two cyanophage strains, and phage-phage interactions (e.g., superinfection exclusion) might occur when two phages coinfect one host cell. Next, we competed P-HM2 with P-SSM2 or P-HM1, which do not replicate in the dark. P-SSM2 outnumbered P-HM2 under continuous light and also at different times of a light-dark cycle, suggesting that the light-dark cycle did not affect the relative fitness of two phages that do not replicate in the dark. Consistently, the competition of P-HM2 and P-HM1 was not affected by light either. Objective 1 has resulted in two publications Liu et al. PNAS 2019 and Demory et al. mSystems 2020. Another manuscript is under preparation and has been deposited onto bioRxiv (https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/167650v1.abstract). In Objective 2, we investigated the dark infection patterns of cyanophage isolates purified from day and night water samples from the South China Sea and found that cyanophages with different dark infection patterns have different temporal rhythms in the ocean. In total we purified 73 cyanophage isolates using Prochlorococcus marinus MED4 and Synechococcus sp. WH7803, including 36 isolates from the day sea water sample and 37 from the night sea water sample collected in Yong Xing Island in the South China Sea. There were three dark infection patterns identified from the total 73 isolates: P-HM2-like with neither adsorption nor burst under dark (47 isolates), P-SSM2-like with adsorption but no burst under dark (25 isolates) and P-SSP7-like with both adsorption and burst under dark (1 isolate) (Figure 1, Chen et al. under preparation). For the 49 cyanophage isolates exhibiting P-HM2 like dark infection pattern, 22 of them were isolated from the day sea water while the other 25 were from the night sea water (Table 1, Chen et al. under preparation). For the 25 cyanophage isolates showing P-SSM2 like dark infection pattern, 14 of them were from the day sea water and the other 11 were from the night sea water (Table 1, Chen et al. under preparation). There was only 1 isolate found to show P-SSP7-like dark infection pattern, which was from the night sample (Table 1, Chen et al. under preparation). Comparing the contribution of cyanophages with different dark infection patterns of the day and night sea water, the night sea water has more P-HM2-like phages with light-dependent adsorption and the night sea water has more P-SSM2-like cyanophages. Our finding shows that the cyanophages with light-independent adsorption would be more abundant in the day while the cyanophages with light-dependent adsorption would be relatively more abundant in the night, suggesting that cyanophage with different dark infection patterns would show different diel patterns in their abundance in the ocean. Results of Objective 2 are included in a manuscript under preparation (Chen and Zeng, attached in Part C). In addition to cyanophage populations in the South China Sea, we also studied cyanophage populations in the North Pacific Subtropical Gyre. We reanalyzed the published time-series marine metatranscriptomic dataset and revealed the diel infection rhythm of cyanophages in the ocean. These results have been published in Microbiome (Chen and Zeng, 2020). In objective 3, we identified host receptor candidate genes from the 52 selected resistant mutant sub-strains of Prochlorococcus marinus MED4 and Synechococcus sp. WH7803. In objective 2, we have purified 73 cyanophage isolates and have their genome sequenced. These 73 isolates include 49 cyanomyoviruses and 24 cyanopodoviruses. Pair-wise genome comparison was conducted to group those isolates with similar genomes (>=93% whole genome Average Nucleotide Identity) into genotypic populations. The 49 cyanomyoviruses felt into 20 genotypic populations, with 18 mutant sub-strains selected to be resistant to phages from 4 genotypic groups (Figure 2, Chen et al. under preparation). We have identified 68 mutation sites in 14 mutant genes from these 18 mutant sub-strains (Figure 4, Chen et al. under preparation). The mutation profiles of different resistant sub-strains were quite different. As cyanobacteria would employ diverse mechanism to stop the infection of cyanomyoviruses. We found 4 mutate genes related to cell membrane. Those genes are all strong candidates for Synechococcus receptor genes (Figure 4, marked with an asterisk, Chen et al. under preparation). The 4 sub-strains that are resistant to S-SCSM4a with P-SSM2 dark infection pattern (Syn_R15-18) have one unique mutant gene (TolC family protein) that was not found to be mutated in the other 14 sub-strains all resistant to cyanophages with P-HM2 dark infection pattern (Figure 4, Chen et al. under preparation). As we hypothesized before, cyanophage with different dark infection pattern would bind to different receptors. Likely TolC family protein is not affected by light thus cause the light-independent adsorption, while the other three candidates might be regulated by light in some way. The 24 cyanopodovirus isolates were divided into 3 different genotypic groups, with 34 mutant sub-strains against phages from 2 different genotypic groups (Figure 3, Chen et al. under preparation). We identified 115 mutation sites in 46 mutant genes from the 34 Prochlorococcus mutant sub-strains. 12 mutant genes related to cell membrane were identified (Figure 5, Chen et al. under preparation), all of which are receptor candidate genes. In summary, we found 4 receptor candidate genes for cyanophages with P-HM2-like dark infection pattern and 1 receptor candidate gene for cyanophages with P-SSM2-like dark infection pattern in Synechococcus. We also found 12 receptor candidate genes in Prochlorococcus for different cyanophages with P-SSM2-like dark infection pattern. This study has already been finished with the manuscript under preparation. Results of Objective 3 are included in a manuscript under preparation (Chen and Zeng, attached in Part C).

16144416.label: Major findings and research outcome
16144416.value: In this research project, we studied how cyanophages use light-dependent and light-independent adsorption strategies to adapt to the natural light-dark cycle. We conducted our research from three aspects: laboratory cultures, field samples, and host receptors. Using lab cultures, we found that the time of infection affects the relative fitness of cyanophages with different adsorption strategies. These results generated one publication (Liu et al. PNAS 2019) and one manuscript under preparation (https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/167650v1.abstract). Using the data collected from this project, we collaborated with Prof. Joshua Weitz at Georgia Institute of Technology to build a mathematical model to describe the infection kinetics of cyanophages with different adsorption strategies. This collaboration has resulted a joint publication with Prof. Weitz and the PI as co-corresponding authors (Demory et al. mSystems 2020). Using field samples from the South China Sea, we found that cyanophages with light-independent adsorption are more abundant in the day and those with light-dependent adsorption are more abundant at night. These results are included in a manuscript under preparation (Chen and Zeng, attached in Part C). In addition to the South China Sea, we also found diel infection rhythms of field cyanophage populations in the North Pacific Subtropical Gyre, which has been published recently (Chen and Zeng, Microbiome 2020). To study host receptors, we sequenced 52 mutant Prochlorococcus and Synechococcus strains that are resistant to the cyanophages we isolated from the South China Sea. We identified many candidate genes that are related to the different adsorption strategies of cyanophages. These results are described in a manuscript under preparation (Chen and Zeng, attached in Part C). In total, our research has resulted in four published papers and two manuscripts under preparation that will be published next year (listed in Part C). One Ph.D. student and one M.Phil. student have been trained during this project.

16144416.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16144416.value: We used laboratory cultures to show that the fitness of cyanophages with light-dependent and light-independent adsorption strategies can be affected by the time of infection. We also collaborated with Prof. Joshua Weitz to use a model to describe the infection kinetics of each cyanophage. In the future, we plan to continue to collaborate with Prof. Weitz to build a more complicated model to describe the competition of two or even more cyanophages with different adsorption strategies, which can eventually be used to model the interactions of cyanophages and cyanobacteria in the marine ecosystem. We also plan to use the potential membrane receptor genes to study the molecular mechanisms of light-dependent and light-independent adsorption. These light-sensitive membrane receptors can be developed into drug delivery systems that can be triggered by light.

16144416.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16144416.value: In the oceans, lytic viruses (cyanophages) infect the unicellular cyanobacteria Prochlorococcus and Synechococcus, which fix a significant amount of carbon dioxide. The first step of successful infection is adsorption of a cyanophage onto the host cell, which can be either light-dependent or light-independent. In this research project, we examined how the daily light-dark cycle affects the fitness of cyanophages with light-dependent and light-independent strategies. We found that the time of infection affects their relative fitness. In the South China Sea, we found that cyanophages with light-independent adsorption are more abundant in the day and those with light-dependent adsorption are more abundant at night. We also identified many host receptor genes that may be responsible for different adsorption strategies. Our project gives us a complete picture of how cyanophages use different adsorption strategies to adapt to the daily light-dark cycle in marine ecosystems. Since Prochlorococcus and Synechococcus are the most abundant photosynthetic organisms in the oceans, our work will help to understand how the interaction of cyanophages and cyanobacteria influences carbon cycling in the marine ecosystem.

16146516.label: Project Objectives
16146516.value: Identify Rab GTPase that binds to PICK1-ICA69 complexes and elucidate how they interact with each other Rab GTPases are master regulators in different protein trafficking pathways. Our initial screening has identified Rab2A as a binding partner of PICK1-ICA69 complexes. We plan to map the regions in both Rab2A and PICK1-ICA69 complexes mediating their interaction and answer how this provides the specificity of Rab2A binding to PICK1-ICA69 complexes based on its activity. Explore the spatial and temporal relations of Rab2A and PICK1-ICA69 complexes We found that the proteins for both Rab2A and PICK1-ICA69 complexes are co-expressed in the same subset of tissues. We plan to further resolve this spatially and temporally at subcellular level. First, which subcellular compartments do Rab2A and PICK1-ICA69 complexes localize? Second, what is their relationship with the moving dense-core vesicles during stimulated secretion? Understand how Rab2A regulates PICK1-ICA69 complexes in protein trafficking The questions that we would like to address are how Rab2A activity determines the sub-cellular localization of PICK1 and ICA69 as well as the trafficking of dense-core vesicles. The Golgi localization of PICK1 and ICA69 will be defined by super-resolution imaging. In addition to expressing the dominant-negative and constitutively active mutants of Rab2A, we will deplete endogenous Rab2A by shRNA-mediated knockdown. Elucidate the physiological functions of Rab2A and PICK1-ICA69 We plan to investigate whether Rab2A is the upstream regulator of PICK1-ICA69 complexes in animals by the ablation of Rab2A gene expression animal models. We plan to map the regions in both Rab2A and PICK1-ICA69 complexes mediating their interaction and answer how this provides the specificity of Rab2A binding to PICK1-ICA69 complexes based on its activity.

Explore the spatial and temporal relations of Rab2A and PICK1-ICA69 complexes We found that the proteins for both Rab2A and PICK1-ICA69 complexes are co-expressed in the same subset of tissues. We plan to further resolve this spatially and temporally at subcellular level. First, which subcellular compartments do Rab2A and PICK1-ICA69 complexes localize? Second, what is their relationship with the moving dense-core vesicles during stimulated secretion?

Understand how Rab2A regulates PICK1-ICA69 complexes in protein trafficking The questions that we would like to address are how Rab2A activity determines the sub-cellular localization of PICK1 and ICA69 as well as the trafficking of dense-core vesicles. The Golgi localization of PICK1 and ICA69 will be defined by super-resolution imaging. In addition to expressing the dominant-negative and constitutively active mutants of Rab2A, we will deplete endogenous Rab2A by shRNA-mediated knockdown.

Elucidate the physiological functions of Rab2A and PICK1-ICA69 We plan to investigate whether Rab2A is the upstream regulator of PICK1-ICA69 complexes in animals by the ablation of Rab2A gene expression animal models. This will validate our biochemical data at the organism level.

16146516.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16146516.value: Our body is composed of millions of cells with diverse roles. Inside the cells, different organelles are compartmentalized to carry out specialized functions, therefore preventing proteins from freely exchanging among them. To cope with this, our cells have developed carriers called vesicles to pack and transport different proteins in cells. This logistic process, which is known as protein trafficking, relies on complex machinery for the budding and fusion of the vesicles and also sorting of different cargo proteins to the vesicles. For example, insulin in pancreatic beta cells needs to be packed in insulin granules, which bud off from the Golgi, move to the cell periphery and then fuse to the plasma membrane to secrete insulin. PICK1 and ICA69 are two lipid-binding proteins which form tight heteromeric BAR-domain complexes. They are co-expressed at high levels in brain, pancreas and testes. Deficiency of PICK1 in mice leads to male infertility and insufficient insulin release. Despite the diverse phenotypes, one common feature in both scenarios is that complexes of PICK1 are closely associated with a specific type of vesicles called dense-core vesicle. Dense-core vesicle is responsible for transporting various kinds of hormones from the Golgi to the plasma membrane in regulated secretion. During the biogenesis of dense-core vesicles from the Golgi, the crescent-shape of BAR domains in PICK1-ICA69 complexes may sense and bend the membrane of Golgi. Despite their importance, we still do not know which upstream regulatory protein recruits PICK1-ICA69 complexes to the Golgi. Here we propose to identify the protein that recruits PICK1-ICA69 complexes to the Golgi, study the molecular mechanism of the recruitment and elucidate its functional significance. We have performed a systematic screening and identified a small G protein that could recruit PICK1 and ICA69 to the Golgi. Our preliminary data indicate that this small GTPase interacts with heteromeric PICK1-ICA69 complexes specifically. Additionally, the Golgi localization of PICK1 and ICA69 are dependent on the activity of this small GTPase. We will further investigate how the small GTPase binds to PICK1-ICA69 complexes and subsequently recruits them to the Golgi. Through studying the phenotypes of C. elegans and mice deficient in the small GTPase, we expect to fully reveal the mechanism and function of the regulatory machinery involved in the biogenesis of dense-core vesicles from the Golgi. 人体是有成千上万个不同的细胞组成的。细胞内部被各种细胞器分割成不同的亚细胞功能区域，这样使得不同的蛋白质只能在特定的区域内起作用。而不同的亚细胞区域之间的物质运输则是通过囊泡介导的蛋白质转运来实现。囊泡转运是一个复杂的系统，包括货物分拣，囊泡形成以及融合等步骤。比如说胰岛素要先装进胰岛素囊泡，然后这个囊泡从高尔基体上形成，移动到细胞的外周，最后和细胞膜融合把胰岛素分泌出去。 PICK1和ICA69是两个膜相关蛋白。它们可以形成紧密的BAR结构域异聚体，在大脑，胰腺和睾丸中分布比较高。小鼠中的PICK1缺失可以导致雄性不育和胰岛素不足。虽然这两者差别很大，它们的一个共同点是都需要一类囊泡叫做致密囊泡。致密囊泡从高尔基体转运荷尔蒙到细胞膜然后分泌到细胞外。PICK1-ICA69可以形成新月形的BAR结构域复合体来感知弯曲的膜，从而促进致密囊泡从高尔基体生成。我们对于PICK1-ICA69复合体是如何被招募到高尔基体上去的并不清楚。这里我们提议寻找招募PICK1-ICA69复合体到高尔基体上的蛋白调控因子，并进一步研究它的分子机制及功能意义。我们已经做了一个系统性的筛选，找到了一个小G蛋白可以招募PICK1-ICA69到高尔基体。我们初步的结果显示这个小G蛋白可以和PICK1-ICA69异聚体特异性结合。此外，PICK1和ICA69在高尔基体的定位需要这个小G蛋白。我们计划进一步研究这个小G蛋白是如何结合PICK1-ICA69，以及如何把PICK1-ICA69招募到高尔基体上去的。通过研究小G蛋白缺失的线虫和小鼠，我们可以进一步了解致密囊泡从高尔基体生成的分子机制和功能。

16146516.label: Major findings and research outcome
16146516.value: In this project, we first conducted a screening to search for the small G protein(s) that associate with PICK1 and ICA69. A panel of mammalian Rab and Arf GTPases were used in the screen. We found that Rab2A was the only small GTPase interacting with PICK1-ICA69 complexes in an activity-dependent manner. Intriguingly, active Rab2A only bound to the heteromeric form of PICK1 and ICA69 via their lipid-binding BAR domains, which is rarely observed among other homomeric BAR domain-containing proteins. We further mapped key residues in the switch regions of Rab2A responsible for binding with PICK1-ICA69 complexes and demonstrated that this physical interaction determined the Golgi localization of PICK1-ICA69 complexes, as inactive or mutated switch regions of Rab2A failed to recruit PICK1-ICA69 complexes to the Golgi. Endogenously, we showed that Rab2A and PICK1-ICA69 complexes colocalized with the newly formed DCVs budding from the Golgi in a stimulation-chase experiment. Depletion of PICK1-ICA69 complexes significantly reduced DCV biogenesis in cultured secretory AtT-20 cells and similarly decreased the fluorescence signal of DCVs in C. elegans. In addition, our study also found that the heteromeric PICK1 and ICA69 complexes in pancreatic beta cells are critical for insulin granule biogenesis and maintenance of glucose homeostasis. In summary, our results demonstrated that activity-dependent recruitment of heteromeric PICK1-ICA69 complexes by Rab2A initiated the cytosolic cascades important for the biogenesis of DCV from the trans-Golgi networks. Three papers were published with the support of this grant. Another manuscript with major data supported by this project is under preparation.

16146516.value: Our findings that Rab2A binds and recruits PICK1-ICA69 heteromeric complexes, and regulates biogenesis of dense core biogenesis have important implication in the secretion of insulin and other neuroendocrine secretion. We plan to explore the possibilities of further extend this study to better understand the molecular mechanism of diseases such as diabetes and use that as a target to develop potential therapeutic treatment.

16146516.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16146516.value: Cell is a basic unit of our life. Inside each cell, molecules are transported in specific vehicles called vesicles. Different molecules are packed into vesicles that surrounded by lipid membranes. There are proteins on the membranes to help us sort, load, and package different molecules into different vesicles. How these proteins were recruited to the vesicles were not very well known, especially for a kind of vesicles called dense-core vesicles. In this study, we identified a small GTPase called Rab2A that could recruit PICK1-ICA69, a heteromeric complex protein pair, to dense-core vesicles. We further demonstrated that Rab2A acts like a switch, changing from an active state and in-active state, and only recruits PICK1-ICA69 in active state. Interestingly, we found this mechanism plays important roles in the secretion of insulin secretion, a key factor in our glucose control with important implication in the pathogenesis of diabetes. In pancreatic beta cells, Rab2A regulates the insulin granule biogenesis and maintenance of glucose homeostasis by recruiting the heteromeric PICK1-ICA69 complexes in an activity dependent manner. It would be interesting to further study this as a target for better diagnosis and treatment of diabetes.

16148816.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16148816.value: 世界衛生組織2014年的統計資料顯示, 全球39%(> 19億)的成年人超重, 13%(> 6億)的成年人存在肥胖問題。 肥胖會導致嚴重的疾病, 包括心血管疾病, 第二型糖尿病, 肌肉骨骼疾病, 以及某些類型的癌症等等。 目前迫切需要創新的治療方法來有效治療肥胖患者, 抑制肥胖人群的增長。 在此,我們提出開發一種無需標記的活體成像技術, 為發展治療肥胖的新療法提供獨特的視角。 肥胖的根本原因是能量攝入和消耗之間的慢性失衡。 因此,有效的治療策略是維持體內能量的動態平衡。 白色脂肪組織(WAT)和褐色脂肪組織(BAT)是兩類已知的脂肪組織。 其中, 白色脂肪組織是最大的能量儲存組織, 而褐色脂肪組織可以把食物中的能量轉化為熱能, 這就是產熱過程。 2009年, 在成年人體中發現了保持產熱活性的褐色脂肪組織以及一種叫做「米色脂肪」的新型的消耗能量的組織。 此後,許多研究表明, 褐色脂肪和米色脂肪的熱調節功能可以説明燃燒多餘的卡路里, 這可能為發展對抗肥胖的新療法提供新的思路。 雖然人類的褐色脂肪和米色脂肪已經通過正電子發射斷層掃描(PET)成像技術確定, 但是正電子發射斷層掃描成像的空間解析度較差(>幾個毫米), 這限制了它在細胞水準上的生物過程的研究方面的應用。 在這裡, 我們提出了利用無標記顯微技術對脂肪組織實現亞細胞解析度的成像。 我們的成像技術是基於兩個內源性光信號: 脂質的受激拉曼散射信號以及線粒體輔酶(NADH)的自發螢光信號。 本項目申請人的研究團隊最近開發出了一套集成多種成像技術的非線性光學(NLO)顯微系統, 包含了受激拉曼散射(SRS)和時間分辨的雙光子激發螢光(TPEF)成像技術。 在對活體老鼠的試驗研究階段, 我們證明了利用集成非線性光學成像系統可以實現同時對脂肪組織中的脂滴和線粒體的無標記成像。 其中, 我們可以依據其獨特的形態將白色脂肪組織和褐色脂肪組織有效地區分出來。 在此研究中,我們將在小鼠模型中探索褐色/米色脂肪的形成和啟動過程。 為此, 我們將進一步發展非線性光學顯微鏡系統, 利用受激拉曼散射的後向檢測, 以實現對脂滴的即時活體成像。 利用該技術,我們將有機會直接通過成像手段觀察活體小鼠的脂肪組織在各種具有治療潛力的生化和物理刺激下的應激反應。利用受激拉曼散射的後向探測技術, 我們可以研究米色脂肪細胞形成過程中脂滴的形態變化, 以及褐色/米色脂肪組織在產熱過程中脂滴形態的改變。 另一方面, 由於米色脂肪細胞形成過程中會新產生大量的線粒體, 我們可以利用NADH自發螢光成像將具有較高線粒體密度的米色脂肪細胞從周圍的白色脂肪細胞中區分出來。 更重要的是, 褐色/米色脂肪細胞中NADH 自發螢光的壽命變化可以揭示它們對各種產熱刺激的反應。 我們的成像技術可以對褐色/米色脂肪組織的形成和啟動過程實施連續,即時和長期的監測。 這項技術如果研究成功, 將可能有助於解決和褐色/米色脂肪的功能和治療潛力有關的重要的生物學問題。

16148816.label: Realisation of objectives
16148816.value: The objectives of the proposed research have been fully realized. Objective-1: “To developed an integrated epi-detection stimulated Raman scattering and time-resolved two-photon excited fluorescence imaging system” As proposed, we develop technologies to investigate the metabolic characteristics of different types of adipocytes in mice during adrenergically stimulated thermogenesis in vivo. First, the rise in temperature of the adipose tissue, revealed through thermal imaging, confirms that intensive thermogenesis is successfully activated by norepinephrine (NE) treatment. Next, we built a multimodal nonlinear optical (NLO) microscope system and conducted high-resolution functional imaging of fat tissues and characterize the redox states of brown and white adipocytes on live mice. Moreover, we developed a fiber-based spectroscopy technology to measure the thermogenic dynamics in deep adipose tissues. Detailed work are described as follows: An infrared camera was used for the in vivo thermal imaging of adipose tissues of mice. After surgical removal of skin, the anesthetized mice were placed dorsalor ventral-side-up onto a cage for thermal imaging of BAT and WAT, respectively. The mice were injected with NE (1 μg/g of body weight) or saline with a single-use intravenous infusion needle. The intravenous infusion needle was embedded intraperitoneally prior to thermal imaging, so that the injection process would not disturb the thermal imaging procedure. After imaging, the thermal images were analyzed using Altair (FLIR Systems) to obtain the time-lapse temperature curves of the adipose tissues. Regions of interest (ROI) were selected in the interscapular or inguinal region of each mouse. The average temperature in the ROI of each thermal image was calculated to plot the temperature profile. The multimodal NLO microscope system integrated twophoton excited fluorescence (TPEF) and stimulated Raman scattering (SRS) imaging modalities. Briefly, for SRS imaging, a pump-laser-integrated optical parametric oscillator system (picoEmerald S; APE, Berlin, Germany) was used as the light source. The Stokes beam (1031 nm, 2.1 picoseconds, 80-MHz repetition rate) was modulated at 20 MHz and the pump beam (1.9 picoseconds, 80-MHz repetition rate) was tunable from 780 to 960 nm to sweep the SRS spectra. For the SRS imaging of lipid droplets in adipocytes, the differential wavenumber of the pump-Stokes beams was 2863 cm−1, matching the CH2 stretching vibrational frequency of lipids [30]. A water immersion objective was used to focus the pump-Stokes beams onto the sample. The backscattered polarization-scrambled SRS signal was collected by the same laser-focusing objective and reflected onto a photodiode through a polarizing beam splitter (PBS). A filter set was used in front of the photodiode to block the Stokes beam and transmit the pump beam. A high-frequency lock-in amplifier was used to demodulate the SRS signal. The output of the lock-in amplifier was imported into an acquisition card to reconstruct the SRS image. In the TPEF imaging modality, a femtosecond Ti:sapphire laser with a pulse duration of 140 femtoseconds was tuned at 740 nm to excite individual NADH fluorescence, or 810 nm to excite the NADH and FAD signals simultaneously. The femtosecond laser was changed from p-polarization to s-polarization with a halfwave plate and combined with picosecond lasers through a PBS. The backward TPEF signal was collected by the objective and reflected onto a fluorescence detection system by a dichroic mirror. In the fluorescence detection system, a spectrograph equipped with a linear array of 16 Photomultiplier tubes (PMTs) was used to record NADH and FAD signals simultaneously. The spectrograph detected light of wavelength ranged from 403 to 598 nm with 13 nm resolution. A pair of galvanometer scanners was used to scan the laser beams to generate SRS and TPEF images. The laser powers used for SRS imaging were 20 and 40 mW for pump and Stokes lasers, respectively. For the TPEF imaging, the power of the femtosecond laser was 15 mW. A 405-nm picosecond diode laser was used to simultaneously excite the NADH and FAD fluorescence from adipose tissues. A multioptical-fiber catheter was used to deliver laser light and collect the fluorescence signal. The excitation laser was delivered through the central fiber and the fluorescence signal was collected through the 6 fibers surrounding the central fiber. The emitted fluorescence signal was directed through the 6 collector fibers into a spectrograph equipped with a linear array of 16 PMTs. TPEF signals ranged 420 to 615 nm were recorded in 16 consecutive spectral bands at a 13-nm resolution. In this study, the power of the 405-nm laser on the tissue surface was 10 μW and the integration time used for the acquisition of the autofluorescence signal was set as 4 seconds. Objective-2: “To study the changes in morphological features and biochemical characteristics during the transformation of WAT to beige cells for understanding of WAT browning process” We first developed a unique label-free method to quantitatively assess the metabolism and thermogenesis of mouse adipose tissues in vivo. Specifically, an optical redox ratio (ORR) based on the endogenous fluorescence of mitochondrial metabolic coenzymes (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide and flavin adenine dinucleotide) was used to measure the metabolic state of adipocytes. Our findings demonstrate that the ORR provides a label-free and real-time biomarker to determine the thermogenic response of brown, beige and white adipose tissues to a variety of physiological stimulations. In addition, the redox ratio also can be used to evaluate the degree of browning in the white fat of cold-acclimated mice. This technique is important to understand the recruitment and activation of thermogenic adipocytes in mammals and thus can help to develop therapeutic strategies against obesity. Next, we investigated the metabolic characteristics of adipose tissues in live mouse model using a multiphoton redox ratio and fluorescence lifetime imaging technology. By analyzing the intrinsic fluorescence of metabolic coenzymes, we measured the optical redox ratios of adipocytes in vivo and studied their responses to thermogenesis. The fluorescence lifetime imaging further revealed changes in protein bindings of metabolic coenzymes in the adipocytes during thermogenesis. Our study uncovered significant heterogeneity in the cellular structures and metabolic characteristics of thermogenic adipocytes in brown and beige fat. Subgroups of brown and beige adipocytes were identified based on the distinct lipid size distributions, redox ratios, fluorescence lifetimes and thermogenic capacities. The results of our study show that this label-free imaging technique can shed new light on in vivo study of metabolic dynamics and heterogeneity of adipose tissues in live organisms.

16148816.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16148816.value: The statistics of World Health Organization in 2014 showed that 39% of adults (> 1.9 billion) were overweight and 13% (> 600 million) were obese worldwide. Obesity causes an array of severe diseases, including cardiovascular diseases, type 2 diabetes, musculoskeletal disorders, certain types of cancers. Innovative therapeutic approaches are urgently needed to effectively treat the obese patients and restrain the epidemic. In this proposed research, we have developed label-free and in vivo imaging technology that could provide a window for continuous, real-time and long-term monitoring of adipose tissue. The results demonstrated that the innovate technologies developed in this research project will potentially help to understand the biological processes controlling the activities and differentiation of brown/beige adipocytes and to design brown/beige fat based strategies to fight against obesity via rebalancing the energy homeostasis.

16148816.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16148816.value: Fat tissue dysfunction is a key factor in the development of obesity-related chronic diseases, such as diabetes mellitus type 2 and cardiovascular diseases. There are 2 major types of fat tissues in mammals with diametrically opposing functions: white adipose tissue (WAT) and brown adipose tissue (BAT). WAT stores the excess energy in the form of triacylglycerol to regulate energy homeostasis, while BAT dissipates energy as heat via thermogenesis. The recruitment and activation of these human BAT may therefore constitute new approaches to increasing whole-body energy expenditure and thus developing novel therapies against obesity. In this study, we developed a unique label-free method to quantitatively assess the metabolism and thermogenesis of WAT/BAT in vivo. Our study uncovered significant heterogeneity in the cellular structures and metabolic characteristics of BAT. Subgroups of fat cells in BAT were identified based on their unique biochemical and biophysical characteristics. Our findings demonstrate that our technology provides a label-free and real-time biomarker to determine the thermogenic response of WAT/BAT to a variety of physiological stimulations, which is important to understand the recruitment and activation of BAT in mammals and thus can help to develop therapeutic strategies against obesity.

16149316.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16149316.value: Damage to axons in the CNS typically results in permanent functional deficits. Boosting intrinsic programs such as mTOR signaling can dramatically augment the axon regenerative capacity of injured neurons. Because certain types of neurons respond to axotomy by maintaining their mTOR activation, we hypothesized that it might be helpful to utilize this property to promote axon regeneration. We found that the light-responsive GPCR melanopsin could promote axonal regeneration after optic nerve crush by activating mTOR. We also showed that light, Gq/11 signaling, and neuronal activity contribute to the mechanism that underlies this effect. Activating Gq signaling through a pharmacogenetic approach promoted axon regeneration. The overall goal of this proposal is to examine whether modulating melanopsin/GPCR signaling can promote corticospinal tract sprouting and regeneration, and develop strategies to further enhance functional recovery after spinal cord injury. 中樞神經系統軸突損傷後通常會導致永久性的功能障礙。提高受損神經元mTOR信號通路可顯著增強軸突再生能力。利用某些類型的神經元在損傷後維持mTOR活性的特點， 我們發現，光感應蛋白可以通過提高神經元的興奮性來激活mTOR，并促進損傷後的視神經再生。本項研究的目標是檢驗通過此方法提高神經元的興奮性是否可以促進皮質脊髓束的發芽和再生，以進一步提高脊髓損傷後的功能恢復。

16149316.label: Realisation of objectives
16149316.value: Injuries to the adult mammalian CNS often result in permanent functional deficits. Severed axons cannot regenerate to restore lost functions. Failure of axonal regeneration is mainly attributed to the diminished growth capacity of neurons as well as an inhibitory environment. Retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) have been used to study the intrinsic mechanisms that hinder axonal regeneration. Modulating several molecular pathways including Pten/mTOR, KLF family, Socs3/Stat3, Raf/MEK has recently been shown to promote axonal regeneration after optic nerve crush. Furthermore, similar strategies can also enhance corticospinal tract regrowth after injury, pointing to the therapeutic potential through manipulating the intrinsic mechanisms. One of the critical determinants of the intrinsic regenerative ability of mature neurons in the adult CNS is neuronal mTOR activity. Pten deletion activates PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling and promotes axonal regeneration, including corticospinal tract after severe spinal cord injury. To develop a non-genetic method, adeno-associated viruses (AAVs) expressing Pten small hairpin RNA (shRNA) have been delivered into the cortex to elicit a growth-enhancing effect, and even promoted functional recovery when a combination strategy was used. However, directly targeting Pten, a tumor suppressor, raises safety concerns and may not be the ideal strategy to develop translational approaches. Manipulating mTOR signaling in a controllable and effective manner to enhance axonal regeneration therefore remains as a possibility and also a challenge. During development, neuronal activity is essential for axon growth and wiring. In adult animal, neuronal activity has been shown to regulate S6 phosphorylation (pS6), an indicator of mTOR activation, and different activity-related stimuli may induce pS6 expression with varying efficiency and kinetics and for varying durations. We then asked whether modulating neuronal activity could enhance mTOR activation and even axon regeneration. In vitro, postnatal RGCs respond to growth factors by elongating axons following depolarization. In adults, electrical stimulation has been shown to promote the regeneration of crushed optic nerves over short distances. Optogenetic stimulation enhances axon regeneration in worms after laser axotomy by regulating localized calcium release. We found that the light-responsive GPCR melanopsin could promote axonal regeneration after optic nerve crush by activating mTOR. We also showed that light, Gq/11 signaling, and neuronal activity contribute to the mechanism that underlies this effect. Activating Gq signaling through a pharmacogenetic approach promoted axon regeneration. In this proposal, we aim to test whether modulating neuronal activity through either the optogenetic and or the chemogenetic approach can promote mTOR activation and axon regrowth in corticospinal motor neurons. We assessed the effects in the corticospinal tract sprouting and whether it can further enhance functional recovery after pyramidotomy. Melanopsin overexpression can induce regeneration in the optic nerve. In addition, when injected into the cortex of neonatal mice, AAV-melanopsin promotes the sprouting of CST axons after pyramidotomy. However, whether the injury-induced down-regulation of the growth capacity can be reversed in adult CSMNs by enhancing neuronal activity is unknown. We then took a chemogenetic approach to activate Gq signaling by overexpressing DREADD-Gq (designer receptor exclusively activated by a designer drug), which is widely adopted as a tool to enhance neuronal activity. We injected AAV-DREADD/control into the cortex of neonatal mice. After 6 weeks, we performed a unilateral pyramidotomy, and examined the sprouting of intact CST axons into the denervated side of the cervical spinal cord. We analyzed the distribution of labeled axons in the spinal cord 4 wk after the pyramidotomy. Compared with the limited sprouting of adult CST axons in controls, AAV-DREADD injection elicited more trans-midline sprouting of CST axons from the intact side of the spinal cord into the denervated side. Daily CNO administration could not only boost neuronal activity in the cortex but also pS6. Gq can also further enhance the effect of Pten deletion on the CST sprouting in the pyramidotomy model. Then, we investigated whether the chemogenetic approach can be used to enhance functional recovery after pyramidotomy. Adult WT mice were injected with AAV-GFP or AAV-DREADD-Gq into the cortex. Four weeks later, they were trained to perform the food grasp test. Then we did unilateral pyramidotomy. All mice were given CNO and underwent daily training for the food grasping. We recorded one day per week as a data point for quantification up to 8 weeks. Then, BDA were injected into the cortex to trace CST axons. Two weeks later, mice were sacrificed for histology. Although a transient improvement trend was detected, CNO activation on DREADD-Gq did not significantly improve functional recovery when compared with control mice. Our interpretation is that the sprouting may not be robust enough to be reflected by the functional assay. In addition, daily training itself could be a neuronal activity modulator that might shadow the effect of Gq.

16149316.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16149316.value: Our finding that neuronal activity can promote axon regeneration and sprouting in at least two different types of CNS neurons is quite interesting. It may imply that non-invasive strategy to stimulate neuronal activity could lead to a therapeutic strategy with safety. It may also expand our understanding on the potential mechanisms of some of the clinical improvement based on the rehabilitation training, which can stimulate neuronal activity.

16149316.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16149316.value: Central nervous system neurons do not regenerate their axons after injury. We found that the axon regenerative capacity could be boosted with the right stimulants on neuronal activity through either an optogenetic or a chemogenetic approach. The the light-responsive GPCR melanopsin could promote axonal regeneration after optic nerve crush by activating mTOR. We also showed that light, Gq/11 signaling, and neuronal activity contribute to the mechanism that underlies this effect. Activating Gq signaling through a pharmacogenetic approach promoted the corticospinal tract sprouting. The findings may potentially lead to the development of clinically useful methods to facilitate neural repair.

16149516.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16149516.value: Class I myosins (Myo1s) were the first unconventional myosins identified. Among the total of 24 unconventional myosins encoded in the human genome, eight of them are Myo1 (Myo1a to Myo1h). The class I myosins are widely expressed among eukaryotic cells and have very diverse physiological functions including hearing, vision, nutrient absorption, body fluid filtration, etc. Not surprisingly, mutations of myosins are frequently associated with different hereditary human diseases such as hereditary deafness. In contrast to the dimeric myosins (e.g. myosin V) that are capable of transporting cargos efficiently along actin filaments, Myo1s exist as monomers and can function as force or tension sensors and in some cases as slow transporters. Since their motor heads are highly homologous to each other, the diverse cellular functions of Myo1s are largely attributed to the distinct tail cargo binding region of the motors. However, very little is known regarding the molecular basis governing specific cargo recognitions by any one of Myo1s, at least partly due to the lack of clearly investigated protein targets of the motors. In this proposal, we will use Myo1c as a representative member of the Myo1 family to investigate its cargo recognition mechanisms. The proposal builds on our recent structural and biochemical characterizations of the entire Myo1C tail (Lu et al (2015), NSMB), showing that the motor tail adopts a rigid conformation ideally suited for function as a mechano-force coupling “device”. In this proposal, we plan to investigate whether the Ca2+-dependent regulation of the conformational rigidity observed in Myo1c is a conserved property for other Myo1s as well. We will also investigate possible structural alterations and functional consequences of several Myo1c mutations found in patients suffering from hearing impairments. To better understand cellular functions of Myo1c, we plan to biochemically and structurally characterize the interactions and regulations of Myo1c binding targets identified by our various targeted affinity purifications coupled with mass spectrometry approaches. If successfully executed, this proposed research will uncover the mechanistic basis governing cargo recognition and regulation by Myo1c specifically, as well as by other Myo1 members in general. 16149516.label: Major findings and research outcome
16149516.value: Unconventional myosins are a superfamily of actin-based molecular motors playing diverse roles including cellular trafficking, mechanical supports, force sensing and transmission, etc. The variable neck and tail domains of unconventional myosins function to bind to specific cargoes including proteins and lipid vesicles and thus are largely responsible for the diverse cellular functions of myosins in vivo. In addition, the tail regions, together with their cognate cargoes, can regulate activities of the motor heads. In this project, we have systematically studied cargo recognitions and cargo-mediated molecular assemblies of unconventional myosins using the Myo1 sub-family and Myo1-related myosins as examples. One line of the study that are particular proud is the organization of unconventional myosins in microvilli structures in various tissues including intestine, kidney, and eyes in animals. These tissue are all enriched with Myo1, but a number of other myosins (e.g. Myo7 and Myo3) are also critically required. We have established that the organization of microvilli structures require a set of Myo7b/Ush1c/Anks4b complex (Li et al, (2016) Dev Cell). We elucidated the structural basis of the assembly of the Myo7b/Ush1c/Anks4b complex (Li et al, (2017) PNAS, see Part C). We showed that the Myo7b/Ush1c/Anks4b complex forms condensed molecular assemblies via phase separation thereby forming stable structural bases for the microvilli tip-links (He et al (2019) Cell Rep, see Part C). This line of our work has made conceptual contributions to the unconventional myosin-organized and mechanosensitive apparatuses such as microvilli and stereocilia in animals including humans. Our work has also explained numerous mutations on unconventional myosins that can cause diseases including digestive diseases, blind and deafness. We have also studied the mechanism of lever arm length and structural stability regulation by binding of calmodulin to myosin IQ-motifs of the Myo7 sub-family unconventional myosins (Li et al, (2017) Structure). This is an extension to what we have described for the calmodulin-regulated conformational changes and force-sensing mechanism of Myo1c (Lu et al. (2015) Nat Struct Mol Biol), the foundation work leading to this project.

16149516.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16149516.value: Unconventional myosins are very divergent in the regions outside their motor domains and correspondingly play extremely diverse cellular functions. Not surprisingly, numerous human diseases are caused or related to malfunctions of unconventional myosins. Despite numerous advances made in the past decades of research, many outstanding questions remain to be answered. First of all, although auto-inhibition has been observed for several myosins and is regarded as a general property for the majority, if not all, of myosins, the lack of atomic-resolution structure of any of the auto-inhibited myosins has prevented us from detailed understanding of their auto-inhibitions and corresponding activation mechanisms. Moreover, regulations of cargo loading/unloading of myosins have always been fascinating questions, as myosin-mediated cellular trafficking and other events should be precisely controlled processes in living organisms. Again very little is known in this regard. Elucidating such regulatory mechanisms are important for understanding cellular functions of unconventional myosins. These are just a few directions for future studies. I am confident that Drs. Lu and Li will advance these and other new aspects of unconventional myosin research in their independent labs.

16149516.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16149516.value: Sensing mechanoforces is incredibly important for well beings of animals including humans. For example, we sense sounds by detecting vibrations of sound waves via stereocillia in our ears. Our intestine sense flow of foods in our digestive systems by microvilli. Both stereocillia and microvilli are actin filament-based molecular assemblies and their force sensing critically depends on a class of motor proteins called unconventional myosins. In this project we have elucidated how intestines microvilli are linked together to form the brush boarder structure by unconventional myosins in concert with their binding proteins. We uncovered that the myosin assembled complexes can form highly dense molecular condensates via a process called phase separation. The formed myosin-containing condensed structure can stabilized the microvilli and stereocilia assemblies with an action the mechanism in a way analogous to the roots of trees. Importantly, our research reveals that mutations of myosins destabilizing such condensed assembly can cause diseases including digestive disorders, deafness and blind in humans.

16149616.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16149616.value: Hippocampal synaptic plasticity is essential for learning and memory; its disruption impairs hippocampal function, contributing to cognitive dysfunctions in Alzheimer’s disease (AD). We previously found that blockade of the activity of the receptor tyrosine kinase EphA4 alleviates synaptic plasticity impairment in an AD mouse model, demonstrating that EphA4 overactivation is critical for mediating the hippocampal synaptic plasticity impairment in AD. However, the spatiotemporal regulation of EphA4 activity during AD progression remains unclear. The proposed study will continue to examine the molecular and cellular mechanisms underlying the pathological role of EphA4 in AD progression. We will identify and examine the upstream signaling that stimulates EphA4 activity during AD progression. Specifically, we will study the causative role of astrocyte–neuron communication in EphA4 overactivation in AD. Furthermore, we will examine the regulation of EphA4 activity in different hippocampal regions in an AD mouse model, using both EphA4 activity imaging and biochemical methodology. Finally, we will validate the in vivo role of EphA4 in mediating network and cognitive functions in an AD mouse model. We will elucidate the functions of EphA4 in AD in vivo by examining network excitability and memory performance after region-specific deletion of EphA4. The findings of the proposed study will increase our understanding of the molecular basis of EphA4 overactivation during AD pathogenesis and may expand possibilities of AD treatment through the specific manipulation of EphA4.

16149616.label: Realisation of objectives
16149616.value: The project objectives have been fully met. Below is a summary of the key findings. Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a major type of dementia and is highly prevalent among aged people. Patients with AD exhibit memory loss and other cognitive dysfunctions. AD is a multifactorial disease, but its precise pathophysiological mechanisms remain unclear. Soluble oligomeric amyloid-beta (Aβ) peptide is believed to be a synaptotoxin that mediates the dysfunction and loss of hippocampal synapses, which lead to the impairment of neurotransmission and neuronal activity. Moreover, the modulation of the homeostasis of intercellular signaling within neurons can contribute to Aβ-mediated synaptic deficits. Notably, the receptor tyrosine kinase EphA4 is prominently expressed in hippocampal excitatory neurons and plays critical roles in the regulation of homeostatic synaptic plasticity. We previously found that Aβ triggers aberrant activation of EphA4 during AD progression (Fu et al., 2014), which contributes to the hippocampal synaptic impairment in AD. Furthermore, in AD transgenic mouse models, blockade of EphA4 activity by inhibitors or RNAi approaches rescues hippocampal synaptic impairment. Accordingly, these findings prompted us to conduct the current project and further examine how Aβ modulates EphA4 activity and how the activation of EphA4 signaling contributes to the pathogenesis of AD. As such, we first examined the cellular expression of EphA4 expression in AD by performing single-nucleus transcriptome analysis of the hippocampi of APP/PS1 mice, an AD transgenic mouse model. We found that APP/PS1 mice exhibit aberrant induction of EphA4 in various neural cell types including excitatory neurons, astrocytes, and endothelial cells (Wang et al., in preparation). Single-nucleus transcriptome analysis also showed that Epha4 transcription is aberrantly induced in endothelial cells in the prefrontal cortices of patients with AD (Lau et al., 2020). To determine how such dysregulated EphA4 activation is associated with the progression of amyloid pathology, we also utilized RNAscope (an in situ hybridization technique) to characterize Epha4 transcript expression in the hippocampi of APP/PS1 mice at 6 and 12 months of age, which correspond to the initial occurrence and severe accumulation of amyloid plaques, respectively. Consistent with previous findings, Epha4 transcript was prominently expressed in the pyramidal neurons in both the CA1 and CA3 regions of the hippocampus in wild-type (WT) mice at both 6 and 12 months of age; there was no significant difference in Epha4 transcript levels between these stages. Meanwhile, compared to that in WT mice, Epha4 transcript level was higher in the CA1 region in APP/PS1 mice at 12 months but not at 6 months. Interestingly, the Epha4 transcript level in CA3 pyramidal neurons did not change during AD progression (Wang et al., in preparation). We also detected very low Epha4 transcript levels in hippocampal astrocytes in WT mice. However, there was significant induction of EphA4 transcript expression in astrocytes specifically in the stratum radiatum within the CA1 region. Notably, these astrocytes were closely associated with amyloid plaques. Thus, our results show that EphA4 expression is specifically induced in CA1 pyramidal neurons and astrocytes in APP/PS1 mice, suggesting that aberrant expression of EphA4 in AD progression is region specific and may be associated with aberrant neuronal activity and amyloid plaque accumulation. Given that the initial increase of Aβ in AD is due to aberrant neuronal activity and the dysfunction of extracellular glutamate clearance at synapses, we subsequently examined whether extrasynaptic glutamate accumulation is associated with Aβ-mediated EphA4 hyperactivation. Accordingly, treatment of mouse acute hippocampal slices with soluble oligomeric Aβ dramatically induced EphA4 tyrosine phosphorylation. However, pretreating the hippocampal slices with glutamate scavengers (i.e., oxaloacetate and pyruvate), which facilitate the clearance of extracellular glutamate, significantly reduced the Aβ-induced tyrosine phosphorylation of EphA4. These results suggest that glutamate mediates the observed Aβ-triggered EphA4 activation (Wang et al., in preparation). The aberrant expression of EphA4 in amyloid plaque-associated astrocytes in AD-afflicted brains suggests that EphA4 signaling might not only impact synaptic functions. Therefore, to further explore the pathological roles of dysregulated EphA4 signaling in AD pathogenesis, we examined the amyloid pathology in 12-month-old APP/PS1 mice using the EphA4 inhibitors KYL and a Traditional Chinese medicine small molecule rhynchophylline (Rhy), which both bind the ligand-binding domain of EphA4 receptors. Administration of Rhy or KYL for 3–4 weeks significantly reduced the Aβ content and area of amyloid plaque deposition in both the cortex and hippocampus in APP/PS1 mice (Fu et al., in preparation; Wang et al., in preparation). Furthermore, in APP/PS1 mice, the extent to which microglia surrounded amyloid plaques was associated with amyloid plaque deposition, while Rhy or KYL administration significantly reduced microgliosis, activation of the microglia (Fu et al., in preparation; Wang et al., in preparation). These results collectively show that blockade of EphA4 signaling not only reverses synaptic impairment but also reduces amyloid pathology and ameliorates the neuroinflammation in AD mouse models. We subsequently explored the mechanisms by which EphA4 signaling ameliorates AD pathology. As such, we performed a microarray analysis on the cerebral cortices of Rhy-treated APP/PS1 mice. Transcriptome analysis identified a set of genes whose expression was higher in APP/PS1 mice than WT mice. Meanwhile, Rhy administration reverted the elevated expression of these genes in APP/PS1 mice to levels similar to those in WT mice. Gene Ontology analysis of this gene cluster identified numerous genes with biological functions related to immune and neuroinflammation responses (e.g., Spp1, Mef2b, Itgax, and Gpnmb). These results suggest that EphA4 signaling is involved in the regulation of the neuroinflammatory responses of neural cells and helps ameliorate amyloid pathology and repair synaptic deficits (Fu et al., in preparation). To further understand the underlying mechanisms whereby EphA4 signaling in hippocampal excitatory neurons causes synaptic deficits, we administered another EphA4 inhibitor, KYL, to APP/PS1 mice for 4 weeks. Thereafter, we collected the hippocampi and subjected them single-nucleus RNA sequencing analysis. We performed unbiased uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) clustering to cluster different neural cell types. We subsequently categorized the hippocampal excitatory neurons according to specific markers (e.g., CAMK2A). We first determined the differential transcriptomic profiles in hippocampal excitatory neurons by comparing the transcriptomes between the WT and APP/PS1 mice. Accordingly, 19 and 59 genes were upregulated and downregulated, respectively, in hippocampal excitatory neurons in APP/PS1 mice compared to those in WT mice. Furthermore, in APP/PS1 mice, KYL administration reverted the expression of some of these differentially regulated genes. Most of these differentially regulated genes are involved in the regulation of dendritic spine development (e.g., Camk2d and Lrrc4c), the regulation of synapse assembly (e.g., Lrrtm3 and Mef2c), or the regulation of glutamatergic synaptic transmission (e.g., Gria4 and Tshz3) (Wang et al., in preparation). Concordant with our previous findings, these results suggest that EphA4 signaling regulates hippocampal synaptic functions by modulating multiple processes including synapse maintenance and synaptic plasticity.

16149616.label: Major findings and research outcome
16149616.value: This study aimed to understand the mechanisms whereby Aβ modulates EphA4 activity and how the activation of EphA4 signaling contributes to AD pathogenesis. Our major findings and research outcomes are as follows: • Aberrant EphA4 expression in the hippocampus is confined to the CA1 region and is associated with amyloid pathology: EphA4-positive neurons are prominently expressed in both the hippocampal CA1 and CA3 regions in WT mice, whereas elevated EphA4 expression is only present in the CA1 pyramidal neurons in APP/PS1 mice at the age when severe amyloid plaque deposition occurs (Wang et al., in preparation). This suggests that the aberrant induction of EphA4 is associated with amyloid plaque deposition and is involved in the modulation of the hippocampal CA3–CA1 circuit. Moreover, EphA4 is also aberrantly induced in other neural cell types, such as astrocytes, associated with amyloid plaque deposition (Wang et al., in preparation; Lau et al., 2020). • Extracellular glutamate accumulation is involved in Aβ-mediated EphA4 activation: The administration of glutamate scavengers in hippocampal acute slices attenuates Aβ-mediated EphA4 activation (Wang et al., in preparation). This demonstrates that the failure of glutamate clearance is involved in mediating the Aβ-triggered EphA4 activation. • Blockade of EphA4 signaling ameliorates the amyloid pathology and neuroinflammation in the brain in AD transgenic mice: APP/PS1 mice treated with specific EphA4 inhibitors exhibit reduced severity of amyloid plaques and microgliosis, which are the 2 major pathological features of AD. This suggests that aberrant EphA4 signaling not only impacts synaptic functions but also the inflammatory and immune responses of the brain (Fu et al., in preparation; Wang et al., in preparation). • Determination of the potential mechanisms whereby EphA4 signaling mediates synaptic function impairment: To understand how dysregulated EphA4 signaling is involved in AD pathogenesis, we performed transcriptome analysis of the brains of AD transgenic mouse models treated with different EphA4 inhibitors. Of note, impaired signaling associated with the regulation of synaptic plasticity and immune responses was rescued upon the attenuation of EphA4 signaling in AD mouse models (Fu et al., in preparation; Wang et al., in preparation). In addition, as p39 and α2-chimaerin are the known downstream mediators of EphA4 receptors in neurons, we performed transcriptome analysis of p39-knockout mice and α2-chimaerin–knockout mice (Su et al., 2019; Ouyang et al., 2020). Accordingly, we identified multiple intracellular signaling pathways that participate in adult neurogenesis, dendritic development, synapse development, and synapse maintenance. Thus, these findings further delineate how EphA4 signaling mediates the homeostatic functions of the brain and how its dysregulation contributes to AD pathogenesis.

16149616.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16149616.value: Our current findings demonstrate that aberrant EphA4 signaling is associated with the amyloid pathology in AD. Besides being involved in the attenuation of synaptic functioning, we also corroborated that EphA4 signaling is a critical signaling pathway that mediates the amyloid pathology and immune responses in AD. Moreover, we found that aberrant expression of EphA4 is not only induced in excitatory neurons but also in other neural cells (e.g., astrocytes and endothelial cells) in the hippocampus in AD mice. Therefore, further studies are required to determine the molecular mechanisms of EphA4 signaling in these neural cells. To achieve this, single-nucleus transcriptome analysis of different neural cell types can be performed to delineate how the dysregulated EphA4 signaling in different neural cell types contributes to AD pathogenesis. Moreover, EphA4 expression can be specifically knocked down in different neural cell types in the hippocampus in APP/PS1 mice followed by the characterization of how EphA4 signaling in certain neural cell types contributes to the various pathological changes observed in AD. Taken together, our current findings can help expand our knowledge about the mechanistic roles of dysregulated EphA4 signaling in AD, making EphA4 a potential target for AD therapeutic development.

16149616.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16149616.value: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is the most common type of dementia in the aged population. However, there is no effective treatment for AD owing to its multifactorial nature and incompletely understood pathological mechanisms. Meanwhile, EphA4, a member of the Eph (erythropoietin-producing hepatocellular) family of receptor tyrosine kinases—together with its cognate ligands ephrins—signal bidirectionally to regulate various cellular processes of the central nervous system. Multiple studies show that improper regulation of EphA4 signaling is involved in the development of AD. However, it is unclear how EphA4 is activated in AD or how improper regulation of its signaling contributes to the development of AD. Herein, we demonstrated that the aberrant expression of EphA4 is associated with the occurrence of amyloid-beta (Aβ) pathology and failure of glutamate clearance, which are key characteristics of AD. Further analysis showed that in AD model mice, EphA4 signaling is involved in Aβ pathology and neuronal synaptic deficits by altering immune responses and synaptic stability. Taken together, our findings support that EphA4 signaling is one of the major mechanisms underlying the development of AD and suggest that EphA4 signaling is a potential treatment target for AD.
