16234816.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16234816.value: Wind is fast becoming a popular source of renewable energy. Nowadays significant investments are being made in wind turbine technology. Unfortunately, the large rotating wind turbines typically used to produce electrical power from wind are usually vulnerable to fatigue and must withstand many load cycles during their design life. Operational experience indicates that the major components of wind turbines experience many more fatigue cycles than other rotating machines. Therefore, long-term fatigue monitoring is urgently needed and has become a high-priority research area in the wind turbine research community. The goal of this proposal is to develop a wireless sensor monitoring system for automated and reliable assessment of the fatigue damage of typical wind turbines. In this project, reliable and efficient algorithms for fatigue damage assessment of wind turbines will be developed using output-only vibration measurements (e.g., strains, accelerations, etc.) collected from a wireless sensor system. A comprehensive probabilistic framework will be developed to quantify the uncertainties of the fatigue damage accumulation and to predict the residual life as well as the failure probability of critical components. Fast and reliable computing techniques will be developed to drastically reduce the computational demands of the proposed algorithms. Since stress responses are often quite irregular due to varying environmental conditions, fatigue damage accumulation and failure probability will be updated from time to time by employing dynamic response data collected continually from strategic structural locations to reflect the real-time operational conditions. The hardware of the system will be comprised of wireless sensing units, which combine sensing, computing and communication capabilities. Power supply is one of the major considerations in the design of wireless sensor networks. Energy harvesting devices will be specially designed to enable an appealing self-powered system. This project will provide an off-the-shelf solution for governments or other agencies owning a large stock of wind turbines to implement condition-based (as opposed to time-based) maintenance.

16234816.label: Realisation of objectives
16234816.value: With regard to the first objective, popular variants of the Kalman Filter (KF) have been used for updating and calibrating dynamical models and making predictions of local strains in wind turbine structures. However, we observed that the quality of strain predictions heavily relies on the parameters of filtering processes, e.g., the parameters of process and measurement noise covariance matrices. In the literature, these parameters are presumed using practical rules of thumb. Nevertheless, they are also unknown quantities that should be calibrated based on the data. Seeing that these parameters are not optimal in any sense, the estimations obtained by the filtering techniques turn out to be suboptimal, if not inaccurate. As presented in Journal paper #2 and Conference paper #4, we have developed a novel sequential Bayesian approach that acts as an effective remedy and updates the noise covariance matrices adaptively. It is shown that this method delivers more accurate and reliable estimates of the dynamical responses and input forces when compared to the other filtering techniques. This method has improved the stability and accuracy of strain predictions through the real-time identification of noise parameters (Conference paper #6). In connection with the first objective, the estimation of local strain time-histories at unmeasured locations has been realized by developing probabilistic system identification and response prediction methodologies. Specifically, Hierarchical Bayesian Modeling (HBM) framework has been developed by the PI’s team, which allows for calibrating the dynamical characteristics of Finite Element (FE) models (Journal papers #1 and #4; Conference papers #1-3). It has been demonstrated that the HBM accurately estimates the unknown parameters while providing reasonable and realistic uncertainty bounds and offering extensive improvements over classical Bayesian tools. This framework also attains reliable predictions of unmeasured dynamical responses and their uncertainties, as documented in Journal papers #1 and #4. Since the modal properties of structures are crucial for response predictions, we have further developed the HBM for inferring modal properties from vibration response-only measurements (Journal paper #5; Conference paper #4). Along the same line of research, we have conducted a theoretical investigation into identifying modal parameters from multi-setup sensor configurations, which provides insights as to how different factors, such as the data length and frequency bandwidth play out (Journal paper #3). In realization of the second objective, we have formulated the optimal sensor placement based on the steady-state solution of the filtering techniques. The methodology and applications exist in the MPhil thesis of Mr. Ka Kin Lau, who was trained and graduated under the PI’s supervision. We have seen that the collocated placement of acceleration sensors with unknown input forces will lead to superior accuracy and stability compared to other sensor configurations. We have also shown that the quality of response predictions in the absence of input forces heavily relies on the types of sensor devices. We have demonstrated that the quality of input and response reconstruction can adversely be affected by fictitious low-frequency drifts when only acceleration responses are used. This challenging problem is resolved through a new Bayesian approach presented in Journal paper #2, where we have imposed a priori constraint on the temporal variation of input forces, which mitigates fictitious low-frequency noise effects up to a great extent and offers accurate estimates of dynamical responses and input forces. We have theoretically investigated this problem to dig up a deeper understanding of the problem, and as a result, we have realized that it is rooted in the ill-posedness of the joint transfer matrix of the process and observation models (Journal paper #7). Thus, in our works, this significant issue is addressed by including input pseudo-observations, which stabilize low-frequency components of input and response predictions and mitigate low-frequency drifts considerably (Journal paper #7; Conference paper #7). With regard to the 2nd and 3rd objectives, a novel approach to fatigue damage monitoring has been developed by the PI’s team (Journal paper #6; Conference paper #6). This approach adopts the joint input-state estimation and virtual sensing tools to provide predictions of the strain and stress time histories when there is no knowledge of input forces. Then, the stress estimations can feed into multi-axial fatigue damage models to produce contours of fatigue damage accumulation. In this framework, the temporal variation of stress response histories was accounted for through the Rainflow cycle counting method, and the multiaxiality of stress states was incorporated through a critical plane approach associated with the modified Wöhler stress-lifecycles curves. The proposed framework has also been formulated on a reliability foundation in the Ph.D. thesis of our student Mr. Victor Flores Terrazas, which accounts for the uncertainties arising from modeling errors and measurement noise. The framework presented in Journal paper #6 was applied for fatigue damage diagnosis and prognosis in wind turbine structures, aiming to showcase the realization of project objectives and goals. To this end, realistic finite element (FE) models of wind turbine towers have been developed and calibrated based on the benchmark model released by the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL). The number and location of sensors, including strain gauges and accelerometers, were optimized using an entropy-based optimal sensor placement algorithm. The synthetic responses of this structure are employed to test and verify the proposed framework and to calculate equivalent forces at the interface of the superstructure and the tower, as well as local strains and stresses at critical locations of wind turbine towers. The contours of fatigue damage accumulation were produced whereon fatigue-prune positions can be realized (Journal paper #6). These contours provide a data-informed assessment of fatigue damage in the wind turbine, which can aid take preventive and corrective actions throughout the operational life of the structure.

16234816.label: Major findings and research outcome
16234816.value: This project has led to numerous publications in prominent peer-reviewed journals, and its research findings have been presented in top international conferences. It has significantly contributed to the area of vibration-based structural health monitoring, as well as data-driven fatigue diagnosis and prognosis. A list of research achievements and scientific contributions is provided below: 1) Have developed Bayesian filtering techniques for joint input-state estimation and response reconstruction of dynamical responses using sparse output-only measurements (Journal papers #2 and #7) 2) Have reported new insights on the reasons behind the low-frequency drifts appearing in the state and input estimations and have proposed two effective remedies to overcome this problem (Journal papers #2 and #7). 3) Have proposed new methodologies for the calibration of noise parameters in Bayesian filtering techniques (Journal papers #2 and #7) 4) Have developed a streamline fatigue monitoring framework through the integration of system identification and virtual sensing tools with multiaxial fatigue damage models (Journal paper #6) 5) Have proposed the hierarchical Bayesian modeling (HBM) framework for structural identification and response predictions at unmeasured locations (Journal papers #1 and #4). 6) Have developed novel probabilistic methods for the identification of modal parameters from vibration response-only measurements (Journal papers #3 and #5) 7) Have attained theoretical insights as to the propagating properties of operational modal analysis in multi-setup sensor configurations (Journal paper #3)

16234816.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16234816.value: While linear structures have been the subject of recent studies, little has been done on structural identification, virtual sensing, and fatigue monitoring in non-linear dynamical systems. Thus, future research can concentrate on the development of real-time structural identification and virtual sensing tools, particularly for structures where dynamical parameters may vary in real-time. Such a problem would entail the development of new tools for the estimation of joint input-state-parameter estimation in nonlinear systems.

16234816.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16234816.value: Fatigue damage refers to the gradual degradation of material strength due to cyclic loadings. This destructive mode of failure is of great concern for engineers who deal with the maintenance and inspection of structures that perform under cyclic loadings, including wind turbines, bridges, railways, and offshore structures. While traditional monitoring and inspection methods shape the present practice, the need to develop new sensing technologies for fatigue monitoring is felt now more than ever before. In this regard, vibration-based fatigue monitoring has grown to an emerging research direction in structural engineering, which is developed further in this project. We have developed new methodologies to estimate local strain and stress response histories based on a limited number of measurements obtained from an optimized sensor network. Then, these estimations are fed into multiaxial fatigue damage models to produce fatigue damage accumulation contours that visualizes the severity of damage in the entire body of structures throughout their operational life. This data-informed assessment detects fatigue-prune positions and aids direct maintenance activities.

16235616.label: Project Objectives
16235616.value: Holistically modeling MPSoC process variations and analyzing their impacts at system level: We will systematically model process variations in MPSoC power delivery networks, processing units, memories, and NoC with different configurations. We will analyze their effects on the complex temporal and spatial behaviors of MPSoC, and study their impacts on the interactions among power delivery networks, processing units, memories, and NoC. An MPSoC process variation simulation and impact analysis platform will be developed. The platform will model MPSoC along a large number of dimensions, including (i) power delivery network structures, (ii) processing unit types, functions, energy consumptions, and locations, (iii) on-chip memory sizes, energy consumptions, and locations, (iv) NoC topologies, protocols, and floorplans, (v) 2.5D and 3D integration structures of on-chip memories, processing units, and NoC, (vi) on/off-chip voltage regulators, (vii) package structures, (viii) thermal effects on parasitic elements, (ix) through-silicon vias in 2.5D and 3D MPSoC. Establishing adaptive tolerant protocols and corresponding scalable low-cost architectures: We will establish light-weight runtime protocols and develop corresponding low-cost scalable system architectures to adaptively tolerate chip-specific process variations. The adaptive protocols will predict, monitor, report, and mitigate process variation impacts at runtime through efficient hardware-software collaborations. The protocols and architecture will holistically tolerate process variations on MPSoC power delivery networks, processing units, memories, and NoC through their interactions. Developing a static-runtime cooperative task mapping and scheduling scheme: We will develop a two-stage cooperative task scheduling scheme including an offline task scheduling algorithm and a light-weight runtime companion algorithm to adaptively optimize performance and energy efficiency under chip-specific process variation impacts on MPSoC. The first stage will statistically schedule and map tasks based on estimated impact distributions of process variations during product development periods. In the second stage, the static task schedule will be adjusted at runtime based on the exact impacts of process variations detected by sensors and the actual application and MPSoC runtime status. Evaluating the chip-specific holistic process variation tolerant method and system: We will perform rigorous evaluations of the chip-specific holistic method and the scalable low-cost architectures and protocols in multiple embedded application domains. We will compare the chip-specific method with existing methods in terms of yields, performance and energy variation tolerance, and area overheads under different MPSoC usage scenarios.

16235616.value: 多處理器系統的片上（MPSOC）已經成為用於嵌入式系統的一個有吸引力的平台，因為在單個芯片上集成的系統或一個複雜的子系統可以提供更好的性能和能量效率。納米技術使MPSOC集成越來越多的處理單元和存儲器，縮小特徵尺寸和降低電源電壓也使MPSOC越來越易受工藝變化的影響。工藝變化可引起晶體管，互連，以及其它裝置的物理性質的波動。他們往往表現為時序，噪音，並在MPSOC邏輯電路，存儲器和電力輸送網絡能效的問題。他們可能會嚴重降低MPSOC產量和增加成本。傳統工藝變異耐受方法顯著增加MPSOC開發的複雜性，並需要大量的保護開銷。這大大限制MPSOC的可擴展性和靈活性。這個問題的根源在於傳統的方法依賴於對複雜MPSOC芯片特定的工藝變化的運行時動態影響靜態統計模型。該項目旨在開發系統的低成本芯片的具體方法和可擴展的系統架構和協議在運行時自適應容忍工藝變化。該方法將整體通過他們的時間和空間的相互作用容忍MPSOC電力輸送網絡，處理單元，存儲器和網絡芯片上的工藝變化。具體芯片方法預測，監測，報告和自適應減輕通過硬件，軟件合作下可變MPSOC運行狀態工藝變化的影響。

16235616.label: Realisation of objectives
16235616.value: As application complexity and versatility burgeon, multiprocessor system-on-chip (MPSoC) has become an attractive platform for embedded systems, because integrating a system or a complex subsystem on a single chip provides better performance and energy efficiency and lower cost per function. While nanotechnologies enable MPSoC to integrate a growing number of processing units and memories, shrinking feature sizes and lowering power supply voltages also make MPSoC increasingly susceptible to variations in fabrication processes. Process variations can cause large fluctuations in the physical properties of transistors, interconnects, and other devices. They often manifest themselves as timing, noise, and energy efficiency issues in MPSoC logic circuits, memories, and power delivery networks. They can severely lower MPSoC yields and increase costs. Traditional process variation tolerant methods significantly increase MPSoC development complexity and require large protection overheads. This greatly limits the scalability and flexibility of MPSoC. The root of this problem is that traditional methods rely on static statistical models against the runtime dynamic impacts of chip-specific process variations on complex MPSoC. They often utilize tolerance techniques designed for extreme cases. However, extreme cases only account for a small portion of total MPSoC runtime. Furthermore, it has become increasingly difficult to determine the exact scales and distributions of process variations at design time due to the burgeoning complexity of MPSoC and fabrication technologies and broad usage scenarios of embedded systems. These difficulties have eroded the foundation of traditional process variation tolerant methods. We systematically develop a low-cost chip-specific method and scalable system architectures and protocols to adaptively tolerate process variations at runtime. The method can holistically tolerate process variations on MPSoC power delivery networks, processing units, memories, and network-on-chip through their temporal and spatial interactions. The chip-specific method can predict, monitor, report, and adaptively mitigate process variation impacts under variable MPSoC runtime states through hardware-software collaborations. Both industry and academic researchers showed strong interests on the research results. The objectives of the project have been completed. We systematically model process variations in MPSoC power delivery networks, processing units, memories, and NoC with different configurations. We analyze their effects on the complex temporal and spatial behaviors of MPSoC, and study their impacts on the interactions among power delivery networks, processing units, memories, and NoC. We establish light-weight runtime protocols and develop corresponding low-cost scalable system architectures to adaptively tolerate chip-specific process variations. The adaptive protocols can predict, monitor, report, and mitigate process variation impacts at runtime through efficient hardware-software collaborations. The protocols and architecture can holistically tolerate process variations on MPSoC power delivery networks, processing units, memories, and NoC through their interactions. We develop a cooperative task scheduling scheme to adaptively optimize performance and energy efficiency under chip-specific process variation impacts on MPSoC. Results show that the method can tolerate more energy penalty and performance penalty caused by process variations than traditional methods. Additionally, parts of the project are being integrated into JADE heterogeneous multiprocessor design and simulation platform and will be publicly released online as an open-source research and development tools for academic and industrial projects. Several realistic multiprocessor application models developed during the projects are being added to COSMIC multiprocessor benchmark suite and will be publicly released online as an open-source research and development tools for academic and industrial projects.

16235716.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16235716.value: Owing to their reliability and efficiency, gas turbines are widely used for power generation and aircraft propulsion. However, they emit harmful pollutants such as nitrogen oxides (NOx), threatening public health and the environment by contributing to acid rain, respiratory illness, and global warming. To reduce NOx emissions, gas turbine manufacturers are switching to lean premixed combustion, but this tends to cause thermoacoustic oscillations in the combustor. These are pressure oscillations arising from the feedback between heat-release-rate oscillations and acoustic oscillations. If severe, they can increase pollutant emissions, exacerbate thermal and mechanical stresses, reduce flame stability, and even lead to catastrophic structural damage. Currently, both passive and active methods are available to control thermoacoustic oscillations, but most assume a priori that the oscillations are periodic with a dominant frequency and a fixed amplitude. Recent studies, however, have shown that in both simple and industrial thermoacoustic systems, the oscillations are not necessarily periodic but can be quasiperiodic or chaotic, especially when the system is operating near its lean stability limits. In developing the next generation of low-emissions gas turbines, it is therefore essential to have effective methods of controlling thermoacoustic oscillations that are quasiperiodic or chaotic. We propose to investigate whether such aperiodic (i.e. quasiperiodic or chaotic) thermoacoustic oscillations can be controlled by open-loop periodic forcing. We will perform lab-scale experiments on a premixed combustion system that has previously been shown to exhibit a wide range of nonlinear phenomenon, including multiple aperiodic states, bifurcations and routes to chaos. We will acoustically force this system using both sinusoidal and square waveforms, and measure its response via pressure transducers and OH* chemiluminescence. We will analyze the data using nonlinear tools from dynamical systems theory and interpret the findings in a synchronization framework so as to better understand the lock-in boundaries and their bifurcations, particularly those associated with chaos destruction, which our pilot study shows is a promising method of suppressing chaotic oscillations. We will use this forced synchronization database to develop accurate low-order models of the system, and then analyze those models in order to find new ways of weakening quasiperiodic and chaotic oscillations. This study will clarify the complex nonlinear interactions between aperiodic thermoacoustic oscillations and open-loop periodic forcing, and will determine whether the latter can be used to weaken the former. If successful, this concept will be very beneficial for the next generation of low-emissions gas turbines. 得益於其出色的可靠性和效率，燃氣輪機已經被廣泛應用於發電機組和航空發動機中。但是它會在工作過程中排放有害污染物如氮氧化物（NOx）引起酸雨，呼吸系統疾病和導致全球變暖，進而危害公眾健康以及環境狀況。為了減少氮氧化物的排放，燃氣輪機的研發設計者們開始轉向使用一種貧油燃燒技術，但是這種技術的使用會引起燃燒室內熱聲耦合振動問題，即由於熱釋放率和聲振動相互耦合導致的壓強振動。如果嚴重的話，他們反而會增加污染物的排放，加劇設備中熱應力以及機械應力，減弱火焰穩定性，甚至導致災難性後果。盡管主動控制以及被動控制目前都能控制熱聲振動，但是他們大都假設熱聲振動是以某個頻率為主的，週期性的，具有固定振幅的振動類型。然而近些年來研究證明，在簡單的實驗熱聲系統和複雜的工業熱聲系統中，熱聲振動並不一定是週期性的而可能是準週期性的或者混沌的。因此，我們建議對這種非週期性的熱聲振動（例如準週期性的或者混沌的）是否可以使用週期性聲源進行開環控制這一問題進行研究。我們將在一個預混燃燒器上開展實驗室尺度的實驗研究。對於該問題的前期研究發現，系統存在一系列非線性動力學現象，其中包括不同的非週期振動，分岔類型以及通往混沌的路徑。我們計劃使用正弦和方波聲源來對系統進行激勵並且通過壓強傳感器和OH*化學發光法對系統的反應進行測量。我們將使用基於動力學理論的非線性時序分析方法對數據進行分析，同時在同步化的框架下對實驗發現進行解讀以便更好地理解鎖定邊界和其分岔，特別是那些與混沌抑制有關的情況，因為我們的先期的研究表明該方法很有希望被用於抑制混沌振動。為了發現抑制準週期和混沌振動的新方法，我們將使用強制同步的數據庫來開發準確的系統的低維模型並且對其進行分析研究。這一研究將更加清晰地闡釋非週期熱聲振動與週期聲源的開環控制之間的複雜非線性作用。並且將決定後者是否可以被用作減弱這種非週期熱聲振動。如果順利的話，這一概念將在在下一代低排放燃氣輪機中得到應用。

16235716.label: Realisation of objectives
16235716.value: To achieve the project objectives, we built a prototypical thermoacoustic system based on a Rijke tube powered by a conical laminar premixed flame. The system consists of an axisymmetric burner that slides within a cylindrical tubular combustor made of quartz. We conducted lab-scale experiments at atmospheric pressure so as to reduce complexity whilst retaining the essential physics of synchronization. We conducted the experiments over a range of lean equivalence ratios and flow rates so as to produce a variety of nonlinear dynamics. To induce synchronization, we applied open-loop periodic forcing (sinusoidal and square-wave) to the flame base using a loudspeaker. We varied the forcing frequency and amplitude independently using a programmable function generator, and measured the pressure response in the combustor using a set of probe microphones. To measure the heat-release-rate (HRR) response of the flame, we used a photo-multiplier tube and a high-speed digital camera capturing the OH* and CH* chemiluminescence emission. To achieve objective 1, we created periodic, quasiperiodic and chaotic thermoacoustic oscillations by varying (a) the flame position within the combustor, (b) the equivalence ratio and (c) the overall flow rate of the reactants. At each dynamical state of the system (i.e. period-1 limit cycle, quasiperiodicity, and chaos), we applied sinusoidal forcing over a range of frequencies and amplitudes so as to determine the full synchronization map. We then identified the specific bifurcations (e.g. Hopf, Neimark-Sacker, saddle-node) and routes to lock-in/chaos (e.g. period-doubling, Ruelle-Takens-Newhouse, intermittency) with the aid of tools from nonlinear time-series analysis, synchronization theory, and complex systems theory. In this way, we were able to collect and analyze forced synchronization data on a self-excited thermoacoustic system oscillating periodically, quasiperiodically and chaotically. To achieve objective 2, we deployed the two-step control strategy proposed in our pilot study, and found that it can reduce the oscillation amplitude by more than 80%. We also combined the measured pressure data with the HRR data to construct a map of the Rayleigh index so that the exact mechanism of oscillation quenching (Rayleigh driving/damping vs acoustic damping) could be identified. In this way, we were able to demonstrate the validity of the two-step control strategy on both quasiperiodic and chaotic oscillations in a self-excited thermoacoustic system. To achieve objective 3, we repeated the steps described above but with square-wave forcing instead of sinusoidal forcing. The use of square-wave forcing, with its flexible control over the duty cycle, provided an extra degree of freedom in our optimization of the open-loop control laws. We were able to show that, under most conditions, square-wave forcing produces synchronization dynamics similar to sinusoidal forcing. However, under some conditions, square-wave forcing can outperform sinusoidal forcing in reducing the oscillation amplitude of a self-excited thermoacoustic system oscillating quasiperiodically and chaotically. To achieve objective 4, we adopted the universal oscillator framework that has been successfully used in various fields of science and engineering to understand and predict the synchronization dynamics of self-excited systems. We modeled the overall thermoacoustic system (flame and combustor) using variants of the van der Pol oscillator and the Anishchenko-Astakhov oscillator. We calibrated the low-order models using the experimental data collected for objectives 1-3, and then used the models to understand, predict and control the forced synchronization dynamics of the thermoacoustic system. We were able to develop low-order models of a self-excited thermoacoustic system oscillating quasiperiodically and chaotically, subjected to external forcing. To achieve objective 5, we analytically and numerically studied the low-order models developed for objective 4. In particular, we searched for ways to force the periodic, quasiperiodic and chaotic oscillations so that their amplitudes can be reduced and/or their frequencies can be shifted to other, less dangerous, frequencies. We were able to discover new ways of weakening periodic and aperiodic thermoacoustic oscillations using open-loop acoustic forcing, which were validated experimentally.

16235716.label: Major findings and research outcome
16235716.value: Major research achievements: (i) we showed that studying open-loop control from a synchronization perspective can provide valuable insight into the optimal forcing conditions; (ii) we showed that the optimal forcing condition for weakening period-1 thermoacoustic oscillations is that which causes the onset of lock-in via a torus-death bifurcation, as this is where asynchronous quenching occurs; (iii) we showed that the forced synchronization dynamics of real combustors can be modeled with low-order universal oscillators; (iv) we showed that, when forced strongly, a phase-locked thermoacoustic system does not necessarily remain phase locked but can transition to more complex states, such as strange nonchaotic and chaotic attractors; (v) we discovered a new method of weakening thermoacoustic oscillations, one that combines transient forcing with hysteresis and mode switching to avoid the need to continuously supply energy to the control system; (vi) we showed that forced synchronization in a T2 quasiperiodic thermoacoustic system occurs via a more intricate route than that observed in a classic period-1 thermoacoustic system; specifically, three steps are involved: as the forcing amplitude increases at a fixed forcing frequency, the system transitions first to ergodic T3 quasiperiodicity, then to resonant T2 quasiperiodicity as the weaker of the two natural modes synchronizes first, and finally to a period-1 limit cycle as the remaining natural mode also synchronizes; we thus extended the applicability of open-loop control from classic period-1 systems with just a single time scale to ergodic T2 quasiperiodic systems with two incommensurate time scales; (vii) we showed that chaos-destroying synchronization can occur in a chaotic thermoacoustic system subjected to periodic acoustic forcing, and that this phenomenon can be accurately modeled with canonical oscillators, providing inspiration for the development of new strategies to control chaos in self-excited combustion systems. In terms of student training, four PhD students (Yu Guan, Abhijit Kumar Kushwaha, Bo Yin, Manikandan Balasubramaniyan) have participated in this project and other relevant projects. In terms of research output, we have published 9 journal papers, while 2 further papers are currently in preparation. We have also delivered 9 presentations at international conferences, including The 70th, 71st and 72nd Annual Meetings of the APS Division of Fluid Dynamics (USA), The 12th Asia-Pacific Conference on Combustion (Japan), and The 24th International Congress on Sound and Vibration (UK).

16235716.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16235716.value: In the future, the synchronization-based control strategies identified in this project can be combined with state-of-the-art machine learning algorithms to create a new framework for controlling complex nonlinear oscillations in self-excited flow systems.

16235716.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16235716.value: Gas turbines are routinely used for power generation and aircraft propulsion. However, they emit nitrogen oxides (NOx), threatening public health and the environment. To reduce NOx emissions, lean premixed combustion can be deployed, but this tends to provoke thermoacoustic oscillations. These are pressure oscillations arising from the feedback between flames and sound. If severe, such oscillations can increase pollutant emissions and reduce system reliability. In this project, we investigated whether various types of thermoacoustic oscillations can be controlled with open-loop periodic forcing. We performed experiments on a prototypical combustion system exhibiting a variety of nonlinear dynamics, such as multiple periodic/aperiodic states, bifurcation cascades and routes to chaos. We acoustically forced this system using both sinusoidal and square waveforms, and measured its response via microphones (pressure signal) and OH*/CH* chemiluminescence (heat-release-rate signal). We analyzed the data using tools from complex systems theory to better understand the bifurcations leading to lock-in and the associated quenching mechanisms. We used this forced synchronization database to develop low-order models of the system, and then analyzed those models to identify new ways of weakening thermoacoustic oscillations. This project has helped clarify some of the complex nonlinear interactions between periodic/aperiodic thermoacoustic oscillations and open-loop periodic forcing, contributing to the development of cleaner gas turbines.

16236716.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16236716.value: Pseudo-ductile cementitious composites (PDCC) are materials exhibiting tensile hardening behavior up to several percent strain, accompanied by the formation of multiple fine cracks with opening below 50-60 microns until crack localization occurs at the end of the hardening regime. In structural applications, these properties translate into very high deformation capability and energy absorption as well as excellent durability and potential for self-healing through the tight control of crack width. Experimental research over the last two decades has demonstrated the advantage of PDCC over conventional cementitious materials in various structural applications. However, relatively little work has been done on the constitutive behavior of PDCC which is essential for the analysis of structural components. In many potential applications of PDCC, such as coupling beam, beam/column joint and regions with stress concentration, the PDCC is under combined tension and shear. Currently, the only available constitutive model for PDCC under combined tension/shear is based on a questionable assumption that the fiber is deforming in pure shear, without bending or length change. The major goal of the proposed investigation is to develop a more accurate constitutive model for PDCC based on micromechanical modeling. For a fiber oriented at an arbitrary angle to the crack, the bridging forces along the normal and tangential directions to the crack plane due to combined opening/shearing of a crack are first derived and verified with results from the mixed mode fiber pull-out test. In the derivation of fiber bridging force, a new approach considering large deflection will be employed. Then, by averaging the effects of fibers at all possible orientations and embedded lengths, with proper consideration given to the probabilistic distribution of these two parameters, the relations between composite crack bridging stresses (in both crack opening and shearing directions) and corresponding crack displacements are obtained. These relations will be employed as constitutive relations in a finite element program to simulate the behavior of various PDCC components under combined bending/shearing effects. Corresponding members will be prepared and tested to provide results for comparison with the theoretical prediction. The validity of the derived constitutive behavior can then be assessed. The successful completion of the proposed work will (i) improve current understanding and modeling approach of crack bridging mechanisms in PDCC, and (ii) provide a general micromechanics-based constitutive model of PDCC for the analysis of structural members, which can facilitate the development of design guidelines for PDCC members in practical applications.

16236716.label: Realisation of objectives
16236716.value: To fulfil the first objective, we have developed a new micromechanical model for the crack bridging stress by considering fibers lying at inclined angles to the crack as beam-struts under combined bending and tension when crack opening occurs. To improve on existing models, the part of fiber within the crack is modelled as a beam under large deflection. This is of particular significance to pseudo-ductile cementitious composites (PDCC) where the crack opening under normal operating condition is only slightly larger (1-2 times) than the fiber diameter. Due to the small span/depth ratio, the deflection is not negligible compared to the fiber length. Also, the effect of axial tension on fiber bending is considered in the new model. With these additional considerations, a new set of governing equations for the problems are derived and a numerical framework for solving the equations is developed. Results of bridging stress vs crack opening were first obtained under Mode I condition (i.e., there is only opening displacements but no shear displacements along the crack). For mode I cracks, the maximum fiber bridging stress vs fiber inclination angle shows an increasing trend that is consistent with test results. In previous work, such a trend has been modelled by assuming the fiber to change angle over an imaginary frictional pulley at its exit point. The new model based on large deflection theory is the first physical model that can provide an explanation to the increase of maximum bridging stress with fiber inclination angle. Based on parametric studies with the model, it is further shown that the stress increase with angle is more significant for increasing fiber/matrix stiffness ratio and decreasing fiber embedded length. Besides the large deflection beam bending model, a modified small deflection model considering the resistant moment resulted from axial tension has also been developed. By comparing the results from the two models, it is shown that (i) for large crack opening, the modified small deflection model may significantly over-estimate the fiber bridging stress, and (ii) for small crack opening within the operating range of PDCC, the predictions from the two models are similar. This result is of great practical significance, because it implies the modified small deflection model, which is much easier to implement and more efficient computationally, can be employed under practical situations where the crack opening remains small. With both the large deflection and the modified small deflection models, the normal and shear crack bridging force under mixed mode condition (where there is combined opening and shearing displacements along the crack) are derived. Using this model, the crack bridging behavior of fibers at different orientation, subjected to various crack displacement histories, were generated. Several interesting observations were obtained. First, under most situations, the modified small deflection model is applicable. However, if significant shearing occurs at small crack opening, the fiber deflection within the crack will become so high that the small deflection is no longer valid, so results are not accurate. Second, while crack opening has an effect on the shear bridging stress vs sliding relation, shear displacement is also found to have a significant effect on the normal bridging stress. Third, the normal and shear bridging stresses are affected by various parameters in the opposite sense – higher normal bridging stress is associated with lower shear bridging stress, and vice versa. For the second objective, a fiber pull-out system has been designed and fabricated. Uniaxial pull-out experiments (simulating mode I crack opening) on fibers lying at different directions to the crack surface was performed with polypropylene fibers and the results were compared to (i) the large deflection beam bending model, (ii) the modified small deflection model and (iii) the conventional pulley model. With (i) and (ii), much better agreement between test data and model results can be achieved. Besides accurate prediction of the maximum pull-out force, the overall shape of the pulling force versus pull-out displacement curve can also be captured. On the other hand, the pulley model predicts similar shapes of the curve for various fiber orientations, which is inconsistent with test results. Mixed mode pull-out test was included in the original proposal but was removed as the funding was significantly reduced. However, some preliminary pull-out tests have been performed under combined pulling and shearing. The limited results showed reasonable agreement with model predictions. For the third objective, based on (i) the bridging force vs crack opening relation derived for a fiber at arbitrary inclination angle and embedment length, and (ii) the probability density function of fiber inclination and embedment length, the bridging stress vs crack opening relation for a crack under pure opening displacement was derived through averaging. Using the bridging stress vs crack opening relation, and an approach for modeling multiple crack formation developed in a previous GRF project, the direct tensile stress versus strain relation of the PDCC can be derived. We have applied the model to a PDCC made with polyethylene fiber (PE), for which experiments were performed at various scales, including fiber pull-out test to obtain interfacial parameters, testing of a notched specimen (with a single crack) to obtain the bridging stress versus crack opening relation and direct tensile test on a dog-bone specimen. Based on the derived interfacial parameters at the microscale, the predicted bridging stress versus crack opening relation and direct tensile behavior with the modified small deflection beam model were found to be in good agreement with test results. Again, the beam model gives more accurate results than the conventional pulley model. To perform numerical simulation of structural members, the derived direct tensile behavior was directly used as input to a finite element program. For the program ATENA we employed, the shear bridging stress at a crack is obtained by assuming pure shearing of the fiber within the crack. As a first work on linking the shear bridging stress to micromechanics, we adopted this simple approach with the use of an equivalent shear modulus of the fiber. Using the micromechanical model, the shear bridging stress was derived by assuming the crack opening and shearing displacements to increase in proportion to each other. This relation was then fitted with the finite element model in ATENA using various values of the fiber shear modulus, until reasonable agreement with the micromechanical modeling results was found. For objective 4, two kinds of PDCC beam specimens were prepared and tested. The first type was a beam under four-point testing, and the major cracks governing failure were under Mode 1. Using the micromechanics-based tensile behavior derived above and implemented into the ATENA finite element program, the relation between applied loading and curvature (within the constant moment span) was calculated and found to be in good agreement with test results. The second type is a beam with notches from both the top and bottom surface at the middle section, and shear loading applied to induce the formation of inclined cracks. For this case, the finite element model was able to predict the overall cracking behavior observed from test specimens but underestimated both the load capacity and deformation capability. Generally speaking, mixed mode cracking in cementitious materials is a complex problem still under study by many researchers and further work on the mixed cracking in PDCC is clearly warranted.

16236716.label: Major findings and research outcome
16236716.value: The most important finding of this work is a novel model for the determination of crack bridging force for fibers lying at an angle to the crack. Conventionally, the inclined fiber is modelled as a string passing over a frictional pulley at its exit point to the crack. The snubbing friction over the pulley which leads to increase in bridging force with fiber angle is then obtained from the empirical fitting of pullout test results. Such an approach is physically unsound because the bending stiffness of the fiber is not negligible and the ‘pulley’ does not actually exist. In this study, by treating the fiber as a beam under large deflection, the fiber bridging force versus pull-out displacement curve can be directly derived. While providing a proper explanation to the empirical snubbing friction effect, the predicted crack bridging behavior with the new model is in better agreement to test results than the conventional pulley model. As the new model can predict the effect of inclination on fiber bridging force, pullout testing of fibers at different inclination angles, which is very tedious, is no longer necessary. The details of the model can be found in the first research output in Section C. While the large deflection beam model correctly describes the physics of the problem and lead to accurate prediction of crack bridging behavior, the highly nonlinear formulation makes it computational inefficient, so difficult to apply in the design of composites through micromechanics. A computationally efficient model based on small deflection analysis but incorporating the P-delta effect is hence developed. The results from this modified small deflection model is found to be comparable to the large deflection beam model especially for small crack opening which is of most interest in PDCC. Details of the work can be found in the second research output in Section C. An important goal of the work is to derive micromechanics-based constitutive model which can be employed as input to finite element model, so member behavior can be linked to the micro-parameters (such as fiber, matrix and interfacial properties, fiber volume fraction, etc.). In this study, the derivation of crack bridging stress and complete tensile behavior from pull-out test results is performed for a PDCC made with polyethylene (PE) fiber and the theoretical results are found to be in good agreement with test results. Details are reported in the third research output in Section C.

16236716.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16236716.value: The present study has focused on the development of a new model for fiber bridging force and its application to the development of crack bridging stress and constitutive behavior of pseudo-ductile cementitious composites (PDCC). The applicability to Mode I cracks is well demonstrated so the next step is to apply the model to the design of new PDCC systems where little information is available. The PI has recently written a Collaborative Research Fund proposal on the development of strain-hardening cementitious composites (which is another name for PDCC) with the use of recycled PET fibers and limestone calcined clay cement matrix. If the proposal is funded, the new model will be employed to simulate the effect of various micro-parameters on the behavior of LC3-SHCC, and then identified the proper range of parameters for specimens to be prepared and tested. For Mode II cracks, the present work has demonstrated the promise of the new model for deriving the constitutive behavior, but further experimental verification is required. Also, there is a need to develop new numerical approach to consider the effect of crack displacement history on the bridging stresses. These will be topics for future research proposals of the PI.

16236716.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16236716.value: Pseudo-ductile cementitious composites (PDCC) exhibit very high deformation capacity under extreme loading conditions and excellent control of crack width at the serviceability state. In practical applications, these properties translate into high energy absorption and good structural resilience as well as high durability (as it is difficult for water and chemicals to penetrate through very fine cracks). The proper design of PDCC is, however, not trivial because its behavior is affected by many parameters at the micro-scale, including the properties of fiber, matrix, fiber/matrix interface as well as fiber size, length and volume fraction. For given performance requirements, finding the most cost-effective PDCC composition by pure experimentation is very difficult. There is hence a need to develop micromechanical models to link the constitutive behavior of PDCC to the micro-parameters. Simulations can then be performed first to identify the proper range of parameters for specimens to be made and tested. The most fundamental information for the micromechanical model is the bridging force versus crack opening relation of fibers. In this project, a new model for the crack bridging force which is significantly improved over conventional models has been developed. It can therefore facilitate the design of PDCC for various applications.

16237016.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16237016.value: 计算机，手机，视频游戏机等电子产品以快速的技术更新，频繁的产品升级换代著称，此举意在增强电子产品公司的竞争优势，进而扩大市场份额。但是，策略型消费者在面对频繁的产品升级换代时可能会推迟购买产品，特别是当他们预计新一代产品即将发售。为了吸引消费者购买新一代的产品，同时再利用旧产品，一些环保公司推出了以旧换新的业务。目前的实践是以一个固定的价格回收旧产品。 但是，即使面对同样的产品，消费者对旧产品回收随着时间的变化有不同的估值。特别是当新一代产品就要上市时，旧产品回收会更吸引消费者。另一方面，仍有使用价值的旧产品可以被重新组装再销售到二手市场。公司到底应该回收多少旧产品一般取决于产品库存水平和公司从二手市场获利的能力。总之，如何动态的控制以旧换新业务及其价格非常重要。我们的主要研究任务就是开发一个新型的销售策略 - 动态以旧换新。 动态以旧换新具体言之就是要求消费者在购买当前产品时还要支付一个以旧换新的价格，这样消费者在下一代产品上市时，就可以用当前使用的产品去换领崭新的新一代产品。我们所提出的新型销售策略的最显著的特点就是公司要动态的决定是否提供以旧换新的业务，如果提供，要根据销售剩余时间，产品库存水平以及已经回收的旧产品数量来动态的决定以旧换新的价格，从而动态的划分消费群体谋取更大的利润。 我们的主要研究课题是针对快速更新换代的产品和策略型消费者提出动态的以旧换新业务从而阻值消费者的延迟购买行为，吸引消费者频繁更新产品进而扩大市场份额。我们研究应该何时，如何利用动态的以旧换新在不同的市场环境和消费者群体中最大获利。我们将模型应用于订货型生产和备货型生产两种生产系统，研究不同的生产系统对动态以旧换新的影响。 据我们所知，目前的文献中还没有动态以旧换新的研究。我们的研究如果成功将会对环保公司如何更加有效的利用以旧换新引导策略型消费者购买频繁更新换代的产品具有指导意义。

16237016.label: Realisation of objectives
16237016.value: The project studies the firm’s several selling strategies when it sells successive generation products faced with strategic customers. To achieve the research objectives, we carry out the following works: We first analyze the optimal markdown policy under which the firm dynamically adjusts the price of the current version of the product. In order to induce purchases for both the current version and future version of the product, we propose a dynamic trade-up (also called exchange-old-for-new, EON in short) policy. Specifically, the firm sells one generation of product within a finite time horizon. At the end of the horizon, a new generation of product is launched in the market. Under a markdown policy, the firm determines the dynamic discount level, and customers who have heterogeneous valuations and arrive sequentially decide whether to purchase the current product or wait for the new version. Under an EON policy, the firm determines the dynamic trade-up price, and customers decide whether to purchase the current product, join the trade-up program, or wait for the new version of the product. When a customer waits for the new version, the customer may renege on the decision and leave the system before the new version is released. We characterize the customers’ utilities for different purchase options and generate the demand functions for the current product and the new version of the product. Then the firm’s problem can be formulated as a standard dynamic program. We characterize the firm's optimal markdown price and trade-up price over time under both the markdown policy and the trade-up policy respectively. We show that neither the markdown price nor the trade-up price always decreases over time; instead, during some period they may increase with time. We find that the optimal markdown or the optimal trade-up policy is only effective in the middle of the selling horizon. In other words, the price is not marked down, and the trade-up program should not be offered in the early selling horizon. Although the price is marked down, and the trade-up program is offered in the late selling horizon, no customers choose to purchase the old product at the markdown price or join the trade-up program. There is no absolutely dominant relationship between the markdown and trade-up strategies over the entire selling horizon. This result prompts us to combine both options and develop a hybrid strategy where the firm offers both the markdown and the trade-up program. We find that a hybrid strategy should be adopted only when the current product's residual value is medium and the likelihood of waiting customers leaving the system is not low. We conduct extensive numerical experiments and find that the hybrid strategy is more profitable when waiting customers are more likely to renege on their decisions, the current product is more value-preserving, the customers’ discount rate is low, and the new version of the product is greatly superior to the current product. To gain more insights into how the firm can best manage successive-generation products when faced with strategic consumers, we investigate two collection policies for used products, that are commonly observed in practice. Based on whether or not the compensation for returning used products is associated with further purchases, we study trade-in and buyback policies. Specifically, under a trade-in policy, customers who return the used product are granted a rebate, which can be redeemed only at the replacement purchase of the upgraded product. Under a buyback policy, a reward is offered unconditionally whenever a customer returns the used product. We decompose the potential value generated by a collection policy into three parts: (i) the residual value of the used product that can be extracted directly after collection, (ii) the replacement purchase revenue derived from selling an upgraded product to repeat customers at a lower effective price under collection compensation, and (iii) the valuation premium that strategic customers are willing to pay for the base product in the initial period in anticipation of a future collection opportunity. We analyze customers’ choice behavior and use backward induction to solve subgame perfect equilibrium, and discuss the interactions of these three parts under the trade-in and buyback policies respectively. The results show that the manufacturer is better off under the trade-in policy if the unit production cost is low or the residual value of the used product is low, otherwise it is worse off than under the buy-back policy. We also explore the impact of the secondary market on the firm’s used product collection policies. The secondary market acts as a buffer that adjusts the market clearing price flexibly, and indiscriminately collects used products from repeat customers, thus negating the discriminative power of a trade-in policy. Specifically, when the residual value of the used product is low, two policies generate the same profit. When the residual value of the used product is higher, the buy-back policy yields higher profit. The result yields important implications particularly relevant to the introduction of new series of generation products, where it is likely that substantial customers who, after making purchase, find their realized valuation turns out to be low and hence expect to resell the used product to the secondary market. Our results suggest that the manufacturer should be cautious about the secondary market when it designs its collection policy. Another interesting result is that the existence of a secondary market can increase the manufacturer’s profit when the customers are highly strategic.

16237016.label: Major findings and research outcome
16237016.value: This project investigates two demand management policies - markdown and trade-up - that have the potential to induce early purchases from strategic customers in the presence of product rollover. We analyze the firm’s optimal dynamic markdown policy and trade-up policy. We first find that both the markdown price and the trade-up price do not necessarily always decrease over time. Both the prices can increase in time during some period. We also find that the optimal markdown or the optimal trade-up policy is only effective in the middle of the selling horizon. In other words, the price is not marked down, and the trade-up program should not be offered in the early selling horizon. Although the price is marked down, and the trade-up program is offered in the late selling horizon, no customers choose to purchase the old product at the markdown price or join the trade-up program. There is no absolutely dominant relationship between the markdown and trade-up strategies over the entire selling horizon. This result prompts us to combine both options and further develop a hybrid strategy where the firm offers both the markdown and the trade-up program. We find that a hybrid strategy should be adopted only when the current product's residual value is medium and the likelihood of waiting customers leaving the system is not low. These results are discussed in details in the paper "Markdown or Trade-up? Incentives to Induce Early Purchases in the Presence of Product Rollover." In a related area of used products collection, the paper "(Un)conditional Collection Policies on Used Products with Strategic Customers" (under the major revision of POMS) considers the optimal design of a manufacturer’s collection policy to encourage strategic customers to return used products and make replacement purchases for upgraded products with/without an independent secondary market. The paper "Managing Return Policies with Consumer Resale" (under the minor revision of NRL) considers a retailer selling products to customers with uncertain valuations under a return policy. We investigate how the existence of consumer resale affects the retailer’s return and resale policy. Another paper "Contract Unobservability and Downstream Competition" (accepted by MSOM) considers a supply chain with a manufacturer and two retailers who are contracted through wholesale prices or two-part tariffs. We depart from the existing literature by assuming that contract terms between the manufacturer and a retailer are not observed by the rival retailer.

Incentives to Induce Early Purchases in the Presence of Product Rollover." Eventually, we hope all these works can be published.

16237016.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16237016.value: Frequently releasing successive generation products can help to increase a firm’s market base and maintain its competitive edge. However, it creates a challenge of strategic waiting by customers; that is, strategic customers may choose to wait when they anticipate the release of a new generation product in the near future. How to induce strategic customers to make early purchases becomes an important problem for the firm that sells successive generation products. In this project, we analyze two policies to tackle this problem. One is a dynamic markdown policy under which the firm varies the price of the current product over time; and the other is a trade-up policy under which the firm sells one unit of the current product with the promise of upgrading to a new version when it is released. We show that neither the markdown price nor the trade-up price always decreases over time; instead, they may increase with time during some period. We also find that the optimal markdown or the optimal trade-up policy is only effective in the middle of the selling horizon. There is no absolutely dominant relationship between the markdown and trade-up strategies over the entire selling horizon.

16237816.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16237816.value: Solar energy is free, clean and abundant, however the cost of converting solar energy to electricity is relatively high due to a number of reasons including relatively low energy intensity for sunlight, low energy conversion efficiency and high cost of solar photovoltaic devices. Although crystalline Si-based solar photovoltaic technology is a dominant photovoltaic technology, large effort has been invested in developing more affordable and efficient photovoltaic technologies. In line with this effort, various types of thin-film photovoltaics have been developed using either organic or inorganic materials. The organic solar cells are typically lightweight, flexible and compatible with low temperature fabrication processes. However, they suffer from low cost and stability issues. On the other hand, inorganic thin film solar cells have presented higher efficiency close to that of crystalline Si solar cells. However, their material and fabrication cost still limits their competitiveness over crystalline Si solar cells. Recently, organic-inorganic hybrid perovskite materials are emerging as highly attractive candidates for cost-effective solar cells, due to their appealing optical and electrical properties and earth abundance. The device performance is already comparable to the best devices made of inorganic thin films. Meanwhile, extensive research has shown that the stability of solar cells based on perovskite materials can be largely improved via various approaches. In this proposed project, we aim to explore scalable fabrication of high performance solar cells based on perovskite materials by utilizing various nanostructures. Scalable device fabrication is of paramount importance for any practical photovoltaic applications. Our preliminary study shows that large area and uniform perovskite thin films can be deposited on nanostructured substrates. And by using the nanostructured substrates, not only is the light harvesting capability of the device and material enhanced due to light trapping effect, the device mechanical stability and flexibility can also be largely improved. Systematic investigations will be performed to achieve further device performance enhancement. Moreover, effort will be made to addressing the challenges for large-scale fabrication of nanostructured perovskite solar cell devices. 16237816.label: Major findings and research outcome
16237816.value: Our major findings can be summarized as: -The integration and stability issues of CH3NH3SnI3 was solved by embedding CH3NH3SnI3 nanowire arrays in nanoengineering anodic aluminum oxide (AAO) templates. The AAO templates effectively alleviate the perovskites decomposition caused by the diffusion of water and oxygen molecules. As a result, the perovskite degradation process has been slowed down by up to 500 times, compared with a planar thin film. -We have found that the stabilized cubic phase inorganic CsPbX3 at room temperature can be achieved by synthesizing the CsPbX3 nanowires inside anodic alumina membrane. Moreover, photodetectors based on these cubic phase CsPbX3 nanowires were fabricated, illustrating a potential application for optoelectronics in the visible wavelength range. -We also found that the unique 3-D INPOS architecture was constructed via anodization of an Al alloy. This structure inherits all the structural merits, including a large surface area, and efficient electron transport, and excellent structural stability, of the 3-D nanopores. It is superior to the 3-D nanopores as it has a higher porosity and better ion accessibility. -We discovered a novel alloying technique of fabrication Sn-rich perovskite film through the reaction of Sn/Pb binary alloy metal precursors and methylammonium iodide vapor. Using Pb–Sn eutectic alloy, perovskite films with large grain sizes up to 5 μm can be grown directly from liquid phase metal. Consequently, a less-toxic and efficient perovskite solar cell with a PCE of 14.04% is demonstrated. It is found that this technique can open up a new direction to further explore different alloy systems (binary or ternary alloys) with an even lower melting point. -We have developed a sequential vapor deposition to fabricate high-quality and uniform mixed-cation mixed-halide perovskite films with microscale grain sizes for the PSC application. Also, sputtered SnO2 is implemented into all-vacuum-deposited PSCs as an electron transport layer. Together with evaporated copper phthalocyanine as a thermally and chemically stable low-cost hole transport layer, a respectable PCE of 15.14% is achieved with promising device stability and negligible hysteresis. -We have pioneered the implementation of radio frequency magnetron sputtered SnO2 as an electron transport layer for vapor-deposited-MAPbI3-based perovskite solar cells on both rigid and flexible substrates. PSCs of 12.82% PCE on rigid glass substrates and 5.88% PCE on flexible substrates were achieved. -We have achieved large scale nanostructured flexible substrate fabricated with a roll-to-roll method, perovskite thin film solar cell devices have been successfully fabricated on it with decent efficiencies.

16237816.value: -We found the device stability still has room to improve. We have explored nanoengineering approach to improve perovskite material stability. In the future material composition can also be explored to further improve stability. -Here we have successfully demonstrated that we can fabricate large scale nanostructured substrate and we have demonstrated that large scale solar cell can be fabricated with evaporation method. In the future, high throughput approach such as slot die coating and roll-to-roll coating method can be explored to deposit perovskite materials to realize fast production of flexible perovskite solar cells.

16237816.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16237816.value: In this project, we have explored scalable fabrication of high performance solar cells based on perovskite materials by utilizing various nanostructures. We have developed a nanoengineering approach to enhance perovskite material stability against water, oxygen and phase change. Large scaled nanostructured substrates have been fabricated with a roll-to-roll compatible method. We have explored solution process, physical vapor deposition method and chemical vapor deposition method to fabricate perovskite thin film solar cells on the nanostructured substrates. And by using the nanostructured substrates, not only is the light harvesting capability of the device and material enhanced due to light trapping effect, the device mechanical stability and flexibility can also be largely improved. Systematic investigations have led to device performance enhancement. The results of the project help researchers in the field to obtain a better understanding of perovskite solar cell device physics and design, as well as achievement of scalable and high performance devices that will have high impact on the solar industry.

16238016.value: To design a novel DTBFP power MOSFET. To develop process modules for the DTBFP power MOSFET. To experimentally demonstrate the DTBFP power MOSFET. 16238016.label: Realisation of objectives
16238016.value: As stated in the mid-term report, we began the project by first working on the design of the novel deep-trench buried-field-plated (BFP) power MOSFET. We used the 2D/3D device simulator Sentaurus to study the BFP device structure and finalized the device and process designs. Our approach is to first demonstrate the most important effect of the buried-field-plate in the drift region with proper impurity doping concentration required for charge balancing. That does not require the implementation of the entire MOSFET device. A simple high-voltage (HV) diode built using the buried-field-plate will be good enough. Once the electric field shaping effect is demonstrated by the implementation of the BFP HV diode, performance of the novel DTBFP MOSFET can be accurately obtained using the device simulator mentioned above. After the mid-term report, we have continued our experimental implementation of the BFP HV diode. We have successfully developed all the critical modules for building of the HV diode and finally built the HV diode experimentally. After that, we have characterized the breakdown characteristics of the HV diode and obtained the performance of the novel DTBFP MOSFET. The TFP structure employed in the drift region modulates the electric field in the off-state, resulting in a higher breakdown voltage than that of conventional power MOSFETs. Simulation results show that the specific on-resistance of the TFP power MOSFET is approximately one third that of the conventional power MOSFET and about 50% lower than that of the silicon limit for the same breakdown voltage. In addition, compared with super-junction devices, the TFP power MOSFET is able to provide better reverse recovery characteristics, including reduction in peak reverse recovery current (IRRM) and reverse recovery charge (QRR) by 24% and 37%, respectively.

16238016.label: Major findings and research outcome
16238016.value: Power MOSFETs are widely used in power electronic systems because of the fast switching speed, simple gate driver design, and compatibility with CMOS technology. However, conventional power MOSFETs suffer from high on-state conduction loss due to the trade-off relationship between specific on-resistance (Ron,sp) and breakdown voltage. Some solutions based on super-junction and field plate approaches have been proposed to break the ideal silicon limit. For the super-junction solution, alternating n/p pillars are used to replace the drift region in conventional power MOSFETs. The fabrication techniques for implementing the alternating n/p pillars can be grouped into three categories: multi-layer epitaxy, trench etching with epitaxy regrowth, and trench sidewall doping. However, for the multi-layer epitaxy technique, many times of the lithography, implantation and epitaxy growth steps are indispensable and complicated, resulting in high cost and low throughput. For the trench etching with epitaxy regrowth, micro voids are easy to form during trench refilling, which causes the reduction of breakdown voltage and increase in leakage current. For the trench sidewall doping approach, the ion implantation doping leads to serious ion reflection when ions reach the trench sidewall, resulting in non-uniform impurity distribution. If vapor phase doping is used, it is difficult to precisely control the total impurity dose to meet the charge balancing requirement. For the field plate solution, a field plate is used to modulate the electric field distribution in the drift region. Thus, the doping concentration of the drift region can be increased by an order of magnitude without degrading the breakdown voltage. However, to achieve a high breakdown voltage, deep and wide trenches are required, and a thick dielectric layer at the bottom of the trench is needed. It is very difficult to achieve a thick dielectric layer at the bottom and is also very costly to refill the deep and wide trenches with polysilicon as the field plate. In this paper, a trench-field-plate high-voltage power MOSFET has been proposed and demonstrated. In this structure, the stringent fabrication requirements for charge balancing in the super-junction devices are eliminated and yet a specific on-resistance which is 50% lower than that of the silicon limit is achieved. In addition, compared with super-junction devices, the TFP power MOSFET is able to provide better reverse recovery characteristics, including reduction in peak reverse recovery current (IRRM) and reverse recovery charge (QRR) by 24% and 37%, respectively.

16238016.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16238016.value: The design and experimental implementation of the novel DTBFP power MOSFET have been demonstrated. It is developed using a CMOS compatible microelectronic fabrication process. The device and process are ready for technology transfer and product development for commercialization.

16238016.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16238016.value: Power semiconductor devices are indispensable parts of any power electronic systems for power management, power conversions, and power control applications. In order to be more environmentally friendly in the future, efficient power electronic systems are needed for efficient use of electrical energy. Thus, efficient power semiconductor devices are needed. In this project, a power efficient high-voltage transistor was developed with an on-resistance which is 50% lower than that of the silicon limit. That will significantly reduce the power losses and also reduce corresponding the amount of carbon emission significantly.

16239316.label: Project Objectives
16239316.value: Different GSG layers will be fabricated in the superelastic NiTi plates by different methods. The key fabrication parameters and the resulting profiles of GS, residual stress and property distributions in the GSG region of the plates will be identified and characterized. Systematic data of fatigue life enhancement will be obtained by fatigue experiment of the plates under cyclic tension or bending tests. Direct observation and measurement of fatigue crack growth at the macro- and sub-macro levels will be conducted to reveal the GSG effects on the enhancement of fatigue crack growth resistance. Intrinsic and extrinsic mechanisms of crack growth suppression and toughening by the GSG layer as well as their GSG profile dependence will be identified.

16239316.label: Realisation of objectives
16239316.value: In this project, we performed an in-depth systematic experimental study, at macro-, micro- and nanoscales, of the grain size gradient (GSG) effects on the fatigue and crack growth resistance of NiTi SMA. The three project objectives have been fully achieved through the successful completion of the following three Tasks. Task I. Fabrication of GSG layer by the surface mechanical attrition (SMAT) and the laser shock peening (LSP) methods and characterization of the microstructures. Task II. Macro- and microscopic experiments of GSG effects on the stress-strain (local and overall), fatigue and fracture responses of the treated NiTi plates. The huge experimental data were summarized and analyzed in terms of the obtained internal microstructure parameters and external loading and plate geometric variables. Physical pictures of GSG effects on fatigue performance were obtained and the mechanism underlying the obtained fatigue life enhancement were identified. The results were further compared with the theoretical analysis in Task III. Task III. Analysis of the experimental data. This task run in parallel with Task I and Task II. Through comparison among SMAT and LSP parameters, experimental data of fatigue life enhancement and analysis, and further improvement of the SMAT and LSP processing parameters and experiment, the roles of the key governing parameters in the fatigue behavior were be verified. Insight into the achieved fatigue enhancement were obtained.

16239316.label: Major findings and research outcome
16239316.value: The research of this project finds that nanocrystalline (nc) NiTi (with grain size of 10nm) can significantly suppress the crack nucleation and enhance the fatigue life but at the expenses of reduced ductility and crack growth resistance. To solve this dilemma, we use new fabrication methods of surface mechanical attrition at elevated temperature and surface laser shock peening to hybridize the properties at different length scales so that an overall optimization of fatigue life together with other functions of NiTi SMA can be achieved. Nanocrystallined Grain-Size-Gradient (GSG) surface layers where grain size (GS) changes gradually from the surface to the interior have been obtained with success to enhance fatigue life of NiTi since most failures originate from the surface. Surface mechanical attrition treatment (SMAT) and laser shock peening (LSP) are promising technique to generate a nc GSG layer on the surface of NiTi material to increase the fatigue life. The key idea of the research is to suppress the surface crack nucleation and growth by the Hall-Petch strengthening and the high residual compressive stress, both due to the severe plastic deformation of the GSG layer. Fabrication parameters of the GSG structure and the resulting intrinsic and extrinsic mechanisms of fatigue are identified. The dual benefits of strengthening and toughening which are usually exclusive to each other for most metals are achieved in the project. We have overcome the numerous difficulties encountered in the significant Hong Kong societal unrest in 2019 and the following COVID-19 in performing the research work of this project. The major research outcome including 4 SCI journal papers (2 in Scripta Mater., 1 in Mater. Sci and Engineering A, 1 in Int. J. Solids and Structures) and 1 paper published in the journal of Superelasticity and Shape Memory Technology. Currently there are 2 manuscripts under preparation. Through this project, research collaborations with the CityU of Hong Kong, the Southern University of Science and Technology in Shenzhen and the Wuhan University of mainland China have been established.

16239316.value: This project has revealed the scientific and practical importance of hybridizing the size dependent material properties in developing the next generation fatigue resistant NiTi alloy by grain size engineering. The research work has also led to the funding of new GRF project in developing high fatigue resistant NiTi via nanostructure engineering.

16239316.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16239316.value: Superelastic polycrystalline NiTi shape memory alloys (SMAs) are increasingly used in many fields due to superelasticity, shape memory and large elastocaloric effects. Long fatigue life is the key requirement of many SMA devices experiencing cyclic phase transition (PT) under periodic thermomechanical loadings. Unfortunately, the fatigue performance of existing NiTi polycrystalline SMAs with typical grain size ≥ 100 nm has so far proved to be disappointing due to the generation of dislocation and damage accumulation in the cyclic PT. To enhance the fatigue resistances of the material has been an important task for material scientists and design engineers. In this project, we performed a systematic experimental study of the grain size gradient (GSG) effects on enhancing fatigue life of NiTi. Different GSG layers were fabricated at the surface of superelastic NiTi plates by the surface processing techniques using SMAT and LSP method. The SMAT and LSP processing parameters and the resulting surface GSG layer, residual stress and property distributions from the surface to the interior were identified and characterized. Fatigue experiment under cyclic tension and bending were performed to obtain the systematic fatigue life data. Intrinsic and extrinsic fatigue and toughening mechanisms and their GSG dependence were revealed. The project has both the scientific and practical importance in hybridizing the size dependent material properties and in developing the next generation fatigue resistant NiTi alloy by grain size engineering.
