16515316.label: Major findings and research outcome
16515316.value: Using a global sample from 27 developed markets between 1994 to 2016, we document a tightening trend of corporate credit ratings, which parallels the growth of global rating agencies’ market shares. Increased market share precedes a decline in ratings, and the result holds among a set of constant firms. In addition, the trend reverses following the NRSRO designation of a local rating agency. Further supporting the notion that market power strengthens rating agencies’ reputational incentives to issue stringent ratings, we find that rating agencies’ market shares are associated with pessimistic qualitative rating adjustments. We have presented the paper at the 2019 Cambridge Accounting Research Camp, Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, 2019 MIT Asia Conference in Accounting, University of Hong Kong, and University of Michigan. .

16515316.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16515316.value: We are in the process of incorporating feedback and submitting to top finance or accounting journals.

16515316.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16515316.value: Despite extensive U.S. evidence on the incentives of credit rating agencies and their rating properties, international evidence is scarce. Using a global sample of issuer level credit ratings in developed markets, we find that the global CRAs have become more stringent in assigning corporate credit ratings worldwide. We also find that their market shares increase globally over time and are associated with the tighter ratings. Further analyses find that increased competition leads to rating inflation and market power has the disciplinary effect of increasing the reputational incentives of CRAs. Consistent with the reputational incentives associated with increased market share, we find that the global CRAs make more pessimistic qualitative rating adjustments when their market shares are higher. Overall, we contribute to the literature by examining the evolution and determinants of credit rating patterns in global markets and thus improving understanding on the economic consequences of the global CRAs’ dominance.

16515716.label: Project Objectives
16515716.value: To investigate how context behaviors and the manner in which they are judged affects perceptions of immorality, an individual's own immoral consumption behavior and the emotions that result from it. To examine how chronic or situationally induced mindsets affect how the morality of a behavior is judged and one's propensity to engage in it.
rows: To investigate how context behaviors and the manner in which they are judged affects perceptions of immorality, an individual's own immoral consumption behavior and the emotions that result from it.
To examine how chronic or situationally induced mindsets affect how the morality of a behavior is judged and one's propensity to engage in it.

16515716.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16515716.value: The norms that govern morality are socially learned over a period of time. We learn that we should not steal, cheat, or harm others. Yet, the application of these learned moral standards in everyday situations varies considerably. For example, an increasing number of consumers use pirated goods and buy counterfeit products – essentially stealing from others who have developed something. Or, they support illegal wildlife trade, harming communities and the environment. In short, people do not always invoke the moral standards that they have learned while making these behavioral decisions. This research examines how and why people transgress and engage in morally questionable consumption behaviors. We suggest that in some cases, people simply use others’ behaviors to guide their own without considering whether the action is moral or immoral. In other cases, a moral standard might be retrieved or constructed online and used as a basis for judging whether the behavior is moral or immoral. The context and manner in which this standard is constructed has implications for whether consumers will engage in the morally questionable behavior or not, and the feelings of guilt or shame that might result from having done so. In this proposal, we suggest that moral standards acquired from childhood are not always applied unless attention is drawn to the morality of an act. And, even when the concept of morality is made salient, the immediate context behaviors (moral or immoral) exert an impact on how a target behavior (e.g., using pirated software) is perceived. Thus, context-based standards of morality might often be constructed on the spot when the concept of morality is made salient and used as a basis for deciding whether to engage in a morally questionable practice. We also suggest that the manner or process of making judgments about the context behaviors can activate a mindset to either consider situational determinants of a behavior or not. This mindset can then generalize to new situations involving one’s own decisions and can affect the emotions that are experienced as a consequence of this decision. We examine how these mindsets might be situationally induced as well as chronically accessible in two different cultures; namely the United States and China. The proposal suggests that moral standards, although learned, are also constructed and based on situational and social factors. An understanding of these factors will hopefully allow one to design interventions that can foster responsible consumption.

16515716.label: Realisation of objectives
16515716.value: Many types of behaviors that exist in the marketplace are of questionable morality because they involve exploitation of others. These could range from salespeople playing on consumers’ lack of knowledge to exploit them, transgressions by firms, consumption of pirated goods and fakes by consumers, and even a disregard for issues that exploit the planet’s resources (e.g., food wastage and environmental degradation) by both firms and consumers. Our research focused on how people judge behaviors that are of questionable morality. Our assumption was that if people judge these behaviors less harshly, they might not hesitate to engage in such behaviors themselves. Our first objective consists of two parts described below: 1. Understanding the effects of context behaviors and the manner in which they are judged on perceptions of morality Our prediction was that judgments of morality will be affected by the manner in which judgments of whether something is “good” or “bad” are made. We found that context behaviors do not exert much of an impact but rather it is the manner in which these behaviors are judged that affects judgments of morality (Saluja, Adaval and Wyer, working paper). When people have a tendency to make absolute judgments (absolute mindset conditions), it facilitates the use of a global moral standard (i.e., a common principle) in judging transgressions by others. In contrast, when they make relative judgments (relative mindset conditions), it facilitates the use of nuanced moral standards. The use of these different standards can result in harsher judgments of others’ behaviors when an absolute mindset is activated and more lenient judgments when a relative mindset is activated. These effects then generalize to one’s own behavior. Participants who played a dictator game acted more selfishly when they made relative judgments. 2. Understanding how the mindset to think relatively can affect the emotions experienced Challenges arose when we sought to measure the types of moral emotions such as anger, guilt, shame that arise in response to immoral actions. People who judge these types of acts using an absolute standard should experience stronger emotions compared to those who use a relativist standard. The FaceReader we employed to track emotions through facial expressions did not reveal differences in emotions given that we could not show people very graphic content. Further, the manipulation of mindset did not last through the advertising we showed. To address this, we used a measured variable of moral relativism. We examined social messages exhorting people to refrain from using certain things (e.g., plastic, paper, etc.) that harm the environment. Past research has linked the effectiveness of these messages to the political ideology of the recipient. For example, liberals are more likely to express pro-environmental concerns because the issues are framed in terms of moral values of harm and care. We assumed that an increase in liberal values should lead to a stronger experience of moral emotions and stimulate behaviors that support the environment (e.g., activism). However, moral relativism might have a dampening effect on the experience of such emotions. In three studies, we tested a model where an increase in liberal ideology has a direct effect on the intensity of moral emotions experienced in response to a pro-environment ad and leads to activism. However, an indirect effect also exists wherein an increase in liberalism is associated with increased relativism which, in turn, dampens the experience of these moral emotions and decreases the amount of activism participants engage in (Saluja, Kwon and Adaval, working paper). Two other projects that were not directly related to the grant objectives but inspired by them were completed. First, moral decisions often involve making decisions to go against what many might be doing. We found that participants who experienced the sensorimotor experience of going against the flow (e.g., walking in the direction opposite to the flow of traffic) were more likely to choose options that were normatively not preferred (Kwon and Adaval 2018). This finding has implications for morality. Given a situation where people are behaving immorally (e.g., cheating on an exam), will such sensorimotor experiences of going against the flow affect the decision to join in? We plan to extend this project to examine decisions pertaining to immoral behaviors. Second, we examined sales practices where salespeople work to increase their margins by selling higher end products. This practice of up-selling is exploitative. We show that consumers are aware of this and do not trust the salesperson. We identify strategies through which long-term trust can be increased (Maeng and Adaval, working paper). The second objective was to examine how chronic or situationally induced mindsets affect perceptions of a firm’s transgressions. Firms are often involved in scandals (e.g., Exxon’s oil spill). To understand how consumers perceive such transgressions, we provided respondents in three different countries (USA, India and China) with vignettes about transgressions. We varied the perpetrator of the crime (local versus foreign company) and the identity of the victim (members of the ingroup or outgroup). To identify if the effects were due to cultural norms to process information in a particular way, we also varied the cultural mindset within each country inducing either a collectivist or an individualist mindset. Oyserman et al.’s (2009) work suggests that a collectivist mindset leads to a focus on contextual information such as whether the company's actions affects members of one's own group. Actions might be judged more severely when they hurt members inside the collective than outside of it. Two studies found that this was the case. Participants were more likely to judge a crime against their ingroup harshly if they had been primed with a collectivist mindset than an individualist mindset. If the crime was against outgroup victims, the primed mindset had no impact. Further, people with an individualist mindset have a tendency to separate themselves from others and extract rule-based principles to judge whether something is moral or immoral. When participants read about a transgression by a local firm, they were more likely to try to separate themselves from the firm by judging it more harshly when primed with an individualist mindset than when primed with a collectivist mindset. Such a tendency was not apparent when the transgression was by a foreign firm (Adaval, Saluja, Yuan and Wyer, working paper). An additional project related to these mindsets was completed. Wasting food is often considered immoral. Yet 40% of food that is produced is actually wasted because of poor storage and inventory management. Our research on mindsets suggested that thinking relationally allows people to see more variety in smaller assortments of food. Consequently, providing customers who have a collectivist mindset a lot of variety does lead to wastage. In contrast, people with an individualist mindset tend to benefit from larger assortment size. Given that these mindsets can be primed situationally within a culture (as the previous studies show) we suggest that priming these mindsets might affect how large an assortment people seek (Saluja and Adaval, working paper). To summarize, a large number of studies were run in different countries and we were able to accomplish both objectives of the grant despite certain hurdles we encountered along the way. This was a challenging project and we are grateful to the RGC for funding it.

16515716.label: Major findings and research outcome
16515716.value: Three major conclusions can be drawn. First, when people have a tendency to make absolute judgments (absolute mindset conditions), it facilitates the use of a global moral standard (i.e., a common principle) to judge morally ambiguous behaviors. This leads to harsher judgments of whether the behavior was immoral or not. When individuals make relative judgments (relative mindset conditions), it facilitates the use of nuanced moral standards and this leads people to judge morally ambiguous behaviors with leniency. These effects of mindsets have implications for individuals’ own behavior. They behave more selfishly when they have a relativist mindset accessible (Saluja, Adaval and Wyer, working paper). Second, the intensity of moral emotions that one experiences in response to a moral transgression decreases the more relativist the mindset of an individual. When examined in the context of political ideology, the findings suggest that increases in liberal values have a direct effect on the intensity of moral emotions experienced in response to a pro-environment ad and activism. However, an increase in liberalism is also positively correlated with increased relativism which, in turn, dampens the experience of these moral emotions and decreases the amount of activism participants engage in (Saluja, Kwon and Adaval, working paper). Third, mindsets can either be primed situationally or be chronically accessible in a culture. Participants judge a crime against their ingroup harshly if they had been primed with a collectivist mindset than an individualist mindset. If the crime is against outgroup victims, the primed mindset had no impact. Further, people with an individualist mindset have a tendency to separate themselves from others and extract rule-based principles to judge whether something is moral or immoral. When participants read about a transgression by a local firm, they are more likely to try to separate themselves from the firm and judge it more harshly when primed with an individualist mindset than when primed with a collectivist mindset. Such a tendency was not apparent when the transgression was by a foreign firm (Adaval, Saluja, Yuan and Wyer, working paper).

16515716.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16515716.value: As noted in the previous section, there are several instances when consumers behave with questionable integrity and they do so because they observe several others doing the same. To not do what others are doing requires moral conviction and courage. Can experiences that have little to do with the situation in which they find themselves have an influence on their behavior? Our research (Kwon and Adaval 2018) suggests that feelings of going against the flow might make people pick something different from what others choose. Such sensorimotor experiences are all around us. For example, people might go against the flow of traffic, walk against the breeze or simply simulate going in a different direction. If people find themselves in a situation where others are behaving immorally, will such sensorimotor experiences of going against the flow affect the decision to join in? We hope to investigate this next. We would also like to collect additional data on the effects of moral relativism on emotions. We plan to manipulate moral relativism once again using a different technique to see if it affects the emotional reactions of liberals and conservatives.

16515716.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16515716.value: The manner in which people think about whether a behavior is good or bad can affect how they judge others transgressions and their own behavior. Relative judgments about such behaviors typically signal to the individual that moral standards are malleable and this leads them to not only judge others less harshly but also engage in selfish behaviors themselves. Such relativism can also affect the intensity of moral emotions that people experience in reaction to a transgression. Specifically, moral relativism decreases the intensity of feelings that individuals experience and leads to fewer attempts to correct the wrong. Such effects are apparent even among people with liberal values. These individuals typically experience strong moral emotions in response to ads highlighting environmental concerns. However, moral relativism can dampen these effects. Morality is perceived differently within and across cultures based on the mindsets that are accessible. A collective mindset makes people react more negatively to crimes by a firm against people of their own kind compared to an individualist mindset. An individualist mindset on the other hand makes people want to distance themselves from a local firm that engages in such immoral behaviors.

16516116.label: Project Objectives
16516116.value: Collect a large data set that can be utilized to analyze global business cycles and financial cycles. Provide key evidence for structural breaks in time series data. Develop the econometric framework for high dimensional dynamic factor models that are subject to heterogeneous structural breaks. Derive the Bayesian algorithm for estimation and inference. Write a computer program for the method using popular programming package such as Matlab and R. Conduct Monte Carlo Simulations to demonstrate the advantage of the proposed estimation method. 16516116.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16516116.value: Modern information technology has shown researchers the luxury of working with high-dimensional data sets, in which a large number of individual units are recorded over extended periods. These complex data sets bring challenges as well as new opportunities for analyzing economic issues. The large dynamic factor model uses latent factors to overcome the curse of dimensionality in large data, which summarize comovement among a large cross section of economic sectors or countries. For example, the factors provide useful measurement for the global business cycles. The dynamic factor model effectively summarizes the large amount of information in a wide spectrum of economic data series using a few latent but estimable indicators. Yet in empirical studies, researchers have to come to realize the importance of potential structural instability when modelling high-dimensional data sets. Such instability could be due to technological changes, preference shifts of economic agents, and policy regimes switching. Forecasts based on estimated factors will be inaccurate if structural breaks in the model are ignored. The long time dimension also introduces the possibility of new factors, with historical factors phasing out. Econometric analysis of the structural change in large factor models is nontrivial because the factors are unobserved and factor loadings have to be estimated, both objects are of high dimension. This project will provide an econometric framework to analyze heterogeneous structural breaks in high-dimensional dynamic factor models, in which individual units experience different break dates with possible clusters at certain periods. Allowing heterogeneous breaks has both empirical relevance and important theoretical implications. For example, the recent financial crisis and recession may lead to economic reforms among both developed and developing countries, which have different exposure to the global shocks and carry alternative reform agenda. This might lead to heterogeneous structural changes among countries. This project aims to develop the method for high-dimensional data analysis with a flexible framework for heterogeneous structural breaks. The empirical application using the methodology of this project can help us better understand the evolution of global business and financial cycles. 現代信息技術的發展讓研究者開始能對高維數據，亦即大量個體單位的時間序列，進行分析。對於經濟分析而言，這種複雜的數據既帶來了挑戰又迎來了機遇。高維動態因子模型利用潛在因子以克服大數據中的維度詛咒問題。這些潛在因子能夠有效地描述大量經濟部門或多個國家之間的同步運轉。例如，潛在因子能用來度量全球經濟週期。動態因子模型使用少量的可估計因子得以對大量經濟數據中的信息進行很好地總結。不過在實證研究中，研究者逐漸開始意識到當對高維數據進行建模時，機構的不穩定性是一項非常重要的考慮。這種不穩定性可能來源於技術的變遷、經濟個體的偏好改動、以及政策的遷移。如果預測模型沒能考慮到結構的不穩定性的可能，那麼預測準確性會大為降低。時間序列的長度增加也會引入新的因子，以及弱化舊的因子的影響。對於高維因子模型的結構變遷的研究較為複雜，這主要是因為因子不能被直接觀測，因子的敏感係數也需要被估計出來，這兩個隱藏的變量都是高維變量。此研究項目着眼於提供一個計量的研究框架，來分析高維動態因子模型中的異質性結構變遷問題，不同的經濟變量可能在不同的日期發生結構變遷，總體看來，這些結構變遷日期可能會集中在幾個凝聚點。這樣的建模方式既考慮到實證的相關性也提供了重要的理論推廣。例如，最近的金融危機可能導致了發達國家以及發展中國家的經濟改革，而這些國家對全球衝擊的反應程度可能大為不同，很自然的，這些國家的改革日程也可能迥異。在建模中，此類異質性改革日程導致了不同國家的異質性結構變遷。此研究項目會構建出一個靈活的經濟計量分析框架，來處理高維數據中的結構變遷問題。在實證應用中，此框架能有效地促進我們對全球經濟週期和金融週期的理解。

16516116.label: Major findings and research outcome
16516116.value: This paper provides a Bayesian estimation framework for the analysis of heterogeneous structural breaks in high-dimensional dynamic factor models. The method is a more general setup that existing approaches to the structural break analysis. In the same time, the method applies the Kalman filter with time-varying parameters to handle the latent factor problem. Monte Carlo simulations show that the method works well for a variety of sample sizes. Both the latent factors and the break dates can be well-identified.

16516116.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16516116.value: Due to the computational cost, Monte Carlo simulations for higher-dimensional cases are not feasible. According to the current simulation results, the accuracy of break date estimates increases with the sample size. Possible extensions of the current framework include modelling multiple breaks over time. For example, a feasible modeling strategy for multiple breaks can be Chib (1998) combined with the dynamic factor structure for cross-sectional dependence.

16516116.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16516116.value: In empirical studies, researchers have to come to realize the importance of potential structural instability when modeling high-dimensional data sets, in which a large number of cross-sectional units are recorded over extended periods. Such instability could be due to technological changes, preference shifts of economic agents, and policy regimes switching. Econometric analysis of the structural change in large factor models is nontrivial because the factors are unobserved and factor loadings have to be estimated. Structural change can happen to either the factor loadings or the dynamic process of factors or both. This paper provides an econometric framework to estimate heterogeneous structural breaks in high dimensional dynamic factor models. As our model nests a few popular structural break models as special cases, it can provide a unified framework for model selection.

16516316.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16516316.value: In research and development projects, investments are often allocated over time as uncertainties about potential rewards resolve, and an investor or project manager has the flexibility of changing his actions in response to new information. In particular, project reviews provide an opportunity to make continue-or-abandon decisions in order to maximize the project's expected payoff. In this project, we intend to study how a behaviorally biased project manager may make project decisions that deviate from the optimal rational solution. In reality, we observe that unprofitable projects are often continued for much longer than they should be, resulting in huge losses of money and resources. Infrequent project reviews may further exacerbate this problem. We consider a project manager who is reference-dependent and loss averse. We intend to investigate: 1) How does the behaviorally-biased project manager's continue/abandon decisions deviate from the normative solution? 2) Does the project manager have an incentive to skip reviews, hence forgoing valuable information provided by a review? 2) How does a project's path history affect the project manager's decision to review, or continue/abandon the project? 3) How does sunk cost affect the project manager's decision to review or continue/abandon the project?

16516316.label: Major findings and research outcome
16516316.value: In uncertain environments, project reviews provide an opportunity to make "continue or abandon" decisions and thereby maximize a project's expected payoff. We experimentally investigate continue/abandon decisions in a multi-stage project under two conditions: when the project is reviewed at every stage and when review opportunities are limited. Our results confirm findings in the literature that project abandonment tends to be delayed, yet we also observe premature termination. Decisions are highly path dependent; in particular, subjects are more likely to abandon after observing reduced project value, and abandonment rate is higher near the middle|rather than near the beginning or end|of a project. Interestingly, when reviews are limited, subjects are less likely to continue a project that should be abandoned. At the same time, subjects are more inclined to review again after receiving negative (rather than positive) news. Our data are explained well by a model that incorporates three behavioral concepts|gains or losses from comparing the project value with an internal adaptive reference point, sunk cost bias, and status quo bias. Our work suggests that more frequent reviews need not lead to better project performance, and it also identifies contexts in which outside intervention is most valuable in project decision making.

16516616.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16516616.value: What kind of information catches attention? As cognitive ability is limited, people are more likely to pay attention to exciting and interesting events that generate entertainment utility. A suspenseful movie with a surprising ending is preferred to an ordinary and undramatic plot. Elections that have more uncertain outcomes are closely followed, even by non-voters. This research plans to quantify suspense and surprise in soccer matches, and analyze their impact on attention. A soccer match is suspenseful if the final result is unpredictable, for example, when two even teams play against each other. A surprising event changes people's prior beliefs significantly, for example, when the trailing team scores two quick goals and now has a chance to win the game. Using soccer betting odds obtained from one of the largest online betting exchanges, we will calculate market participants' beliefs and define suspense and surprise based on probabilities. Attention is measured by attendance in the stadium and total betting activity. Controlling for other variables such as teams' supporter base and skill level, we expect that fans and bettors participate more actively in tight matches with unexpected developments. We will also examine price efficiency in betting odds when suspense and surprise are high. Prices are expected to be less informative because of the additional bettors who react to attention-grabbing events. We would like to apply these findings to financial markets. While the literature shows plenty of evidence on investors' limited attention, there is a lack of objective ways to characterize salient financial information. The current methods usually rely on other observations such as large price movements, internet search frequency, and appearance on the front page of newspapers. Our study will help shed light on how to measure attention and its impact, as well as make new empirical implications. Investor reactions may be stronger when an unknown outcome is more unpredictable, and if there is a huge swing in expectations. 什麼樣的信息引人注目？由於認知能力是有限的，人們容易關注到會產生娛樂效用的刺激有趣活動。有一個令人驚訝的結局的懸疑電影比一齣平鋪直敘的電影吸引。即使是非選民也會密切關注一場激烈的選舉。 這項研究計劃將量化足球比賽的懸念和驚喜，並分析其對注意力的影響。一場難以預測最後結果的足球比賽是緊湊和有懸念的，比如當兩支實力相當的球隊對壘時。一個令人驚訝的事件顯著改變人們的先驗信念，例如當落後球隊迅速攻入兩球，並有機會贏得比賽。我們將使用一個大型網上博彩交易所的足球賠率，用概率去計算市場參與者的信念及量化懸念和驚喜。球場內觀眾數目和總投注金額可以量度人們的注意力。在控制了其他變量之下，如球隊的支持者和技術水平，我們認為球迷和投注者應更積極參與緊湊而意想不到的的比賽。 我們也將研究當懸念和驚喜都處於高水平時的賠率價格效率。賠率價格效率會因投注者對引人注目的事件作出反應而減少。我們希望這些研究結果能應用到金融市場。雖然文獻表明很多證據證明投資者的關注有限，但就缺乏了客觀的方式來刻畫金融信息的吸引力。目前的方法通常依賴於其他觀察，如大的價格變動，互聯網搜索頻率，以及報紙的頭版新聞。我們的研究將有助於闡明如何衡量注意力和其影響，以及作出新的研究預測。當一個未知的結果是難以估計，或預期的結果有一個巨大轉變時，投資者的反應可能會更強。

16516616.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16516616.value: The majority of scientists (97%) agree that humans cause climate change, but Yale Climate Opinion Maps 2019 show that only 67% of adults in the U.S. think global warming is happening. One reason for the discrepancy between scientific findings and aggregate beliefs is that limited cognitive resources force people to focus on attention-grabbing events. Climate change is a long-term trend and its effect may not be immediately visible; people are likely to revise their beliefs about climate change based on current local temperatures, which contain little information about the long-term average global temperature but affect them personally. Our paper tests this notion by estimating people’s opinions in 74 cities around the world with major stock exchanges and studying their follow-up actions, revealed by how investors trade on their beliefs and move stock prices.

16516916.label: Project Objectives
16516916.value: The first step of the project is to extract information from prices of options written on individual stocks to construct risk-neutral distributions of future stock returns, calculate nonparametrically the projected pricing kernels conditional on the state variables, and obtain condition physical marginal distribution for individual stocks. Using a similar, but more sophisticated approach, the conditional physical joint distribution between individual stock return and market return can also be constructed. The second step is to use the constructed conditional marginal and joint distribution of stock returns to recalculate various existing downside risk measures that are based on past returns, and to analyze their persistence properties and their return-predictive power. The various asset pricing models based on asymmetric risk measures will be tested using options-based measures.

16516916.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16516916.value: There have been many theoretical models on how rare but severe downside risk may affect asset prices and risk premiums. There are also quite a few empirical measures of downside risk proposed in the literature. These measures have been successful in predicting future returns on stock indexes and large portfolios, but not so successful in predicting future returns and explaining the cross-sectional differences in expected returns on individual stocks. The problem comes from the fact that rare disasters may not realized in a finite sample, especially for individual stocks. Therefore, both downside risk measures based on a finite sample of realized return in the past and tests using a finite sample of future returns do not work well for individual stocks. Cross-sections of prices of options on individual stocks contain distributional information which is forward looking and do not depend on realized returns. Therefore, downside risk measures based option prices can sidestep problems faced by realized-return based downside risk measures. The purpose of this project is to develop methodologies of using option prices to construct downside risk measures, which improve realized return based downside risk measures. 16516916.label: Major findings and research outcome
16516916.value: In this project, we set out to investigate how skewness of the idiosyncratic component of the individual stock returns can be inferred from the prices of options written on the stocks. The skewness of the idiosyncratic component of individual stocks is different that the skewness of the index returns, which is contributed by all stocks jointly. To this end, we use the usual market model in which an individual stock return has one component related to the entire market through beta and the idiosyncratic component with its volatility and skewness. We use options data to infer risk-neutral market beta and the risk-neutral idiosyncratic volatility and skewness. We relax the assumption of zero risk-neutral idiosyncratic skewness imposed in the literature and assume an exponentially modified normal distribution for the idiosyncratic component of the market model under the risk-neutral probability. We find that the idiosyncratic skewness is mostly negative and has large variations. The resultant conditional market beta estimates possess nicer properties than those estimated under the assumption of zero idiosyncratic skewness. They are on average lower those estimated by other methods in the literature, and closer to the physical beta estimate. Allowing non-zero risk-neutral idiosyncratic skewness is the key to improve the risk-neutral beta estimation since assuming zero risk-neutral idiosyncratic skewness when it is in fact negative (positive) biases the risk-neutral beta upwards (downwards). The paper is accepted and presented in the 31st Australasian Finance and Banking Conference and New Zealand Finance Meeting 2018. It is currently under review.

16516916.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16516916.value: Downside risk of an individual stock, view from investors’ point of view, refers to the probability and the magnitude of a large decline in the stock price, in addition to its usual fluctuation with the entire market. Such an event causes huge losses to investors, so the assessment of the probability and magnitude is important before it happens, so investors can make decisions on whether the stock is worth holding. But since large declines do not happen frequently, so the probability and the magnitude are difficult to estimate from the historic data by an average investor. Such information exists in options, which are traded more by institutions and experienced investors. Extracting such information, however, is non-trivial, involving separating the usual fluctuation with the entire market and the magnitude and skewness of the idiosyncratic component of the stock returns. This project proposed one methodology in doing that and achieved success to certain extent.

16517316.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16517316.value: Media outlets have linked a dramatic increase in white-collar crime in recent years to the Global Financial Crisis and the subsequent economic recession. This project examines whether the financial crisis spurred white-collar crime as has been suggested by the press. To answer this important question we will use data from detailed administrative registers on reported crime, criminal charges, and criminal convictions linked to demographic and financial data. The Global Financial Crisis might have led to increases in white-collar crime for several reasons: First, the crisis affected individuals' income and wealth through financial losses or by worsening labor market conditions, and resulting financial difficulties might spur white-collar crime. Second, the financial crisis might have impacted norms in society. As the crisis (by many) is viewed as a crisis resulting from unethical behavior in the financial sector, the crisis might have changed norms about white-collar crimes. Third, the crisis might impact enforcement and/or punishment capabilities, resulting in an increasing number of detected and convicted white-collar crimes. We hypothesize that negative experiences in the banking sector has increased the propensity to commit white-collar crime. We propose to test this hypothesis by investigating the determinants of white-collar. Our preliminary analysis suggests that most white-collar crimes are committed by repeated offenders. The crisis is unlikely to change their behavior, and they would have continued it anyway. The main question is therefore whether the financial crisis has led to an increase in white-collar crime on the extensive margin. To establish a causal link between the financial crisis and white-collar crime, we propose to use stock market losses due to bankrupties as exeogenous variation in financial losses. Our identification strategy exploits individuals' exposure to the financial crisis through investment in bank stocks. In the aftermath of the crisis, some banks defaulted, while others did not. Using a difference-in-differences strategy we propose to examines whether these financial losses increased the incidence of white-collar crime. Preliminary evidence suggest that the incidence of white-collar crime increases by more than twofold for investors with first-hand experiences with bank defaults, while remaining relatively constant for a control sample of individuals with similar investment styles. To this end, we expect to devliver new insights on the determinants of white collar crime, and whether experiences in financial markets have negative externalies in the form of white-collar crime. 媒体都把在急剧增加的白领犯罪和近年来全球金融危机和随后的经济衰退联系在一起。 本项目研究金融危机是否刺激了白领犯罪。我们将使用在犯罪报道，刑事指控和刑事定罪详细的行政寄存器中的数据把这一重要问题挂钩。 全球金融危机可能已经遭受白领犯罪而增加有以下几个原因：首先，金融危机影响个人的收入和财富通 金融卸载或恶化的劳动力市场状况，及由此产生的经济困难可能会刺激白领犯罪。其次，金融危机可能会影响社会的常态。随着危机（许多）被看作是危机在金融领域的不道德行为致使，这场危机可能会改变有关规范白领犯罪。第三，危机可能会影响执法和/或处罚的能力，在越来越多的检测和被定罪的白领犯罪而造成的。 我们假设在银行业负面经验增加的倾向2犯下白领犯罪。我们提出了两种测试这个假设被调查白领的决定因素。 我们的初步分析表明，大多数的白领犯罪被屡犯者承诺。这场危机是不可能的2转换自己的行为，价格比它的花哨无论如何都会继续它。主要的问题是有存在无论是金融危机已经经历了两次上升项白领犯罪的粗放边际。二，建立金融危机和白领犯罪之间的因果关系，提出了两种使用卸载股市本月两次bankrupties作为exeogenous变化在金融卸载。 我们识别战略利用个人接触到的金融危机通过 投资银行股。在危机之后，一些银行违约，而 另一些则没有。使用不同的功能于不同的策略，我们提出了两个检 无论这些金融卸载增加白领犯罪的发生。初步证据表明，白领犯罪提高了两倍于与银行违约的第一手经验的投资者更多的发病率，同时保持具有相似的投资风格的个体的对照样品相对稳定。 为此，我们期待在发表白领的决定因素的新见解 金融市场的犯罪，以及是否有经验的负面externalies 白领犯罪形式。

16517316.label: Realisation of objectives
16517316.value: The objectives of the project have been fully realized, and resulted in the working paper "Do Financial Misconduct Experiences Spur White-Collar Crime?". The results in the paper follow the outline of the reseach objectives, and are summarized below: Considering these plausible explanations for the increase in white-collar crime, we estimate a simple econometric model which enables us to make an out of sample prediction of the prevalence of white-collar crime in the aftermath of the financial crisis. In the pre-crisis period, we fit a logit model to variation in individuals propensity to commit white-collar crime using individual characteristics such as age, gender, family status, income, wealth, and employment status. We also include variables to capture differences in economic conditions, such as becoming unemployed or changes in financial wealth. To control for heterogeneity in policing across location and time we account for changes in municipality-level rates of criminal reports to criminal charges and municipality fixed effects. Based on this model, we predict the level of white-collar crime in the post-crisis period using the post-crisis observed individual characteristics and policing rates. Changes in socioeconomic conditions around the crisis does an inadequate job at explaining the growth in the incidence of white-collar crime after the crisis. Adverse economic conditions (like unemployment or declining wealth) or increased policing only explains about 43 percent of the increase in white-collar crimes after the crisis, leaving the majority percent accounted for. In comparison, economic conditions and policing rates explain about 97% of the incidence of white-collar crime in the pre-crisis period. In summary, our simple predictive model cannot account for the increase in the incidence of white-collar crime, and motives a more careful analysis of our main hypothesis that individuals' experiences with financial misconduct are so powerful that they lead to future criminal activity. We investigate whether financial misconduct experiences spur white-collar crime, we exploit a unique institutional setting affecting the retail banking sector in Denmark. As a plausible source of experiences with financial misconduct, we identify individuals who were customers (i.e. depositors and/or investors) of regional retail banks—a common phenomenon in Denmark prior to the financial crisis—some of which defaulted due to financial misconduct in the aftermath of the crisis. In total eight banks defaulted of which the Danish Financial Supervisory Authority charged senior executive in five banks with financial misconduct, fraud, insider trading and of breaching trust with banking customers. We find strong evidence that first-hand experiences with financial misconduct have significant implications on the rate of convicted white-collar crimes for those exposed. Our results suggest that financial misconduct experiences increased the incidence of white-collar crime convictions after a bank’s default by more than two to three times. These individuals are subsequently more likely to engage in fraud-related white-collar crime such as tax, credit card, check, or unemployment related frauds and were primarily driven by the extensive margin of financial crime: individuals without prior criminal records. Furthermore, the convictions constitute serious economic crime. More than 60% of the convictions identified in our empirical setting result in prison sentencing – a rare penalty in Denmark. To convincingly identify the effect of financial misconduct experiences, we perform a difference-in-differences estimation that compares the probability of conviction for customers of banks which defaulted after the financial crisis and where senior executives subsequently were charged with financial misconduct to customers of banks which also defaulted, but where the senior management where not charged. The difference-in-differences setting allow us to disentangle three potential mechanisms behind the motive for white-collar crime: i) a pecuniary effect due to financial losses, ii) information or social learning about penalties and benefits of white-collar crime, and iii) a non-pecuniary effect driven by changing views on what is morally just or the social utility associated with committing white-collar crime, either because individuals view the norms of society differently, or because they feel cheated and seek some form of retribution. The strength of our difference-in-differences setting is that the between subject differences effectively eliminates the wealth effect, because all customers face financial losses, while the inclusion of time fixed-effects effectively eliminates the social learning or information channel, because news about the financial misconduct were disseminated nationwide. We can further ensure that the results are not driven by differences in the salience of the financial misconduct events in specific geographic locations by including location-time fixed effects in our specification. This specification also ensure that our results are not driven by geographic or time differences in policing. To this end, our results suggest that first-hand experience with financial misconduct may loosen a ‘moral constraint’ among individuals, which induces them to partake in behavior they may have previously perceived as wrong. In our setting, the financial misconduct experience is likely to have been a significantly large and salient shock to individuals’ beliefs on what is morally justifiable. Retail banks charged with financial misconduct were given a focal point in national and local media. Many media organizations in Denmark reported how senior level executives contributed to their bank's demise, costing tax payers and shareholders billions of Danish Kroner, yet were retiring with generous pension packages.

16517316.value: We use police records on individuals’ criminal activity to investigate whether personal experiences with financial misconduct spur white-collar crime. 16517616.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16517616.value: Legal protection for shareholders is one of the most important governance mechanisms among others such as product market competition, large shareholders and corporate control market (Shleifer and Vishny, 1997). While shareholders’ power can discipline managers’ opportunistic behavior that hurt both shareholders and debtholders, granting stronger power to shareholders may not necessarily benefit debtholders. This is because interests of shareholders and debtsholders are not fully aligned, and strong power of shareholders enables them to expropriate debtholders opportunistically. The existing literature also shows that governance mechanisms addressing agency conflicts between shareholders and managers may or may not benefit debtholders. For example, while monitoring by institutional investors appear to benefit both shareholders and debtholders, other governance mechanisms, such as product market competition and shareholder rights that facilitate corporate control market, benefit shareholders but could hurt debtholders. Shareholder litigation is an important element of legal protection for shareholders. Research (e.g., La Porta et al., 2006; Hail and Leuz, 2006) shows that laws that facilitate private enforcement through shareholders litigation benefit stock market development and enhance shareholder value. However, there is relatively little evidence on how shareholder litigation rights affect welfare of debtholders. Answering this question is important because debt is an important source of finance for corporations and agency conflicts faced by debtholders also hinder economic development. This project will examine the effect of shareholder litigation rights against directors and officers on debtholders using the 2001 Nevada legislative change in corporate laws as a natural experiment. The 2001 legislative change significantly reduces directors’ and officers’ legal liabilities for breaking their fiduciary duties to shareholders and therefore weakens shareholders litigation rights. In particular, this project will examine how the 2001 Nevada legislative change affects the cost of debt and how the effects vary across firms. To further identify channels, this project will also examine the effects of the 2001 Nevada legislative change on corporate decisions of operation, investment, and financing that may affect debtholders’ interests, and on firm risks. Finally, I will examine whether Nevada firms change their executive compensation and accounting policies in order to adjust the incentives of managers after the legislative change. 對股東的法律保護是最重要的公司治理機制之一。儘管股東權力可以約束管理者傷害股東及債權人的機會主義行為，但給予股東過大的權力並不一定有利於債權人。這是因為股東与債權人的利益并不完全一致。現有的文獻也表明有利於緩解股東及管理層利益衝突的公司治理機制未必有利於解決股東与債權人之間的利益衝突。股東訴訟權利是股權法律保護的一個重要組成部分。現有研究表明，便於股東訴訟的法律制度安排能夠促進股票市場發展及提高股東價值。但關於股東訴訟權利如何影響債權人利益的研究卻相對較少。回答這個問題很重要，因為債務融資是企業融資的重要來源。債權人面對代理衝突也會阻礙了經濟的發展。本課題將利用2001年美國內華達州公司法的變化來研究股東對於公司高管及董事訴訟權利是如何影響債權人利益的。2001年華達州變更了公司法，顯著減少董事及高管受股東起訴其違反受託責任的法律風險，削弱了股東訴訟權利。本課題將研究2001年內華達州的立法變化如何影響債務成。為了進一步明確該公司法變更影響債權人的機理，本課題還將研究2001年公司法變更對公司經營，投資和融資決策,以及高管薪酬和會計政策的影響。

16517616.label: Realisation of objectives
16517616.value: I have achieved all the project objectives. This project has generated a working paper titled “Litigation Risk and Debt Contracting: Evidence from a Natural Experiment". This paper is under revision for resubmission to the 3rd round review in Journal of Law and Economics (JLE). This paper examines the impact of the reduced litigation risk caused by the 2001 Nevada legislative change on Nevada firms’ loan contract terms and related borrower-lender agency conflicts. Using a difference-in-differences analysis, this paper finds that this legislative change leads to less favorable loan contract terms for Nevada firms: higher spread and more restrictive covenants. In addition, after the legislative change, Nevada firms with severe borrower-lender agency conflicts take more risk, increase payout through stock repurchase, and reduce capital investment and equity issuance. Collectively, these results suggest that the reduced litigation risk exacerbates the borrower-lender agency conflicts. I have also found that Nevada firms increase their accounting conservatism after the 2001 Nevada legislative change. As accounting conservatism may not be the interests of readers of JLE, we do not include this result in the submission to JLE.

16518816.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16518816.value: Are women given worse financial advice than men? Although numerous studies show evidence consistent with gender bias in labor market (hiring) and bargaining contexts (negotiations), contexts that are clearly vital for the well-being of an individual, no study has specifically looked at gender bias in financial advice. Financial decisions, which are also significant for the well-being of an individual, are often influenced by advice from others, including professional financial advisors. It is therefore important to examine whether the quality of advice of investment advisors varies based on the gender of the advisee. If we do find gender bias, we would also like to learn whether this bias is attenuated if the competition amongst financial advisors increases, and whether this bias is attenuated if the advisees are more financially sophisticated. An important aspect of our study would be to test for evidence of gender bias with a field experiment – specifically using an audit study methodology. This involves sending trained actors to engage with real financial advisors in Hong Kong and documenting the kind of interaction and advice provided. A second important aspect of our study is that, by restricting the scope of financial advice to just asking advice on which Hang-Seng index fund to invest in, the “quality” of advice is easily measured: it is negatively related to the fee on the fund. As investing in the lowest fee index fund is the optimal choice for everyone, irrespective of gender and other advisee characteristics or other advisor characteristics, any differences in advice across advisee gender has to be interpreted as gender bias. Such unambiguous interpretations of bias are not possible in the large number of gender bias and discrimination assessment studies that have been done in the context of labor markets. The reason is that gender (or race) may still be informative about the productivity of the potential employee, thereby making it a justifiable input in the decision to hire. That is not so in our case. This is the third important aspect of our study. This study would be of interest to financial market regulators and self-governing bodies of financial advisors in Hong Kong. In addition, we would obtain an independent assessment of the quality of financial advice provided by financial advisors in Hong Kong. Furthermore, understanding the details of a typical interaction between financial advisors and clients would be of interest to retail investors in Hong Kong.

16518816.label: Realisation of objectives
16518816.value: On March 1, 2018, RGC permitted me to drop Project Objective no. 2. The other four objectives were completed 100%. To be specific, Objective 1: We found that women receive worse financial advice than men from financial planners, but not from security firms. The bias was particularly acute for women with higher risk tolerance, with higher confidence, and with a domestic outlook. The research design involved sending undercover trained men and women to all firms in Hong Kong that advise retail investors. These auditors pretended to be clients, and asked for advice. Advisors and auditors were matched randomly, and auditor attributes like risk tolerance, confidence and geographic outlook were experimentally varied. Objective 3: We found that the above gender bias is not attenuated by financial sophistication, suggesting that discrimination was taste-based rather than statistical. Objective 4: We found in the same study that the quality of financial advice provided in Hong Kong is bad. About 40% of advisees are told to buy just single risky securities or only Hong Kong stocks. Objective 5: Our study was covered in Bloomberg News on September 5, 2020. Hopefully, regulators read it. The trade body of financial advisors certainly did. I quote from the Bloomberg media report: "Sally Wong, chief executive officer of industry organization the Hong Kong Investment Funds Association declined to comment on the findings of the study."

16518816.label: Major findings and research outcome
16518816.value: We conduct an audit study in Hong Kong to find out if women receive worse financial advice. Specifically, we send trained undercover men and women, posing as potential clients, to visit all 65 local financial advisory firms in Hong Kong that cater to local retail investors. Since financial advice can include recommendations to buy different financial products that vary simultaneously along many different dimensions, it is difficult to classify the advice as unilaterally good or bad. We rely on the observation from classical finance that regardless of risk appetite, it is smarter for an investor to purchase a basket of securities than a few risky securities, and it is smarter for an investor to purchase a portfolio of securities from many countries than a portfolio of securities only from the investor’s home country. This is because, by purchasing just a few risky individual securities or by purchasing only risky securities from the home country, the investor bears idiosyncratic risk that is not rewarded by extra expected return. Accordingly, we define the financial advice as “undiversified” if only individual risky securities were recommended, and as “home-biased” if it only includes local Hong Kong securities. We interpret undiversified or home-biased advice as dominated advice, and estimate whether men or women are more likely to receive dominated advice. We then randomly assign attributes – risk tolerance, confidence, and home-biased outlook – to the auditors, and then randomly random assign the auditors to financial advisors. Results from our study suggests that the incentive structure of the advisers affect the propensity to offer worse financial advice. While the advisors who focus more on short-term relationships (securities firms) offer worse financial advice on average than the ones who emphasize long-term client relationship (financial planners), it is the latter whose advice differs across client’s gender. We find that financial planners are more likely to provide undiversified and home-biased advice to female clients than to male clients. Delving deeper, we show that the financial planner’s response to change in client’s attributes – risk tolerance, confidence and home-biasedness – differs between male and female clients. The financial planner’s propensity to give worse advice increases with client’s risk tolerance, confidence and home-biasedness more for the female clients than for the male clients. This leads to our main result: financial planner’s gender discrimination is concentrated among the large confidence, big risk tolerance or domestic outlook auditor clients.

16518816.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16518816.value: Based on our research, we would like to write a policy brief to HK regulators on how to ameliorate gender bias in financial advice in Hong Kong.

16518816.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16518816.value: 1) Trained undercover men and women, posing as potential clients, visited all 65 local financial advisory firms in Hong Kong that cater to local retail investors. 2) Each individual was assigned to an “avatar” consisting of a specific combination of risk tolerance, confidence and geographic outlook attributes. 3) We conservatively define financial advice as “bad” if only individual or local securities are recommended, and find that securities firms are more likely to give bad advice than financial planners are.Financial planners, but not securities firms, provide bad advice to women more often than to men. 4) This gender difference in advice is driven by the more risk-tolerant, more confident, and more domestic outlook women. 5) Our theoretical model interprets these results in terms of advisors’ conflicts of interest and statistical discrimination. However, the data do not allow us to rule out taste-based discrimination.

16520116.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16520116.value: In this project, we study collusion among experts who provide both diagnoses and repair services. It is well known that experts have a natural incentive to defraud their clients by exaggerating the severity of their problems in order to charge them for an expensive instead of cheap repair (Wolinsky, 1993, Emons, 1997, 2001, Fong, 2005, Dulleck, and Kerschbamer, 2006, Liu, 2009). Consumers' threat to search for second opinions upon recommendation of the expensive repair mitigates this incentive problem and improves efficiency of the market, compared to the alternative that they do not search for second opinions. However, consumers' search for second opinions can also raise the highest profits achievable among colluding experts. This is because after a consumer rejects an expert's recommendation for an expensive repair, if she continues to visit other experts, she will eventually accept the treatment by another expert in the industry. In this research project, we propose an unexpected consequence of consumers’ search for second opinions: it makes it easier for experts to collude. In the typical commodity market where n sellers collude, the sellers each will get 1/n of the industry profit. When a seller undercuts the other sellers, the seller will capture the entire industry profit, i.e., scale up its profit by n folds, for one period before triggering a price war and losing all future profits. When experts collude, on the other hand, the deviating expert is no longer able to capture the entire industry profit before triggering a price war. When experts are colluding, part of their profits come for clients' first visits and part of their profits come from clients searching for second opinions after visiting another expert. When an expert undercuts other experts with attractive prices, the expert is able to attract all the clients. However, he is unable to capture the entire industry profit. This is because some of the customers who visit him will go to other experts to search for second opinions upon his recommendation of an expensive repair. This implies that some of the industry profits will still be captured by non-deviating experts, preventing the deviating experts from capturing the entire industry profit for one period before triggering a price war. This explains why colluding experts have a weaker incentive to deviate from the collusive equilibrium, rendering collusion easier to sustain. 本項目主要研究專家在為客戶提供診斷和維修服務時所產生的合謀行為。眾所周知，專家存在激勵去誇大客戶問題的嚴重性從而欺騙客戶，以收取更昂貴的維修費用 （見Wolinsky, 1993, Emons, 1997, 2001, Fong, 2005, Dulleck, and Kerschbamer, 2006, Liu, 2009）。消費者因維修費用過於昂貴而質疑專家給出的診斷意見時，可能會繼續尋求其他專家的意見以做出決策，從而緩解上述的激勵問題并提高市場效率。然而，這種不斷尋求專家意見的可能性也會提高專家在合謀時所能獲得的最大利潤。這是由於，消費者即使暫時拒絕了某位專家提供的維修服務并繼續訪問其他專家，最終也會接受行業內另一位專家的意見并支付維修費用。在這一研究項目中，我們提出了消費者不斷尋求專家意見所導致的意想不到的結果：使得專家之間的合謀更為容易。在典型的商品市場中，如果有n家廠商合謀，每一家廠商將得到行業利潤的 1/n。其中一家廠商通過略微降低價格就能獲得整個行業利潤，即在引發價格戰之前將其當期的利潤擴大n倍。另一方面，如果專家合謀，沒有任何一位專家能通過降價在引發價格戰之前獲得整個行業利潤。這是因為，專家合謀的利潤一部分是來自於第一次尋求意見的客戶，另一部分則來自於已經得到過其他專家的意見的客戶。其中一位專家即使能通過提出更有吸引力的價格去暂时搶奪其他專家的所有客戶，也無法阻止這些客戶中的一部分人在得知需要支付昂貴維修費用的診斷時繼續尋求其他專家的意見，從而最終無法獲得這部分客戶的利潤。這就解釋了為什麼專家在合謀時有較弱的激勵去偏離均衡，從而使得合謀更容易持續。

16520116.label: Realisation of objectives
16520116.value: We achieved object 1 by 100%. We construct a model in which infinitely lived experts serve a sequence of short-lived customers, each with a serious or minor problem, through competition in price. Each problem requires a specific treatment to repair and these treatments are not substitutable. Customers do not know the type of their problems and rely on the experts for both diagnosis and treatment. Also, customers do not know which of the two treatments has been actually provided as long as the problem is repaired. At the beginning of each period, experts simultaneously announce two prices respectively to charge for the minor and serious treatment respectively which become public information. A customer arrives in the market and Nature draws the loss of her problem according to the prior distribution. After observing the prices, the customer decides whether to visit any expert and which expert to visit. When a customer visits an expert, the recommendation subgame begins. The expert first observes the customer's problem, and recommends a minor treatment, a serious treatment, or refuses to provide any treatment. If the expert offers to fix the problem, the customer decides whether or not to accept the offer. If the customer accepts the expert's offer, the expert must repair her problem at the quoted price. If the expert refuses to provide any treatment or the customer rejects the expert's offer, the customer decides whether to visit another expert and which expert to visit again. If the customer visits another expert, a new recommendation subgame begins. This process goes on within the same period until the customer's problem is treated, the customer gives up treating the problem, or there is no more expert to visit. We assume that, except for the first visit to an expert, a customer has to incur a sufficiently small search cost for each additional expert she visits, and the search cost converges to zero. The model is general, flexible, and easily extended. 2. We achieved 80% of the second objective. We first characterize the collusive equilibrium when search cost is sufficiently high that second opinions is not allowed as a benchmark. Experts play the equilibrium in Fong (2005) on the punishment path, where all experts gain zero profit. In the collusive equilibrium, experts truthfully recommend the treatment for the customer with either problem. A customer randomly visits an expert when arriving at the market. The customer accepts a minor treatment with probability one but may reject a serious treatment. By undercutting the collusive prices, a deviating expert can capture the entire industry profit in one period before losing profits in all future periods. Thus, collusion among experts is as easy to sustain as in the standard search good case without search for second opinions. However, the first-best profit cannot be attained as the industry profit even under collusion. Then we characterize the collusive equilibrium when search cost is very small so customers find it optimal to search for second opinions. We assume that experts play the equilibrium in Wolinsky (1993) on the punishment path, where all experts gain zero profit. In the collusive equilibrium, for the customer with the serious problem, experts recommend the serious treatment with probability one; for the customer with the minor problem, they recommend the minor treatment with a probability less than one and recommend the serious treatment with the complementary probability. A customer randomly visits an expert when arriving at the market. If recommended the minor treatment on the first visit, the customer accepts it with probability one. If recommended the serious treatment on the first visit, the customer accepts it with a probability less than one and searches for a second opinion with the complementary probability. If recommended any treatment on the second visit, the customer accepts it with probability one. Whenever a customer is recommended no treatment, she exits the market. When an expert deviates in price, even if he can attract the customer to visit him first, the customer will reject his recommendation with positive probability to ensure that the expert makes honest recommendations, making it unable to capture the entire industry profit before triggering a price war. Thus, collusion among experts is easier to sustain than in the standard search good case with search for second opinions. Also, we show that experts can attain (almost) the first-best profit under collusion when the search cost is sufficiently small. On the equilibrium path, even though a customer rejects the first expert's serious treatment recommendation with positive probability, her problem will be treated by the next expert she visits. It is prohibitively challenging to characterize equilibria for all search costs levels. So our comparative statics results are incomplete. 3. We achieve objective 3 by 100%. We show that consumers gain zero expected surplus in the collusive equilibrium that we characterize, whether search for second opinions is allowed or not. Thus, the consumer harm due to experts’ collusive behavior depends on consumers’ expected surplus without collusion in both cases. Suppose each customer has a problem which is either serious (s), with probability α, or minor (m), with probability 1-α. For a customer with the problem i∈{m,s}, denote the customer’s loss as l_i if the problem is left untreated and the repair cost to treat the problem as r_i. Also denote the search cost as k where k converges to zero. Then in the case where search for second opinions is not allowed, the consumer harm due to experts' collusive behavior is given by (1-α)( l_m-r_m); in the case where search for second opinions is allowed, the consumer harm due to experts' collusive behavior is given by (1-α)( l_m-r_m)+ α( l_s-r_s-k). 4. We achieve objective 4 by 80%. When search cost is sufficiently high that consumers don't search for second opinions, efficiency is unambiguously higher under collusion. Moreover, when search costs are low and consumers search for second opinions, efficiency may be higher under collusion, which happens when search cost is sufficiently close to zero or when the prior probability of a serious problem is high enough. These findings suggest that the welfare effects of enforcing competition policies on markets for expert services can be very different from enforcing competition policies on regular products or services markets. We believe these are insightful policy implications. It is unclear whether there can be more which we have not identified.

16520116.label: Major findings and research outcome
16520116.value: This paper studies tacit collusion among experts with private information about customers' problems. We provide a canonical framework for analyzing collusion among experts which incorporates search costs. One interesting discovery we made is that collusion among experts is facilitated by customers' search for second opinions which ironically is the customers' defense against the experts' incentive to defraud them. When search for second opinions is not allowed, collusion among experts is as easy to sustain as in the standard search good case. This is because a deviating expert can capture the entire industry profit in one period before losing profits in all future periods. On the other hand, when search for second opinions is allowed, we show that collusion is more readily sustainable among experts than among sellers of typical products or services. On the equilibrium path, through search for second opinions, a customer's problem is fixed with probability one, and the total surplus from repairs is split evenly among experts. Even though a deviating expert can attract the customer with probability one by undercutting the equilibrium prices as in collusion among search-good sellers, the attracted customer will search for second opinions with positive probability and have her problem fixed by non-deviating experts. The deviating firms' inability to capture the entire industry profit before triggering a price war renders collusion among experts easier to sustain than collusion among search-good sellers. Finally, although collusion among experts harms consumer welfare unambiguously, we show that it may improve efficiency if the search cost is sufficiently small. This is because under collusion, each consumer's problem is still fixed with probability one, while the frequency of searching for second opinions becomes lower.

16520116.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16520116.value: For future research, one extension is to consider the possibility that the type of the goods or services provided is observable and verifiable, but the outcome is not, so experts cannot be held accountable for an unresolved problem. This assumption is termed Verifiability by Dulleck and Kerschbamer (2006). Under the Verifiability assumption, an expert may provide goods or services which are either insufficient to fix the serious problem or unnecessary to fix the minor problem. Furthermore, it would be interesting to introduce adverse selection on prices. For example, suppose prices are observable but are subject to change after diagnosis so that the customer can infer her type from the prices offered. Moreover, some assumptions can be relaxed in the analysis to get more general results. For example, we can consider the case where customers are allowed to revisit the same expert within the same period, and the case where experts only get noisy signals in the diagnosis of the customer’s problem.

16520116.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16520116.value: Services provided by experts such as doctors, lawyers, car mechanics, and home improvement contractors are different from typical commodities or services because these experts not only provide repair services but also provide diagnoses of their customers' problems. Studies have shown the market inefficiencies caused by the asymmetric information between experts and their customers. However, to the best of our knowledge, no research specifically studies collusion among experts which can further harm consumer welfare. This gap in the literature is significant because collusion among experts is empirically relevant and potentially different from collusion among typical sellers of goods or services. First, experts post multiple prices for problems of different severities and they also decide which price to charge after diagnosing each customer's problem. Second, the customer does not have to accept the expert's recommended treatment after his diagnosis and can search for second opinions. The current project aims to provide a canonical framework for analyzing collusion among experts which incorporates search costs. The results of this study will help us understand how collusion among experts will affect consumer welfare and social efficiency and may help us draw practical policy implications from our welfare analysis.

16528116.label: Project Title(Chinese)
16528116.value: 投票率對美國總統選舉的影響

16528116.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16528116.value: 民主國家依靠選舉聚集其公民的不同意見和選擇。然而，選舉所聚集的資訊, 只限於有參加投票的人。有關選舉權 擴大的文献己羅列參加選者的重要性, 有涉及南非種族隔離後選舉情況（Kroth et al，2013年），美國南方1965年投票權後訂法案 (Cascio and Washington, 2013; Husted and Kenny, 1997）和美國各州婦女參選權法律後（Miller，2008年）的各種狀態。減低某類選民的投票成本會確定影響選舉政策（Fujiwara，2015年）。 雖然大多數民主國家享有普選權，但投票率卻強往往差人意。選民因投票成本高而不投票, 他們的選擇因沒參與而煙沒。如果他們和因投票成本低的人有異, 選舉結果便有偏頗。因此，選舉能否反映公民的選擇，代表性有否不足，在成熟的民主國家也是一大命題。 選舉意願聚集和代表性不足的也是政策問題。某類選民的代表性不足引出 “強制投票” 的建議（見例如，Lijphart，1997）。較為溫和的政策建議有, 網絡投票，限制較少的註冊，選舉日為假期，也是由類似的擔憂推動。了解投票成本如何影響選民的意願, 可以提供關於這些政策建議更明智的討論的基礎。 在這個項目中，我們將探討是如何聚集選民的意願，這關鍵取決於是否投票成本和選擇是否相關。特別是，我們將表明投票成本，偏好和投票有效性感知可以被識別，並使用從2004年美國總統大選的縣級投票數據來作估算。然後，我們將模擬下強制投票的選舉結果。模擬和實際結果之間的差異將容許我們量化選擇性非參與的效果。 這項目將揭示哪些公民團體投票成本高, 而對選舉有效性存疑。因此，結果將顯示誰代表性不足。此外，我們將恢復這些未被充分代表的群體的選擇。結合這些結果將顯示美國大選有否聚集公民的選擇。此外，這項目將調查全民皆投栗的選舉結果。

16600916.label: Project Title(Chinese)
16600916.value: 雨傘傘運動後, 香港公眾支持民主的原因

16600916.label: Project Objectives
16600916.value: Measure and explain the level of public support for democracy in Hong Kong, based on related theoretical literature and Hong Kong’s context. Emancipative values and different conceptions of democracy will be especially heeded in explaining the support for genuine democracy, while socio-demographic factors will be included to assess any societal division concerning support for democracy. The theory of human emancipation maintains that the spread of “emancipative values” can advance democracy and revitalize civil society in different parts of the world. This research will be the first test in Hong Kong for investigating whether the emancipative values enhance the support for democracy here (Welzel & Alvarez, 2014; Welzel, 2013). The research will provide the pioneering investigation of its kind in Hong Kong, against the backdrop of the epochal event of Umbrella Movement. Public conceptions of democracy in Hong Kong will be studied, using measures developed by the World Values Survey (Welzel and Alvarez, 2014). The varied conceptions of democracy in Hong Kong will help more reliably assess the level of support for genuine democracy in Hong Kong. The study will also illuminate whether the exclusively liberal conception of democracy will shape the level of mass support for democracy.
