17138616.label: Realisation of objectives
17138616.value: Summary of project towards realization of objectives -------------------------------------------------------- 1. Brief background: Respiratory motion is a significant challenge for liver diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI). To date, free breathing is one of three major motion control methods for liver DWI data acquisition and shows better reproducibility than breath holding and respiratory gating. However, the image quality of free-breathing liver DWI is still suboptimal when using single-shot echo-planar imaging for the data acquisition. 2. Goal: The ultimate goal of this project is to development a robust MRI technique that can enable high-quality free-breathing liver diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI). 3. Research activities and outputs: In the 24 months of projection duration, we have completed three objectives and successfully extended the technical developments to benefit other MRI studies. The brief summary of research activities and achievements of each objective is shown at below. Objective 1: We have successfully developed a DW-Propeller-EPI pulse sequence on clinical MRI scanner that is compatible with arbitrary oblique plane slice orientation and off-center field-of-view (FOV) acquisition. The velocity compensation (VC) diffusion preparation gradient feature has been integrated into the developed DW-Propeller-EPI pulse sequence as well. We have tested the developed DW-Propeller-EPI on 40 subjects with and without VC diffusion preparation, and examined the blade images before Propeller-EPI reconstruction. The VC diffusion preparation could significantly reduce the signal loss due to cardiac and respiratory motions. However, we have found that the prolonged TE caused by the use of VC diffusion preparation scheme could lead to reduced signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), resulting in significant change of measured apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) values. This finding is coherent to the result observed in a collaborative study related to parotid gland ADC measurement (KM Chien, et. al., “Is ADC Affected by Distortion of EP-DWI for Distinguishing Parotid Gland Tumor- To Compare ADC of Parotid Gland in Echo-Planar DWI and PROPELLER DWI”, ISMRM 2018, #3214). Besides, the developed DW-Propeller-EPI pulse sequence has enabled the high-quality DWI for other applications, such as the brain diffusion-tensor imaging. We have used the developed pulse sequence and a joint reconstruction algorithm to accelerate the conventional Propeller-EPI acquisition, which usually takes longer scantime than other multi-shot techniques. In the light of this improvement, we can obtain better balance between acquisition time and image quality. This development can also benefit the imaging-guided robotic system for intra-operative MRI for enabling high-quality real-time MRI. Objective 2: We have successfully developed a reconstruction algorithm for the free-breathing liver DWI data acquired with the DW-Propeller-EPI pulse sequence developed in Objective 1. Our development was based on the original Propeller-EPI reconstruction algorithm. We have firstly applied and refined the phase cycled reconstruction (PCR) method for the Nyquist ghost correction of each blade data. We have found that the non-linear phase correction along phase-encoding direction was very time consuming by using PCR method, although it is effective for reducing the ghost artifact in Propeller-EPI acquisition. To improve the efficiency of ghost correction before Propeller-EPI reconstruction, we have developed a self-reference method and successfully extended it to eliminate ghost artifact in 2D and 3D interleaved-EPI acquisition with arbitrary number of shots for different applications (i.e., functional MRI). This development made the reconstruction of DW-Propeller-EPI data more robust and efficient. Afterward, we have embedded a motion correction scheme into Propeller-EPI reconstruction pipeline. The proposed motion correction scheme included the measurement of correlations, and non-rigid body registrations among blade data. In the light of above developments, we have successfully reconstructed free-breathing liver DWI data acquired with DW-Propeller-EPI sequence, with less image blurring compared with the same data reconstructed with original Propeller-EPI algorithm. Objective 3: We have collected in-vivo data from 40 healthy subjects that included three routine single-shot acquisition methods (breath-hold, free-breathing, and respiratory-triggering), and two multi-shot acquisition methods (respiratory-triggering interleaved-EPI, and free-breathing DW-Propeller-EPI). After the quantitative and qualitative assessments, proposed DW-Propeller-EPI showed higher SNR and better geometric fidelity than all other acquisition methods. The measured ADC values were also assessed for different acquisition methods. In the assessment of image quality, the DW-Propeller-EPI data showed less misalignment of liver edge than conventional acquisition because the non-rigid body registration was implemented in Propeller-EPI reconstruction. This evaluation study has also provided sufficient evidence for demonstrating that the free-breathing liver DWI using DW-Propeller-EPI acquisition is superior to routine single-shot acquisition under free-breathing condition. Besides, we have also compared the DW-Propeller-EPI to another multi-shot DWI technique (i.e., interleaved-EPI acquisition), and found that the data reconstruction of DW-Propeller-EPI is more robust than interleaved-EPI for liver DWI acquisition. However, due to the limited scan time for each subject (for managing the comfort of subject), only the reproducibility of free-breathing DW-Propeller-EPI and free-breathing routine single-shot acquisition were tested. Although we could not complete the full evaluation of reproducibility for all acquisition methods, the free-breathing DW-Propeller-EPI is better reproducible and less susceptible to respiratory motion than free-breathing routine single-shot DWI. From previous study conducted by another group, the utilization of free-breathing showed better reproducibility in ADC measurement than other motion control methods for routine single-shot liver DWI acquisition. In light of this, by integrating our assessments and previously reported findings, we conclude that free-breathing DW-Propeller-EPI can be a better alternative for liver DWI acquisition.

17138616.label: Major findings and research outcome
17138616.value: The Major findings and research outcomes can be summarized in two main aspects at below. I) Technical development 1. Completion of the development of DW-Propeller-EPI pulse sequence with no restrictions in scan orientation and location of FOV. This pulse sequence can also be used for the DWI data acquisition at different body parts, such as brain (Part C. 9.2 and 9.5). 2. Completion of the development of reconstruction pipeline with non-rigid body registration for the DW-Propeller-EPI data acquired under free-breathing condition (Part C. 9.2). 3. Development of a self-reference Nyquist ghost correction method for DW-Propeller-EPI that has also been generalized for 2D and 3D interleaved-EPI acquisition methods (Part C. 8.1, 9.1, 9.3-9.5). 4. Development of a self-calibrated and collaborative Propeller-EPI reconstruction (SCOPER) algorithm that can substantially improve the acquisition efficiency of Propeller-EPI (Part C. 9.5). 5. Development of DW-Propeller-EPI pulse sequence that can benefit the imaging-guided robotic system for intra-operative MRI for enabling high-quality real-time MRI. (Part C. 11.1) II) Technical evaluation 1. Free-breathing liver DW-Propeller-EPI provides superior image quality to routine single-shot based acquisition method (Part C. 8.2 and 9.2). 2. The apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) measured with DW-Propeller-EPI technique has been evaluated from 40 subjects that can provide the baseline ADC values of normal liver parenchyma for future application of tumor detection (Part C. 8.2 and 9.2). 3. The use of velocity compensation (VC) diffusion preparation gradient can reduce the signal loss caused by the cardiac and respiratory motions, but at the expense of signal-to-noise ratio (SNR).

17138616.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17138616.value: After successful development of proposed free-breathing liver DWI technique, we plan to evaluate the applications of free-breathing live DW-Propeller-EPI for detecting liver tumor and fibrosis, and to further improve the acquisition efficiency of free-breathing liver DW-Propeller-EPI. The brief descriptions of future plans are summarized at below. 1. We plan to add the developed pulse sequence into routine liver protocol for the patients who are being screened for HCC. The liver DWI data acquired with proposed method will be compared with routine method. 2. We plan to acquire the data from the patients diagnosed with liver fibrosis. This patient population will come from another study (assessment of liver fibrosis using T1 mapping), and additional DWI data will be acquired for our evaluation. 3. We plan to test our recently developed Self-calibrated and Collaborative Propeller-EPI Reconstruction (SCOPER) algorithm, which can reconstruct highly accelerated Propeller-EPI data without sacrifice of image quality, on healthy subjects for improving the scan efficiency of free-breathing liver DW-Propeller-EPI.

17138616.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17138616.value: Diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (DW-MRI) is a medical imaging biomarker for assessing liver fibrosis, detecting tumor, and predicting therapy response. However, the respiratory motion is the major challenge during the collection of image data. Although variable motion control methods (e.g., breath holding, free breathing, and respiratory gating) can reduce the problem, the attainable image quality is still very limited when using currently available DW-MRI techniques on clinical MRI scanner. In this project, we have successfully developed a free-breathing DW-MRI technique which is less sensitive to respiratory motion during the scan of liver. Through the evaluation study, our newly developed technique can provide better image quality (e.g., such as less noisy) and better geometric fidelity than other routinely used techniques available on clinical MRI scanner. Our technique has provided an advanced DW-MRI tool for scanning the liver for challenging populations who are unable to perform breath holding or maintain regular breathing rate. The successful development of this project is expected to improve the feasibility of free-breathing liver DW-MRI in routine scan, and potentially benefit the application of liver DW-MRI.

17138916.value: Climate change has been shown to have devastating effects on the world’s ecosystems with many scientists warning that our planet is already on the brink of the next mass extinction. The pivotal question in the debate on the ecological impact of climate change is whether species will be able to adapt fast enough to keep pace with their rapidly changing environment. Our current understanding is that species with either large population sizes or short generation times, or both, have the highest capacity for rapid adaptation. Recent reviews have, however, also highlighted the potential role of sexual selection in modulating the rate of adaptation, suggesting a novel and exciting new theory for scientists to explore. Sexual selection often acts in the opposite direction as other natural selection drivers, but its direction or relative strength can be altered under global warming scenarios. As a result, sexual selection may either act as a driver of evolution accelerating the rate of adaptation; or decelerating the rate of adaption and hence potentially condemning a species to extinction. To precisely assess the overall direction and strength of natural and sexual selection acting on a species, one must use a holistic approach taking into account the whole species life cycle (larval, juvenile and adult stages) as well as both pre- and post-copulatory sexual selection. In this study, we test this novel theory by adopting such an approach using gastropods as model species. The Gastropoda are the second largest animal class but have largely been neglected in studies measuring the importance of sexual selection. Due to the sparse number of studies in gastropods, whether selection pressures act on larval life-stages or during the post-copulatory period remains a mystery. We will fill this knowledge gap by using two marine gastropods from tropical shores as models. These gastropods are excellent models as they are already living close to their thermal limits and hence are subject to strong natural selection pressure under global warming. By investigating the interplay between natural and sexual selection in these species, we aim to strengthen our current understanding of the adaptive capacity of living organisms in the future era of global warming. 氣候變化已經對世界各地的生態系統構成破壞性的影響,有許多科學家也警告說我們的星球正瀕臨下一次生物大滅絕的邊緣。關於氣候變化的一個備受爭論的議題是,物種能否適應迅速變化中的環境。我們目前理解種群較大的或生命週期較短的物種,最具備快速適應的可能性。另外,近年有科學家提出性擇有機會改變物種適應環境的速度,因而有可能在物種適應環境的過程中扮演重要的角色,而這個理論亦成為了一個嶄新的科學研究領域。性擇與天擇有時候會相反地運行,但隨著全球暖化,性擇的強度或方向有可能會改變。因此,性擇有機會增加或減低物種的適應速度,並決定一個物種是否會因氣候變化而絕跡。要能夠準確地評估一個物種受性擇與天擇整體的影響,我們必須用一個整合的研究方案,當中要考慮到物種整個生命週期(包括幻體,幼年及成年時期)。我們會用腹足動物作為研究對象,並將這樣一個整合的研究方案應用在這項研究裡面,以測試這個新的科學理論。性擇在生物演化過程的重要性一直被廣泛研究,但這些研究卻很少用腹足動物作為對象,即使牠們是第二大的動物綱目。正因如此,性擇與天擇在這些動物的生命週期或交配後的時期扮演著怎樣的角色,至今仍然是一个迷。我們會用熱帶海洋腹足動物(海螺)作為研究對象,來填補這個知識缺口。這些海螺是非常適合的研究對象,因為牠們在岸上已經是活在接近牠們可以受熱的極限,所以牠們將會因著全球暖化而承受強大的天擇。我們希望透過探究天擇與性擇在全球暖化底下怎樣決定這些海螺的命運,從而對物種適應全球暖化的能力有更深的認識。

17138916.label: Realisation of objectives
17138916.value: Objective 1: To investigate whether natural selection favours small or large size under increasing temperatures in marine gastropods Survival of Nerita yoldii was tracked using mark recapture at different sites to determine if size was a predictor of survival followed by measures of shell temperatures (= body temperatures) using a thermal camera. Whilst mortality rate varied at times between sites (20 - 50%), shell size was a poor predictor of mortality suggesting natural selection (i.e. temperature responses) does not favour any size class. There was no significant difference in body temperatures between size classes (MSNo5 in prep.). There was no significant difference between LT50 for different size classes of adults, but differences in thermal tolerances were observed for larvae from mothers in different adult size classes (veligers from large mothers having lower LT50 than from medium sized mothers). There was no difference between adult size classes in Arrhenius Breakpoint Temperatures (ABT), and flatline temperatures (FLT). Data loggers revealed that all exposed rock surfaces during the summer would exceed the snails’ thermal safety margins (TSM, measured using ABT, FLT and LT50). TSMs for ABT varied with site, with most of the refuge habitats (crevices and tide pools) being within the nerites’ TSM at one site but not at others (MSNo5 in prep). A new metric, thermal preference (temperature chosen by individuals, reviewed in MSNo2) was also assessed which revealed that snails prefer lower, ‘sub-optimal’ temperatures than are ‘optimal’ for their physiological and behavioural performances (MSNo3 in revision). Thermal preference was measured in comparative studies in Hong Kong and Singapore. This involved training three students from Singapore in Hong Kong in terms of methodology and data collection (two used this work for their Honours dissertations). One methodology paper was published (MSNo1) and TSMs of N. undata on artificial walls in Singapore were measured using identical techniques and compared with Hong Kong (MSNo5 in submission, MSNo7 in prep). Similar patterns were observed where exposed rock surfaces at one site exceeded the animals’ TSM and preferred temperatures, whilst at the sun sheltered site they did not. This work showed the importance of behavioural thermal preference and how this maintains the TSMs of the snails (also see MSNo6, under preparation). This theory is being incorporated into a follow up project investigating latitudinal variation in thermal performance (MSNo7 under preparation). In the original plan LT50, ABT, and FLT were supposed to be measured from two different sites. Given the large number of individuals required for these experiments and the low density of snails at each site, we felt this would significantly impact the local populations and as a result we only completed the experiments for a single site (see Mid Term report). Measures of thermal performance (using heart rates, ABT and FLT etc) were performed at all sites (Objective 3). Objective 2: To investigate whether pre- and post-copulatory sexual selection favours small or large size under increasing temperature in marine gastropods This objective was achieved by quantifying the relationship between female size and fecundity, measuring size assortative mating, sexual selection and trail following (MSNo4 which includes data from different sites for Objective 3). Sex ratios did not differ from 1:1 at the sites and there was clear sexual size dimorphism (female>males). Both female and male sizes were under sexual selection (with the exception of 2 sites out of 12). There was little evidence (one case out of six) of size assortative mating. Female shell length was a poor predictor of fecundity in terms of the eggs laid and number of egg capsules (although total number of eggs at one site increased significantly with female size, size explained only a small amount of the variation). Pre-copulatory trail following behaviour was measured in the mating and non-mating seasons (MSc thesis, Crane, 2019) which showed no evidence of males following the female trails disproportionately during the mating season. Overall, the absence of size assortative mating in the presence of positive sexual selection is unusual and may be due to a lack of mating constraints on size pairings during mating. The original plan was to follow mating pairs and measure time of copulation, size, sex, intra-specific fighting behaviour and fight duration. As noted in the Mid Term report, these snails did not show the same behaviours as other snails we worked with previously. In general densities were much lower, and the behaviour patterns of the nerites did not aggregate large numbers of individuals together. It was not, therefore, possible to follow mating pairs on the shore or observe trail following; mating times were brief and hence there was no competition observed between males for females. We were also unable to get a reasonable number of the animals to mate in the laboratory (again unlike littorinids where we have been able to induce mating very successfully). We attempted this in two consecutive years, and had a full time RA working on this case, mimicking the conditions that have been successful with other species as well as trying new approaches. The differences observed between species may be informative as they suggest a difference in the focus and strength of sexual selection between these sympatric gastropods. As a result, after two years, we were unable to observe a useful number of breeding pairs and examine post-copulation selection. To try and compensate and investigate post-copulation selection indirectly, we checked for multiple paternity in laid egg masses. We collected females from the shore and allowed them to lay egg masses (where we assume females had successfully mated with at least one male) and cultured them until we were could release free swimming veligers which were preserved and genotyped using optimized microsatellite markers (see Mid Term report). The results were surprising in that, in both years, we could identify different maternal individuals (i.e. we could identify which mother the veligers came from) but there was no evidence of paternal contributions to the veliger DNA. These results are very surprising (although some snail species are parthenogenic). Accordingly, we have collected egg capsules and are rearing them to repeat the trials again this year. Objective 3: To elucidate the role of sexual selection in modulating adaptation in marine gastropods under climate change The experiments outlined above were repeated in two years at two sites and extended to two extra sites to cover a range of thermal conditions (this was limited by the lack of sites with high densities of snails). Physical and biological properties of the sites were measured (slope, aspect, rock colour, density of snails, competitors, sessile species cover). Comparison of thermal environments (PCA bubble plots) and thermal performances (heart rates, ABT, FLT and Topt and CTmax) for snails of different size classes from different sites revealed little spatial variation in performance. Whilst the physical and environmental conditions separated the sites, there were only differences in snails’ responses (FLT and size class differences) at one site, which was not associated with the highest environmental temperatures, but biological conditions (snail density). Sexual selection was also measured at the sites. Sexual size dimorphism was present at all (females>males), but positive size assortative mating was only present at one site in one year. Sizes of both male and females were under selection except for two sites (MSNo4).

17138916.label: Major findings and research outcome
17138916.value: Objective 1: To investigate whether natural selection favours small or large size under increasing temperatures in marine gastropods: Although mortality of individuals was high during the summer there was no indication that thermal tolerance or mortality varied with size for adult snails. There was, however, a maternal effect of larger females producing larvae with lower thermal tolerances, although we suspect this may not be a general trend (MSNo6 under preparation investigating Thermal Safety Margins of adults and larvae). On-shore temperatures regularly exceeded tolerance limits of snails in Hong Kong and in a comparative study in Singapore (including development of a bio-mimetic datalogger, MSNo1). By devising a behavioural metric of performance (preferred temperature, as reviewed in MSNo2 in Journal of Thermal Biology) it was clear that snails choose environments below their thermal optima for other measures of performance: as such, to ensure survival, sub-optimal appears to be optimal in these snails (as described in MSNo3 under revision in Journal of Animal Ecology). As such behavioural thermoregulation is a key trait to allow these snails to survive (MSNo3 and MSNo6 in prep). Objective 2: To investigate whether pre- and post-copulatory sexual selection favours small or large size under increasing temperature in marine gastropods: Fecundity selection is commonly used to explain positive selection on female size and sexual size dimorphism (SSD). Both female sexual selection and SSD were common despite little evidence for a relationship between female size and fecundity (eggs laid, number of embryos, only at one site for larvae hatched). As such we propose that fecundity selection should be considered as only one of several potential mechanisms, rather than the default explanation (detailed in MSNo4 submitted to Animal Behaviour). As noted in the Progress Report it was not possible to measure copulation behaviours and post-copulation interactions (see section 6.2). Laboratory experiments, however, revealed no evidence for pre-copulation male selection on female size via trail following as reported in sympatric species (MSc thesis by exchange student MS C Crane and also included in MSNo4). Objective 3: To elucidate the role of sexual selection in modulating adaptation in marine gastropods under climate change: Data on physical and biological characteristics of a number of sites were compared which enabled the separation of sites. There was no, however, strong evidence for either differences in thermal performances of the snails with the recorded thermal environment (from data loggers) or size assortative mating (MSNo4).

17138916.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17138916.value: Sexual selection: Our work demonstrates that positive size assortative mating is a possible, but not necessary, outcome of positive sexual selection on female size. Differences in the patterns of sexual selection between sympatric species is interesting, where N. yoldi shows none of the common sexual behaviours of littorinids. Nerita also inseminate females via spermatophores which can be stored and are often rejected. Investigations of multiple paternity in larvae failed to show evidence of male DNA, which is intriguing. The mating system of this species is, therefore, complex and warrants further investigation and we are currently attempting larval genotyping for a third time. Thermal performance and tolerance: We found considerable interindividual variation in thermal performances particularly of optimal and lethal temperatures. We have hypothesized that variation in thermal environments drives this variation. To test this, we are combining thermal physiology data of two Nerita species and habitat temperature data from the present grant and our collaborators across latitudes at Singapore and Xiamen. This dataset from eight localities will test if the snails' TPCs can be explained by variations in their local environmental temperatures. Our preliminary analyses (see MSNo7 in preparation) suggests that habitat temperatures are strongly location-dependent and over-ride latitudinal variations.

17138916.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17138916.value: We assessed the potentially contrasting roles of natural and sexual selection on thermal stress in a marine snail at multiple life stages across a variety of shores (degrees of thermal stress). We investigated whether the mating process and subsequent fecundity of different sized females (i.e. sexually selected traits) was affected by the thermal environment. There was little evidence that males chose females that match their sizes (i.e. no assortative mating) and they also did not select to follow their trails (a pre-mating means of choosing mates). Fecundity showed little relationship with female size, suggesting little role for sexual selection in these snails, and there was also no difference in thermal tolerance of the snails between sites. Potential habitats the adult snails utilized exceeded their thermal tolerances, but this was not the case for the larvae. Behavioural studies showed snails selected habitats of lower temperatures which was vital for their survival. Thermal stress drives behaviours to ensure snails do not exceed their thermal limits and may override the potential benefits of sexual selection to find and mate with larger females, where snails are required to spend longer periods in habitats where environmental temperatures may exceed their physiological tolerances.

17140916.value: To investigate the effectiveness of group CBT-I as a transdiagnostic early intervention for patients with mood disorders.
rows: To investigate the effectiveness of group CBT-I as a transdiagnostic early intervention for patients with mood disorders.

17140916.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17140916.value: Background: Insomnia is a common complaint often associated with significant distress, functional impairment, and socio-economic cost. There is robust evidence that insomnia is implicated in the onset, presentation, and prognosis of a wide range of psychiatric disorders, including mood disorders. Patients are often left with residual insomnia despite an adequate course of pharmacological or psychological treatment. Among various psycho-behavioral interventions, cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) has the strongest evidence base to suggest that it is safe, efficacious, and durable. Proposed as a transdiagnostic treatment, manualized CBT-I can be administered by healthcare professionals after receiving training and used as an early intervention for mood disorders. Aims: To investigate the effectiveness of nurse-administered 4-session group CBT-I, compared to standard care, for improving sleep and daytime function, enhancing recovery, preventing relapses, and reducing medication burden in patients with the first episode of major depression, mania, or hypomania. Methods: This will be a prospective, randomized, assessor-blind controlled trial. Two hundred subjects, stratified by psychiatric diagnosis of major depression or mania/hypomania, will be randomly assigned to 4 sessions of 60-90 minutes group CBT-I over 8 weeks or standard care in a 1:1 ratio. The CBT-I sessions will cover sleep education, relaxation training, stimulus control therapy, sleep restriction, and cognitive therapy. Patients with the first episode of major depression, mania, or hypomania and comorbid insomnia in addition to having received psychiatric treatment for less than 12 months will be recruited from regional psychiatric clinics. Other than participation in the group CBT-I, patients will be treated by their psychiatrists according to clinical needs. Patients will be assessed 4 times in total at baseline and 3, 6, and 12-month post-baseline. Insomnia Severity Index will be the primary outcome measure. Secondary outcomes include depressive, manic, anxiety, and somatic symptoms, daytime sleepiness, fatigue, functioning, quality of life, medication burden, number and type of relapses, and number of clinic visits and hospitalizations. Data analysis: The difference between intervention and standard care will be assessed using mixed-effects group-by-time interaction or chi-square test. Significance: This will be the first study on the effectiveness of 4-session group CBT-I for early intervention of psychiatric disorders. Nurse-administered 4-session group CBT-I, if proven effective in mood disorders, can be applied as an early intervention in other psychiatric disorders that are commonly associated with insomnia. 背景：失眠是一個常見的案例，它會做成很大的困擾，功能上的影響，及社會經濟成本。很多證據指出失眠對多樣的精神病，例如情緒病的發病，程度，及長期結果起很大的影響。雖然有使用藥物及心理治療，很多病人仍然會長期失眠。在眾多的心理行為治療當中，認知行為療法對治療失眠產生最大效用，而且安全及效力持久。由已受訓的醫療專業人士進行認知行為療法治療失眠可用於早期干預多種情緒病。 目標：研究四節由護士提供的認知行為療法治療失眠，比較標準治療對改善睡眠及曰常功能，提高復原，防止復發，及減少用藥負擔在情緒病患者是否有效。 方法：這是一項預期性，隨機，評估盲的對照試驗。二百位病患者將會已1比1的比率隨機分配接受8個星期四節60至90分鐘小組認知行為療法治療失眠或標準治療。認知行為療法包括睡眠教育，放鬆訓練，刺激控制法，睡眠限制，及認知療法。我們會在地區性精神科門診招募頭12個月接受精神科治療及第一次患有抑鬱症或躁鬱症及失眠的病人。除參與認知行為療法治療失眠外，醫生會以病人的臨床需要給以治療。病人會在底線，第3，6，及12個月時接受4次評估。失眠嚴重程度指數是主要的評估項目，其他評估包括抑鬱，狂躁，焦慮，及軀體症狀，白天嗜睡，疲勞，功能，生活質量，用藥負擔，復發的數目及類型，及拜訪門診的數目。亦會評估可能的中間因素，包括精神病的嚴重程度，壓力程度，與睡眠不相容的思想及行為，采取認知行為療法的程度，是否有內科的疾病，是否有使用補充及替代醫學療法，和是否有足夠的藥物及心理治療。 數據分析：以混合效應對組別/時間的相互作用及chi－square測試分析參加認知行為療法和標準治療的分別。 意義：這是第一項以認知行為療法治療失眠用於早期干預精神病的研究。如證明四節由護士提供的認知行為療法治療失眠對情緒病有效的話，認知行為療法治療失眠可用於早期干預其他經常同時有失眠的精神病。

17140916.label: Realisation of objectives
17140916.value: The study was an assessor-blind randomized controlled trial comparing group CBT-I and routine care in patients with first-episode mood disorders and comorbid insomnia. Major assessments were conducted at baseline, 3 months, 6 months, and 12 months. Patients were recruited from January 2017 to January 2020 at 2 regional psychiatric outpatient clinics in Hong Kong. Patients aged ≥ 18 years with the first episode of depressive or bipolar disorders according to the DSM-5 diagnostic criteria who received less than 12 months of mood disorder treatment and had insomnia disorder for over 1 month were our target population. The study was reviewed and approved by the local Institutional Review Boards (HKU/HA HKW UW-16-057 and KC/KE-16-0164/FR-3) and was registered at clinicaltrials.gov (identifier: NCT03000894) before subject recruitment. After giving written informed consent, and completion of the baseline assessment, patients were randomly assigned to CBT-I and routine care in a ratio of 1:1 by an independent administrator. Researchers who were responsible for assessment, data input, and data analysis were blind to patients’ group allocation. For patients in the CBT-I group, they received 4 sessions of 90 minutes group CBT-I administered by a nurse therapist. Each group involved 6-8 participants and those who dropped out were not replaced. The contents of the group CBTI were based on our self-help CBTI program. The major components included sleep education, sleep hygiene advice, activity scheduling, relaxation training, stimulus control, sleep restriction and cognitive therapy. The treatment period was 8 weeks, with biweekly sessions. On completion of each session, patients were provided with paper or digital CBT-I materials. We contacted those who missed treatment sessions and sent them CBT-I materials. The CBT-I was conducted by trained psychiatric nurses. All treatment sessions given by the trained nurses were audiotaped and reviewed by the Primary Investigator (KC) to monitor therapist adherence to the protocol. Other than participation in the group CBT-I, patients were treated by their psychiatrists according to clinical needs. The respective psychiatrists were not informed of their patients’ group allocation. To mimic a real-world clinical setting, the psychiatrists were not required to follow a standard treatment protocol. For the routine care group, patients were treated by their psychiatrists according to clinical needs as usual without a standard treatment protocol stipulated by this study. Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) was used as the primary outcome. The total score of ISI ranges from 0-28; a score above 14 indicates moderate insomnia. Secondary outcomes included response and remission status, psychiatric and somatic symptoms, daytime functioning and quality of life, medication burden, sleep-related cognition and behavior, treatment creditability, satisfaction and adherence, and adverse events. We used SPSS version 26 for statistical analysis. The intention-to-treat principle was adopted. For continuous variables, the repeated measures were analyzed with the mixed-effects model. The effects of intervention over time were assessed using the mixed-effects group by time interaction. The standardized effect size was computed by dividing the difference in means by the pooled standard deviation. Dichotomous outcomes were assessed using the χ2 test. Planned subgroup analysis was conducted to examine the effect of baseline insomnia severity and treatment attendance on outcomes. A total of 200 patients were recruited, with 102 in the CBT-I group and 98 in the routine care group. Patients had a mean age of 46.8 years; 72.0% were female, 49.5% married or cohabiting and 53.5% were in paid employment. The majority (99.5%) of the sample were having major depression. At baseline, the majority of patients (80.0%) were taking antidepressants; 55.5% were taking selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors and 8.0% were using a combination of antidepressants. More than half (56.0%) were taking hypnotics, mostly non-benzodiazepine hypnotics (38.0%). The mean baseline ISI and Hamilton depression rating scale scores were 17.6 and 12.6, respectively. There was no significant group difference in baseline characteristics, except the history of insomnia. Twenty-one of the 102 patients (20.6%) who were allocated to receive CBT-I did not attend any session; 41 (40.2%) attended all 4 sessions, 18 (17.6%) attended 3 sessions, 11 (10.8%) joined 2 sessions, and 11 (10.8%) attended only 1 session. One-hundred fifty-eight patients (79.0%) finished 3-month follow-up, 151 (75.5%) finished 6-month follow-up, and 138 (69.0%) completed 12-month follow-up. There was no significant difference in the attrition rate between the groups (χ2 test, p > 0.05). The mixed-effects analysis showed that there was a significant time effect but no significant group by time interaction in ISI total score, but several secondary outcomes had significantly greater improvements in the CBT-I group including higher depression remission at 12 months (59.7% vs. 37.9%, χ2 = 6.57, p = 0.01); lower anxiolytic use at 3 months (18.1% vs. 33.3%, χ2 = 4.72, p = 0.03) and 12 months (12.5% vs. 25.8%, χ2 = 3.26, p = 0.047), and lesser sleep-related dysfunctional cognitions at 3 months and 6 months (mixed-effects model, F = 5.12, p = 0.001 and 0.03, respectively). Subgroup analysis showed that the beneficial effect of CBT-I was more noticeable in patients with at least moderate insomnia and in those who attended 3-4 treatment sessions compared to patients who did not attend any session. In conclusion, we found that group CBT-I integrated into clinical service for first-episode mood disorders was beneficial to patients in the medium-term. In particular, the remission rate of depression was higher in the CBT-I group compared to the routine care group. Further studies are needed to examine the benefits of modification of CBT-I for the treatment of mood disorders with comorbid insomnia among Chinese people.

17140916.label: Major findings and research outcome
17140916.value: Efficacy Primary outcome The mixed-effects analysis showed that there was a significant time effect but no significant group by time interaction in ISI total score. The magnitude of improvement was similar in the CBT-I and routine care groups, with an effect size of 1.44 and 1.30, respectively, from baseline to 12 months. The response rate, defined as the proportion attaining at least a 6-point reduction in ISI total score, was 36.4% in the CBTI group and 22.2% in the routine care group at 3 months, but the difference cannot reach statistical significance (χ2 = 3.83, df = 1, p = 0.05). Secondary outcomes There was a significant group by time interaction in Dysfunctional Beliefs and Attitudes About Sleep Scale total score at 3 months and 6 months (p = 0.001 and 0.03, respectively), with a greater reduction in the CBT-I group. Most of the secondary outcomes had significant improvement from baseline to 12 months. Depression remission rate, defined as the proportion attaining a Hamilton Depression Rating Scale total score of 7 or below, was 59.7% in the CBT-I group at 12 months, which was significantly higher than that in the routine care group (37.9%) (χ2 = 6.57, df = 1, p = 0.01). Medication burden Anxiolytics and hypnotics were more often used in the routine care group compared to the CBT-I group. The difference was significant for anxiolytic use at 3 months (33.3% vs. 18.1%, p = 0.03) and 12 months (25.8% vs. 12.5%, p = 0.047) and marginally non-significant for hypnotic use at 12 months (p = 0.07). However, there was no significant group by time interaction in the dosage of benzodiazepines and antidepressants (mixed-effects model analysis: F = 0.36, p = 0.78 and F = 0.52, p = 0.67, respectively). Symptom exacerbation There was no significant difference between the 2 groups in the proportion of patients who had symptom exacerbation during the study period. Treatment credibility, satisfaction, adherence, and adverse events The mean total score of the credibility scale was 15.1 (SD = 3.3) (scale range = 4-24), mean satisfaction score was 22.6 (SD = 4.8) (scale range = 3-30), and mean adherence score was 14.0 (SD = 3.2) (scale range = 2-20), representing the 56th, 73th and 67th percentile of the scale scores, respectively. None of the 66 participants reported any adverse event.

17140916.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17140916.value: We found that nurse-administered group CBT-I integrated into clinical service for first-episode mood disorders was beneficial to patients in the medium-term. In particular, the remission rate of depression was higher in the CBT-I group compared to the routine care group. The credibility, satisfaction, and adherence to CBT-I were good and no adverse event was reported. The results suggested that CBT-I should be provided as an early intervention for patients with first-episode mood disorders and comorbid insomnia. Study limitations are that most patients were having depressive disorder and only 40% of patients in the CBT-I group completed all treatment sessions. Previous studies have shown that CBT elicits weaker effects on Chinese clients than their Western counterparts. We believe that modifications of the content, technique, and/or duration of CBT-I may be needed in the Chinese population. An example is that Chinese clients may not easily change their dysfunctional beliefs; hence an alternative approach is to help them reframe their beliefs in a less absolute and more positive way. Another modification of CBT-I for Hong Kong Chinese may be adding a preparatory interview and booster sessions for enhancement of participation and continuous practice of learned materials.

17140916.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17140916.value: Early intervention is regarded as a priority for the future of psychiatry since it reduces chronicity and relapse of psychiatric disorders. This randomized controlled study aimed to investigate the effectiveness of group cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) as an early intervention for patients with first-episode mood disorders and insomnia. We hypothesize that add-on nurse-administered group CBT-I to routine clinical service is effective for improving sleep and daytime function, enhancing recovery, preventing relapses, and reducing medication burden in patients with mood disorders and insomnia. We recruited 200 patients and randomly allocated them to receive add-on CBT-I or routine care. Patients in the CBT-I group received 4 sessions of 90 minutes group CBT-I administered by a nurse therapist and those in the routine care group had no add-on intervention. The major finding was that the CBT-I group had significantly higher depression remission at 12 months, lower anxiolytic use at 3 months and 12 months, and lesser sleep-related dysfunctional cognitions at 3 months and 6 months. The credibility, satisfaction, and adherence to CBT-I were good and no adverse event was reported. Our findings suggested that group CBT-I should be integrated into routine clinical service for patients with first-episode mood disorders and insomnia.

17141216.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17141216.value: Metastasis is the cause of >90% cancer deaths, and yet the control of the processes is still poorly understood. Emerging evidences show that interaction between tumors and their microenvironment, but not tumor cells per se, is the key factor that ultimately determines tumor progression and therefore of obvious scientific interest and therapeutic value. In ovarian cancer, a highly metastatic and rapidly lethal tumor, disseminated cancer cells that succeed in infiltrating the peritoneum present the distinct feature of adhering on macrophages, whereas those that unable to coopt also fail to thrive. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying this interaction have not been defined because the lack of tightly controlled, representative cell models. Moreover, traditional bulk measurements to visualize metastasis are unable to differentiate different phenotypes and their kinetics in the same population, masking cell-to-cell variation that is important for therapeutic response. We are the first to relate specific cell adhesion changes to the metastatic potential of ovarian cancer. Recently, we have further successfully developed a new isogenic ovarian cancer model with different metastatic properties, enabling us to unravel key factors mediating metastasis. In our pilot studies, using a live single-cell imaging platform to probe subpopulations and cell-to-cell variability, we show for the first time that HM (highly metastatic), but not NM (non-metastatic) tumor cells, have a selective advantage in activating M1 macrophages to a tumor-associated macrophage (TAM)-like phenotype. In turn, TAMs supported HM tumor cell growth, forming a positive feedback loop. Interestingly, this interaction also significantly increased the ploidy level, which is pivotal for tumor aggressiveness and therapy resistance, in a significant subset of HM. Expression of b-catenin was activated in HM, but not NM, plays a key role in this process through Metadherin. We hypothesize that disseminated ovarian cancer cells expressing Metadherin can survive and progress in macrophage-rich microenvironment via juxtacrine activation of the b-catenin-Metadherin/CEACAM1-CCL3 signaling pathway. In this proposal, we will: (1) elucidate the specific contribution of Metadherin-driven HM on properties of macrophages and how the crosstalk may affect tumorigenic behavior; (2) decipher the molecular mechanism of polyploidization with particular relevance to cytokinesis machinery, mitotic spindle checkpoint, and genome/chromosome stability; and (3) unravel the underlying mechanisms of action of the Metadherin/CEACAM1 juxtacrine loop. This research will provide important new mechanistic insights into the critical step in tumor metastasis, with implications of finding novel treatment options for effective therapies. 癌細胞轉移是多於90％的癌症死亡原因，但我們對於過程的控制仍知之甚少。新證據顯示腫瘤及其微環境之間的相互作用，而非只是腫瘤細胞本身，是最終決定腫瘤進展的關鍵因素。因此，腫瘤微環境有明顯重要的科研價值。卵巢癌是種高轉移性，並迅速致命的腫瘤。成功擴散至腹膜的卵巢癌細胞具有黏附至巨噬細胞的顯著特徵。因缺乏有代表性及嚴謹控制的細胞實驗模型，兩種細胞之間互動的分子機制尚待分析。 此外，細胞的個體差異對治療反應有重要影響。然而，傳統的批量檢測實驗無法區分在同一細胞族群中不同的表型和其動力學。我們是第一個把細胞黏附的特有變化聯繫到卵巢癌的轉移能力。最近，我們成功開發了一個基因同源的卵巢癌自發性轉移模型，使我們能夠從中找出轉移的關鍵因素。在試驗研究中，我們使用實時單細胞成像來探測細胞亞群的變異性。我們首次顯示了HM（高轉移性），而非NM（非轉移性）腫瘤細胞，能把M1型巨噬細胞誘導至腫瘤相關巨噬細胞（TAM）的表型。反過來，TAM支持HM腫瘤細胞的生長，形成一個正反饋環路。有趣的是，這互動過程增加了部份HM 腫瘤細胞的染色體套數，而有非常數染色體的腫瘤細胞已知是有高度侵襲性和抗治療性。β-catenin的表達水平在HM中相對較高，並可能通過Metadherin在此過程中發揮關鍵作用。我們推測播散卵巢癌細胞可以近分泌啟動β-catenin-Metadherin/ CEACAM1-CCL3信號通路，從而存活於有大量巨噬細胞的微環境中。在這個項目中，我們將：（1）研究Metadherin如何驅動HM與巨噬細胞的互動，以及此互動如何影響腫瘤發展; （2）解構HM染色體多倍化的分子機制，並重點分析尤為相關的胞質分裂機械、有絲分裂紡錘體檢查點和基因/染色體穩定性; （3）探討Metadherin/CEACAM1近分泌循環的基本分子機制。這項研究將對腫瘤轉移提供新見解，並為尋找新治療方案帶來特別意義。

17141216.label: Realisation of objectives
17141216.value: Objective 1: It is now increasingly clear that the tumor microenvironment, rather than tumor cells per sec, is the key determining factor to tumor progression. However, previous studies have focused mainly on tumor cells, the microenvironment remains poorly understood, especially cells of the immune system, which are the most important regulators in the microenvironment that can affect tumor behavior. Recently, we have developed a new isogenic ovarian cancer model with different metastatic properties to unravel key factors mediating metastasis. HM was unique in its ability to metastasize consistently to the peritoneum, mimicking the major dissemination route of human ovarian cancer. In contrast, NM failed to form detectable metastases although it was equally tumorigenic. Using this well-controlled HM and NM cells and a robust single-cell based time-lapse microscopy, we identified a positive feedback loop between HM and macrophages that is essential to ovarian cancer metastasis. HM, when cocultured with HM-activated macrophages can induce epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition of HM, in which HM changed from a rounded shape to an elongated one, with loss of cell-cell contact and enhancement of migration and invasiveness. Further, depletion of b-catenin or Metadherin inhibited tumor cell aggressiveness induced by TAMs. Tumor xenografts in humanized mice and patients’ clinical samples corroborate these findings in vivo. Percentage achieved: 100% Objective 2: We showed for the first time a direct role of Metadherin-CEACAM1 interaction in polyploidization and protumor phenotype. We provided further evidence that this process involved the activation of cyclin E. It is also clinically relevant that cyclin E was overexpressed in the clinical samples of ovarian cancer patients, in particular in the giant polyploid cells. The abscission checkpoint is known to be dependent on the persistent activity of the Aurora B and Survivin but not Mad2 and BubR1. We further provide evidence that HM could undergo multiple rounds of failed cytokinesis, suggesting that they could tolerant the presence of multiple sets of chromosomes. Percentage achieved: 100% Objective 3: Until now, there has no understanding of the structure of cell surface Metadherin and its binding partner and how their structures might affect their interactions, and the role those interactions in cancer. Using a series of deletion constructs within Metadherin, we identified a fragment of amino acid residues 75-582 harbors the essential region required for interaction with CEACAM1. In search of the underlying mechanism of how b-catenin may regulate Metadherin, putative TCF binding sites were found in the promoter of Metadherin, and p300, a coactivator of b-catenin/TCF-mediated transcription was involved. Our studies also revealed a previously unrecognized role of b-catenin in the downregulation of multiple microRNAs through attenuating microRNA biogenesis. CEACAM1 transduces a STAT3 metastatic signaling to regulate CCL3. These results uncover new regulatory mechanisms that may control the high degree of aggressiveness and potential for metastasis that are characteristic of ovarian cancer. Percentage achieved: 100% These findings not only reveal a previously unrecognized role for HM tumor cells as TAM activators, but also unveil a novel role for HM and macrophages in mediating the metastatic cascade through a positive feedback loop, which provide new perspectives on tumor cell and microenvironment interaction in the peritoneum, and that its targeting may represent a potential therapeutic advantage for metastatic ovarian cancer. 17141216.label: Major findings and research outcome
17141216.value: Objective 1: Here, using both an isogenic ovarian cancer cell line model with opposite metastatic abilities and humanized mice, we show that highly metastatic (HM) cells, but not non-metastatic (NM) cells, have a selective advantage in skewing the interacting macrophages to tumor-associated macrophages (TAM). Live single-cell imaging reveals that these TAMs subsequently induce failed cytokinesis in a significant subset of HM, leading to the formation of polyploid tumor cells that are pivotal for tumor aggressiveness. This bidirectional interaction between HM and macrophages are mediated by Metadherin expression induced by b-catenin on HM via trans-acting CEACAM1 expressed on macrophages. Moreover, HM-macrophage interaction promotes macrophage secretion of the cytokine CCL3. Tumor xenografts in humanized mice and patients’ clinical samples corroborate these findings in vivo. Publication: Journal article: #1 Conference proceeding: #4-6 Objective 2: We show for the first time that this process involves the activation of cyclin E. It is also clinically relevant that cyclin E is overexpressed in the clinical samples of ovarian cancer patients, in particular in the giant polyploid cells. The abscission checkpoint is known to be dependent on the persistent activity of the Aurora B and Survivin. We also observed the presence of chromosome bridge in the co-cultured HM, which may be a trigger for cytokinesis failure. HM cells could tolerant the presence of multiple sets of chromosomes. Publication: Journal articles: #1 Conference proceeding: #4 Objective 3: On exploring how the Metadherin interacts with CEACAM1, we show that this is mediated through a direct binding at positions of amino acid residues 75-582. Furthermore, we uncovered a new link of b-catenin, Dicer, a key component of the microRNA-processing machinery, and Metadherin activation. Moreover, we also show that CEACAM1 can transduce a STAT3 metastatic signaling cascade to activate CCL3, a strong chemoattractant for monocytes. These findings not only shed new light on the significance of considering tumor cells as heterogeneous populations in cancer progression, but also emphasize the need of a population-informed framework in the development of therapeutics. Publication: Journal article: #1, 3 Conference proceedings: #4-6 Taken together, our data strongly support the important role for a b-catenin/Metadherin/CEACAM1 cascade in mediating a novel positive feedback between macrophages and a subpopulation of cancer cells that is essential for ovarian cancer metastasis and provide a mechanistic rationale for targeting b-catenin or its associated signaling in the treatment of this unique metastatic population. Publication: Journal article: #2 Conference proceedings: #4-6

17141216.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17141216.value: We reveal the novel identification of a polyploid metastatic tumor cell subset that has a pivotal role in the metastatic heterogeneity, aggressiveness, and therapy resistance of ovarian cancer. This reveals a new direction for understanding the regulatory mechanism of polyploidization in ovarian cancer metastasis and implicate that targeting b-catenin/Metadherin could provide a promising therapeutic opportunity to target this unique metastatic subpopulation. Our findings underscore a critical role for b-catenin/Metadherin during the development and maintenance of the polyploid cells. While Metadherin was reported to localize in cellular compartments such as nucleus and endoplasmic reticulum, we showed the cell surface localization of Metadherin. The binding partner of surface Metadherin is unknown, and we identified a functional interaction of Metadherin and CEACAM1. Intriguingly, we found high b-catenin is associated with high Metadherin expression in patients’ samples of ovarian cancer tissues. We also found polyploid cancer cells in ascitic cells collected from ovarian cancer patients’ ascites. We are actively pursuing in this direction to document such effect using more extensive clinicopathological studies. Given that targeting phenotypic heterogeneity is evolving as an important therapeutic concept, it is of great interest to identify the key signaling path in this process. Peritoneal metastasis has also been detected in patients with breast, gastric, and colon cancer. To expand our understanding of the bidirectional tumor-macrophage interaction in polyploidization, we plan to examine if this crosstalk is also seen in other tumor types in which peritoneal metastasis is an important pathological process. We will also examine the level and effect of tumor-macrophage interaction in healthy donors or non-cancerous patients. These findings should highlight the functional importance of tumor-macrophage interaction in impacting malignant cell behavior and implies important clinical implications.

17141216.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17141216.value: One of the greatest unmet needs compromising the successful treatment of cancer is metastasis. A critical, rate-limiting step of metastasis is the ability of less than 0.01% disseminated cancer cells to survive and settle in target tissue, which involves specific tumor-host interaction. The observation that those which fail to coopt to the microenvironment also fail to thrive further suggests the importance of the tumor-host interaction. Unraveling the intricate details of this particular crosstalk is of obvious importance. Our new findings of this project indicate that the bidirectional tumor-macrophage interaction is a pivotal regulator of polyploidization and that it could be a promising target. (i) We show for the first time a preferential activation of the macrophages by the metastatic-competent than the metastatic-incompetent cancer cells. (ii) We uncover a new uncommon genetically unstable polyploid metastatic subset upon this interaction. (iii) We also present evidence that this activation is mediated by a juxtacrine b-catenin/Metadherin/CEACAM1-CCL3 signaling axis. These results reveal a new direction for understanding the regulatory mechanisms of polyploidization and highlight b-catenin/Metadherin as a viable therapeutic target. Targeting b-catenin/Metadherin may thus be a useful approach to decrease this aggressive and therapy resistant subpopulation, the most distressing complication for successful treatment.

17141416.label: Realisation of objectives
17141416.value: All the 3 objectives have been achieved. The achievements are detailed below: Objective 1 - Evaluating the clinical significance and prognostic value of RalA and RalGAP in human HCCs. Using the TCGA database and our in-house HKU RNA-seq database, we observed a consistent significant upregulation of RalA expression in human HCCs. This RalA overexpression was validated in our other cohort of our HCC patients using qPCR (n= 90 pairs of patients’ HCCs). Upon clinicopathological correlation, over-expression of RalA in HCC tumors was associated with more aggressive features, namely more frequent tumor microsatellite formation, venous invasion and absence of tumor encapsulation. Over-expression also correlated with poorer overall survival of HCC patients. On the other hand, with RNA-sequencing analysis in human HCCs and cell lines, we found that RalGAPA2 was the predominantly expressed RalGAP catalytic subunit in the liver. For RalGAPA2, 37.8% of the paired HCC samples (n=90) showed a 2-fold downregulation expression in HCC. Clinically, downregulation of RalGAPA2 significantly correlated with a lower cellular differentiation and a shorter overall survival rate. Interestingly, HCC tumors showing combined RalA upregulation and RalGAPA2 downregulation had more aggressive tumor behavior, including more frequent venous invasion and more advanced TNM stage. Objective 2 - Characterizing the functional role of RalA in hepatocarcinogenesis. Functionally, we established RalA stable knockdown (KD) in three HCC cell lines (PLC, HepG2 and MHCC-97L-Luc). KD of RalA significantly inhibited cell proliferation, colony formation, migration and invasion in vitro. Conversely, ectopic expression of the RalA wildtype and dominant active form G23V promoted HCC cell proliferation, migration and invasion in vitro. Overexpression of RalA also enhanced the tumor initiation using the limiting dilution assay of HCC xenografts in vivo. Orthotopic liver injection model using RalA stable-KD MHCC-97L cells in nude mice demonstrated that KD of RalA suppressed HCC tumorigenicity and reduced lung metastasis. There was also decreased tumor initiation ability of KD MHCC-97L cells using the limiting dilution assay of HCC xenografts in vivo. Moreover, KD of RalA also reduced sphere formation ability of HCC cells. These findings demonstrate that RalA promotes hepatocarcinogenesis and HCC progression (metastasis). Objective 3 - Delineating the molecular mechanisms of RalA dysregulation in HCC. With RNA-Seq analysis of shRalA clones of two HCC cell lines, multiple genes were found to be significantly altered, with some being up-regulated and others down-regulated, when compared with our in-house RNA-seq database as well as TCGA cohort. Further analysis showed that RalA expression level was positively as well as negatively correlated with different pathways and small groups of genes. Taken together, our findings so far have shown that RalA is frequently and significantly upregulated in human HCCs and associated with poorer patient prognosis. Coupled with its functional activities in vitro and in vivo, RalA likely plays an oncogenic role in human HCC.

(2) The abstract was also in the Hong Kong Scholars Annual Symposium, 2018, Hong Kong) (Please refer to Part C) Taken together, our findings so far have shown that RalA is frequently and significantly upregulated in human HCCs and associated with poorer patient prognosis. We have taken to expand this project to delineate the upstream positive regulators and negative regulator of RalA, to make the study more comprehensive. 17142316.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17142316.value: 銅緑假單胞桿菌（Pseudomonas aeruginosa）是一種常見的革蘭氏陰性緻病菌，能造成人類多種器官感染[並併]引[發髮]感染性疾病，比如肺炎，燒傷感染，尿路感染，囊腫性纖維化（cystic fibrosis，CF）病人中的肺部感染。在囊腫性纖維化病人中，銅[綠緑]假單胞桿菌的感染是導緻器官功能衰竭和病人過早死亡（小於37歲）的主要原因。銅[綠緑]假單胞桿菌是一種具有高度適應性的革蘭氏陰性細菌，可以産生一係列毒力因子，以促進其在在不衕感染階段對宿主的侵入和持留宿主的能力。在這些毒力因子中，緑膿菌素（Pyocyanin, PYO），一種吩嗪類（phenazine）微生物次生代謝物，因可以作為多功能的電子穿梭體而在急性和慢性銅[綠緑]假單胞桿菌感染中都發揮相當重要的作用。PYO具有一種特徵性的藍緑色，是銅緑假單胞桿菌侵染傷口膿液和囊腫性纖維化病人唾液的顯著標志。然而，在銅[綠緑]假單胞桿菌對環境壓力的適應過程中，如何調控PYO的[產産]生、這些調控通道和錶達産物對細菌生理和緻病性的意義，卻知之甚少，特別是在細菌生存的自然環境以及臨床條件下多菌種群體共生的情況下。 為了探索此問題，我們首先進行了細菌交叉接種實驗。 我們發現大腸桿菌E.coli MG1655可以誘導銅緑假單胞桿菌ATCC 27853 産生PYO。進一步的研究發現這種誘導是依賴大腸桿菌産生吲哚的能力。吲哚是大腸桿菌産生的一種標志性的微生物代謝物，超過80種細菌可以[產産]生此代謝物。有意思的是，在60株分離於香港瑪麗醫院細菌感染癥病人的銅緑]假單胞桿菌中，有15株被[發髮]現在吲哚存在下誘導産]生PYO。然而，在實驗室常見菌株PAO1中，我們的實驗和之前其他研究都證實吲哚未能誘導其産生PYO，這暗示了臨床菌與實驗菌株對生物源吲哚的不衕反應。由於銅[綠緑]假單胞桿菌和其他吲哚産生菌通常被發現是衕時存在於許多人類感染和自然環境中的，因此，這種吲哚誘導毒力因子增強的現象具有非常重要的意義。已經有報道稱，銅緑假單胞桿菌形態差異的産生和菌株多樣性分化是一種壓力適應性的結果。據此，我們假設，臨床菌和常見實驗菌株對吲哚的不衕反應，可能代錶了臨床菌對富含吲哚的多菌種共生環境的一種適應策略，例如肺炎中（與之共存的流感嗜血桿菌（Haemophilus influenzae），尿路感染中與銅緑假單胞桿菌共生的尿路緻病性大腸桿菌（uropathogenic E. coli，UPEC）和産酸剋雷伯菌（Klebsiella oxytoca），傷口感染及糖尿病潰瘍中常見的中間普雷沃菌（Prevotella intermedia），以及在CF病人肺部感染中的流感嗜血桿菌（H. influenzae）、中間普雷沃菌（P. intermedia）和伯剋氏菌（Burkholderia）等。 該項申請目標是以銅緑假單胞桿菌ATCC 27853臨床菌株為範例，係統探索吲哚誘導PYO産生的分子機製、生理影響和緻病性的特徵。對這些問題的回答，將會促進我們對銅緑假單胞桿菌在感染過程中對其動態環境的適應中所發生的多樣性分化和微進化的理解。從而有助於我們認識細菌感染的發生發展機製以及在此基礎上發展新型抗菌乾擾劑。

17142316.label: Realisation of objectives
17142316.value: Objective 1. Dissect the regulatory mechanisms of indole stimulated PYO production in P. aeruginosa ATCC 27853. We performed RNA-Seq analysis to identify the genome wide gene expression changes in the presence or absence of 0.5mM indole in P. aeruginosa ATCC27853. It was shown that expression of a total of 244 genes (202 genes being up-regulatd and 42 genes being down-regulated) were altered with more than 2-fold upon indole treatment, with . Consistent with the enhanced PYO production during indole treatment, expression of phz genes, including both the phz1 and phz2 operon, were significantly induced (log2 value ranges from 4-10). Moreover, expression of genes encoding three quorum sensing systems in P. aeruginosa, RhlIR (encoded in the rhlABRI operon), PQS (synthesized by genes pqsA-E and pqsH), and IQS (synthesized by the ambA-E) were elevated more than 4-fold in the presence of indole compared to the absence of indole. Consistently, a number of genes within the regulon of RhlIR and PQS is also up-regulated by indole, such as phz1, phz2, lasA, lasB, lecA, hcnABC, cdrA etc.. RT-qPCR analysis confirmed the gene expression changes. To explore the molecular mechanisms underlying the different indole response between ATCC 27853 and the laboratory strain PAO1 as observed in our preliminary study and reported by Lee et al, we also conducted the comparative RNA-Seq analysis in the laboratory strain PAO1 with or without indole treatment (0.5mM). Surprisingly, expression of only 136 genes were altered by indole treatment in this strain (55 genes being up-regulated and 81 genes being down-regulated), much less than the number of genes regulated by indole in ATCC27853. Furthermore, the extent of gene regulation in PAO1 was much less pronounced than that in ATCC 27853. Consistent with the differential response of the two strains to indole treatment, expression of genes phz1, phzH, hcpA, and lecA which were shown to be up-regulated by indole in ATCC27853 were down-regulated by indole in PAO1. The fact that all these genes were controlled by quorum sensing and the QS systems PQS and IQS were regulated in opposite manner by indole in ATCC27853 and PAO1 suggests that indole differentially regulates the gene expression in the two strains via its differential effect on the quorum sensing regulatory systems. Objective 2. Examine global physiological effects of indole on P. aeruginosa ATCC27853. Our RNA-Seq analysis revealed that indole induced a series of virulence genes and genes involved in biofilm formation, such as phz1, phz2, lasA, lasB, rhlAB, lecA, hcnABC, cdrA etc. Hence, in this aim, the corresponding virulence factor production and biofilm formation was assessed to examine the global physiological effects of indole on ATCC27853. We used two different methods to evaluate biofilm formation of ATCC 27853 with or without indole treatment, biofilm formation at the air-liquid interface in polystyrene tubes and on glass submerged glass slides. It was shown that indole enhanced biofilm on both surfaces. Scanning Electron Microscopy revealed that indole also altered the architecture of ATCC 27853 biofilms, especially the type of matrix extracellular polymeric substances. Consistent with the RNA-Seq data, RT-qPCR showed that expression of genes responsible for several extracellular matrix components including the Pel polysaccharides and adhesins CdrA and LecA were up-regulated upon indole treatment. Consistent with the increased biofilm formation, we also showed that ATCC27853 cells treated by indole displayed decreased and swimming and twitching motility. In addition to the pigmented virulence factor PYO which was shown to be elevated in indole treated ATCC27853 cells in our preliminary study, based on the RNA-Seq analysis, we examined the production of the virulence factors exo-proteases (encoded by lasA and lasB) and rhamnolipids (encoded by rhlAB) and found that indole treatment increased their levels in a QS dependent manner. Additionally, RNA-Seq data also suggested an increased level of the RND multidrug efflux pump MexAB in indole treated ATCC27853 cells. Hence, we examined the antibiotic resistance of the ATCC27853 cells. It was shown that indole treatment significantly increased survival of ATCC27853 against several antibiotics, including ciprofloxacin, tetracycline, and gentamicin. These results together suggested that indole elicited a global response in ATCC27853 which led to increased virulence factor production, biofilm formation, and antibiotic resistance. Objective 3. Assess the impacts of indole response on the pathogenesis of P. aeruginosa in nematode infection models. To evaluate the role of indole response in the infection and pathogenesis of ATCC 27853, we conducted in vivo infection assay using the C. elegans fast and slow killing assay. We first showed that indole itself does not affect the survival of C. elegans. Culturing ATCC 27853 in the presence of 0.5mM indole prior to infecting the C. elegans increased the killing of C. elegans, suggesting indole treatment enhanced the virulence of ATCC 27853 to the nematode host. In contrast, indole pre-treatment decreased the killing rate of C. elegans by PAO1. We also examined the effect of indole exposure on the attachment and aggregation of P. aeruginosa ATCC 27853 on cultured human bronchial epithelial cells (16HBE). It was shown that indole treatment significantly enhanced the aggregation of ATCC 27853 on the 16HBE cells. Indole treated cells were recovered 4.5-fold higher than non-treated cells following infection of 16HBE cells for one hour. These data together strongly suggested that indole elicit global physiological and pathogenic changes in the P. aeruginosa ATCC 27853 through its action on RhlIR, PQS, and IQS quorum sensing signaling cascades. More interestingly, these responses are strain specific. In the future, we will examine these responses in a broad range of clinical P. aeruginosa isolates. These findings indicate that presence of indole producing bacteria affects the pathogenesis of P. aeruginosa and therapeutic interventions may need to be adjusted depending on the presence of species that co-infect with P. aeruginosa.

17142316.label: Major findings and research outcome
17142316.value: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a prevalent and pernicious human pathogen with clinical significance. It is a highly adaptable Gram-negative bacterium that can colonize a diverse range of environmental niches and infect various body sites and tissues. In both its environmental niches and infection loci, P. aeruginosa encounters various chemical and physiological challenges including interspecies competition, nutrients starvation, antibiotic treatment, oxidative stress, host immune responses etc.. To adapt to and colonize these niches, the pathogen often undergoes complex genetic and physiological differentiations and generates specific phenotypic variants. The bacterium relies on an arsenal of virulence factors to facilitate its invasion and persistence of the human hosts, including proteases, phospholipases, biosurfactant, siderophores, Pseudomonas specific PQS (Pseudomonas quinolone system) and pyocyanin (PYO) etc.. However, the production and regulation of these virulence factors in the context of natural environmental niches and clinical settings, which are characterized by polymicrobial communities, are poorly understood. This proposal built upon an interesting observation in our preliminary studies which showed that production of a signature virulence factor pyocyanin (PYO) in the P. aeruginosa ATCC 27853 was stimulated by indole producing bacteria, and aimed to delineating the molecular mechanisms underlying this adaptive response and the global effect of indole stimulation on the pathogenesis of the strain. We found that indole indeed elicits differential physiological effects on different P. aeruginosa strains, i.e. it enhances the PYO production in ATCC 27853 and a series of other clinical strains but reduces PYO production in the laboratory strain PAO1. By conducting a series of comparative RNA-Seq analysis and targeted molecular studies, we showed that indole differentially regulate the virulence factors production in P. aeruginosa by differentially regulate the quorum sensing signal cascades. We further showed that indole enhanced the virulence factors production, biofilm formation, and antibiotic resistance, and decreased the motility of the bacterium. It also enhanced the pathogenesis of ATCC 27853 in vivo in the C. elegans infection model and the attachment and survival in the human bronchial epithelial cells. Since more than 80 bacterial species produce indole and co-existence of P. aeruginosa with indole producing species is prevalent in many human infections, unraveling the adaptation strategies of P. aeruginosa in response to indole significantly advanced our understanding of bacterial microevolution during stress adaptation. These findings imply that presence of indole-producing species affect the infection outcome of P. aeruginosa in the polymicrobial infections and adjustment of therapeutic interventions may be needed to treat these infections.

17142316.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17142316.value: Execution of the current proposal led to further development of the research in the following two areas. First, exploring the molecular mechanisms of indole response in clinical P. aeruginosa strains led to the development of native CRISPR-Cas mediated genome editing techniques. These studies have been published in the internationally leading journals Cell Reports (2019), Environmental Microbiology (2020) etc. Second, during investigating the effect of indole treatment on biofilm formation of ATCC27853, we fortuitously found that temperature affected biofilm formation of the strain. These findings have served as the preliminary data to apply for another GRF grant which was successfully funded [GRF 2019/20 (No. 17124719), Title: Unraveling the thermoregulation of biofilm formation in P. aeruginosa].

17142316.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17142316.value: The Gram-negative bacterium Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a prevalent and pernicious pathogen that causes several infectious diseases in humans. P. aeruginosa is highly adaptable to diverse environmental niches and is capable of producing an array of different virulence factors to facilitate its invasion or persistence in host at different infection stages. However, production and regulation of virulence factors during stress adaptation in the infection, especially in the context of polymicrobial communities which are prevalent in natural habitats and clinical settings, are poorly understood. One of the prominent biological feature in the polymicrobial infections involved in P. aeruginosa is the presence of indole-producing bacteria, such as in pneumonia (containing indole producing H. influenza); UTIs (containing uropathogenic E. coli and K. oxytoca); wound infection and diabetic ulcers (containing E. faecalis); and lung infections of CF patients (containing H. influenza, P. intermedia, Burkholderia sp, etc.). However, how indole affect the physiology and pathogenesis of P. aeruginosa and consequently the outcome of infectious diseases, were unknown. In this proposal, we delineated the molecular mechanisms of indole response in the paradigmatic P. aeruginosa strain ATCC 27853 and found that indole affects the global physiological and pathogenic features of the strain which led to enhanced virulence and antibiotic resistance. These findings imply that increased dose of antimicrobials are needed to treat P. aeruginosa infections when indole producing bacteria are simultaneously present in the infection sites.

17142516.value: 肝癌（HCC）是世上其中一種最常見和致命的癌症，每年導致超過60萬人死亡。然而，肝癌發生的分子機理尚不十分清楚。普遍認為，遺傳和表觀遺傳改變的積累是導致肝癌發生的主要因素。肝癌的遺傳病變，包括染色體異常和體細胞突變，在過去已經有深入的研究。表觀遺傳改變，如DNA甲基化和組蛋白修飾異常的重要性也在許多研究中被證實。最近新的證據指出，除了DNA和組蛋白蛋白質外，RNA也存在動態和可逆轉的化學修飾。腺苷N6位置甲基化形成N6 - 甲基腺苷（m6A）是mRNA的一種普遍的轉錄後修飾，並且對調節mRNA的穩定性和基因表達非常重要。現今，mRNA的甲基化已成為一個新的表觀遺傳調控機制。M6A已被證實對幹細胞的維護和細胞分化起著關鍵作用。然而，m6A失調是否參與人類癌變尚有待探索。我們初步的轉錄組測序（RNA-Seq）和 定量RT-PCR分析表明，一種名為 METTL3，負責m6A修飾的基因在肝癌中顯著上調。我們的初步數據還表明，METTL3的上調與腫瘤復發和預後差顯著相關。此外，敲低METTL3明顯抑制肝癌細胞的增殖和遷移。而且，METTL3敲低顯著恢復多個腫瘤抑制基因的表達。這些初步發現促使我們提出METTL3 上調可能導致m6A失調並促進肝癌發生的假設。在這個擬議的項目，我們旨在徹底研究METTL3和m6A失調對人類肝癌的病理作用。我們將 1) 確定METTL3的表達變化對肝癌m6A水平的影響，2) 確立 METTL3 和m6A失調在肝癌患者中的臨床病理及預後意義， 3) 研究促成肝癌中METTL3頻繁上調的機理, 4) 在體外和體內模型裡表徵METTL3在肝癌的致癌功能，5) 探索METTL3介導的肝癌發生的基本機理。我們相信，我們的研究將增進我們對肝臟癌變的分子基礎的認識而且可能促進新的肝癌診斷和治療方法的開發。

17142516.label: Realisation of objectives
17142516.value: All objectives are successfully completed. Details as following Objective 1: Expression of METTL3 and global m6A level in primary HCCs The expression of METTL3 in human HCC was detected in 16 pairs of primary HCC and their corresponding non-tumorous liver by RNA-Seq and validated in additional 104 cases by qRT-PCR. We found that METTL3 was significantly overexpressed in human HCC. Consistent with our findings, analysis of TCGA dataset also revealed a frequent up-regulation of METTL3. In addition, using dot-blot assay we found that the mRNA m6A level was significantly elevated in human HCC. Objective 2: Clinicopathological and prognostic significance of METTL3 and m6A deregulation in primary HCCs Statistical analyses revealed that expression of METTL3 increased during the progression of HCC (from G1 to G4) and was significantly associated with Ki67 expression. High expression of MEETL3 was significantly associated with shorter overall and disease-free survival of HCC patients. However, we found no correlation between METTL3 and HBV infection as well as other clinicopathological features. Objective 3: The functions of METTL3 in HCC growth and metastasis with in vitro and in vivo models Using shRNA and CRISPR/Cas9 systems we generated METTL3 knockdown and knockout cells in HCC cell lines. We showed knockdown/knockout of METTL3 significantly suppressed HCC proliferation, colony formation, and cell migration. In addition, knockdown and knockout of METTL3 also suppressed HCC tumor growth and metastasis in subcutaneous xenograft and orthotopic tumor implantation models. On the other hand, overexpression of METTL4 by the CRISPR/dCas9-SAM system promoted HCC proliferation, colony formation, cell migration in vitro, and tumorigenicity in vivo. Objective 4: the molecular mechanisms underlying METTL3 mediated liver carcinogenesis Using RNA-Seq and m6A-seq we identified tumor suppressor gene SOCS2 as a down-stream target of METTL3-mediated m6A modification. Using MeRIP and qRT-PCR we showed that inactivation of METTL3 significantly decrease SOCS2 m6A level and augmented SOCS2 mRNA expression. Using luciferase reporter assay, we showed that the putative m6A motif is essential for regulate SOCS2 mRNA expression. Using PAR-CRIP-seq, we found that YTHDF2, an m6A reader protein, binds to the m6a motif. YTHDF2 promoted SOCS2 mRNA degradation. Knockdown of YTHDF2 stabilized SOCS2 mRNA expression in human HCC. We further showed that SOSC2 is a tumor suppressor gene that frequently down-regulated in human HCC. Knockdown of SOCS2 remarkably promoted HCC proliferation and migration.
