17149816.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17149816.value: There were >1,800 new cases of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) in Hong Kong in 2011 and it’s the second leading cause of cancer death in man. Liver transplantation (LT) is the curative treatment of choice for patients with HCC and end-stage liver disease. Organ shortage and long waiting time for a liver graft remains the major obstacle for DDLT, due to our low our organ donation rate. Up to 35% of patients listed for DDLT would dropout from waiting list at 1 year either due to disease progression or worsening of liver function. There was no prospective data on stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) as bridging therapy for HCC but 4 prospective series on SBRT for nonresectable HCC showed a promising local control rate of 87-100% at 1-year. Our study aims to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of SBRT in HCC patients on DDLT waiting list. SBRT related complications and aftereffect of SBRT on subsequent transplant surgery will be recorded. Effectiveness of SBRT in terms of local tumor control and extent of tumor necrosis in explant will be assessed. This is a single center prospective study that aims to enroll 40 HCC patients for evaluation of SBRT as bridging therapy during waiting period for DDLT. Patients will receive high dose radiation in 5 sessions over 5-14 days to tumors while limiting exposure to surrounding healthy organs. Patients will be followed up regularly and treatment related complications would be evaluated by clinical symptoms and blood tests. Effectiveness of SBRT for tumor control will be assessed biochemically with tumor marker and radiologically by computed tomography. Dropout will be recorded and analyzed. European Organization for Research and Treatment of Cancer Quality of Life Questionnaire Core-30 (QLQ-C30) and Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy-Hepatobiliary (FACT-Hep) questionnaires will be used for assessment of performance status. Our study will identify side effects of SBRT and its impact to technical difficulty in subsequent LT. Effectiveness of SBRT in local tumor control will be demonstrated as a reduced dropout and a high degree of pathological tumor necrosis of explant. Our study will help to define the role of SBRT in treatment of HCC and will be used to design future prospective study on utilizing SBRT as an ablative therapy for nonresectable HCC patients. 研究背景 肝臟移植是肝癌患者首選的治癒治療，根據米蘭和三藩市大學的標準準則，肝臟移植5年生存率> 70%，由於器官短缺和輪候時間長，在香港，有>30%的患者在等候時腫瘤惡化而退出輪候名單，因此處理等候期間腫瘤惡化是關鍵。目前肝動脈化療栓（TACE）是普遍使用的過渡性療法，它較安全，創傷小，耐受性好，30%的等候患者可有效控制腫瘤生長。但它的副作用包括：造影劑導致的腎功能損傷，潛在的血管內皮和膽管的損傷可能影響隨後的肝移植效果，故希望引進新的過渡療法。而立體定位放射治療是應用立體定位技術和特殊射線裝置，將多源、多線束三維空間聚焦的高能射線聚焦於體內某一靶區，使病灶組織受高劑量照射，周圍正常組織受量減少，因而能逹至臨床療效高但副作用少的放療技術。至目前為止，立體定位放射治療仍不是確立的過渡性療法，但有4個使用立體定位放射治療不可切除肝癌的相關前瞻性研究顯示，一年局部控制率達87-100%，2年的總體生存率達60-69%。 研究目的 肝癌患者輪候肝移植過程中，採用立體定位射治療為過渡性治療的有效性和安全性。 研究方法 這是一項前瞻、非隨機研究，將招募腦死亡肝臟移植等候名單上30位肝癌患者參予，外科和腫瘤科醫生會解釋兩種過渡性療法（TACE 和SBRT）。若患者選擇SBRT，將接受5次立體定位放射治療（隔天一次），療程10天。治療後第一個月及以後每3個月做一次電腦掃描作評估。立體定位放射治療將針對所有的腫瘤病灶，隨後是否重複治療取決於腫瘤對放射治療反應。若患者選擇TACE, 將按目前TACE治療常規處理。

17149816.label: Realisation of objectives
17149816.value: In this prospective study, we have recruited 43 HCC patients for SBRT as a bridge to transplant. The safety and effectiveness endpoints were achieved as planned. Outcomes of SBRT patients were compared to a retrospective cohort of patients who had conventional bridging therapies i.e. transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) and high intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU). Recruitment Forty three patients were assessed for eligibility for SBRT. 7 (16.3%) patients were unsuitable for SBRT: 3 were due to small liver remnant, 2 were due to close proximity to duodenum and stomach and 2 were due to discrepancy of tumor position on planning and treatment CT because of irregular breathing pattern and ascites. Thirty-six patients underwent SBRT during the study period. (i.e. we have achieved the proposed sample size) In the retrospective cohort, 109 patients underwent TACE/ HIFU and they served as control arm. Realization of safety endpoints 1) SBRT related RILD: all patients were followed up prospectively and there was no 30-day mortality and deterioration of liver function after SBRT. None required admission for management of post-SBRT complication and none required urgent transplant. In summary, under our selection protocol, the risk of RILD in HCC candidates on waiting list for DDLT were extremely rare. 2) Post SBRT toxicity was assessed according to CTCAE and compared to TACE/ HIFU patients. We have assessed clinical and biochemical parameters including fatigue (>= Grade 2: 2.8% vs. 0.9%, P=0.407), fever (>=Grade 2: 2.8% vs. 5.5%, P=0.508), bilirubin (>=Grade 2: 38.9% vs. 38.6%, P=0.6), albumin (>= Grade 2: 8.7% vs. 26.6%, P=0.05), AST (>=Grade 2: 8.3% vs. 1.8%, P=0.836), INR (>=Grade 2: 11.1% vs. 14.7%, P=0.928), platelet (>=Grade 2: 80.5% vs. 58.7%, P=0.01), white cell (>=Grade 2: 52.8% vs. 23.9%, P<0.001), hemoglobin (>=Grade 2: 2.8% vs. 17.4%, P=0.167) and creatinine (>= Grade 2: 5.6% vs. 3.7%, P=0.72) up to 30 days after bridging therapies. When compared to TACE/ HIFU group, the impairment of liver function, fever, fatigue and creatinine were similar between the SBRT group and TACE/ HIFU group. There was more hematological derangement including thrombocytopenia and leucopenia in the SBRT group but none was associated with clinically adverse events. 3) Aftereffect of SBRT on technical difficulty in transplant operation. In those who reached DDLT, SBRT patients had similar perioperative outcomes when compared to TACE/ HIFU group. [overall complication (66.7% in SBRT vs. 58.3% in TACE/ HIFU P=0.501), severe complication rate (14.3% in SBRT vs. 18.3% in TACE/HIFU, P=0.673), hepatic artery thrombosis rate (4.8% in SBRT vs. 0% in TACE/ HIFU, P=0.089) and biliary complications (0% in both groups). Hospital mortality after transplant was 0% in SBRT and 3.3% in TACE/ HIFU (P=0.959). Transfusion requirement, ICU and hospital stays were not different. No surgeon reported peri-tumoral or peri-hilar adhesion as a result of SBRT. Realization of effectiveness endpoint 1) Rate of tumor control was assessed in 2 different ways. Firstly we assessed the radiological response according to Modified Response Evaluation Criteria for Solid Tumours (mRECIST) of HCC after SBRT every 3 months and compared to those who underwent conventional bridging therapies. Tumor control was defined as complete response(CR), partial response (PR) and stable disease (SD) whereas objective response was defined as CR and PR according to the mRECIST criteria. The tumor control rate at 1-year was superior in the SBRT group (92.3% vs. 37.8%, P=0.001). The ability of tumor control after SBRT was also better at other time points within 1st year after bridging therapy [3 months: 90.9% vs. 70.6%, P=0.018; 6 months: 95.7% vs. 62.8%, P=0.002; 9 months: 89.5% vs. 50%, P=0.002; 12 months: 92.3% vs. 37.8%, P=0.001]. There were more SBRT patients achieving CR (24.2% vs. 9.8%, 47.8% vs. 16.3%, 47.4% vs. 17.2% and 53.9% vs. 13.5%) and objective response (66.7% vs. 35.3%, 82.6% vs. 34.9%, 78.9% vs. 34.4% and 76.9% vs. 32.4%, P<0.001) at 3-, 6-, 9- and 12-months after bridging therapies. 2) The superior effect of tumor control has translated into a lower dropout rate in the SBRT group. At time of study analysis, the dropout risk was lower in the SBRT group [7/36 (19.4%) vs. 45/109 (41.3%), P=0.018]. 3) Comparing the explant pathology, there was no difference between SBRT vs. TACE/HIFU with respect to tumor size (2cm vs. 2.5cm, P=0.067), tumor number (median 1 in both groups, P=0.33), microvascular permeation (22.7% in SBRT vs. 25.5% in TACE/ HIFU, P=0.773) and macrovascular permeation (4.5% in SBRT vs. 0.9% in TACE/ HIFU, P=0.190). In the SBRT group, there were more pathological CR [11/22 (50%) vs. 13/60 (21.7%), P=0.008). The research team has achieved all proposed objectives listed.

17149816.label: Major findings and research outcome
17149816.value: To the best of our knowledge, this is the first and only prospective study that investigated the use of SBRT as bridging therapy for HCC candidates on liver transplant waitlist. In the present study, SBRT showed a better radiological tumor control and objective response compared to TACE/ HIFU at every time point after treatment. The use of SBRT also reduced the risk of dropout and produced a higher rate of pathological CR in explant histopathology when compared to TACE/ HIFU. An ideal bridging therapy should be effective, non-invasive and safe for HCC candidates. The data from the present study showed that SBRT is close to, if not an ideal bridging therapy. SBRT is completely non-invasive, without an increased risk of peri-procedural complication or RILD. All study patients completed SBRT treatment as an outpatient procedure. SBRT did not induce adhesion which could potentially increase technical difficulty and perioperative complications during the transplant operation. Most importantly, SBRT was very effective. The high dose radiation given in divided doses achieved a “radio-ablative” effect to the tumor. Objective response was achieved in 66.7%-82.6% of SBRT patients when compared to 32.4-35.3% to other conventional bridging therapies. Within the 1st year of SBRT, tumor control was maintained at 90%. This is in great contrast to TACE/ HIFU patients where the effect of tumor control reduced with time; 50% at 9-months to 37.8% at 12-months. Moreover, 50% of transplanted patients reached pCR in the explant histopathology, and 3 were delisted because of treated HCC, with no recurrence to date. This phenomenon shed insights on the effectiveness of SBRT as “radio-ablation” that might be curative for small HCC. The preliminary report of our study was presented in International Liver Transplant Society (ILTS) Annual Congress in Toronto, Canada in May 2019. Our research data and presentation was awarded with "Rising Star Award" (with PI Dr T Wong as mentee and Co-I Prof CM Lo as mentor). The full manuscript of our study was currently under review in the Journal of Hepatology (IF 18.946).

17149816.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17149816.value: In the present study, the post-transplant and recurrence-free survival rates were similar after SBRT and other bridging therapies. However, given the higher rate of tumor control on waitlist and a higher pathological CR in explant, SBRT might lead to a better post-transplant survival in the long-term. The sample size and follow-up time of our study was not powered to test this hypothesis but it will be of interests to follow-up the long-term survival and recurrence in these patients. Furthermore, tumor control was seen in 90% of SBRT patients within the 1st year and such effect was sustained, suggesting that the use of SBRT as downstage therapy should be recommended in eligible patients, given tumor progression accounts for the majority of dropouts in downstage protocols. In HCC candidates when tumor was the only indication for transplant, absence of active HCC(CR on mRECIST and normal AFP) consistently for >=1 year after bridging therapies and actual MELD<15 were considered “treated” and removed from waitlist. As mentioned in part 6.1, 3 patients were considered treated and as for the time of analysis, they have no HCC recurrence. This phenomenon shed insights on the effectiveness of SBRT as “radio-ablation” that might be curative for small HCC.

17149816.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17149816.value: This is the first prospective study on the use of SBRT as bridging therapy for liver cancer candidates were safe. SBRT reduced the risk of dropout and had better tumor control. Postoperative side effects and survivals were similar after SBRT and conventional bridging therapies. Good quality data to support the routine use of SBRT in transplant candidates are lacking, but there are intense interests from researchers all over the world to understand more about the safety and effectiveness of SBRT. Our study fills the current literature gap. The findings of our study provides important foundation for future research. The safety and effectiveness that were demonstrated in our study suggested that SBRT could be used in downstage protocol in transplant population. In non-transplant patients, SBRT could be considered in clinical trial for as curative treatment for small liver cancer.

17150816.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17150816.value: Next generation sequencing (NGS) allows massive parallel sequencing of DNA/RNA in a sample using non-specific primers. Such high throughput ‘deep sequencing’ makes possible to examine the comprehensive composition of microbial species in biological samples (e.g. virome in gut samples). Therefore NGS becomes an important tool used in infectious disease surveillances to investigate the causative pathogens and their genomic evolution in disease outbreaks. However, most current NGS technologies share a common limitation: a huge amount of small fragments (about 75- 400 bases) of a genome are sequenced. These short sequencing reads must be assembled to obtain complete biological sequences. While the current assembly methods, whether de novo or reference sequence based, are successful in many cases, their accuracies are challenged when genomes from a mix of closely related microbial strains are to be sequenced, which is often the case for the original samples from infectious disease surveillance. The failure of existing methods to adequately distinguish the source strains of the reads will mis-assign the reads into a wrong genome assembly. As a result, a false recombinant sequence, or a sequence with incorrectly high variability may be generated. Such data inaccuracy will seriously impede all downstream sequence analyses. We propose to develop a novel assembly method that utilizes the phylogenetic trees of reference genomes to guide the assembly of NGS short reads. The reference phylogeny, which encodes comprehensive evolutionary information among the known strains, will help distinguish the reads between similar strains and allocate them properly into respective assemblies. At the same time, our method will detect recombinant genome sequences, and report the phylogenetic positions of the strains in the sample. We will evaluate the performance of our method using computer simulation experiments. Our assembly method will be applied to deep sequencing data of the poultry samples from China, to construct more accurate genome sequences of frequently co-infecting avian influenza viruses and Newcastle disease virus. We expect that our method will help identify highly accurate genome sequences and distinguish between similar and recombinant microbial strains, which will facilitate molecular epidemiologic studies and investigations of outbreak sources in the future. 二代測序（NGS）通過非專一性引子對DNA/RNA進行大規模並行測序。這些高通量的"深度測序"使得檢測生物樣品中微生物種類的複雜組成（比如腸道樣品中的病毒組）成為可能。因此NGS成為傳染性疾病監控的重要工具，用於追查致病病原體以及它們在疾病暴發中的基因組進化。目前主要的NGS技術都有一個共同的局限性：測序大量短片段（大約75-400鹼基），而這些短片段必須通過拼裝來獲得完整的生物基因序列，當前使用的拼裝方法包括從頭拼裝和基於參考序列在很多情況下都獲得了成功，但是當測序的基因組來自於混和高度相似的微生物菌株/病毒株的情況下，這些方法的精確度是不可靠的，而這種情況在傳染性病毒監控的原始樣品中是經常出現的。現行方法無法準確地區分不同菌株/病毒株來源的短序列會導致將短序列拼裝到錯誤的基因組中，結果將是產生錯誤的重組序列或者不准確的多變序列。這種不准確的數據將嚴重影響下游分析。我們提出新的拼裝方法，利用參考基因組所構建的進化樹來指導NGS短序列的拼裝，參考進化樹編碼了已知菌株/病毒株的全方位進化信息，將幫助區分來自相似菌株或病毒株的短序列，並將其正確地拼裝到相應的基因組中。與此同時，我們的方法將檢測基因組序列重組並報告出相應菌株/病毒株在樣品中的進化位置。我們將使用計算機仿真實驗來評估此方法的性能。我們的拼裝方法將應用於來自中國家禽樣品的深度測序數據，而這些樣品經常共感染了甲型流感病毒和新城病病毒。我們預期這一方法將有助於拼裝出更準確的基因組序列，同時可以分辨出相似和重組的微生物菌株/病毒株。如此可促進分子流行病學研究和未來流行病暴發來源的搜尋。

17150816.label: Realisation of objectives
17150816.value: Realisation of the three objectives: (1) A computation method “Phylogeny-guided assembly method” (PAM) has been successfully developed. This method enables the genome assembly of next-generation sequencing (NGS) short reads with the aid of the reference phylogeny of the target microbial species. Our results (details refer to (2)) showed that PAM is capable to deal with sequencing reads from samples with co-existence of multiple strains on both the simulation and real datasets. PAM has the ability to assemble viral genome sequences from different strains in a high accuracy. In the simulation study of mixed viral infection samples, we showed that PAM had outstanding performance compared to some other existing de novo and reference-based assembly methods (see details in (2)). It could also detect the recombination pattern simultaneously from assembly profiles (by showing crossover pattern in the read coverage plot). The PAM is implemented in a JAVA program with graphical user interface, which could run in Windows, Linux and MacOS operation systems. This provides a visual presentation of the assembly results to the users and their flexibility to examine the results. It will be available for download and use in our GitHub software repository (https://github.com/id-bioinfo). The publication introducing this PAM tool is in the process. Furthermore, in the process of PAM development, we had also developed a novel method for phylogenetic placement of sequences, called “TIPars”, which utilizes the pre-computed ancestral sequences to speed up the insertion process. This TIPars was used in PAM to place the short reads on the reference phylogeny. We implemented TIPars as a standalone computational tool, and share it to the public on GitHub via https://github.com/id-bioinfo/TIPars. The publication of TIPars tool is also in the process. (2) We had conducted extensive simulation study of the performance of our PAM and compared with the performances of some other existing de novo and reference-based assembly methods including SPAdes and Velvet (de novo), and Bowtie2 and BWA (reference sequence-based) respectively. For PAM, we tested with two types of implementations of phylogenetic placement methods for reads: using “TIPars” (our new method described above; parsimony approach), and two existing maximum likelihood methods EPA and pplacer. Simulations were based on the genome sequences of Influenza A virus and Newcastle Disease Virus. In the simulated read datasets mixing with two virus strains (of same virus species), de novo assembly methods produced more fragmented contig sequences than our and other methods. Similarly, the coverage and accuracy of their assembled sequences were also lower (at 65% above, in average) than the other methods. Bowtie and BWA had much higher coverage, almost perfect in average (lower quartile at >96%), given the a priori known closest reference strains. Their accuracies were also high, mostly above 96%, but their performance dropped significantly (e.g. from average at 99% to 95%; p<0.05) when the closest references were not known and instead two random reference sequences were used as template for their assembly process. For PAM, without knowing the closest references, it performed much better than the de novo methods (SPAdes and Velvet) and more accurate than the reference sequence based methods (Bowtie2 and BWA). PAM has about 95% and >99% accuracy in average for using maximum likelihood phylogenetic placement methods and our new parsimony placement method “TIPars”. The improvement on the coverage by using TIPars in PAM is even more substantial (80% to 98%). Overall, PAM had similar performance to reference sequence-based methods that knew the closest strains (but this is usually not practical in dealing with samples in reality). Notably PAM outperformed the other methods by obtaining longer and more accurate genome sequences from the assembly process, given no prior knowledge on which strains present in the samples. For TIPars tool, we also performed extensive simulation assessment comparing it with some other existing phylogenetic placement methods including EPA and pplacer. The results showed that it outperformed other methods in the overall speed and accuracy. (3) We have re-examined the poultry samples from the surveillance in China using PAM. NGS sequencing data from 300 NDV positive samples were analysed. These real data sets from the field surveillance have quite variable abundance of reads matched to NDV, ranging from 17,984 to 259,656 reads in each sample (average 24,418 reads). In general, samples with more NDV reads produced longer consensus sequences from PAM. Interestingly, the number of consensus sequences generated from each sample ranges from 11 to 74, which is significantly more than those from simulated data. This reflected the higher intra-sample diversity of the viral sequences in reality. Notably, majority of the multiple consensus sequences generated from the same samples were highly similar (average dissimilarity 1.05%). Examining the phylogenetic placement of the reads that form these consensus sequences, revealed that most of them clustered in the same lineage. Among the 300 datasets, 159 (53%) dataset had at least one pair of consensus sequences with dissimilarity > 1%. Although the >1% dissimilarity suggest these consensus sequences may represent different NDV strains, the 53% might not be an accurate figure of co-infection rate among NDV only because we also found that some samples have reads related to both NDV (serotype 1 avian paramyxovirus) and non-serotype 1 paramyxovirus. Some of these >1% dissimilarity might have resulted from the comparison between NDV reads and the non-serotype 1 paramyxovirus reads erroneously mapped to the NDV reference tree. These erroneous mapping was usually limited to very few reads (conserved regions across paramyxovirus serotypes), so their consensus sequences were very short. Therefore, if we restricted our comparison on samples with only consensus sequences that covered >60% of expected NDV genomes, among these 86 fulfilled datasets only 6 datasets (6.98%) contained at least one pair of consensus sequences with dissimilarity > 1%. This 6.98% might represent a more accurate estimate of the co-infection rate of NDV (excluding non-serotype 1 paramyxovirus). On the other hand, among all datasets, at least 3 samples show crossover pattern in the assembly profile, thus suggesting at least 1% recombination rate. Overall, we have obtained the estimates of NDV recombination and co-infection rates in the poultry population in southern China. For avian influenza virus (AIV), we re-examined the 1,200 positive poultry samples from our 2013-2014 surveillance in China using PAM. A total of 348 samples (29%) were found to produce consensus sequences with >1% dissimilarity, suggestive of fairly frequent co-infections.

17150816.label: Major findings and research outcome
17150816.value: This research has led to the development of a new type of computational method (called "PAM") that utilises the reference phylogeny of the target microorganisms to guide the assembly of genomes from their short NGS reads. Simulation studies showed that PAM outperformed some existing de novo and reference-sequence based assembly methods - it had high accuracy and coverage in distinguishing multiple virus strains mixed within the samples, particularly when we have no prior knowledge on which strains present in the samples. This research created another new method (called "TIPars") that utilises ancestral sequences to accurately and efficiently perform phylogenetic placement of sequences. Simulation studies demonstrated that TIPars outperformed some existing maximum likelihood methods, with higher accuracy and speed. PAM was used to re-examine the NGS data of AIV and NDV positive poultry samples from the market surveillance in China. It presented evidence of co-infection and recombination between different viral strains.

17150816.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17150816.value: The PAM tool was developed based on the sequences of avian influenza virus and Newcastle disease virus. This method is also applicable to other viruses, theoretically, as well as bacterial genomes. Further research could validate and demonstrate the use of PAM in more diverse NGS data from different viral and bacterial samples. It would also be useful to incorporate these developed computational tools (and other downstream tools) into a complete virus NGS analysis pipeline to facilitate genomic surveillance and epidemiological analysis of the pathogens.

17150816.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17150816.value: In this research, a novel computational method (called "PAM") was developed for assembling next-generation sequencing short reads by utilising the reference phylogeny of the target microbes. We have shown that this new method had outstanding performance in distinguishing multiple virus strains from the sequencing data. It was capable to obtain high-quality assembled virus genomes with higher coverage and accuracy from co-infection samples, compared to some existing assembly methods. Therefore, this method is an useful new tool to enhance the genomic surveillance and molecular epidemiological study of the pathogens. It has a high value for infectious disease monitoring and control using the state-of-the-art genomic approach.

17150916.label: Realisation of objectives
17150916.value: The project objectives have all been 100% achieved. Objective 1. To study the role of CaMK2A and CaMK2A/SOX2 coupling in TIC regulation of non-small cell lung cancer: We first demonstrated the role of CaMK2A in mediating TIC phenotypes by knocking down/out or overexpressing CaMK2A in multiple lung cancer cell lines and showed SOX2 expression was correspondingly increased or reduced. Cell lines with CaMK2A overexpression enhanced TIC in vitro and in vivo bioassays as well as resistance to chemotoxic and targeted therapy. CaMK2A suppression led to the reverse effects, supporting its TIC enhancing actions. Double engineering with CaMK2A overexpression and SOX2 knockdown showed in vitro and in vivo suppression of TIC phenotypes, implicating the actions of CaMK2A were mediated through SOX2. Objective 2. To study the mechanism of SOX2 regulation by CaMK2A through EZH2 and H3K27me3 modification: Using Western blot on cell lines with suppressed or overexpressed CaMK2A, it was observed SOX2 and EZH2 expression were correspondingly reduced or increased. The mechanism was due to CaMK2A-mediated phophosphorylation of EZH2 T487 which, in turn, suppressed methylation of H3K27me3 and thus de-repressed SOX2. The finding was validated using co-immunoprecipitation experiments which showed physical binding of H3K27me3 and EZH2 to SOX2 regulatory regions in lung cancer cell lines with CaMK2A up- or down-regulation, respectively. Functionally, suppression of CaMK2A led to reduced in vitro TIC phenotypes including stem cell marker expression (ALDH) and cancer cell viability, but co-suppression of EZH2 rescued the functional suppression with partial reversal of ALDH expression and cell viability. Together, the findings validated the hypothesis of this study. Objective 3. To study the expression patterns of CaMK2A and its clinicopathological significance in human non-small cell lung cancer: We performed immunohistochemistry analysis of 199 human lung cancers and showed high level cytoplasmic and nuclear staining of CaMK2A correlated with poor recurrence free and overall survival. Using public dataset (KMplot), the relation between CaMK2A and prognosis was validated at the mRNA level. No correlation with other clinical and pathological parameters was observed.

17150916.label: Major findings and research outcome
17150916.value: Tumor initiating cells (TIC) of lung cancer are mainly induced by stress-related plasticity. Calcium/Calmodulin dependent protein kinase II alpha (CAMK2A) is a key calcium signaling molecule activated by exogenous and endogenous stimuli with effects on multiple cell functions but little is known about its role on TIC. In human lung adenocarcinomas (AD), CAMK2A was aberrantly activated in a proportion of cases and was an independent risk factor predicting shorter survivals. Functionally, CAMK2A enhanced TIC phenotypes in vitro and in vivo. CAMK2A regulated SOX2 expression by reducing H3K27me3 and EZH2 occupancy at SOX2 regulatory regions, leading to its epigenetic de-repression with functional consequences. Further, CAMK2A caused kinase-dependent phosphorylation of EZH2 at T487 with suppression of EZH2 activity. Together, the data demonstrated the CAMK2A-EZH2-SOX2 axis on TIC regulation. This study provided phenotypic and mechanistic evidence for the TIC supportive role of CAMK2A, implicating a novel predictive and therapeutic target for lung cancer. The findings of this project were published in a peer-reviewed journal (CAMK2A supported tumor initiating cells of lung adenocarcinoma by upregulating SOX2 through EZH2 phosphorylation. Cell Death Dis 11, 410 (2020). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41419-020-2553-6), and reported in 2 conference abstracts. The funding also supported one PhD student whose thesis was titled "Lung Cancer Resilience and Stem Cell Phenotypes are Enhanced Through the CAMKIIα/NRF2/GSTP1 Axis", and studies have been completed.

Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17150916.value: Tumor initiating cells (TIC) of lung cancer are mainly induced by stress-related pathways. This study has shown a molecule known as Calcium/Calmodulin dependent protein kinase II alpha (CAMK2A) contributes to the support of TIC. In human lung adenocarcinomas (AD), activated CAMK2A was expressed at high levels, and statistically associated with cancers that had shorter survivals. Experimental studies performed in cell cultures and in mice models showed CAMK2A had functions that enhanced the biological properties of TIC, including increasing the resistance of cancer cells to chemotherapy. Mechanistically, CAMK2A regulated SOX2 expression by reducing H3K27me3 and EZH2 occupancy at SOX2 regulatory regions, leading to its epigenetic de-repression with functional consequences. Further, CAMK2A caused kinase-dependent phosphorylation of EZH2 T487 resulting in suppressed EZH2 activity. Together, the data demonstrated the CAMK2A-EZH2-SOX2 axis supported TIC, and implicated CAMK2A was a predictive and therapeutic target for lung cancer.

17151716.label: Realisation of objectives
17151716.value: All proposed objectives in this study have been achieved with major findings in the protective role of kallistatin in renal fibrosis, the mechanism of its anti-fibrotic action and the clinical relevance in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD). First, we showed the inhibiting effect of kallistatin on Wnt/β-catenin signaling in tubular epithelial cells. Kallistatin overexpression reduced β-catenin expression level and its translocation into the nuclei for action, resulting in down-regulation of β-catenin target gene expression (completion of Aim 2). Next, we revealed the functional role of kallistatin in renal fibrosis using both depletion and gene transfer approach in the model of unilateral ureteral obstruction (UUO). Here, we found that depletion of kallistatin by anti-kallistatin antibody injection enhanced Wnt/β-catenin activation and aggravated renal fibrosis, indicating an endogenous protective role in progression of CKD. On the other hand, ultrasound microbubble-mediated kallistatin gene transfer ameliorated TGF-β-induced EMT and fibroblast activation in UUO mice by antagonizing Wnt/β-catenin activation, suggesting a potential novel therapeutic strategy for CKD (completion of Aim 3). The findings were featured in the front cover of the journal. Clinically, reduced kallistatin expression level was detected in renal biopsies from patients with various stages of CKD, and its expression correlated with renal function (completion of Aim 1). In conclusion, our data uncovered an important implication of renal kallistatin expression in progression of CKD since its downregulation in the kidney may lead to the re-activation of Wnt/β-catenin signaling and thus promoting renal fibrosis. Kallistatin may be considered as a potential therapeutic target as well as novel biomarker for CKD.

17151716.label: Major findings and research outcome
17151716.value: 1. Kallistatin (KS) attenuated TGF-β-induced fibrotic changes via antagonizing Wnt/β-catenin signaling in tubular epithelial cells (HK-2 cells) By transfection with KS plasmid, we found that KS overexpression significantly repressed endogenous TGF-β expression and TGF-β-induced phosphorylation of smad3 (p-smad3), and confirmed that such blockade of downstream Smad3 signaling pathway lead to suppression of ECM protein expression such as collagen 1 (Col-1). In addition, KS overexpression also markedly inhibited TGF-β-induced cytoplasmic β-catenin expression and its nuclear translocation, thereby downregulating the expression of β-catenin target genes including fibronectin, PAI-1, Snail and the negative regulator of Wnt/β-catenin signaling, DKK1. 2. Kallistatin prevented fibroblast activation via paracrine mechanism Previous study shows that kallistatin is mainly localized in the tubular epithelium of the kidney. Despite the suppression of epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) of tubular epithelial cells, we showed that pretreatment with secreted KS from transfected HK-2 cells attenuated TGF-β-induced expression of α-SMA and Col-1 in kidney interstitial fibroblast cells (NRK49F cells) compared with that pretreated without secreted KS. 3. Depletion of kallistatin aggravated renal fibrosis in the model of unilateral ureteral obstruction (UUO) via activation of Wnt/β-catenin signaling Immunohistochemical staining showed that KS expression was markedly reduced in kidney tissues of rats than in sham-operated control at day 7 after UUO. To confirm the association between renal KS loss and progression of renal fibrosis, UUO rats were injected with anti-KS antibody to further deplete endogenous KS level. Sirius red staining showed that injection with anti-KS aggravated the ECM accumulation in UUO kidneys compared with UUO received control IgG. Cortical expression of vimentin, α-SMA and TGF-β was upregulated in UUO kidney while induction of these fibrotic molecules was attenuated after anti-KS injection. Furthermore, expression level of phosphorylated GSK3β was induced after anti-KS injection, leading to β-catenin accumulation in the tubular epithelium of UUO kidneys and upregulation of Wnt4, β-catenin and Axin2. Our findings confirmed that endogenous KS regulated Wnt/β-catenin signaling in kidney tubules during UUO. 4. Kallistatin gene transfer ameliorated inflammation and renal injury in UUO model We demonstrated that KS overexpression in UUO kidneys significantly alleviated cytokine production, macrophage infiltration and tubulointerstitial fibrosis via suppression of Wnt/β-catenin and TGF-β signaling pathways. Interestingly, we found that KS overexpression can attenuate the upregulation of renin and angiotensin II type 1 receptor in UUO kidneys, uncovering a novel role of KS in intrarenal renin-angiotensin system. Together, our findings suggested a potential therapeutic strategy for renal fibrosis by targeting KS. 5. Reduction of KS in the progression of chronic kidney disease (CKD) Immunohistochemical staining in human biopsy showed that renal KS expression was progressively decreased in patients with CKD. The magnitude of KS reduction was correlated positively with estimated glomerular filtration rate and negatively with serum creatinine, confirming the association of renal KS loss with the development of progressive renal fibrosis.

17151716.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17151716.value: Based on the findings from this study, we identified an endogenous protective role of kallistatin in renal fibrosis and suggested a potential novel therapeutic strategy for CKD. Importantly, we uncovered a clinical implication of renal kallistatin expression in CKD, suggesting that it may become a biomarker for the progression of CKD. We are currently exploring the relationship between kallistatin and clinical evidence of renal function in patients with CKD from our clinical trial study on diabetic kidney disease. Findings from this study will provide further evidence on the potential use of kallistain as diagnostic and or prognostic marker for CKD.

17151716.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17151716.value: Kidney fibrosis is a key driving process common to all chronic kidney disease (CKD). In this study, we showed that kidney expression of kallistatin, an endogenous serine proteinase inhibitor, was progressively decreased in patients with CKD and its expression correlated with kidney function. Our results showed that kallistatin protected against kidney inflammation and fibrosis via suppressing Wnt/β-catenin and TGF-β signaling pathway and kallistatin exerted these beneficial effects not only on tubular epithelial cells, but via paracrine action on kidney fibroblasts. Taken together, our work provided significant evidence on the importance of kallistatin in kidney fibrosis that made it a valuable clinical biomarker and novel therapeutic target in CKD.

17152116.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17152116.value: Our clinical observation revealed that Gardenia jasminoides Ellis (Shan-Zhi-Zi in Chinese), has beneficial effect of regressing tumour progression in cancer patients. Geniposide is the major active component isolated from Gardenia jasminoides Ellis. However, scanty scientific information is available to reveal anticancer effect of geniposide in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and its underlying mechanism. Is it safe and effective? Our preliminary observation showed that geniposide exhibited minimal systemic toxicity. Live animal imaging of mice bearing hepatic tumour revealed that geniposide could regress the growth of implanted HCC. In vitro assays confirmed that geniposide significantly reduced proliferation of HCC. What are the targets of geniposide in its anticancer activities in cell and animal models? By profiling genomic-wide gene expression with cDNA microarray, we discovered that geniposide, altered the expression of a number of genes in HCC cells. Based on qRT-PCR verification of the genes highly relevant to HCC, Human PIWI-like protein (Hiwi) was mostly down-regulated in geniposide-treated cells. Interestingly, Hiwi is recently identified as a new oncogene in HCC, and over-expression of Hiwi was proved to promote the proliferation of HCC cells. Geniposide suppressed Hiwi expression in multiple HCC cell lines. Over-expression of Hiwi markedly attenuated the inhibitory effect of geniposide. How does Hiwi play its role in mediating anticancer effect of geniposide? Our preliminary study showed that geniposide inhibited NF-κB signalling pathway and repressed the expression of oncogenes including Cyclin B1 and VEGF. Geniposide may suppress Hiwi by inhibiting the induction of oncogenic proteins and the activation of oncogenic signals. Activation of Ras/Raf/MEK/ERK1/2 is known to up-regulate the expression of Hiwi and other genes in the regulation of proliferation and growth of HCC. Interestingly, geniposide suppressed IL1β-induced ERK1/2 activation and Hiwi expression. Importantly, Hiwi may mediate the effect of geniposide on the oncogenic activity of Ras/Raf/MEK/ERK1/2. Thus, we hypothesize that geniposide may exhibit the anti-tumour action on HCC via inhibiting Hiwi and related cell signals. We propose (1) To further validate anti-tumour effect of geniposide using orthotopically HCC-implanted models; (2) To investigate the role of Hiwi in mediating the tumour suppressive effect of geniposide; and (3) To elucidate the regulatory mechanism of geniposide on the upstream and downstream signalling of Hiwi. 17152116.label: Realisation of objectives
17152116.value: The objective 1 has been fully achieved. We have conducted animal study with orthotropic hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) implantation model with different liver cancer cell lines expressing the luciferease reporter. While MHCC97L could successfully generate an implanted tumor, most of the other cell lines are not tumorigenic in vivo. Both oral administration and intraperitoneal injection of geniposide with 30mg/kg once per two days for 5 weeks have yielded the most inhibitory effect of HCC generation, which is achieved via the downregulation of CD31, ki67, Hiwi and Cyclin B1. In addition, mice treated with geniposide combined with capecitabine/doxorubcin can enhance the anti-tumor activity against implanted HCC. The objective 2 has been achieved. Both in vitro and in vivo studies have been conducted to evaluate the role of Hiwi in mediating the tumour suppressive effect of geniposide. Overexpression and knockdown of Hiwi in HCC cell lines was established. In both modified cell lines, we have observed that the anti-tumor effect of geniposide in vitro and in vivo could be attenuated by restoration of VEGF and Cyclin B1. In addition, qPCR, ELISA, and ChIP assay confirmed that geniposide could exhibit anti-HCC effect by mediating Hiwi/Sp1-related pathway. Histological analysis on the liver section including the detection of CD31, ki67, VEGF, Sp1 in geniposide-treated mice further supported our conclusion. The objective 3 has been achieved in line with our hypothesis. We have conducted EMSA assay and verified that the Hiwi-induced increase of transcriptional activity of NF-κB including the subunits of p65, p50,p52 and cRel could be blocked by geniposide. In addition, we confirmed the role of ERK1/2 in mediating transcription of Hiwi by using ERK1/2 inhibitor and siRNA, and further measured that inhibition of ERK1/2 could mediate geniposide-suppressed Hiwi transcription in HCC cells All the proposed experiments have been conducted and research questions have been elaborated.

17152116.label: Major findings and research outcome
17152116.value: 6.1.1 The anti-hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) effect of geniposide has been systematically evaluated in pre-clinical model of HCC implanted mice. Geniposide was found to be a potent inhibitor of liver tumor, and both intraperitoneal injection and oral administration of geniposide could significantly suppress tumor growth. Mice treated with geniposide combined with both capecitabine and doxorubcin can enhance the anti-tumor activity against implanted HCC. In the process of learning, we elaborated that excessive use of geniposide including other Chinese medicine could induce multiple hepatotoxicities rather than their therapeutic effect. Additionally, co-treatment of Chinese medicine with common chemotherapeutics including capecitabine could potently alleviate the adverse effects of chemotherapy. Please refer to Part C publication on peer reviewed journal entitled “Molecular Mechanisms Involved in Oxidative Stress-Associated Liver Injury Induced by Chinese Herbal Medicine: An Experimental Evidence-Based Literature Review and Network Pharmacology Study” and “Multi-Component Herbal Products in the Prevention and Treatment of Chemotherapy-Associated Toxicity and Side Effects: A Review on Experimental and Clinical Evidences” 6.1.2 We observed that Hiwi, Sp1, cyclin b1, and VEGF are the key targets that get involved in the anti-HCC effect of geniposide on liver cancer. HCC inhibition by geniposide could be attenuated by suppressing Hiwi by mediating Hiwi/Sp1-related pathway. This part of study has been concluded and the manuscript is under preparation. In addition, apart from the anti-VEGF effect of geniposide, other Chinese medicine could also exert anti-HCC action by targeting VEGF/VEGFRs, Wnt, and WT1 pathway through multiple layers of regulation as well. Please refer to Part C publication on peer-reviewed journal entitled “Targeting VEGF/VEGFRs Pathway in the Antiangiogenic Treatment of Human Cancers by Traditional Chinese Medicine”, “Repression of WT1-Mediated LEF1 Transcription by Mangiferin Governs β-Catenin-Independent Wnt Signalling Inactivation in Hepatocellular Carcinoma”, and “Identification of WT1 as determinant of heptatocellular carcinoma and its inhibition by Chinese herbal medicine Salvia Chinensis Benth and its active ingredient protocatechualdehyde” 6.1.3 We found that inhibition of NF-κB and ERK1/2 activation have a strong correlation with the anti-tumor effect of geniposide. Besides, we verified that both NF-κB and ERK1/2 can strongly bind to the promoter region of miR-23a. With the experiment platform established in this grant we identified a novel target Atg9b involved in the regulation of autophagy during hepatocarcinogenesis. Please refer to Part C publication on peer-reviewed journal entitled “microRNA-23a in Human Cancer: Its Roles, Mechanisms and Therapeutic Relevance” and “Atg9b Deficiency Suppresses Autophagy and Potentiates Endoplasmic Reticulum Stress-Associated Hepatocyte Apoptosis in Hepatocarcinogenesis”

17152116.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17152116.value: This study has revealed the anti-tumor potential of genipoiside and provided a fundamental evidence of tumor inhibitory effect with multiple mechanisms may be involved. It was noticed that geniposide is a potent inhibitor of hepatocellular carcinoma by regulating Hiwi/Sp1and VEGF secretion. In particular, inhibition of VEGF expression is the case that gets widely involved in various cancer progression, so the potential of geniposide in regulating tumor microenvironment could be further direction. It may be possible that geniposide may suppress the tumor angiogenesis, either by direct action or by mediating VEGF/VEGFR-related signaling pathway in tumor and endothelial cells. Further study may focus on exploring the mechanism between angiogenesis in endotheliocytes and cancerometastasis in the presence of geniposide.

17152116.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17152116.value: Geniposide, a compound from the Chinese herb Zhizi, possesses multiple pharmacological properties, including hepatoprotective, antioxidant, antidiabetic and anti-inflammatory effects. A pre-clinical model that well bioimitated human liver cancer, the orthotropic HCC implantation mice model, was established, and we observe that geniposide treatment, via either oral administration or intraperitoneal injection, could remarkably inhibit the orthotropic growth of liver tumor. This effect of geniposide is dose-dependent and related to inhibition of tumor cell proliferation and tumor angiogenesis. In addition, we found that combination use of geniposide with common chemotherapeutics could enhance the therapeutic outcome. The oncogene Hiwi plays a central role in regulating geniposide-mediated anti-tumor actions, and inhibition of Hiwi by geniposide results in reduced tumor expansion. Our study provides comprehensive pre-clinical evidence of anti-tumor effect of geniposide on liver cancer, and sheds lights on the potential of geniposide as a novel chemopreventive medicine. The data in our study could be translatable in future clinical trials and drug development.

17152316.label: Project Objectives
17152316.value: Measure thermal tolerance (ctmax and ctmin) for a range of diurnal and nocturnal lizards and Lepidoptera species in Hong Kong and South Africa. With these data we can examine if nocturnal ectotherms have comparable thermal tolerance to diurnal ectotherms. Examine diel variation in thermal tolerance for lizards and Lepidoptera. How thermal tolerance (ctmax and ctmin) might vary hourly over the course of a day remains an under-studied topic with possible consequences for climate change responses. In the lab, determine how thermal tolerance is affected by resource restriction for nocturnal and diurnal lizards and Lepidoptera. We will test the hypothesis that fasting/starvation affects thermal tolerance. Using operative temperature models, measure thermal variation at small spatial and temporal scales for lizards and Lepidoptera in Hong Kong and South Africa. In order to contextualize the lab thermal tolerance results we will quantify variation in body temperature for diurnal and nocturnal ectotherms to assess whether activity patterns is likely affect thermal safety margins (the difference between ctmax and operative temperature). Integrate all lab and field data to project warming impacts on nocturnal and diurnal lizards and Lepidoptera across latitude (in South Africa and Hong Kong). 17152316.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17152316.value: Tropical species have recently been highlighted as a group vulnerable to warming due to their natural exposure to high temperatures and adaptation to narrow ranges of thermal variation. However, how diurnal variation in temperature will affect climate change vulnerability and specifically how activity preferences across diurnal times scales, e.g. nocturnal vs. day-active, will structure thermal adaptive responses to warming are not well understood. Furthermore, fundamental to all warming impacts on organismal fitness are underlying energy use patterns mediated by resource availability; in particular, dietary restriction can diminish tolerance to thermal extremes. Lepidoptera and lizards are useful study systems to test diurnal variation influences on biodiversity responses to climatic warming as many species are nocturnal (e.g. moths and geckos) and diurnal (e.g. butterflies and skinks). Additionally, the biophysics and energetics involved in Lepidoptera and lizard eco-physiology have been well modeled for many species. Here, using physiological experimentation and modeling, we will study Lepidoptera and lizards, in both Hong Kong and South Africa, to determine how nocturnality and food/resource availability might structure climate change impacts on ectotherms. First, we will test thermal tolerance in the lab of both diurnal and nocturnal lizards and Lepidoptera in Hong Kong and South Africa to examine possible physiological consequences of nocturnality for warming responses. Second, we will measure diel variation in thermal tolerance to see if such variation is associated with diel activity patterns. Third, we will measure tolerance with added treatments of resource/ feeding restriction at multiple life stages (for Lepidoptera, both adult and larval stages). Fourth, we will characterize thermal variation in Lepidoptera and lizard body temperatures in the field at fine temporal scales across environmental gradients using thermal models (i.e. operative temperature models). Finally, we will integrate all field and lab data using a climate change model within a comparative framework to assess how activity patterns (diurnal vs. nocturnal) and resource availability (full vs. restricted) in different environmental contexts (subtropical Hong Kong vs. temperate South Africa) might alter projections of climate change impacts on ectotherms across latitude. 最近的研究認為熱帶地區的物種生活與溫度較高及溫差較小的熱帶，因而不能適應氣候的急劇變化而容易受到氣候變化的影響。然而，我們對於日溫度變化對於物種對氣候變化的影響了解不多，對不同物種活動節律（白晝和夜晚）更所知甚少。此外，氣候變化對所有物種的影響都作用於影響其對資源的利用，可利用資源尤其是食物資源的減少能夠降低其對極端溫度的適應。鱗翅目昆蟲和蜥蜴是研究上述問題的優良對象，因其均即包含日行性物種（蝶類和石龍子）又包含夜行性物種（蛾類和壁虎）。不僅如此，關於兩者的生物物理學和能量資源分配的生態模型已經在很多物種中建立。據此，我們希望通過研究香港和南非的鱗翅目昆蟲和蜥蜴：首先，利用物理實驗和生態學模型，來檢驗氣候變化對不同活動節律的物種的影響；其次，我們測量溫度適應性是否隨行為節律的不同而變化。第三，測量物種在不同生活史階段（對鱗翅目，成蟲和幼蟲）對溫度耐受的影響及增加或限制食物資源帶來的變化。第四，在野外利用物理溫度模型，在精細的溫度尺度上量化鱗翅目昆蟲和蜥蜴體溫在不同環境梯度下的變化。最後，比較在不同氣候環境下（亞熱帶香港和溫帶南非），利用氣候變化模型整合所有的實驗和野外數據來預測活動節律（日行性和夜行性），以及資源的可利用性（無限和受限）對不同緯度變溫動物對氣候變化的響應。

17152316.label: Realisation of objectives
17152316.value: Over the course of the research we found that some of the objectives were better met by using Lepidoptera as a study system (e.g. resource restriction, Objective 3) while others were better suited to lizards (e.g. diel variation in thermal tolerance, Objective 2). For all objectives we made progress in both Lepidoptera and lizards to some extent but we tended to focus on individual systems for the full completion of the respective objectives. In this case, while the project proceeded as proposed, the final research outputs generally reflect the systems within which successful application of the methods resulted in novel findings and outcomes. The extreme example of this comes from Objective 5 which was proposed as a modelling exercise for ectotherms and activity patterns across latitude but resulted in a model of endotherms and activity patterns across latitude (Bonebrake et al. American Naturalist, 2020). Objective 1 ¬–We measured thermal tolerance for a range of diurnal and nocturnal lizards in both Hong Kong and South Africa. From our results we did not find consistent differences in thermal tolerance between geckos or lizards (Dufour in review, Conservation Physiology – PhD student-led). For Hong Kong moths we found that ctmax increased with increasing body size in some families (crambids and noctuids) but otherwise found high variation in thermal tolerance across species. We also examined body color for a dataset of moths collected in Yunnan China and found that darkness increases with elevation consistent with the thermal melanism hypothesis (Xing et al., Oecologia, 2018 – Postdoc-led). This was somewhat unexpected given the nocturnality of these species and the unclear need for solar input to increase body temperatures for activity during the day (when they are largely inactive). The study then emphasizes the complexity of diel variation in climate and how morphology mediates thermal variation. Objective 2 –We studied variation in thermal tolerance for Hong Kong and South Africa lizards across diurnal scales. We measured both ctmax and ctmin for induvial lizards (both nocturnal and diurnal) during the day and at night. We found no consistent differences between day-time and night-time measurements across all species – however, for one nocturnal gecko we found that ctmin was over 2.5 degrees C lower at night than during the day. This suggests that while consistent differences between day and night thermal tolerance are not likely across ectotherms, there may well be species-specific effects that are important to consider for climate change vulnerability. These are the primary findings of Dufour et al. (in review, Conservation Physiology – PhD student-led). Objective 3 –For lizard species, we took advantage of a steep precipitation gradient in South Africa that results in significant variation in productivity and food resources to test whether this impacted thermal tolerance for diurnal and nocturnal lizards. We found that ctmax did not vary across sites. Ctmin however, was lower in drier and more food-restricted sites (i.e. greater thermal tolerance) counter to expectations (Dufour, presentation at the British Ecological Society 2019). While we had originally planned to execute lab-based trials of resource restriction for lizards we were unable to for logistFor Lepidoptera, we did an intensive examination of food restriction consequences for thermal tolerance in a species of butterfly in Hong Kong, Mycalesis mineus. By focusing on this species, we were able to undertake a mechanistic look at organismal ecophysiology and how starvation at the larval and adult stage impacted not only thermal tolerance, but also mortality and morphology. We found that starvation had little impact on thermal tolerance but it did reduce body size and increased mortality (Ling and Bonebrake, in prep – PhD student-led). We further investigated this by employing stable isotope analysis to see how resource allocation following starvation might impact other aspects of insect physiology, especially reproduction. We found that resource restriction led to delayed times in egg peaks and laid fewer eggs over their lifetime – adult allocation (from nectar) was also found to increase over time for individuals fed normally but not individuals that were starved indicating a reduction in available resources for reproduction (Yu et al., in prep – undergraduate researcher-led). This work on butterfly resource restriction and thermal tolerance indicated that there is not a simple link between the two. However, depending on the life stage (adult vs. larval) and the season (wet season and dry season form), thermal tolerance can vary significantly as can the consequences of resource restriction (e.g. for reproduction and growth). Objective 4 –We deployed operative temperature models for lizards in South Africa and for Lepidoptera in Hong Kong (for both diurnal and nocturnal species in each case). In South Africa, operative temperature models exhibited significant variation across sites (several degrees between maximum temperatures) and greater variation (more than ten degrees in one site) between microhabitats (sun vs. shade). Comparing to thermal tolerance data available for species across those sites, the diurnal skink (Trachylepis variegate) had a narrower thermal tolerance breadth relative to the nocturnal gecko (Chondrodactylus bibronii). While all sites exhibit mean operative temperatures within the thermal tolerance range of both nocturnal and diurnal species, maximum temperature (but not minimum temperatures) do exceed thermal tolerance. To contextualize the thermal data from the operative models we also developed novel methods to measure thermal preference for both lizards and Lepidoptera. For lizards we constructed thermal gradients and used Deep Learning techniques to analyse video data and estimate thermal preference. For Lepidoptera, we built an arena with a steep thermal gradient. We then released field-caught moths and butterflies and used a thermal camera to estimate body temperature and thermal preference. From these experiments, moths (nocturnal Lepidoptera) appear to have a preference for lower temperatures relative to butterflies (diurnal Lepidoptera). Objective 5 – In 2018 the PI went to Chile on a Universitas 21 award to work with Enrico Rezende and Francisco Bozinovic (Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile) to execute this objective collaboratively. However, after initial discussions we determined that, somewhat counterintuitively, endotherms might be a more tractable system for answer the question of how species activity patterns might structure climate change vulnerability across latitude. We therefore developed a model for endotherms (mammals specifically) and climate change vulnerability given thermoregulation and variable activity times. We found strong morphological differences between nocturnal and diurnal mammals in that nocturnal mammals tend to be much smaller. We also found through the thermoregulatory model and projected climate change impacts that diurnal mammals are likely to lose habitable space from warming (especially in the tropics) but that nocturnal mammals may find greater availability of habitat in the future (especially at higher latitudes) (Bonebrake et al., American Naturalist, 2020). Endotherms have capacity to regulate their body temperatures and are likely better able to manage climatic change in the presence of greater food availability, an important element of the thermoregulatory model developed. While we did not model climate change projections in the context of ectotherms as planned, the results for endotherms and mammals have broad relevance for understanding the relationship between activity patterns and climate change vulnerability. Tropical species (endotherms and ectotherms alike) that are obligate in their diurnal activity could be especially vulnerable to warming given their exposure to high temperatures and inability to use diel variation to avoid increasing extreme thermal conditions under climatic warming.

17152316.label: Major findings and research outcome
17152316.value: We investigated how activity patterns (nocturnal vs. diurnal) affected thermal tolerance and climate change of species, especially lizards and Lepidoptera. We furthermore examined how food resources modulated thermal tolerance and vulnerability to warming. Using the diverse ecosystems of Hong Kong and South Africa, we measured thermal tolerance and performance of a range of nocturnal and diurnal species. Across several lizard species we found that thermal tolerance rarely differed between night and day measurement. However, for the one species that did differ, we found a difference of over 2.5 degrees C which highlights how in some contexts such diel variation in thermal tolerance could be key (Dufour et al. in review). We also found no consistent differences in thermal tolerance between diurnal and nocturnal lizards. For Lepidoptera, interestingly, we found that moths (in Yunnan, China) tend to increase in darkness up elevation consistent with the thermal melanism hypothesis (Xing et al., Oecologia, 2018). We also developed methods for quantifying thermal performance in lizards and Lepidoptera – moths appear to have a lower thermal preference than butterflies (in Hong Kong). Altogether our results show that while moths are active at night and therefore not subject to extreme temperatures during their activity period, they are still vulnerable to warming impacts. We also investigated the effect of resource restriction on thermal tolerance for a Hong Kong butterfly species, Mycalesis mineus. Larval and adult starvation did not affect thermal tolerance of the species (ctmax) but did reduce body size and increase mortality (Ling and Bonebrake in prep). We also used stable isotope analysis to see whether starvation affected resource allocation or reproduction in the species. We found reduced overall fecundity under starvation conditions and also that starved individuals were unable to maintain resource allocation to reproduction compared to fully fed counterparts (Yu et al. in prep). This case study then highlights the complexity of food and thermal tolerance interactions. Finally, we developed a framework for modelling endotherm thermoregulation in response to diurnal and nocturnal climatic variation globally and applied it to mammals. The results demonstrated that climatic suitability is likely to be lost for diurnal species (especially tropical species) under future warming but that nocturnal species will see increases in climatic suitability. Body size will also critically determine the vulnerability of species to future warming. The model shows the importance of the consideration of activity time in structuring warming responses (Bonebrake et al., American Naturalist, 2020).

17152316.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17152316.value: During the course of this research we tended to shift our focus from thermal tolerance to thermal preference of species. While thermal tolerance data can yield important insights, there is significant potential in understanding how warming impacts that do not approach ctmax may still alter performance and be reflected in vulnerability assessments of species. Further development of this component of our work would be ideal and we continue to test experimental and analytical techniques to ease the collection and interpretation of this data. The modelling study of endotherms highlighted the utility of global approaches for understanding thermoregulation, activity patterns, and climate change projections. A major challenge in this for ectotherms is the relative lack of data – for mammals, this was a significant strength. But data is accumulating and the recent recognition of global insect declines (in 2019) has accelerated the urgency in these kinds of analysis. We will continue the development of models (and data collection to feed into the models) to better understand how climate change is likely to impact nocturnal ectotherms.

17152316.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17152316.value: We studied lizards and Lepidoptera (butterflies and moths) across South Africa and Hong Kong to examine variation in thermal tolerance and how access to food might buffer or exacerbate warming impacts for nocturnal species. Broadly, we found no consistent differences in thermal tolerance between diurnal and nocturnal species. We also found that thermal tolerance, if measured during the day or night in lizards, did not vary consistently (except for one species). In moths, interestingly, we found a clear pattern of darkness increases with increasing elevation indicating important thermal consequences of temperature for these nocturnal species. We also tested whether starvation affected the thermal tolerance of a Hong Kong butterfly species. There was no effect of starvation on thermal tolerance but body size was reduced and mortality increased. Butterflies that were starved also exhibited reduced fecundity and lower allocation of adult resources to eggs. Resource restriction and climate change effects have complex interactions in ectotherms. Finally, in a modelling study, we found that nocturnal mammals will have increased climatic suitability under climate change while diurnal species will have reduced suitability (especially in the tropics). Altogether these results demonstrate the importance of considering activity patterns in understanding climate change impacts on biodiversity.

17153016.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17153016.value: 傳統觀點認為線粒體功能缺陷促進衰老。然而, 越來越多的證據表明，某些線粒體電子傳遞鏈（ETC）功能的改變可誘發細胞的防禦機制，包括線粒體未折疊蛋白反應（UPRmt），線粒體活性氧應激響應(mitohormesis)和線粒體自噬(mitophagy)。這些應激反應機制互相協調防止老化引起的器官損害。 SIRT1屬於一類NAD依賴性蛋白脫乙酰酶, 具有各種有益的抗老化活性。SIRT1在脂肪組織的高表達顯著減慢小鼠代謝老化，改善能量平衡和胰島素敏感性。我們最近的數據顯示，在這種類型小鼠的脂肪組織，線粒體的形態和功能明顯不同于野生型小鼠。早在八週的年齡，線粒體基因組編碼的ETC組分都顯著下調，導致UPRmt，觸發mitohormesis和mitophagy。此外，通過生命早期階段的線粒體動態重構， ETC的最大呼吸能力顯著增加。 在這裡，我們提出生命早期脂肪細胞線粒體功能的及時重置能夠確定小鼠衰老表型。本研究將揭示SIRT1如何誘導mitohormesis和mitophagy並刺激線粒體重塑, 从而減緩代謝老化。研究結果有望揭開長壽通路的分子機制, 和開闢老化藥物研發的新前景。

17153016.label: Realisation of objectives
17153016.value: Our results demonstrated that over-expression of human SIRT1 selectively in adipose tissue protected mice from ageing- and dietary obesity-induced metabolic abnormalities. SIRT1-triggerred mitochondrial stress and UPRmt represent the major underlying mechanisms to instigate the defense response against adipose tissue dysfunction, including ER-stress an dinflammation. Detailed cellular and molecular studies revealed that SIRT1 was located in a specific subcellular compartment, named mitochondria-ER contacts (MERCs). A UPRmt downstream signaling molecule, clusterin, was found to mediate SIRT1's effects on the regulation of ER stress. SIRT1 and clusterin cooperated to control the lipid and protein composition at MERCs, in turn facilitating the communications between the two important organelles and the biogenesis of high density lipoprotein particles (HDL) enriched with omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids. The latter contributes to the systemic anti-inflammatory and insulin-sensitizing effects of adipose SIRT1.

17153016.label: Major findings and research outcome
17153016.value: Major findings 1. Mitohormesis is invoked by overexpression of human SIRT1 in adipose tissue via enhanced mitochondrial ROS production. Modulation of mitohormesis abolishes the metabolically healthy ageing and anti-obesity function mediated by adipose SIRT1. 2. Adipose SIRT1 is located at the interface between mitochondria and ER, referred to as MERCs, which are a specific subcellular microcompartment that mediates effective intraorganellar communications and lipoprotein biogenesis. 3. Clusterin is upregulated by SIRT1 in adipose tissue and acts at MERCs to prevent the hyperactivation of ER stress and facilitate the biogenesis of HDL enriched with omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids. 4. Hyperactivated ER stress downregulates SIRT1 expression, whereas inhibitors of ER stress signaling restores adipose SIRT1-mediated beneficial effects on systemic energy metabolism. Research outcomes: 1. Publication of four journal articles and a number of conference papers 2. Training of three PhD students 3. Establishing and strengthening the international collaborations

17153016.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17153016.value: The discovery of SIRT1's location at MERCs is unexpected and opens a new field for metabolic aging research and development. Importantly, not only SIRT1, but also the machinery of NAD biosynthesis as well as the CDK5/P25 signaling molecules are located at MERCs. Collectively, the information suggest an important micro-compartment where SIRT1 is regulated, in turn coordinating the various stress signaling pathways in adipose tissue. To uncover the detailed molecular interactions at MERCs will pave the way for SIRT1-based translational research and development. Based on these important discoveries, a grant application was submitted to bid for the 2022/2023 round of RGC-GRF, entitled "SIRT1 signaling and NAD homeostasis in adipose tissue – focusing on the contact sites between mitochondria and endoplasmic reticulum".

17153016.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17153016.value: SIRT1 is a longevity regulator that possesses potent anti-ageing activity. Our research reveals that SIRT1 in adipose (fat) tissue governs the whole body's energy metabolism and homeostasis. Enhancing SIRT1 function in adipose tissue represents an effective approach to develop drugs for obesity and metabolic diseases.

17153116.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17153116.value: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains as one of the most lethal cancers in the world due to late symptom presentation and lack of curative therapy. Currently, only one FDA-approved drug, Sorafenib, is available for HCC patients and its effect is modest. Metabolic reprogramming is recently considered a hallmark of cancer. Better understanding of the metabolic programs of HCC and its underlying molecular mechanisms is important for the development of effective diagnostic and therapeutic platforms for HCC patients. Cancer cells have increased demands for 1) macromolecules to support rapid cell division, and 2) antioxidants to counteract oxidative stress. The folate cycle, through the transfer of a carbon unit between tetrahydrofolate and its derivatives in the cytoplasmic and mitochondrial compartments, produces precursors for nucleotides and methionine, as well as the antioxidant, NADPH. Interestingly, we observed that folate depletion in the culture medium greatly inhibited HCC growth, suggesting folate as an important nutrient for HCC cells. Folate cycle is carried out by different members of the methylenetetrahydrofolate dehydrogenases (MTHFDs) and we found that a member from the mitochondrial compartment of the folate cycle, MTHFD1L, was significantly over-expressed in human HCC. We showed that NRF2, a transcription factor that acts as the master regulator of REDOX homeostasis, bound to the antioxidant response elements in MTHFD1L to regulate its expression in HCC cells. Furthermore, knockdown of MTHFD1L decreased NADPH production, thereby elevating oxidative stress in HCC cells. Knockdown of MTHFD1L also impeded the growth of HCC. Importantly, knockdown of MTHFD1L or the use of an anti-folate drug, methotrexate, worked synergistically with Sorafenib to suppress HCC proliferation in vitro. These preliminary data led us to hypothesize that MTHFD1L, by maintaining the folate cycle, provides metabolic and survival advantages for HCC cells. Therefore, targeting the folate cycle might create metabolic vulnerability in HCC cells for drug treatment. In this proposal, we will first investigate the clinical relevance of MTHFD1L over-expression in human HCC. Second, we aim to elucidate the upstream regulatory pathway that leads to MTHFD1L over-expression in HCC. Third, we will comprehensively investigate the metabolic and biological functions of MTHFD1L in HCC. Fourth, we will explore the therapeutic potentials of folate inhibitor as single and/or combined therapies in HCC treatment. Taken together, our study will substantially expand our knowledge on the molecular basis of the metabolic machinery of HCC and shed light on new therapeutic regimens for HCC patients.

17153116.label: Major findings and research outcome
17153116.value: 1. We confirmed MTHFD1L over-expression in an expanded cohort of HCC patients by RT-qPCR. MTHFD1L over-expression was present in 50.59% of HCC patients. HCC transcriptome sequencing data available in TCGA echoed our findings. We found that MTHFD1L over-expression was closely associated with aggressive clinicopathological features of HCC including the presence of tumor microsatellite formation, venous invasion, and more advanced tumor stages. HCC patients with high MTHFD1L expression also have lower overall and disease-free survival rates. Western blotting further confirmed that MTHFD1L was also over-expressed at the protein level. 2. NRF2 initiates transcription of genes that counteract oxidative stress. We found three putative AREs in MTHFD1L and confirmed that NRF2 bound to these AREs by ChIP assay in a human HCC cell line, MHCC97L. We generated NRF2 over-expressing (OE) MHCC97L cells by CRISPR-dCas9 Synergistic Activation Mediator (SAM) system and found that MTHFD1L mRNA expression was significantly induced. Reversely, MTHFD1L mRNA and protein expressions were reduced upon knockdown of NRF2 in different HCC cell lines. These data converged to show that MTHFD1L is transcriptionally regulated by NRF2. 3. We found that MTHFD1L drastically increased NADPH production and reduced intracellular ROS level. Knockdown of MTHFD1L reduced NADPH production leading to the accumulation of ROS and oxidized DNA in multiple HCC cell lines. Knockdown of MTHFD1L markedly reduced mitochondrial function. Knockdown and knockout of MTHFD1L markedly repressed cell proliferation, arrested cell cycle, and induced apoptosis in HCC cell lines. Metabolomic profiling using capillary electrophoresis time-of-flight mass spectrometry (CE-TOFMS) was performed. Knockdown of MTHFD1L greatly altered the metabolic profiles of HCC cells. MTHFD1L knockdown resulted in the truncation of folate cycle therefore blocking the transfer of 1C from serine to THF, ultimately causing an accumulation of serine and its precursors G3P and 3PSer. 4. We performed orthotopic liver implantations with MHCC97L-NTC and –shMTHFD1L cells. Knockdown of MTHFD1L in HCC cells drastically suppressed the growth of primary tumors and lung metastasis. We found that HCCs with knockdown of MTHFD1L were more sensitive to Sorafenib in subcutaneous tumor model. Next, we investigated whether pharmacologic inhibition of folate cycle by methotrexate (MTX) would sensitize HCC cells to Sorafenib treatment. MTX worked synergistically with Sorafenib to suppress the growth of subcutaneous HCC tumors derived from MHCC97L as well as patient-derived tumor xenografts (PDTXs). Consistently, we observed synergism between MTX and Sorafenib.

17153116.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17153116.value: We have established MTHFD1L as a prognostic indicator for aggressive HCC and also confirmed that folate cycle inhibitor, methotrexate, is effective in treating HCC in preclinical mouse HCC models. Our study will benefit the development of novel therapeutic strategies involving methotrexate for HCC treatment.

17153116.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17153116.value: HCC cells experience higher level of oxidative stress due to the over-production of metabolic side-products, reactive oxygen species (ROS) or oxidative stress. Our study demonstrated that HCC cells are able to survive this adversity through activating anti-oxidant-producing metabolic pathway, the folate cycle. This is done through the activation of the NRF2/MTHFD1L pathway. We found that MTHFD1L as a novel indicator for poor prognosis in HCC patients and confirmed that targeting the folate cycle through methotrexate could effectively suppress HCC growth in preclinical mouse HCC model.
