17609516.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17609516.value: The rise of China as a global power has witnessed the paradoxical coexistence of both cosmopolitan and nationalistic sensibilities among its population. If China is cosmopolitan, why is it also anxious and xenophobic? How might we understand this tension between two poles that are also coterminous in cultural and social expressions of the cosmopolitan? One way of investigating this paradox is through a focus on media representation and popular imaginaries of masculinities in China as a response to global hegemonic masculinity. As nationalism is often regarded as masculinist, with the status of the male (and also the female, albeit in a very different way) often linked to national confidence and ambition, one would expect media representation to indicate the fault lines of the a) confidence and b) anxiety that the paradox suggests. Through critical analysis of a wide range of male identities and images (both Chinese and foreign) on the Chinese TV screen and their reception by the audience, the proposed project will investigate how masculinity is constructed, negotiated and performed in an increasingly globalizing China and, in particular, in the context of the tensions and negotiation between state-sanctioned nationalistic ideology and neoliberal globalization. The project thus responds to the limitations of exiting studies on hegemonic masculinity by demassifying the monolithic “transnational business masculinity” and offering a nuanced account of the Chinese masculine order and its interactions with the state and global capitalism. Television in China, which combines the roles of a state-controlled propaganda tool and a highly commercialized entertainment industry, is both globalized and localized. It is gaining a new level of cultural importance in the 21st century with technological convergence with other media platforms and unprecedentedly widespread influence. The focus on television thus makes possible new understandings of contested and shifting discourses around the imaginaries of masculine identities and in the intersection of state ideology, market demand and popular desire. Through multi-dimensional explorations of the interrelationship between gender and national identities in TV entertainment, the project promises to not only reveal significant insights into the role played by television in the production of gender identities in present-day China but also provide a well-focused account of China’s cultural engagement with the world in the era of globalization.

17609516.label: Realisation of objectives
17609516.value: 1. The study has examined more than 30 TV programs aired in mainland China during 2015 to 2019. Through close reading of and audience study on a number of male images in these programs, the study constitutes a dialogical inquiry into televisual texts and their various readings. Postsocialist subject-making and knowledge production by and through television are approached from the perspectives of nationalism, cosmopolitanism, and gender construction. Most of the TV programs discussed are TV dramas, the most popular genre of storytelling in China today, although a number of popular reality shows and variety shows, such as the yearly Spring Festival Gala (chunwan) are also involved. However, it did not cover news, current affairs, documentary, education, sports, or children’s programs. In other words, the focus is on entertainment television alone. Program selection was based primarily on three criteria: (a) quantifiable widespread appeal (confirmed through ratings); (b) relevance to the themes and focus of the study; and (c) societal impact (as evidenced by online comments and discussions). Further programs were identified during the process of audience research, as new programs mentioned by the informants were added to the discussion pool. The selection process was therefore iterative, resembling snowball sampling. Instead of collecting a representative sample of Chinese TV programs, I was more interested in collecting programs that have provoked debate in terms of masculinity, Chineseness, and subject-making. 2. The study examined the dynamic negotiations between national and global identities through the lens of the televisual construction of masculinity. Postsocialist Chinese television has produced a wealth of popular male images, ranging from the wartime heroic man to the metrosexual urbanite. Instead of a comprehensive survey of the masculinities depicted on Chinese TV, however, the study is more interested in masculinities in transnational settings, focusing on the development and dynamics of certain forms of manliness that are closely related to the discourses of nationalism. All the male images are discussed in the context of the increasing transnationality of Chinese media and society and treated as a lens through which to productively analyze the politics of subjectivity. As the study reveals, representations of masculinity on Chinese TV are entangled with the paradoxical dynamics of national confidence and anxiety in a global age and contribute to a vision of Chineseness that appeals to the domestic audience. In this sense the role played by the state in the construction of the hegemonic masculinity can never be overestimated. A critical study of these male images reveals how competing forms of masculinity in Chinese media respond to global hegemonic masculinity, legitimatizing male dominance in postsocialist China in various ways, and reflect both the engagement with the global and discourses that are deeply rooted and embedded in the local sociopolitical context. Outcomes of the study thus help deepen our understanding of hegemonic masculinity in a non-Western context and will contribute to a genuinely global vision of this concept. 3. The study has examined the rapid transformations of television in China in recent years. The mechanism of TV production and censorship in China makes this form of culture an important site to examine the tension and complicity between state agenda and global capitalism in the construction of gender identities. The study thus contributed to the mapping of television and its cultural politics in today’s globalized and digitalized era. The resilience of state control over and the social engineering function of Chinese television, as well as the interaction between power and capital, attest to the possibility that current instantiations of media formats, audience behaviors and technological apparatuses might reinscribe—rather than challenge—existent power relations. 4. The textual analysis of select TV programs was supported and supplemented by an empirical study of the programs’ consumption and reception and their influence on people’s perception of masculinity. Three rounds of focus group discussions were carried out in Beijing and Zhuhai in July 2016, June–July 2017, and October 2018 respectively. These two cities were selected because, as the national capital and an economically robust new coastal city, respectively, they are representative of the demographic diversity of Chinese TV viewers. The TV viewers who attended focus group discussions include people with both urban and rural household registrations. During focus group discussions, TV audiences of different age, gender and class background were invited to express their opinion toward certain male images and how these images impact their perception and performance of masculinity. These focus groups were followed by in-depth and open-ended interviews with some informants (through phone calls, emails, and face-to-face communication). Drawing on the theory of the “active audience”, audience study explores how televisual texts are given meaning to by viewers of different gender, age, and educational backgrounds. Outcomes of the ethnographic study have significantly enriched the arguments in each chapter of the book and have brought forth new discoveries and new directions of the critical study of men and masculinities in the context of contemporary China

17609516.label: Major findings and research outcome
17609516.value: The research has so far produced 4 peer-reviewed journal articles/book chapters, 5 conference papers and 1 unpublished book manuscript. A monograph entitled Televising Chineseness: Gender Politics and Nationalism has been completed and is now in the stage of last-minute polishing and copyediting. It is expected that the full manuscript will be submitted to a university press for publication by May 2020. One MPhil student has been trained during the project term with a relevant research topic. In addition, I have been invited to deliver talks about the interim research outcomes at a number of universities, such as Oxford University, University of Texas at Austin, Lancaster University and Australian National University. My research on Chinese masculinities in television has been widely featured by major international media outlets, such as the South China Morning Post, Nikki Asian Review, China Daily, Los Angeles Times and CNN. The study has extensively examined a variety of male images in Chinese television and web dramas, especially new types of images and new aesthetic trends. Drawing on the theory of the “active audience”, audience studies were conducted to explore how televisual texts are given meaning to by viewers of different gender, age, and educational backgrounds. As illustrated by several articles resulted from the research, TV drama and the emergent drama serials on online platforms have become the primary form of storytelling in today’s China. Male images in these dramas reflect not only the resilience of patriarchal ideology in China but also the recent official stance about the necessity of regaining “cultural confidence” in the global age, a stance that has catalyzed an imagined gender order as part of the country’s national essence. In addition, gender hierarchy and ideals are closely associated with the “positive energy” moral values, which underscore optimistic and aspirational attitudes in the face of challenges and thus serve a new mode of governance in China. As a result, the socialist discourse on gender equality and women’s liberation has to coexist and negotiate with the interests, desires, and aspirations of a market that pragmatically promotes neoliberal self-governing subjects. The “straight-man cancer” misogyny, “bossy CEO” arrogance, for instance, can be readily traced back to entrenched traditions in Chinese culture and, at the same time, reflect the profound economic and social changes that have taken place in the reform era, as well as the political agenda of perpetuating both national and male chauvinism.

17609516.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17609516.value: With the rapid convergence of media platforms, it is now increasingly difficult to define the boundaries of “television” in China and alike. Web dramas adapted from online literature, or “IP dramas,” as it is known in China, has emerged as an important yet little studied form of narrative in recent years. They reach out to the younger generation of audiences in urban China and reflect shifting discourses of masculinity and femininity in a globalized era. In a subsequent GRF project, I plan to focus on this form of popular culture and investigate a variety of new gender aesthetics and discourses as seen in these dramas.

17609516.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17609516.value: With an over one billion-strong domestic audience and growing transnational influence and accessibility, Chinese television has become a new symbol and carrier of China’s soft power in an era of increasing global connectivity and is playing a prominent role in cultural governance within the country. The study, echoing recent interest in the interplay between subjectivity and communication in the context of contemporary China, regards television as an effective and dynamic medium of communication and explores the roles it has played in the formation of postsocialist Chinese subjects, especially gendered subjects. In doing so, it offers a new angle on, and reads critically, a selection of Chinese TV programs, mostly TV dramas, that have proved overwhelmingly popular nationwide in recent years (most of them aired since 2015), and investigates how a state-sanctioned, globally negotiated version of “Chineseness” is being articulated through the discourse of masculinity. Popular male images that have been analyzed and discussed in the study include the anti-Japanese heroes, middle-aged entrepreneurs, and the “tall, rich and handsome” returnees from overseas, among others. Textual readings of TV dramas have been supplemented by reception studies conducted with TV audiences.

17612916.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17612916.value: Mentally incapacitated persons (MIPs) are often unable to manage their own financial affairs. With the advent of smaller families, a declining birth rate and a rapidly ageing society, there is an urgent need for a safe and affordable mechanism to manage the assets of MIPs when their ageing parents or caregivers are no longer around to look after them. In Hong Kong, there are currently a few legal asset management tools available to MIPs, at least in theory. In practice, however, none is really suitable. First, while a parent can make a gift of their properties to the MIP by will, it is hard to find a suitable individual to serve as executor of the will. Second, while donees of an enduring power of attorney can be given power to manage financial affairs of the donor, most MIPs do not have the capacity to execute it in the first place. Third, statutory guardianship, while giving the guardian decision-making powers over the MIPs’ affairs, caps the guardian’s power of management to not more than HK$14,000 per month for the MIP. Fourth, only those who are exceptionally financially well off can afford to establish a private trust and engage a professional trustee to manage the assets. To address the drawbacks of these mechanisms, some countries have developed the Special Needs Trust (SNT). Only individuals with special needs, typically defined as individuals who lack mental capacity, are eligible to become beneficiaries under such trusts, which operate as pooled trusts with individualised accounts for clients. The pooled assets of these individual trust accounts are transferred to a trustee, who either manages the assets itself or with the help of a custodian cum fund manager. The trustee devises a care plan and budget for the special needs dependent in consultation with his or her caregiver. The budget provides the basis for the caregiver to apply for distributions for the dependent’s maintenance. Our research will compare the laws and operational experiences of laws pertaining to fiduciary management of property of MIPs in select jurisdictions in Asia and the West. In particular, we will examine two exemplary models of SNTs in the US and Singapore respectively. We seek to distill best practices from these jurisdictions, explore the desirability and feasibility of setting up an SNT in Hong Kong, as well as formulating recommendations to enhance the legal regime for financial management of property of MIPs more generally. 智障人士通常缺乏管理自己的財政事務的能力。隨著小型家庭日趨普及、出生率下降與人口日益老化，智障人士急需一個安全可靠與收費相宜的資產管理機制，以確保他們的資產在其家長或照顧者不在世時，仍能得到妥善管理。 現時，理論上香港有少數適用於智障人士的法定資產管理機制。然而實際上，這些機制幾乎無一切合智障人士的需要。首先，雖然家長能透過訂立遺囑轉贈資產予其智障子女，要找到一個合適而可靠的人選執行遺囑實在非常困難。其二，儘管授權人能利用持久授權書委任受權人，以允許受權人在自己日後變得精神上無行為能力時照顧其財務事項，大多數智障人士根本由始至終連委任一名受權人的能力也欠缺。其三，在政府監護令下，監護人雖然獲授權為智障人士的生活、醫療及財政事項作決定，其權力只限於每月為智障人士處理不超過港幣$14,000的金錢。其四，由於成立私人信託及聘用專業受託人所涉的費用高昂，只有財政較富裕的一群有能力承擔此等費用以管理智障人士的資產。 為了克服上述困難，一些國家成立了專為只有特殊需要⼈士(包括如智障⼈⼠)合資格成為信託受益人的特殊需要信託 。信託把不同家長或照顧者設定的資產集中管理和投資，但每人將獲設一個度身訂造的獨立帳戶。組合起來的資金會轉予一名受託人管理，或會由一名兼任基金經理的保管人一同協助管理。受託人會在徵詢照顧人的意見後為有特殊需要的受益人訂立照顧方案及財政預算，而預算將會成為照顧者日後申請資產分配，以供養受養人的依據。 我們的研究將會比較在亞洲及西方一些國家的法律，以及當地為特殊需要人士而設的資產信託的法律實踐經驗。美國與新加坡兩地的特殊需要信託制度尤其值得我們研究。藉著借鑒外國的最佳經驗，我們期望探討在香港成立特殊需要信託的可取性和可行性，並提出相關建議，以改善及完善針對智障人士資產管理的法律制度。

17612916.label: Realisation of objectives
17612916.value: There was complete achievement of all 4 Objectives. Objective 1: We thoroughly examined the Hong Kong laws, regulations, and operational experiences pertaining to the fiduciary management of property of MIPs. Specifically, we examined the following existing mechanisms for financial planning for MIPs in Hong Kong: (1) the will; (2) enduring power of attorney; (3) adult guardianship and (4) trust. The research findings were published in two journal articles in Trusts & Trustees and a book chapter in an edited collection by Cambridge University Press. Objective 2: We undertook research to compare laws, regulations, and operational experiences pertaining to the fiduciary management of property of MIPs in Singapore, Japan, England, the US, Australia and Canada. An international symposium was organised by us to study the latest developments in special needs financial planning in various jurisdictions, including US, UK, Australia, Canada, Japan, South Korea, Singapore and Hong Kong. We published an edited collection of papers examining (1) adult guardianship, (2) lasting/enduring powers of attorney and (3) special needs trusts from international and comparative perspectives with Cambridge University Press in 2019. Objective 3: We applied the research findings from Objective 1 and recommended the government to reform the laws on fiduciary management of assets of MIPs. Specifically, we proposed the introduction of a Special Needs Trust (SNT) fiduciary management of assets of MIPs. Objective 4: We conducted, in collaboration with a local NGO, the first territory-wide survey the desirability and feasibility for introducing SNTs in Hong Kong. The questionnaire survey received an overwhelming response of over 2,500 valid returns. A detailed bilingual report on the key findings and observations of the survey was published. A large-scale press conference attended by about 200 members of the public and the media was organised. The report was also presented to the Hong Kong Government for consideration. Based on the survey findings, we devised a structural model of SNT for Hong Kong taking into the account the strengths and constraints of the existing institutional framework: the proposed SNT model saves costs by pooling the funds contributed by parents for investment; it’s also operated and managed by the government and charges annual fees of not more 1% of the entrusted assets. The Government announced in its Chief Executive’s Policy Address in January 2016 the establishment of “a working group to explore the feasibility of setting up a public trust”. The Co-I was appointed to the Working Group. In October 2017, the Chief Executive announced the Government’s decision to set up the SNT, adopting the key finding of our research to act as trustee of the SNT. The 2018 Budget earmarked HK$50 million to set up an SNT office and the SNT was formally launched the SNT in December 2018.

17612916.label: Major findings and research outcome
17612916.value: 1. The most significant research outcome of the project is that our research has successfully convinced the Hong Kong Government to introduce an innovative SNT service that was not previously available. The SNT benefits the families of some 250,000 individuals whose disability (be it intellectual disability, mental illness, or autism) renders them unable to manage their own property affairs. In addition, the following are major findings and outcomes of our research: 2. Our research on Hong Kong laws pertaining to the fiduciary management of property of MIPs showed that affordable legal tools such as wills, statutory guardianship and enduring powers of attorney for managing the assets of individuals with cognitive impairment are inadequate. 3. We also completed reviews of the laws and operational experiences of guardianships and enduring powers of attorney in Australia, Canada, Taiwan, Irelend, Singapore, and the UK. 4. We completed a survey of parental opinions on guardianship, enduring power of attorney and SNT and published a detailed bilingual report on the survey findings. 5. We studied in particular the SNT models in Singapore and the US and formulated a model of SNT which is government-run and -managed for the HK government’s consideration. 6. We conducted presentations on the inadequacies of adult guardianship and enduring power of attorney in Hong Kong, as well as features and controversies of the Hong Kong SNT. 7. We published an edited collection with Cambridge University Press on special needs financial planning from international and comparative perspectives.

17612916.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17612916.value: Whilst our current research project is able to convince the government to introduce an SNT for people with special needs, our research has also identified major gaps in the laws on personal and financial protection of people with special needs in Hong Kong that remain to be addressed. Our current research has enabled further work on specific issues about the protection of people with special needs. These issues include, for example, continuing/enduring powers of attorney, advance directives, elder abuse and supported decision-making. The current research has also identified the strengths and pitfalls in the approaches of different jurisdictions on these issues. We propose to work closely with the government, legal and medical practitioners, the civil society and the international experts to conduct further research in these areas. We also plan to seek further collaborative and/or interdisciplinary research funding in the near future for this purpose.

17612916.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17612916.value: For many years, parents of children with special needs have expressed concerns that after their passing, their assets will not be allocated to the care of their children, and the well-being of their children will be disrupted. Affordable legal tools such as wills, statutory guardianship and enduring powers of attorney for managing the assets of individuals with cognitive impairment are inadequate. The trust is an ideal mechanism for professional asset management, but it is beyond the means of most families. Our research examined the inadequacy of existing legal mechanisms for financial planning for people with cognitive impairment. The research enabled us to formulate a model of the SNT that saves costs by pooling the funds contributed by parents for investment. We also convinced the Government that a government-managed SNT was both desirable and feasible. The research directly led to the setting up of the special needs trust (SNT) in Hong Kong. The scheme benefits the families of some 250,000 individuals with special needs. It reassures parents that upon their passing, their children’s well-being will not be unduly affected. The SNT was launched in December 2018. The impact has now reached South Korea, which decided in 2018 to launch an SNT.

17613316.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17613316.value: This project aims to examine and compare the processes and challenges of identity formation among young gay men in three Chinese societies: Hong Kong, mainland China and Taiwan. There is a growing body of literature on Chinese gay identities, some of which detail the life experiences of men born between the 1950s and 1980s. However, the research on young Chinese gay men is limited and tends to be location specific rather than comparative in nature. This project fills that gap by collecting 90 life stories of young gay men aged 18-27 years through in-depth interviews and self-reported visual narratives in three specific locales: Hong Kong, Shanghai and Taipei (n=30 each), which explore how participants understand and negotiate being ‘gay’ (sexuality), ‘young’ (age) and ‘male’ (gender). Unlike previous generations of Chinese gay men, young gay men who were born in the 1990s in Hong Kong, mainland China and Taiwan have grown up in an era where homosexuality is no longer seen as a crime and/or mental illness and there is a substantial infrastructure of queer consumer markets, visible online and offline queer communities and even the emergence of queer activism. Do they experience their lives in qualitatively different ways from the previous generations? Do they experience ‘being gay’ in the same way or differently in Hong Kong, mainland China and Taiwan? The first question will be addressed through a cohort study of young gay men that examines how identity is historically situated and sensitive to changing local, national, regional and even global contingencies, comparing against the previous generations as documented in the existing literature. The second question will be addressed through a trans-local study of the queer flow of circulation of ideas, bodies and capital among and within the three Chinese locales (Hong Kong, Shanghai and Taipei) that constitute, inform and shape identities, practices and desires. In doing so, the project investigates the processes and challenges of identity formation of Chinese young gay men in Hong Kong, mainland China and Taiwan through a qualitative study that offers a unique trans-local study of Chinese gay identities. This project will contribute to Chinese gender and sexuality studies in general but Chinese youth sexuality studies in particular as well as informing international debates about the theorization of (Chinese) homosexuality. 這項計畫聚焦中港台三地，旨在分析當地年輕男同志建構自我身分的過程，以及當中面對的挑戰。有關華人同志身分建構的學術文獻正不斷發展，部分更詳盡地記載了出生於50至80年代間的男同志的人生歷程。然而，涉及華人年輕男同志的研究相對不足，而且範圍大多局限於某個特定地域，甚少進行跨地區的比較。為填補這些不足，此計畫將通過深度訪談和視像日記，收集90位來自香港、上海和台北、年齡介乎18至27歲的年輕男同志的生命故事(各地30人)，探索他們如何理解和面對自己作為「同志」、「年輕人」和「男性」的三重身分（即性傾向、年齡和性別）。 有別於以往幾代的華人男同志，在1990年代出生於香港、內地和台灣的年輕男同志彷彿成長在一個截然不同的世界：同性戀不再被視為罪行和精神病，社會上亦出現了略有規模的同志消費市場，同志在網上和現實世界均逐漸凝聚成清晰可見的社群，酷兒運動更應運而生。跟以往幾代人相比，他們的生活和經歷是否有基本的不同？在香港、內地和台灣三地「搞基」，又是否存在差異？為回應第一個問題，這項計劃將針對年輕男同志進行世代研究，分析身分建構如何與歷史脈絡緊緊相連，並受到本土、國內、區內以至全球的各種形勢影響，進而呼應現存學術文獻，與過往同志的經歷作出比對；為回應第二個問題，計劃將針對三個華人地區（香港、上海和台北）進行跨地域研究，從而了解各種價值、身體和資本如何在社會內和三地之間流動／流通，塑造出不同的身分、常規和情慾。 這項計劃代表了一個獨特的切入點，通過質化研究的方法，就華人男同志身分展開跨地域研究，探討中港台三地的華人年輕男同志建構自我身分的過程，以及當中的挑戰。此計劃主力推進有關年輕華人性／別的學術研究，但同時亦將為整體的華人性／別研究帶來新貢獻，有助深化國際間有關開創華人性／別理論的討論。

17617416.label: Project Objectives
17617416.value: To provide a systematic comparative review of med-arb systems and the ways in which they are reformed in Asia. To contribute to the international comparative literature on Asian experiences of med-arb reform that balance local conditions and international expectations (particularly East Asian experiences which have great relevance to China). To study the issues that require exploration for the reform of the med-arb system of mainland China, by comparing the experiences of those most recently reformed Asian jurisdictions, such as Japan, South Korea, Hong Kong and Singapore. To examine Chinese local dispute resolution circumstances (legal, economic, and cultural), and formulate ways of framing those circumstances for the reform of the med-arb system in the legal and socio-economic contexts of China. To apply research findings and formulate recommendations for reforming the med-arb-related laws and institutions (arbitral tribunals and commissions) in China with reference to the Asian experiences by employing proper procedural safeguards to accord with international standards while taking into account Chinese dispute resolution realities. To contribute to China’s rule of law progress as med-arb is prevalent in China's dispute resolution system.

17617416.label: Realisation of objectives
17617416.value: In the GRF research proposal, the PI has suggested that a conference is desirable for the sharing of experience of not only Asian med-arb jurisdictions but also other major jurisdictions in the West which have had recently developed med-arb system. The conference is also intended to conduct a comparative study on med-arb regulatory development and reform trajectories between the Eastern and Western jurisdictions and between the common law and civil law world, and to shed light on China’s future reform, with particular impact on China’s active development of a one-stop multi-tiered dispute resolution platform for commercial disputes arising out of the Belt and Road Initiative. To prepare for the conference, since the beginning of the project, the PI has been in active contact with potential country experts in Asia and the West. After sufficient preparation, a GRF-projected one-day conference was successfully organized by the PI. The conference was entitled, “Multi-tiered Approaches to the Resolution of International Disputes: A Global and Comparative Study”, held on 28 September 2018, at the University of Hong Kong Faculty of Law. The conference has attracted wide interests, in particular, interests from leading arbitration institutions in Asia and beyond such as the Hong Kong International Arbitration Center (HKIAC) based in Hong Kong, China International Economic and Trade Arbitration Commission (CIETAC) based in Beijing, Japan International Mediation Center (JIMC) based in Kyoto, Chartered Institute of Arbitrators (CIArb) based in London. The PI is indeed honored that those leading arbitration institutions in Asia such as HKIAC and CIETAC finally accepted my offer to become collaborators in the conference. Sarah Grimmer (HKIAC’s Secretary-General), Wenying Wang (CIETAC Hong Kong’s Secretary-General), Naoshi Takasugi (JIMC’s Secretary-General), Mary Thomson (CIArb East Asia’s then Chair) all took time off their busy schedules to participate in the conference and offer their comparative and international views on med-arb reform with special reference to China and its Belt and Road dispute resolution development. HKIAC is the arbitration institution outside Mainland China which handles the largest number of China-related med-arb cases. HKIAC’s Secretary-General, Ms. Sarah Grimmer, gave the keynote speech for the conference and shared HKIAC’s unique med-arb handling experience with respect to China from an institutional leader perspective. The conference received high interests from international, regional, national, and local levels. The PI is grateful for the GRF project’s support which enables her to invite the country experts to the conference (which later became contributors to the book) to share their expertise on this emerging but innovative dispute resolution design. The GRF project has also enabled the PI to employ a research assistant to support in the organization and logistics management of the conference. To achieve research objectives and research outcomes, while planning for the conference, the PI has already been working tirelessly on book proposals (with a unanimous template to be applied to all investigated arbitration jurisdictions to answer relevant research questions envisaged by the GRF project). The PI has also been working hard on preparing sample chapters, and approaching potential publishers. The PI has been in strong wish to turn the outputs in the conference into a published book with internationally reputable publishers. Cambridge University Press (CUP) finally approved our book proposal at its Syndicate and the peer review reports by all the six international reviewers were positive. Though the peer review process took longer than we had expected, everything had been worthwhile. The CUP publishing agreement was signed in September 2019, and the entire book manuscript has been submitted to CUP. According to CUP’s consolidated peer-review comments, “this book will become the leading academic, judicial and practitioner guide on med-arb and multi-tiered dispute resolution that is not only heavily relied on in East Asia, it will also contribute to international dispute resolution innovation that is paid much attention to globally”. In the Acknowledgements of the book, the PI has devoted a special paragraph to thank the support by the GRF project scheme under the RGC. The book will be published in Spring 2021 at Cambridge. During the final stage of the manuscript submission, the PI employed two research assistants for helping edit the chapters to comply with the CUP house styles. The budget item, “Research Assistants”, allocated in the project has been used to some extent for the purpose of the edit of the CUP book. The PI has also conducted a few research trips to China and Asia and the rest of the world to contextualize the research findings. Some of the research trips were conducted while the PI was invited to attend conferences and invited talks there and others were just made for purpose of research investigation. Through research trips, the PI met the country experts on med-arb system and reform in respective jurisdiction, conducted relevant interviews and collected important research materials. The budget item, “Field Trip”, allocated in the project has been mainly used for such purpose. The PI has benefitted tremendously from the GRF budget item, “Research Assistants”. The budget for hiring research assistants (RAs) has been deployed effectively in the sense that the RAs helped a lot in collecting literature in the initial period of research, in analysing the interviews and materials the PI collected from the field trips, in logistics support of the conference in the middle of the project. The RAs were again critical in the footnote checking and bibliography compilation stage when the manuscripts were completed to be submitted to journals and book publishers. The PI, with the capable assistance of the RAs, have published quite prolifically in this project. The research outputs include 1 book, 2 book chapters, and 9 journal articles. Moreover, all the book chapters and journal articles have been solely authored by the PI herself. The PI is happy to report that all research outputs have been published by, or will be forthcoming with, world leading law publishers and world leading law journals. As aforementioned, the book output will be forthcoming with the Cambridge University Press in Spring 2021. Of the 9 journal articles, all had been published at the time when this GRF Completion Report was prepared and some were published by global leading law journals, such as the American Journal of Comparative Law (in 2017) which enjoys the reputation of being the world’s best and foremost law journal on comparative law issues and one of the most prestigious law journal globally, the Vanderbilt Journal of Transnational Law (in 2018) which is ranked as the 5th best in international law among all the US law journals and considered one of the most reputable international law journals worldwide, the Journal of Comparative Law (in 2018) which is deemed as one of the foremost law journals on comparative law issues in the UK, the Peking University Law Journal (in 2018) which is among one of the top-three law journals in China generally, and the Proceedings of the American Society of International Law Annual Meeting (in 2019) which is one of the flagship journals of the prestigious American Society of International Law. To conclude, the PI is happy to submit that the research objectives have all been satisfactorily achieved, and the research funds are well and properly used. 17617416.label: Major findings and research outcome
17617416.value: 1. The book provides a comprehensive analysis of how med-arb systems have recently been developed and reformed in major jurisdictions in Asia and beyond. The book first analyses the ways in which med-arb develops, whether “judicially” or “legislatively”. In common law jurisdictions such as Hong Kong and Singapore, med-arb is motivated by landmark cases, and the development depends heavily upon judicial decisions that determines the validity of the med-arb process. In civil law jurisdictions such as Japan, legislations usually play a more important role. This is so even if the legislation is not comprehensive. Second, the book analyses varying degrees of procedural safeguards applied to med-arb proceedings which is of particular importance to China. Through the study, common law jurisdictions (such as US, UK, Australia, Hong Kong, Singapore) generally have more procedural safeguards and are more skeptical towards having the same neutral as both arbitrator and mediator. Common law jurisdictions in the East (Hong Kong and Singapore) require the mediator-turned-arbitrator to mandatorily disclose all material confidential information obtained during mediation. The same requirement is not present in civil law jurisdictions in the East where mediation has a strong cultural root (China, Japan). Finally, the book analyses varying patterns of med-arb development, whether “top-down” (Japan, Singapore), “bottom-up” (US, UK), or from a “hybrid” impetus (China, Hong Kong). The book findings present a first-time cross-jurisdiction comparative study of the med-arb regulatory framework, practices and reforms in the Asia and beyond and significantly contributes to international dispute resolution innovations design combining mediation and arbitration. 2. The journal articles and book chapters contribute to the reform of the med-arb system in China, by comparing the Chinese med-arb law and operational experiences to those investigated jurisdictions. The comparative research shows that the Chinese way to med-arb development is largely “judicially”, and “top-down” driven, pushed by China’s Supreme People’s Court, reflecting its prevailing controlling approach on dispute resolution. In the meantime, despite the lack of national level med-arb legislative mechanism, the Chinese state has been reliant on and even accommodating of regulatory and institutional competition by Chinese arbitration and mediation institutions at the local level. The Chinese trajectory of med-arb reform is thus an attempt to synthesis a unique socio-economic dynamic, with both controlling element and free market features, and the free market features have become a more important force driving med-arb reform in China.

17617416.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17617416.value: Future research could aim to identify a global enforcement standard for med-arb such that the divided development levels of and approaches to med-arb between the common law and civil law jurisdictions and between Asia and the West could be mitigated at an internationally harmonized level to facilitate enforcement of the outcomes of med-arb. Now that for the enforcement of outcomes of international commercial arbitration, there is the 1958 New York Convention; and for the enforcement of outcomes of international commercial mediation, there is the 2018 Singapore Convention. It is worthy of further studies to have on international framework which draws inspiration from both the New York Convention and Singapore Convention to make informed guide on how to facilitate enforcement of med-arb outcomes globally. Towards that end, empirical case studies on med-arb enforcement in world leading jurisdictions are also targets of future research. The rising use of med-arb in both the Eastern- and Western-based arbitration jurisdictions deserves a global answer, from both international law and policy perspectives. This has been mentioned in PI’s published articles and in the conclusion chapter of PI and Co-I’s co-edited book, Multi-tiered Approaches to the Resolution of International Disputes (Cambridge University Press), forthcoming, 2021.

17617416.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17617416.value: Med-arb entails an early attempt at mediation followed by arbitration if mediation is unsuccessful. Med-arb is innovatively attractive due to its combination of the flexibility and informality of mediation with the rigour and formality of arbitration. This project studies the recent emergence of med-arb as a dispute resolution innovation mechanism. The project (1) provides an up-to-date and comprehensive comparative analysis of the regulatory approaches to and development patterns for med-arb within Asia and beyond, (2) compares trends in med-arb in Asia and the wider world, (3) identify med-arb’s strengths and weaknesses, (4) prescribe ways to address med-arb’s weaknesses in China by benefitting from the comparative study, and (5) propose regulatory design for med-arb system in the Belt and Road Initiative which is of influence to both China and Hong Kong. The project presents a first-time cross-jurisdiction comparative and contextual study of the med-arb development in Asia and beyond and significantly contributes to international dispute resolution innovations design from the Eastern vantage point. The project also identifies that, in the wake of the economic recession post the pandemic, med-arb offers a cost-effective and time-efficient means of resolving disputes and should be more widely used than at present.

17617916.label: Project Objectives
17617916.value: Examine how social background influences the ways in which rural students navigate the elite university environment over four years. Identify and analyze the selected factors that act as obstacles or contribute to the academic and social success of rural students in the four elite universities.

17617916.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17617916.value: Gaining admission to universities is an important step toward upward social mobility for rural students. Adjusting to higher education institutions constitutes the next crucial one. There is evidence in China that rural students experience obstacles to their academic success that increase with each year at university. This is particular the case when they enter the most elite universities. They can barely benefit if the challenges on campus hinder them from a successful transition into the new social settings. Recent policies introduced by Chinese government have increased the number of rural freshmen in China’s key universities. Yet, current literature seldom look at how rural students navigate the elite academic milieu and how this is associated with their social backgrounds. The PI and CIs have conducted preliminary research on rural students in their at four elite universities, which indicated that obstacles grow as social activities on campus become more important to academic success and readiness for graduation. Our proposed rural student university survey (RSUS) will document social origins and experience, including academic performance, interactions with faculty/staff members, peer group interactions and participations in extracurricular activities. The proposed research will provide data to analyze how rural students navigate their university environment. The research is grounded in Tinto’s model of social integration in universities, with insights from Bourdieu’s cultural capital theory. The project uses a mixed-method research design. We plan to document the patterns of academic and social success achieved by the participants and its associations with their social origins by surveying 2000 students selected using a two-stage cluster sampling method. A questionnaire is adapted from a pre-established instrument, the validity of which has been tested by a pilot study. We also propose face-to-face interviews involving around roughly 100 students whom we purposively sampled. This will provide qualitative data to illustrate the possible associations between the social origins of students and the results of their navigation in elite universities. The findings of this study are expected to contribute to the literature on the relationship between education and social equity, as well as provide useful knowledge for university counselors to help rural students become better adjusted and integrated into the university environment. 对农村学生而言，获得进入高等教育机构学习的机会仅仅是他们实现社会流动的第一步。适应大学的环境是下一重要步骤。有研究表明，农村大学生在大学学习期间会面临不同类型的障碍——在进入中国最精英的高校学习时，犹如为此。对于他们而言，倘若在进入大学时不能克服所面临各种障碍，顺利融入大学的环境，则有可能不能充分地利用大学的学习机会。中国政府近些年来的政策有效地增加了重点大学的农村生源学生数。但是，针对农村学生在重点大学学习和生活状况的研究却付之阙如。 本研究的主调研员和副调研员在中国大陆的四所精英大学已经开展过初步的研究工作。这些工作显示农村生源学生在社会活动方面面临着一定的障碍，但社会活动对于他们学业以及毕业准备而言，又较为重要。我们所设计的研究将会对农村生源大学生的社会背景和大学体验状况（包括学业成就，与教师的互动，与同辈群体的互动以及课外活动的参与状况）进行调查。 本研究的基本理论模型以Tinto的大学生发展理论和Bourdieu的文化资本理论为基础。基本的设计为混合研究方法。我们将通过问卷调查对研究参与者的学业和社会成就状况进行了解。样本数量为2000左右，通过多阶段整群抽样的方式获得。将要采用的问卷为宾州大学的学者所使用的《大学生学习和社会生活体验调查问卷》，该问卷已经过汉化，并在中国高校中通过预研究工作经过检验。问卷调查之后我们还计划选择样本学生中的约100名学生开展访谈工作，质性访谈部分的数据将有助于我们对学生的社会背景与他们在精英大学学习结果之间的关系有更深入地了解。在理论上，本研究将有助于丰富教育和社会平等之间关系研究的相关文献。在实践上，本研究将有助于大学的服务人员设计更好的方法帮助农村生源学生更好地融入大学的环境。

17617916.label: Realisation of objectives
17617916.value: The two objectives have been completely achieved. The research teams in Hong Kong and Shanghai conducted a random sampling, resulting in selecting 5% of all of the 29,900 senior university students (i.e.,1,495 students, with a usable sample size of 1,072) in nine elite (Project 211 and Project 985) universities in Shanghai. These institutions included Fudan University; Shanghai Jiaotong University; Tongji University; East China Normal University; Shanghai University; Shanghai University of Finance and Economics; and Shanghai International Studies University. The dataset is one of a kind and will be used as a basis for long-term charting of the career development of final-year university students in Shanghai. Shortly after winning the project, the Principal Investigator (Professor Gerard A. Postiglione) was required to surrender it because of HKU’s retirement age. He had to either return the grant or identify a colleague in the Faculty of Education who had the expertise, experience, seniority, and access to the data needed to achieve the research objectives. I was deemed to be a suitable PI. Despite the fact that I had other research and publication projects (including my GRF project on the academic profession - Reference: 17604015), book contracts, as well as several administrative roles, I was able to organize a research team in Shanghai (including Professor Weiqiao Fan of Shanghai Normal University, who led a team of research students) to have successfully collected the data. The research results have been widely disseminated. In addition to the two international conferences and the research outputs we reported in the last mid-term report (March 2019), we have the following achievements. First, the original PI has been working on a book contract based on the data from this GRF research. The book is expected to be in press in 2021. Second, another article was published and won the Outstanding Award for The Third National Educational Empirical Research. Third, the PI has been invited to give talks at two international conferences. Finally, in the past several months, we have submitted four manuscripts to peer-reviewed international journals. We are happy to say that we are still preparing for several more manuscripts for submitting to peer-reviewed international journals because the data set contains so much valuable information on rural university students attending elite universities in Shanghai.

17617916.label: Major findings and research outcome
17617916.value: The key findings are: First, while students from rural lower socio-economic status families significantly underperformed academically (as represented by their GPAs) than their peers from urban higher SES families in their final year, it was not the case in their first two years of study (see Postiglione et al., 2017a; Xie et al., 2018). Second, while urban students sought more opportunities to participate in high-impact educational activities such as research projects and academic competitions (which become influential factors in graduate employment), rural students were more engaged in time-consuming and low-paid part-time jobs such as distributing leaflets and working as restaurant waiters or waitresses. Compared with urban students, rural students had fewer opportunities to take on a leadership position in student organizations on campus (Postiglione, April 2019; Postiglione et. al, 2017b; Xie et al., 2018) Third, while rural students tended to rely on themselves to make decisions and gather information for making those decisions from the internet, urban students had a wider social network from which they gather information and seek advice (Xie et al., 2018). Fourth, compared with their urban counterparts, rural students were significantly less creative in their thinking; had a significantly weaker sense of vocational identity (career exploration and career commitment); showed a significantly lower level of career adaptability; exhibited a significantly lower level of career self-efficacy (e.g., self-appraisal, goal setting, and problem solving); and perceived less parental support. All of this indicated that rural students were at a disadvantageous position at various aspects of university student learning and development (see the abstracts of the four journal articles under review – full articles available upon request; see also Zhang, 2017). Finally, irrespective of the differences found between rural and urban students, several common findings were obtained across the two groups: 1) creativity-generating thinking styles were conducive to the development of students’ vocational identity (Zhang, 2017; Zhang, LF et al., under review); 2) career-related positive emotion experience contributed to career self-efficacy and that social support played a major role in the relationship between social class and career self-efficacy (Zhang LL et al., under review); 3) career adaptability significantly positively contributed to career choice satisfaction (Li et al.A, under review); and 4) living up to parental expectation on academic achievement negatively predicted vocational identity, while living up to parental expectation on personal morality positively predicted vocational identity; parental support played a critical role in these relationships (Li et al.B, under review).

17617916.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17617916.value: Our research has been of interest to the career offices of Shanghai’s elite universities. We have arranged for a Shanghai colleague, a former HKU doctoral graduate, now a professor and director of career counselling in Shanghai to follow up. The area for further development of the research concerns the differential patterns of social engagement in 3rd- and 4th-year students as they consider employment after graduation and the way that cultural capital and social capital play a role in their job search, interviews, and selection of employment or postgraduate study. The significance of the previous research for how cultural capital from pre-university socialization loses some influence as students go through their university education and the way to measure the extent of that influence ¬is worth further investigation. We are confident from our research that household income, parents, education, and social capital would become strong predictors during the four years of university study. However, we would like to focus more on institutional interventions in future research.

17617916.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17617916.value: The proportion of Chinese senior secondary school graduates from poor rural areas entering elite universities has continued to decline. Since 2013, our team has been studying how those rural students who do gain admission to elite universities navigate their learning, development, and campus life. We found that first- and second-year rural students performed equally well with, or at times, better than, their urban peers in academic work. However, they were less engaged socially. By the final year, compared with their peers from urban areas, students from rural China lagged behind not only in terms of academic achievement and social development but also in various dimensions of career development. Our findings have enriched the literature on student learning and development, as well as that on higher education in general. The findings would be of interest to university career guidance counselors, senior managers, and academic staff at elite universities in mainland China, particularly those in Shanghai.

17618216.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17618216.value: Hong Kong: Uncertain(ci)ty will be the first scholarly monograph focused on themes of risk, crisis, and vulnerability in relation to Hong Kong’s architectural and urban history. My research attends specifically to the tensions engendered by physical, environmental, financial, geopolitical, and viral destabilization within the city over time, and the ways these tensions have shaped architectural and urban design, practice, as well as discourse, in Hong Kong since its founding as a British colony in 1842. Preexisting scholarship tends to depict Hong Kong’s built environment as little more than successful concretizations of the free market--an urbane “World City” best known for its dense urban form and unyielding efficiency. My research, by contrast, illuminates themes of precariousness underlying these well-worn characterizations. Through this work, I aim to demonstrate the historical relationship between architecture and the perception and reality of instability in Hong Kong. My project is structured around several architectural case-studies, few of which have attracted any previous scholarly attention. Each building or site is grouped within a particular category of crisis; these include war, governance, immigration, natural disaster, financial panic, contagion, as well as anxieties of identity. Individually, each theme constitutes a chapter that illuminates how singular moments of crisis inscribed themselves within specific examples of architecture. Collectively, these themes reveal the history of architecture’s broader relationship to change. Of key concern in this work is how Hong Kong’s architectural design has managed crisis. More than a study of particular architectural styles and individual designers, Hong Kong: Uncertain(ci)ty challenges readers to reconsider the notion that architecture simply represents or reflects broader political, economic, social, or cultural trends in society. Rather, it examines the very real ways that architecture actively defines and conditions how people engage with society. In this way, my work highlights architecture’s participation in crisis—its ability to both ameliorate as well as aggravate the disruptions at work in processes of modernization. Theorizing Hong Kong’s architectural history in relation to these issues offers new insight into how and why the city physically developed over time. Architecture occupies the intersection between the territorial logics of political authority on one hand and the fluid dynamics of capitalism on the other. In this respect, and as my project argues, architecture has played a crucial, mediatory role between people, institutions, the economy and the environment over the course of Hong Kong’s history as a colony and Special Administrative Region (SAR). “香港：易变的城市”是第一个用风险与危机来分析香港建筑历史的专著。我的研究调查这些话题对城市的环境，经济，国际关系，等等，有什么影响，以及如何从这些紧张塑造了建筑和城市设计，实践，以及话语，在香港的作为创始于1842年英国的殖民地 多半的香港的学习描绘香港的建筑环境比自由市场的成功具体化而已 - 一个文雅的“世界城市”，其密集的城市形态和不屈的效率而闻名。香港的建筑环境比自由市场的成功具体化而已 – 亚洲的“世界城市”，其密集的城市形态和不屈的效率而闻名。我的研究，通过对比，阐明不稳定这些陈腐的表征背后的主题。通过这项工作，我的目标是展示香港建筑与感知和不稳定的现实之间的历史关系。 我的项目是周围的几个建筑个案研究，其中没有收到任何学术上的注意。每个建筑或网站危机的一个特定的类别中进行分组; 这些包括战争，治理，移民，自然灾害，金融恐慌，危机蔓延，以及身份的焦虑。单独来看，每个主题构成照亮危机的奇异时刻如何架构的具体例子内自己题写的一章。总的来说，这些主题揭示架构的更广泛的关系，改变历史。 在这项工作中主要关注的是香港的建筑设计跟危机有什么关系。对于读者考录的概念，”香港：易变的城市” 提出他们怎么了解香港的建筑历史，架构仅仅代表或反映社会更广泛的政治，经济，社会或文化的发展趋势。这个研究会检查非常真实的方式，积极的架构定义和条件，人们的社会参与如何。这样一来，我的工作亮点架构在危机的能力，参与双方改善和现代化进程的工作加重中断。 关于理论化香港的建筑史，我想用这个研究来提供新的见解。建筑就是一个跟政治和资本主义有关系的学习。在这方面，建筑对机构，经济和对香港的历史过程作为殖民地和特别行政区（SAR）环境之间至关重要的，调解的作用。

17618216.label: Realisation of objectives
17618216.value: My final project addresses all of the objectives as laid out in the original application. "Hong Kong: Uncertain(ci)ty" is a book-length manuscript offering the first critical study of Hong Kong's architectural history to pay particular attention to the affects of crisis and uncertainty upon the city. It engages in a range of archival material in Australia, Hong Kong, and England and offers a number of historically over-looked case-studies to develop its argument. Various notions of crisis are introduced and assessed in particular relationship to architectural design practices, materials, and construction processes. It offers new perspective on the architectural history of Hong Kong and global architectural history more generally. The book is under contract with HKU Press and has undergone a rigorous, double-blind peer review process. In addition, a section of Chapter 3 detailing the architectural history of the Hong Kong Observatory received a Commendation from the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) President’s Award for Research, 2020. It was published in the Journal of Architecture in October 2021 as “Constructing Climate: The Hong Kong Observatory and meteorological networks within the British imperial sphere, 1842 – 1912.” I did encounter challenges during the research. The protests of 2019 and the passage of the National Security Law in 2020 cast some doubt upon my project's potentially controversial nature. In addition, COVID-19 prevented me from completing a second research trip to London to consult the papers of Sir Peter Hall and visit the Jardine Matheson Company archives at the University of Cambridge. During the spring of 2020, I had a research sabbatical related to this project but was unable to satisfy all of my objectives due to personal and professional strain caused by the pandemic. Despite these obstacles, however, I successfully applied for extensions and have completed the project while meeting my original research objectives. The book is currently organized both chronologically and thematically into eight chapters, each of which attends to a particular, uncertain condition. In an effort to challenge the hoary characterizations of Hong Kong as a meeting place between East and West, each chapter’s title offers a new thematic bifurcation though which we may understand the city’s uniqueness. Chapter 1, “From Stone to Architecture,” examines the port’s first colonial-era buildings, and the ways in which Hong Kong’s physical ground, composed of distinctive soil and granite deposits, shaped British perceptions of Hong Kong’s barrenness, which proved consequential not only to the first narratives of failure to emerge from the colony, but to its first architectural successes. Chapter 2, titled “Flow and Regulation,” studies the influx of residents from mainland China and their consequential influence upon the Hong Kong’s built environment, with particular focus paid on the period between 1861 and 1881. Seemingly uncontrolled movements of people from Qing China in and out of Hong Kong supplied the world with a new supply of cheap, unregulated labor that required designed water-based networks and buildings. By the 1860s and 1870s, Hong Kong’s climate had become an increasingly urgent social and political concern. Drought, typhoons, and landslides, among other natural crises, necessitated complex and productive architectural and infrastructural systems. “Gardens and Weather” shows how two key sites, the Hong Kong Zoological and Botanical Gardens, founded in 1864, and the Hong Kong Observatory, built in 1883, responded to growing public and official interest in environmental management. Chapter 4, titled “Heath or Wealth,” explores pathogenic concerns circulating within the colony between the late nineteenth century and the 1930s and the rise of sanitation as a driving social, political, and architectural concern. Chapter 5, “Plans and Types,” offers an architectural analysis of the colonial British government’s ambitious postwar design and construction plans in relation to the study of types and plans, in particular the government’s efforts to provide large-scale emergency housing for tens of thousands of Chinese refugees capable of ameliorating their integration into colonial society. “Antitype and the Non-Plan” addresses countervailing interest in non-planned spaces within which unregulated economic activity and loose, informal architectural and corporate assemblages might occur. Collectively, both chapters present the conflicted visions and contradicted ideology of spatial control and economic emancipation in Hong Kong, and the extent to which architecture—and architects—aimed to mediate between the two. Chapter 7 is titled “Money and Time;” it examines the effects of economic and political abstraction upon architectural design and construction in the city between the late 1970s and mid-1990s, amid Sino-British negotiations over the city’s future. Many of Hong Kong’s most prominent architectural landmarks were conceived during this era, and they served to both initiate and index the city’s rise as an epicenter of international finance. Chapter 8, “Simultaneity and Surface,” reflects upon the architectural implications of public and official anxiety surrounding the city’s identity in the wake of 1997, following Hong Kong’s return to China. Three important architectural events help to encapsulate the shifting political and spatial dynamics that have dominated the city over the past twenty-five years, including the construction of the new Central Library, the government headquarters at Tamar, designed by Rocco Yim Associates in an effort to centralize the city’s major administrative bodies, and the Occupy-related movements that reverberated around the city in 2011 and 2014, followed by the anti-extradition protests of 2019. The book’s conclusion anticipates uncertainties still to come.

17618216.label: Major findings and research outcome
17618216.value: My major research finding concerns the historically integrated role of architectural design not simply in crisis, but in its management. Existing scholarship tends to depict Hong Kong’s built environment as little more than successful concretizations of the free market—an urbane “World City” best known for its dense urban form and unyielding efficiency. My project, by contrast, works to draw readers’ attention to the physical, social, geopolitical, viral, and climatic precariousness underlying well-worn characterizations of Hong Kong to demonstrate the historical relationship between architecture and the perception and reality of instability in the city. Theorizing Hong Kong’s architectural history in relation to these issues has produced new knowledge that will contribute not only to the study of the city but also to methodological shifts currently underway within the discipline of architectural history. Scholars are increasingly moving beyond the notion that architecture passively represents or reflects broad political, economic, social, or cultural forces in society, and toward the very real ways that architecture defines and manages how we engage with society. As my research suggests, architectural objects actively participated in Hong Kong’s history, with spaces, practices, and operational mechanisms that mediated the various uncertainties posed by the city’s colonial condition, transient population, and vulnerability to viral outbreaks, among others. In this respect, and as my book argues, architecture has played a crucial, mediatory role between people, institutions, the economy and the environment over the course of Hong Kong’s history as a colony and Special Administrative Region (SAR). My book is currently under contract with HKU Press and has undergone a rigorous, double-blind peer review process. In addition, a section of Chapter 3 detailing the architectural history of the Hong Kong Observatory received a Commendation from the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) President’s Award for Research, 2020. It was published in the Journal of Architecture in October 2021 as “Constructing Climate: The Hong Kong Observatory and meteorological networks within the British imperial sphere, 1842 – 1912.”

17618216.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17618216.value: There is always an opportunity for further development of a research project. Over the course of writing my book manuscript, I was not able to include all of the material I collected. There are numerous projects and architects I would like to study further. In addition, Hong Kong will undoubtedly encounter crises in the future, and this book offers a theoretical framework through which students, scholars, and the public at large may better understand how those crises might relate to architectural production. Ideally, this project offers themes and methods of study that will be further developed by other scholars. In that sense, this research and its impact may continue on through the work of other academics and interested members of the public over time. Recent interest in Hong Kong’s architectural heritage, for example, has prompted significant public inquiry into the nature and history of the city’s architectural development. It would be interesting to consider my research on crisis in relation to the increased attention paid to architectural conservation and reuse in the city, and how recently completed or proposed heritage work may be situated within my theoretical framework.

17618216.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17618216.value: Hong Kong is often dismissed as a city lacking in architectural quality--an unfair assessment that tends to privilege architecture as something based primarily on appearance or location. My work offers a counter-narrative of the city's architectural history. I'm particularly interested in how architectural design and construction participated in moments of crisis within the city, and the extent to which buildings helped to manage these moments. I'm particularly interested making readers aware of the physical, social, geopolitical, viral, and climatic precariousness that has shaped Hong Kong for much of its colonial and post-colonial history, and the extent to which architecture has contributed to the perception and reality of instability in the city. By reframing Hong Kong’s architectural history in relationship to the notion of crisis, I hope to redefine how we understand the development and history of an architectural culture in the city. In this respect, my book has the potential to contribute significantly to the overall study of Hong Kong’s history and its built environment, with implications for how we understand Hong Kong as a place.

17623016.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17623016.value: For the purposes of this project, cyber-bullying refers to situations in which a child is harassed by another child (children) through the use of technology. Of pertinence to Hong Kong is the problem of ‘uncovering’ through exposing others’ personal data by unknown netizens. Social networking sites (SNS) have greatly intensified this form of bullying because their very nature and design encourage and facilitate individuals to share information. In addition to SNS (e.g. Facebook), there are online discussion forums (e.g. Golden Forum) dedicated to the sharing and disclosure of others’ personal data, as well as apps that allow individuals to broadcast their own lives in real time (e.g. app 17). In response, privacy protection (including personal data protection) has been invoked as a legal remedy to this worrying situation. Emerging legal attempts to address privacy violations in contexts such as cyber-bullying include recognising new legal concepts, such as the right to be forgotten. However, these remain to be isolated attempts. Besides, the resort to direct and pure legal means to tackle cyber-bullying and to check abuse of children’s widespread sharing of information remains controversial. In addition to the fact that legal actions are lengthy and costly, many suggest that legally punishing children engaged in cyberbullying is unlikely to be effective in the long term because it fails to address other environmental factors, including the way in which SNS are structured to encourage disclosure and incent peer monitoring and surveillance. Therefore, our team decides to adopt a legal, technological and socio-educational approach to tackle the problem from an interdisciplinary perspective. We advocate an alternative anti-cyberbullying regime examining the role of personal data disclosure on SNS by youths, and evaluating their conceptualisation of privacy to identify effective legal solutions, appropriate technological policies and education strategies. Methodologically, we will carry out theoretical legal analysis and empirical research to find out the attitudes of young people on personal data sharing and cyberbullying. In addition, we will adopt a comparative approach by drawing on existing lessons from Canada and the European Union (EU). In the long run, this research aims to bring about a paradigm shift on the legal protection of privacy in the Internet age and exert transformative effect on violent behaviour. The results will also contribute to digital media policy and development of a privacy literacy framework for youths.

17623016.label: Realisation of objectives
17623016.value: This study on cyberbullying from a comparative and an interdisciplinary perspective has culminated in the publications of 2 articles in international journals, one book chapter, and one edited volume. In addition, an interdisciplinary symposium was organised, and a workshop was delivered to the education sector. We conducted a large scale survey among more than 2000 high school students in Hong Kongm which shows that cyberbullying is a prevalent phenomenon among high school students, with more than 12% of the respondents having conducted doxing before, and more than 50% of them experienced personal information being disclosed online without consent. Further, we find that the reasons for doxing may not necessarily be hostile doxing, but can be social doxing. We also detect a slight difference of doxing pattern between female and male students, which reveals female students were more likely to engage in social doxing. In addition, our study also confirms the finding that females are more likely to experience sexual harassment as a form of doxing. Regardless of the reasons behind doxing, there is a definite association between doxing and negative emotional states as depression, anxiety and stress. Our study reveals that youngsters in Hong Kong have little understanding or awareness on the legal protection on data privacy. Nevertheless, our study has also analysed the inadequacy of existing law in Hong Kong to protect one's against doxing and cyberbullying. In comparison, different countries have come up with their legal solutions to specifically address the issues of doxing and cyberbullying either by having specific law, or having specific regulatory bodies to prevent and monitor online harms. We realize that tackling cyberbullying and doxing requires a multi-disciplinary approach, and has to be examined in the context of a fast changing technology world. An edited volume on technology facilitated violence with contributions from our team and other international scholars will be published in February 2021. The complex issue has been studied in depth from a legal, socio-educational, techno-regulatory and socio-educational perspective in the volume.

17623016.label: Major findings and research outcome
17623016.value: A study to examine adolescents’ doxing participation was carried out by using a school survey covering different types of secondary schools and students of differing socioeconomic backgrounds in Hong Kong. A sample of 2120 secondary school students participated in the study. The major findings of the study are that: 1. 12.1% of students conducted doxing on the Internet. Personal information of 54.7% of students was disclosed on the Internet without their consent. Girls were also found to be more likely than boys to be doxed. 2. Social and hostile doxing were the two most common forms of doxing. Girls were more likely than boys to engage in social doxing while boys were more likely to conduct hostile doxing than girls. 3. Students who had perpetrated doxing acts were more likely to have experienced information disclosure as victims, perpetrators, or bystanders. 4. Unauthorized disclosure of most types of personal information resulted in negative feelings in victims, including depression, anxiety, and stress. Signiﬁcant associations were found between emotional problems and the disclosure of mobile phone numbers and personal photos and videos, between doxing conducted by schoolmates and anxiety and depression, and between doxing through Instant Messenger and anxiety. (Chen, Q.Q., Chan, K.L. & Cheung, A.S.Y. (2018), Doxing victimization and emotional problems among secondary school students in Hong Kong; Chen, M, Cheung, A.S.Y. & Chan, K.L. (2019), Doxing: What Adolescents Look for and Their Intentions) Existing Hong Kong laws were studied to assess the adequacy of combating cyberbullying. Hong Kong has no statute law which specifically governs the issue of cyberbullying. A patchwork system of anti-cyberbullying laws makes legal remedies being inadequate uncertain and inaccessible. Hong Kong can take reference from New Zealand and Australia to create a single criminal offence of causing harm by posting digital communication and establish an agency to investigate cyberbullying cases and regulate social media services (Cheung, A.S.Y. (2018), Cyberbullying: In Search of a Legal Definition and a Legal Response). Although doxing is often denounced as a form of technology-facilitated violence and abuse, it serves the purpose of revealing wrongdoings. Court judgments concerning doxing in Hong Kong were analyzed to reveal that Hong Kong courts granted broad and vague injunction orders to prohibit doxing. Society should strike a balance between public accountability and privacy by establishing a public interest defense to doxing (Anne Cheung (Forthcoming, 2021), Doxing and the Challenge to Legal Regulation: When Personal Data Become a Weapon).

17623016.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17623016.value: The study focuses on the problem of doxing in Hong Kong. Yet it is only one type of violence. Further exploration of integrated cyber-violence prevention programmes is strongly recommended for schools with regard to preventing doxing victimization. At the same time, legal reform is urgently required to address the issue of doxing and its entailing problems. The PI already has a solid publication record on data privacy. She will discuss with her collaborators about the possibility of developing a legal policy framework. She will also explore with social network media (e.g. Facebook) on the technological challenges brought to data privacy in the age of artificial intelligence such as trolling, disinformation and fake news.

17623016.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17623016.value: This project is a study on doxing in Hong Kong, focusing mainly on the behaviour of high school students. It discovers that more than 12% of high school students in Hong Kong have conducted doxing for different reasons. Amongst them, more than 50% had been victims of doxing, experiencing various kinds of negative emotions such as depression and anxiety. There is a slight gender difference concerning the reasons behind doxing and the targets of doxing. Despite the prevalence of this phenomenon, the legal response in Hong Kong is far from adequate. Hong Kong does not have legislation which specifically governs the issue of cyberbullying or doxing. A patchwork system of anti-cyberbullying laws makes legal remedies being inadequate, uncertain and inaccessible. Our team has studied the problem of doxing and cyberbullying in the larger context of technology facilitated violence. We have produced journal articles, a book chapter, an edited volume; hosted symposium and workshop. We have been advocating for a multi-disciplinary response including legal reform, policy changes and new practices from online intermediaries.

17628816.label: Project Title(Chinese)
17628816.value: 二十 世紀初現代園境設計在中國城市規劃中日趨重要的地位

17628816.label: Project Objectives
17628816.value: Reposition the early 20th century as a historical moment in which landscape designs began to play a prominent role in China’s modernization and conception of the nation’s urban future. Illustrate the conflicting forces that shaped urban milieus and the impetus of producing new knowledge and pedagogies of the built environment amongst Chinese intellectuals. Illustrate how a new, unified logic of “developmental thinking” came to be rationalized across different professional fields. Challenge the previous “diffusionist” and “derivative” models of development by showing how concepts emerged in the "West" had been “vernacularized” in China via local agents. Act as a catalyst for interdisciplinary research and use of diverse local sources in the study of the built environment.
