To provide an in-depth analysis of three case studies of urban reconfiguration in Guangzhou: the construction of new streets in the western part of the city in the 1920s and 1930s, the "socialist housing transformation" project in the old city center in the 1950s and 1960s, and the reconstruction of an "urban village" in the new city center in the contemporary context;

To make a contribution to recent debates on infrastructures, material powers, and techniques of modern governance in the fields of urban studies, anthropology, post-colonial studies, and STS, adding a much-needed non-Western critical perspective into these debates.

17636016.label: Realisation of objectives
17636016.value: 1. The PI and Co-I have conducted research to examine the process of urbanization with a focus on bottom-up changes. Specifically, the PI conducted research that allowed for in-depth understanding of how ordinary urban citizens handled changes initiated by a series of policy shift, and how citizens' engagements complicate the development of urbanization. The Co-I focuses on the rural household holders who migrated to cities for jobs and life, and challenged the boundaries set by the household registration system. 2. The PI has conducted thorough archival research, supplemented by fieldwork, on the construction of new streets in the 1920s and 1930s. The PI started to rethink the issue of continuity in terms of governance rationale and government structure between the Republican era and the socialist period through the case of urban governance. This part of the research inspired the PI to develop another project that looks into the historical process of urbanization in Guangzhou that fundamentally changed the rationale and structure governance of cities. 3. Both researchers have conducted fieldwork (including participant observation, semi-structured interviews and informal hangouts) and textual analysis on the "socialist housing transformation" project in the old city center in the 1950s and 1960s, and the reconstruction of an "urban village" in the new city center in contemporary Guangzhou. These research activities have generated rich materials. That said, the reconstruction of an urban village has been put on hold in the past two years, a contingent development that researchers did not anticipate at the time of drafting the proposal. As the PI was trying out to find out the different forces that shaped the unexpected development, the outbreak of COVID-19 has prevented researchers from doing fieldwork. Nonetheless, the PI will follow closely with the development once cross-border travelling is open again. Meanwhile, the tightened political atmosphere in the mainland, our key informants (urban planners and government officials) requested us not to use information they provided directly regarding the specific cases for publications. Bounded by the ethical rules, both the PI and the Co-PI will not use the concerned information for publication now. However, one the one hand, the researchers will use the individual stories and materials obtained through observations and textual analysis to discuss spatial politics in the process of urbanization without directly implicated the key informants. On the other hand, the researchers will keep good records of the interview data for possible future publication. 4. Both researchers have developed nuanced analysis in their research that attend to the interactive process of the built environment, forms of governance and political economy in the process of urbanization, as shown in their research output. 5. Research outputs made possible by this grant contribute the recent debates on infrastructures, material powers, and techniques of modern governance in the fields of urban studies, anthropology, post-colonial studies, and STS, adding a much-needed non-Western critical perspective into these debates, as shown in research output.

17636016.label: Major findings and research outcome
17636016.value: -- The research on urban transformation in the Republican era has led us to problematize the often perceived break in terms of government before and after 1949. Both researchers are working on the human waste collection paper that illustrates the substantial re-organization of structural change in this period (see 8.1, 8.5, & 9.1). The PI therefore developed a new research project on the emergence of urban governance in Guangzhou in the Republican era (for details, see 6.2). -- From the perspective of ordinary urban citizens in Guangzhou, the periodisation of urbanisation is different from that in the grand narrative of Reform and Opening. For many, the late 1970s, which was often seen as the beginning of the Reform era, did not make much a difference in their lived experience regarding urbanisation. It is the twenty-first century that many feel substantial changes in urban life, regarding the size of the city, the population size, means of transportation, infrastructural networks, the built environment, and lifestyle. This finding is written into the draft "Urbanisation in China" for an encyclopaedic entry (8.6). -- Our research on "socialist housing transformation" and the reconstruction of an urban village led us to realise the persistent urban poverty in a wealthy city like Guangzhou, poverty that is not simply a result of economic reform but a continuation since the 1950s. Due to the tightened political atmosphere in the mainland, the sensitivity of some issues and the protection of some key informants, we decided not to discuss explicitly the two cases specified in the proposal. Instead, we use our research finding to discuss important socio-spatial issues in process of transformation (see 8.2, 8.4, 9.2 & 9.4).We also use materials collected during the fieldtrips to develop other articles (8.3 & 9.3). -- All three case studies suggest the complexity of the concept of public space in the China context. We discuss this issue in the several articles in preparation (8.2, 8.4, 8.7, & 9.2). -- Our research output analyze the dynamic process of population flow, forms of governance, infrastructural building, and political economy in the process of urbanization (8.4, 8.6, 8.7, 9.2 & 9.4).

This book project was awarded an Early Career Scheme grant for a period of three years to conduct archival and field research. Research will be carried out to further our understanding. -- We will continue to work on the articles that we have presented in conferences and workshops and get them published. -- We may publish some of the most sensitive materials in the future when risks for our informants are significantly reduced.

17636016.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17636016.value: This research tries to explore the complexity of urbanisation in China. Combining archival research with ethnographic investigation, the project will concentrate on three different critical moments of the process of urbanization in Guangzhou (Canton): first, street construction in the Thirteen Factory area in the western part of the city during the Republican era; second, the socialist housing transformation of an old city center neighborhood in the 1950s and 1960s; and, third, a contemporary urban village reconstruction project in the new city center. These three case studies of old neighborhood reconstruction will exemplify a nuanced analysis of urbanization that takes into account historically distinctive combinations of and evolving relations between actors, political rationalities, government capacity, material constraints, expertise and economic practices. This approach adds significant historical complexity to conventional accounts of post-Mao processes of urbanization, while challenging master narratives of urban transformation that give too much agency to state actors. Outside the China field, the project will make an important contribution to recent debates on infrastructure, power, and governance in the fields of urban studies, anthropology, post-colonial studies, and STS, adding a much-needed non-Western perspective into what remains a largely Western-centric research agenda.

17636116.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17636116.value: Population ageing is increasing across societies. However, data on ageing lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender adults (LGBT) is lacking as same-sex sexualities are seldom acknowledged in national census data collection and sexual orientation is not included in large scale gerontological research studies. A large portion of the research literature that does exist tends to focus on health disparities among older LGBT adults in comparison to older heterosexuals. Few studies address sex and intimacy among older LGBT adults, with even fewer studies focusing on lesbian sexualities and on non Euro-American contexts. We propose to explore the relationship between ageing and sexuality through a qualitative ethnographic study of 45 lesbians aged 60 and above in Hong Kong, Taiwan and Singapore. A minimum of 15 participants will be recruited from each research site for in-depth interviewing. The proposed comparative study of older lesbians’ lives in the three sites of Hong Kong, Taiwan and Singapore, is informed by the concept of “inter-Asian referencing” and intersectionality theory. Two were British colonies and one Japanese, and all were “Asian Tiger” economies, now developed with Taiwan trailing behind in GDP per capita. Chinese ethnicity is dominant in the three societies, with 94% in Hong Kong, 98% in Taiwan and 74.2% in Singapore. On the cultural front, Confucian values and beliefs are common in these societies. Taiwan has been known for its recent progressive attitude towards LGBT communities while Singapore still criminalises homosexuality. Homosexuality is decriminalised in Hong Kong yet social stigma remains for most LGBT persons. The project will improve our understanding of changing social, cultural and material conditions and lived experiences of older lesbians in three Asian societies and contribute to the sociological literature on gerontology, gender and sexualities in Asia. We aim to investigate the critical issues facing older lesbians in the realm of sex and intimacy amid ageing concerns. We also intend to find out whether older lesbians are marginalized in contemporary LGBT communities and, if so, why this is the case. By shedding light on the everyday lives of older lesbians living in predominantly ethnic Chinese societies, the proposed study will: (1) enrich the academic literature on ageing and the sociology of sexuality; (2) address a research gap in lesbian history; and (3) open up Euro-American debates on the definitions of elder sexuality to include those circulating in Asian societies. 世界各國人口老化現象日益顯著。然而，由於全國性的人口普查資料收集甚少承認同性傾向，大規模的老年學研究亦很少納入性傾向項目，以至於老年女同志、男同志、雙性戀以及跨性別 ( lesbiangay、gay、bisexual 以及 transgender，以下簡稱LGBT )之資料至今依然付之闕如。既有的文獻則多數關注於老年LGBT族群與老年異性戀者之間的健康差異。少有研究提出老年LGBT族群之性與親密關係議題，其中關於非歐美女同志之關注更是少數。 本研究期望透過質性民族誌研究方法了解老年與性傾向之關係。預計訪談45位在香港、台灣以及新加坡之60歲以上(含60歲) 老年女同志。預計在上述每一地區招募至少15位研究參與者進行深度訪談。上述香港、台灣以及新加坡三地老年女同志生命之比較研究主要是參考「亞際互為參照」概念以及交織性理論。其中二處曾是英國殖民地，一處則是前日本殖民地。三者均曾是「亞洲四小龍」經濟體之一，如今屬已開發國家，三者之中人均本地生產總值以台灣最低。 三者皆為華人為主之社會，其中香港華人佔94%，台灣佔98%，而新加坡則佔74.2%。文化方面，儒家的價值信仰皆普遍存在於這三處社會。台灣近幾年以其對LGBT社群之進步態度聞名，然而在新加坡同性戀仍屬刑事犯罪。香港雖已通過同性戀非刑事化，然而大多數LGBT個人仍遭受社會歧視。 本計劃將增進我們對於上述三個亞洲社會之社會、文化與物質條件變遷以及老年女同志生命經驗的理解，並對亞洲老年學、性別與性傾向之社會學文獻有所貢獻。我們旨在探討女同志面對年老問題，在性與親密關係方面出現的重大議題。我們亦企圖了解老年女同志在當代女同志社群中是否處於邊緣地位，若結果為是，則其原因為何。透過呈現華人社會老年女同志的每日生活 ，本研究將 (一)豐富老年與性社會學之學術文獻 ; (二) 補女同志歷史之研究空缺; (三) 拓展歐美論辯中對於老年性欲特質之定義，以納入亞洲社會的脈絡。

17636116.label: Realisation of objectives
17636116.value: This project explores the relationship between ageing and sexuality through a qualitative ethnographic study of 31 lesbians aged 60 and above in Hong Kong, Taiwan and Singapore. As mentioned in the last report, Dr. Tang T.S. Denise has been replaced by Dr. Travis S.K. Kong due to a change in Dr. Tang’s title and later institutional affiliation as of January 2018. Dr. Tang has remained as the Co-Investigator of the project. Another key factor that occurred during the project duration was the ill-health of Dr. Tang which resulted in limited physical mobility during Stage 2 and 3 of the project’s research field trips to Taiwan and Singapore. In summary, the core research team has completed 31 in-depth interviews including primary and secondary data collection, participant observation and numerous meetings with stakeholders in the older lesbian communities across 3 research sites. Research findings were shared in 6 seminars/international conferences. Two manuscripts have been submitted to highly-esteemed journals within the specialized field of gender and sexualities. Two more articles are currently in progress. Details are provided as follows in response to project objectives. In the final stage of our project, we focused on transcription and coding of data and data analysis. Two qualified research assistants have been hired to assist us with translation in terms of linguistic complexities as well as cultural nuances within the interviews. Multiple languages were used during the interviews including Cantonese, English, Hokkien, Mandarin and Singlish. During Stage 4 and 5, two more fieldtrips were conducted to Singapore and Taiwan for follow-up interviews with informants and face-to-face meetings with Co-Investigators. As a result of earlier interviews with informants in Stage 2 and 3, we had a chance to spend more informal time with informants and their wider circle of friends in the last segment of our project. Participant observation was carried out as we were invited to join social gatherings involving family members and their peers. Through these gatherings, we have become aware of more potential informants yet their reluctance to be formally interviewed remain strong. It has become clear that formal ways of documentation in terms of writing and recording were perceived as threatening to some of our informants’ friends. Rather, casual conversations over food and drinks provided key information and at times, long narratives of love and intimacy among older lesbians and bisexual women. Combined with empirical data collected from the completion of qualitative in-depth interviews in earlier stages of the project, Tang organized a panel on “Ageing & Sexuality: Qualitative studies and methodological notes on older gay men and lesbians in Hong Kong and Singapore” at the Association of Asian Studies in Asia conference (July 1-3, 2019). Presentations included Kong’s project on older Chinese gay men, Tang’s study on Hong Kong lesbians and the project’s other Co-Investigator, Dr. Shawna Tang’s research on older lesbians in Singapore (Objectives 1, 3 and 4). Organizing of the panel also allowed us to further discuss ways of developing a comparative framework to address issues of ageing and lesbian sexualities across connected histories in predominantly Chinese societies (Objective 2). In the later phases, we have also begun to notice differences among older lesbians and bisexual women primarily in healthcare provision, marriage and family, peer relations, sexual and romantic relations, gender roles, retirement and financial arrangements (Objectives 1 & 3). New and pressing issues also arose out of later informal gatherings with informants and their family members and friends. Data analysis has pointed to rising concerns of state provision in elderly care across the three research sites. A spectrum of commonly discussed elderly care services ranging from leisure activities to residential facilities was mentioned by informants. The younger cohort of informants was placed in a position to take care of their elderly parents, in particular when their parents were married at a very young age often in their late teens or early twenties. This phenomenon appears to be more common among informants in Hong Kong and Taiwan, whereas Singaporean informants appeared to be less worrisome about their own elderly parents (Objective 2 and 4). This may be partially explained by increasing disparities between social classes in Hong Kong and Taiwan as living standards rose while their life savings diminished. Although Taiwan has the benefit of a larger social welfare net in terms of healthcare provisions, there has been increasing discussion of medical examinations and prescription drugs outside of state healthcare. By caring for their own elderly parents, informants discussed about their own anxieties of growing old (Objective 3). Singaporean older lesbians, on the other hand, were slightly more confident in their state affairs. Prior to presenting at the Association of Asian Studies in Asia conference, Tang was invited to share preliminary research findings at two occasions in Hong Kong. The Gender Research Centre & Sexualities Research Programme at the Chinese University of Hong Kong (April 10) and the HKU – UC Berkeley Summer Institute (July 22) invited Tang to give guest lectures on the project. Students and faculty members at both seminars offered insights and asked critical questions on the project’s research findings. Tang has incorporated their feedback in eventual publications. On October 2, Tang was invited by an elderly queer women group in Vancouver B.C., Canada, called “The Queer Imaging & Riting Kollective for Elders (Quirk-e)” to give a presentation on issues facing Chinese lesbians in Asia. This transnational knowledge exchange has allowed me to further explore future possibilities in research. In the last months of the project, Tang wrote up two journal articles for submission with two other manuscripts in progress. Please refer to point number 6.1 Major findings and research outcome for more information. Recruitment of informants remained our biggest challenge for this project. As mentioned in the last progress report, we encountered unprecedented difficulties in recruiting participants for our Singapore cohort. In the end, we had to lower the age requirement from 60 to 55. Even though our Co-Investigator for the Singapore phase, Dr. Shawna Tang, has put in tremendous efforts in locating informants through gatekeepers, community leaders, friends and family relatives, only 5 women were willing to be interviewed by us. Stigmatization of lesbian sexuality and their lived experience under penal code was a constant reminder among Singaporean older lesbians.

17636116.label: Major findings and research outcome
17636116.value: This project explores contemporary lesbian subjectivities through a historical analysis of lesbian spaces in different Chinese locales. More specifically, we examine same-sex intimacies formed by and among older Chinese lesbians and bisexual women who were born between early 1940s to late 1950s through qualitative interviews and participant observation conducted in Hong Kong, Singapore and Taipei. As an emerging field, gay and lesbian gerontology tends to focus on clinical and social issues surrounding ageing and ageing bodies. Later research speaks to evolving lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender (LGBT) identity-driven social movements and the role of sexual identities play in the life experiences of older LGBT adults. Rather than only focusing on identity formations, experiences of discrimination or healthcare needs, we aim at complicating cultural notions of love, romance and intimacies, that were brought up within interstices of connected histories, gender roles and marginalized sexual subjectivities. Based on ethnographic data collected during 2016-2018, we elaborate on the moments of longing and waiting as redefining modern notions of love and intimacy across time and spatial dimensions. We also bring up a methodological episode where inter-Asian referencing intersects with Chinese modernities to illustrate how gender and sexuality meet, intersect and influence each other in the cultural imagination and eventual materialization of women’s same-sex desires. Moreover, we examine the politics of butchness as protection and as a form of politeness. We contend that older Chinese lesbian and bisexual sexualities in three Asian societies are linked through multiple understandings of Chinese modernities and its implications on understanding social institutions such as work, marriage and family in everyday life. She investigates how same-sex desires and practices were actualized within a historically contingent and culturally influenced understanding of gender roles within a social order that is often conflictual and contradictory.

17636116.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17636116.value: One of the key indications in conducting research with stigmatized subject as in elderly lesbian subjectivities is the critical importance of time. It has become clear to the core research team that a project of this topic often needs time for participant recruitment and saturation of trust among participants. We anticipate more opportunities for research activities and more productive dialogues with participants as word gets out through our current pool of informants as well as exposure gained through publication of research articles. This project has the potential to be of a longitudinal nature as we follow the everyday lives of our current informants. We anticipate to build on our current scholarship and to develop our comparative model by expanding our research scope to include other Asian societies. We also hope to locate funding opportunities to bring elderly participants together for sharing sessions and to build connections with other community groups in the Asia region.

Special consideration is given to the assessment of damages for PSLA. To construe, characterise and reshape a large number of judicial decisions rendered in Hong Kong in the past 40 years, with a view to formulate a sufficiently well-defined conceptual framework out of a broad notion of “pain and suffering”. To perform a statistical analysis of the factors that are influential in determining the levels of PSLA awards in Hong Kong, using data from cases collected in Objective (2), and Hong Kong's economic statistics. To explore the feasibility of using PPO as an alternative to the conventional multiplier-multiplicand approach. For this purpose, an indexation methodology will be tailor-made to address the uniqueness of Hong Kong’s social and economic situation.

17636316.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17636316.value: In this project, we will examine the rationales behind and the effectiveness of the compensation for pecuniary and non-pecuniary losses in Hong Kong’s personal injury disputes. We will give special consideration to the assessment of damages for pain, suffering and loss of amenity (“PSLA”). On the other hand, the potential use of structured settlements or periodical payment orders (“PPO”) as a substitute for (or together with) lump-sum awards will also be examined. The primary sources of data comprise all judgments on personal injury issued by all levels of the Hong Kong Judiciary during 1976-2016. Damages are broadly divided into four categories: (1) expenses incurred before the trials; (2) PSLA; (3) future nursing and medical expenses; and (4) future loss of earnings. Concerning (3) and (4), we previously proposed the move to a standard method of capitalising future financial needs by using actuarial tables. The figures in the tables had to reflect the mortality statistics and economic data of Hong Kong. The proposals and the actuarial tables constructed by the present investigators have now been formally endorsed by the Court of First Instance (Chan Pak Ting, 2013) and the Court of Appeal (Chan Wai Ming, 2014), constituting an indispensable part of Hong Kong’s common law system. The present research proposes further reforms, focussing on PSLA and the use of PPO regarding future medical and other expenses. PSLA involves converting pain into dollars, which is not a process of mathematical measurement. It involves sound judgment and principled discretion guided by moral norms. We will propose a solution to this predicament by systematically analysing the damages awarded by the Hong Kong Judiciary in the past 40 years as guidelines for constructing a coherent and logical framework. In particular, the statistical relationship between PSLA awards and other relevant factors, such as medical/nursing expenses, will be scrutinised. We will present the framework as an accessible judicial tool for judges, lawyers and mediators involved in dispute resolution. In catastrophic personal injury cases, the lump-sum awards hinge on estimates of the claimants’ life expectancies and investment returns over inflation. However, claimants may exhaust their funds by surviving longer than their projected life expectancies, or due to lower-than-expected investment returns. PPO provide for regular payments over their lifetime, which are adjusted annually based on an inflation index. In this project, we will recommend reforms, focussing on PSLA and the use of PPO regarding future medical and other expenses. 在這個項目中，我們將先研究在香港人身傷害糾紛中金錢與非金錢損失補償訂額的基本原理及其有效性。其中，我們會較專注受害人之痛苦及損失人生樂趣（“PSLA”）的補償估算。在另一方面，我們亦研究以定期付款 (“PPO”）方式替代現行一筆過支付人身傷害賠償之可行性。 主要的數據來源包括在1976至2016年間由香港各級司法部門發出的所有人身傷害案件之判決。賠償大致可分為四類：（1）原訟前費用; （2）PSLA; （3）未來的護理和醫療費用; （4）未來的收入損失。關於（3）和（4），我們先前已經制訂及發表有關計算該兩項損失之精算表。而該表中的數字已經反映香港死亡率及經濟情況數據。該組精算表最近由原訟法庭（Chan Pak Ting，2013年）和上訴法院（Chan Wai Ming， 2014年）正式採納，構成香港普通法律制度中不可或缺的一部分。 是項研究之目的是提出了進一步的改革，側重於PSLA之議題及未來的醫療有關費用通脹對採用PPO制度的挑戰。PSLA涉及轉換痛苦成賠償金額，這不是純粹數學的計算。它涉及到在適當道德規範指導下之判斷原則和合理裁量權。我們將通過有系統地分析由香港司法機構在過去的40年之判決及案例，構建一個有連貫性和邏輯性之PSLA賠償制訂的框架指南。特別是對PSLA賠償金與其他相關因素(如醫療及護理費用)之間的統計關係進行審查。我們冀望是項研究提出之框架能作為參與解決糾紛的法官、律師和調解員可依據的司法工具。 在災難性的人身傷害案件中，一筆過賠償金額取決於索賠人的預期壽命和撇除通脹之淨投資回報率。可是當索賠人存活的時間比其預期壽命為長，或實際的淨投資回報結果比預期的差，他們的賠償金會過早被耗盡。 PPO提供保証分期支付賠償金給予索賠人直到他們過世為止，而分期金額亦每年根據通貨膨脹指數而調整。在這個項目中，我們將提出改革建議，重點放與未來的醫療有關費用通脹掛鉤之PPO制度。

17636316.label: Realisation of objectives
17636316.value: The rationales behind and the effectiveness of the compensation for pecuniary and non-pecuniary losses in Hong Kong’s personal injury disputes are examined in this project. A key objective of the project is to critically evaluate the assessment of damages for pain, suffering and loss of amenity (“PSLA”). The primary sources of data are derived from all the judgments on personal injury issued by the Hong Kong judiciary during 1976-2016. As rightly pointed out by Professor Geistfeld: “…even if tort awards for pain and suffering are desirable in principle, they may be undesirable in practice if there is no defensible method for calculating the appropriate award. The problem is that there is no obvious relationship between money and a nonmonetary injury. Consequently, different ways of conceptualizing how these damages should be determined could yield significantly different damages awards.” (“Placing a Price on Pain and Suffering” (1995) 83 California Law Review 773, at 778-9). In 1996, the Law Commission of England and Wales issued a Consultation Paper titled “Damages for Personal Injury: Non-Pecuniary Loss”, followed by the Commission Report issued in 1999. It was recommended that the level of damages for non-pecuniary loss for personal injuries (mainly PSLA) should be increased. The Commission’s recommendation was examined judicially and followed by the English Court of Appeal in Heil v Rankin ([2001] QB 272 (CA)). The Heil v Rankin uplift has not been followed explicitly in Hong Kong courts. Our research findings based on a computational analysis of more than 1,200 judgments support the thesis that there was a de facto uplift of the PSLA amounts in Hong Kong after 2000. We argue that even though the Heil v Rankin uplift was not expressly followed in Hong Kong courts, the impact of this landmark decision rendered by the English Court of Appeal cannot be overlooked. We therefore argue that a comprehensive review is needed in Hong Kong, and propose a framework for uplifting different categories of PSLA compensation. Furthermore, we also propose a way to construct a mechanism for keeping the levels of compensation up to date and inflation-adjusted. Another objective is to examine the potential use of structured settlements or periodical payment orders (“PPO”) as a substitute for (or together with) lump-sum awards. The primary sources of data comprise all judgments on personal injury issued by the Hong Kong judiciary during 1976-2016. In catastrophic personal injury cases, the lump-sum awards hinge on estimates of the claimants’ life expectancies and investment returns over inflation. However, claimants may exhaust their funds by surviving longer than their projected life expectancies, or due to lower-than-expected investment returns. PPO provide for regular payments over their lifetime, which are adjusted annually based on an inflation index. In this project, reforms focussing the use of PPO are recommended. We argue that the court must be satisfied that the continuity of payments under a PPO is reasonably secure. Otherwise, the court should not make the order. It is unreasonable for plaintiffs to bear the default risk. For instance, if the source of the payments under a PPO is the Hong Kong Government or the Hong Kong Hospital Authority, the continuity of payments should be considered as reasonably secure. The HK Mortgage Corporation Annuity Limited (“HKMCA”) should also be considered as a reasonably secure paying party for making periodical payments. Even though technically speaking HKMCA a limited company, it is wholly owned by the Hong Kong Mortgage Corporation Limited, which is in turn wholly owned by the Hong Kong Government through the Exchange Fund. HKMCA launched a life annuity scheme in 2018 for Hong Kong residents. We believe that HKMCA should possess sufficient capital and expertise to offer PPO annuity to be purchased for a personal injury victim, either by the defendant directly or by the defendant’s insurer. On the other hand, if the source of the payments under a PPO is an insurance company (either self-funded by the insurance company or funded by an annuity provided by another insurance company), the continuity of payments must be fully protected irrespective of the insolvency of the insurance company honouring the PPO obligations. In Hong Kong, the Policyholders’ Protection Scheme Bill was introduced to the Legislative Council for debate during the 2018-19 legislative year. Under the proposed Policyholders’ Protection Scheme, insurance policyholders are entitled get protection coverage of up to HK$1 million if their insurance company goes into liquidation. If the source of the payments under a PPO is an insurance company, we propose that the Policyholders’ Protection Scheme should be extended to protect the recipients of periodical payments under PPOs. We also propose that the cap of HK$1 million should be lifted for PPOs, so that the recipients of periodical payments under PPOs can have a direct claim under the PPS to cover 100% of the periodical payments. PPOs, if implemented, will cover serious personal injury claims in which victims are in need of lifelong medical care for lengthy periods of time. In other types of claims, lump-sum awards will continue to operate. It is necessary to consider the multipliers and discount rates used in ascertaining the lump-sum awards. In Hong Kong, the Court of First Instance determined the discount rates based on the economic evidence adduced in 2012 (in Chan Pak Ting No.1). However, the economic and population landscapes of Hong Kong are constantly changing. Accordingly, the factors and driving forces shaping the discount rates in Hong Kong are also changing in a dynamic way. In our opinion, regular reviews of the discount rates should be in place. It is prudent for the Hong Kong judiciary to take steps to review the discount rates, at least on a triennial basis. We put forward the proposal that the Chief Justice of Hong Kong should set up a panel of independent experts. The panel will play an advisory role in formally reviewing the discount rates. The Chief Justice should be empowered to announce the discount rates. Membership of the panel may include judges, representatives from the Government (e.g. Census and Statistics Department, Hong Kong Monetary Authority), actuaries, economists, statisticians, accountants, financial advisors and academics. It is hoped that an effective mechanism to conduct regular reviews of the discount rates, a holistic framework to consider the adjustment of PSLA awards, together with the enactment of legislation to implement PPOs will lay the cornerstone of full compensation in the tort of personal injury in Hong Kong.

17636316.label: Major findings and research outcome
17636316.value: We have collected and presented the empirical evidence in support of the introduction of periodical payment orders (PPOs) in Hong Kong. We argue that PPOs can significantly alleviate the longevity risks borne by the victims. In recent decades, longevity risk has become a major concern for governments, private pension providers and individuals in most jurisdictions. Hong Kong is no exception. In the context of personal injury litigation, longevity risk refers to a situation where the plaintiff’s lump-sum award for daily and medical expenses has been exhausted because the plaintiff lives longer than expected. If implemented successfully with adequate security for payments, PPOs will afford a higher degree of protection to victims of serious personal injuries in need of lifelong medical care. Our research outcome indicates the urgent need to make sure that the continuity of payments under a PPO is reasonably secure. Otherwise, the court should not make the order. A variety of methods for providing the security and continuity of payments have been thoroughly analysed, and a proposal based on the research findings is put forward for judicial consideration. Lump-sum compensation will remain relevant in the near future, new edition of the actuarial tables have been published in HK in 2019. Based on the same common law principles, the publishers Sweet and Maxwell also invited us to publish the Singapore edition of the tables in 2021. Another key objective of the project is to critically evaluate the assessment of damages for pain, suffering and loss of amenity (“PSLA”). Systematic analysis of the PSLA awards has never been conducted in Hong Kong. The only judicial guideline, which is very brief and general, can be found in the Hong Kong Court of Appeal’s decision in Leung On v Chan Pui Ki (1996). Under the guideline, PSLA are broadly categorised into 4 groups: (1) serious injury; (2) substantial injury; (3) gross disability; and (4) disaster. Apart from this, very little judicial guidance is provided under the Hong Kong common law system. In this project, we have systematically analysed more than 1,200 judgments on personal injury claims rendered by the Hong Kong judiciary during 1996-2016. Our research findings based on a computational analysis support the thesis that there was a de facto uplift of the PSLA amounts in Hong Kong after 2000. With empirical evidence in support, we put forward a framework for uplifting different categories of PSLA compensation in Hong Kong.

17636316.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17636316.value: On 25 April 2018, the Hong Kong Law Reform Commission published a consultation paper titled “Periodical Payments for Future Pecuniary Loss in Personal Injury Cases”. One of the goals of the consultation paper is to invite public views on whether the court should be granted, by way of legislation, the power to make PPOs in relation to compensation for future pecuniary loss in personal injury cases. The key objective of the consultation paper is to highlight the problems of the existing law and practices in assessing damages, in particular, future pecuniary losses in personal injury cases, and whether reform is desirable to permit periodical payments for future pecuniary loss to be awarded. In August 2018, we have submitted a written response to the Hong Kong Law Reform Commission during the consultation period. It is hoped that the proposals we put forward will be implemented by means of legislation. If requested, we will be pleased to provide the relevant data regarding our research outcome and findings to the Law Reform Commission, so that they can make an informed assessment and decision in respect of different proposals put forward by the stakeholders.

In addition, the potential use of structured settlements or periodical payment orders (“PPO”) as a substitute for (or together with) lump-sum awards is also examined. 17641716.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17641716.value: General Studies, Chinese History, and History are three main subjects for schoolchildren in Hong Kong to learn about society around them, past and present. However, recently some educators have suggested that primary resources for teaching these subjects misrepresent societal diversity, with biased portrayals of minorities. To date no academic studies have focused on how these subjects represent the overall social world. This study builds upon the principal investigator’s previous research on Hong Kong Liberal Studies, to complete a systematic examination of how Hong Kong education achieves its multicultural aim of helping students understand diversity in society through major social studies-related subjects. It focuses on textbooks: primary educational resources used exclusively by many teachers to frame content, which are also promoted today by government officials as tools for student self-guided learning. The primary objective of this research is to analyze how ethnic and religious minorities in Hong Kong and Mainland China are represented in past and current textbooks for General Studies, History, and Chinese History. In line with the principal investigator’s past research on the multicultural content of Liberal Studies, the analysis focuses on depictions of people/groups who appear as not part of the Han ethnic group (Chinese ethnic minorities, Indians, Whites, etc.); and/or as part of a religious group and/or involved in religious practice. It includes texts and other government-sanctioned educational resources commonly used for the subjects today, as well as commonly used texts historically, since the 1970s. The study will employ quantitative and qualitative content analysis methods. The proportion of multicultural content in texts will be identified, while Key Words in Context and text and picture coding will be used to provide a nuanced overall portrayal of content. Parallel analyses by the principal investigator and research assistant and teacher surveys will be used to establish reliability and validity of findings. Building on past research, this study will lead to a comprehensive, historically-framed view of the quantity and quality of curriculum content related to multicultural diversity in Hong Kong education (primary and secondary). It will lead to articles, presentations, and a monograph articulating the extent, substance, and evolution of multicultural elements in Hong Kong school curricula since the 1970s. The monograph will be foundational for theorizing multiculturalism in the Hong Kong context in light of the political and educational changes of the last half-century, valuable for comparative analysis and future reforming of curriculum, teacher education, and use of educational resources. 本研究致力於分析香港和中國內地的通識教育、世界歷史和中國歷史三門學科的新舊教科書中少數族群和宗教是如何被表述的。正如主研究員曾研究過的通識教育中的多元文化內容，主要的分析對象為教科書中關於非漢族的少數族群（如，中國少數民族、印度人、白人等等）和宗教人士、宗教相關行為的描述。此項研究不僅涵蓋了現在正在被普遍使用的政府審查合格的教學材料，還包括1970年代以來使用過的舊版材料。研究將同時採用質性和量性方法來進行內容分析。（教科書中的）多元文化相關內容所占的比例將被識別，通過關鍵字編碼分析文本和圖片資料從而精確地呈現相關內容。同時，主研究員及其研究助理的平行分析及教師調查將被用來保證研究結果的信度和效度。

17641716.label: Realisation of objectives
17641716.value: The first objective of this study was to analyze how ethnic and religious minorities in Hong Kong and Mainland China are represented in primary and secondary school textbooks and related resources for Hong Kong social studies subjects (General Studies, History, and Chinese History). To achieve this objective, I critically examined related content in textbooks for Chinese History, History, and General Studies. In Chinese history textbooks, I found that the representation of the relationships between groups reflects majority perspectives, cultural superiority, and plural monoculturalism. The majority perspective means that multicultural content was expressed from the perspectives of members of the majority (i.e. the Han) group in society, while minority perspectives were only included in textbooks when they benefited a majority view. For example, the history of China reflects the assimilation of ethnic minority groups by the central governments of the territory over time. In this case, history is mainly told from the perspective of central government leaders past and present, rather than from a minority view, to provide a complementary and celebratory connotation in describing interactions which had mixed impacts when seen from minority perspectives. In particular, this is seen in the way the Chinese history textbooks positively describe and normalize practices of assimilation and territorial expansion by central government leaders throughout Chinese history. Cultural superiority refers to how the Han Chinese viewed minority cultures as backward and saw the culture of the Han as advanced and superior. In all periods in Chinese history, the culture of the Han is described as advanced, superior to others, and beneficial to ethnic minority groups. While cultural spreading from minority groups is depicted as superficial in textbooks, they narrate the assimilation of ethnic minorities by the Han as deeply beneficial. Plural monoculturalism is another useful lens to examine Chinese history textbooks. In contrast to the types of inclusion and recognition of different cultures sought under pluralistic multiculturalism, plural monoculturalism suggests or creates an illusion that mutual contact naturally or necessarily leads to assimilation and the disappearance of minority cultures, which reinforces exclusion and segregation. In relation, narratives in textbooks suggest that mutual contact leads to cultural extinction, concealing the possibility that communication and dialogue can help minority cultures and develop mutual respect. This naturalizes the extinction of cultural groups within the national community, because it obscures the possibility for minority groups to positively influence and peacefully coexist with the majority. In this sense, Chinese history textbooks do not provide any possibility for minority groups to protect their culture in a period of assimilation, as the only apparent choice is to seclude themselves. In this situation, disparities and boundaries among diverse groups are created and reinforced as they are naturalized and justified through a plural monocultural mentality. In both history and Chinese history textbooks, I found a focus on national identity over local identity. Promoting a sense of national identity has arguably been the ultimate goal of teaching Chinese history in Hong Kong from a historical view. After 1997, Hong Kong history was added to the Chinese history syllabus for the first time. This was done to boost students’ interest in Chinese history, by enhancing students’ perceptions of Hong Kong as having been a part of China since ancient times. The history textbooks are traditionally seen as reflecting a western and liberal perspective in contrast to Chinese history texts. Nonetheless, in these textbooks, national identity is prioritized over local identity, to strengthen students’ sense of national identity toward Mainland China (especially in sections on local history). In addition to tracing Hong Kong history back to ancient times, the situation of contemporary Hong Kong is also used in history textbooks to strengthen national identity. However, the discrepancy between textbooks and the ‘reality’ in students’ minds can intensify a sense of tension among Hong Kong youth in relation to societal concerns regarding nationalism and patriotism. Moreover, I found the role of general studies and history textbooks in facilitating cosmopolitan values, balancing identities, and global citizenship limited. Cosmopolitanism and cosmopolitan values are described as good for Hong Kong people to embrace. However, although texts encourage students meet and engage with students from other places, learn to respect one another, and welcome everyone, they are given in textbooks as slogans, without specifying instruction or examples that could guide students regarding what aspects of diversity they should respect, and what they should do to show respect to others, or rectify discrimination in reality. The details of how to think about and treat ethnic and religious minorities beyond abstract and idealistic slogans is never articulated. Worse, textbooks risk impeding cosmopolitan values and global citizenship among students, as they reinforce and reproduce prejudice, stereotypes, and misunderstanding of people, especially Mainland Chinese and ethnic and religious minorities. The second objective was to compare the extent, substance, and evolution of multicultural elements (focused particularly on ethnic and religious minorities) in Hong Kong government schools’ curriculum since the 1970s. I explored the development of political and cultural contexts of Hong Kong and its influence on social studies subjects. In particular, I examined to what extent the interplay of globalization, nationalization, decolonization, and localization shape the depiction of Hong Kong society in curriculum development. By comparing multicultural content in Chinese history textbooks since the 1970s, this study provides a perspective for understanding current discussions about Hong Kong curricula.

17641716.label: Major findings and research outcome
17641716.value: This project has conducted a comprehensive examination of how Hong Kong schools' curriculum for General Studies, History, and Chinese History reflect upon cultural diversity, particularly in relation to representations of ethnic and religious minorities. It found that despite including many broad statements about the positive value of diversity in society, curricula and textbooks at the same time do not represent ethnic minorities in a way that effectively educates students towards multicultural aims. Instead, they often depicted ethnic and religious minorities and cultural difference as problematic and as a source of social tension. In this sense, prejudice and stereotypes towards ethnic minorities – particularly those from South Asia and Africa, is quite commonly discussed, but not without sufficient criticality, in textbooks. Meanwhile, beneath the surface curricula promote experiences and perspectives from the majority ethnic Han people, and encourage an assimilationist stance by emphasising Hong Kong as ethnically Chinese. Both history and Chinese history textbooks prioritise Chinese and particularly Han ethnic identities, in the contemporary time period and across historical eras, reflecting assimilation to the mainstream as virtuous. These findings have been reported on in academic articles and conference presentations, and in various seminars open to the public, facilitated by university research centres and academic units, and other organizations.

17641716.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17641716.value: By examining the extent and nature of depictions of ethnic and religious minorities in resources for social studies subjects, this project comprehensively responded to the question of whether school resources aid students to develop multicultural values which are major aims of primary and secondary education identified by the Curriculum Development Council. This enables more informed decision making by policymakers, educators, teacher trainers and textbook publishers, regarding the production and use of resources for teaching toward multicultural aims across Hong Kong curricula. Additionally, this research provides opportunities for future research to examine multicultural content in curricula in other Chinese societies (e.g. Mainland China, Macau, and Taiwan), and to compare similarities and differences in terms of their approaches for representing cultural diversity in curricula. Future research could focus on textbooks in subjects most relevant to multicultural education used in government schools in these societies. These include History, Moral and Character Education, and Moral and Political Education in Mainland China; Moral and Civic Education, and Social and Humanities Education in Macau; and Social Studies, Civics and Society, and History in Taiwan. Potential methods include quantitative and qualitative content analysis.

17641716.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17641716.value: Hong Kong is a multicultural society which seeks to accommodate and positively recognise and include diverse groups. Recognition of diversity is one of the core values of the society and central aims of education in Hong Kong. General Studies, Chinese History, and History are three main subjects for schoolchildren in Hong Kong to learn about diversity. However, recently some educators have feared that resources for teaching these subjects misrepresent societal diversity, with biased portrayals of minorities. This study is the first academic study that focuses on how these subjects represent the overall social world. With a focus on textbooks, as primary educational resources used exclusively by many teachers to frame content, which are also promoted today by government officials as tools for student self-guided learning, this study completed a systematic examination of how Hong Kong education achieves its multicultural aim of helping students understand diversity in society through major social studies-related subjects. It is foundational for theorizing multiculturalism in the Hong Kong context in light of the political and educational changes of the last half-century, and it is also valuable for conducting future comparative analyses and for reforming curriculum, teacher education, and use of educational resources.

17646216.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17646216.value: Urban Rooftop Farming (URF), is a component of the zero-acreage farming (ZFarming) concept of using built urban surfaces for the production of food crops, and a recent development of the strong interest in greening city roofs. In addition to the benefits of green roofs (reduced solar heat gain; improved building energy conservation and sound insulation; storm water amelioration; reduced urban heat island; improved air quality; increased biodiversity; and contribution to urban greening), collectively URFs may help address issues of food security, and promote healthy lifestyles and community interaction amongst urban populations. URF has been enthusiastically embraced by architects, urban designers, environmentalists and community groups. Ad hoc projects have been initiated in high density cities across the world, using a variety of building types, construction methods, farming modes, etc., and with differing motivations and outcomes. Broadly these can be categorised as community-based or commercial-scale URF projects. The nature, operational requirements and performance criteria (economic, environmental, social) of URFs have not been clearly defined, and city regulatory authorities have yet to be able to codify URF initiatives and bring them within building development and land use planning processes. This is a significant restraint on the number and scale of URF projects being developed, and their potential collective benefit at a city-scale is not being realised. This study seeks to first to define URF typologies, their requirements and performance criteria through a systematic review of published project case studies and academic literature, verified through field investigations of established URFs in Hong Kong, Singapore and Bangkok. Based on the understanding generated, a method to assess the potential feasibility for both community based and commercial URFs will be developed using GIS spatial analysis of building and land use data to map potential sites, and to evaluate these against commercial and community factors. The method will be tested using data from Hong Kong. Potential environmental and social impacts on the city of the comprehensive application of URF projects will be assessed, including an evaluation of the implications on current building regulations, land use planning processes, strategic planning policy for the city. The impact of this study would be to advance our understanding of the nature URF practices and create a framework for the consistent evaluation and regulation of potential URF projects. The findings will be presented to government agencies and professional groups as a basis for technical research and consideration of changes in public policy. 城市屋頂農場(URF)是零種植面積農業(ZFarming)的一部分，運用城市建成表面種植食物及增加屋頂綠化。除了綠色屋頂的益處（減少太陽熱能，有助建築節約能源及隔音，改良屋頂排水，降低熱島效應，改善空氣質量，改善生物多樣性，增加城市綠化）之外，屋頂農場還可以幫助解決食物安全問題，提倡健康生活方式，以及增強城市居民的社區交流。屋頂農場得到了建築師，城市設計師，環境學家及社區組織的熱烈歡迎。 在世界上很多高密度的城市中，眾多屋頂農場項目被實施於各式建築物之上，運用不同建造及種植方法得出不盡相同的結果。屋頂農場類型大致可分為社區屋頂農場及商業屋頂農場。但其基本性質，操作要求，（經濟，環境及社會）性能標準都還未被明確定義，而且城市管理機構也還未能將屋頂農業項目納入到建築設計及土地規劃程序的法律條例中。這使得屋頂農場在城市規模的公眾效益無法實現，是屋頂農場發展的巨大障礙。 此研究將首先通过文獻查和分析香港，新加坡及曼谷的現有屋頂農場案例來定義屋頂農場的類型，其操作及性能標準。在此基礎上，以香港為例，運用GIS對城市用地現狀數據進行分析得出潛在屋頂農場場地，再考慮各場地的商業或社區因素進行再次篩選 。項目同時也會研究屋頂農場對城市潛在的環境，社會影響， 及現有建築規範，土地規劃程序的相關政策。研究目的是為了加深公眾對屋頂農場的了解，以及為科學評估與管理屋頂農場項目創建框架。最終研究結果將提供予政府機構或專業團體用於屋頂農場相關的技術和公共政策研究。

17650416.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17650416.value: This research project explores how the European Union (EU) regime on tax evasion impacts on Singapore and Hong Kong - Asia’s major financial centres. It capitalises on the recent tightening, driven by France and Germany, of EU regulation on tax evasion over non-EU jurisdictions and examines why the EU has altered its traditional strategy of norm entrepreneurship (advocacy of best practices) to norm coercion (imposition of fines, threats of prosecution, blacklisting). By casting doubt on the reputation of Hong Kong and Singapore as ‘clean’ financial centres, the EU may have found a powerful mechanism to achieve its regulatory preferences without hurting its other commercial and economic interests in Asia. In order to understand this shift, this research project examines (a) the differences and similarities between the French and German governments in spearheading EU regulation on tax evasion, (b) the responses to EU pressure to combat tax evasion by authorities in Singapore and Hong Kong, and (c) the role of reputational risk in the pursuit of coercive mechanisms to get non-EU jurisdictions to adopt EU regulatory preferences. This will be achieved by comparing the case studies of France and Germany in EU policy formation on tax evasion, and of Hong Kong and Singapore in responding to this pressure. Significant data collection is required, especially regarding EU directives, national legislation, and policy initiatives on tax evasion, as well as regulatory frameworks developed through multilateral channels such as the Organisation of Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) and the G20. This shift in EU policy is under-researched and so are its consequences on Asian financial centres. The EU regime on tax evasion and its behaviour vis-a-vis Hong Kong and Singapore needs to be analysed by taking account of the French and German models of capitalism and the electoral and economic pressures that facilitate a more coercive policy posture by the EU. Likewise, as Singapore and Hong Kong continue to attract increasing capital inflows from Europe, especially for their growing wealth management and private banking industries, it is important to analyse their response to adopt regulations that are at odds with their own models of capitalism. The outcome of this research project will be a major monograph and high-impact journal article dedicated to the analysis of a complex and highly topical issue that is rapidly becoming a bone of contention in the competitive relations between European and Asian financial centres. 此項研究旨在考察歐盟反避稅機制的發展及其對亞洲兩大主要金融中心——香港和新加坡的影響。它重點關注歐盟最近強化對非歐盟司法區避稅行為的管制并分析其對亞洲帶來的影響。 在歐元區金融危機的背景下，歐盟兩大重要成員國——法國和德國緊急推行了反避稅規則，在歐盟內部引領了超出經濟合作發展組織（OECD）框架的規範轉變。由歐盟委員會以及法、德兩個政府倡導的新管制標準有意針對和影響非歐盟司法區。這些地方如今既面臨重大壓力和動力採用歐盟的法律和管制標準，鬆動銀行秘密法，對避稅質控提供援助，并與歐盟成員國的稅務機構分享信息。新加坡與香港持續吸引著來自歐洲的資本入境，尤其是在他們日益增長的財富管理以及私人銀行業，因此他們發現自己不得不採納往往與自己的資本模式相悖的規範。 本研究將論證這樣一個假設，即歐盟能夠成功擴散其管制規範是源於其策略的改變，即由創造性規範(倡導最好的實踐)轉向強制性規範(征收罰款、威脅指控、列黑名單以及針對其他金融中心的聲譽)。為了更好地理解這一轉變，本研究將考察：a) 德國以及法國政府在醞釀和實施反避稅規則上的相同與不同點；b) 新加坡與香港監管部門對歐盟出台反避稅政策的反應；c) 歐盟如何有意識地通過強制性的機制促使非歐盟司法區（尤其是新加坡和香港）的監管部門採用歐盟的政策規範。此研究需要大量的數據支撐，尤其是關於歐盟的指令、成員國的立法、針對避稅的相關政策，以及在經濟合作發展組織（OECD）和20國集團（G20）等多邊渠道建立的管制框架。 反避稅政策是一個複雜而迫切的問題，這一問題正迅速成為歐洲與亞洲金融中心競爭性關係中的焦點。此項研究將分析這一問題，并將發表專著和高影響力的期刊論文。

17650416.label: Major findings and research outcome
17650416.value: The EU has exerted considerable influence to steer the global regime against tax evasion, money laundering and terrorist financing in way that is congruent with its political, economic and commercial interests. The main contribution of this research project is to sketch out the pathways of this influence beyond legal and technical regulatory isomorphism. Much of the scholarly literature on tax evasion is technical and legalistic, thus assuming that the global regime on something as essential as taxation and financial crime exists in a political vacuum. This research project adds significant analytical value by illustrating the ways in which reputations, identities, norms and perceptions are mobilised to either motivate jurisdictions to push for regulatory action or to stop it. The main benefit of the comparative approach chosen for this research project is that it was able to process trace how two distinct financial centres in Asia - Hong Kong and Singapore - respond to this European pressure.

17650416.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17650416.value: This research project has generated a lot of research material for future research on money laundering and terrorist financing. In particular, two avenues of future research stand out: the ability of states to learn from each other when it comes to security matters (organised crime, terrorism, money laundering) and the disjuncture between the EU's leadership on regulatory matters and its deficient enforcement mechanisms. Both avenues of research will be explored further and lead to more publications down the line.

17650416.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17650416.value: The EU has been a leading actor pushing for the development of a more comprehensive international regime against tax evasion, harmful tax competition, money laundering and terrorist financing. This research project has shown that the influence of the EU is not only legal, technical and diplomatic, but that it also involves the mobilisation of 'soft' factors such as reputations and perceptions. As Asia's main financial centres, Hong Kong and Singapore have been exposed to European pressure to adopt regulatory frameworks in line with EU preferences and standards. By tracking the evolution of the regime against tax evasion and money laundering in Hong Kong and Singapore, this research project illustrates the extent to which repetitional damage and coercion influence state behaviour in jurisdictions over which the EU has no direct control.

17651016.label: Realisation of objectives
17651016.value: By June 30, 2019, we have completed all the relevant work of the whole project. First, we completed running all the groups for the two experimental conditions, cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) and cognitive behavioural therapy with parental involvement (CBT-PI), and the control condition, social activity groups. A total of 136 adolescents and 46 parents participated in the study. We achieved several research outputs. First, a CBT group workbook for Chinese adolescents with anxiety problem was developed. Second, two academic articles have been completed. One of them has been published in a high ranking peer-review journal in psychology and family studies, and another one is under a second review in a high ranking peer-review journal in social work. Third, we have invited the world-renowned CBT expert in children and adolescents with anxiety problems, Professor Philip Kendall to travel to Hong Kong and conducted a two-day workshop to disseminate clinical CBT skills on working with adolescents with anxiety problems. Besides, a one-day symposium was held by the research team, Professor Kendall, and several other local experts in the academic and clinical fields to share the clinical CBT skills and part of the research outputs to frontline social workers, other mental health professionals, teachers, academics etc. The following sections report in specific how Objectives 1, 2, and 3 have been achieved. For objective 1, the CBT group workbook for Chinese adolescents with anxiety problems in Hong Kong was first developed by the research team. After evaluating the content according to the implementation and feedback during CBT and CBT-PI groups for several times, we have finalized the workbook after all the CBT and CBT-PI groups were run. In addition, the research team held a two-day workshop and a one-day symposium from December 7 to December 9, 2017, to disseminate some materials of the workbook and part of research results to frontline social workers, nurses, counselors, school teachers, and academics. Around 130 participants joined the workshop and symposium. Therefore, objective 1 has been fully achieved. For objective 2, six CBT groups (N=45), six CBT-PI (N=46), and six social activity groups (N=45) were run for 136 adolescents with five to ten participants per group. For the CBT group, the mean session attended is 5.43 sessions, and over 60% of participants completed more than six sessions. For the CBT-PI group, the mean session attended is 6.00 sessions, and over 69% of participants completed more than six sessions. For the social activity group, the mean session attended is 5.62 sessions, and around 60% of participants completed more than six sessions. Parents attended an average of four sessions out of the total five sessions. Five (CBT groups), four (CBT-PI groups), and nine (social activity groups) participants failed to return the questionnaire at post-test. Six (CBT groups), five (CBT-PI groups), and nine (social activity groups) participants failed to return the questionnaire during the six-month follow-up period. Data analysis was performed on the intention-to-treat principle. All the participants who have gone through the randomization have been included for the data analysis. A series of multilevel models (MLMs) with random intercepts and slopes were conducted using HLM 6.08 to examine the effectiveness of CBT and CBT-PI on various outcomes, including anxiety (i.e., Spence Child Anxiety Scale, SCAS), emotion regulation skills (i.e., Cognitive Emotion Regulation Questionnaire, CERQ), and self-esteem (i.e., Rosenberg Self-esteem Scale, RSES). MLM is useful in conducting ITT analyses, as it can accommodate missing data by including participants with data at only one time point in the analysis. The below findings indicate the short and longer term effects of the CBT and CBT-PI treatment model. First, the comparison between CBT, CBT-PI, and social activity group unfortunately yielded insignificant results. A further look at the simple effect test results found out that participants in CBT and CBT-PI conditions both reported significant improvement in six types of anxiety problems. CBT condition revealed significant decreases in all the negative emotion regulation strategies, and CBT-PI condition yielded a significant decrease in rumination. In contrast, no changes were found in the social activity condition regarding all the emotion regulation strategies, and slightly significant decreases were found on five subtypes of anxiety problems. But all the differences did not reach significant results. It is somewhat surprising that the effects of social activity on adolescent anxiety were comparable to CBT and CBT-PI. As we mentioned in our paper reporting the efficacy of the current study, several possible reasons for these unexpected findings are discussed. Specifically, participation in social activities is conducive to adolescents’ adjustment (Dumont & Provost, 1999). Moreover, social activities may generate social support, which in turn may mitigate adolescents’ anxiety symptoms (Compas, Slavin, Wagner, & Vannatta, 1986). Furthermore, as Hong Kong adolescents spend a large amount of time in school and on homework and have a packed daily schedule with extracurricular activities and supplementary tutoring (Sivan, Tam, Siu, & Stebbins, 2019), they may regard the social activity group as an opportunity to avoid academic stress. Future studies are suggested to examine the impact of social activities on Chinese adolescents’ anxiety symptoms. To conclude, we conducted a rigorous three-arm randomized controlled trial (RCT) to examine the efficacy of our CBT and CBT-PI treatment models against a social activity control condition. Results showed that social activity group produced comparable effects in reducing anxiety problems among adolescents with CBT and CBT-PI treatment but inferior efficacy in changing emotion regulation strategies among adolescents. We tried to explain the results and advocated for future research in exploring how social activity programme influence anxiety among adolescents and replicating such design in other settings. Objective 2 has been achieved. For objective 3, we compared CBT and CBT-PI conditions, MLM results found that significant Time × Contrast interaction effect on the SCAS physical injury fears score (γ=-.14, p=.042), suggesting that the CBT-PI condition showed a significantly greater reduction in the SCAS physical injury fears score compared with the CBT condition. Besides, three interaction effects were in the expected directions but not statistically significant (i.e., in a marginal significant range). In particular, CBT-PI condition showed a greater reduction in the SCAS generalized anxiety score γ=-.06, p = .073) compared with the CBT condition. Moreover, the CBT-PI condition exhibited greater increases in the RSES score (γ= .11, p = .088) and the CERQ refocus on planning score (γ= .16, p = .081) compared with the CBT condition. A further look at the data found that changes in negative emotions among parents significantly related to changes in social phobia (r=.41, p<.05) and self-esteem (r=.45, p<.05) among their children. On the other hand, improvement in one of the parenting stress index, social isolation, among parents significantly related to changes in self-esteem (r=.41, p<.05) and positive reappraisal (r=.43, p<.05) among their children. To conclude, by adopting statistical strategies, we have uncovered that CBT-PI was more effective in alleviating one dimension of anxiety than child-focused CBT. In addition, CBT-PI showed a promising trend in better improving emotion regulation strategies among Chinese adolescents. Also of note, the reductions in anxiety symptoms did not decelerate over time, suggesting that the treatment effects were sustainable. Objective 3 has been achieved.

17651016.label: Major findings and research outcome
17651016.value: Both academic and practical outputs have been generated from the project. First, we have attended two international conferences (listed in Part C.9) to introduce the research nature, significance and findings at different stages to a diverse group of audiences across the world, such as academics, scholars, students, mental health professionals etc. Second, we have published one journal article based on the data collected in the project and one journal article was submitted under the second review (listed in Part C.8). The first paper entitled “Cognitive-Behavior Therapy With and Without Parental Involvement for Anxious Chinese Adolescents: A Randomized Controlled Trial” evaluated the effectiveness of our culturally-attuned group CBT intervention for Chinese adolescents at risk for anxiety disorders in Hong Kong and the additive effects of parental involvement. This paper was the first attempt in its kind to examine culturally-attuned CBT intervention and the role of parental involvement in addressing adolescent anxiety. Remarkably, parental participation may provide improvement in treatment efficacy as findings suggested a significantly greater decrease in physical injury fears in the CBT-PI condition than in the CBT condition. Furthermore, the effectiveness on anxiety symptoms reduction was sustained over time. The preliminary findings on the positive parental influence on relieving adolescent anxiety suggested the benefit of including parental involvement to enhance the treatment effect of CBT in future intervention for Chinese children and adolescents. In the second paper entitled “The differential functions of cognitive emotion regulation strategies in Chinese adolescents with different levels of anxiety problems in Hong Kong”, investigated different effects of emotion regulation (ER) strategies on anxiety symptoms in two groups of Chinese adolescents with clinical and at-risk levels of anxiety. Multiple-group Structural Equation Modelling (SEM) analyses indicated that maladaptive ER strategies, including self-blame and rumination significantly predicted anxiety among the clinical group while adaptive ER strategy of reappraisal predicted anxiety among the at-risk group. The study provides insight on how differently ER strategies function in the etiology of psychopathology contingent on different levels of anxiety. The findings have practical implications for the local mental health services and intervention direction targeting Chinese adolescent anxiety. Third, we have finalized a culturally-adapted workbook to meet the needs of Chinese adolescents with anxiety problems for future utilization among social work practitioners. Coupled with the evidence from the data, we believe this workbook could be a handy guide to the local social service practitioners who work with adolescents with anxiety problems.

17651016.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17651016.value: There are several future research directions based on the present findings of the project. First, our research showed that involving parents in the treatment of anxiety produced better results among Chinese adolescents with anxiety problems in Hong Kong. However, this study only included Chinese adolescents with anxiety problems. Further research is needed to determine whether parental involvement may enhance the treatment effect of CBT for both Chinese children and adolescents with anxiety problems and anxiety disorders. In addition, this study did not assess parental factors (e.g., parenting strategies) across all the three conditions. Future studies may include parental factors in the assessment so that whether the superior efficacy of CBT-PI relative to traditional CBT is due to improvements in parental variables can be explored. Second, our findings on the differential impacts of emotion regulation on anxiety among adolescents with at-risk and clinical levels of anxiety disorders provided primary evidence that emotional state (i.e., anxiety levels) might influence the process of flexibly adopting ER strategies. Future studies are needed to further examine the functions of adaptive and maladaptive ER strategies contingent on different levels of anxiety, depression, or other negative emotions among both clinical and non-clinical populations.

17651016.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17651016.value: The study developed a culturally-attuned cognitive-behavioural model for Chinese adolescents with anxiety problems and provided evidence on the treatment effectiveness. It is a first study evaluated child-focused cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT) and CBT with parental involvement among Chinese adolescents. Self-reported data affirm that the treatment protocol could successfully improve anxiety symptoms and the effects were sustained through the six months follow up period. Parental involvement with CBT potentially have an additive small effect on alleviating physical injury fear. Furthermore, the study identified the differential effects of adaptive and maladaptive emotion regulation (ER) strategies on Chinese adolescents with different levels of anxiety. While maladaptive ER strategies, self-blame and rumination, significantly predicted anxiety among the clinical group, adaptive ER strategy of reappraisal predicted anxiety among the at-risk group. These findings provide insights to target specific ER strategies in designing interventions for people with clinical anxiety disorders and at-risk of developing anxiety problems. Besides, our results also highlight the potential to explore parental involvement in CBT anxiety treatment for Chinese adolescents.
