18603516.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18603516.value: Objectification is defined as being treated as an object that can be instrumentally manipulated. Despite the fact that prior studies have accumulated substantial knowledge about the impacts of objectification, what we currently know is still very limited. Whereas prior studies have mainly focused on sexual objectification (i.e., treating women as objects that satisfy men’s sexual desires), relatively little research has examined how non-sexual forms of objectification influence people’s psychosocial well-being. The present research aims to fill the research gap by testing whether non-sexual objectification increases aggressive behavior. Objectification is a process of subjugation. When people are objectified, they are treated as mere tools or instruments that aid others to achieve certain goals, and whose autonomy, needs, feelings, and opportunities are being denied. Therefore, objectified people should perceive a lack of control over their situation. Because people have a strong need to master their destiny and actualize their potential, people should be motivated to behave in ways that can restore the thwarted feelings of control following objectification. We propose that objectification should increase aggression because aggressive behavior can restore thwarted feelings of control as it symbolically asserts superiority and control over others. When objectified people’s thwarted feelings of control are restored through interventions, they should no longer behave aggressively. In addition, the present research will also explore the role of context in influencing the relationship between objectification and aggression. We propose that objectification should only increase aggressive behavior when the context of the objectification is detrimental to their well-being. Objectified people should not behave aggressively when the context of the objectification is beneficial. The present research will include a series of correlational and experimental studies which aim to examine when and why objectification increases aggression and how to weaken the relationship between objectification and aggressive behavior. Given the ubiquitous nature of objectification and aggression in daily social interactions, it is critical to understand how objectification can influence aggressive behavior. A deeper understanding of the mechanisms and contexts involved in triggering and weakening objectified people’s aggressive behavior can help further develop existing theories and design intervention strategies that enable people to better cope with the detrimental impacts of objectification. 物化是指被當作是可以利用的工具。雖然以往的研究對於被物化的影響積累了一定的認識，但是我們目前所知道的仍然十分有限。以往的研究主要集中探討性物化(即把女性當作是一件物品來滿足男性的性慾)對女姓的影響，相對較少的研究曾探討與性無關的物化會如何影響人們的身心福祉。本研究旨在探討被物化會否增加人們的攻擊行為。當人們被物化時，他們只是被當作是可以幫助別人實現某種目標的工具，但他們的自主性，需求，情感和機會往往會被剝奪。因此，被物化的人應該會感覺對自己的處境缺乏控制感。因為人們對於掌握自己的命運和實現自己的潛力有著強烈的需求，人們在被物化後應該會積極地通過不同的方法來恢復所失去的控制感。我們提出被物化會增加人們的攻擊行為是因為攻擊行為可以通過肯定自己的優越地位和控制他人而恢復被物化後所失去的控制感。當被物化後所失去的控制感被恢復時，被物化的人將不會將進行攻擊行為。此外，我們亦會探討被物化時的處境會否影響物化和攻擊行為之間的關係。我們預計只有在被物化時的處境對人們不利時，物化才會增加攻擊行為。當被物化時的處境會對人們有利時，物化並不會增加攻擊行為。我們將進行一系列的相關性和實驗性研究以探討被物化在什麼情況下會增加攻擊行為，和探討如何削弱被物化對攻擊行為的影響。鑒於物化和攻擊行為在日常生活中各個方面都無處不在，了解物化和攻擊行為之間的關係是一個非常重要的心理學課題。本研究的發現可望有助於推進現有理論和制定干預方案，使人們能夠更好地克服物化所帶來的負面影響。

18603516.label: Realisation of objectives
18603516.value: Realization of Objectives 1 and 2: The project team formulated an innovative theoretical model that advances current knowledge of objectification. This conceptual model provides a new theoretical framework that explicate why objectification increases aggression through thwarted sense of control. Adopting a multi-method approach, we conducted a series of studies to test whether objectification, a detrimental interpersonal experience, increases people’s tendencies to engage in aggressive behaviors. We also empirically examined whether thwarted sense of control mediates the effect of objectification on aggression, and whether other psychological processes may mediate the link between objectification and aggression. In particular, the results of our studies showed that participants who experienced objectification reported lower levels of sense of control and higher tendencies to behave aggressively than participants who did not experience objectification. In addition, thwarted sense of control significantly mediated the effect of objectification. We also empirically examined and ruled out an alternative explanation that changes in negative mood after the objectification experience can explain objectified people’s aggressive tendencies. Specifically, we found that negative mood could not mediate the effect of objectification on aggression and that thwarted sense of control still significantly mediated such an effect after controlling for the effect of negative mood. We also experimentally demonstrated that not all negative experiences would induce aggression. In particular, we found that participants who experienced objectification behaved more aggressively than participants who experienced misfortunes. Realization of Objective 3: Our new theoretical model also explains why restoring objectified people’s thwarted sense of control would reduce their aggressive tendencies. We empirically tested the effectiveness of a short intervention in weakening the effect of objectification on aggression. The result demonstrated that a short control-restoration exercise (i.e., offering objectified participants a chance to restore their thwarted sense of control) reduced objectified people’s aggressive tendencies. Realization of Objective 4: Our new theoretical model also highlights the significance of context in influencing the consequences of objectification and related forms of interpersonal maltreatment. In particular, we tested and found that the effects of objectification and related forms of interpersonal maltreatment are weakened if people perceive the context where the negative interpersonal experience occur as nondetrimental to themselves.

18603516.label: Major findings and research outcome
18603516.value: In the present research, we developed a new theoretical model to explicate why objectification increases aggression through thwarted sense of control and how a brief control-restoration exercise weakens the effect of objectification on aggression. A multi-method approach was adopted to empirically test the hypotheses that were directly derived from the theoretical model. The results of our studies showed that when compared with participants who did not experience objectification, participants who experienced objectification had higher levels of aggression, for example, reporting higher aggressive inclinations in hypothetical situations and assigning more painful and harmful treatments to others (Poon, Chen, Teng, & Wong, 2020; Poon & Jiang 2020). It is noteworthy that objectified people showed higher levels of both retaliatory aggression toward the perpetrators of objectification or provocateurs and even displaced aggression toward innocent strangers (Poon et al., 2020). Moreover, the current studies also showed that thwarted sense of control can mediate the effect of objectification on aggression, even after controlling for the effects of negative mood (Poon et al., 2020). Significantly, our results further demonstrated the effectiveness of a short control-restoration exercise in weakening people’s aggressive tendencies following objectification (Poon et al., 2020). More broadly, the current research revealed that the effect of objectification-related interpersonal maltreatments on antisocial tendencies can be moderated by both individual differences and contextual factors. For instance, our studies showed that people who perceived that their aggression has significant costs reported lower antisocial tendencies following interpersonal maltreatments (Poon & Wong, 2019). These findings were published in top-tier peer-refereed international journals in psychology, such as Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, Aggressive Behavior, and Psychology of Violence. They were also presented in international conferences, including the Association for Psychological Science (APS) Annual Convention and the Biannual World Meeting of the International Society for Research on Aggression (ISRA).

18603516.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18603516.value: The current research provided converging empirical evidence showing that objectification thwarts people’s sense of control, thereby increasing their tendencies to behave aggressively. In future studies, researchers may examine whether other psychological mechanisms can account for the effect of objectification on aggression. Moreover, the current research demonstrated that a short control-restoration exercise effective was effective in weakening objectified people’s aggressive tendencies. Future studies may examine whether it can also weaken other negative impacts of objectification and help people to cope with objectification adaptively. Lastly, the present research centered on the general form of objectification, yet it is noteworthy that objectification experiences lie in a spectrum of degrees, ranging from being mildly objectified by having personal needs neglected to being blatantly objectified by being manipulated as a tool to achieve certain purposes. Similarly, people can be objectified by different motives and reasons (e.g., role-prescribed, oblivious, or punitive motives). To get a fuller picture of the impacts of objectification, future studies may examine how various degrees and forms of objectification influences people’s aggression and other psychosocial outcomes.

18603516.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18603516.value: The current research demonstrated that objectification increases people’s aggressive tendencies through thwarted sense of control. Moreover, restoring objectified people’s sense of control can effectively reduce their tendencies to behave aggressively. Through showing when and why objectification increases aggression and how to weaken the effect, these new findings advance our existing knowledge of objectification. The current research also carries both theoretical and practical significance. Theoretically, it advances current theories of objectification and creates new avenues for future research to further examine various consequences of objectification and identify the corresponding psychological mechanisms. Practically, it provides insights for practitioners to design theory-driven intervention programs to combat objectification and related forms of interpersonal maltreatment.

18603716.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18603716.value: In the ITE4 document (2014), the fourth strategy on information technology in education proposed a new ‘e-learning policy’ to unleash the learning power of students. In the field of music education, the use of ICT in music composition has been studied since 2000. From the framework of Webster's (2003) model of creative thinking, the connection between music composition and creativity has been established. In 2013, Webster claimed that musical intelligence that involves composition is intimately connected to the model of creative thinking in music. He suggests two reasons why compositional thinking by students is vitally important. One is to increase musical intelligence and the other is to increase the likelihood of creative achievement. The definition of music composition intelligence is that students have a natural capacity for thinking in sound for compositional purposes and this capacity is not just a talent for ‘gifted’ individuals but a natural part of what might be considered musical intelligence that is present to some extent in all. However, no empirical study has been conducted to support music composition intelligence. To extend my doctoral study, the research objective is to examine how secondary students demonstrate their innate abilities in using computers to compose by observing their compositional approaches under the musical intelligence (MI) of Gardner’s framework (2006) and compositional thinking within Webster’s model of creative thinking (2003) in order to validate their compositional intelligence. To further investigate the compositional intelligence in secondary students aged from 12 (F.1) to 15 (F.4) during their computer-assisted compositional process at a band one secondary school, this empirical research is a one-year study to capture their compositional process through collecting quantitative data (file analysis) and qualitative data (reflective journals, focus group interviews and video observations). A songwriting project for F.1 students and a classical composition project for F.4 students will be taught. The ICT music curriculum will be framed into 12 weeks with a prescriptive task in the first semester and a free task in the second semester. Digital composition files and reflective journals are collected each week. During the digital file analysis, different compositional approaches in popular and classical music are observed. From the reflective journal, different stages of students’ compositional behaviours are mapped under the framework of Webster (2003). Therefore, students’ compositional approaches and compositional thinking are revealed, from popular music to classical music, and open-end to closed-end tasks, in a proposed model of music composition intelligence. 研究計劃簡介 A) 闡述研究計劃的目的 1. 確認作曲智能的存在，該智能是革拿(Gardner) 所提出的音樂智能架構中的一環。 2. 透過觀察學生運用不同音樂智能 － 音高、節奏、音色及曲式，在電腦的輔助下創作的流行音樂和古典音樂，研究中學生不同的作曲方法。 3. 透過觀察學生的作曲思維如何體現韋伯斯特(Webster)於二零零年提出的四項創作重要階段：一) 預備；二）時間；三）實現；四）確定。 研究方法 A) 參與人數 - 六十位選擇ICT in music課堂的學生。 B) 說明工作及步驟 - 這是一個以個案形式進行的研究，數據將會透過四項渠道收集：雲端系統、學生自我紀錄、小組討論、錄影。 - 參與的時間： 每星期六十分鐘的課堂。 - 所需時間：一個學年 - 是次研究將為準老師和在職老師提供寶貴的資料，以便將來用ICT來編寫有關課程。 - 是次所搜集數據將有助全港所有中學，於將來發展學生作曲智能。

To examine the translation market in East Asia from the historical, economic and social perspectives in order to have a clear and current context for analyzing translator professionalism perceived by translators and clients. 18604416.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18604416.value: In recent years, there has been a growing interest in studying translator status empirically in Translation Studies. However, the topic is relatively under-researched in East Asia. More empirical work is necessary in the region, to give a fuller picture of translators, who are important mediators during the translation process. The objective of this research project is to empirically investigate how non-literary translation practitioners and translation clients perceive translator professionalism, which is understood as not only involving knowledge and expertise but also the virtues of trustworthiness and altruism. The regions in East Asia to be studied are China, Hong Kong, Macau, Japan, Korea and Taiwan. A two-phase mixed-methods approach, combining both quantitative and qualitative methods, will be employed in order to gain a thorough understanding of the topic. For this project, “translators” include people who do translation and/or interpreting as part of their job and are paid accordingly, full-time, part-time, or by project. It does not include interpreters who only handle oral renditions of spoken discourse from one language into another. In addition, it does not include those who translate for free or treat translation as a kind of hobby. This project not only aims to understand practitioners’ perceptions but also those held by translation clients because the viewpoints of the latter are seldom researched in Translation Studies. This is true even though translators consider clients as king, and clients’ satisfaction is paramount. Little about clients’ opinions of translator professionalism is known in Translation Studies. More precisely, the research questions for this project are: How do non-literary translation practitioners in East Asia perceive their professionalism? Does the background of the practitioner affect the person’s perception? For example, is there any relationship between gender, level of education, age, years of translation experience, mode of working (full-time, part-time, freelance, in-house), materials rendered (financial, media, technical, marketing etc.) and translator professionalism? How do translation clients perceive the professionalism of non-literary translators in the region? In addition, are there any differences in the perception of translator professionalism among translators in different East Asian regions? And, are there any differences in the perception of the topic between translators and clients? If so, why do such differences exist? What implication do these similarities and differences have? 近年，翻譯學以實證研究方法探討譯者地位的關注日益增多，不過，這種研究於東亞地區較為不足。本研究計劃分為兩階段，以實證研究方法 (結合量性和質性) 調查東亞地區 (包括中國、香港、台灣、澳門、日本和韓國) 的非文學翻譯工作者和翻譯委託人，如何理解譯者的專業。本研究的「譯者」指以筆譯 (或兼口譯) 為工作，全職、兼職或按項目受薪的人，而不包括純粹以口譯為工作的傳譯人員，也不包括那些作免費翻譯，或把翻譯當作興趣的人。翻譯學甚少研究委托人的意見，雖然譯者視委托人為尊，盡力滿足他們的要求，但學界有關委托人對譯者專業的研究郤十分匱乏，而且中國翻譯學一直以來較著重文學文本及文學譯者，對非文學譯者的研究不足，所以是次計劃不僅會了解非文學譯者的看法，還會研究委托人的意見。 更準確地說，本計劃探討以下問題：東亞地區的非文學翻譯工作者如何理解其專業？譯者的背景有否影響其對譯者專業的看法？例如譯者的性別、教育程度、年齡、翻譯年資、工作模式（全職、兼職）、翻譯題材（財務、媒體、科技、市場學等）和譯者的專業有沒有關係？翻譯委托人怎樣理解非文學譯者的專業？此外，東亞地區的譯者對於譯者專業有沒有不同的看法？還有，譯者和委托人的看法又有沒有任何不同？如有，為何會出現這些差異？此等相似與差異又有何含意？

18604416.label: Realisation of objectives
18604416.value: This two-year project (January 2017 to December 2018) empirically investigated the way non-literary translators and clients in East Asia perceive translator professionalism. The project used a two-phase mix-methods approach, the first, a quantitative phase and the second, a qualitative, phase. Some of the findings were published in two academic journals (Liu 2019a, 2019b) and disseminated in one research seminar and two academic conferences. In addition, a paper comparing the similarities and differences in translator professionalism for translators and clients was originally accepted for presentation in the “Translation Studies in East Asia: Tradition, Transition and Transcendence” conference in Hong Kong in December 2019. However, the conference was cancelled because of the social situation in the city. As of this writing (November 29, 2019), I am looking for another venue to present the findings and publish the paper. Also, I am currently finishing two papers which will be submitted to journals for review in early 2020. Furthermore, this completed GRF project motivated me to develop a new GRF proposal which has recently been submitted to Research Grants Council for review. Objective 1: To review the existing Translation Studies literature related to translator status, the role of translators, translator professionalization and translator professionalism. Objective 2: To examine the translation market in East Asia from historical, economic and social perspectives, in order to have a clear and current context for analysing translator professionalism perceived by translators and clients. To address these two objectives, traditional concepts of translators’ role and status in society were reviewed. Then, an overview of seminal empirical studies dealing with the mentioned topics was carried out. The focus was on the empirical studies, because this project employed this method to carry out an investigation. In Translation Studies (TS), subservience and invisibility have been traditionally used to describe the role and status of translators in the workplace and society. Some TS some scholars (for example, Angelelli 2001, 2004; Dam and Korning Zethsen 2008, 2009, 2010, 2011, 2012; Katan 2009; Sela-Sheffy 2008, 2011, 2014; Wolf 2006) used empirical methods to carry out investigations. As most of the empirical studies were done for Western countries, they provide me with important data because I can further compare my results with the results of those studies. This is the sixth objective of this project. The concept of translator professionalism was thoroughly reviewed, as it is the central theme of this project. Traditionally, TS literature associated translator professionalism with a person’s capacity to produce acceptable target texts (Jiménez-Crespo 2017). However, the past two decades have witnessed a change wherein translation is increasingly viewed as a social practice (Kafi et al., 2018; Wolf 2010). Translator professionalism is not simply limited to the person’s capacity to produce acceptable target texts. Rather, it is a multidimensional term that also covers the translator’s professional status (Sirén & Hakkarainen 2002), the behaviour of the translator at and outside work (Cragie et al. 2016; Kiraly 2014; Kościałkowska-Okońska 2012), the translator’s adherence to ethical practice principles, professional identity and pride (Robinson 1997). The first two objectives have been achieved. I shared the findings in a research seminar at the Hong Kong Education University on April 28, 2017. I also included the literature review and relevant discussion in two papers (Liu 2019a, 2019b). Objective 3: To develop a construct for measuring translator professionalism perceived by practitioners and clients. This study adapted the framework proposed by Carter et al. (2015) to develop a translator professionalism construct covering six dimensions: professional identity, professional status, pride in the profession, translators’ adherence to ethical practice principles, translators’ proactive behaviour at work and translators’ behaviour outside work. I shared the way I developed the construct in the Asian Conference on Asian Studies in Japan on June 2, 2018. I also explained in detail the development of the construct in two papers (Liu 2019a, 2019b). Objective 4: To empirically examine the way non-literary translation practitioners in East Asia perceive their professionalism. The perspectives held by practitioners in different East Asian regions will be compared. Objective 5: To analyse and compare similarities and differences in translator professionalism for translators and for clients. These two objectives were handled together via a two-phased mixed-methods approach. The first, quantitative, phase: Guided by the translator professionalism construct, two sets of questionnaires, one for translators and another for clients, were prepared. From May 2016 to June 2018, 425 completed questionnaires from translators were returned. Also, 72 clients returned their questionnaires from July 2016 to July 2018. The majority of the clients were fairly experienced in hiring translators. In the questionnaire, clients were asked how many translators they hired the previous year. The data show that, on average, they hired 24 freelance, 17 full-time and 5 part-time translators. This study targeted collecting data from East Asian translators and clients. However, translators and clients from other Asian countries also sent in their questionnaires and shared their valuable comments, because snowball techniques were used for data collection. As a result, the majority of participants were from East Asia (80%) and about 20% were from other Asian countries. This geographical distribution of participants (from ten Asian countries/cities but mainly East Asia), unexpectedly, allows me to make in-depth comparisons of participants in different Asian countries. The analysis of translators’ perception was reported in detail in Perspectives: Studies in Translation Theory and Practice (Liu 2019a). I also shared some findings in the “Asian Conference on Asian Studies” on June 2, 2018, and in the “Asian Conference on Media, Communication & Film” on October 10, 2018. Besides, the analysis of clients’ perceptions was published in International Journal of Translation, Interpretation, and Applied Linguistics (Liu 2019b). The second, qualitative, phase: I started inviting translators and clients who completed the questionnaire to participate in my interviews in May, 2018, via email. Even after the completion period of this project (Dec 2018), replies were received from translators and clients saying that they were willing to take part in interviews. As a result, interviews continued to be done until October 2019. Over 70 translators and about 20 clients were interviewed. I am currently writing two papers to report on the qualitative findings. They should be finished in early 2020 and will be submitted to international TS journals for review. Comparison between translators and clients The similarities and the differences in translator professionalism for translators and for clients were compared. I planned to present the findings in the “Translation Studies in East Asia: Tradition, Transition and Transcendence” conference in Hong Kong in December 2019, and submit the full paper to the conference organizers for consideration for publication in Translation Quarterly 2020/21. My abstract had been accepted for presentation, but the conference was cancelled due to the social situation in Hong Kong. At the time of writing (Nov 29, 2019), I am looking for another venue to present my findings and submit my paper for publication. Objective 6. To compare the findings obtained from the project and related empirical studies conducted by other TS scholars. My literature review located seminal empirical studies examining the status and role of translators in Western countries. Comparison of the findings obtained from the present project and those from related empirical studies was reported in Liu 2019a, 2019b and the two papers that I am writing.

18604416.label: Major findings and research outcome
18604416.value: The findings this GRF project suggest that translators in the region have positive associations with their identity although they tend to perceive having a middling status. A close comparison of the perspectives of translator professionalism held by practitioners in the ten Asian countries/ cities found that translators have similar viewpoints on professional identity, their behaviour outside work and pride in the profession. However, there are statistically significant variances in their perceptions of professional status, adherence to ethical practice principles, and proactive behaviour at work. To seek an explanation, the quantitative data have been complemented by qualitative data for analysis. It was found that the differences were due to cultural factors, because the qualitative data suggest that translators in bilingual or multilingual cities perceive having a lower professional status than translators in other Asian countries do. It was found that Asian clients have slightly divergent views on whether translation is a profession although they perceive that the translation occupation is vital to society and recognize that translators have a high degree of expertise and knowledge. In addition, the Asian clients, no matter where they live, lay emphasis on translators’ adherence to ethical practice principles. Although the clients attach importance to translators’ proactive behaviour at work, such as reliability, they have different viewpoints on translators’ behaviour outside work. Also, the clients point out that the lack of a certification system affects the professional image of translators and the healthy development of the field. The problem has become particularly serious in the digital era, because it is not easy for clients to verify a translator’s curriculum vitae and assess his or her skills. Clients may have to undergo processes of trial and error to identify suitable candidates to handle their assignments. One important finding from comparing the viewpoints between translators and clients is that the two parties have similar attitudes towards translators’ adherence to ethical practice principles in the workplace, as no statistically significant difference was found. However, both parties view translators’ behaviour outside work differently in a statistically significant way. Translators attach greater importance to practitioners’ professional manner outside work and their behaviour in online communities than clients do. These findings are important because translators’ behaviour outside work has seldom been empirically examined in TS. However, this topic has become increasingly important in the digital world, because online communities, such as Facebook and Instagram, may introduce complex transference issues in the translator-client relationship.

18604416.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18604416.value: This completed GRF project offered me a valuable opportunity to directly communicate with translators and clients to share their insights. One important topic that they discussed with me is the way translator professionalism should be maintained in this digital era. They said that online translator-client social networking sites (SNSs) such as Proz.com have become pervasive in the professional lives of translators and clients. However, these online communities posit new challenges to the industry. Some translators noted that, in reality, their status can be certified by traditional signals such as academic qualifications. However, in SNSs, they find it difficult to signal their status or have no idea how to do so. Also, some clients said that they underwent processes of trial and error to identity suitable candidates, because it is not easy for them to access a translator’s suitability and professionalism in online communities. Both parties even worry that this may lead to a possible de-professionalization of the field. This project did not examine translator status signalling mechanisms and online communities, but this is an important topic for future research. Therefore, in November 2019, I submitted to RGC a new GRF proposal which specifically investigates translator status signalling mechanisms in SNSs.

18604416.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18604416.value: Professionalism is a much-discussed topic in various ﬁelds, such as legal, medical and teaching, but has not been a central theme in Translation Studies. Although the past decade has witnessed a growing interest in studying translators in the workplace via an empirical lens, the topic is relatively under-researched in Asia. More empirical work is necessary to give a fuller picture of translators, who have gone through a ‘long march from slavery to professionalism’ (Pym 2010: 160) to become mediators in society. This GRF project empirically examines how non-literary translators and clients in East Asia perceive translator professionalism. A two-phase mixed-methods approach, combining both quantitative and qualitative methods, was employed to gain a thorough understanding of the topic. This project not only aims to understand practitioners’ perceptions but also those held by translation clients because the viewpoints of the latter are seldom researched in TS. This is true even though translators consider clients as king, and clients’ satisfaction is paramount. Little about clients’ opinions of translator professionalism is known. The data and analyses are valuable because relevant associations and stakeholders can benefit from the findings. This project contributes to the understanding of translators as mediators and their professionalism in Asia.

18608816.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18608816.value: Student revision of their drafts is recognized as an important strategy to support the development of their writing skills. It involves a complex process of evaluating text, diagnosing problems and making changes to improve the text. Early research found that novice and experienced writers make different kinds of changes in the course of revision, and indicated that success in revision could be influenced by the effectiveness of the feedback received. More recent studies in English as a Second Language (ESL) writing have been overwhelmingly concerned with written corrective feedback (also known as grammar correction) and its effectiveness in improving the accuracy of student writing. However, there have been surprisingly few studies exploring what features of teacher written feedback influence student revisions. In most studies that investigated the impact of teacher feedback on student revisions, only a very limited number of ESL students at a single university in a English-speaking country were involved. Arguably, the small size of samples and the specific settings limit not only the generalization of research findings to other student populations, but also their applicability to practice in real educational settings. To address the limitations of previous research, this project will adapt the existing frameworks to support fine-grained categorization of student revisions and teacher feedback. Based on the adapted frameworks and Natural Language Processing (NLP) methods, the project aims to design and implement an automatic classification system for identifying the types of student revisions and teacher feedback as well as detecting the connections between them. Additionally, the impact of the system on the teaching and learning process of writing will be investigated. This project is a collaboration between information technology (IT) and ESL researchers from four higher education institutions in Hong Kong and Taiwan, which builds a strong research partnership in the Chinese communities working towards the project's objectives. The project opens up opportunities for students to be promptly informed about their uses of different revision types and the links of their revisions with teacher feedback, adding a new layer of feedback to allow students to review their writing strategies. It also provides an efficient way for teachers to identify those students who have problems in revising their drafts and are in need of early assistance. Equally importantly, the project proposes a promising approach for researchers on revision and feedback to systematically analyze data collected from a large sample of students and teachers. 草稿的修訂被視為發展學生寫作技巧的一項重要策略，當中涉及評估內容、找出錯處並作出相應的修改，以改善寫作的質素。早期的研究發現缺乏經驗的和資深的作家在草稿的修訂過程中會作出不同類型的修改，而成功的修訂往往是受著回饋訊息的有效性所影響。近年，有關英語作為第二語言（ESL）寫作的研究主要是關心寫作糾正性回饋（亦被稱為文法改正）及其對改善學生寫作精準度的有效性，僅有少量的研究著重於探討具備什麼特質的教師回饋才能夠影響學生草稿的修訂。在大部份探討教師回饋對學生修訂影響的研究中，參與者均為極少數來自英語國家同一所大學的ESL學生。由於這些研究的參與人數較少，且在特定的設置下進行，因此不單未能把研究的結果普及至其他的學生族群，同時亦限制了其在真實教學環境中的應用性。 為了解決先前研究的限制，本研究將調整現有的分類架構以支援學生草稿及教師回饋的細緻化分類。透過利用經調整後的分類架構及自然語言處理技術，本研究旨在設計及開發一個自動化分類系統，把學生草稿及教師回饋加以分類，並檢測它們之間的關係。此外，本研究亦會探討該系統對寫作教與學過程之影響。本研究團隊是由來自香港及台灣四所高等院校從事資訊科技及ESL研究的學者所組成，成員間能建立起緊密的研究夥伴關係，以達致研究的目標。本研究為學生提供了機會，讓他們能即時知道自己使用了什麼類型的草稿修訂，並了解此等修訂類型與教師回饋類型之間的連繫，從而協助他們檢視自己的寫作策略。另外，本研究為教師提供了一個有效率的途徑，讓他們能及早發現學生在草稿修訂時所遇到的困難，藉此提供適當的協助。最後，本研究能為對修訂及回饋方面有興趣的研究人員展示一個可行方案，讓他們能有系統地分析來自大量學生及教師的數據。

18608816.label: Realisation of objectives
18608816.value: The project has satisfactorily fulfilled the four stated objectives, as explained below: Objective 1. To develop an automatic classification system for identifying the categories of student revisions and teacher feedback as well as detecting the connections between them. This objective was successfully achieved by drawing on the literature on feedback and revision to propose fine-grained classification frameworks for teacher feedback and student revision. To characterize the ways that teachers frame their feedback, a classification framework was initially proposed to include six categories including: praise (T1), criticism (T2), imperative (T3), advice (T4), closed question (T5), and open question (T6). Since the six categories emphasises on the feedback mode but they are of little concern to text-specific features, four more categories were added to the framework, including content (T7), language (T8), organisation (T9), and referencing and formatting (T10). On a similar note, a classification framework was designed to distinguish various categories of revision in terms of both syntactic and semantic features. In this classification framework, eight categories of revision were identified. They include lexical choice (R1), grammar and mechanics (R2), organisation (R3), referencing and formatting (R4), claim (R5), evidence and details (R6), reasoning (R7), and analysis (R8). A corpus of 530 data entries were collected from English as Foreign Language (EFL) undergraduate students in three different universities during the project period. Every data entry consists of a draft essay with teacher feedback and a final essay of a student. The entry was manually and independently annotated by two researchers. The researchers were trained to perform the manual annotation with reference to the classification frameworks for feedback and revision. The training was followed by discussions about non-trivial cases to reach a consensus on the annotation standard. The basic unit of annotation was either a single sentence or an aggregate of consecutive sentences indicating the emergence of a particular category. Each unit of annotation could be labelled as one or more categories depending on its properties. A set of syntactic rules and a bag of semantic keywords were then extracted to represent the feature space of each category based on Latent Semantic Analysis. A web-based system (http://gp.ied.edu.hk:8080) was designed and developed to classify teacher feedback and student revision into different categories and to detect the connections between them. The system was driven by the corpus-based computerised model and implemented using Python, Ajax, D3.js, Django Web Framework and Natural Language Toolkit (NLTK). In addition to the provision of classification and tracking functions, the system serves as a platform to showcase the project and its outcomes to the public. For example, the system offers a detailed description of the classification frameworks, a video demonstration of how the automatic classification system works, as well as a list of publications produced from this project. Objective 2. To evaluate the agreement of the classification results between the system and human assessors. This objective was successfully achieved by measuring the accuracy of the automatic classification system. Accuracy refers to the percentage of the automatic classifications that agree with the manually annotated results in the data set. It could be illustrated by confusion matrices. Furthermore, Cohen’s kappa coefficients (K) were computed to evaluate the accuracy of the system while taking the possibility of chance agreement into account. Our results show that the classification accuracy of teacher feedback ranges between 96% and 98% (T1: 97%; T2: 96%; T3: 98%; T4: 97%; T5: 98%; T6: 97%; T7: 98%; T8: 96%; T9: 98%; T10: 98%), while the classification accuracy of student revision ranges between 82% to 98% (R1: 96%; R2: 94%; R3: 92%; R4: 97%; R5: 90%; R6: 96%; R7: 86%; R8: 83%). They also show that all K values (0.86 – 0.96) are within the range of near perfect agreement (0.81 – 1.00), indicating that the results of machine classiﬁcation are closely comparable to those of human classification. Objective 3. To examine the impact of the system on the quality of students’ final drafts. This objective was successfully achieved by investigating whether the use of automatic classification system can improve the quality of students’ final drafts. Specifically, this research question was addressed by comparing the scores on the final essay prepared by the students who were given access to the automatic classification system (i.e. the experimental group) and those who were not (i.e. the control group). A research procedure was undertaken in a 13-week, credit-bearing English course entitled Advanced English for University Studies (AEUS) offered by a Hong Kong university. Two classes (with 36 students) were assigned to the experimental group and two other classes (with 32 students) were assigned to the control group by convenience sampling. All participants in the experimental and control groups studied the same content, received the same instructions and followed the same assessment requirements. There was initially no significant difference between the experimental and control groups in the assessment results of the draft essay. The experimental group was then given individual login accounts to access and use the automatic classification system, while the control group was not. Our results indicate that both the experimental and control groups showed improvement in the writing performance of the final essay. However, the experimental group outperformed the control group in the aspects of content, organisation and language. The overall results suggest that the automatic classification system is effective in improving student writing, but the effectiveness may to a certain extent be influenced by the quantity and quality of teacher feedback. Objective 4. To explore the views of students and teachers on the role of the system in teaching and learning process of writing. This objective was successfully achieved by gathering and analysing questionnaire and interview data. An online questionnaire was designed to solicit students’ views towards using the automatic classification system to support their essay writing. The questionnaire consists of four self-report items. To cross-validate the questionnaire results and to elicit further views on the effectiveness of the automatic classification system, a purposeful sample of students and teachers were invited to attend focus group interviews. The online questionnaire was administered to 212 participants who had tried the automatic classification system during the project period. A total of 157 completed questionnaires were returned, yielding a response rate of 74%. Furthermore, four focus group interview sessions were arranged. Sixteen participants were selected to share their views and experiences towards the use of the automatic classification system during the interview sessions. According to the interview results, most interviewees found it helpful in using the automatic classification system to identify the gaps between their revisions and the changes the teacher wants to see. Given these gaps, the interviewees reported that they were engaged in a reﬂective process to review the feedback received again and trigger more eﬀective revisions before the submission of their ﬁnal essays. From the questionnaire results, it is found that most respondents were satisﬁed with the helpfulness of the analysis generated by the automated classification system. The highest level of agreement was seen with the classiﬁcation of teacher feedback and student revision. This was followed by the mapping between feedback and revision, and then by the percentage of feedback and revision types.

18608816.label: Major findings and research outcome
18608816.value: The research has successfully yielded the following findings and outcome: (I) Frameworks for classifying teacher feedback and student revision in EFL writing A fine-grained framework was designed to classify teacher feedback in terms of feedback modes and text-specific features. Ten types of feedback were identified, including praise, criticism, imperative, advice, closed question, open question, content, language, organisation, as well as referencing and formatting. In the same vein, another framework was designed to classify student revision in terms of surface and text-based revisions. Eight types of revision were identified, including lexical choice, grammar and mechanics, organisation, referencing and formatting, claim, evidence and details, reasoning, as well as analysis. (II) An online classification system for automatic tracking of student responses to teacher feedback in draft revision Based on the classification frameworks and Latent Semantic Analysis, an online system was developed at http://gp.ied.edu.hk:8080 to automatically classify teacher feedback and student revision. The system can also track whether revisions are made in response to teacher feedback. According to our results, a high classification accuracy (ranging from 82% to 98%) could be achieved by the system. (III) Impact of the automatic classification system on the quality of student essays Our results indicate that the automatic classification system could enhance the overall quality of students’ final essays, especially in the aspects of content, organisation and language. It is also found that teacher feedback in the mode of open question was strongly associated with text-based revisions. Open question could even be more effective than criticism and imperative in promoting changes to meaning. Our findings add further weight to the argument in favour of teacher feedback in question form. (IV) Students’ and teachers’ views on the role of the automatic classification system The questionnaire and interview data suggest that the automatic classification system could bring benefits to students by encouraging critical reflection on the gap between their actual and desired revisions. Furthermore, the system could help teachers reflect on and refine their feedback practices. (V) Publications, scholarly activities and awards The results of this research project were presented in five international conferences (ICERI2017, ICCE2017, IConEGS2018, ISTEL2018, LICE2018) and one keynote presentation in ABID2019. Two peer-reviewed journal papers have been published by Interactive Learning Environments and International Journal of Information and Education Technology, respectively. Besides, the project has received the following awards: Silver Medal (SVIIF 2019), Best Extended Abstract (LICE 2018) and Excellent Presentation Award (ICERI 2017).

18608816.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18608816.value: As the intended purpose of the automated classification system was to track whether students revise their drafts in response to the teacher feedback received but not to add extra feedback to what teachers already provide, the effectiveness of the system relative to enhancing student writing may be limited by the quantity and quality of teacher feedback. Going forward, further research would be conducted to explore the feasibility of adding new functions to the system, such as offering students suggestions and links to relevant learning resources on how to revise their text. In addition, this project was primarily designed to focus on the effects of teacher feedback on student revision. Due to its increasing prevalence in language learning, peer feedback (also known as peer review or peer response) is another possible source of feedback that would also be investigated in future research. Furthermore, a study into the effects of a standalone approach (either teacher feedback or peer feedback only) and a hybrid feedback approach (comprising both teacher feedback and peer feedback) on student revision is worthy of consideration in EFL writing.

18608816.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18608816.value: The research project has two major implications for researchers and practitioners in English as Foreign Language (EFL) writing. First, the project contributes to the development of an automatic approach for classifying teacher feedback and student revision and tracking the connections between them. Not only can this approach support students in identifying the gaps between what the teacher feedback suggests and their actual revisions, it can also play a beneficial role in encouraging students to reflect on the gaps for further revision and improvement. The approach can additionally be used to support teachers in understanding their feedback practices. Teachers can compare their own feedback practice with other teachers to ensure consistency across multiple teachers in a large course. Second, the project adds evidence to the literature highlighting the effectiveness of question-type comments in encouraging text-based revisions when compared with other comments such as criticism and imperative. This finding can help teachers gain insights into which feedback types are more likely to be appropriate for students in the revision process of EFL writing.

18613716.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18613716.value: When humans are enlisted to judge competency in many fields, for example academic examinations, psychological assessments, selecting personnel, singing competitions, and peer assessment in classroom, rating errors are inevitable and can have serious consequences. Rater errors include degrees of severity/leniency, inconsistency, centrality/extremity, similarity and the so-called halo effect. Severity/leniency is referred to as the tendency to assign predominantly lower/higher scores than the ratees should receive. Inconsistency occurs when a rater exhibits more random variability than expected. Centrality/extremity is the tendency to overuse middle/extreme scores. Similarity is the tendency to gravitate towards ratees who are similar to themselves. Halo is the tendency to overgeneralize based on only one or a few aspects of a ratee’s performance. It is important to take rater errors into account so the resulting scores are free from rater errors and thus fair and valid. Item response theory (IRT) and Rasch measurement has contributed significantly to the assessment of rater errors. There are two frameworks of IRT models, each representing a distinct philosophy about raters: the framework of facets models and the framework of hierarchical rater models (HRM). Each has its supporters, although the former is more commonly used. Historically, rater errors of severity and inconsistency are the two major foci; leaving centrality and similarity almost untouched. Given they are common in rater data, failing to consider such errors makes test scores unfair and subsequent decisions erroneous (e.g., college admission). This project aims to overcome this by inventing new IRT models in both frameworks that consider not only severity and inconsistency but also centrality and similarity. It will involve simulation and empirical studies to evaluate the new models and demonstrate their applications. Computer source codes and examples will be made available to researchers and practitioners. Pilot studies will be conducted to extend the new models and create new research lines for future studies. The project will make theoretical and practical contributions to the assessment of rater errors. Theoretically, new IRT models will be developed to fix the deficits, which in turn will generate new research lines. Practically, test scores will become fairer when the major rater errors are considered and fairer scores will lead to fairer and better decisions. 在許多領域，譬如能力測試、心理測評、人事甄選、歌唱比賽、課堂中的同儕互評等，常常需要評分員進行評分。在給分數時，評分者的錯誤是難以避免的，並且可能產生嚴重的後果。評分者錯誤包括評分過於寬鬆或嚴苛，評分標準不一致，趨中或極端評分，評分過於相似，以及所謂的月暈效應。評分過於寬鬆或嚴苛指的是評分者持續地給予高於或低於考生應得的分數。評分標準不一致指的是評分者在給分時，表現出過高的隨機性。趨中或極端評分指的是評分者過多地使用中間或極端的分數。評分的相似性指的是評分者傾向於對跟他們相似的被評者，給予高分。月暈效應指的是過於誇大被評者的某些方面表現，而對他的其他表現也給予過高的分數。偵測評分者錯誤可以使評分更公平和有效，其重要性不言而喻。 試題反應理論在檢測評分者錯誤方面貢獻良多。目前存在兩種分別代表不同哲學理念的理論模式框架：多相模式和階層評分者模式。這兩種模式各有支持者，但多相模式更為廣泛使用。過去的研究主要集中於探討評分者嚴苛度和評分不一致，而甚少探討趨中或極端評分及相似評分。事實上，這些錯誤在評分者中都是很常見的。如果不予考慮，考生就可能得到不公正的分數，從而產生錯誤的決定（例如大學錄取）。 本研究計劃旨在通過發展兩種理論框架下的新試題反應理論模式，以克服目前的研究不足。新模式不單考慮評分者嚴苛度和評分不一致，同時還考慮趨中或極端評分及相似評分。本研究利用模擬和實證研究以評估新模式，並為使用者提供自由下載的電腦程式和實例，同時也為未來研究進行先導性探索。 本研究將為檢測評分者錯誤作出理論及實務貢獻。就理論而言，新模式將彌補過去研究的不足，並創造新的研究方向。就實務而言，當評分者的主要錯誤都予以考慮之後，考生分數將變得更公平，從而導致更公平和更好的決策。

18613716.label: Realisation of objectives
18613716.value: To achieve Objective 1, we have successfully developed new rater error IRT models within the facets and the hierarchical rater model (HRM) frameworks. The new models feature more general statistical formulations, more flexible use for practical testing, and more accurate and fairer results. Specifically, we: (1) Created a New IRT Model for Centrality in a Facets Model Framework Our team has successfully developed new IRT models in a facets model, in which both raters’ severity and centrality are considered simultaneously, by adding a weight parameter for each rater to the item threshold of the standard Rasch facets model. The parameter of the new models can be estimated with the customized JAGS freeware. Our studies showed that if rater centrality exists but is ignored, the parameter estimates will be biased. (2) Incorporated Rater Centrality into an HRM Our team has developed a class of IRT models that account for various rater errors in the HRM framework. By incorporating specific parameters into the traditional latent class HRM, the new models can handle raters’ severity, inconsistency, and centrality simultaneously. The new model can be estimated using the customized JAGS freeware. The new model estimates with greater accuracy: the item difficulties, student abilities, raters’ errors (including their severities, inconsistency and centrality) and test reliability. (3) Created New IRT Models for Rater Effects in Examinee-Selected Items (ESI) Some high-stake tests (e.g., Hong Kong Diploma of Secondary Education Examination) employ ESI items which require examinees to select and answer a fixed number of items from a given list of items (e.g., select one of three possible items). Usually, ESI items are constructed-response items that human raters evaluate. Therefore, rater errors are inevitable and yield unfair scores. Our team developed new IRT models that account for rater errors in the ESI items to yield unbiased estimates. Moreover, we developed two estimation methods, namely, conditional maximum likelihood estimation and pairwise estimation method, to estimate the new model. To achieve Objective 2, we have conducted comprehensive simulation studies to examine the parameter recovery, model-data fit of the new models, and the consequences of ignoring rater errors. For example, in simulation studies for the new HRM of rater errors, we have manipulated the variables of number of items, number of latent classes, degree of centrality/extremity, and linking design. As these variables arise from practical testing situations, they are critical for simulation studies. We investigated parameter estimation bias, the accuracy of test reliability, and the selection of correct models under different conditions. The results revealed good parameter recovery for the new model. Ignoring centrality yielded poor item and person parameter estimates, and underestimated test reliability. The deviance information criterion (DIC) is useful for comparing how well different models fit the data. The simulation studies provide much needed guidelines to practitioners to create efficient and successful rating designs. Because of the novel natures of the new models, our team has developed Bayesian estimation with Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method for the estimation of the new models. We tested the free program, which is now available for public use. To achieve Objective 3, we applied the new models to empirical data to illustrate the implications and possible applications. In the study, we developed a new model for centrality in a facets model framework. Then, we applied the new model to analyze data collected in an experiment on perceptual judgment of Chinese-accented speech with dozens of students. Next, we developed new model for ESI items, and we applied it to analyze responses of college entrance exams. Then, we developed a new model incorporating rater centrality into a HRM, which we applied to analyze national language assessment of thousands of examinees and hundreds of raters. The examples range from small scale to large scale tests, from low-stake to high-stake tests, from tests with incomplete linking designs to tests with complete linking designs. The applications illustrate the feasibility and benefits of the new model that accounts for various rater errors simultaneously to yield higher accuracy estimates of item parameters, person parameters and test reliability. To achieve Objective 4, our team has conducted pilot studies to extend the new IRT models for rater errors. For example, we have developed a new model on rater halo effects in which raters tend to overgeneralize ratings of a ratee’s performance who have backgrounds (e.g., education, ethnicity) similar to them. This manuscript is under preparation and will be submitted to conferences for presentation and to journals for publication.

18613716.label: Major findings and research outcome
18613716.value: Major findings include: 1. A new class of IRT models that account for different types of rater errors (i.e., severity, sensitivity, centrality, similarity, and halo effects) has been successfully developed within the frameworks of facets models and hierarchical rater models. The new models are more general and flexible. They subsume many traditional IRT models as special cases. For example, the new facets model for centrality includes the conventional facets model as a special case; the new HRM that incorporating latent class includes the traditional HRM as a special case. Thus, the project advances the methodologies of measuring rater errors. In practice, a rater is very likely to show various rater errors from time to time. These models can estimate various rater errors simultaneously, thus, they are more practical, flexible, and useful. 2. New estimation methods are developed for the new class of models. They include the computationally efficient MCMC method and the conditional maximum likelihood estimation method which can quickly converge and complete the estimation in several minutes. All these new methods can recover the parameters of the new models. 3. Customized computer programs that implement the new estimation methods for the new models are available for the public. Researchers and practitioners can directly apply the new methods or models developed in this project to their real-life test data. The outcomes from this project have substantial impacts both theoretically and practically. Theoretically, the findings of this project provide an approach to obtain more accurate estimates of item difficulties, student abilities, rater effects, and test reliability by correcting the bias caused by rater errors. Practically, it enables customized training interventions for reducing rater biases. For example, supervisors can use the information from the new models to evaluate raters, identify low-performing raters, and train them to counter-act their bias(es), which might improve the accuracy of their ratings. Thus, this study can benefit assessment practice as well. Findings have been widely disseminated in an article published in a world-class journals and in conference papers. The detailed information can be found in Part C of this report. The project team will continue to prepare manuscripts for publication and generate more outcomes.

18613716.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18613716.value: Although we have conducted pioneering work for developing new IRT models for rater errors, more studies are in need. Three issues are listed as an example: (1) When raters’ evaluations take a long time, their errors may change across time, which is known as rater drift. The latent traits might change or grow. So future studies can model this by extending the new models to multilevel models with time points nested within raters and students, (2) rater errors might be linked to rater attributes (e.g., gender), so future studies can test whether adding explanatory variables can accurately model these relations. Such research might provide much needed guidelines to inform rater training, thereby reducing their biases, and (3) future research can create a user-friendly and stand-alone computer program to facilitate researcher use of the new models.

18614716.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18614716.value: This study will engage various levels of school implementers, including school leaders and teachers, to investigate their concerns and sense-making regarding the New Senior Secondary Curriculum Reform (NSSCR) in Hong Kong. Studies on curriculum policy implementation show that policy implementation is an ongoing and interactional process and is affected by different actors in school contexts (Ball, 2008; Datnow and Park, 2009; Veselý, 2012). The proposed study will add to ongoing international research on educational policy to investigate the interactional processes of individuals and groups in school contexts, and fill gaps in the research as to how school systems can work effectively. In particular, school leaders’ and teachers’ concerns and sense-making will be brought together to form the lens for understanding the NSSCR policy implementation. A mixed-method approach will be adopted in this study, with survey and case study methods directed at identifying the multi-levels of school implementers’ concerns and their sense-making processes during implementation. The Concerns-Based Adoption Model (CBAM), which is widely used for understanding implementation, will be employed to determine the concerns of the school implementers (Hall, Dirksen and George, 2006; Hall and Hord, 2011). The Stages of Concern Questionnaire will be adopted to tap into the concerns of a stratified representative sample of school implementers in Hong Kong. Subsequently, case studies will be used to probe the school implementers’ sense-making processes, which will help unveil the process of how multi-level actors in schools pave the way for adapting the curriculum policy in developing their students, colleagues and school organisation. Significant outcomes are expected from this study. Firstly, the concerns of school implementers will be identified, whose patterns will be categorized, and further be investigated of how school implementers at various stages of concern implement curriculum policy through sense-making processes in school contexts. Through case studies, an in-depth investigation will help identify and analyse issues related to how different actors in schools interact with self, others and contexts in paving the way through the dilemmas of policy implementation, particularly in a context which typically has a centralised policy-making characteristic. Finally, the results will provide insights into the relationship between policy itself and its context, and will respond to issues regarding international studies on curriculum policy implementation regarding school leaders’ and teachers’ roles and their professional development in effective school systems. 本研究探討各層級的學校實施者，即學校領導與教師，對香港新高中課程改革的關注與意義建構。根據課程政策實施的文獻研究顯示，政策實施是一個持續且相互作用的過程，受到學校環境中不同實施者的影響（Ball, 2008; Datnow and Park, 2009; Veselý, 2012），本研究在探討學校環境中個體與團體的相互作用之時，不僅為當前國際教育政策研究提供啟示，也將填補有關學校系統如何作有效運作之研究空白。具體來說，本研究結合學校領導與教師的關注和意義建構，並以此作為研究的視角，以理解新高中課程改革政策的實施。 本研究採用混合研究方法來揭示政策實施中學校實施者的關注與意義建構過程的多個層面，研究方法包括問卷調查與個案研究。對學校實施者的關注研究採用「關注為本採用模式」（Concerns-Based Adoption Model，以下簡稱CBAM）作為理論框架 (Hall, Dirksen and George, 2006; Hall and Hord, 2011)。研究將採用關注階段問卷（The Stages of Concern Questionnaire），並選取學校實施者的分層代表性樣本，藉以測量參與者的關注度。隨後，本研究會採用個案研究法，探索學校實施者的意義建構過程，深入探討學校各層級的實施者如何調適課程政策來促進其學生、同事，與學校組織的發展。 本研究有其重要的貢獻，首先，研究結果能辨認學校實施者不同程度的關注，按其不同的模式分類，並進一步探討處於不同關注階段的學校實施者如何通過意義建構，在學校環境中實施課程政策。第二，本研究將通過個案研究的方法，呈現並分析有關的議題，例如學校不同實施者在含中央集權政策制定的特徵環境下，如何與自身、他人、以及環境相互作用來解決政策實施中所遇到的困惑。最後，研究結果將為理解政策本身與其環境的關係提供啟示，並回應有關課程政策實施的國際研究議題—即在有效的學校系統中學校領導與教師角色以及其專業發展。

18614716.label: Realisation of objectives
18614716.value: In general, the research project has achieved all the objectives that it stated. Data was collected through survey, interviews and documentary analysis. First, around 1200 teachers filled in the questionnaires and the data collected was sufficient to help revising the instrument. The study has started from 1 October 2016 and is comprised of 3 stages, namely stage I, II and III. Stage I takes about 6-8 months with its focuses on quantitative research and data collection, stage II will proceed in the next 8-10 months focusing on qualitative research and data collection, and stage III will be the overall coordination and reporting in general for the rest of the remaining period. By now, the research team has already refined the questionnaire tool as adapted from Hall and Hord (1987) especially designed and contextualized for local schools’ use, with relevant validity and reliability established as well. Selection of sampled schools and administration of the questionnaires in some invited schools are done. A total of 20 schools participated in stage I, contributing to 1045 respondents to the Stages of Concern Questionnaire (SoCQ). Within each sampled school, different implementers of the NSSCR are included. For example, the school leaders such as the principal and vice principals, the middle management such as the panel heads of different subjects, and also the teachers at the frontline. In this stage, different types of schools, i.e. ‘Government’, ‘Aided’ and ‘Direct Subsidy’ are involved. Meanwhile, Stage II of the project has kicked off to probe more deeply into how teachers and different implementers make-sense of the NSSCR, 4 school cases were identified based on their survey results. So far, the research team has paid visits to all schools and several formal interview sessions have been conducted. In short, interviews, observations together with data analyses are underway. The project has completed good progress in all stages. Through survey, the researchers in this research found out the patterns of school leaders and teachers’ concern about the implementation of Senior Secondary Curriculum reform in Hong Kong. The statistical data showed that educators in schools were concerned about the information and practicality of reform, feasibility of reform implementation within school culture and the results obtaining from curriculum reform. In the survey, 1045 questionnaires (from 30 schools) were collected and being analysed. Hall’s Model of Stage of Concern Questionnaire (SoCQ) has been extensively used for measuring teachers’ concerns about curriculum reform in the past four decades. It has become a famous instrument for stage of concern of teachers for implementation. Cheung (2001) re-examines the questionnaire and proposes a 5-stage SoCQ. Using the Hall’s stage of concern model, the reliability test scores fall between 0.548 and 0.824. Delete two stages and items with low reliability and Item-total correlations. Thus, only 21 items are being retained. (See appendix 1 and 2) Moreover, through interviews and documentary analysis, the researchers identified the sense of stages of concern when implementing the curriculum reform. Over 40 teachers are being interviewed and documents from 4 schools (with over 30 documents in each school) are being analysed. Through the collecting data, the researchers reviewed the 7-stage model of Hall and 5-stage model of Cheung, attempts to construct a 5-stage model for studying Hong Kong teachers’ concerns about senior secondary curriculum implementation. The methodology of the current study, using the new curriculum implementation in Hong Kong as the context, shows the validity and reliability of the instrument. The revised model is consisted of 5 subscales namely time-constraint, informational, collaboration, refocusing and consequences, which are culturally bounded. The nature of the five stages of concerns is discussed. It is found that this revised model fits the time-constraint (heavy workload of teacher in both lessons, administrative affairs and extracurricular activities) and consequences nature (mainly public examinations) of Hong Kong society. To certain extent, all three objectives in this project are attained. In precise, the researchers understand and explore the patterns of school leaders’ and teachers’ concerns about Hong Kong's Senior Secondary Curriculum Reform. Moreover, we analyzed how school leaders and teachers at different stages of concern implement the NSSCR through sense-making processes with respect to interactions with others and school culture. Finally, the researchers framed the sense-making processes co-constructed by school implementers that work towards an effective school system.

18614716.label: Major findings and research outcome
18614716.value: There are three main findings in this research. First, Hall’s Model of Stage of Concern Questionnaire (SoCQ) has been used for measuring teachers’ concerns about curriculum reform in past 40 years. In 2001, Cheung (2001) re-examines the questionnaire and proposes a 5-stage SoCQ. This research, using curriculum implementation in Hong Kong as the context, applies the SoCQ and revises the instrument. The current research shows the validity and reliability of the revised instrument. The revised model is consisted of 5 subscales namely time-constraint, informational, collaboration, refocusing and consequences, which are culturally bounded. The nature of the five stages of concerns is discussed. In other words, the Hall and Hord (1991) model is not fitting the societal context of Hong Kong as teachers did not distinguish 7-stage concern and stressed the complexity of the instrument. The Hong Kong teachers show that the stages of concern in different order as listed: Unaware; informational / personal; management; consequence / collaboration; refocusing. Second, it is found that this revised model fits the time-constraint and consequences nature of Hong Kong society. As far as the teachers’ concern, heavy workload of in lessons, administrative affairs and extracurricular activities are the major obstacles for curriculum reform. Nearly all teachers rated “Time and Effort Constraint” as the lowest factor (mean = 3.99 out of 7) for implementing reforms in schools. Moreover, all teachers rated “Consequences” (especially public examination results as stressed in interviews and documents) as this highest factor (mean = 5.39 out of 7) for reform (see Table 1). The researchers observed that interpreting through this revised instrument suits the cultural context of Hong Kong. Table 1: Factor loadings of HK teachers’ concerns in Senior Secondary Curriculum Reform Mean N1 Time & Effort Constraint 3.99 N2 Informational 5.05 N3 Refocusing 4.77 N4 Collaboration 4.69 N5 Consequence 5.39 Finally, factor loading of two items have significant implications on curriculum implementation in Hong Kong. One is teachers’ suspicious about merging consequence & collaboration (esp in senior secondary school teaching). On the one hand, they are more concerned about consequences (esp public examination). On the other hand, they are less favoured in collaborate with colleagues in curriculum implementation. Second is teachers’ concern about management of school heads. In precise, this research shows the special features in Hong Kong which are not similar to those stated in SoC of Hall (1991). The researchers advocate that applying SoC should take culture context into consideration. In this research, the “time and effort constraint” and “consequences” matter!

18614716.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18614716.value: There are two aspects for further development or action from this research. One is the application of the revised SoC instrument to similar research of curriculum reform in Hong Kong or other localities. The application may lead to justifications or testing of the instrument. The researchers expect that this will be helpful to understand and address teachers’ concern on curriculum reform in East Asia regions. Second, the government should pay attention to the concerns of teachers take the pressure of public examinations and the workload of teachers.

18614716.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18614716.value: Hall’s Model of Stage of Concern Questionnaire (SoCQ) has been extensively used for measuring teachers’ concerns about curriculum reform. It has become a famous instrument for stage of concern of teachers for implementation. Cheung (2001) re-examines the questionnaire and proposes a 5-stage SoCQ. This research, collecting data through surveying 30 schools and interviewing 40 teachers, reviews the 7-stage model of Hall and 5-stage model of Cheung, attempts to construct a revised 5-stage model for studying Hong Kong teachers’ concerns about senior secondary curriculum implementation. The methodology of the current study, using the new curriculum implementation in Hong Kong as the context, shows the validity and reliability of the revised instrument. The revised model is consisted of 5 subscales namely time-constraint, informational, collaboration, refocusing and consequences, which are culturally bounded. With the support from interviews and documents, it is found that this revised model fits the time-constraint and consequences nature of Hong Kong society. This research has both conceptual and policy significances. On the conceptual aspect, the revised SoC instrument should benefit scholars for investigating teachers’ concern of curriculum implementation in East Asia. On policy aspect, the policy makers should address to pressure of public examinations and workloads of teachers.
