22502016.label: Major findings and research outcome
22502016.value: Given that this study employed a longitudinal design, it was able to demonstrate the temporal effect on the sports event impact. In reference to the hypothesis made in the research proposal, we found there was a significant positive relationship between residents' perceptions of event benefits and their support towards the event, as well as a negative relationship between their perceived costs and support, for both near- and distant-past samples. Regarding event attachment, we confirmed there was a pronounced positive influence of residents' event attachment on their perceptions of positive event impact in the near-past sample, as well as in the distant-past sample. However, the proposed negative effect of event attachment on the perception of event costs was not detected in either period. Conversely, the level of residents' concern on their community had a significant influence on their perceptions of event impacts with enhanced evaluation on the positive outcomes, while reduced assessment on the costs, regardless of the time-lapse. Moreover, we were able to observe the perceived benefits derived from the hosting of a sport event was positively associated with residents' overall evaluations of life quality across time. The perceived negative impact was found to influence the perceived quality of life (QOL) negatively within the near-past group. However, for the distant-past sample, this study failed to identify a significant relationship between residents' perception of costs and their QOL assessment. Collectively, findings indicated that residents' perceptions and attitudes towards the event, as well as their evaluations on QOL, did not change significantly after the event as time passes by in a recurring event context. Instead, residents' perceptions and attitudes towards the event formed based on a direct experience regarding the event show stability over time. Overall, residents generally perceive the impact of SCHKM as positive and favorable. Their perceptions of benefits generated from the event were above the midpoint (Mnear=4.926, Mdistant=4.914) while the perceptions of costs were below the midpoint (Mnear=3.207, Mdistant=3.267). This positively skewed evaluation of event impacts translated to positive attitudes about the event as suggested by the above middle point mean of support (Mnear=4.768, Mdistant=4.793). More importantly, residents' perceptions of event impacts influence their support for hosting of a recurring event in their community both directly and indirectly through their perceptions of the QOL. It highlights the critical role of QOL perceptions in formulating residents' support towards an event.

22502016.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
22502016.value: As QOL was measured aggregately and as an overall evaluation of life quality, future research can provide a more comprehensive picture of the event impact by examining individuals' evaluations of specific life domains. A previous study has indicated that it is plausible that the reflections on various life domains could generate different effects on their QOL perceptions. Thus, a more specific investigation of different life domains should provide additional insights for relevant stakeholders. Furthermore, event organizers often cite one of the significant functions of sports events is to promote the participation of sport/physical activity among the citizen. While the research team has attempted to address this proposed impact in this study preliminarily, a more extensive study on this issue should be a priority in the future. Researchers can investigate how an individual's perception of the other facets of social impacts (e.g., economy, host city reputation, culture development, environment) may influence the intention to engage in physical activity. More specifically, the study can also incorporate the temporal effect into the mix, to explore any potential diminishing effect of this sport development impact, both within one event cycle and between different event cycles.

22502016.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
22502016.value: This study mainly examined the different social impacts (both positive and negative) of an annual sport event on the residents. Specifically, the study investigated five different areas of social impact- economic and recognition, cultural development, cultural diversity, social problems, and traffic congestion and pollution. As significant amounts of resources are being invested in this sporting event each year, it is crucial to appraise the event’s non-monetary impact on society. Through the residents’ perceptions of these five areas, event organizers would be able to have a better understanding of how residents form their attitude and support toward the event. They would also be able to observe how the relationship of these factors changed over time, as this study conducted surveys at multiple times over two event cycles. Another focus of this study involved investigating how residents’ perceptions of quality of life are impacted by the perceived impacts of the marathon event, as well as how QOL influence residents’ support to the event. Collectively, the data gathering from this study confirmed the value a sport has for the local community. Further, it also provides relevant information for different stakeholders to continuously improve and sustain the event.

22602316.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
22602316.value: The proposed study will look at how Chinese military officers from different parts of China envisioned future warfare and tried to prepare their forces, states, and societies accordingly between the First World War and the outbreak of the Second Sino-Japanese War. The First World War witnessed a comprehensive transformation of warfare. The effectiveness of modern weaponry and the massive scale of fighting forced the belligerents to fight a protracted conflict. The pace of technological advancement turned war into a contest not only of military strength but also of research and industrial capabilities. To survive, European states mobilised and controlled all aspects of national resources at an unprecedented level, even in democracies such as France and Britain. The idea that a new understanding of the relationship between the military force, the state, and the society would be required for a nation to fight a modern war prevailed in the postwar world. This study is a logical extension of the principal investigator’s (PI) previous GRF project on the institutionalisation of modern military science in the Fengtian Army and the Nationalist Army during the 1920s and 1930s. The previous study illustrated that officers from the two armies formed intellectual communities and forged military paradigms for their respective forces instead of merely copying lessons from abroad. This study, in turn, will reconstruct the discussions among the officers over the issues of new tactics, the role of technology in future warfare, and the reforms necessary for the state and society. These discussions were governed by the social, political, economic, and geographical contexts faced by different military factions in China. To illustrate the importance of the regional context, this study will cover not only the above-mentioned armies but also the Guangxi Clique (guixi) and the Guangdong Clique (yuexi). The reform measures taken by these officers will also be studied and evaluated. By looking at the officers’ vision of future warfare during the 1930s, we can gain a better understanding of the Chinese military between 1918 and 1937, a period that was usually overshadowed by the wars between the Chinese Nationalist and Communist parties and the role of German advisors. It will also allow us to gain a better understanding of the process through which the Chinese officers transformed their military according to foreign experiences and conditions in China, and enhance our understanding of the spread of military science in the world after the First World War. 本課題嘗試研究在第一次世界大戰至第二次中日戰爭期間，來自中國各地的軍官如何思考未來的戰爭，並以此為其軍隊、國家機構，以及社會作出相應準備。第一次世界大戰使戰爭形式出現全面的變化。現代武器的威力和戰爭規模擴大迫使各交戰國進行長期戰爭。科技快速轉變，使戰爭成為軍事力量與工業實力的較量。各國為求生存，遂於國內進行前所未見的動員和統制，甚至英、法等議會民主制國家亦不能倖免。為應付現代戰爭，時人逐漸認為軍隊、政府和社會之間需要一種全新的關係；此想法在戰後成為共識。 主研究者曾研究奉系與國民革命軍的軍人如何在1920至1930年代把現代軍事科學在中國制度化，其研究顯示兩軍均出現了知識軍人的群體，並在其軍中逐漸形成範式，亦不只是從外國照抄軍學。此課題則更進一步，從戰術發展、科技在未來戰爭的角色，以及政府與社會需要的改革等方面重構這些軍官的討論。為了突出地域因素的重要性，本課題亦嘗試把桂系和粵系的軍人納入研究。研究時亦會檢視他們提倡的實際改革。 研究兩次世界大戰期間中國軍人對未來戰爭的思考與想像，使我們可以對1918至1937年的中國軍事歷史有更深刻的了解，特別是關於國共兩黨的內戰和國民政府聘請的德國顧問以外的問題。此課題不單使我們可以更深入地了解中國軍人如何利用外國軍學，在中國的背景下進行軍事改革的過程，更有助我們理解第一次世界大戰後軍事科學在世界的傳播。

22602316.label: Realisation of objectives
22602316.value: The PI of the project is pleased to report that the objectives of the project have been achieved during the period after the Mid-term Report was submitted in 2018. The PI acquired a deeper understanding of the Chinese officers' changing theoretical understanding of warfare between the establishment of the Republic in 1912 to the outbreak of the Second Sino-Japanese War in 1937, such as but not exclusively on issues such as the nature of modern warfare, the importance of technology, the changing tactics and strategy, the new aerial dimension of war, China's geopolitical and international situations, and the need to organise the society for "total war". This was largely done through a continuous collection of the publications of the Chinese officers as well as the contemporary intellectuals in the form of books, professional journals, training manuals, and post-action reports. In all, hundreds of such materials were found and critically read, and the PI has published articles about some of the more salient points raised by the Chinese officers during this period, such as the Chinese officers changing understanding on the nature of war, the ideal civil-military relations, and the changing face of aerial warfare. The PI also addresses the ways in which the Chinese officers learned from the wars that occurred during the period concerned and institutionalised modern military knowledge by establishing education institutions, creating an intellectual community, and constructing a common language and paradigm. This was done through a critical examination of the institutionalisation of military education and the formation of an officer corps in China during the period concerned. Moreover, the PI also wrote about how Chinese armies tried to learn from their combat experience from the late 1920s to the first months of the Second Sino-Japanese War in 1937. It shows that at least some of the better organised Chinese armies, such as the Fengtian Army, the Nationalist Army, and the Cantonese Army all attempted to learn from their combat experiences by writing detailed combat reports, and even organised meetings among the officers to discuss the lessons learned. Lessons learned from combat would lead to changes in tactics, doctrine, training, and equipment. This created a knowledge loop for branches of the Chinese military during the first half of the 20th century and played a role in helping the Chinese armed forces to face the Japanese invasion during the Second Sino-Japanese War. This project also located the influence from Japan, Germany, and the Soviet Union on the theoretical development of modern Chinese military thoughts, and enhanced our understanding of the process of localisation of foreign military science in China. This is done through a critical reading of the translations of foreign military writings by the Chinese officers as well as their works, such as journal articles, training manuals, and war plans. The procurement of arms and equipment by the Chinese military before the Second Sino-Japanese War was also examined. It is found that of the different powers, the Japanese had been the most influential on the development of the Chinese military during the period concerned. This overthrows the assumption held by many that the Chinese were deeply influenced by the Germans and the Soviets on military science from the late Qing to the mid-twentieth century. The PI also found that the influence of different branches of the Chinese military also differed and changed over time. The theoretical and actual changes in the Chinese Air Force was a case in point (the PI published an article about this). The Chinese Air Force has been under the influence of many powers before the Second Sino-Japanese War. While the German advisors advocated for an air force that mainly supported land operations, the planners of the Chinese Air Force opted for an air force that could operate independently from the Army and the Navy, as they needed a rationale for more resources and attention. The planners then turned to the American and Italian advisors, who argued that the air force alone could be the deciding factor of the war, by concentrating on the enemy's ability to sustain the war, namely its industrial capabilities and the cities. This led to a tendency to exaggerate the capabilities of aircraft and air force in general by the advisors, and the over-estimation of their air force's power by the planners. A similar pattern was also seen in the modernisation of the land forces of the Nationalist Chinese government. The result was the emergence of a series of ill-conceived war plans and tactical doctrines that led to heavy losses and early defeats suffered by the Chinese during the early stage of the Sino-Japanese War. To examine the emergence of and changes in the Chinese professional officer corps before the Second Sino-Japanese War through an in-depth study of the infrastructural and institutional changes in the Fengtian Army and the NRA and the composition, world view, and features of the officer corps. The PI used the example of the Anguojun officers (many of whom from the Fengtian Army and many later joined the National Revolutionary Army) as to illustrate the emergence of the officer corps in China and the diverse background and experience of these officers from the late Qing period to the 1990s. Also, through an in-depth study of the writing of the officers, the PI also explored their understanding of modern warfare and their attitude towards civil-military relations. The most important lessons they learned (almost entirely from other countries and especially Japan) were the importance of firepower in modern warfare and of the state's ability to mobilise manpower, capital, and resources to fight a protracted war of attrition. It was with such understanding that many Chinese officers (especially those from the Fengtian Army and the NRA) supported a more authoritarian form of government led by Chiang Kai-shek, as he advocated for introducing military discipline to control not only the Nationalist Party but also the society in general, as the country faced an imminent threat from Japan. However, such a solution was also seen by many as an excuse for Chiang to expand his power. The PI also commented on the state of the Chinese armies during the 1920s and 1930s and the impact of modern military science on the performance of the Chinese armies, especially using the Chinese air force and the army as examples. The PI found that the Chinese air force had been deeply influenced by competing foreign theories, and the result was an unbalanced force that was assigned with roles that it was not equipped to perform. Similarly, although the Chinese Nationalist decision-makers spent a large sum of money on arms, equipment, and advisors, the Nationalist Army remained far from ready to fight a modern war. In fact, the obsession with state-of-the-art technology actually distracted the Chinese Nationalist army from solving the more pressing problems in areas of command, organisation, training, and logistics. The PI also laid a foundation for further studies on Chinese military history by gathering the historical sources concerning military developments between 1911 and 1937, mainly in the form of articles written by the Chinese officers during the period, the after-action-report of the Chinese armies, and the related literature.

22602316.label: Major findings and research outcome
22602316.value: This study enhanced our understanding of Chinese military changes during the first half of the 20th century by mapping the ways that the Chinese officers understood modern warfare and the impacts of such understanding. It challenged the idea that the Chinese officers during this period only copied from the more 'advanced' militaries such as Germany and the Soviet Union without critically examining their own strategic needs and resources available. Instead of assuming a straight-forward one-way influence of the Chinese officers copying from others, this study identified the existence of 'knowledge loops' that illustrates the complexity of military change in China during this period. While the Chinese officers did pay much attention to the perceived lessons of the First World War, especially those digested and discussed by the Japanese military, they too tried to put the new knowledge in China's context and examined the practicability of adopting new equipment and tactics. Meanwhile, they were being influenced by a variety of factors such as incomplete information, suggestions from foreign advisors, advice from officers who participated in study tours, and officers who were educated aboard. Of equal importance were other factors such as the perceived threat by the decision-makers, politics between the branches of the armed forces, and internal political needs. All these factors shaped the Chinese armed forces that were to fight Japan in 1937. This study also identified the major sources of the influence on the Chinese officer class during this period, namely the lessons of the First World War, the perceived threat from Japan and the Soviet Union, the need to ensure national unity to meet external threats, and the idea that it was necessary to empower the state to the extent that it could control all elements of war from manpower to the so-called spiritual force so that China could survive the next world war that was seen as inevitable. This project also mapped the changes of the Chinese military during the early Republican period, up to the outbreak of the Second Sino-Japanese War, especially in terms of equipment procurement, training doctrines, and organisation. In addition, the PI had collected various primary sources not only for this project but also future works.

22602316.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
22602316.value: An obvious extension of this project would be the process in which the Chinese armed forces learned from their combat experience during the Second Sino-Japanese War, 1937-1945. During the early stage of the war, the Chinese forces suffered from a series of defeats that disproved many of the pre-war assumptions and understandings. The Chinese armed forces had to extract meaningful lessons and implement changes amidst a rapidly deteriorating strategic situation. In the meantime, a war started in Europe and later in the Pacific, leading to the involvement of the United States, the Soviet Union, and Britain in the war. These powers provided material and training and also help shape the Chinese military. As the PI has already collected a critical amount of primary and secondary sources concerned the topic and have explored the relevant archives and databases, the PI can continue this study almost immediately. Moreover, an extension of the study would allow the PI to construct a coherent narrative about the transformation of the Chinese armed forces during the first half of the 20th century, and the factors that shaped it such as the impact of the First World War, foreign influence, technological transformation, and the internal politics.

22602316.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
22602316.value: This study looks at the Chinese military officers' understanding of modern warfare during the first half of the 20th century by studying their writings about war, a group of important primary sources that have been previously overlooked. It also addresses the various factors that shaped their understanding such as perceived lessons of the First World War from aboard, technological development, competing foreign military theories, assessment of foreign threats, politics in China, the tension between the branches of the armed forces, and civil-military relations. The study highlighted the difficulties facing the Chinese military decision-makers when they were trying to modernise the Chinese armed forces amidst increasing foreign pressure, internal disunity, and rapid technological changes. They had to make hard choices when selecting tactical doctrines and investing in equipment that had not been tested by actual combat. This study also discussed how Chinese officers improved the capability of their forces by learning from their combat experience. This project allows us to better appreciate the complex process of a military trying to learn from the experience of themselves and others and make informed choices amidst rapidly changing situations before the outbreak of the Second Sino-Japanese War in 1937.

22606916.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
22606916.value: This project will open up new ways of understanding medieval Chinese society by examining epigraphic sources for eunuchs, a group still little understood despite its enormous impact on all areas of politics, society, and culture. The project is the first systematic study of the military role of eunuchs and the ‘palace domestic service’ (neishi sheng 内侍省), the eunuch agency of the Tang 唐 dynasty (618–907), during the period of its radical transformation after the Rebellion of An Lushan (安史之亂, 755–63). In that time, the neishi sheng took control of much of the military, and eunuchs forged kinship ties with members of the military and civil elites of the empire through marriage and adoption. While past research on eunuchs has relied on traditional sources – depicting them as morally corrupt and politically subversive –, this study undertakes close readings of newly discovered epigraphic sources and thereby reconstructs the life worlds of eunuchs, their gender, family, and other relationships with members of the Tang elite. That way, it breaks new ground in taking eunuchs as a social entity with a group interest and agency of its own. In addition, it utilizes hitherto neglected literary sources on the homo-social bonds between eunuchs and other men at court. As this study will show, those bonds were not, as the traditional record suggests, all political in nature and constantly fraught with tension, but often characterized by friendship and common cultural (religious and literary) pursuits. Until recently, research on Tang eunuchs was greatly restricted by a scarcity of sources and mostly based on historical writings (Jiu Tangshu 舊唐書, Xin Tangshu 新唐書, and Zizhi tongjian 資治通鑑). The excavation of thousands of muzhiming 墓誌銘, tomb epitaphs buried with the dead, around the Tang capitals of Chang’an 長安 (Xi’an 西安) and Luoyang 洛陽 since the mid-20th century has changed that situation dramatically. At the moment, ca. 250 of those epitaphs are believed to be dedicated to eunuchs, their spouses, and adopted children. Apart from papers at international conferences, the project will produce articles in internationally peer-reviewed journals and a monograph on the social networks of eunuchs with other elites, and a searchable database of images, transcriptions, and translations of epitaphs into English and modern Chinese. In addition, the PI will seek further funding to host a conference with international experts in Hong Kong, to look at the military eunuch from a cross-cultural perspective. N/A

22608316.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
22608316.value: Situated within the wider arena of public art, socially engaged art is defined as art-in-the-public-interest, as it foregrounds social issues, political activism and community collaborations. (Kwon 2002) Because of this nature, it operates beyond the gallery–museum nexus and has a problematic relationship with the art market system, which predominately favours household decorations. However, because of its site-orientedness, there is great potential of symbiosis between artistic work and the economic paradigm. Instead of critiquing capitalism with straightforward antagonism, there is a possibility for penetrative approaches to hack the system. The research aims to focus on this strand of socially engaged art, which situates itself in a symbiotic relationship with the market through creating alternative art economies. Such possibilities have been explored by international artists; for instance, Project Row Houses, started by artist Rick Lowe, turned dilapidated and abandoned “shotgun houses” into a supportive community for single mothers and visiting artists; Conflict Kitchen by Jon Rubin and Dawn Weleski takes the form of a take-out restaurant which serves only ethnic foods from countries with which the United States is in conflict. This area has also been addressed by international research, such as in Art Production beyond the Art Market? (van den Berg 2013), a compilation of essays surveying global tendencies and case studies. Universities such as the Rhode Island School of Design also rolled out practical action kits, loosely under the name of “artonomics” and “artrepreneur”, to aid students in creating new economies through their creative practices. While a rising number of artists in Hong Kong have been endeavouring to explore in this type of art over the last decade, there is however limited literature in framing this global phenomenon in the local context and their work has not been well examined. This research will be an inquiry into the subject in four successive phases: 1) to synthesize knowledge across parallel research fields, including socially engaged art, theory and critique of capitalism, creative economy and social innovation; 2) to re-examine local projects in socially engaged art; 3) to embark on research-led, practice-based inquiry and prototype experimental projects; 4) to consolidate and review the research processes and findings in a project documentation publication. For second and third phases, the research will be conducted through three distinctive lenses: the projects’ artistic criteria, the viability of an alternative art market approach, and their systemic potential for creating sustainable and extensive impact. 社會參與式藝術涉及社會議題、政治上的社會運動以及社區協作，在廣義的公共藝術之中，定義為以公眾利益為大前提的藝術。(Kwon 2002) 因為這種性質，它在畫廊、藝術館等傳統機制以外運作，跟主要偏好物質藏品的藝術市場關係不明。可是，因為它重視特定場域的面向，藝術創作跟經濟有共生的可能性。除了以直接歒對的態度批評資本主義，滲透性的手法，有可能入侵資本主義的系統。這項研究對焦這種社會參與式藝術，透過創造另類的藝術經濟模式，與市場共生。 不少國際的藝術家都曾探索這種可能性：例如由Rick Lowe發起的「排屋計劃」 (Project a Row Houses)，將廢置的傳統房屋轉化成支援低收入人士、年輕母親和術藝家的社區；Jon Rubin和Dawn Weleski的「衝突廚房」 (Conflict Kitchen)是一間外賣餐廳，專門出售與美國處於衝突關係中的國家的傳統食物。這個領域亦是國際研究的題目，例如《藝術市場外的藝術生產？》（Art Production Beyond the Art Market?） (Van den Berg 2013) 收錄了與全球趨勢和案例有關的文章。羅德島設計學院（Rhode Island School of Design）等大學也設計了以「藝術經濟」及「藝術創業家」命名的實用行動套件，幫助學生透過創作，創造新的經濟模式。 在過去十年，越來越多香港藝術工作者奮力從事這種藝術，可是，將本地脈絡置於全球現象中的文獻有限，他們的作品亦未有被充分研究。這項研究探討這個議題，設四階段：1）綜合平行領域的知識（包括社會參與式藝術、資本主義的理論與批判、創意經濟以及社會創新）；2）研究本地社會式參與藝術的項目；3) 展開研究主導、實踐為本的踏查，以及嘗試實驗項目；4) 整合及回顧研究過程及發現，並以結集成項目紀錄出版。在第二及第三階段，研究會著眼於以下三方面：項目的藝術準則、另類藝術市場方案的可行性，以及創造可持續及廣泛影響的系統性潛能。

22608316.label: Realisation of objectives
22608316.value: Objective 1: The PI and his research assistants have conducted literature reviews, under the following topics or keywords: alternative economies, art and community, art and economy, cultural theory, research methodology, socially-engaged art, and the commons. The range of authors include Giacomo D’Alisa, Alberto Vanolo, Namoi Klein, Peter Barnes, Albert Mills, Victoria Foster, Dominique Lammli, Brett Scott, Trebor Scholz, Sunquan Huang and Charles Simpson. While this research explores the potential of alternative art economies for sustainable development of socially engaged art, the intersection between socially engaged art and alternative art economies is rare because both categories take a long time to develop, and it requires many factors for either to emerge. For instance, many of the above case studies only check one of the two boxes. Considering this situation, I propose to expand the research slightly for results that can be more realistically explored within the research period. The suggested change is to expand the notion of “socially engaged art” as a stringent mode of practice to “creative practice with social relevance”, so that the criterion of sustainability through alternative economics can be approached as the key area of investigation. Objective 2: With the re-focus on “creative practice with social relevance,” third exemplary cases were selected for in-depth study. The list includes: • Chan See-kwong, Ray, Chuen Lung Cups (ceramics, local culture and community building) • Kevin Cheung (product design and upcycling) • Coutou Woodwork Studio (carpentry, sustainability and heritage preservation) • Creativity Is (film, experience design and self-discovery and empowerment) • Crossroad Foundation (experience design and aid to the Third World) • Fashion Clinic (fashion and sustainability) • Flower plaques (crafts and heritage preservation) • Okapi Studio (incense making and cultural diversity) • MUDWORK (art, object making and autonomous living) • Sanwood Kids Club (parent-and-child activities and sustainability) • work, sheet. Studio (product design and sustainability) • Yip Kai-chun, Hakkaoke (new media art, heritage preservation and community building) • Zine Coop (independent publishing and various social issues) In view of the three specific areas of inquiry, the following observations are made: A) Artistic criteria: These projects all transcend conventional criteria of assessment for their respect disciplines. While rigour by disciplinary standard is still an important factor in evaluating their merit, other criteria, especially those pertaining to the causes they pledge should be indispensable in recognising the projects’ achievements. B) Alternative economic models: Below is a list of alternative models deduced from the empirical experiences of the above projects: • Running activities (typically workshops) that can be subscribed by corporations as CSR programmes, staff development, etc, or by individuals for interest, health and well-being, etc. • Generation of educational materials that can be subscribed by schools or individuals • Products that can be purchased by individuals who are willing to pay a bit more for the value they represent • Operating with not monetary support, such as mutual help in a community of likeminded practitioners C) Systematic impact: Most of the projects are not fully sustainable and still rely on a mix of funding models. A high degree of perseverance is needed for their continual survival. However, there seems to be growing optimism among a young generation of value-drive practitioners, who felt that their endeavours are increasingly supported by a growing critical mass who are also looking for alternatives as consumers. Expansion of this critical mass, as well as provision of infrastructural support before the market is sufficiently ready, are vital for promoting such practices. Objective 3: Tapping into the emerging trend of value-driven undertakings among a new generation of creative practitioners, the research-led practice was conducted as an expanded pedagogical experiment by engaging MA graduates to further develop their socially relevant graduation projects into potentially sustainable undertakings. Below is an overview of the incubated projects: • Angel Yam, Name: An interactive art experience promoting communication between hearing and non-hearing participants • Chi Chi Cheung, Belonging Cookies: An interactive art experience engaging participants from diverse backgrounds to converse on the notion of “belonging” and “displacement” • Terence Leung, The Use of No Use: An interactive installation for participants to reflect on and share “useless” items with emotional value • Walter Ma, Everlasting Moment: A photographic project enabling elders with dementia and their families to capture cherished memories Each of the above graduates went through a mentored process to develop their works into potentially sustainable models. Developing these prototypes has been a great challenge. A key reason is that a diverse range of skills, such as user-sensitivity, market awareness, promotional and communication savvy, production known-how, etc, alongside artistic competency, is needed for connecting personal creative works to marketable outputs, and many of these skills are beyond conventional art school training. While it takes time for the projects to mature into marketable outputs, their potential has been evaluated through qualitative interviews with related stakeholders. Objective 4: On top of the above incubated projects, quantitative survey has been conducted at a number of occasions when massive numbers of participants attended art activities (presented by the PI with other art fundings) with social relevance and potential marketability. These surveys form the basis of a market research on the viability of alternative art economies. A mixed approach is thus seen as a more viable yet progressive model to expand the funding system for socially relevant art projects. Along this line, a prototype was conducted in collaboration with the West Kowloon Cultural District Authority (WKCDA) and the Hong Kong Society for the Deaf (HKSFD). We synthesised three of the MA’s students projects into a theatre-based, art-driven experience of social inclusion, in which people with hearing impairment are bridged with people with regular hearing. The programme was presented with capital costs covered by the research’s funding and partial sponsorship from WKCDA. However, it can be a ticketed event and potentially sustain itself in a model similar to that of the performing arts, which is rarely practiced in other art disciplines in Hong Kong so far. Another form of alternative economies practiced in the project is creation of additional value through creative and financial synergy. The sponsorship from WKCDA actually comes from a budget for audience expansion, while the in-kind contribution of HKSFD is supported by their mandate to enhance the deaf community’s social participation. By weaving existing needs together, resources from different sources can be pulled together for art projects with multifaceted impact. Objective 5: While the prototypes contribute to an enrichment of practice in creative practices with social relevance, knowledge generated through research is made available to the general public through an accessible website: www.creativesocialhk.net. Exemplary local cases are presented in a laymen-friendly manner to inform readers of the availability of such works in Hong Kong. Findings and insights derived from the research are also presented in a number of international conferences, including at the 14th International Conference on the Arts in Society. The discussion touches on multiple dimensions such as expanding art practice, the social relevance of art, models of sustainability, etc. Objective 6: The PI was invited to give a plenary presentation at the HKADC’s International Arts Leadership Roundtable. It was to be attended by international and local policymakers, and is themed “Art as Game Changer.” The PI originally planned to present the research findings as directional recommendations for diversity and community development. However, it was postponed due to social disruptions. Meanwhile, based on the prototype scheme developed through this research, the WKCDA Learning and Participation team is interested to implement some of the strategies in their long-term planning and development.

22608316.label: Major findings and research outcome
22608316.value: • A list of exemplary creative projects with social relevance in HK • Lack of training of relevant skills in art schools; this can be improved by expanding the range of training for aspiring creative entrepreneurs, or through collaboration among professionals with different skills. • While the provision of space is the mainstay of many current schemes for emerging creative entrepreneurs, other forms of support, such as promotion to cultivate consumers, clustering to facilitate collaboration, cross-disciplinary mentorship, are also needed. • Findings from 507 questionnaires suggest that over 90% of the respondents are willing to pay partially for attending such activities, while the average percentages of funding suggested to be 43% from public, 39% from private sector, and 18% from ticketing. 22608316.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
22608316.value: Refocused to examine alternative economies for sustaining creative practice with social relevance, the research identifies a list of exemplary local cases that demonstrate an emerging trend of value-driven creative practice beyond the conventional art market. By experimenting with a range of alternative models of sustainability, these projects strive to reach out to diverse demographics while pursuing their social goals. The merits of such projects should be considered with regard to both artistic and social criteria. While most such projects are still struggling to sustain, enhancement of infrastructural support is needed for more substantial impact. A pedagogical experiment informs the research’s practice-led inquiry. Four art graduates were supported to develop their graduation projects into potentially sustainable undertakings. Enterprising is proven to be challenging for art graduates, as the vast range of skills needed is beyond the existing scope of training in art schools. This can be overcome by expanding cross-disciplinary learning, mentorship and collaboration, as well as other infrastructural support, eg. cultivation of consumers who are receptive to value-driven creative outputs, clustering to facilitate collaboration, more imaginative expansion of “market place”, etc. To disseminate information relevant to the general public, exemplary local cases are listed in a website: www.creativesocialhk.net. Besides informing readers of these examples, the website also serves as a contact point for these projects to reach out to potential supporters.

22608716.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
22608716.value: Interpreting into the B language, or retour interpreting, has often been regarded as unacceptable, mostly because of language idiomaticity concerns. However, this kind of interpreting is frequently an unavoidable reality for Chinese to English interpretation owing to the lack of English-native interpreters who are proficient in Chinese. This is especially so in political and diplomatic settings, where the interpreter is required to be of the same nationality as the speaker to avoid potential conflicts in political stances. When interpreting political speeches, interpreters, in addition to rendering the message and political stances accurately and faithfully, also play the role of a mediator to help reduce unnecessary hostility or displeasure. Existing research has seldom addressed the specific communicative strategies of interpreters working in a non-native language. In this respect, the use of pragmatic markers (PMs), i.e. the linguistic signals concerning the communication functions of the language, not only displays an interpreter’s proficiency in B language orality, but also the level of communicative skills core to professional interpreters. This project aims to study PMs in interpreted political speeches from Chinese to English. The research work consists of two parts. The first part involves the collection and compilation of three corpora of political speeches, including one of interpreted speeches from Chinese to English, and two of speeches by native speakers of English and Chinese, respectively. These speeches are delivered by, and interpreted from those by, state leaders and key political figures from the Chinese mainland and Hong Kong, in addition to speeches delivered by their counterparts from the United States and the United Kingdom. In the second part of the research, the three corpora will be annotated with different types of PMs. Cross-genre and cross-modality analysis on the corpora will be conducted to examine and compare PMs in interpreted political speeches in the B language and those in the non-interpreted speeches in the A language. The analysis will also assess the extent to which PMs of the original speeches in the A language interfere with the interpretation into the B language. The project will provide insights into how PMs of interpreted political speeches operate in interpreters’ B language. The research findings will contribute to enhancing our understanding of the functions of PMs in political interpreting and help advance the professional practice of retour interpreting. The corpora compiled will constitute a pool of useful resources for training interpreters in discourse competence. 在傳譯中，如果傳譯員由A語言（母語）譯入B語言（非母語），常常會引致譯文語言是否地道的質疑，從而被視為是不可接受的做法。然而，在中—英傳譯中，由於以英文為母語並精通中文的譯者不足，傳譯員常常需要以中文為母語的人士擔當。尤其在政治和外交場合，基於政治立場和國家安全問題的考慮，擔任傳譯的必須是本國人員。因此，譯入B語言常常在所難免。 在傳譯政治演辭時，傳譯員不僅必須保證原語信息和政治立場傳遞的正確性和忠實性，同時需要起到外交協調的作用，避免出現不必要的政治不快甚至糾紛。過往的研究甚少涉及傳譯中譯入B語言時的交際策略問題。在言語交際中，語用標記的使用蘊含和傳達了豐富的語言交際功能，成為反映傳譯員B語言的表達及交際能力的重要指標。 本項目旨在研究政治演辭中—英傳譯之語用標記的使用。研究分兩個主要階段。第一階段涉及政治演辭語料的收集和語料庫的建立：包括中文原語語料庫、中—英傳譯語料庫、以及英文原語語料庫三部分。這些演辭源自中國大陸、香港、美國以及英國四大地區，講者為國家領導或重要政治人物。項目第二階段涉及語料庫的語用標記標註和分析。本研究將就不同語用標記的使用進行跨語料庫和跨語料類型的分析和比較，找出A語言（中英文原語）和B語言（英文譯入語）中語用標記使用的異同，并探討A語言語用標記遷移的問題。 本項目將揭示語用標記在譯入B語言的傳譯中的影響和作用。研究成果不僅有助於提升我們對政治及外交傳譯中語用標記的作用的了解，且可推進譯入B語言的傳譯專業發展。項目所開發的語料庫亦可用於培訓傳譯人員的語用能力。

22608716.label: Realisation of objectives
22608716.value: The project aimed to achieve seven objectives, all of which have been fully realised. First all, the use of PMs were compared in native and interpreted English speeches and a clear pattern was identified (Objective 1). The findings are reported in a number of publications (Pan, 2019a; Pan & Wong, 2017b, 2018b, 2019, under preparation). Specific cases of overuse/underuse were further explored (ibid). Interpreters were found to employ strategies such as intensification, total equivalence, mitigation and omission when interpreting PMs into B language, and their employment of strategies vary in different political settings or on different PMs (Objective 2; see Pan, 2018a; Pan & Wong, 2017a, 2018a). In addition, possible influence of A language was identified when interpreting PMs in political speeches into a B language, particularly on some PMs, although sensitivity of political topics or stress of political settings may be a greater contributor to certain differences of PMs use in interpreted English speeches (Objective 3; Pan, 2019a; Pan & Wong, 2018a, 2019, under preparation). The rendition of PMs were also compared by different parameters including mode of interpreting, source speech type, source language and speech modality, all of which were included in the metadata of the corpora data (Objective 4; Pan, 2019b). The nuances of differences were identified to provide light on both research and teaching (Pan, 2018b; Pan & Wong, under preparation). A semi-automatic annotation procedure has been developed, using advanced editing and regular expression functions of Word and Excel and an example base of the annotated PMs for speeding up the checking process and ensuring the consistency of annotation (Objective 5; Pan & Wong, under preparation). The project website (https://digital.lib.hkbu.edu.hk/cepic/index.php) features free search and downloadable resources for practitioners and students who aim to enhance their skills of Chinese/English language interpreting, including the possibility of searching for paralinguistic features (Objective 6). The corpora of the study, amounting to 6.5 million words, are included in the project website (https://digital.lib.hkbu.edu.hk/cepic/index.php), which provides open access to the corpora, and features introductory text about the corpora, manual of the search platform of the three corpora, the main search platform, a Q&A page, as well as list of publications relevant to the project (Objective 7). The website received 11,114 views till 12 Dec 2019. A FaceBook and Twitter account were also created for the corpora. In addition, till the date of this final report, a total of 3 journal articles have been published and 11 conference papers (2 invited ones) published/presented, all of which are about the project and its findings. There are also 2 journal articles/book chapters and a monograph under preparation. The aforementioned deliverables (the project website, online corpus, and over 14 publications), plus the spin-offs of the project (the organisation of an international conference and post-conference publications, and supervision of an undergraduate dissertation using the project materials), are far beyond the original plan for Objective 7, which can help to increase the impact of the project.

22608716.label: Major findings and research outcome
22608716.value: This project aims to study PMs in interpreted political speeches from Chinese to English based on the collection and annotation of Chinese/English corpora of political speeches. The major outcome of the project include: 1. A 6.5-million-word open-access corpus of political interpreting, transcribed, POS tagged and annotated with paralinguistic features (Pan, 2019b, 2019c; Pan & Wong, under preparation). The corpus can serve the needs of not only researchers, teachers and students of interpreting/translation, but also the general public, for purpose of understanding political speeches and their interpreting/translation, and/or simply language enhancement. Researchers interested in features such as PMs can access the corpus and obtain downloadable search results. 2. A project website (https://digital.lib.hkbu.edu.hk/cepic/index.php) that features the aforementioned online corpus. It also includes a list of relevant publications and notes on political interpreting, which help to deliver the project outputs to academics as well as the general public. The website received 11,114 views till 12 Dec 2019. 3. According to the project findings, there is in general a pattern of underuse of PMs in interpreted political speeches in English (Pan & Wong, 2017b, 2018b, 2019, under preparation), but the pattern is complicated by the use of specific PMs (Pan, 2018c, Pan & Wong, 2017a, 2018a) and by different parameters including mode of interpreting, source speech type, source language and speech modality (Pan, 2019a, 2019d; Pan & Wong, 2017b, 2018b, under preparation). 4. Interpreters were found to employ strategies such as intensification, total equivalence, mitigation and omission when interpreting PMs into B language, and their employment of strategies vary in different political settings or on different PMs (Pan, 2018a; Pan & Wong, 2017a, 2018a). Possible influence of A language was identified when interpreting PMs in political speeches into a B language, particularly on some PMs, although sensitivity of political topics or stress of political settings may be a greater contributor to certain differences of PMs use in interpreted English speeches (Pan, 2019a; Pan & Wong, 2018a, 2019, under preparation). 5. Apart from 14 journal articles and conference papers (and a monograph and 2 more articles under preparation), spin-offs of the project include an international conference (convened by the PI, with an edited volume and a special issue as the post-conference publications [under preparation]), a special issue of a journal, and an undergraduate student dissertation, which was accomplished using the project data and materials, under the supervision of the PI.

22608716.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
22608716.value: The project will be further developed in the following ways: 1. The project website (https://digital.lib.hkbu.edu.hk/cepic/index.php) will be further enhanced and kept updated with new relevant publications. 2. The corpus will be further expanded to include more speech types, language combinations and newer materials. 3. Workshops and seminars will be given to help promote the use of the online corpus. 4. In addition, 2 journal articles/book chapters and a monograph are under preparation, to help to disseminate the project findings.

22608716.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
22608716.value: This project aims to study pragmatic markers (PMs), i.e. the linguistic signals concerning the communication functions of the language, in interpreted political speeches from Chinese to English. The research work consists of two parts: the first part involves the collection and compilation of corpora (i.e., computer readable texts transcribed and annotated based on relevant videos/audios) of Chinese/English political interpreting, and the second part the annotation and analysis of PMs. The project findings indicate a specific pattern of PM use by interpreters, which is indicative of their communicative strategy preference. Interpreters' communicative strategies are significantly different from native speakers. The differences, apart from showing possible influence from the mother tongue (and culture) of the interpreters, demonstrate possible stress caused by interpreting in political settings. These findings help us to learn more about the work of the interpreters and the special features of political speeches, both of which require high-level communication skills. Moreover, the project website (https://digital.lib.hkbu.edu.hk/cepic/index.php), which feature the online search of the corpora of the project, provides valuable resources for researchers, teachers and students who are interested in knowing about interpreting in political settings, and those who are looking for resources for the improvement of communication skills in general.

22609216.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
22609216.value: This project examines two of the critical transformations of the nineteenth century: the rise of the modern corporation and the development of the modern city. By looking at the relationship between the first railroad corporation in the United States, the Baltimore & Ohio (B&O), and its terminal city, Baltimore, this project shows that these two processes were intertwined in ways that historians have not yet recognized. Studying the corporation through the lens of urban history will contribute to a rapidly developing field, the history of capitalism. Historians have been attentive to the cultural dimensions of nineteenth-century capitalism, but this project will emphasize its spatial dynamics: the ways in which the development of capitalist institutions and ideologies entailed remaking urban space and reimagining economic geography. The railroad is widely recognized as a crucial agent in the development of the global economy, noted particularly for its critical role in the nineteenth-century’s “annihilation of time and space.” The unprecedented challenges of coordinating operations across hundreds of miles led railroad companies to develop business practices that later became standard procedures for large corporations. Yet the earliest railroads began not as engines of private profit but as agents of urban ambition. Baltimore’s municipal government launched the B&O in 1827 as a public project in the hopes that it would bolster the local economy. By 1877, though, the B&O’s private stockholders unhinged the company from its local moorings in order to manage it as an independent profit-seeking entity. This project suggests that to understand how an ambitious municipal project became a modern capitalist enterprise, we must look to an unlikely place – the city street. Applying tools of spatial analysis from urban studies to the field of business history, it will argue that competing visions of capitalism developed amid conflicts over the use of public space. As the railroad placed iron tracks in public thoroughfares to funnel shipments through Baltimore, it remade the street as a place of mechanized movement within a privately controlled communications system. In doing so, railroad executives reimagined the city as a “mere place of transit,” a node in a transnational economic network. It is a conception of the city that survives to this day in the notion of the “global city,” a place defined by its position in worldwide information systems. This project aims to show that the streets of nineteenth-century Baltimore can help us understand the origins of twenty-first century urbanism. 本研究項目探討十九世紀兩項至關重要的變革：現代企業的興起和現代城市的發展。通過考查美國首家鐵路公司——巴爾的摩與俄亥俄鐵路（巴俄鐵路）——與終站城市巴爾的摩之間的關係，本研究展示這兩項變革實際上是以史學家尚未洞悉的方式相互牽繫的。透過城市史的視角研究企業，有助於探討資本主義歷史這一發展蓬勃的學術領域。史學家對十九世紀資本主義的文化層面多有關注，但本研究項目著眼於其空間動態層面：資本主義體制及意識形態發展以何種方式重塑城市空間、重新構想經濟地理學。 巴俄鐵路被公認為經濟全球化發展的重要動力，尤以其對十九世紀“消滅時空”的關鍵作用著稱。跨越數百英里整合營運，這項前所未有的挑戰促使鐵路公司開展商業管理，這些管理措施及後成為大企業的標準規程。然而，最早的鐵路公司並非私人利益的動力泵，而是城市化藍圖的推進器。1827年，巴爾的摩市政府創立公共項目性質的巴俄鐵路公司，希望它拉動地方經濟。不過到1877年，該公司的私人股東使之與當地泊船區脫鉤，經營為一個獨立的盈利性企業。 本研究項目指出，要理解一個構想宏偉的市政項目如何轉變成現代資本主義企業，必須考察一個看似無關的地方——城市街道。通過將城市研究中的空間分析應用於商業史領域，本研究項目指出，一些新的資本主義觀點正是在對公共空間運用的爭議中產生的。當鐵路公司在城市大街鋪設鐵軌，使漕運貨物通過巴爾的摩集散，它就將街道重塑為私人操控的交通系統內一個機械化調度場所。由此，鐵路公司主管便將城市重新構想為一個“純粹的運輸場所”，跨國經濟網中的一個交匯點。當今“全球城市”的概念正來源於巴爾的摩的城市定位，即以其在世界信息系統中的位置來界定的城市。本研究項目旨在展示，十九世紀巴爾的摩的街道有助於我們理解二十一世紀城市化的起源。

22609216.label: Realisation of objectives
22609216.value: The Early Career Scheme Grant enabled me to complete research and writing on a monograph that will, I hope, make a critical contribution to the historiography of capitalism and the city. Funding from the ECS enabled me to hire research assistants who tracked down new material and prepared visual aids for the final manuscript, to attend conferences at which I disseminated and tested my ideas, to conduct additional archival research that has materially shaped by findings, and to take the time necessary to accommodate and respond to feedback from peer reviewers. The outcome of this work is a book contract with the University of Chicago Press. I expect that my manuscript, now titled Steam City: Railroads, Urban Space, and Corporate Capitalism in Nineteenth-Century Baltimore will be published in 2020 or 2021 (objective 4). This book intervenes in a number of fields: urban history, the history of capitalism, cultural and historical geography, railroad history, and nineteenth-century U.S. history. It argues that two of the signal transformations of the nineteenth century—the rise of the industrial metropolis and the proliferation of railroad routes—were intertwined in ways that scholars have not yet recognized. Typically, historians portray these as complementary, even symbiotic phenomena: railroads, after all, facilitated the concentration of trade at urban centers, while cities’ burgeoning populations and manufacturing enterprises furnished traffic for the railroads. This received narrative takes for granted that railroad corporations were the agents and municipalities the sites of economic development. Yet at the dawn of the railroad age, as my research has shown, people understood the railroad quite differently. Rather than think of railroads as private corporations, they envisioned them as urban improvements, means by which to bolster cities’ economic development. This represented an expansive vision of urbanism, one in which cities—that is, urban publics, acting collectively as investors or through the agency of their mayors and city councils—launched projects that were to stretch hundreds of miles beyond the city limits, rewriting economic geography itself. This project sought to understand how the nineteenth-century railroad went from being an adjunct of urban prosperity to the epitome of private enterprise. To do so, I focused on the Baltimore & Ohio, the first railroad in the United States, and its relationship to its terminal city, Baltimore (objective 1). In 1827, the citizens of Baltimore, seeking to reverse their city’s ailing economic fortunes, placed their hopes in a novel technology, the railroad. By building a railroad across the Appalachian Mountains to the Ohio River Valley, they hoped to capture a hinterland and channel commerce toward their harbor, counteracting the effects of New York’s Erie Canal. They thought of the railroad as a public enterprise and accordingly lavished it with public funds: between 1827 and 1853, when the B&O reached its destination on the Ohio River, the mayor and city council devoted in excess of $10 million to the enterprise, an extraordinary sum for that era. Yet the railroad’s long-awaited completion to the Ohio also marked in many ways the end of its commitment to the urban public weal. Starting in the 1850s, private stockholders pushed a new vision for the B&O, one that privileged profits over urban development. To do so, however, they needed first to shed their urban origins and define the outlook and purpose of a private corporation. This was, at its core, a spatial process, a struggle over the physical form of the city itself. Stockholders laid the groundwork for the privatization of the railroad and the subordination of the city long before the B&O reached the Ohio River. Fights between public and private objectives on the rail line began in the 1830s as conflicts over control of the street. In 1831, the B&O pioneered the practice of laying tracks through city streets in order to bring goods to the port and forge connections with other rail lines. Railroads in other cities heeded the B&O’s example and followed suit. But railroads found that urban space posed unique challenges to their operations, as the presence of a dense urban population subjected their traffic to interruption, protest, and regulation. Over fierce public outcry, advocates of a privatized B&O articulated a new vision of the city, one that cast Baltimore and other municipalities not as economic agents, but as sites for investment. They argued that goods should circulate as freely within the city as without. To realize this vision, they built specialized port and depot facilities, lobbied for unrestricted use of steam power, and ultimately routed rail traffic around the urban core through a system of tunnels, deep cuts, and harbor ferries. In converting the nineteenth-century walking city into a site of mechanized movement, they opened up new ways of thinking about urbanism, the corporation, and capitalism itself. They formulated a new spatial logic for corporate capitalism, one that tied the free movement of goods to the free flow of capital in a system that located competition and economic agency in private enterprise (objective 2). Examining Baltimore’s trajectory from an urban public capable of projecting a major rail line to a place of transit whose economic fortunes are determined by forces beyond its control sheds new light on the spatial logic of globalization. Today the city is bounded, its field of legitimate action circumscribed territorially. The corporation, by contrast, owes little allegiance to place and can shift the site of production as costs of labor or tax burdens warrant. As I argue in the book, turning our attention to nineteenth-century Baltimore can help us understand the place of the city in contemporary global capitalism (objective 3). I could not have written this book without the RGC’s generous support. The ECS provided me with funds to hire research assistants and student helpers, and to attend academic conferences. Research assistants scoured nineteenth-century newspapers for useful materials and prepared maps that I will use in the final manuscript. Their contributions have made this a richer and more professional-looking book. At the conferences, meanwhile, I presented papers on railroad tunnels, the Civil War, and locomotive policy, receiving helpful feedback from an international audience of scholars that has in turn shaped the way I frame my arguments in the book. The most substantial and most important assistance from the ECS came in the form of teaching relief. Teaching relief furnished the time I needed to conduct additional research and revise the manuscript. This proved especially important after I received the first round of readers’ reports from the peer reviewers, who offered productive but challenging comments. In the first semester of teaching relief, in addition to doing the work required to bring my chapters in line with their suggestions, I conducted additional research in Baltimore, locating materials in the B&O archive that helped me understand the company’s internal dynamics and its relationship to its terminal city. The second round of peer review coincided with my second semester of teaching relief. This round – which ultimately led to a book contract – called for revisions that broadened the scope of the project, and spoke to the significance of the Baltimore case study for a broader national and even global narrative. I could not have executed these revisions in a timely fashion without this support.

22609216.label: Major findings and research outcome
22609216.value: As noted above, the earliest American railroads were conceived as urban improvements, ways to bolster cities’ economies; within a generation, though, they became the country’s premier private corporations. Examining the urban history of the railroad thus affords an opportunity to rethink the role of the city in the history of capitalism and the development of private enterprise more generally. In Steam City (forthcoming, see Part C), I argue that the rise of the private corporation as an economic agent and the spatial configuration of the industrial metropolis were structurally intertwined: the development of modern capitalist institutions and ideologies was predicated on the cultivation of new understandings of economic geography and the production of new types of urban space. Making corporate capitalism meant making the capitalist city – a space for investment and movement, its political powers contained by its borders. I reach these conclusions through close attention to material found in municipal and corporate archives, two sources rarely used in tandem. Reading internal corporate documents alongside petitions to the city council, complemented with a rich print culture (including newspapers, pamphlets, and maps), I was able to track the ways in which citizens’ and railroad managers’ understandings of the city diverged in the nineteenth century, and reconstruct the ways in which the city became a place of transit in a capitalist network managed and coordinated by private corporations. In addition to the major historiographical contributions noted above, Steam City also intervenes in a number of historical subfields. It contains, for example, a chapter on the circulation of money in the 1830s and 1840s. Paper money was highly controversial at that time, as its opponents deemed it too far removed from real value; by reconstructing a scheme through which the B&O issued its own currency, I contribute to scholars’ understanding of “the money question.” Similarly, through this manuscript and a conference presentation (see Part C), this research has shed new light on popular attitudes towards the steam engine in American cities at this time. Other contributions include a reconsideration of the origins of postbellum populism, the reconstruction of alternative ways of thinking about labor and its relationship to corporate enterprise, and discussion of the urban history of the Civil War (see Part C).

22609216.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
22609216.value: Having received a contract from the University of Chicago Press, I am now making final revisions before submitting the manuscript to the editors. From that point, there will be one more round of revisions (though not of peer review), followed by a production process that should bring the book into print in 2020 or 2021. Steam City raises new questions about the varieties and meanings of movement in the nineteenth century city, and I hope to take these up in my next project, a study of traffic before the automobile in New York City. Research for this project will take me into new archives, and allow me to explore the contested practices of mobility in nineteenth-century Manhattan.

22609216.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
22609216.value: We tend to think of the American railroad as the epitome of nineteenth-century private enterprise. Railroads were the first modern, large-scale businesses; they reshaped the economy and pioneered corporate organizational structures. In the United States, though, before the railroad was a private business, it was a public venture—an instrument designed to funnel trade into particular cities, and funded by urban governments. To understand the railroad’s transition from an urban improvement to a private enterprise, we have to look to an unlikely place: the city street. The same years that saw the rise of the railroad also saw significant transformations in urban form, as compact walking cities gave way to sprawling industrial metropolises. This project argues that these developments, usually understood separately, were closely intertwined. Building railroad networks involved laying tracks through city streets and ultimately remaking the city as a place of transit. Drawing on archival research, I demonstrate that as railroad executives fought with urban citizens over the right to use urban space, they also came to think of their enterprises as private corporations. Understanding the urban history of the railroad sheds new light on the origins of both the private corporation and the modern city.

22611516.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
22611516.value: Global health ethics is a sub-field of bioethics and the philosophy of public health. One of the most important questions in global health ethics concerns the ethics of human rights to health. Rights to health are not the same as rights to be healthy. Rights to health simply refer to the obligations that governments or other agents should establish policies to promote health and prevent fatal diseases, so that suffering and premature death could be prevented. If human rights to health are universal moral rights, then everyone has these rights morally and hence there are questions about moral obligations we have to each other. On the one hand, some scholars argue that we do have moral obligations to global health and everyone has human rights to health as specified in international documents. On the other hand, some scholars argue that we do not have these rights, or these rights seem impossible to satisfy in the current conditions of the world, and so it is unrealistic to claim that everyone has human rights to health. The PI will investigate the ethics of human rights to health in this research project. Particularly, the PI will answer why human rights to health are universal moral rights. The PI will evaluate and compare different ethical theories and seek out a moral foundation for the universality of human rights to health. The following ethical theories will be discussed in detail: the capability approach in the ethics of global development, both the feminist and non-feminist versions of the ethics of care, and different versions of contemporary Confucian thoughts. The PI will evaluate them and investigate how the interaction among these ethical theories provides a moral foundation for human rights to health, and compare this moral foundation with other ethical traditions such as Kantian deontology and utilitarianism. The PI will also reply to challenges to human rights to health from different ethical perspectives. Although this project mainly aims at solving philosophical problems, it is also related to some practical issues, such as using and analyzing social media data pertaining to global health ethics. The PI will discuss how the practical issues in global health affect the ethical theories, apply the philosophical findings of this research project to the practical issues of global health, reply to some empirical challenges to human rights to health, and discuss how to apply these findings in the current global public health system. 全球衛生倫理學可說是生命倫理學和公共衛生哲學的分支。而全球衛生倫理學的其中一個重要課題就是衛生人權倫理學。衛生權利並不是說每個人都要有健康的權利；衛生權利更多是關於政府和每一個人應該有甚麼責任去建立公共衛生政策、促進大家的健康、防止致命疾病的擴散以避免無謂的受苦和過早的死亡等等。如果衛生人權是普遍的道德權利，那就是說每個人道德上都有這樣的權利，亦因此帶來了我們彼此有甚麼道德責任的問題。一邊廂，有些學者論證我們確實有對全球衛生的道德責任，而每個人亦都有國際文件中明確列出的衛生人權。另一邊廂，有些學者卻論證我們沒有這樣的權利，又或者當今世界的情況令我們不可能滿足這些權利的內容，亦因此要求所有人都有衛生人權是不切實際的。 本研究項目是關於衛生人權倫理學，目的是為了回答為何衛生人權是普遍道德權利的問題。首席研究員會評估和比較不同的倫理學理論以嘗試尋找衛生人權的普遍性的道德基礎。涉及的倫理學理論包括全球發展倫理學中的能力進路、女性主義和非女性主義的關顧進路，和一些現代儒家思想。首席研究員會評估和研究這些理論能否為衛生人權提供道德基礎， 亦會與另一些諸如效益主義或康德義務論的倫理學傳統作出比較。首席研究員亦會回應一些來自不同道德觀點對衛生人權的挑戰。 儘管這個研究項目的主要目標是探討哲學問題，但亦會涉及一些現實的課題，例如社交媒體與全球衛生倫理學的關係。首席研究員會討論這些全球衛生的現實課題對倫理學的影響、把本研究項目的哲學發現應用在全球衛生的現實課題、回應一些從經驗上對衛生人權的挑戰、和討論如何把研究所得成果應用在全球公共衛生系統。

22611516.label: Realisation of objectives
22611516.value: This research project has achieved all five objectives. These objectives are interconnected with each other and so it is hard to discuss the realization of each of them separately. Instead, it is better to describe all of them together. This research project is a philosophical investigation of the discourses on human rights in global health ethics (in short, ‘the ethics of human rights to health’). Human rights to health are part of family of economic, social and cultural rights, which are known as the “second generation of human rights.” Human rights to health are affirmed in many international documents, such as Article 25 of Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Article 12 of the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights and the Preamble to the Constitution of the World Health Organization. Nevertheless, these documents are not philosophical papers. The ethical issues concerning these rights remain controversial. Therefore, a theory of human rights to health can be considered as a developing topic in the field of global health ethics, which is a new sub-discipline within the broader fields of bioethics and the philosophy of public health. In order to construct comprehensive philosophical arguments that explain why human rights to health are universal moral rights, and show how these arguments deal with various philosophical challenges to those rights, we need to examine and compare different ethical theories so that a moral foundation of human rights to health can be identified. To achieve these goals, we also need to explore the possibility of developing a conceptual framework for the study of bioethics and the philosophy of public health within the context of human rights to health. Based on these understandings, the Principal Investigator (PI) conducted philosophical research in the discourses on ethical theories concerning a moral foundation for the human right to health. There are various normative accounts of human rights, and philosophers usually disagree on which ethical theory is the best, and it is unclear how different ethical theories may apply in the discourses on human rights to health. In this research project, the PI has evaluated and analyzed various ethical theories, and the result is that the PI argues for a consequential evaluation of international human rights. It is important to emphasize the importance of human rights in international legal documents (in short, “international human rights”). Some scholars, such as Allen Buchanan, argue that international human rights are morally significant in their practice and international human rights are not necessarily justified by deontology or a rights-based approach only; indeed, some international human rights are not traditional absolute rights. The PI agrees with this claim and argues further that consequential evaluation, especially the version suggested by Amartya Sen, is at least one of the possible ways to develop a normative account of international human rights. There are now more and more discussions on how consequential evaluation is relevant to human rights. One may assert that Sen’s consequential evaluation is a methodology for practical reasoning, not a comprehensive moral theory. One implication of Sen’s idea is that consequential evaluation is unavoidable in normative ethics. Consequential evaluation deserves more attention in the current human rights literature. The PI argues that such a consequential evaluation of international human rights can further develop and explain the idea on the minimal account of human rights (roughly, it means that human rights are some minimal mora values) even better. Based on this understanding of the ethics of human rights, the PI has argued further how to use this in the discussion of human rights to health. The PI has investigated how the interactions between his idea and different ethical theories and traditions, and how the project has contributed to and reformulated the ethical theories concerning the human rights to health. This research project has also provided philosophical replies to some of the challenges to the ethics of human rights to health through a discussion of what these arguments call for in practice. The ethical theories and challenges discussed in this project include the challenge from Christianity, Confucianism, Ubuntu ethics, and Utilitarianism. For example, the PI has argued that that it is better to use consequential evaluation than cultural evaluation to justify human rights to health. Although Confucianism or Ubuntu are not any form of consequentialism, this does not mean that they cannot tell us what good consequences are in some situations. The project has also covered ideas such as the moral significance of International human rights to health and the capability approach. The PI has also replied to the challenge from cultural relativism, the challenge of moral obligations, and the challenge of resource-allocation in the project. The replies to these challenges have clarified the issues and advance both the study of bioethics and the philosophy of public health. These discussions also help people to build a moral consensus for global health. In practical terms, this research project has also examined empirical cases of public health issues as a means of developing practical arguments for an ethics of human rights to health, and as a way to show how these ethical principles can be applied in the current global public health system. The PI has investigated the feasibility of various solutions to the issues surrounding human rights to health. The PI has also closely examined the challenges involved in applying ethical principles for meeting major challenges in global public health. For example, this project has involved different cultural traditions, such as East Asian and African traditions, which are related to many empirical cases. The PI has also discussed the ethical issues of the involvements of American health professionals in enhanced interrogation. The PI has also investigated some practical privacy issues related to human rights to health. In general, the findings of this project has contributed to the discussion about how practical issues of global health affect ethical theories, and how developments in ethics can be applied to global public health operations. More precisely, this project has indicated how the principles of human rights to health can be implemented for reducing suffering worldwide, how human rights to health can guide practical and realistic solutions (even with the limited resources available), and how the findings of this research project can be applied within the current global public health system. Lastly, it is also important to notice that the PI has published some journal articles and a book chapter, and another journal article has been accepted already. Some preliminary findings are presented in different international conferences as well. The details of these outputs are discussed in other sections of this report.
