22611516.label: Major findings and research outcome
22611516.value: As mentioned in the realization of objectives (section 5.3), the PI has evaluated and analyzed various ethical theories, and the major findings and research outcome is that the PI argues for a consequential evaluation of international human rights. The PI also finds that such a consequential evaluation of international human rights can further develop and explain the idea on the minimal account of human rights. The PI has also used these ideas to discuss some human rights debates on Christianity, Confucianism, Ubuntu ethics, and Utilitarianism. For example, the PI has argued that that it is better to use consequential evaluation than cultural evaluation to justify human rights to health. The PI has also examined empirical cases of public health issues in the ethics of human rights to health. These findings are published in one academic book chapter, three academic journal articles, and presented in various academic conferences. Particularly, the book chapter “Are International Human Rights Universal? – East-West Philosophical Debates on Human Rights to Liberty and Health” represents the work from the PI on applying minimal account of human rights into the debate on human rights to health. This chapter is published in an academic book in Europe for the 70th anniversary of Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR). The book is later translated in Italian and published in Italy in 2020. The article “A Preliminary Consequential Evaluation of the Roles of Cultures in Human Rights Debates” discusses consequential evaluation of international human rights, Confucianism, and Ubuntu ethics. “Enhanced Interrogation, Consequential Evaluation, and Human Rights to Health” discusses consequential evaluation, utilitarianism, and the ethical issues of the involvements of American health professionals in enhanced interrogation. Lastly, “A Consequential Evaluation of a Christian Approach to International Human Rights” discusses consequential evaluation of international human rights and Christianity. This paper is already accepted and going to be published in 2020. The PI has also presented some new ideas in different conferences. For example, the PI has investigated some practical privacy issues related to human rights to health, and how the capability approach can be related to his idea on human rights to health. For further details, please see Part C, Section 8 and Section 9.

22611516.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
22611516.value: There are various possibilities for further development of the research project. Theoretically, a minimal account of the consequential evaluation of international human rights can be further compared with other theories such as the capability approach, deontology, and other natural law and natural rights theories. In general, it is important to compare consequential evaluation with non-consequential evaluation. The comparison between consequential evaluation and cultural evaluation is also a potential direction that this research project can develop further. Another related research development is about what moral values are important consequences in the debate on human rights to health. In practical terms, this research project can further examine the challenges involved in applying ethical principles for meeting major empirical challenges or applications in global public health. For example, one of the practical issues considered will be the analysis and use of social media data in relation to global health ethics. Other practical problems of pandemic or epidemic are also related to human rights to health. In general, further development of this research project will contribute to the discussion about how practical issues of global health affect ethical theories, and how developments in ethics can be applied to global public health operations.

22611516.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
22611516.value: In the era of globalization, many health issues are not confined by national boundaries, but also problems for the whole world. Global health issues raise a lot of questions in ethics. Global health ethics is a sub-field of bioethics and the philosophy of public health, specifically focusing on answering these ethical questions. One of the most important questions in global health ethics concerns the ethics of human rights to health. This research project uses a minimal account of the consequential evaluation of international human rights to explain the moral significances of human rights to health. This research project evaluates and analyses various ethical traditions, including Christianity, Confucianism, Ubuntu ethics, and Utilitarianism. This research project also provides philosophical replies to some of the challenges to the ethics of human rights to health through a discussion of what these arguments call for in practice. These challenges include the challenge from cultural evaluation, the challenge of moral obligations, and the challenge of resource-allocation. In practical terms, this research project investigates the feasibility of various solutions to the issues surrounding human rights to health.

22612016.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
22612016.value: 中文摘要 全球化往往伴隨著家庭成員的離散各地。過往的研究已經證實，許多移居海外的華人，其父母卻因為各種理由仍然留在故鄉。然而，現有的跨國家庭的研究，往往偏重從子女的觀點，探討跨國家庭代間關係與老人照顧的協商。另一方面，留在故鄉的父母，與其主要照顧者的經驗則往往被系統性忽略。為了補強以往研究的不足，本研究將以中國大陸作為個案，探討跨國家庭中的年長者與其主要照顧提供者，在實際面、情感面，與文化面所面對的種種挑戰與變化。透過訪談父母與其主要照顧者，本研究將探討跨國家庭中的年長者， 如何思考與因應老化過程中出現的各種需求。此外，本研究也將分析，父母與子女（包括海外子女與其他國內親屬）在協商與提供照顧工作的過程中，如何重構彼此間的權利義務關係，並且發展出對應的處理方式。換言之，本研究試圖呈現跨國家庭中留居故鄉的父母，其感受、體驗與實踐如何受到跨國親族網路的左右與模塑。藉此，筆者試圖補足甚至挑戰既有文獻單單關注移民子女經驗的缺失，進而對現有的跨國家庭文獻作出貢獻。

22612016.label: Realisation of objectives
22612016.value: To date, we have interviewed 120 caregivers for left-behind parents – parents who have children emigrating abroad – in mainland China (Shenzhen, Guangdong Province and Beijing). These caregivers include (1) 85 stay-behind siblings and (2) 35 paid caregivers. All of the respondents we included in this sample are the primary caregivers for parents who are no longer independent or self-sufficient. In addition, we interviewed 80 left-behind parents in mainland China (Shenzhen, Guangdong Province and Beijing). Our qualitative interviews generate rich data on (1) how family caregivers back home negotiate relationships with their emigrating siblings abroad, (2) how paid and unpaid caregivers differentiate spatial and social boundaries between one another, and (3) how emigrating adult children position themselves in a cross-border network. We initially encountered some problems when recruiting the siblings who are responsible for taking care of stay-behind parents. Many of these siblings refused to be interviewed because they were reluctant to talk about the conflicts that they experience with their siblings who live overseas. We ended up recruiting sufficient sibling to be interviewed through our personal and professional networks.

22612016.label: Major findings and research outcome
22612016.value: Findings on Parents The findings suggest that most of the parents fashion their expectations of intergenerational reciprocity and emphasize the importance of staying independent and self-sufficient as they transition to a later stage of life. At the same time, these parents valued their connections to their children and reported a number of strategies (e.g. gifts, money, visits, communication, practical care, and the provision of emotional as well as moral support) that they and their globally-dispersed children fostered to sustain relationships. The constellation of material and symbolic resources that parents and their children have profoundly shapes their thoughts, perspectives, and feelings about how they consider family ideals and how they address life transitions. Findings on Caregivers Back Home Our findings point to the necessity of a relational analysis of how caregivers reflect upon their membership within care networks. More specifically, we shows that transnational relocation creates four type of relational patterns: (1) collaboration, (2) intrusion/interference, (3) voluntary takeover, and (4) feeling left behind. To delineate how intimate relations are constructed in the context of transnational aging, we identify two primary analytical axes on the perspectives of the caregivers in the homeland: (1) how these caregivers perceived roles that emigrating siblings play in family networks of support (e.g. active participation and minimal/lack of participation) (2) whether these roles are aligned or misaligned with the expectations of primary caregivers back home. Based on these two proxies, we carve out four types of intimacies in the context of long-distance elder care. These typologies are (1) collaboration, (2) intrusion and interference, (3) voluntary takeover, and (4) feeling left behind. To be sure, these typologies are conceptually distinct, but empirically interrelated. The relationship between respondents and their emigrating siblings varies across time and situations. Some are able to repair the relationships after experiencing tension and conflicts that stem from managing family crisis, but most aren’t. Importance of Time and Temporalities Finally, we found that temporal factors – such as length of stay in the home and host societies, age at the time of migration, and life-cycle stage – are essential to analyzing migrants’ experiences. These findings have significant implications for the study of transnational families, testifying to the ways in which time, age, or life stage affects the emotional responses of members of transnational families.

22612016.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
22612016.value: I will start to care out publications from the data that has been collected. The target journals include Social Problems, Aging and Society, and Journal of Aging Issues. In addition, I am in the process of applying for grants to conduct a new research on emigrant children with parents who remain back home. Doing so will allow me to triangulate the perspectives of migrant adult children with their stay-behind family members.

22612016.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
22612016.value: The impact of geographic proximity on family intimacy should be analyzed through the myriad ways in which caregivers align expectations with perceived reality. To date, gerontological research tends to view physical distance as barriers that prevent from siblings to sharing the responsibilities of caring for aging parents. By contrast, scholars of transnational aging has underscored the ability of emigrants to transcend physical distance and share the responsibilities of elder care with siblings back home. To reconcile the competing explanations that exist in gerontological research and transnational family studies, we call for a relational approach to analyzing the dynamics internal to cross-border care network. Using the concept of “relational alignment,” we argue that understanding solidarity, conflicts and ambivalence in the contexts of family crisis requires a close examination of how members of a care network assess each other’s roles and contributions. This explains why the ongoing circulation of advice, information, money, people, and emotions is thought of as helpful resources in some cases but perceived as constraints in others.

23100216.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
23100216.value: 在亞洲，淡水龜類正走向滅絕之路。龜類不僅是中國傳統文化的重要標誌之一（代表智慧、健康和長壽），而且在生態系統的營養循環中（如分解物質）扮演著重要的角色，因此野生龜類的尋找和保育工作迫在眉睫。香港在龜類的保育方面具有得天獨厚的優勢，這是由於在當地仍然存在龜類的野生種群，然而在實際的保育工作中仍存在一個主要瓶頸即如何找到野生龜類，傳統的籠捕調查法不僅耗時耗力，而且成功率低，就好比在一個巨大的湖泊中尋找稀少的魚類。 新的環境DNA技術（以下簡稱eDNA）在尋找野生龜類方面具有很好的前景，該技術通過從空氣、水或土壤樣本中提取動物向環境中釋放的DNA（來自皮膚，配子，唾液，糞便和血液等）來尋找物種，因此相比傳統的籠捕法，eDNA技術更為快速、廉價和準確。目前eDNA技術在水生脊椎動物領域已有很多成功的應用先例，包括龜類。本項目的目標是通過改進現有的eDNA技術來尋找、監測和保護香港的龜類。我們會利用eDNA技術達到三個目的，首先我們會找到並評估五種香港本土龜類的豐富度，這些信息將服務於今後的研究並作為長期監測的基礎數據；其次我們要實地檢驗已有的針對紅耳龜（Trachemys scripta elegans）的eDNA檢測方案。紅耳龜在香港屬於入侵物種，它們會與本土龜類競爭並導致它們的滅絕，因此分析紅耳龜的eDNA可以幫助我們尋找和追踪紅耳龜並了解它們對本土龜類的影響；最後我們會定期（每年四次，共三年）從研究地點採集水樣來系統檢測eDNA的時間變化趨勢。這些信息可以幫助研究人員判斷eDNA是否存在時間變化規律，如果存在，那麼可以在生物釋放eDNA最多的時期採樣以提高檢測的準確率。 本項目的成功實施將產生兩個主要成果。首先，這些數據可以直接促進香港淡水龜類的保育工作。我們會與政府部門和非政府組織合作，為他們制定有效的保育措施提供科學數據；其次，這項工作可以檢驗和改進eDNA技術在龜類保育中的實用性，今後可以將該技術推廣至中國大陸，亞洲以及世界其他地區的瀕危龜類研究和保育工作。

23100216.label: Realisation of objectives
23100216.value: 1) Refine an existing eDNA method to detect and monitor Hong Kong’s five endangered freshwater turtle species: Cuora trifasciata, Mauremys reevesii, Pelodiscus sinensis, Platysternon megacephalum, and Sacalia bealei. (90% complete) This objective required 2 steps. I detail each of the steps below. (a) Develop a species-specific assay for five turtle species Originally, I had planned on developing assays for five species native to Hong Kong (Cuora trifasciata, Mauremys reevesii, Pelodiscus sinensis, Platysternon megacephalum, and Sacalia bealei). The success of developing assays depends on the available data in GenBank, as well as the relationship of the target species to closely related non-target species. The more closely related a target and non-target species are, the more similar the DNA sequences are, and the more difficult it is to make species-specific primers. After laboratory testing, I found out that it was difficult to develop assays for three of the target species. Due to limitations of time and money (developing and testing qPCR probes is expensive), and the non-guarantee that I could be successful with additional work, I decided to stop pursuing the development of three species-specific assays (Cuora trifasciata, Sacalia bealei, Mauremys reevesii). However, I was still successful in developing species-specific assays for the other two species (Platysternon megacephalum, Pelodiscus sinensis). This work was published in a peer-reviewed paper (Lam et al. 2020, Developing quantitative PCR assays to detect threatened and invasive freshwater turtles in Hong Kong using environmental DNA, Conservation Genetics Resources). (b) Collect and screen water samples. A total of 492 water samples were collected for this study (41 sites x 3 years x 4 times/year = 492 samples). Despite rigorously testing the three assays against a variety of eDNA samples, the only reliable assay was for Platysternon megacephalum. It is unclear why the performance of the eDNA assay for Pelodiscus sinensis was inconsistent. The data from the work on Platysternon megacephalum was prepared for a publication that is under review (Lam et al., Using eDNA techniques to find the endangered big-headed turtles [Platysternon megacephalum], PLoS One). The first round of reviews was completed (major revision), and I have edited and resubmitted the manuscript. I consider this objective to be 90% complete since I was unsuccessful in developing assays for three proposed species, and the implementation of one assay. Being unable to develop a species-specific assay is likely due to two factors out of our control—the presence of closely-related species and/or the limited amount of publicly available data. I spent almost two years testing, trying different primer sets. In the end, I decided to stop testing to make progress and complete the other objectives. 2) Field-test the eDNA method developed by Davy et al. (2015) to track T. s. elegans, a nonnative, invasive turtle species in Hong Kong, and study its effect on native species. (90% complete) Originally, I planned to use the species-specific primers for T. s. elegans developed by Davy et al. (2015), developing a qPCR probe. However, through the PCR specificity tests, I found that the primers were not species specific, amplifying other turtle species in the Emydidae family. Therefore, I started from the first step and developed new species-specific primers-probe for T. s. elegans. As the Davy et al (2015) assay was not suitable for our purpose, I proposed in the 2018 annual report to revise Objective #2 to state “Develop and test an eDNA assay to track T. s. elegans, a non-native, invasive turtle species in Hong”. I successfully developed a new qPCR assay for T. s. elegans, which was published in a peer reviewed paper (Lam et al. 2020, Developing quantitative PCR assays to detect threatened and invasive freshwater turtles in Hong Kong using environmental DNA, Conservation Genetics Resources). Unfortunately, the performance of the assay for T. s. elegans was inconsistent, so the data were not suitable for publication. I consider this objective to be 90% complete because I was unsuccessful in screening field samples. I was successful in developing a species-specific assay, but the results were inconsistent when dealing with field-collected water samples. I repeatedly tested water samples, but was unable to achieve consistent results. Due to time and money constraints, I felt it was necessary to stop this work. 3) Study temporal variation in eDNA detection. (100% complete) Each of the sites was sampled each of the four seasons (spring, summer, autumn, winter) for three years. In our successful screening for Platysternon megacephalum, I included an analysis of whether eDNA detection varied across seasons. I found that it did not. Instead, eDNA detection seemed to be influenced more by the population size. These results are included in the manuscript currently under review (Lam et al., Using eDNA techniques to find the endangered big-headed turtles [Platysternon megacephalum], PLoS One). 4) Use results to develop effective conservation of Hong Kong freshwater turtles by working with non-governmental organisations (Kadoorie Farms and Botanical Gardens, Hong Kong Society of Herpetology Foundation) and governmental departments (Agriculture, Fisheries, and Conservation Department). (80% complete) As required by the formal collaboration with Kadoorie Farms and Botanic Gardens, I submitted all annual and final reports. I have also informally discussed the results with Hong Kong Society of Herpetology Foundation and Agriculture, Fisheries, and Conservation Department. I consider this objective to be 80% complete because no tangible conservation measures have developed from this work. I have spoken to each of the organizations and the response has been positive. Unfortunately, due to the COVID-19 situation, work priorities in these organizations have shifted and progress has slowed. However, after this final report is submitted, I will continue to contact these organizations to leverage this project towards improved turtle conservation in Hong Kong.

23100216.label: Major findings and research outcome
23100216.value: In this study, there were two major accomplishments: (1) developing eDNA assays for local Hong Kong turtles, and (2) applying the assay to study the big-headed turtle (Platysternon megacephalum) in Hong Kong. First, we developed species-specific eDNA assays for two native (Pl. megacephalum, Chinese softshell turtle [Pelodiscus sinensis]) and one introduced (red-eared slider [Trachemys scripta elegans]) turtles in Hong Kong. This work was published in a peer-reviewed, international journal (Lam et al. 2020, Conservation Genetics Resources). In this paper, we detail the methodology on how to apply these assays, as well as provide a framework for future studies to develop their own species-specific eDNA assays. Second, we applied the assay of Pl. megacephalum to study its populations in Hong Kong. A manuscript of this work was reviewed (major revisions), and we have resubmitted and are awaiting results (Lam et al., PLoS One). This species provides a unique opportunity to evaluate the effectiveness of this assay because it has been the focus of a 10-year ecological study in Hong Kong, and streams with different population sizes are known. We are able to compare results from streams with known populations, historical populations, and unknown status. We found that eDNA detection varies over time and space, and as expected, larger populations are more consistently detected. Additionally, we located new populations, which we verified through turtle observation and trapping. Lastly, we provide recommendations to advance eDNA studies, such as the influence of temperature and pH on detection. Additional impacts of this work came in the form of collaborations with other organizations (Kadoorie Farm and Botanic Garden, University of Hong Kong, Hainan Normal University, Qufu Normal University, Kasetsart University [Thailand]). So far, these collaborations have produced two scientific publications (Rujirawan et al. 2019, Journal of Natural History; So et al. 2020, Ecosphere), five successful research grants (~ HK$ 2.2 million), and a Memorandum of Understanding. These collaborations will continue to be nurtured, with a focus on eDNA and turtle conservation.

23100216.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
23100216.value: I envision two potential avenues of development of this work: (1) expanding of use of developed assays, and (2) developing new eDNA assays for other organisms. I imagine expanding the use of developed assays locally and internationally. Locally, I will continue working with NGOs and the government to find ways to apply this research to local conservation. Internationally, The big-headed turtle is also found in mainland China, Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, Thailand, and Vietnam. I have begun to contact researchers to explore extending our eDNA work in these regions. I hope to develop collaborations now, with the prospect of going overseas to do this work after the COVID-19 pandemic. For developing new eDNA assays, I have already done so collaborating with Dr. Ken SO (University of Hong Kong) to monitor the rice fish (Oryzias curvinotus). Additionally, in collaboration with Dr. Anthonu Lau (Lingnan University) we have successfully received a grant to study invasive fish and crayfish in Hong Kong. I will continue efforts to apply my experience to new eDNA projects.

23100216.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
23100216.value: Turtles are one of the most endangered animal groups in the world. The first step to study and conserve them is to capture them in the wild, which involves setting traps in streams. This work is difficult because turtle species are rare and secretive. Scientists have developed a method to help locate organisms using environmental DNA (eDNA). eDNA is the DNA left in the environment (air, water, soil) by an organism via their cells. In this study, we successfully developed an eDNA method to locate three turtle species—big-headed turtle (Platysternon megacephalum), Beale’s eyed turtle (Sacalia bealei), and red-eared slider (Trachemys scripta elegans). Next, we applied the eDNA method to study the big-headed turtle in Hong Kong. We sampled water from 41 sites across Hong Kong, four times each year, for three years. We located new populations of this endangered species, which we verified by turtle trapping. Also, we helped clarify some general details of an eDNA method—detection of turtle eDNA varied across locations and time, and as expected, streams with larger populations have more consistent detection. Our work demonstrates the effectiveness of eDNA methods and we will continue working with the government to apply it to turtle conservation.

23600416.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
23600416.value: 隨著英語遍及世界各地，過去十年，英語作為通用語的研究在應用語言學領域中有顯著發展。不過，英語作為通用語作為相對較新的學術範疇，仍然需要多作探究，尤其是英語作為通用語在亞洲的使用情況。亞洲大部分英語作為通用語的溝通牽涉英語為第二語言的使用者，他們的英語運用卻往往被學術研究忽略。世界各地的高等院校大力推廣國際化，以致大量能操多種語言的師生遍佈校園，大專院校因此為研究英語作為通用語的溝通提供一個良好平台。在香港，隨著日漸增多的內地及國際學生來港升學，英語作為通用語於課室內外都非常普遍。 是次研究旨在探討在一所使用多種語言的大學裡，以英語作為第二語言的內地及國際學生在課室內外使用英語作為通用語的交流情況。這項研究會探討內地及國際學生在使用英語作為通用語交流下的語言應用。根據研究員早年針對本地大學學生使用英語作為通用語交流的研究成果，這項研究著重於內地及國際學生為求達到互相理解及化解誤會所運用的溝通策略，並探討他們的身份建構，特別針對他們作為第二語言使用者及學習者的身份。 是次研究以定性研究方法為主，採用多種方法，進行為期一年半的數據收集。這個過程包括五名內地學生及五名國際學生作為重點參加者。除了觀察數據和相關文件資料，研究會使用兩組主要數據，分別是（一）口語交流數據（即是學生平日於校園課室內外交流中所得的電子錄音）；以及（二）訪問數據（即是與十位學生進行的深入訪談）。研究將會深入分析十位重點研究對象在使用英語作為通用語的交流情況，以辨別他們的溝通策略。另外，研究人員會與十位重點研究對象進行五輪深入的個人訪談，以便取得他們對在校園內使用英語作為通用語交流的見解及個人感受。這項縱向研究有利深入了解學生在使用溝通策略中可能出現的轉變及他們作為英語為第二語言使用者及學習者對自身身份的看法。 研究將對研究人員及教育工作者帶來顯著意義。研究將對英語作為通用語在亞洲的研究帶來貢獻，並增加對中國內地及國際學生在校園裡使用英語作為通用語溝通的理解，有助內地及國際學生融入香港校園生活。此外，調查結果對了解大學國際化也 有重要意義。最後，調查結果有助加深大學語文教師對使用英語作為通用語溝通的交際策略的理解，有助教師協助學生為應付使用英語作為通用語帶來的挑戰。

23600416.label: Realisation of objectives
23600416.value: The research project successfully achieved the original objectives as set out in the proposal. (1) The study contributed to the growing body of research on English as a lingua franca in the Asian context. It investigated the language experiences of two groups of ‘non-local’ students’ in a Hong Kong university, namely, mainland Chinese students and international students, with particular attention to their use of English as a lingua franca and other languages in the university context. The study also added to the existing body of work on language issues in international universities by pointing to international students’ complex and sophisticated understandings of English as a lingua franca in the university context, the tensions arising from the language choice between English and the local language, the co-existence of different language ideologies concerning monolingualism/multilingualism, as well as the intersections of language, social inclusion/exclusion and linguistic advantage/disadvantage. (2) The findings of the study deepened our understanding of the language practices in English as a lingua franca from the unique perspectives of mainland Chinese and international university students in Hong Kong. The study found that the majority of international students relied on English for their academic and social integration in the university, and local students’ reluctance to speak English could lead to the exclusion of international students from participating fully in the university. Moreover, the non-local students’ negotiation of participation and identities in different communities within the university appeared to involve their appropriation of different sets of discursive practices. In particular, these discursive practices were not necessarily carried out in a monolingual manner, but in a multilingual mode. Non-local students’ awareness of the monolingual/multilingual norms associated with particular communities within the university context would be important for their participation and memberships in these communities. (3) The study advanced our understanding of the complexity involved in second language identity construction and negotiation among mainland Chinese and international students in ELF settings. The study found that the non-local students’ identity negotiation in English as a lingua franca communication could be shaped by the types and amounts of linguistic capital they possessed. The findings of the study also point to the role of agency in mediating the non-local students’ negotiation of their academic and social identities in the university. Agency involves a person’s ability to make decisions and take actions. With their exercise of agency, the non-local students could make decisions as to how to draw on their existing capital in exchange for other forms of capital in their bid to (re)construct desirable identities. (4) The research project made contributions to the theorizing of the relationship between English as a lingua franca and identity by understanding mainland Chinese and international students’ language experiences. It pointed to the usefulness of linguistic capital in understanding non-local students’ identities and language experiences when using English as a lingua franca. The differential forms and amounts of linguistic capital the students possessed could shape their forms of participation in the university community, which in turn could position them in different ways. In particular, the degree of (in)compatibility of the forms of linguistic capital they possessed and the linguistic competences expected of them in specific academic and social contexts could contribute to their level of success in negotiating their desirable identities. Depending on the level of (in)compatibility, their different forms of linguistic capital could act as affordances for, or constraints upon, their negotiation of desirable identities. Students who possessed the right kinds of linguistic capital could convert such valued linguistic capital into affordances for gaining other forms of capital, including social and symbolic capital, for identity transformation. On the contrary, students who lacked the appropriate kinds of linguistic capital struggled to achieve desired identities in both academic and social contexts. (5) The research project identified specific ways to support mainland Chinese and international students’ language developments, which could facilitate their integration and enhance their learning experiences. The research project suggests that universities should provide adequate support for these students to maximize their opportunities to learn and use English both inside and outside the classroom. For example, universities could offer language enhancement courses that support students’ continued second language development in speaking and writing throughout their academic studies. Universities should also run workshops to raise non-local students’ awareness of the various opportunities to learn and use English outside the classroom, especially how different contextual conditions (including social networks) could afford different language learning possibilities. Apart from language courses and workshops, one-to-one language consultation services on should be provided to cater for students’ individual needs. It is also important for universities to organize networking events for non-local students to meet exchange students so as to increase their opportunities to interact with exchange students for cross-cultural exchanges through English and develop their intercultural communicative competence. (6) The study informed the development of compulsory English-enhancement courses to prepare university students for English as a lingua franca communication in today’s globalised world. In particular, the study provided recommendations for improving the design of existing compulsory English enhancement courses in order to prepare students to use English not just for academic purposes, but for English-mediated intercultural communication on campus. The study also identified forms of additional language support that are needed for mainland Chinese and international students so that they could continue to improve their English proficiency during their studies. (7) The research study successfully generated multiple research outputs, including four articles in SSCI journals (Compare, Research Papers in Education, Language, Culture and Curriculum, Journal of Multilingual and Multicultural Development) and nine conference presentations.

23600416.label: Major findings and research outcome
23600416.value: MAJOR FINDINGS The research project investigated the language experiences of two groups of non-local students, namely, mainland Chinese and international students, in a university in Hong Kong, with particular attention to their use of English as a lingua franca and other languages both inside and outside the classroom. The study found that the international students embraced a pluralistic conceptualization of English as a lingua franca and emphasized the role of accommodation in order to make themselves understood in the university context. For example, they showed a high level of sensitivity to interlocutors’ English proficiency levels and made use of accommodation strategies in English as a lingua franca communication (e.g., reducing speaking pace and repeating keywords). They also chose to use a kind of ‘simplified’ English in terms of vocabulary and sentence structure in order to get their message across in English as a lingua franca communication. While they stressed the importance of English for their academic and social integration in the university, they experienced local students’ resistance to the use of English. It was also found that while the international students expressed monolingual ideologies with respect to the use of English as a result of their concerns about social exclusion and linguistic disadvantage, they also engaged in multilingual language practices. The study also found that the international students’ identity negotiation in English as a lingua franca communication could be shaped by the types and amounts of linguistic capital they possessed and their ability to exercise agency in drawing on their linguistic capital for identity (re)construction and transformation. Furthermore, the study found that mainland Chinese students were motivated to improve their English during their cross-border studies, since English was perceived as a marketable commodity. Their participation in English-mediated practices was shaped by the contextual conditions in different communities within the university and mediated by their agentic responses to the contextual realities of these communities. While they gained fuller participation in English-mediated activities in the local student community and the classroom community as a result of their appropriation of the associated language practices, they struggled to gain access to English-mediated interactional opportunities in the community of exchange students, where their negotiation of positionalities was subject to the perceived unequal power relations between native and non-native speakers of the English. RESEARCH OUTCOME The outcomes of the research project included four journal articles and nine conference papers.

23600416.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
23600416.value: Two further research directions were identified in the project. (1) The research study suggests that it is important not only to investigate English as a lingua franca in international universities, but also to understand the non-use of English as a lingua franca. Even though English may be available to all university students as a ‘shared’ medium, some local students may not use English with non-local students, but choose to speak in the local language or other languages, whether or not in combination with English. Further research on English as a lingua franca should be situated within the framework of multilingualism and investigate the roles of English in relation to multilingualism, the language choices regarding the use and non-use of English, as well as the monolingual and multilingual uses of English in international universities. (2) Future research could also consider the role of individual differences in shaping mainland Chinese and international students’ English learning and use experiences during their university studies, especially with respect to how students with varying quantities and volumes of capital strategise to convert their capital into affordances for them to gain English learning and use opportunities both inside and outside the classroom.

23600416.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
23600416.value: The research project investigated the language experiences of two groups of non-local students, namely, mainland Chinese and international students, in a university in Hong Kong, with particular attention to their use of English as a lingua franca both inside and outside the classroom. The findings of the study have significant implications for both researchers and educational practitioners. In particular, the study made a valuable contribution to the growing body of research on English as a lingua franca and multilingualism in Asia and advanced our understanding of cross-border university students’ language-related experiences in higher education. In practical terms, the study identified ways for universities to support the language developments of mainland Chinese and international university students, which could in turn facilitate their integration into the Hong Kong educational setting. In addition, the findings have practical implications for universities’ internationalisation initiatives by raising their awareness of the language-related difficulties encountered by non-local students in English as a lingua franca communication. Finally, the findings provided university language teachers with insights into the language and communication challenges faced by non-local students.

To illustrate the crucial role played by translation in writing for the early modern English stage. To provide a more unified and complete picture of the functions of translation in early modern literature. To investigate early modern theories of translation, adaptation and imitation, and to connect and compare these theories with current trends in translation studies.

23600516.label: Realisation of objectives
23600516.value: By the end of this research project, the objectives that are set out in the beginning have been realized. Since these five objectives are interrelated, I shall explain how they are accomplished together. I have discussed how Jonson and Shakespeare are relevant to, and can be studied and examined with, the notion of translation in two separate articles. The reason for not writing an article that is solely devoted to the discussion of playwrights other than Jonson and Shakespeare is only because as soon as I started researching and writing on the relationship between translation and writing on Jonson and Shakespeare, I realized that the materials are abundant enough for me to develop them into, at least, two articles. Indeed, I plan to develop them into one monograph as I have already started developing these materials into multiple chapters. There is a vast amount of works that can be and need to be done on how Shakespeare and Jonson are related to the early modern notion of translation. In my first article, I examine how Jonson borrows, imitates, and, in fact, translates, the satire of Juvenal in his tragedy Sejanus. Seeing this process from the notion of translation allows us to learn that Jonson does not only borrow or reference previous texts, as usually suggests, in his works. He is in fact transforming, or translating, from one genre to another, namely, from satire to tragedy. I continue my discussion in the article on how Jonson, once again, translates Juvenal’s Satires into Volpone, a comedy that was written three years after Sejanus. This comparison is important as the whole discussion is relevant to the subject of genre. I discuss how the same materials can be translated differently in a tragedy and a comedy. In other words, it is not enough for us to only “trace” how Jonson uses classical materials in his works. We need to examine this from the notion and concept of translation as it allows us to realize how Jonson works and deals with previous materials. The discussion of the change of genre in this translation process illustrates the intricate and complicated relationship between writing and translation. The two processes are inseparable: Jonson is not only writing a tragedy and a comedy, he is translating satire into the two genres. My second article discusses how Shakespeare portrays the concept of translation in his sonnet, tragedy and comedy, discussing if we can understand the concept of translation from, once again, the notion of genre. Moreover, I have discussed whether the notions of translation in these different genres are relevant to the translation activities that are carried out within the texts. In other words, I have examined if the borrowing and translating of Shakespeare of Ovid in, for instance, A Midsummer Night’s Dream, can be thought and discussed together with the concept of translation that is portrayed in this comedy. It means that I have linked translation as a theoretical concept, as portrayed by Shakespeare, with the actual practice of translation in his works. I have also suggested how the concepts of translation as portrayed in the three genres can be discussed together and if they share any similarities and differences. In my discussion, I have proposed that the understanding of translation by the characters in Shakespeare’s comedy is closer to the concept portrayed in the sonnet, whereas Hamlet, as a tragic character, shows a distinctive difference on how perceives translation. As suggested above, the materials that I found during my research process are so abundant that I have started developing them into a monograph. I plan to finish two more articles relevant to Shakespeare on how he “translated” previous works in his comedies and tragedies respectively. The two articles in this current project have proved how translation played an important role in the works of Jonson and Shakespeare. In other words, it would be too simplistic for us, as readers, to treat them as two creative geniuses who compose their works “originally”. However, it is also not enough for us to just trace their “sources” and “origins” and see where they “borrowed” previous ideas for their works. It is important for us to ask how they borrow, or even translate, previous materials. In the words of contemporary translation studies, these “sources” and “origins” should be regarded as their source or original texts, and their works have thus become target texts. In addition, this analysis provides us insights on how the notion of translation can enrich our understanding of their works. For instance, as suggested above, Jonson is not only translating Juvenal in Sejanus and Volpone, he is translating and transforming the boundary, or the nature, of genre. On the other hand, the characters in the plays of Shakespeare can be used as tools to discuss how the concept of translation is portrayed and understood in his works. There may be a comic and a tragic perspective of translation, which in return can be used to enhance our understanding and appreciation of Shakespeare’s comedies and tragedies. Finally, I want to conclude by suggesting how objective 5, which is about the theoretical investigation of translation in the early modern period, is accomplished. Apart from the issue of genre, my research is theoretically related. In my first paper on Jonson, I discuss how for him, the notion of translation is relevant to the concept of transmigration, a subject that he is hugely interested in, for instance, Volpone. In my previous works, I have discussed how Jonson’s notion of translation and imitation is different from the Restoration concept. In this paper, I suggest how the connection between the author (Juvenal) and translator (Jonson) can be understood through the relationship between translation and transmigration. In other words, the notion of translation for Jonson is related to how one author passes his soul or spirit to another. While a text of Jonson can be read as a single target text composed of numerous source texts, Jonson may perceive himself as the author who inhabits the souls of all the previous authors. Similarly, the article on Shakespeare and translation is theoretically informed. It discusses the concept of translation that is portrayed in his works, linking it with contemporary translation theories such as those of Walter Benjamin and Jacques Derrida while at the same time acknowledging and addressing their differences. While I want to develop a more complete understanding of how translation is perceived in the early modern period, I want to illustrate the possible continuations and discontinuations between the early modern notion of translation and the current one.

23600516.label: Major findings and research outcome
23600516.value: With the support of this research funding, I have successfully finished two journal articles which are under external review by the time of writing this report. The first article is entitled “‘Be a satire to decay?’ – Translating Satire into Tragedy and Comedy in the Works of Ben Jonson”. Focusing on Jonson, this article aims at untangling the similarities and differences between satire, comedy and tragedy from the perspective of translation. It discusses how the works of the Roman satirist Juvenal were translated and transformed into Sejanus (1603) and Volpone (1606). Comparing with Sejanus, the use of Juvenal in Volpone is somewhat different, giving us a picture on how translation was adopted in comedy. Through rereading and reexamining the presence of references and quotations from the works of classical authors in Sejanus and Volpone, this article argues for the intricate relationship between writing and translation – in the language of translation studies, these great works of Jonson are individual target texts which are derived from multiple source texts. In other words, the act of writing is inseparable from translation. The second article is entitled “Metaphors for translation in Shakespeare’s sonnets, tragedies and comedies”. Focusing on Sonnet 96, Hamlet and A Midsummer Night’s Dream, this paper examines the metaphors of translation in Shakespeare’s sonnet, tragedy and comedy. Whereas Shakespeare links translations with notions such as faults, errors and betrayal in his sonnet, Hamlet, as a character in tragedy, seems to disdain the notion of translation as he does not believe honesty and beauty could coexist simultaneously. Comparing the perceptions of translation in Shakespeare’s tragedy and comedy, this article shows that while Hamlet, as a translated subject, reminds us of Walter Benjamin’s discussion of translation and madness in ‘The Task of the Translator’, the translation that happens in A Midsummer Night’s Dream resembles more of Derrida’s ‘Des Tours de Babel’ and is more similar to the notion suggested in the sonnet. In short, this paper suggests there are different metaphors of translation in Shakespeare’s various genre of works. These portrayals in return help us rethink the characteristics of tragedy and comedy. The final part of this essay argues how translation can be read from the perspective of comedy and tragedy, and at the heart of translation is the act of repetition, whether it is that of reading, writing, or translating.

23600516.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
23600516.value: With the research outcome of this project, I have submitted a new funding application for the General Research Fund. The new proposal is a continuation of the Early Career Scheme project. As I have gathered a lot of materials on how Jonson and Shakespeare were influenced by the works of classical authors, the new project will conduct an in-depth analysis on how the two playwrights are relevant to the notion of “translation”. Both Jonson and Shakespeare infused a great deal of classical materials into their works. These materials were sometimes directly translated into their works, as in the case of Jonson, or occasionally indirectly, as in Shakespeare, as some of the materials are based on translated texts of that period. The new project proposes that the works of these two authors can be regarded as a single target text composed of numerous source texts. While this writing practice is usually examined using the concept of imitation, the new project re-considers this suggestion through the notion of translation, a term that in the 16th and 17th centuries conveyed much more meaning than it does now.

23600516.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
23600516.value: The underlying question of this research project is the importance of translation in an author’s creative process, in cultural exchange, and, eventually, in our daily life. It also aims at promoting the status of translation in academia. While traditionally speaking, literary studies often claim a more primary, and therefore significant, position as an academic discipline, by suggesting and demonstrating how certain “authors” such as Jonson and Shakespeare were indebted to the notion of translation, this project illustrates that the traditional primary and secondary roles that we associate with literary studies and translation studies are unsustainable. The notion of an “original” author is problematic, and the concept of “originality” needs to be redefined. Perhaps it is time for us to place translation as a more primary activity and the notion of “originality” should be examined together with translation and how an “author” deals with his/her previous materials, instead of simply imagining their creativity as something that is originated from their geniuses. The result of this research project encourages us to acknowledge the process of translation as something that happens continuously in our mind. We cannot do without translation whenever we are reading, writing and speaking.

23600616.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
23600616.value: The proposed project will develop a theoretical understanding of the relation between information and communication technologies (ICTs) and young people’s political engagement in Hong Kong. The recent rise of political activism around the world has made such a study timelier than ever, as increasing internet uses, in parallel with youth politicization, have been seen as hastening the pace of democratization. The project will contribute to existing research that overemphasizes the impact of ICTs on protests by focusing on how people’s daily uses of online media shapes their political perceptions, beliefs and identities. To avoid technological determinism, the project will see political culture as a range of codes, meanings and emotions and social relationships brought together through online and offline practices. The notion of “political participation‟ used in the project will refer to different forms of participation (including discussion, expression and social action) pertaining to government administration, political parties, social disputes and social action. The members of local young cohort born after the 1980s, as many scholars and critics have noted, are more politically active than their predecessors and they have developed a distinct formula for political engagement. This study will explore how they make use of the ICTs to immerse themselves in the online media activities of daily life and as a tool for political engagement. A multi-faceted qualitative approach will be taken, adopting the methods of ethnographic study, individual and focus group interview, archival research, and discourse analysis. The project will attempt to provide an understanding of the very terms “politics” and “participation” within the new political and communicative environment. People perceive contestations, share emotions and envision a mediated and imagined world that they find compelling and intensely dramatic. This techno-mediated interaction triggers a shift in communication, grouping and political contestation. Thus the project will examine the new interactive modes reflected in dynamics such as individualization, distrust of authorities, the abrupt incursions of youth into the public sphere and how youth are distancing themselves from institutional politics. Even though young people in Hong Kong are entering into a bustling political life primarily through the Internet, this project will also address the local political contexts restricting other channels for political participation. Further, attempts will be made to develop a theoretical understanding regarding the transformation of Hong Kong’s communicative dynamics and the social-political relationships generated by its youth’s political engagements with the city’s difficult and tortuous path to democracy.

23600616.label: Realisation of objectives
23600616.value: Objective 1. A typology has been developed as follows: Type I: "Nostalgic nationalism" (nativists) Young people, largely of lower-middle class and attending or graduating from non-elite school, derive a sort of “uncanny sense of closeness” to their inner self and imagined community from the digitally mediated environment. They got involved in sectarian political campaigns and conflicts over the past few years but experienced political setbacks and frustrations. They have eventually shifted their media use from political propaganda to sentimental monologues. Type II: "Sectarianism" (nativists) Young people, largely of lower-middle class and attending or graduating from non-elite school, actively engage in propagating their sectarian views. Social media, along with active participation in street politics, serves as enhancing the confidence of their abilities to deal with adversity. They share the similar political views and rhetoric with Type I. Type III: "Closeted participation" (nativists) Young people, largely of middle-class and from elite school, strive to develop their medium-term political careers. While some mix their partisan views with their mainstream and professional images on social media, others blend themselves in with the pro-democracy camp and distance themselves from Type I & II. They prefer not to share much of their personal life and stories on social media. Type IV: "Voluntarism in civil society" (pan-democrats) Young people, largely of middle-class and from elite school, immersed themselves in the network of civic groups, grassroots organizations, and pan-democrats' parties. They fashion their political positioning, public activities, and networks in social media. Like Type III, they rarely share their personal life on it. For details, please refer to the research outputs, including the journal articles and some chapters of my book (especially Chapter 7). Objective 2 The typology largely captures the dynamic between online expression and offline activities. Some nativists, especially those sectarians with pro-independence views, derive a strong sense of ownership on social media. Their language uses on social media are also more mixed (e.g. mixing civic codes with verbal abuses), colloquial, and seditious. They also successfully combine their public causes with their private uses on the Internet. In doing so, their online and offline activities, with a strong populist favor, serve as an embodied form of media and media contents for advocating their peculiar political causes. It has challenged the dominant role of mainstream media outlets, such as newspapers and television, and shaped the political landscape of Hong Kong in recent years. Those with stronger allegiance to the organizations of civil society and community politics tend to use social media for networking and advocating political causes. Their language uses largely follow civic codes. Objective 3 The typology serves as a conceptual and theoretical framework for understanding civic engagement in the digital age, especially the aspects related to social media. I further develop some discussion on its implications for young people's senses of time and organizational affiliations. Social media opens up a non-organizational space for individual activists to engage in politics without sticking to institutional process, but in a sectarian manner. This populist form of engagement bears the temporal oscillation between the emotionally charged moment of mobilization and the banality of everyday life. The activists got trapped in it. This kind of activism, despite forceful in street politics at spontaneous moments, is less sustainable than that grounded in civic and grassroots organization. In my published articles, I further associates it with the global trend of the disappearance of the vision for interim changes. Whether and how the pan-democrats and the community-based nativists facilitate a new interaction between online expression and offline engagement remains to be further developed, especially after their victory of the District Council election in 2019. And the temporal vision enabled by formal democracy still remains resilient in engaging people in politics in a more gradual manner despite more challenges to it. Objective 4 This research is conducted during 2017-2018, the period after the Umbrella Movement (2014) and the Mong Kok riot (February 2016). This phase is politically calm. Therefore, this research overlooks and underestimates the evolution of their uses of information technologies other than social media. The anti-Extradition Law Amendment Bill (anti-ELAB) movement in 2019 evidences the increasing importance of encrypted communication to social mobilization (e.g. their uses of Telegram and interactions on LIHKG in anonymous manner). It is not covered by this research. Therefore, I estimate that I only achieve about 70% of this objective. In the recent movement, the interactions between online activities and offline actions are even more intense but less discernible. This form of online interactions involves less expression in public arena than intensive in-group discussion, action planning, and collaborations. And the social actions are immediate outcomes of online interaction, sometimes even on the scenes of street politics. More research is needed for catching up the advancement of information technologies and the innovative uses of them. In order to fill this gap, more methodological adjustment and advancement are needed. This research relies too much on interviews, recording of online activities in public, and very limited ethnographic field observation. All these are not adequate for tracking the everyday life of activists and their intensive uses of information technologies in social mobilization. Another limitation is timing. No large-scale mobilization happened during the period of this research (2017 and 2018). And the principal investigator did not have the budget for relief teacher to spare more time for in-depth ethnographic research which is extremely time-consuming. And with the budget constraint, it is also difficult to recruit an experienced researcher to conduct field work deeply. One or two full-time experienced ethnographers are needed for addressing the new dynamic and relationship between political engagement and online activities.

23600616.label: Major findings and research outcome
23600616.value: In the journal article titled "The Collapse of the Hong Kong Dream" (2018) and "Chapter 2. The Fall of the Hong Kong Myth" of my book, I elaborate the historical contexts out of which the new forms of youth activism emerged. The late colonial authority premised on the Hong Kong Dream has evolved into an authoritarian-neoliberal power in the post-handover years. It fails to articulate a new dream and accord agency to Hong Kong. Instead, this power is essentially anti-democratic for its rejection and repression of the popular demands and evacuating the agency of "Hong Kongers". Therefore, more people, especially the new generation, strive to "reclaim" Hong Kong, i.e. their political agency. In the book chapter of“Political De-institutionalization and the Rise of Right-wing Nativism", I further elaborate the context mentioned above and associates it with the rise of right-wing nativism. I analyze the nativists' discourses on the Internet and how they interact with the offline and political world. I highlight the nativists' political existentialism, featuring a will to power, in response to their alienation from political institutions. In my book titled Hong Kong's New Identity Politics : Longing for the Local in the Shadow of China, chapter 2, 6 & 7 are the most related to this project. I discuss the contexts, neoliberal populism, and temporal impasse. I finally point out that Hong Kong's identity politics shifts to a will to power. In "After Mobilization: Youth, political engagement and online performance in Hong Kong" (forthcoming), I focus more on the major features of online performance of the young activists and how they are related to political engagement. I highlight three divergent forms of agency embodied in their cultural representations. They represent three discrete and contested contexts and effects, different in scope, efficacy, and nature. These contestations increasingly alienate the politicized crowd from the civil society and the establishment.

23600616.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
23600616.value: During the research, I have come up with some related and new research ideas. I found that online verbal abuses play an important role in the political expressions of many young activists, especially among the nativists. While there are some research on it with focus on online incivility, almost no one studies it in Hong Kong. With this topic, I re-submitted a GRF application this year. I am also planning to develop some teaching kits for addressing political types of verbal abuses in a reflexive, critical and alternative way. In this research, I found that managing and creating selfhood are crucial to online expressions and political engagement in the digital age. However, in the digital environment, characterized by the development of big data and the idea of "smart city,", the encroachment of private domain is ubiquitous. And new forms of privacy are also generated. In collaboration with three local scholars, I applied for Public Policy Research Scheme (PICO) to study privacy challenges and big data. We received the grant in August 2019. Now we are working on it.

23600616.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
23600616.value: This research contributes to developing a theoretical understanding of information and communication technologies (ICTs) and young people's political engagement in Hong Kong. The recent rise of youth radicalism is often attributed to the advancement of ICTs. But there is no simple cause-and-effect relationships. More rigorous examinations of the social and cultural mechanisms between them are needed. This research, with focus on social media, develops a typology of political engagement and using patterns of ICTs. The ways the young people engage themselves in social media vary with their political experiences and affiliations. Put it simply, there are two forms of engagement. The first one is individual-based and populist-sectarian. It features a mixtures of personal feelings and public advocacy, and civic codes of languages and verbal abuses. It contributes a lot to the recent radical agitations. The second form is an extension of the civil society and community groups and features civic codes. It is also more grounded in civic groups and community politics.

23603516.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
23603516.value: This project involves the critical interpretation of a classical Chinese text, the Zhuangzi, from a philosophical perspective. The project aims to articulate Zhuangzi’s conception of knowledge and argue for its relevance and contribution to contemporary epistemological research. There is continuing debate about Zhuangzi’s attitude towards ‘zhi 知’ (knowing, or knowledge). One prominent view, which I tentatively name the ‘skill-over-concept’ interpretation, is that Zhuangzi approves of ‘skill knowledge’ but rejects ‘conceptual knowledge’, that Zhuangzi’s zhi 知 equates either to ‘ji 技’ (skill, art), which should be exalted, or to conceptual knowledge, which should be discarded. In my research project I argue against this view to offer a more accurate and balanced interpretation, and reorient Zhuangzi’s relevance to contemporary epistemology. I plan to do this in three steps: The first step is to argue that Zhuangzi does not reject conceptual knowledge and exalt skill knowledge. When Zhuangzi criticises those views that oppose his, Confucianism and Mohism, the issue is not about the status of conceptual knowledge as neither of his opponents relates knowledge to abstract concepts or definitions. If the skill-over-concept interpretation is applied here, it is difficult to understand how Zhuangzi’s criticism is motivated. In fact, Zhuangzi sometimes comments on the inadequacy of skill knowledge and points to its limitations rather than exalting it unconditionally. The second step is to argue that even if we place Zhuangzi’s views in a contemporary epistemological debate, the skill-over-concept interpretation remains misleading. The main reason is that Zhuangzi’s epistemology excels at blurring distinctions rather than firmly establishing them. It is questionable whether Zhuangzi aims to uphold the distinction between skills and concepts. After all, the ability to use concepts can be regarded as a skill. Rather than applying the skill-over-concept interpretation, Zhuangzi’s epistemology can be described as a form of ‘practicalism’, which suggests that all knowledge, including what we call conceptual knowledge, is basically skill. The third step is to argue that when Zhuangzi contrasts ‘great knowledge 大知’ and ‘petty knowledge 小知’, the point is not the content of the knowledge (what the knower knows), but the way of valuing knowledge. Zhuangzi’s point is that certain ways of valuing knowledge－even skill knowledge－harm our well-being. From this, I will show that Zhuangzi’s accounts of knowledge and ethics are intertwined, which is a distinctive characteristic of his philosophy.

23603516.label: Realisation of objectives
23603516.value: 1. This objective is achieved in the paper, “Zhuangzi’s Knowing-How and Skepticism”, published in Philosophy East and West 68 (4): 1062-1084. In the paper I criticize a common interpretation of the Zhuangzi, namely that it is only skeptical about propositional knowledge but not practical knowledge, for the reason that Zhuangzi argues against thinkers who uphold practical knowledge, but not propositional knowledge. Both Zhuangzi and his opponents start from the assumption that knowledge is practical in some sense. 2. This objective is achieved in the paper, “Zhuangzi’s Knowing-How and Skepticism”, published in Philosophy East and West 68 (4): 1062-1084. In the paper I articulate Zhuangzi's skepticism as probing Confucian and Mohist notion of correctness in the context of practical knowledge and suggesting that there is no determinate form of correctness. Any form skill knowledge is complete, but completion always comes with loss, so every practice is imperfect. 3. This objective is achieved in the paper, “Spontaneity, Perspectivism and Anti-intellectualism in the Zhuangzi”, accepted by Dao: A Journal of Comparative Philosophy. In the paper I defend the interpretation that Zhuangzi primarily does not entertain the distinction between knowledge-how and knowledge-that. His view can help us to construct arguments against intellectualism, in particular the idea of spontaneity and perspectivism. Spontaneity points to a dimension of knowledge that cannot be captured by propositions, especially if we consider the process of improving one's knowledge. Perspectivism suggests that ambiguity is an inevitable part of knowledge, even when it comes to factual knowledge. 4. This objective is achieved in the paper, “Zhuangzi’s knowledge and its evaluation of qing”, accepted by ISCP 2019 conference at the University of Berne in Switzerland (with a plan of submitting to a journal afterward). In this paper, I articulate Zhuangzi’s twofold view towards "qing", which has two apparently contradictory translations: "emotions" and "facts". I propose it refers to reality being viewed from something or somebody’s perspective, contrary to reality viewed from nowhere. Furthermore, I argue that on one hand, humans’ qing is the habit of making emotions and judgments, which under certain conditions may generate a self-inflicted tension that clouds our perception or response. On the other hand, through detaching from this qing, one can freely access to things’ and humans’ qing as well as experience authentic emotions. This detachment also marks one's becoming an authentic person.

23603516.label: Major findings and research outcome
23603516.value: The major finding of this research is threefold: i) That the distinction between propositional knowledge and practical knowledge creates difficulties in interpreting the Zhuangzi as well as its relationship among other schools of thought. Since this distinction is applied by many scholars, showing the difficulties can remind us of the influence of modern philosophical concepts we use when interpreting ancient philosophies. ii) That some of Zhuangzi's idea of knowledge and skill can be extracted and reconstructed to support an anti-intellectualism stand. This can shed light on revitalizing ancient classics and highlighting its contribution to modern philosophical debates. iii) That Zhuangzi has a twofold view of knowledge, which is parallel to his view of emotion, as well as reality-as-perceived. This can contribute to the holistic view of knowledge in pre-Qin philosophies, as well as inform the current research on epistemology and philosophy of action. Research outcomes are listed in part C. There are totally three papers. One paper is published in Philosophy East and West. One paper is accepted by Dao. One paper is going to be presented in 2019 ISCP Conference in Bern and submitted to journal afterward.

23603516.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
23603516.value: After clarifying the Zhuangzi's view on knowledge and its emphasis on skill, this research can serve as a basis for a detailed analysis of the unique account of skill and agency in the text. In order to accomplish this, another research proposal was submitted to RGC, titled "Skill stories in the Zhuangzi".

23603516.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
23603516.value: The nature of this research is threefold: i) offering a philosophical interpretation of key ideas in a Daoist text, the Zhuangzi. ii) challenging an existing interpretation of the Zhuangzi. iii) showing the Zhuangzi's contemporary significance. The significance of this research lies in its criticism of a popular interpretation of the Zhuangzi as well as introducing the text to contemporary debate in epistemology. The value of this research lies in positioning the Zhuangzi under the general picture of pre-Qin philosophy as well as contemporary comparative philosophy.
