27615616.label: Major findings and research outcome
27615616.value: This research has revealed that early modern Japanese doctors' thinking about epidemics was strongly influenced by the novel ideas of Chinese doctors who lived through the epidemics that afflicted southern China during the mid-seventeenth century, particularly Wu Youxing and Guo Zhisui. These Chinese doctors argued that epidemics could not be interpreted in terms of a fixed range of disease categories from the ancient past, but needed to be understood as temporally and geographically specific phenomena. When these doctors' books became available in Japan during the early eighteenth century, they provoked some controversy but eventually became widely accepted. During the later half of the eighteenth century, they inspired Japanese doctors to investigate local diseases in Japan that had not previously been explored by mainstream scholarly doctors. When global cholera pandemics arrived in Japan during the nineteenth century, Japanese doctors further adapted these ideas to describe the previously unfamiliar disease. Sino-Japanese medical interpretation of the disease developed in dialogue with the new European medical ideas that were becoming increasingly popular during this period. Throughout this period, the development of ideas about epidemics was shaped by exchanges of information between elite metropolitan doctors and the wider urban and rural populations. During times of crisis, the central government of the Tokugawa bakufu and the regional governments of individual domains, distributed information about simple remedies that could be used to combat epidemics, and during the nineteenth century health advice pamphlets offering advice on how to avoid contracting epidemic diseases such as measles and cholera circulated widely among the population. Some of the ideas in these pamphlets were derived from Chinese sources familiar to elite doctors, but others were folk remedies of local origin. The flow of information was often bidirectional: the publication of books allowed orthodox medical ideas to spread beyond the urban centers into the countryside, but metropolitan doctors also learned from their rural counterparts about local diseases, healing techniques, and practices such as the isolation of diseased individuals. This knowledge of local practices informed their response even to newly introduced European techniques such as bloodletting, as well as ideas about contagion in the nineteenth century.

28300016.label: Project Objectives

rows: To obtain global-in-time wellposedness of the three-dimensional magneto-geostrophic (MG) equation for different cases depending on the diffusion parameters with the presence of damping and forcing terms.
To address the convergence problems of solutions of the three-dimensional magneto- geostrophic (MG) equation in the vanishing diffusion parameters limits.

28300016.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
28300016.value: Geodynamo theory describes the relation between the fluid motion in the liquid iron core of Earth and the magnetic field generated in the process. Such magnetic field is essential to Earth which protects the Earth’s surface environment from the harmful effects of solar wind and cosmic rays. The study of geodynamo theory also contributes deep understanding to the dynamics of Earth’s fluid core, which associates to many different natural phenomena including earthquakes and volcanoes. In view of its importance in geophysics, we aspire to strengthen the mathematical understanding of geodynamo mechanism. The present project focuses on different mathematical questions relating to a three-dimensional active scalar equation called the magneto-geostrophic (MG) equation, which was proposed by Moffatt and Loper as a model for the geodynamo processes in the Earth’s fluid core. The first topic in this proposal focuses on the global-in-time wellposedness of solutions of the MG equation with the presence of damping and forcing. The proposed problem is particularly difficult because of the presence of time-dependent external forces and the correlation between kinematic viscosity and thermally diffusivity, which give hurdles in controlling the growth of norms of solutions. New mathematical methods for proving existence, uniqueness and regularity will be developed in this project which are also applicable to the study of other types of active scalar equations including surface quasi-geotropic equation (SQG) and Euler equation. The second topic in this proposal addresses the convergence problems of solutions in the vanishing diffusion parameters limits, especially the convergence of the rate of dissipation of kinetic energy of solutions as inspired by the case of incompressible Navier-Stakes equations. The proposed problems are challenging because of the unknown behaviour of the transition from “smoothing to singular” of the functional operator relating velocity and temperature. New Fourier analysis methods will also be needed for the study of abstract functional operators. 本項目的重點探討三維活性標量方程（磁地轉方程）的數學問題。在這個項目中的第一個主題集中研究磁地轉方程在外力和阻尼影響下的適定性問題，第二個主題則涉及解決消失的擴散參數極限收斂的問題。

28300016.label: Realisation of objectives
28300016.value: The objectives of the project have been fully addressed, the global-in-time wellposedness of the three-dimensional magneto-geostrophic (MG) equation has been studied in Sobolev space and Gevrey-class, together with some convergence results in different vanishing diffusion parameters limits. Specifically, as described in Part C Section 8, the research outcome has been written in two papers, which have been published in Annals of PDE and Journal of Mathematical Fluid Mechanics. The first objective of this project was to obtain global-in-time wellposedness of the three-dimensional magneto-geostrophic (MG) equation for different cases depending on the diffusion parameters with the presence of damping and forcing terms, as a first step in realising the problem, we studied a more general class of forced drift-diffusion equations, which included and generalised MG equation for the case when the thermal diffusivity is positive. We successfully proved the global existence of classical solutions to such class of forced drift-diffusion equations with L^2 initial data and divergence free drift velocity u^ν in BMO^{−1} space, where ν are some non-negative parameters resembling the physical diffusion parameters. The approach we used is based on De Giorgi iteration which allowed us to obtain estimates on the L^∞ norm of scalar field, which gave uniform estimates on solutions independent of ν. This strengthened the previous results on such abstract class of drift-diffusion equations. On the other hand, when the thermal diffusivity is zero, we addressed a family of non-diffusive active scalar equations where a viscosity type parameter ν enters the equations via the constitutive law that relates the drift velocity with the scalar field. The resulting operator between the velocity and scalar field is smooth when ν is present but singular when ν is zero. Depending on the values of ν, different wellposedness results were obtained: for the case when ν > 0, the smoothing effect from ν is strong enough which enables us to obtain a priori bounds on approximate solutions and prove global-in-time existence of solutions in Sobolev spaces; for the case when ν = 0, the singular operator given by the constitutive law does not allow any wellposedness result in Sobolev space, and we obtained Gevrey-class local wellposedness results which generalised previous results for analytic solutions. We made full use of the smoothing effect from ν, which was critical for closing a priori estimates on approximate solutions in Sobolev space. With the absence of ν, the derivative loss in the velocity field could be overcome by introducing Gevrey-class of solutions, which can accommodate a larger class of solutions compared with analytic solutions. The second objective was to address the convergence problems of solutions of the three dimensional magneto-geostrophic (MG) equation in the vanishing diffusion parameters limits. To overcome the difficulty, we subdivided the problem into different scenarios which depend on the thermal diffusivity. For the case with positive thermal diffusivity, we successfully obtained strong convergence of solutions as the parameter ν vanishes for the class of forced drift-diffusion equations as mentioned above, which can be applied to the three dimensional MG^ν equation. This gave an answer to the convergence problem of solutions of the three-dimensional (MG) equation when the viscosity vanishes but the thermal diffusivity remains positive. We further addressed the problem in the context of global attractors, and by introducing a new class of “vanishing viscosity solutions”, we proved the existence of global attractors including the critical case when ν = 0. The limiting behaviour for the global attractors as ν vanishes was carefully addressed, and we proved that the attractors are upper semicontinuous at ν = 0. For the case with zero thermal diffusivity, we proved convergence of Gevrey-class solutions as ν vanishes. The results were successfully applied to MG equations and incompressible porous media Brinkman (IPMB) equation, which is a new physical model initiated by our research team. The introduction of IPMB equation inspires us to apply similar method on other related physical methods, and we shall also investigate some other general classes of active scalar equations by exploiting the smoothing effects benefited from the diffusive parameter ν.

28300016.label: Major findings and research outcome
28300016.value: The research output was written in two papers with detail given as follows. In the first paper (refer to [1] in Section 8 Part C), we prove the global existence of classical solutions to a class of forced drift-diffusion equations with L^2 initial data and divergence free drift velocity, and we obtain strong convergence of solutions as the viscosity ν vanishes. We then apply our results to the three dimensional magneto-geostrophic (MG) equation, which address Objectives 1 and 2 for the case when the thermal diffusivity is positive. We further prove the existence of a compact global attractor for the MG equations including the critical equation where ν = 0, and we obtain the upper semicontinuity of the global attractor as ν vanishes. These are new results for the MG equations which certainly deepen our understanding on the subject. In the second paper (refer to [2] in Section 8 Part C), we consider a family of non-diffusive active scalar equations where a viscosity type parameter enters the equations via the constitutive law that relates the drift velocity with the scalar field. The resulting operator is smooth when the viscosity is present but singular when the viscosity is zero. We obtain Gevrey-class local wellposedness results and convergence of solutions as the viscosity vanishes, which address Objectives 1 and 2 for the case when the thermal diffusivity is zero. We apply our results to two examples that are derived from physical systems: firstly a model for magnetostrophic turbulence in the Earth’s fluid core and secondly flow in a porous media with an effective viscosity known as incompressible porous media Brinkman (IPMB) equation. These are new and fundamental results for the IPMB equation which sets a new benchmark for the subject.

28300016.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
28300016.value: The results of the research project inspire the PI to address an abstract general class of active scalar equations, with emphasis on the wellposedness and inviscid limiting behaviour in the long time regime. We hope that by analysing the general results for active scalar equations, we can deepen our understanding on physical models which include MG equation, IPMB equation and SQG equation. The success of the research project also leads the PI to develop a new research project, which is funded by General Research Fund (GRF) from Research Grants Council (RGC) (Ref: 18300720).

28300016.value: Geodynamo theory describes the relation between the fluid motion in the liquid iron core of Earth and the magnetic field generated in the process. Such magnetic field is essential to Earth which protects the Earth’s surface environment from the harmful effects of solar wind and cosmic rays. The present project focuses on the wellposedness and vanishing diffusion parameters limits behaviour of solutions of a three-dimensional active scalar equation called the magneto-geostrophic (MG) equation, which was proposed by Moffatt and Loper as a model for the geodynamo processes in the Earth’s fluid core. The first topic in this proposal focuses on the global-in-time wellposedness of solutions with large data that are consequences of the correlation between the divergence free drift velocity and the scalar temperature. The second topic in this proposal addresses the convergence problems of solutions in the vanishing diffusion parameters limits, especially the convergence of the rate of dissipation of kinetic energy of solutions as inspired by the case of incompressible Navier-Stakes equations. We believe that the progress made in the project enriches the mathematical theories of the MG equation, and the overall activity described in the project will stimulate new collaborations between applied mathematics and geophysics.

28600216.label: Project Title(Chinese)
28600216.value: 政府資助的英語教育外判：新的教育私有化是否可以確保香港中學教育中的“全民品質教育”？

28600216.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
28600216.value: The study aims to examine and theorize the practice of state-funded outsourcing of English language education (ELE) focusing on its quality and equity, with reference to the Hong Kong (HK) context. Many governments have turned to state-funded outsourcing of education (Ed-outsourcing) to enhance the quality and economic efficiency of education, and ultimately, the competitiveness of their societies (Barrera-Osorio, Guaqueta & Patrinos, 2012). The quality of state-funded Ed-outsourcing, what Burch (2009) termed new education privatisation, however, is disputed in the international literature (Ball and Youdell, 2008). It has also been documented that new privatization techniques have reproduced or even increased disparity in learning opportunities in many contexts (ibid.). Although some concerns related to quality and equity in Ed-outsourcing have been echoed in HK (e.g. the need for quality-control systems) (Chan & Ng, 2015), few, if any, attempts have been made to investigate changes and impacts at the school and government-regulation levels. Thus, this project intends to explore and theorize the emerging phenomenon of providing schools with state funds to buy and integrate third-party services into their delivery of education. Focusing on ELE, where students’ achievements correlate with their socio-economic status (SES) (Lai, 2013), this exploratory study will pursue the following objectives: 1) to understand the current policies driving state-funded ELE outsourcing and their implementation; 2) to analyse the outsourcing in HK secondary schools with reference to schools’ SES profiles; 3) to identify any factors impacting quality and equity related to outsourcing ELE within and across four in-depth case studies; 4) to draw out implications for international scholarship and effective practice at the government and school levels. Drawing on the applicant’s previous research (Choi, 2015) and three pilot studies, the study is designed to comprise 1) an analysis of policy documents and telephone interviews with 2-3 government officials, 2) a HK wide document-based research, analyzing grant reports of 138 schools from six districts with different SES profiles, 3) in-depth case studies in 4 schools involving; document analysis, around 30 observations of selected outsourced programmes, and about 70 interviews with staff from schools and outsourcing providers, and 4) a synthesis of findings through cross-case and cross-level (government, schools, programmes) comparative analysis. NVivo will assist data management and thematic content analysis. This research will contribute to building empirical and theoretical foundations to inform relevant practices and policy regulations to ensure that the private sector’s involvement in public schooling helps provide “a quality education system for all.” 許多外地政府已轉變策略，透過資助外判教育的模式增強教學質素和社會整體的競爭力。不少學者研究發現，教育私營化的模式所提供的質素保證成疑並加劇學習機會不均等。縱然上述情況見於香港有關調查和研究並不多，本研究將彌補其不足。本研究探討購買第三方私營教育服務的現行政策、比較在香不同經濟社經地位的學校使用政府資助的差異、並深入硏究四間學校的現況。本研究建議第三方教育服務機構為學校提供有質素的和機會均等的教學。

28600216.label: Realisation of objectives
28600216.value: The project objectives have all been achieved. Below the findings are summarised for each objective. Objective 1. Describe and understand the current policies driving state-funded ELE outsourcing and their implementation at government and school levels 1-1. Policies driving ELE outsourcing The policy on educational outsourcing in Hong Kong was introduced as part of the New Public Management (NPM) in the Public Private Partnership (PPP) introduced by the The Efficiency Unit (EU). The rationale behind the institution of PPP is efficiency, quality and choice (Bates, Choi, & Kim, 2019). The policy which creates ‘markets’ in public education is influenced partly by the global trend to create markets in the public services. The funding for public services is limited by government budget constraints, so service improvements are induced through tapping into existing services in the private sector, rather than training the teaching workforce to learn new skills created by the changed needs of students and dynamic nature of the society. The Education Bureau (EDB) spread educational outsourcing by introducing the School-based Management policy. As I noted in project reports (Choi et al, 2018), the EDB gave autonomy in deploying annual school budget as long as they meet the principle of prudence and propriety. The EDB enabled outsourcing by setting aside funds for marginalized students, through which schools outsource services for students with SEN, new migrants, cross-borderers to promote equity in educational opportunities and outcomes. Some funds could be used for all subjects while others were allocated for a single subject. The EDB guides how to use these funds and the manage outsourced education. It requires schools to upload the fund proposals and reports. Schools share content of the programmes, target beneficiary groups and measures they implement to monitor and assess their quality. Schools responded positively to these initiatives. As I reported in Choi (2018), which draws on annual school reports, fiscal reports, and grants reports obtained from a third of publicly funded secondary schools, for the year of 2014, schools used 23 funds which allowed for the purchase of services and programs from third parties, and annual budget to purchase educational services. Three-quarters of the schools engaged in outsourcing English education, purchasing more than three items, on average, per year. Out of sixteen identified types of ELE programs and services, the most frequently purchased were the foundational program for reading, writing, speaking and listening. Schools purchased one-off, independent programs, while directly running those which require school-wide systematic changes and coordination. 1-2. Implications for quality and equity The involvement of third parties in outsourcing has reduced workload, added diversity to curriculum, and implemented reforms (崔太僖, 2019). However, there are issues regarding quality management and public accountability (Choi, 2018): i) the laws concerned the procurement of services and programs; ii) there were fund-level guidelines to report on the quality of programs and services and submit separate reports and make them publicly accessible, but one-third of the schools did not report information for some of the programs, suggesting that the guidelines have a limited impact in quality control. This is because there are no specific laws or policies governing the quality of the purchased programs and services. Issues with equity are explicated below. Objective 2. Analyse the ELE outsourcing in HK secondary schools with reference to schools’ SES profiles Case studies show that some schools use funds differentially across groups of students with different SES backgrounds. While affluent students are required to pay a minimal amount to participate in the outsourced programmes, those from households that earn less than the minimum income are allowed to participate in the programmes for free, by submitting documents that prove they qualify to be a beneficiary of the arrangement. Schools serving economically underprivileged communities catch up with the ones in more affluent districts by investing 50 per cent more in purchasing English subject related items, perhaps partly to compensate for the fact that in those schools English is often not the main medium of instruction. For the schools in low SES districts, building basic English skills was prioritized. They invested more in developing the curriculum and teaching materials. For schools in high SES districts, the top priority was on competition or public performances, or advanced skills programmes such as debates and essay writing, and e-learning. Schools in high SES districts provided programmes developing soft skills that help their competitive performance in exams, whether for higher education or job seeking, and those required in navigating through the ICT-based society. Objective 3. Identify factors affecting quality and equity of the outsourcing within and across four in-depth case studies As discussed in Choi (2018), the factors that have shaped ed-outsourcing quality and equity included policy features, people and contextual features. This study has indicated that Hong Kong ed-outsourcing policies promote and hinder educational equity. The fact that quality management of the outsourced educational programmes was not covered in the legislation, but only through grant guidelines, however, may need consideration. Quality assurance through monitoring and looking into what is offered via ed-outsourcing is required to ensure educational equity around ed-outsourcing. The equity of the outsourced programmes also interact with impact from other policies. The trilingual and biliteracy policy is promoted through the relatively high minimum academic achievement in language subjects in the HKDSE required for local university admission. The language policies work adversely for underprivileged students because EMI schools concentrated more in high SES districts, where the affluent students already have greater exposure to English outside of school. People involved in ed-outsourcing in ELE varied, but in the study, their roles in shaping educational equity were not conclusive. It is noted that government entities, charities and even higher-educational institutes join educational partnerships through the state-funded ed-outsourcing policy. Whether the participation of diverse third parties in public education is for the better or worse in terms of achieving greater equity in education remains an open question, because they differ across schools, and how differential practices are experienced by students across high and low SES districts is yet to be explored. Finally, contextual features in terms of the SES profiles of the communities in which the schools are serving appear to have had a significant role in shaping the equity involved in outsourced ELE. Schools in districts of low SES invested more in English to level the playing field; however, they had to use the money mostly in building the foundation of ELE, as most of these schools have received students with more limited English proficiency and exposure, whereas the schools in districts of high SES, spending less money in ELE, were able to prioritise investment in programmes that aimed to help students develop, or be recognized for, a much higher level of English proficiency. Objective 4. Draw out implications for international scholarship and effective practice at the government and school levels As I recommended in Choi et al (2018), considering varied quality-control practice across schools and programmes, the government need to formulate related laws and regulations that address the quality of delivered items, in addition to current regulations for transparency in the tendering process. Although the allocation of funds on a need basis on support potentially marginalized students is helpful, the government could consider whether further support is needed to ensure greater equity through improved learning outcomes, beyond the provision of access to services.

28600216.label: Major findings and research outcome
28600216.value: Outsourcing of education, introduced by policies on public private partnership and school-based management, is a prevalent practice in the secondary schools. The document research reveals that three-quarters of the case schools outsourced more than three items, on average, per year, to count only English subject related purchases. Seventeen areas of purchase were identified including developing four areas of language skills (e.g., speaking) and remedial classes. In terms of outsourcing providers, NGOs were the most prevalent, followed by educational service companies and travel agencies (to organise learning trips). The funds that can be used for outsourcing have four main purposes, including the promotion of more equitable education. The practice of outsourcing of education is, in general, recognised by school teachers as being useful and helpful. Most teachers value the additional funding that can support their teaching and address students’ needs that cannot otherwise be met due to lack of resources or capacity. While most schools do their utmost to ensure quality of the outsourced education, quality monitoring may need review because practice to ensure student learning varies considerably across schools and programmes, and required public access to outsourcing information is not always provided. The current distribution of funding contributes to educational equity, by allocating additional funding to schools serving less affluent communities and to students with more needs to some degree at the government level, and schools are using them to address the needs of the less privileged students. However, it is also evident that what schools can achieve with these funds is shaped by the contextual features such as the socioeconomic status of the districts and student intakes. Thus, rather than access, the learning outcome may need to be considered in terms of fund distribution, though it is rather complex. Sustainability of funds can also be considered. Successful schools ensured the quality and subsequently the equity of the outsourced education through close partnership and monitoring throughout the programme (see Choi et al., 2018 for further details): 1) the use of needs analysis in determining programme choice and content; 2) writing a proper contract; 3) monitoring of the programmes throughout and setting clear objectives for such monitoring; 4) leadership and teacher development on managing partnerships, and 5) building in the sustainability of the partnership and learning through considering the partners as part of the school and aligning the contribution with the regular curriculum. Such practice can be shared and scaled up.

28600216.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
28600216.value: The project identified needs for research on the following: (1) The diverse models of government monitoring and the respective impacts on the practices of outsourcing; (2) The impact of outsourcing on teacher professionalism and public schooling; (3) The impact of outsourcing on students’ life chances. Drawing on the findings from this project, future research should explore following questions: 1. Are the factors identified as affecting the practice and policy in Hong Kong relevant to other contexts and in what circumstances? 2. How will the factors change due to the maturity of the outsourcing policy in the context? 3. What is the impact of outsourcing on teacher professionalism? The raised questions will be explored in my next project, which was just funded by the UGC through the GRF scheme. Recommendations for government The quality monitoring should focus on student learning as well as the transparent use of public funds. Quality service providers can be encouraged through a flexible approach that allows for sustainability, rather than mandatory annual renewal of contracts. The government may want to consider developing and funding professional development activities on outsourcing activities for school leaders and teachers, as the capacity required for managing the relationship with third parties involves new skills. An information portal could be created as a resource for schools. Differential funding which prioritises schools serving poorer districts may be worthwhile to consider. The sustainability of grants allowing for outsourcing will be useful, integrating the funds into the regular budget (further details in Choi et al. 2018).

28600216.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
28600216.value: The study investigated the policies and practice of state-funded outsourcing with an emphasis on its quality and equity in Hong Kong. Many governments have turned to state-funded outsourcing of education to boost the quality of their education provision, and consequently their economic performance and competitiveness. There is not sufficient research on the topic and available findings are inconclusive, thus, the research was valuable. The research found that, in general, Hong Kong is efficiently managing educational outsourcing. However, some improvements can be made to enhance the quality and equity in outsourced education further. For instance, quality monitoring may be integrated into regular school evaluation, and focus on learning rather than transparency of fund use. The current distribution of funding contributes to educational equity. Additional funding is given to schools serving less affluent communities, and schools are creatively using funds to best serve the less privileged students. Distributing funds focusing on learning outcome, as well as access, may further enhance equity. Further findings are available in the free copies of its reports downloadable at https://sites.google.com/view/eprhub/research-reports. The impact of outsourcing on teacher professionalism and the best management model for different societies will be investigated through the next project, accessible at https://www.researchgate.net/project/New-Education-Privatisation-NEP-in-English-Education-for-Speakers-of-Other-Languages-ESOL-A-four-nation-comparative-study.

28601616.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
28601616.value: 近年來，專研宋代的中國學者以及漢學界均指出：僅以現代的「藝文」觀念分析北宋文學現象，無法全面呈現當時「文人」概念的全部內涵。 以歐陽修、曾鞏、蘇軾為例，他們不僅是文學大家，也是當時的思想領袖，他們以「士」自居，任職中央或地方官員，並撰寫官式禮文。例如：由於職責所在，儒家的歐陽修、曾鞏不得不撰寫佛、道祭文，蘇軾在《蘇氏易傳》中以「氣」的觀念解釋鬼神；可蘇軾也曾奏告朝廷，請求賜封「祈雨有應」的山神。那麼，三人如何處理他們個人的思想觀念，與朝廷對「士」的要求的差異？ 針對這些現象，本研究計劃試圖以歐陽修、曾鞏、蘇軾對「鬼神」的認識為切入點，把他們的「文道觀念」和「祈祭禮文」、「禮法行為」相聯繫。一方面作精細的個案研究，同時希望從更宏觀的角度，分析北宋文人如何理解「禮文」、「禮法」和「道」的關係。主要探討的問題包括： 一． 儒家的天、上帝、鬼神觀念，及其祭祀禮儀，對於歐陽修、曾鞏、蘇軾的「文道觀念」有何影響，又有何意義？ 二． 在禮法的框架內，歐、曾、蘇如何處理個人的鬼神觀念，與禮文規範的差異？ 三．祈祭文、悼文、廟碑體現了怎樣的文類和思想範式？ 四．以鬼神觀念為例，是否能夠找到一種核心精神，足以貫穿上述三人的祭文和私人撰述？ 五．「神」、「鬼」等帶有神秘色彩的詞彙，在他們的「文」中呈現了怎樣的美學效果？這些效果，與官式文章中的鬼神形象有何異同？ 本計劃分三部分： 一．以歐陽修、曾鞏、蘇軾為中心，分析北宋「文人」的鬼神論述、鬼神觀念和形象； 二．配合北宋禮法，分析上述三人的祭文特徵，及其所呈現的鬼神與文、道觀念； 三．探討上述觀念與北宋文學(特別是文體學)、思想、宗教、禮法、經學、政治的關係。 (400 words in English version) 近年來，專研宋代的中國學者以及漢學界均指出：僅以現代的「藝文」觀念分析北宋文學現象，無法全面呈現當時「文人」概念的全部內涵。 以歐陽修、曾鞏、蘇軾為例，他們不僅是文學大家，也是當時的思想領袖，他們以「士」自居，任職中央或地方官員，並撰寫官式禮文。例如：由於職責所在，儒家的歐陽修、曾鞏不得不撰寫佛、道祭文，蘇軾在《蘇氏易傳》中以「氣」的觀念解釋鬼神；可蘇軾也曾奏告朝廷，請求賜封「祈雨有應」的山神。那麼，三人如何處理他們個人的思想觀念，與朝廷對「士」的要求的差異？ 針對這些現象，本研究計劃試圖以歐陽修、曾鞏、蘇軾對「鬼神」的認識為切入點，把他們的「文道觀念」和「祈祭禮文」、「禮法行為」相聯繫。一方面作精細的個案研究，同時希望從更宏觀的角度，分析北宋文人如何理解「禮文」、「禮法」和「道」的關係。主要探討的問題包括： 一． 儒家的天、上帝、鬼神觀念，及其祭祀禮儀，對於歐陽修、曾鞏、蘇軾的「文道觀念」有何影響，又有何意義？ 二． 在禮法的框架內，歐、曾、蘇如何處理個人的鬼神觀念，與禮文規範的差異？ 三．祈祭文、悼文、廟碑體現了怎樣的文類和思想範式？ 四．以鬼神觀念為例，是否能夠找到一種核心精神，足以貫穿上述三人的祭文和私人撰述？ 五．「神」、「鬼」等帶有神秘色彩的詞彙，在他們的「文」中呈現了怎樣的美學效果？這些效果，與官式文章中的鬼神形象有何異同？ 本計劃分三部分： 一．以歐陽修、曾鞏、蘇軾為中心，分析北宋「文人」的鬼神論述、鬼神觀念和形象； 二．配合北宋禮法，分析上述三人的祭文特徵，及其所呈現的鬼神與文、道觀念； 三．探討上述觀念與北宋文學(特別是文體學)、思想、宗教、禮法、經學、政治的關係。

28602416.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
28602416.value: In his 2014 novel 10:04, Ben Lerner frankly states that he writes as “the Whitman of the vulnerable grid.” Through this “autobiographical moment” (de Man 1979), Lerner opens a double perspective on the meaning of self-representation in contemporary American literature. On the one hand, autobiographical writing in the United States has long referenced Walt Whitman’s equation of the author’s appearance on the page, with the citizen’s right to representation within democracy. On the other hand, Lerner recognizes that his writing not only participates in a democratic public sphere, but that it also appears on the “vulnerable grid” of what has been called “surveillance society” (Lyon 2001). In this project, I argue that through such autobiographical moments, contemporary authors are exploring the emergence of mass surveillance within democratic culture, focusing on what democracy and surveillance both enjoin: the appearances and self-representations of twenty-first century citizen-subjects. When an author announces his or her presence within an otherwise fictional or poetic text, their appearance can be experienced as a relationship between foreground and background, between main and paratext, or between manifest and encrypted meanings. In such moments, which take place without the identity of author, narrator, and subject guaranteed via conventional autobiography’s implicit “pact” (Lejeune 1989), contemporary authors are advancing arguments about the shifting meanings of appearance and representation. While contemporary authors are responding to the emergence of “mass self-communication” (Castells 2009), in which both practical and enculturated barriers to representing oneself in public are dissolving, and while such communications are sometimes celebrated as democratic self-expression, this same externalization of the self also enables what has been called the “surveillant assemblage” (Haggerty and Ericson 2000)—the coalescing of strands of personal data into a far more complete knowledge of the individual than previously possible. In this context, the contrast between a “totalitarian” surveillance and a democracy based on the right of the citizen to be represented no longer seems to hold. In response, contemporary authors are using partial, compromised, and strategic self-representations to understand the substantial continuities between surveillance society and democratic culture. Exploring varieties of the autobiographical moment in two pivotal contemporary writers, David Foster Wallace and Lyn Hejinian, and in three newly prominent writers (Claudia Rankine, Miranda July, and Tao Lin), this project shows that the autobiographical moment is at the core of contemporary literature’s cultural politics. 於此研究，我主張當代作者正透過其作品中的自傳式時刻，探究於民主文化當中大規模監控的形成。當一位作者於其虛構或韻文的文本當中，表面其自身的存在，他們的出現便為存在與再現的意義變換做出了論證。儘管當代作者正就「大眾自傳播」(mass self-communication)，當中對公眾再現自己之實際的障礙和同化的障礙兩者都正在消逝，作出回應；及當這種傳播往往獲頌揚成民主的自我表現，同樣的自我外在化亦使所謂的「監視者聚集」(surveillant assemblage) 成為可能──令個人資料得以串聯起來，使對個人之完整了解，遠比過去可能。

28602416.label: Realisation of objectives
28602416.value: The four objectives of this project have been fully achieved. Working according to the schedule as originally planned, I have conducted research, given a series of conference papers, published journal articles and book chapters, and worked on a book manuscript and book proposal. Below I discuss each of the four project objectives in turn. 1) To identify the autobiographical moment as a prominent feature of contemporary American literature. I have examined a large number of texts which foreground the divide between autobiography and other genres of literature. This boundary work is reflected across contemporary American writing, including for example Ben Lerner’s 10:04, from which this project takes its title phrase: “Whitman on the grid.” As this phrase suggests, the tradition of US autobiographical writing, first seen as related to democracy in the US by the poet Walt Whitman in the 19th century, continues to evolve in the 21st. During the period I have been working on this project, American literary studies has seen increasing use the term “autofiction” to describe the same body of work I have been researching. This term, taken from French criticism, where it has been commonplace since the 1970s, has recently become a keyword of 21st century US literary studies, which has never really needed to distinguish between “autofiction” and other forms of postmodern literature. The increasing attention to this term and to this area indicates the validity of my overall hypothesis. My own monograph draft now bears the title Whitman on the Grid: Surveillance in Contemporary American Autofiction, reflecting this new usage and joining a growing conversation. The course of research described in my original project proposal indicated five strophes of inquiry, each focused on a particular author. These included research about David Foster Wallace, Lyn Hejinian, Claudia Rankine, Miranda July, and Tao Lin. I have conducted research on each of these authors and published about both Hejinian and Rankine already. In the case of David Foster Wallace, I did extensive archival research at the University of Texas using this grant’s funding, but decided to retain the resulting material for my book monograph rather than publishing a stand-alone essay. I have given several conference presentatations containing this material. Additionally, while I was at the archive in Texas, I was also able to make use of the Robert Lowell archive, and I have published an essay about Lowell which forms part of the project’s research outputs. In the cases of Miranda July and Tao Lin, I have already given conference papers reporting the results of my research into their work, as described in the abstracts attached to this report. I have therefore produced research outputs related to all five of the authors I originally mentioned in the proposal, with an additional significant output related to Robert Lowell. However, I have not by any means limited my attention to these figures or their works. My monograph in progress will analyse autofictional texts by many authors, providing a deeper and more compelling case that, as I suggested in this project objective, “the autobiographical moment” is a central feature of contemporary American literature. The monograph will—at minimum—analyse works by the following writers in the following configurations: Introduction: Philip Roth and Lisa Halliday Chapter 1: David Foster Wallace and Joshua Cohen Chapter 2: Miranda July and Sheila Heti Chapter 3 Susan Choi and Tao Lin Chapter 4: Teju Cole and Claudia Rankine Chapter 5: Ben Lerner and Dana Spiotta These arguments, currently in different stages of development, will provide a wide-ranging description and theorization of American autofiction in the twenty-first century that fully demonstrates this project’s first research objective. 2: To show how the autobiographical moments in contemporary literature explore the changing relationship between surveillance and democracy. Many of the texts I have researched in this project, intensively investigate the nexus of relationships between surveillance and democracy. My archival research in Texas can provide an example. David Foster Wallace’s important novel The Pale King, which has often been understood as an attempt to reconfigure the notion of American citizenship for the twenty-first century, actually began as a series of sketches of surveillance operations by internal revenue agents. This is an archival discovery which clearly demonstrates the growing relationship between surveillance and democracy in the United States and which represents an important contribution to studies of David Foster Wallace. Other works, some of them published since this project was begun, also bear out similar conclusions. Lisa Halliday’s novel Asymmetry (2018), which has been widely discussed in the US in the last couple of years, specifically picks up on the autofictional work of Philip Roth, but juxtaposes the element of metafiction with an examination of US surveillance and security practices in the post 9/11 era. As one might hope, my hypothesis that autofiction, surveillance, and democracy are closely related in the group of texts I originally identified has also been borne out in later cases. 3: To examine the symmetry between practices of surveillance and practices of contemporary democracy, which both work with experiences of appearance and representation. My first three versions of this argument, in papers about Robert Lowell, Claudia Rankine, and Lyn Hejinian, have been warmly welcomed by editors and reviewers and published in good venues with high visibility. Additionally, important theoretical texts recently published in the United States and focused on the culture of social media have helped to substantiate this way of reading contemporary US culture. For example, Clare Birchall’s Shareveillance: The Dangers of Openly Sharing and Covertly Collecting Data (2017) and Kris Cohen’s Never Alone Except for Now: Art, Networks, Populations (2017) both make cases similar to mine, and such works will help substantiate my argument. For both of these authors, the strange proximity of the democratic and egalitarian imaginary to the one underlying contemporary surveillance—something like an “aesthetics of transparency”—has enabled the growth of surveillance practices in the United States. 4: To assess the relationship between mass surveillance and democratic society with the use of insight from sociology, political science, and critical theory. This project, which was timely when I proposed it, has only grown more so in the intervening period. Major works of theoretical insight, like Shoshana Zuboff’s The Age of Surveillance Capitalism: The Fight for a Human Future at the New Frontier of Power (2019) and Steven Levitsky and Daniel Ziblatt’s How Democracies Die (2018) have borne out the project’s sense that the homology between surveillance and democracy made on the basis of self-representation is largely a false one, and that contemporary structures of self-representation replace or subvert, rather than enhancing or strengthening, the ability for contemporary citizen-subjects to govern themselves. The works of autofiction I examine in the project invariably involve both a melancholic outlook on the future of democratic society, and a distinctive attempt to refigure literary self-representation as a model for political representation. This grant project has therefore provided crisp new arguments about contemporary US literature while at the same time offering insight into epochal changes in contemporary US society.

28602416.label: Major findings and research outcome
28602416.value: Part C of this report refers to three specific published outputs that have come directly from this project. These publications document the development of my thinking during the project period and articulate the theoretical concepts that I will deploy in the monograph. The publication about Claudia Rankine (2017) depended on this project’s conference travel funding. The paper examines the culture of United States surveillance and United States democracy with reference to the culture of racialization in the US. Rankine’s re-reading of citizenship as something other than community or belonging, but rather as an element of bureaucratic modernity with deep ties to race and discrimination, has been widely recognized as a major insight. My paper shows that her work regularly develops an analysis of citizenship that depends on images of surveillance and on the figure of “hypervisibility” as a description of the exposed contemporary citizen-subject. The publication about Robert Lowell (2018) depended directly on this project’s archival travel funding. The article argues that it is possible to see today’s culture of ubiquitous surveillance—both visual and informatic—emerging in the previous surveillance panic of the 1970s, which was predominantly focused on auditory surveillance. By examining both Lowell’s contemporary poems of “overhearing” and the rhetoric surrounding Richard Nixon’s White House taping system, I was able to show that the “performance space” defined by ubiquitous surveillance has many meanings, some of which are empowering and enabling—rather than merely disciplinary, as in Foucault’s familiar account of panoptic subjectivity. This paper thus provides a cultural and theoretical backdrop to the always-on culture of self-representation that typifies the 21st century US. The publication about Lyn Hejinian (2019) depended directly on this project’s archival travel funding. Documents in the archives in San Diego showed that Hejinian’s work has taken a distinctive recent turn, one I was able to theorize—just as Hejinian herself has done—via a reading of Hannah Arendt. Arendt’s vision of the public sphere, as many have noticed, depends on a very stark distinction between public and private. While it has long been a matter of consensus that this distinction does not really hold in the way that Arendt imagined, my reading of Hejinian shows how important this distinction remains. Hejinian herself has expressed her appreciation of my careful reading of her archival materials, and her general agreement with my analysis of how her work engages emergent “surveillance capitalism.”

28602416.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
28602416.value: The major themes of this project, which are surveillance and democracy, have only become more urgent and more salient in the last several years. Large strides have been made, for example, in the use of facial recognition technology in public places. At the same time, these surveillance technologies have increasingly been used for the purpose of increasing transparency in democratic governments. Moreover, writers, artists, and filmmakers have continued to produce an extended body of work that engages and critiques contemporary surveillance practices and contemporary cultures of democracy. From this vantage, a wide of array of continued further studies may be considered. The path I have chosen, however, leaves the issue of mass surveillance to one side. My next body of research will be primarily about the faltering and even retreat of democratic self-governance in many parts of the world. In the new project I explore contemporary fiction in English, focusing on its many means of representing what I call “democratic formalism”: the actual mechanisms by which democracy is operated. The project has already begun, with the publication of a book chapter about fiction and democracy in India, and a related GRF grant has been submitted.

28602416.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
28602416.value: This project explored a trend in contemporary American literature: books that stand on the border between fiction and reality. The project proposed that the popularity of such books—both from the point of view of those who write them, and those who read them—results from two major aspects of contemporary American culture: the emergence of mass surveillance in everyday life, on the one hand, and a crisis of faith in representative democracy, on the other. The project further proposed that the emergence of mass surveillance and the crisis of democracy were related phenomena. However, this relationship is not the one that might be expected, in which a totalitarian surveillance practice challenged a faltering system of democracy. Instead, contemporary American literature shows that surveillance and democracy have profound continuities, insofar as both work with experiences of appearance and representation. In works of “autofiction,” authors both appear and do not appear, both represent themselves and fail to do so. The project demonstrated that this pattern of ambivalence indicates the extent to which surveillance has proven congruent with democracy in the United States.

28604616.label: Project Objectives
28604616.value: To examine whether computational characteristics constitute an integral factor that can determine the learnability of a sound sequence along with other factors that have been identified by the field (e.g. phonetic naturalness). To test whether adults can learn a plausible, but unattested phonological pattern (accidental gap). To test whether adults can learn a plausible, but unattested phonological pattern (accidental gap).

28604616.label: Realisation of objectives
28604616.value: In order to examine whether computational characteristics constitute an integral factor that can determine the learnability of a sound sequence (objective 1) and to test whether adults can learn a plausible, but unattested phonological pattern (objective 2), the following experiment was run. An experimental study using the artificial language learning paradigm was carried out to test and compare the learnability of the following processes in the tonal domain and the vowel domain. A total of 132 native speakers of Cantonese were tested. Participants were first placed in the training phase, during which they had to listen to a list of words that either conform to a very well attested harmony grammar (left-to-right harmony, LR), or a harmony pattern that is only attested in the tonal domain but not in the vowel/consonantal domain (Plateau) or received no training (Control). During the test phase, a two-alternative-force-choice task was administered. The participants had to judge which word within a test pair was more likely to belong to the language they heard during the training. The duration was roughly 20 minutes for the entire procedure. There were two domains for each condition (tonal and vowel) and three conditions (LR, Plateau and Control), a total of 6 groups of participants were run. The LR process only triggers harmony from the leftmost high tone/vowel and spreads to the right. Since it is computationally less complex than Plateau and it is attested in both tonal and segmental domain, we predicted that LR should be 1. more learnable than Plateau, and 2. Learnable in both Vowel and Tonal domains. The control condition did not contain any training. The participants were only given the test items to judge which word within the pair they liked better in order to ensure they had no inherent preferences and to establish baseline. The results show that the accuracy rates of both LR and Plateau are significantly higher than the Control condition (p= 1.56e-10and p=0.0004285). We further analyzed the accuracies of the LR and Plateau conditions and found that the difference in accuracies between the vowel and tonal domain in the LR condition is significant (p=0.02511), with tonal domain (73.6%) being higher than the vowel domain (58.7%). However, the differences between the vowel and the tonal domains are not significant in the Plateau condition (p=.442). The participants were able to internalize both harmony patterns (LR and Plateau), but the performance of the vowel group is better than the tonal group’s. This is only evident in the LR but not in the Plateau condition. The results are consistent with the hypothesis that the learnability of tonal processes and vowel processes are different. However, this difference is only observable in the computationally less complex pattern, LR, not in Plateau. In order to explore whether it is necessarily true that if adults can learn a pattern in a linguistic domain, the same pattern can also be learned in a non-linguistic domain (objective 3) and to critically evaluate the domain-general and domain-specific hypotheses (objective 4), two non-linguistic experiments (visual and audio) haven been run. The design includes a set of audio stimuli consisted of a sequence of drumbeats and a set of visual stimuli consisted of a sequence of non-canonical shapes with different patterns and colors (3 domains). The sequence is determined by the training conditions (LR/Plateau/Control) and were therefore identical to experiments 1 and 2 in terms of their abstract grammars. The experimental procedures were also identical to experiments 1 and 2. The results show there is a significant Domain effect (chisq= 30.99, p < .001), a significant Training effect (chisq = 12.76, p < .001) and a significant interaction of Domain*Training (chisq = 31.65, p < .001). Post-hoc analysis reveals that the accuracy rates are higher when the patterns are instantiated in shapes than when they are instantiated in patterns (z.ratio = 5.242, p < 0.001) and colors (z.ratio = 3.249, p = 0.003), and are also higher when instantiated in colors than in patterns (z.ratio = 0.229, p < 0.001). However, further analyses reveal that only the accuracy rates of the Plateau Training in the Color domain are significantly higher than the LR Training (p= .04) and neither Training is significantly higher than the Control condition. This suggests that neither pattern is learned in the Color domain. In the domain of Shapes, only the accuracy rates of LR are significantly higher than Control (z.ratio = 3.277, p = 0.003) and those of Plateau are only marginally higher than Control (z.ratio = 2.162, p = 0.08). This suggests that the LR (simpler) pattern is learned whereas the computationally more complex pattern, Plateau, is not in the Shapes domain. In the Pattern domain, the accuracy rates of LR and Plateau are significantly lower than the Control (LR vs. Control: z.ratio = -6.282, p < 0.001; Plateau vs. Control: z.ratio = -2.855, p = 0.01), which are unexpected. This suggests that the participants reacted to the experimental conditions differently, and that the participants consistently chose the wrong answer during the test phase. In the drum experiment, two domains were designed to imitate the differences between tones and vowels in experiments 1 and 2 (the patterns of the stimuli in the ‘tone’ domain are created by drumbeats that are different in pitch, and those in the ‘vowel’ domain are instantiated by the drumbeats that are different in sound quality). The analyses show that there is a main Domain (chisq = 128.00, p < .001) and Training effect (chisq = 9.71, p = .002) and a marginally significant interaction between Domain*Training is found (chisq = 5.70, p = .074). Further post-hoc analyses show that only the accuracy rates of the Plateau but not the LR pattern are significantly higher than the control in the ‘tone’ condition (Control vs. Plateau: z.ratio = -.6.812, p < .001). In the ‘vowel’ condition, similar results are found, only the accuracy rates of the Plateau training is significantly higher than the control condition (z.ratio = 5.932, p < .001). This suggests that the nonlinguistic audio are learned differently than the speech stimuli and the visual stimuli, and that the more complex pattern (Plateau) is learned more successfully than the simpler LR pattern. These results suggest that the patterns that are readily learned in speech pattern are not necessarily learned in non-linguistic context (objective 3), and reversely, a pattern that is readily learned in the non-linguistic context does not necessarily mean that it can be learned in speech. The results of experiments 1 to 4 suggest that the same abstract patterns are learned differently within linguistic context (tone vs. vowels), and they are also learned differently across linguistic and non-linguistic contexts (visual vs. audio). This suggest that the learning mechanism is domain-specific rather than domain-general, as the former predicts different learning results in different contexts (objective 4).

28604616.label: Major findings and research outcome
28604616.value: A series of artificial language/pattern learning experiments were run to test the learnability of typologically attested and unattested patterns of various degrees of computational complexity in two linguistic contexts (tones vs. vowels), and in two non-linguistic contexts (visual and audio). The main findings of these experiments show that the computationally more complex pattern (Plateau) is learned less well than the simpler pattern (predicted by the Computational Complexity hypothesis), but the two linguistic conditions showed different learning effects. The LR vowel pattern was less learnable than the LR tone pattern, and this suggests that the there is a discrepancy in the learnability of the same abstract pattern when they are coded in supersegmental and suprasegmental domains. The results are consistent with the hypothesis that the learnability of tonal processes and vowel processes are different. However, this difference is only observable in the computationally less complex pattern, LR, not in Plateau. In the non-linguistic contexts, the Computational Complexity hypothesis is partially supported as the abstract patterns of LR and Plateau were tested with shapes, colors and patterns in the visual domain, and only the results in the shapes conditions are consistent with the Computational Complexity hypothesis. These findings have been reported in The 41st Generative Linguistics in the Old World (GLOW41). In the nonlinguistic audio experiment, the results are different from the previous two contexts: the more complex pattern was learned more readily than the simple pattern, which means the Computational complexity hypothesis was not supported in this domain. Our findings are consistent with the domain-specific hypothesis, suggesting that the extraction of statistical details from the training stimuli and inferring their relevant grammars may be different for different domains. The difference could be due to the saliency of different features (e.g. tones vs. vowel and shape vs. color/pattern), or there is a more fundamental reason for the bias of extracting one pattern over the other i.e. participants being exposed to shape and tone stimuli are biased towards extracting the computationally less complex pattern whereas those who are exposed to drumbeats are biased towards extracting the more complex pattern. The non-linguistic findings have been reported in the Annual Meeting of the Society of Computation in Linguistics (SCiL2020). A journal article that will be submitted to the Journal of Cognition is under preparation.

28604616.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
28604616.value: A series of studies have been planned to investigate the development of the extracting statistical patterns of different computational complexities. As described in the major findings, the learnability of different patterns are partially dependent of their computational complexity, and it is yet unknown when and how the ability to acquire different phonological patterns that are characterized by different classes of complexity are developed. An investigation on the development of these abilities is the natural next step of the current study. Pilot experiments have been run to confirm a suitable experimental paradigm for infants to participate in. Our preliminary data suggests that 14-months-olds toddlers were able to learn a full harmony pattern, but not the more complex first-last harmony pattern. 12-months-olds were not able to learn either. We are currently also testing a set of simpler patterns on 5- and 7-months old to investigate the learnability boundary for younger infants.

28604616.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
28604616.value: Despite the many different variations of phonological patterns in the world's languages, it is not plausible to assume that any logically possible pattern is humanly learnable. The aim of the present study is to uncover which patterns are less learnable than others and investigate the underlying reason for the learnability of different patterns. Moreover, we aimed to examine whether humans’ learning mechanism is the same for all cognitive domains, and designed experiments to test whether abstract patterns of the same nature are learned equally well when presented as linguistic stimuli and as non-linguistic stimuli. We found that a simple pattern is learned more easily than a complex pattern when the stimuli are presented as linguistic and non-linguistic shapes but the complex pattern is learned more readily than the simple pattern when it is presented as drumbeats. This suggests that the learnability of pattern differs when they are presented in different cognitive domains, and supports the claim that humans’ learning mechanism is domain-specific. These findings help us better understand the limitations of humans’ linguistic and non-linguistic learning mechanisms and advance our understanding of the infrastructure of human cognition.

28604916.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
28604916.value: The emergence of women’s white-collar jobs in the 20th century marked an important chapter of women's history. In the Hong Kong context, the secretarial profession was considered one of the first white-collar jobs for women, and became an indispensable component of the city’s economy in the latter half of the 20th century when Hong Kong gradually evolved into an international financial center. This project will trace the history of this phenomenon by using Sacred Heart Canossian College of Commerce (SHCCC) as a case study. Founded by the Catholic Daughters of Charity order in 1905, SHCCC was the first professional training institution to provide secretarial training in Hong Kong. After training thousands of secretaries over the years the college was known as “Hong Kong’s cradle for secretaries.” Nevertheless, it closed its doors in 2014. “It is a pity to see the college close after having turned out so many secretaries whose service has been an important part of the territory’s economic success,” wrote the Standard in its editorial on 30 January 2013. This project will start from SHCCC’s foundation in 1905 until 1970, when other white-collar jobs opened up for women. By using SHCCC as a case study, this project will examine how a previously foreign profession was introduced by female missionaries to the colony, and analyze the college’s secretarial training in terms of women’s work, education and religious identity. From the perspective of women’s work, this research will focus on how the secretarial training influenced the lives and status of Chinese women as Hong Kong developed into a major commercial hub, and how SHCCC students embraced their new profession by connecting East and West, “tradition” and “modernity,” and family and work. From the perspective of women’s education, this study will look at the influence of this specialized training on the development of women’s schooling in the colony and assess the value of SHCCC’s vocational education. From the perspective of women’s religious identity, since most of SHCCC’s students in the early years were Christians, this project surveys the correlation between their religious identity and socio-economic status.

28604916.label: Realisation of objectives
28604916.value: 1. Reconstruct the history of Sacred Heart Canossian College of Commerce (SHCCC)'s secretarial training and identify SHCCC's role in the development of the secretarial profession in Hong Kong: The PI completed all the archival research, retrieving most of the existing school publications, mission documents, newspaper articles and government records directly related to SHCCC. In particular, the PI has conducted archival research at the Sacred Heart Canossian College, and found all the school publications about the commercial school. The PI also went through all the school publications stored in major University and public libraries in Hong Kong. Some of the mission documents were also discovered in Pavia and Verona, Italy. The PI also went to the Hong Kong Public Records Office and retrieved all the official government documents about and correspondences with the Canossian Mission. Subsequently, the PI also did extensive research at the Hong Kong Catholic Diocesan Archives to look for relevant documents about the Catholic Missions in Hong Kong, as well as the Canossian Daughters of Charity. Lastly, the PI went over the major Chinese and English newspapers (香港工商日報, 香港工商晚報, 華僑日報, 香港華字日報, 香港華字晚報, 大公報, 天光報, 遐邇貫珍, 循環日報, China Mail, Hong Kong Daily Press, Hong Kong Sunday Herald, Hong Kong Telegraph, Hong Kong Weekly Press) and collected all the relevant articles about the secretarial training school. The PI has presented the development of SHCCC’s secretarial training curriculum in his research paper (see section C). 2. Examine the influence of SHCCC's secretarial training on women in Hong Kong and analyze the collected narratives of these white-collar women: In order to identify the right informants, the PI went through the 70 initial survey responses received from the former students and teachers of SHCCC. The PI and the research assistants carefully selected 25 informants from the pool; the research team has completed all the oral history interviews and transcribed all interviews. These oral history interviews focused on how secretarial training influenced the lives and status of Chinese women as Hong Kong developed into a major commercial hub, and how SHCCC students embraced their new profession by connecting East and West, “tradition” and “modernity,” and family and work. In our analysis, which was presented in the research paper (see part C), reflected on the secretaries’ struggle between their new professional role in the outer sphere and their traditional family role in the inner sphere throughout the process. 3. Survey the influence of SHCCC's secretarial training program on the overall development of girl's schooling in Hong Kong and reflect upon the value of this specialized vocational education in the colony: In addition to doing archival research, the PI has surveyed the existing publications and research projects on the topic of women’s education in Hong Kong. The findings in this particular field are still scarce. The PI attempted to place SHCCC’s development under the context of education trends and practices of the colony, especially the important roles Christian and Catholic schools played in shaping the educational system in Hong Kong. This project suggested that SHCCC was unique because the religious charity was not the sole factor behind the establishment of the secretarial training curriculum; instead, this was also the reflection of the trend of the rapid increase of women entering into office in the West at the turn of the century. As a result, the school’s goal was to equip these women with basic knowledge and specialized skills. The PI also inquired about the school curriculum in the oral history interviews, and has learned interesting perspectives about how the public perceived SHCCC in the 60s and the 70s. The analysis was presented in the paper (see part C). 4. Investigate the socio-economic status of SHCCC's students by inspecting the correlation between their Christian identity and their education/employment opportunities as secretaries under the colonial context: The findings of this research project confirmed that Christianity indeed played a significant role in changing people's socio-economic status in the colony. Often negotiations and compromises had to happen for Chinese to embrace their new religious identity, but what often followed was opportunity. When education and employment became important mission strategies, these Christians became the first group of women to receive education and professional training. Due to the secular nature of the secretarial training, the PI learned that the religious elements of SHCCC were rather obscure; the short prayer during the morning assembly was the only religious ritual that the students were asked to perform. Nonetheless, according to former students, most students who apply to SHCCC had either Catholic family background, or they came from a Catholic primary or secondary school. Therefore, these students continue to embrace their religious identity when they enter into the commercial realm. 5. Contribute to Hong Kong's oral history project by transcribing interviews with former secretaries and promote further studies on the history of white-collar women in Hong Kong: With the help of research assistants and student helpers, the PI has transcribed all the oral history interviews. The PI is in the process of publishing a book that will feature the detailed stories of these Hong Kong secretaries (see part C). While working on this research project and promoting the practices or oral history, the PI was invited by schools and churches to be the advisor of their oral history projects. The PI has organized a number of oral history workshops, and supervised the process of their oral history interviews. The PI hopes the book will inspire more institutions in Hong Kong to preserve their valuable memories of the past. Problems Encountered: The progress of this project was delayed due to the closing of Canossian Mission Archive in Hong Kong. After talking to many experts in the field of history of Catholic Missions in Hong Kong, including Father Louise Ha, I was able to reach the supervisor of the Canossian Archive, Sister Teresa Chien. She, however, informed us that the archive is currently under renovation, therefore it was impossible for the research team to access any information. The problem was eventually resolved when Sister Vernoica Fuk, and former principal Sister Law were willing to provide timely assistance and received relevant archival materials from the school. In addition, the recruitment of former students and teachers was also very challenging and time-consuming. Luckily, former vice principal Cecilia Wu joined the project at the later stage and helped the research team to distribute the survey and identify potential informants for the research team.

28604916.label: Major findings and research outcome
28604916.value: At the end of the 19th century, with the invention of the typewriter, women began to enter the commercial realm, and the structure of European and American offices began to change⸺making the white-collar female class that symbolized "modernity" appeared in the West. When Hong Kong developed into an important trading port at the end of the 19th century, Sisters from Canossian Daughters of Charity from Italy took up the task of training secretaries, and established the first secretarial training curriculum in Hong Kong, The Sacred Heart Canossian College of Commerce (SHCCC). This project used SHCCC as a case study to analyze this newly-introduced white-collar female profession in Hong Kong. After completing the archival research and collecting oral histories from the school’s former students and teachers, the PI discovered that the religious charity was not the sole factor behind the establishment of Sacred Heart Commercial School; instead, this was also the reflection of the trend of the rapid increase of women entering into office in the West at the turn of the century. As a result, SHCCC’s secretarial training curriculum produced a new class of professional white-collar women for Hong Kong. In particular, when Hong Kong became the Asian financial center in the 70s, secretaries have become an indispensable part of the colony’s economy. The PI discovered that even though the secretarial profession has offered these women economic ability and eventually elevated their social status⸺the reason why secretarial professional was appealing to the grassroot families, what Hong Kong secretaries faced in the workplace was the extension of the "traditional" gender roles in the office. In other words, becoming a secretary did not help these professional women change the traditional gender power dynamics, but somehow reinforced the traditional gender constraints and stereotypes, making Hong Kong female secretaries the “professional servants” in this international financial center. The PI has completed a paper based on the findings of this project; the paper has been submitted to Journal of Women’s and Gender Studies for review. Please find the submitted paper in Part C. The PI is in the process of completing a book that features the oral histories of the secretaries; the PI has selected 15 detailed stories to present in this book. Joint Publication (H.K.) has shown initial interest in publishing this book, and has agreed to review the manuscript soon. Please find the draft of the introduction in Part C as well.

28604916.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
28604916.value: The PI will complete the book manuscript before the end of 2020, with the hope to publish the book before the summer of 2021. The PI will also try to promote the book by delivering public lectures and talks in Hong Kong, so that the public will have a better understanding of the history of the secretarial profession, as well as raise awareness of the gender issues that still exist in our society. The PI has offered oral history workshops regularly in secondary schools and churches in Hong Kong while doing this research project; the PI will continue to do so when the book comes out, so that we could preserve the precious history of different schools, institutions, and individuals in Hong Kong. Lastly, in the long run the PI will consider doing a project on the history of Hong Kong school teachers, another “gendered” profession in Hong Kong.

28604916.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
28604916.value: In Hong Kong, the secretarial profession was considered one of the first white-collar jobs for women, and became an indispensable component of the city’s economy in the latter half of the 20th century when Hong Kong gradually evolved into an international financial center. This project investigated the secretarial profession by using Hong Kong’s first secretarial training school, Sacred Heart Canossian College of Commerce (SHCCC), as a case study. Sacred Heart has cultivated a large number of professional secretaries in the past 100 years, thus contributing to the development of commerce in Hong Kong. This project examined how a previously foreign profession was introduced by female missionaries to the colony by analyzing SHCCC’s school history and examining the stories of the school’s former students and teachers. This was the first research conducted on this subject, and is one of the more comprehensive research on the history of white-collar women in Hong Kong. This research project discovered that the secretarial profession did indeed provide a pathway for some women in Hong Kong to enter into the middle-class, on the other hand these white-collar women still expected to play the subordinate role when “serving” their superiors in the office.
