28605516.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
28605516.value: Workplace bullying is prevalent worldwide, suggesting that it is a widespread social and organizational problem. Despite the profound impact of workplace bullying on victims, a major limitation of the literature is that existing studies essentially focus on the consequences of workplace bullying on victims, including the psychological, physiological and socioeconomic impacts, and on the factors causing bullying in the workplace, but research on the impact of workplace bullying on the victims’ relatives and loved ones, such as their children, is lacking. It is however evident that the consequences of workplace bullying have a spillover effect on the victims’ family members. Since many victims of workplace bullying have young children, and given that young children are particularly vulnerable to a negative family environment, which puts their ability to develop into healthy and accomplished human beings in future at risk, examining the impacts of the type of parental stress induced by workplace bullying on children’s physical health, psychological well-being (self-esteem and depression), problem behaviors (aggression, lying, disrespect) and school adjustment (academic performance and school conduct) is urgently needed. The overall aim of this study is to examine how the physical health, psychological well-being, school adjustment and problem behaviors of children whose parents are victims of workplace bullying may be related to the impact that workplace bullying has on parenting practices. The proposed study is a quantitative research using a 2-year longitudinal design. Data will be collected from class teachers, employed Chinese parents whose children are studying in primary schools in Hong Kong, and their children. To ensure that the sampling is representative, one primary school will be recruited from each district. A total of 18 primary schools will be invited to join the study. The proposed study is the first attempt to explore the way parents who are victims of workplace bullying may influence children’s physical health, psychological well-being, problem behaviors and school adjustment. The originality of the proposed study lies in the innovation of its research topic, which covers several areas simultaneously. Workplace bullying belongs to the area of organizational psychology, while child development belongs to the field of developmental psychology. Studying the selected variables simultaneously will therefore enable researchers to better understand the impact of workplace bullying as a growing social problem. This study shows significance at different levels, at the individual (i.e., children’s health), familial (parenting), economical and societal levels.

28605516.label: Realisation of objectives
28605516.value: 1. Execution of the Project to achieve the research objectives: (i) Formative Research - Focus group interviews To achieve the research objectives 1-3 as stated in section 5.1, some additional research activities were conducted prior to the main study. Since workplace bullying is an under-researched area in Asia, including Hong Kong, and the majority of empirical data come from the West, gaining an understanding of how Hong Kong people define workplace bullying and the types of negative acts or bullying behaviors that they encounter at work was crucial for the development of our questionnaire. In addition, since the Chinese Workplace Bullying Scale (CWBS) (Li et al., 2010) measuring workplace bullying was developed in China, it is essential to know whether the items of the scale are applicable in the local context. Qualitative interviews (three focus groups and one individual interview) have been arranged to interview 15 participants to understand their definition, perceptions of workplace bullying, types of bullying behaviors, and their comments on the questionnaire. The participants came from a multiplicity of backgrounds - (i) age (12 participants aged ≤40 years old and 3 participants aged >40 years old), (ii) occupations (blue-collar workers to professionals and managerial posts - construction worker, clerical staff, activity assistant in a community centre, professionals, financial manager, and self-employed), (iii) educational levels (master’s degree or above to high school graduates), and (iv) years of working experience (from less than one year to over 20 years). The qualitative interviews provided us with insights into the definition of bullying in the workplace, different types of bullying behaviors and the appropriateness of items of the CWBS. Revisions were made to the CWBS by including more items of the scale and wordings to suit the local context. The interviews also helped refine the preliminary draft of the questionnaire. (ii) Pilot study Two randomly selected primary schools from the full list of Hong Kong primary schools published by the Hong Kong Education Bureau (EDB) were invited to join the pilot study. One class from each of those two primary schools, located in Kowloon and the New Territories respectively, joined the pilot study. A total of 108 consenting participants were recruited (34 fathers, 32 mothers, 40 students, and 2 teachers). Individual interviews with four parents, two teachers and three students were conducted and the participants were asked to give comments on the questionnaires. The results from the pilot study showed that the measurements of parent questionnaires showed good psychometric properties, with Cronbach’s alpha ranging from .74 to .95 while the Cronbach’s alphas of measurements in students’ questionnaire ranged from .75 to .90. (iii) Main study One primary school from each district was randomly selected and invited to join the study. International primary schools, special needs schools, and two primary schools which previously joined the pilot study were excluded. Emails were first sent to a primary school in each district based on the full list of primary schools in the 18 districts, followed by phone calls to school principals to elaborate the objectives and significance of the study and invite them to join. If the primary school refused to join the study, the next school in each district on the said list would be invited using the same process (i.e. email invitations followed by phone calls). However, three primary schools did not respond despite repeated emails and calls before the deadline, so we assumed that the schools were not interested. The three primary schools responded only after the next school on the list was successfully recruited, therefore, we ended up recruiting two primary schools for 3 of the districts included in the study (Central and Western, Shatin, and Islands), which amounts to a total of 21 primary schools, yielding a larger sample size. At baseline, there were 1507 working fathers, 1252 working mothers, 2141 students, and 215 teachers, while at follow-up, 1157 working fathers, 1024 working mothers, 1794 students, and 206 teachers joined. Structural equation modelling was used to do the analysis for objectives 1 and 2. For objective 3, the prevalence of workplace bullying was assessed and presented in terms of frequency and the proportion of those experiencing bullying at work. Prevalence estimates (%) were presented at 95% confidence intervals (CI) calculated from the standard error. The results of three objectives were presented in section 6.1. 2. Challenges faced during data collection 2.1 Recruitment of participating schools: The recruitment of the participating schools was one of the biggest challenges for the study. First, the study recruited one school from each district, which made the recruitment more difficult. Second, the design of the study consisted of two waves, so it was a longer commitment for the participating schools. Most schools preferred to join a study with one time point only. Third, the study involved students, parents and teachers. Many principals expressed that involving parents and teachers in surveys was very challenging because they needed to issue a letter to parents to explain the rationales of the study which resulted in additional administrative work for the schools. In addition, teachers had very heavy workloads and they did not have enough time to complete the questionnaires on students’ academic performance and behaviors at school. All these were hindrances for the schools to join the present study. To encourage school participation, we provided (i) a school report on aggregated results, (ii) free talks to students, parents, and teachers upon request, and (iii) administrative support to alleviate the additional work incurred by joining the study, for example, upon request, administrative support was provided to prepare the list of consenting students and parents based on all the consent forms collected and the draft of letters to parents. As a result, the PI delivered four talks (two for parents and two for students) to three participating schools in 2017 and 2018 (see Other Impact section). Over 1000 student and parent participants attended the four talks. We also provided on-site administrative support to three other schools. 2.2 Adequate retention of research participants: The study consisted of two waves with a 1-year lapse. A few retention strategies have been used, for example, paragraphs showing appreciation for the participation of parents/students/teachers in the study have been included and the importance of completing the follow-up survey was stated in the sheet of instructions for completing the questionnaires. Repeated calls have been made to the relevant school coordinators to understand the difficulty in collecting parent questionnaires such as extending the deadline and providing necessary support. The loss of follow-up was due to several reasons: (1) students withdrew from schools because they changed schools (emigration or moved), (2) at the time of collecting follow-up data, there was social unrest which made the collection of parent questionnaires more difficult. Despite all the challenges, the objectives of the study were successfully and fully achieved.

28605516.label: Major findings and research outcome
28605516.value: For objective 1, the mediational model was evaluated using structural equation modelling. Since there were no significant relationships between school adjustment variables and other variables, school adjustment was not included in the model. The correlation matrix of latent variables were significantly positively correlated. The model provided a good fit to the observed data, as suggested by the goodness-of-fit indices (χ2(38)=127.24, CFI=0.93, SRMR=0.05, RMSEA=0.07 with 95% CI, 0.06 to 0.09). Workplace bullying reported by parents had a significant direct effect on child adverse psychological well-being (standardized coefficient = -.39, p < .0001), child’s poorer physical health (standardized coefficient = .59, p < .0001) and problem behaviors at home and at school (standardized coefficient = .57, p < .0001). However, the indirect effects of workplace bullying through parenting on the three outcomes (health, psychological well-being, and behaviors) were not significant. Therefore, workplace bullying had a direct effect on children's poor health, negative psychological well-being, and problem behaviors. This finding provides evidence that workplace bullying not only affects working adults, but also their children, and, importantly, this impact on children is felt without any significant mediation via parenting behaviors, suggesting that parents are not doing anything different in terms of parenting while being victim of workplace bullying, but despite not behaving differently, children are being affected by the situation. For objective 2, workplace bullying reported by parents at baseline was positively related to child’s poorer physical health (standardized coefficient = .51, p < .0001) and problem behaviors at home and at school (standardized coefficient = .90, p < .0001) at follow-up, suggesting that the more parents said they experienced workplace bullying at baseline, the more children had poor physical health and problem behaviors at follow-up. Parents being bullied at baseline were negatively related to child’s psychological well-being (standardized coefficient = -.30, p < .0001) at follow up, meaning that the more parents experienced bullying, the less workplace bullying was associated with positive psychological well-being for children. This finding shows that workplace bullying undermines children’s health over time. For objective 3, the annual and lifetime prevalence rates of workplace bullying were 39.0% (95% CI: 36.5% to 40.2%) and 58.9% (95% CI: 57.0% to 60.8%), respectively (see manuscript 2 for details). Workplace bullying was associated with adverse mental health consequences and a low level of life satisfaction, with bullied employees reporting high levels of stress, anxiety, and depression and low life satisfaction.

28605516.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
28605516.value: 1) Research implications: Workplace bullying, which is a growing serious public health issue, is an under-researched area in Hong Kong. The prevalence of workplace bullying was high and its direct effects on children’s health, psychological well-being, and behaviors have been confirmed, in addition to the adverse impacts on victims’ mental health and life satisfaction. Therefore, more future studies are needed to explore the risk factors of being bullied, bullying processes, the characteristics of the perpetrators and victims as well as the impacts on neutral bystanders of workplace bullying. The organizational factors for bullying at work is also worth investigating, which will provide us with insights into the environmental and managerial factors which induce workplace bullying. Examining interactions of different factors, including environmental, organizational and personality factors, will enable us to understand more about workplace bullying. The results can inform us on how to design intervention programmes. In addition, the mixed-method approach is an optimal research method to better understand the phenomenon. 2) Policy implications: The results constitute a wake-up call. With its adverse impacts on victims and their families, relevant measures and legislations should be implemented to ensure that a safe working environment is guaranteed for our working population.

28605516.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
28605516.value: Workplace bullying is a serious public health issue. Little is known about workplace bullying in Asia as most studies were conducted in high-income countries and on Caucasian samples. The sample consisted of 1507 fathers, 1252 mothers, 2141 students, and 215 teachers from 21 randomly selected primary schools at baseline. They completed a survey at baseline and follow-up. The results provide empirical evidence of the high annual and lifetime prevalence of workplace bullying. Parents being victims of workplace bullying at baseline were associated with their child’s poor health, low level of psychological well-being and problem behaviors at follow-up. An indirect association of workplace bullying with child’s poor health, adverse psychological well-being, and problem behaviors was not observed. The study is one of the pioneer studies which reported the epidemiology of workplace bullying among Chinese employees in Asia, which is lacking in the field. Furthermore, the study is among the first study in Asia which reported the impact of workplace bullying on the family environment of the victims, of which children constitute an essential part as the existing literature largely explored the effects of bullying on victims. The results supported the implementation of appropriate legislation to eliminate workplace bullying in our society.

28606216.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
28606216.value: This study aims to examine the effectiveness of using mobile sequencing software namely Garageband for iOS and Walk Band for Android as a tool to facilitate music creation for the Hong Kong Diploma of Secondary Education (HKDSE) Music Examination. Paper 3, Creating I, is one of the core papers of the HKDSE music examination. Although it is a core paper, there is a lack of teaching and learning materials specifically designed for this paper with the use of technology. GarageBand and Walk Band are multifunctional applications which can realize and record music in real-time. With this handy device, students can create music anytime and anywhere. There are two phases in this study: in Phase 1 a selected group of music teachers and senior secondary students will be interviewed and perceptions and suggestions will be derived to formulate a composition pedagogy with the use of the application with a theoretical framework and practical teaching approaches. Phase 2 will be a multi-case study in which three pilot schools will be involved and music classes will be observed with the launch of the pedagogy for three months. In addition, teachers and students will be interviewed in order to validate the pedagogy. This study will provide a practical and validated pedagogy for school music teachers to prepare students for the HKDSE Music Examination. 這項研究旨在探討使用流動科技的音樂排序軟件GarageBand（運作於iOS平台）和Walk Band（運作於Android平台）作為一種工具來促進香港中學文憑音樂科考試卷三（創作I）的成效。卷三（創作I）是香港中學文憑音樂科考試其中之一的必修部分。雖然這是必修考卷，但卻缺乏配合科技的教材。GarageBand和Walk Band是一個可以實時錄製音樂的多功能軟件。有了這個便利的裝置，學生可以隨時隨地創作音樂。 本研究將分為兩個階段：在第一階段中，經篩選的音樂教師和高中學生將會被訪問有關音樂創作的教學議題。其看法和建議將被分析並制定出一個作曲教學理論框架和教學法。第二階段會是一個多案例研究，三間試驗學校將運行新的教學法，並會被觀察三個月。參與的教師和學生將接受訪問以驗證此教學法的成效。這項研究將會為學校的音樂教師提供可行和有效的教學法，讓參與香港中學文憑音樂科考試的學生作準備。

28606216.label: Realisation of objectives
28606216.value: The four objectives have been archived within the 27 months project period, and the realisation of the objectives will be discussed in the following. Regarding Objective 1: To examine the feasibility of using GarageBand or Walk Band as a tool to teach music composition at the HKDSE level, a group of teacher participants from the selected pilot school were invited to attend a two-day workshop on how to make use of GarageBand or Walk Band as a tool to teach music composition at the HKDSE level in July 2019. The teachers develop a school-based curriculum plan collaboratively which apply GarageBand to teach composition at HKDSE level. During the development of the curriculum plan, the PI provided consultation and suggestion for improvement with necessary technical support to the teachers. The curriculum plan developed by the teachers were field-tested in the pilot school. Lessons were observed by PI and Research Assistant which have been videotaped. One teacher who mainly implemented the creating class and five students were selected for a semi-structure interview. The interview was developed based on Graham Wallas's Stages in the Creative Process to investigate what functions are most commonly used, how does GarageBand facilitate idea generation, the development of melody writing, harmony and timbral exploration, the role of GarageBand in the creative process and the composing experience with and without GarageBand in the four stages of creativity. The student compositions were archived and analysed. Regarding Objective 2: To study the problems of teaching and learning composition at the HKDSE level, a questionnaire was conducted for music teachers, composer-instructor and students respectively in 2017. The questionnaire aimed to investigate the participants' background, the current teaching and learning quality, content, activities and technological support. Twenty-four were received from music teachers, and composer-instructors while forty-two were received from students. Then, semi-structured interviews were conducted to investigate the HKDSE Course structure, pedagogy, assessment, facilities, resources and difficulties in teaching and learning. Regarding Objective 3: To develop a pedagogy to provide solutions and/or guidelines for teachers teaching composition using mobile technology application, the PI has invented the Grid Notation for notating GarageBand instruments so that students were able to write down their musical ideas during the creative process with the use of GarageBand. The innovative Grid Notation created a new presentation of pitch and rhythm with grids, provided large databank of articulation symbols for Chinese and Western instruments, visualised dynamics and tailor-made notation for virtual instruments. Based on the Grid Notation, a cloud-based software The Grid has been developed for teachers to create grid score in a standardised format. Teaching and learning activities of composition have made use of such notation to be the bridge between virtual instruments and traditional staff notation. The invention A System for Creating a Grid Notation Music Score has obtained a patent in Hong Kong and China in 2019. Regarding Objective 4: To study the current trend of teaching music composition, a semi-structured interview was conducted for one HKEAA HKDSE Music Subject past committee member, three music teachers and three composer-instructors. It aimed to investigate what to teach, how to teach, when to teach in composition as well as what is the role of technology.

28606216.label: Major findings and research outcome
28606216.value: The first part of this study aims to investigate the current teaching and learning phenomena of creating at the Hong Kong Diploma of Secondary Education. The interview finding shows that the subject knowledge of music composition of music teachers who received pre-service training before the 1990s, for example, transformative techniques, motivic development, orchestration is inadequate which is not enough for teaching composition. On the other hand, composer-instructors have a different music training from the music teachers in which they were trained with skilful craftsmanship in music composition. However, they received no training in music pedagogy. All interview participants (n = 6) addressed the difficulties of teaching composition at the HKDSE level. One-third of the participants felt that their students do not have adequate musicianship to realise their creativity from idea to notation. The recourse, to some extent, affects the teaching of composition. Nearly all the participants mentioned that resource is one of the main issues which affect the teaching of composition, which include minimal lesson time per week. Besides, most of the composition reference books are too advanced, which is not suitable for senior secondary students. Teachers teach composition mainly by past experiences. Selected findings of the survey from students showed that the teaching of composition is generally useful (mean = 3.72). Students found that composition training can enhance their creativity (mean = 3.62). Teachers can effectively comment on student works (mean = 3.81). However, teachers seldom encourage group composition activities (mean = 2.30) and without much opportunity to perform (mean = 2.88) or play the audio realisation of student compositions (mean = 3.13) during the class. Students agree that music software is essential to facilitate their creative process (mean = 3.30). The second part of this study aims to provide solutions for teachers teaching composition using a mobile technology application and examine the feasibility of using GarageBand as a tool to teach music composition. The patented Grid Notation developed by PI provides a user-friendly experience in notating musical idea with the use of GarageBand to both teachers and students. The interview shows that students found that the application of GarageBand provides instant playback and easy manipulation facilitate the creative process, especially in the stages of incubation and verification. The simple interface with scale function enables students to explore various virtual instruments at the very beginning and able to hear the audio realisation in high quality at a later stage. The recording function is essential to students due to the inadequate skills in dictating rhythm and pitch in which the function helps students to reflect and revise their works.

28606216.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
28606216.value: The study has already investigated the current situation of teaching and learning of music composition at HKDSE level with a pilot study on the feasibility of using GarageBand, which provided a concrete foundation for further research and development. The potential for further research development would be the investigation of the motivation of learning composition with the use of technology under the HKDSE Music curriculum and the pedagogical development of teaching and learning of composition after eight years of HKDSE Music curriculum implemented.

28606216.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
28606216.value: The project studied the current trend of teaching and learning of music composition at the HKDSE level. The findings showed how the teacher-training affect the teaching and learning of composition, what is the teaching content, and what is the role of technology and resources. The project also examined the feasibility of using GarageBand or Walk Band as a tool to teach music composition at the HKDSE level where semi-structured interview sessions were conducted with school music teachers, HKDSE music part-time tutors and students. A new pedagogy making use of the patented Grid Notation was tested in the pilot school.
